terms.name: 400 Design Rules
terms.text: A project to collect game design rules that have proved useful, written as instructions. Each rule has an imperative statement, a domain of application, dominated and dominating rules, and examples.

terms.name: The 400 Project
terms.text: Hal Barwood and Noah Falstein's effort to collect 400 game design rules, which reached 112 in five years. Each rule has an identifier, title, short description, a domain and a contributor.

terms.name: 80/20 rule
terms.text: The rough pattern that about 80 percent of effects come from 20 percent of causes. Pareto saw it in incomes around 1900.

terms.name: AAA game
terms.text: A game made by a large studio with a large budget. The book mostly draws its examples from small independent makers instead.

terms.name: Abject failure
terms.text: The most final failure, such as missing the final goals or the team breaking up.

terms.name: Abondance
terms.text: In Solo Whist, a bid to take nine of the thirteen tricks, with a chosen trump suit.

terms.name: Absorption
terms.text: Being drawn deeply into play and giving oneself over to it, without needing a match between challenge and skill. The folk game ninja is an example.

terms.name: Abstract (in a game)
terms.text: A game or part of a game shown with plain shapes or numbers instead of pictures of real things, such as a health bar or coloured squares in place of Mario.

terms.name: Abstract game
terms.text: A game with little or no theme that uses plain shapes on a grid, such as Go, chess or Hive.

terms.name: Abstract game
terms.text: In Chateau's scheme, a game of arbitrary rules, prowess and competition, which looks ahead to sport.

terms.name: Abstract game
terms.text: A game with no story or picture standing in for real events, such as an abstract strategy game. Koster notes many players disagree on whether fiction helps one.

terms.name: Abstract space
terms.text: Lefebvre's name for space defined so that it can be set up anywhere and changed at will. Flanagan says many urban games treat a city this way, as a board with no history.

terms.name: Abstract strategy game
terms.text: A board game, such as Go or chess, where players move pieces on a board and each move sets the next puzzle for the other player.

terms.name: Abstract strategy game
terms.text: A game whose pieces and board stand for nothing in particular, such as Go.

terms.name: Abstract subgame
terms.text: A simpler game that sits inside a bigger game, such as rock-paper-scissors among unit types in a strategy game.

terms.name: Abstraction
terms.text: Reducing a complex thing to a simpler game form. The book names three uses: no representation at all, simplifying an everyday activity, and simplifying a real-world system.

terms.name: Accumulating game
terms.text: A game in which the aim is to win all the cards in the pack.

terms.name: Accumulation of deeds scenario
terms.text: A design where a game lets players make moral choices and tracks the results, often on a scale, so choices carry consequences (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Achievement play
terms.text: Playing for the sake of winning, either for its own sake or for what follows, such as prize money. Goal and purpose are the same thing.

terms.name: Achievement tracking
terms.text: Recording special accomplishments, from baseball statistics and high-score tables to badges in computer games.

terms.name: Achiever
terms.text: In Bartle's list, a player who wants to set and reach goals, whether the game's or their own, such as completing every mission or running a speed run.

terms.name: Acquaintance tie
terms.text: A loose link to someone you know slightly. Mark Granovetter found these helped people find jobs more than close friends did, because they reach groups outside your own circle.

terms.name: Action
terms.text: Something a player gets to do in a game, such as kicking a ball or running on a field.

terms.name: Action item
terms.text: A task that comes out of a meeting. A meeting without them is described as just a conversation.

terms.name: Action theory
terms.text: A sociological idea of the loop a person goes through in any situation: beliefs, reaction, desire, intention, action, then repeat. The book uses it to ask what a game demands of its player.

terms.name: Action-outcome unit
terms.text: A pairing of one action and the result it brings, which then leads to the next action. Play is a long chain of these.

terms.name: Action/event
terms.text: The player plays a card that shows both action points and an event, and chooses to use one or the other.

terms.name: Active skill
terms.text: Skill in physical timing and movement, such as the precise jumps of Super Meat Boy.

terms.name: Activist game
terms.text: A game that takes up a social issue, mostly through its theme, story, roles, setting and goals, and less often through its mechanics or win condition.

terms.name: Adaptation
terms.text: A new work based on an earlier one, repeating it with changes. In the book, a board game made from a video game.

terms.name: Adaptation
terms.text: What the carer does to fit herself to the infant's needs. Nearly complete at birth, it falls away step by step.

terms.name: Adaptive process
terms.text: A way of working that moves through cycles and leaves room for mistakes and new ideas. Iterative design is one.

terms.name: Add-on
terms.text: An extra item backers can buy on top of their pledge in a crowdfunding campaign, such as an expansion or older games from the same company.

terms.name: Adventure (Chore Wars)
terms.text: A chore written up as a fantasy task with a set reward in experience points and gold. Players write their own adventures.

terms.name: Adventure game
terms.text: A game of exploring places, talking to non-player characters, carrying an inventory and solving puzzles or quests. Mission US used the form for its turn-based, reflective pace (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Advertise
terms.text: In poker, to make a bluff that is meant to be found out, so that later bets are believed to be sound.

terms.name: Aesthetic design values
terms.text: One of Holm's five kinds of design value: values about form and experience.

terms.name: Aesthetic measure
terms.text: A formula from George Birkhoff around 1930 that scores an image as the ratio of order, meaning the regularities in it, to complexity, meaning the number of its elements.

terms.name: Aesthetic responsibility
terms.text: The question of who is credited for the qualities of a play experience, the designer who built the conditions or the player who acted in them.

terms.name: Aesthetic striving play
terms.text: Play pursued for the quality of the struggle itself, such as grace, an elegant solution or a tense turn of events.

terms.name: Aesthetics
terms.text: In the MDA framework, the feelings a game calls up in its players. The chapter also uses the older sense of how a game looks and feels to the senses.

terms.name: Affective conflict
terms.text: A team disagreement over feelings, goals and needs, often rooted in differences of values or background.

terms.name: Affinity space
terms.text: Gee's name for a space within and around a game where players take part in it as a shared discourse (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Affordance
terms.text: What an object lets a person do, given its shape and material. The book uses it for what a piece's weight, size and surface allow in the hand.

terms.name: Affordance
terms.text: What a thing seems to be for before anyone uses it, such as a handle that suggests gripping.

terms.name: Affordance (of a piece)
terms.text: What a game piece can do under the rules, such as a pawn that moves forward and captures on a diagonal.

terms.name: Agency
terms.text: A player's ability to affect the result through their own choices and performance. Burgun says heavy randomness weakens it.

terms.name: Agency
terms.text: The sense that your actions cause what happens in the game.

terms.name: Agency
terms.text: The capacity to act for a reason. The author treats a game as something that shapes the player's agency by setting goals, abilities and obstacles.

terms.name: Agency (Murray)
terms.text: Janet Murray's definition: the satisfying power to take meaningful action and see the results of our decisions and choices.

terms.name: Agenda setting
terms.text: The choice of which indicators count, which decides what gets attention and what is neglected.

terms.name: Agent
terms.text: Any party that tries to win. It can be a person, the game system itself (the viruses in Pandemic), or the same player measured against an earlier score.

terms.name: Agential
terms.text: Describes a characteristic that depends mainly on the people who play, so it can change without any change to the rules.

terms.name: Agential center of gravity
terms.text: The part of a player's activity where their agency was most active, which draws their attention when they look back on play.

terms.name: Agential distance
terms.text: The gap between what a designer makes, such as rules and pieces, and what the player appreciates, which is their own activity. The designer has to reach the effect through the player's agency.

terms.name: Agential fluidity
terms.text: The human ability to take up new goals and abilities quickly and drop them just as quickly, as a player does when a game starts and ends.

terms.name: Agential layering
terms.text: Holding a temporary game agency inside one's lasting agency. The inner layer wants to win; the outer layer chose the game and can stop it.

terms.name: Agential mode
terms.text: A focused way of being an agent: one set of goals paired with one set of abilities, such as mending a house with a carpenter's skills.

terms.name: Aging effect
terms.text: The way a paper's novelty fades as later work takes its ideas in, so its citations drop over time.

terms.name: Agon
terms.text: Caillois's word for competitive games, where players start with equal chances and one quality, such as speed or skill, decides who wins. Chess, football and races are examples.

terms.name: Agon
terms.text: A Greek word for contest. Isidore of Seville treats contest, with chance, as the central theme of war and of the games of the circus, theatre and amphitheatre.

terms.name: Agon
terms.text: In Roger Caillois's scheme, games where competition is the main feature, such as most sports.

terms.name: Agon
terms.text: Roger Caillois's word for games of competition, where skill decides the winner.

terms.name: Agon
terms.text: Competition between players who strive for rank and distinction, with a winner and a loser. Caillois uses it for one of his four kinds of play.

terms.name: Agonistic
terms.text: Having the form of a contest. Huizinga uses the word for customs, thinking and institutions built on rivalry for the first place.

terms.name: Agôn
terms.text: Caillois's name for games of competition where skill decides who wins. Chess is the example the book gives.

terms.name: Airfield
terms.text: Bell's image for an empty point or group of empty points touching a Wei-ch'i group. A group with at least one is not captured, and when the last is filled the group is removed.

terms.name: Alea
terms.text: Caillois's word for games of chance, where the result comes from fate and not from the player's effort. Dice, roulette and lotteries are examples.

terms.name: Alea
terms.text: In Caillois's scheme, games of chance, such as dice or bingo.

terms.name: Alea
terms.text: Caillois's name for games decided only by chance, where the result does not depend on any decision the player makes.

terms.name: Alea
terms.text: Roger Caillois's word for games of chance, where luck decides the winner.

terms.name: Alea
terms.text: Games of chance, where dice, cards or luck decide the result and skill does not. Caillois's word for the second kind of play.

terms.name: Aleatoric method
terms.text: Making a work by chance, as the Surrealists did when they used dice-like operations to remove the maker's control.

terms.name: Aleatory
terms.text: Made by chance, as in music or art composed by dice or random rules. John Cage's music and Jackson Pollock's drip paintings are the book's examples.

terms.name: Algebraic notation
terms.text: A way to record any game on a grid by naming each space with a letter for its file and a number for its rank, and writing a move as the start and end spaces.

terms.name: Algorithm
terms.text: A finite list of instructions for making something, in this book's example a ranking, the way a recipe makes a meal.

terms.name: Algorithm
terms.text: A finite list of instructions that turns a starting condition into a clear end condition. A recipe in The Sims and the requirements for a career are both examples.

terms.name: Algorithmic game
terms.text: A game in which calculations or rules underneath decide how it answers what the player does. The term is Costikyan's.

terms.name: Alien power
terms.text: A special ability in Cosmic Encounter that lets a player break or change the rules in a set way.

terms.name: Alienation
terms.text: A social state in which people are forced to act against their own goals, such as on an assembly line or in queues for rationed goods.

terms.name: Alienation (in mimicry)
terms.text: Caillois's word for the state of a player who stops pretending and believes the role is real. He says the limits of stage and time protect an actor from it.

terms.name: Alignment
terms.text: How far everyone on a team shares one aim and vision. More alignment leaves less room for individual freedom.

terms.name: All-consuming instrumental attitude
terms.text: Treating every resource and opponent as a tool for one aim, which many games ask of players for a short time.

terms.name: Allegorithm
terms.text: Wark's coined word. It names the double relation of a player to a game's algorithm: the player learns the hidden rules by playing, and that learning stands for how people relate to the hidden rules of daily life.

terms.name: Allegory
terms.text: A way of speaking in which one thing is said and another is meant. Medieval writers described it as a distinction between words and meaning.

terms.name: Allegory
terms.text: A story or scene whose parts stand for something else, so that one thing can mean another. Wark says games work as allegories of the world around them.

terms.name: Alliances
terms.text: Players keep formal relationships with one another.

terms.name: Ally
terms.text: A partner player on the same side. In four-handed Shaturanga a rajah who takes an ally's throne controls the ally's pieces as well.

terms.name: Ally
terms.text: A player who works with another for one hand only, as when two players join against a single one.

terms.name: Alternate reality dashboard
terms.text: A page that reports invented news and figures from a scenario, with meters that rise and fall as players act.

terms.name: Alternate reality game
terms.text: A game played inside everyday life, not in a virtual world, in order to take more from that life. The book calls it the antiescapist game.

terms.name: Alternate reality game
terms.text: A game set in the real world where participants play as themselves, not as made-up characters (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Alternate version
terms.text: Two texts of the same scene kept for one slot, of which only one is played in a given year. The Chester Shepherds play has two comic readings of the angels' song in different metres.

terms.name: Altgames
terms.text: A loose grouping of games and makers who move away from genre and market concerns, tending to be smaller and more experimental in the search for expressive play.

terms.name: Altmetrics
terms.text: A score for research that adds up mentions in news, blogs and social media with set weights, such as 8 for news and 1 for Twitter.

terms.name: Amateur
terms.text: From the Latin for love. Originally a person who loves an activity, with no sense that their skill is lower.

terms.name: Ambient sociability
terms.text: Sharing a space with other players without talking or working with them, so that their presence still counts as company. Researchers also call it playing alone together.

terms.name: Ambiguous decision
terms.text: A choice where the player cannot tell for sure which option is correct, even after the result is in. Burgun names this as the feature that separates a game from a contest.

terms.name: Ameritrash
terms.text: A board game of mostly American origin with heavy theme, many components and many dice. The name began as an insult and was then adopted.

terms.name: Amusement
terms.text: In Thoreau's use, play for its own sake and not to recover for work. He set it against diversion.

terms.name: Anagram
terms.text: A word made from the same letters as another word in a different order, such as LARGE and GLARE.

terms.name: Anagrams
terms.text: A word game in which letter tiles are turned up one at a time and players call words they can make, take the tiles, and may later have the word stolen.

terms.name: Analog
terms.text: Variation by more and less along a line, a continuous movement such as pushing a stick a little or a lot.

terms.name: Analog stick
terms.text: A control on a game pad that can be pushed by degrees in any direction. In Katamari Damacy it moves the ball, though the game turns the movement into yes and no decisions.

terms.name: Analogic listening
terms.text: A way of hearing music in which sound brings up feelings and pictures, such as a sleigh in snow. It sits between plain sensory listening and analysis.

terms.name: Analysis paralysis
terms.text: A stall in turn-based play where a player takes a very long time to choose because too many options are open.

terms.name: Analytic listening
terms.text: A way of hearing music in which attention goes to its structure and to comparisons between versions or performers.

terms.name: Anchor
terms.text: In tug-of-war, the player at the end of the rope who secures it round the body.

terms.name: Anchoring effect
terms.text: Feeling that a number you learned first is the right one, such as a price held fixed for decades.

terms.name: Animatic
terms.text: A sequence of storyboards that shows motion and pacing.

terms.name: Annotated schematics
terms.text: Schematics with notes added so they can stand in place of a design document, which suits simple games.

terms.name: Anomie
terms.text: A social state in which the rules of behaviour are muddled. People cannot tell what is worth putting effort into.

terms.name: Answerer and questioners
terms.text: In Twenty Questions, the one who knows the subject and the others who try to guess it.

terms.name: Ante
terms.text: The sum each player puts in at the start of a round of poker before cards are dealt, also called buying in.

terms.name: Ante
terms.text: A stake put in the pool before the cards are dealt in Poker, so there is something to win.

terms.name: Ante
terms.text: A fixed stake every player puts into the pool before a hand begins.

terms.name: Ante
terms.text: A stake each player puts into the pot before the cards are dealt.

terms.name: Anticarnival
terms.text: A feast that keeps its food to itself. The master shepherds hide their food from the apprentice, which refuses the open sharing of a carnival banquet.

terms.name: Antilogia
terms.text: Arguing both sides of a question in turn. Sophists used it to show that a thing can be put one way or another.

terms.name: Antiludic tradition
terms.text: The long run of church rules from the thirteenth to the seventeenth century against rowdy games and dishonourable play. The author separates it from the later Puritan attack on the stage.

terms.name: Antitheatrical tradition
terms.text: A line of writing that attacks stage play. The book argues England had none against vernacular drama in the Middle Ages, which helped plays last into the sixteenth century.

terms.name: Anxiety
terms.text: The state a person feels when challenges are higher than their skills.

terms.name: Apathy
terms.text: The state of low challenge and low skill, in which people report feeling passive and dull. The work study found it far more common in leisure than at work.

terms.name: APM
terms.text: Actions per minute, or clicks per minute. In a real-time strategy game, a player who can do far more actions has a large advantage.

terms.name: Apollonian and Dionysian
terms.text: Two styles the arts swing between, the first reserved and formal and the second exuberant. Koster says games have mostly stayed formal.

terms.name: Aporia
terms.text: A question that cannot be answered conclusively. The Greeks used it as a parlour game and philosophers used it to trap an opponent.

terms.name: Appeal to authority
terms.text: Treating a claim as true because a person with standing made it. The book notes there is no causal link between who says it and whether it holds.

terms.name: Appeal to fear
terms.text: Pushing people to an action by making them afraid of what happens if they do not take it.

terms.name: Applicable skill
terms.text: The skill a player can actually turn into wins, which rises with skill and falls with luck. It is what the skill chain measures.

terms.name: Archbishop and chancellor
terms.text: Pieces in Capablanca's Chess. The archbishop moves as a bishop or knight and the chancellor as a rook or knight.

terms.name: Area control
terms.text: A game where players compete for influence inside regions, and several players can have a presence in one region at once.

terms.name: Area-control game
terms.text: A game where players try to hold more territory than their opponents, such as Go or Carcassonne.

terms.name: Arrow's impossibility theorem
terms.text: A result that no voting system that ranks candidates can meet every one of a short list of fairness conditions in all cases.

terms.name: Art action
terms.text: A staged intervention that takes an artwork out of the gallery into untraditional places, often with instructions for the people present.

terms.name: Art game
terms.text: A game made on the view that games can be as expressive as painting or film and that the expression lies in the mechanics and the play (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

terms.name: Art implementation
terms.text: Turning the planned look and sound into production work such as animation, modelling, rigging and sprites.

terms.name: Art prototype
terms.text: A trial of a game's look, such as its colour palette, typography and style of illustration or modelling.

terms.name: Artificial situation
terms.text: In Boyd's account, the made-up setting of a game, set up by the players' acceptance of its rules and roles. She set it against the genuine situation of work.

terms.name: Artist's work
terms.text: The stable thing a maker produces, such as the rules, pieces and software of a game.

terms.name: Artistic medium
terms.text: The set of technical resources an artist works with, as opposed to the raw material. For painting this includes brushstrokes as well as pigment.

terms.name: Asset list
terms.text: A sheet listing every piece the team has to make, such as models, sprites, sounds and text, by the prototype that needs it.

terms.name: Asymmetric game
terms.text: A game where each side has different rules and aims, so the sides in effect play different games. Root and Android: Netrunner are examples.

terms.name: Asymmetric information space
terms.text: A game where players know different things and think from different roles, as in Android: Netrunner.

terms.name: Asymmetric victory conditions
terms.text: Different players needing different things to win, as in a wargame where the historically losing side wins by holding out.

terms.name: Asymmetrical competition
terms.text: Competition where players have different actions, objects or goals, as in a sniper hunting a spy.

terms.name: Asymmetrical cooperative play
terms.text: Cooperation where players have different roles and abilities, as with the Medic and Dispatcher in Pandemic.

terms.name: Asymmetrical forces
terms.text: A set-up where each side starts with different powers, such as different characters in Street Fighter. Each matchup becomes its own game.

terms.name: Asynchronous competition
terms.text: Players compete by comparing scores or performances, not by playing against each other at the same moment.

terms.name: Asynchronous play
terms.text: Play in which players take turns at different times and need not be online together. Lexulous and FarmVille work this way.

terms.name: Asynchronous play
terms.text: Play where people take their turns at different times, not together. A high-score list that family members compare over days is an example (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Atom
terms.text: The smallest complete unit of play that players feel is really playing the game, such as two possessions in football or one level of Donkey Kong.

terms.name: Atomic and compound ludeme
terms.text: In the definition the paper uses, a ludeme can be a single element (atomic) or a combination of elements (compound).

terms.name: Atopia
terms.text: Wark's name for a place with no fixed location, where a game's values run through every space. In Vice City each part of the map carries a score.

terms.name: Attention
terms.text: The process that picks a few items out of the many a person could notice and holds them in awareness. It can hold only a small amount at once.

terms.name: Attention
terms.text: The act of picking out the relevant parts of what the senses take in, which turns raw data into information.

terms.name: Attentional resources
terms.text: Sport psychology's term for the finite attention a person can spend on a situation. Skills not yet automatic fail when attention runs out (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Attentive focus
terms.text: What the audience is told to attend to. For a painting it is the painting; for an aesthetic striving game it is the player's own activity.

terms.name: Auction
terms.text: A stage before play in which players take turns saying how much they will try to achieve. The highest call sets the task for the hand.

terms.name: Auction
terms.text: A way of selling something in which players call higher and higher offers until nobody will go further. In Auction Monopoly every unowned property landed on is sold this way.

terms.name: Auctioneer
terms.text: In Bell and Hammer, the player who sells the five picture cards to the highest bidders and pays out of the pool.

terms.name: Auctor
terms.text: A Latin word for the person who gathers and shapes a collection of texts, as against an author who writes one consistent work. The book asks whether the Wakefield Master was the auctor of the Towneley manuscript.

terms.name: Auditor-spectator participation
terms.text: The first step on Boyd's scale of social relations, in which people listen to or watch an activity, as in theatre, radio or watching a sport.

terms.name: Auguste
terms.text: The clown who wears ill-fitting clothes and a red wig, tries to copy the others and fails, and is mocked and drenched. Caillois links him to figures in myth who parody the gods.

terms.name: Auspices
terms.text: The people or body that sponsor and put on a play. The book says assumptions about genre, mode and auspices stop us reading what the playwright did.

terms.name: Authentic power and external power
terms.text: Gary Zukav's pair. Authentic power comes from matching your talents and values to your work, and external power comes from rank, title or possessions.

terms.name: Automatic double
terms.text: A variation in which matching numbers on the first roll turn the cube to 2 with the cube left unowned.

terms.name: Automatic doubling
terms.text: A rule that a tie on the opening throw doubles the stake, or adds one to it.

terms.name: Automatism
terms.text: Making writing or drawing without conscious control, whether from the unconscious or from a physical process, with chance operations used to organise the results.

terms.name: Autonomy
terms.text: How much freedom a team member has to carry out their role in their own way.

terms.name: Autotelic
terms.text: Describes an activity done for its own sake, not for a later reward. The word joins the Greek for self and for goal.

terms.name: Autotelic
terms.text: Describes an activity done for its own sake, which rewards itself.

terms.name: Autotelic family context
terms.text: A home where children know what is expected, feel noticed in the present, can choose, trust their parents and meet rising challenges.

terms.name: Autotelic job
terms.text: A job built like a game, with variety, flexible challenges, clear goals and immediate feedback. Hunting, cottage weaving and surgery are the examples.

terms.name: Autotelic personality
terms.text: A person who finds it easy to turn ordinary or hard situations into flow. They notice chances for action, set goals and watch feedback.

terms.name: Autotelic self
terms.text: A self whose main goals come from its own evaluated experience and not from instinct or social habit. It turns threats into challenges.

terms.name: Auxiliary piles
terms.text: The packets of cards dealt to the table in Solitaire from which cards are moved to build families.

terms.name: Availability bias
terms.text: Judging an event as likely because a similar one happened recently or left a vivid feeling.

terms.name: Avalanche rule
terms.text: In Avalanche Chess, the rule that after each normal move the player has to push one enemy pawn forward one square.

terms.name: Avatar
terms.text: The character that a player controls and improves in a game world.

terms.name: Avatar
terms.text: The character through which a player acts in a game world; its abilities and limits set what the player can do there (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Avatar
terms.text: A figure through which a player acts in a game. Wark says the gamer is also an avatar of the game itself.

terms.name: Avatar-self
terms.text: Gee's idea that a player and the character they control combine into a new joint self, each bringing different knowledge and teaching the other (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Awase
terms.text: Japanese matching games in which players pair or group related images, often painted on shells, as a talking game for comparison and judgement.

terms.name: Awe
terms.text: The feeling of being in the presence of something larger than yourself. Chills, goose bumps and a choked-up throat are its signs.

terms.name: Back game
terms.text: A style of play in which a player lets the opponent get far ahead while holding points in the opponent's home table to hit later.

terms.name: Back score
terms.text: A running total kept for each person across many hands, so winnings and losses can be settled at the end.

terms.name: Backgammon (the result)
terms.text: A gammon in which the loser still has a piece in the winner's home board. In the United States it scores triple.

terms.name: Backstory
terms.text: The background tale that explains why the player is acting, such as the story of Eden in Rez. Wark says the player may read it once or not at all.

terms.name: Bad guy
terms.text: In 'SuperBetter', the author's recovery game, anything that makes your symptoms flare, written on a list so you can avoid it.

terms.name: Balance
terms.text: Putting all available actions on the same level of value for the player. A more damaging move can still be balanced if it costs more or is slower.

terms.name: Balanced difficulty
terms.text: A state in which, with equal skill and luck, every player has the same chance to win. Burgun calls it an aim that is never fully reached.

terms.name: Balk line
terms.text: A line drawn on a billiards table that restricts how many successive shots may be made while both balls stay in one marked space.

terms.name: Balking the crib
terms.text: Giving away cards to the other player's crib that are unlikely to score, such as a King with a Nine.

terms.name: Balking the crib
terms.text: Putting cards into the opponent's crib that are unlikely to score, such as widely spaced ones.

terms.name: Ball (Phutball)
terms.text: The black stone in Philosopher's Football. It is moved by jumping over lines of white stones, which are removed.

terms.name: Banco
terms.text: A call by a player to bet against the whole of the bank.

terms.name: Bank
terms.text: The sum of money or chips a banker puts up to cover bets, which limits how much players may bet against him.

terms.name: Banker
terms.text: A player who takes the stakes and pays the winners in a gambling game. The bank may pass round the players, as in Crown and Anchor, so the advantage is shared.

terms.name: Banker
terms.text: The person who owns the chips at the start and sells equal stacks to each player, keeping the record of who holds what.

terms.name: Banking
terms.text: In pool, playing a ball off a cushion. Players also bank a cue ball to decide the choice of lead.

terms.name: Banking game
terms.text: A game in which one player or the house takes bets from the others, instead of all players betting against each other.

terms.name: Banns
terms.text: A public announcement of a coming play or game. New Romney paid town criers from neighbouring places to proclaim banns, and was paid in turn when its own play was cried in other parishes.

terms.name: Banns-crier
terms.text: A person who went through nearby towns calling out the announcement of a coming play. The Castle of Perseverance text has gaps where the crier names the town of the performance and the towns visited.

terms.name: The bar
terms.text: The strip between the inner and outer tables of a backgammon board, where hit pieces wait until they can re-enter.

terms.name: Bar
terms.text: The raised strip across the middle of a backgammon board. A hit piece waits on it until it can enter again.

terms.name: Bar
terms.text: The centre divider of a backgammon board, where hit stones wait to re-enter.

terms.name: Bar
terms.text: The divider in the middle of a backgammon board where a captured piece waits. Its owner can move nothing else until it has re-entered.

terms.name: Bare king
terms.text: In Shatranj, the position in which a player has lost all pieces except the king. Capturing all the rest of the opponent's pieces won the game.

terms.name: Bare king
terms.text: In Shatranj, a win by capturing every opposing piece except the king, unless the other side can bare the king on the next turn.

terms.name: Barred player
terms.text: A player who has to pass at every turn in an auction as the cost of an error.

terms.name: Barrier position
terms.text: A position where a player has made a wall behind which his own pieces move safely. The game stalls and the player with more pieces wins on points.

terms.name: Barter
terms.text: A swap of cards between players with no payment. In Commerce a player cannot refuse unless they are content with their hand.

terms.name: Base
terms.text: A marked place or posture, such as a tree or a squat in stoop tag, where a player is safe but cannot play. The player is in the game without taking part for a while.

terms.name: Baseline (ball games)
terms.text: A line from which players throw, kick or bat in a game.

terms.name: Basic empathy
terms.text: An intermediate form of perspective-taking where a player knows others have feelings like their own but has trouble keeping in mind how others differ from the self (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Basic value
terms.text: In Haggle, the points a card is worth by itself, apart from bonuses and limits that depend on the rest of the hand.

terms.name: Basta
terms.text: In Solo, the Queen of Spades, the third trump.

terms.name: Batch (taking from the pile)
terms.text: Taking two or more cards from the top of the discard pile in one turn, allowed if the bottom card taken can be melded at once.

terms.name: Batman problem
terms.text: The clash in a licensed game over who gets to play the main character when the story has only one or two and the game needs many.

terms.name: Batting order
terms.text: The fixed sequence in which a team's players take their turns to bat.

terms.name: Battle array
terms.text: In Shatranj, the opening positions reached when each player made ten or twelve moves at once to set up his forces. Bell gives the name Ta'biyat.

terms.name: Battle of the Sexes
terms.text: A coordination game with two equilibria, where each of a couple prefers a different outing but both prefer being together.

terms.name: Battle royal
terms.text: A staged fight in which several blindfolded boys hit each other at once while onlookers watch. In Ellison's novel white townsmen run one for their own amusement, and the boys have no say in it.

terms.name: Bearing off
terms.text: Taking a piece off the board once it has come to the end of the track. Backgammon allows it only when all of a player's pieces are in the home table.

terms.name: Bearing off
terms.text: Taking pieces off the board once all of them have reached the home table. The first player to bear off every piece wins backgammon.

terms.name: Bearing off
terms.text: Removing stones from the board once all of them are in the home table.

terms.name: Bearing off
terms.text: Taking pieces off the board once all of them have reached the home field. It is how a backgammon game is won.

terms.name: Beg
terms.text: In Seven-Up, to hand to the dealer the choice of whether to accept the turned-up suit as trump.

terms.name: Begging
terms.text: In All-Fours, a non-dealer who dislikes their hand may ask for a new deal. The dealer either gives one point or deals new cards and a new trump.

terms.name: Being versus doing
terms.text: A distinction found in law: who you are, such as your skin colour, is protected, while what you do, such as a hairstyle or a way of speaking, is not. A person can lose a case for refusing to hide a cultural habit.

terms.name: Benchmarking
terms.text: Systematically comparing your practice and results with those of similar bodies.

terms.name: Bent rule
terms.text: An exception that everyone sees and accepts, made for one player to help the game along. In volleyball a tired player asked to play near the net and was allowed.

terms.name: Bete
terms.text: In Solo, a forfeit put into the pool after a failed bid or a mistake.

terms.name: Bete
terms.text: A condition of the player who accepted the trump and then scored less than his opponent. He loses, and the opponent scores both totals.

terms.name: Betting interval
terms.text: A set period in a betting game when players, one after another, add to the pot or give up, until all stakes are level.

terms.name: Betting limit
terms.text: The most that any player can bet at one time, agreed before the game starts.

terms.name: Betweenness centrality
terms.text: A score for how often a member sits on the shortest path between two others. A member with high betweenness and few links is a broker between groups.

terms.name: BGG rank
terms.text: A ranking built from a Bayesian average of user ratings, which pulls games with very few votes towards the overall average so that a handful of high scores cannot push a game to the top. A game needs at least 30 ratings before it is ranked.

terms.name: Bid
terms.text: A statement of the points a player will win. In Forty-two, each bid has to beat the one before.

terms.name: Bid
terms.text: A promise in Bridge to win a stated number of tricks with a stated suit as trumps. Each bid has to outrank the one before.

terms.name: Bidder's temporary partnership
terms.text: Two players who normally play for themselves join against whoever won the bidding, for that hand only.

terms.name: Bidding
terms.text: Players stating how many tricks or points they will take, to win the right to name trump or lead.

terms.name: Bidding for turn order
terms.text: Letting players pay for the right to move first, in place of rolling dice. The price paid shows how much the first position is worth to them.

terms.name: Bidding game
terms.text: A game where players offer resources for an item that several want, and the highest bid wins it.

terms.name: Bidding rule
terms.text: A balancing rule in which players bid how well they will do with the favoured side, such as escaping in fewer moves, and the lowest bidder takes that side and has to keep the promise.

terms.name: Big urban game
terms.text: A game played in the physical streets of a city, often with phones only as a minor aid, using public space and city layout as the playing field (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Bingo
terms.text: In Scrabble, a play that uses all seven tiles on the rack at once.

terms.name: Bingo (domino)
terms.text: The double blank in a domino game played like Sixty-Six, counting as 14 spots and the highest tile.

terms.name: Black mask
terms.text: A small plain mask worn at balls and plots. Caillois says it gives anonymity and a promise of secrecy, and marks a game of flirtation or conspiracy.

terms.name: Black-or-white fallacy
terms.text: Presenting two options as the only ones, so that anyone who does not choose one is taken to have chosen the other.

terms.name: Blank tile
terms.text: A Scrabble tile that stands for any letter chosen by the player.

terms.name: Blind
terms.text: An ante put in by the eldest hand in Poker before the cards are looked at.

terms.name: Blind
terms.text: A bet made before the cards are looked at, so that there is always something in the pot.

terms.name: Blind
terms.text: In Texas Hold'em, a bet placed by the two players left of the dealer before the cards are dealt.

terms.name: Blind follower model
terms.text: A design where the player carries out what the game tells the avatar to do and so passes moral responsibility to the game's authority, which may later be shown to have been wrong (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Blind kingmaking
terms.text: A player out of contention who changes who wins by random choices, without favouring any one contender. A low-skilled player in a poker pot does this.

terms.name: Blind Man's Buff
terms.text: A party game where a blindfolded player tries to catch someone and guess who they are.

terms.name: Blind test
terms.text: Handing a new game's rulebook and parts to players who know nothing about it, with nobody else in the room, to see whether they can learn it.

terms.name: Blissful productivity
terms.text: The feeling of being deeply absorbed in work whose results are immediate and obvious.

terms.name: Blitz
terms.text: In Thirty-One, an ace, king and ten of one suit, which ends the hand at once and makes the others pay.

terms.name: Block
terms.text: A position in dominoes in which no player can play. The player with the fewest spots left wins the count.

terms.name: Block game
terms.text: A domino game in which a player who cannot play loses his turn.

terms.name: Blockade
terms.text: A position in which neither player can break the other's line. In the suggested rules, thirty moves without a capture ends the game.

terms.name: Blocked (solitaire)
terms.text: A solitaire game that has ended because no play is possible in a whole deal.

terms.name: Blocked game (dominoes)
terms.text: A game where nobody can play a tile. Players then count the spots left in their hands and the lowest count wins.

terms.name: Blocked piece
terms.text: A piece that cannot move because the points ahead hold enemy pairs. In Tabula such a piece was incitus.

terms.name: Blocked point
terms.text: A point held by two or more enemy pieces. The other player cannot move onto it, so it limits which dice numbers can be used.

terms.name: Blocker
terms.text: An item that has to be settled before team members can finish their tasks. It goes on the for-discussion list.

terms.name: Blocking
terms.text: Playing a card so that an opponent cannot play the card they need. In Grabouche, players avoid helping the other side reach the top card of its pile.

terms.name: Blot
terms.text: In backgammon, a single piece alone on a point. It can be hit by an enemy piece moving onto the point.

terms.name: Blot
terms.text: A single piece alone on a backgammon point, which the opponent can hit by landing on it.

terms.name: Blot
terms.text: A single stone on a point, which an opponent can hit.

terms.name: Blot
terms.text: A single piece alone on a point in backgammon, which can be hit.

terms.name: Blot
terms.text: A single piece alone on a point. An enemy piece that lands there sends it back off the board.

terms.name: Bluff
terms.text: In bidding, raising the price beyond an item's value to make a rival pay too much.

terms.name: Bluff
terms.text: A play where a player says something untrue about their cards or hand. In I Doubt It the whole game rests on putting down the wrong card without anyone suspecting.

terms.name: Bluff
terms.text: Acting as if you have a particular word or card in mind when you do not. In Ghost a bluffer who is challenged earns a penalty letter if caught out.

terms.name: Bluff call (I doubt it)
terms.text: A challenge in which the last cards played are turned over. Whoever is wrong picks up the pile.

terms.name: Bluffing
terms.text: Betting on a low-ranking hand in the hope that every other player gives up.

terms.name: Board game experience profile
terms.text: The set of scores a game receives on the paper's traits, shown as a bar graph so two games can be compared at a glance. Each trait is scored low, medium or high, and a trait that is absent is scored nil, which still counts as a score.

terms.name: Bold stand
terms.text: In Division Loo, a round in which every player has to play their hand, and only the eldest hand may swap for the dummy.

terms.name: Bolotoudou
terms.text: A game from the Sudan played with twelve sticks and twelve pebbles on thirty boxes in five rows. A player who gets three in a line takes an opponent's piece.

terms.name: Bonding capital and bridging capital
terms.text: Robert Putnam's words for the value of ties inside your own group and the value of ties across groups.

terms.name: Boneyard
terms.text: The face-down pile of unused dominoes from which players draw.

terms.name: Boneyard
terms.text: The face-down dominoes left over after dealing. A player who cannot play draws from it.

terms.name: Bonus card
terms.text: A card that is never melded but scores a fixed amount when held, such as a red three in Canasta. It is replaced by a draw.

terms.name: Bonus stroke
terms.text: An extra shot earned by scoring a wicket or hitting another ball in croquet. It is also called a continuation shot.

terms.name: Boodle cards
terms.text: Cards laid in the middle with chips on them. A player who plays the matching card collects the chips.

terms.name: Book
terms.text: A set of four cards of one rank collected in Authors and Fish.

terms.name: Book
terms.text: In Whist, the first six tricks, which score nothing. In Go Fish, a set of four cards of one rank collected by a player.

terms.name: Book (Go Fish)
terms.text: A set of all four suits of one rank in Go Fish. The most books at the end wins.

terms.name: Boredom
terms.text: The state a person feels when challenges are lower than their skills.

terms.name: Boredom
terms.text: The state Koster says arrives when a game stops offering new patterns to learn. He treats it as the signal that a game has stopped teaching.

terms.name: Borrowed rule
terms.text: A rule taken from another version of a game and attached to the one being played. In solitaire a player can switch from turning every third card to turning each card.

terms.name: Boss
terms.text: An enemy larger and more powerful than those before it, usually met at the end of a run of linked levels.

terms.name: Boss
terms.text: The large opponent at the end of a run of levels. Wark uses the big boss as a picture of time, always out ahead of the player.

terms.name: Boss level
terms.text: A hard unit that makes a player use everything learned so far, as a boss monster does in a video game. At Quest to Learn it is a two-week team project.

terms.name: Bottom-feeding
terms.text: Choosing low-skill opponents or easy levels again and again to gain safe wins or lives. Koster says it follows when easy encounters pay out as much as hard ones.

terms.name: Bottom-up simulation
terms.text: A model that puts the player in one small role to show a larger system from within, as Papers, Please does.

terms.name: Boundary
terms.text: The line between a game and everything outside it. It lets a player step out without stopping the game, and keeps outside matters from entering.

terms.name: Bounded rationality
terms.text: Herbert Simon's idea that people decide within limits of time, information, money and thinking, so they cannot search for the exact optimum.

terms.name: Bounding, temporal and objective components
terms.text: Bounding components are goals, rules and game modes, and say what is allowed. Temporal components are actions, events, end conditions, evaluation functions and closures, and cover what happens over time. Objective components are players, interfaces and game elements such as tokens, dice, cards and tiles.

terms.name: Bourd (bourding)
terms.text: Middle English for jesting or joking, especially with a familiarity unfit between unequals. The Tretise uses it for people making a game out of sacred events.

terms.name: Bower
terms.text: In Euchre, the two Jacks that rank highest in trumps. The right bower is the Jack of the trump suit, and the left bower is the other Jack of the same colour.

terms.name: Bower
terms.text: In Euchre, a jack that has been raised to the top of the trump suit. The right bower is the trump jack, and the left bower the other jack of the same colour.

terms.name: Boy bishop
terms.text: A choirboy who held the bishop's role on the feast of Saint Nicholas, with ceremonies he led. Some monasteries and cathedrals called these ceremonies miracula because a boy was acting as a bishop he was not.

terms.name: Brahmodya
terms.text: A Vedic contest in which priests asked each other questions about holy things at a sacrifice.

terms.name: Brainstorming
terms.text: A process with set rules for exploring every possibility round an idea or question, which produces many what if questions.

terms.name: Brawl
terms.text: A multiplayer game made by adding players to a two-player game that cannot be reduced to one player, such as Risk. Players hurt each other directly.

terms.name: Break (Mahjong)
terms.text: The point in the wall where tiles start to be drawn, found by dice throws.

terms.name: Breaking a suit
terms.text: The rule that a suit may not be led until someone has first played a card of it on an earlier trick.

terms.name: Breaking hearts
terms.text: In Hearts, the first time a heart is discarded. Until then a player may not lead a heart unless holding nothing else.

terms.name: Brisques
terms.text: The aces and tens in Bezique, each worth a few points when taken in play.

terms.name: Broken
terms.text: Said of a game or object so powerful that once players find it, it is the only choice, as if the game stopped working as intended.

terms.name: Broker network
terms.text: A set of contacts who do not know each other, held together by one person, also called a connector or boundary spanner. Three contacts from separate circles reach eleven people, where three in one clique reach three.

terms.name: Buck
terms.text: A token marking the next dealer.

terms.name: Bughouse
terms.text: A four-player chess game on two boards in which a captured piece is handed to your partner, who may drop it onto his own board.

terms.name: Build-up
terms.text: Boyd's word for correcting behaviour by feeding the whole person with developing experience, in place of fixing the fault or punishing it.

terms.name: Building
terms.text: In Casino, laying a card on one or more cards on the table to make a total that you hold a card to capture later.

terms.name: Building
terms.text: In Casino, stacking cards on the table and announcing a total, to capture them on a later turn. The other player can take the build first.

terms.name: Building (Casino)
terms.text: Laying a card from your hand on table cards to make a total, which then only a card of that total can capture.

terms.name: Built-in customization
terms.text: A game letting each player choose rules or pieces for themselves before or during play, as with a Magic deck or an MMO character.

terms.name: Bull-roarer
terms.text: A flat piece of wood whirled on a cord to make a roaring sound. In some ceremonies it is the secret sound of the spirits.

terms.name: Bulls and cows
terms.text: The paper-and-pencil game MasterMind came from. Bulls are right digits in the right place and cows are right digits in the wrong place.

terms.name: Bumper cars
terms.text: A fairground ride where players steer small cars and collide on purpose. Caillois says they combine the pleasure of driving with paidia, doing freely what road rules forbid.

terms.name: Bundle of standards
terms.text: A group of standards that come together in a genre, such as track, piece and dice in track boardgames. Knowing the bundle lets players start an unknown game quickly.

terms.name: Burnt card
terms.text: The top card of the pack, put on the bottom unseen before dealing so nobody knows it.

terms.name: Burying
terms.text: Putting cards face down out of a hand after taking the widow. They count for the bidder at the end.

terms.name: Bushy game tree
terms.text: A game tree with many choices at a point.

terms.name: Bust
terms.text: Going over 21 in Twenty-One (or 21 on a die), which takes the player out of the round.

terms.name: Bust
terms.text: Going over 21 in Blackjack, which loses the bet at once.

terms.name: Bust
terms.text: In blackjack, going over 21. The player loses the bet at once.

terms.name: Bust (darts)
terms.text: In 301 darts, a turn that would take the score below 2 or not exactly to zero, so the score goes back to what it was.

terms.name: Busywork
terms.text: Rote activities a player has to do that involve no real decisions and cannot be done well or badly, such as shuffling, dealing, setting up and adding scores.

terms.name: Busywork
terms.text: Predictable, repetitive play that occupies hands and mind and gives a clear result, such as swapping jewels or harvesting virtual crops.

terms.name: Busywork component
terms.text: A part that serves the bookkeeping and not the game's world, such as an instruction manual or a mat. The term comes from Elias, Garfield and Gutschera.

terms.name: Button mashing
terms.text: Pressing buttons rapidly with no thought. Burgun says if it works, the game has stopped asking for decisions.

terms.name: Calculation
terms.text: A formulaic mental effort in which paper or a computer would help, such as counting cards, reading out moves or working out odds.

terms.name: Call
terms.text: In poker, matching the current bet to stay in the hand. It is also called seeing the bet.

terms.name: Call (Poker)
terms.text: Matching the last bet and so ending the betting, after which the hands are shown.

terms.name: Call, raise, fold
terms.text: The three choices in a round of poker betting: pay the current wager, increase it, or drop out of the hand.

terms.name: Called Ace
terms.text: In Solo, a bidder names an Ace and the holder of it becomes their secret partner until the Ace is played.

terms.name: Called ace
terms.text: A secret partnership made by naming an ace. Whoever holds it is the partner, and nobody knows who until it is played.

terms.name: Called shot
terms.text: In pool, naming the ball a player intends to pocket before the stroke. The ball only counts if it goes in as called.

terms.name: Caller
terms.text: The person who draws and reads out the numbers in Bingo.

terms.name: Calling
terms.text: In Puritan teaching, the work a person is called to do, either the general calling to serve God or a particular job that makes the person useful to neighbours.

terms.name: Calling the bluff
terms.text: Challenging a player's claim. In I Doubt It the challenged card is shown, and whoever was wrong takes the whole pile.

terms.name: Calling the turn
terms.text: Betting on the exact order of the last three cards of the pack.

terms.name: Camel and wildebeest
terms.text: Pieces in Wildebeest Chess. A camel leaps like an elongated knight across a 2x4 rectangle, and a wildebeest combines knight and camel moves.

terms.name: Campaign
terms.text: A series of games or sessions that are linked in some way, such as a weekly poker night, a sports season or an ongoing role-playing game.

terms.name: Campbell's law
terms.text: The claim that the more a number is used to decide things in society, the more it is pushed to be corrupt and the more it distorts the process it was meant to track.

terms.name: Canasta
terms.text: A set of seven or more cards of one rank, which carries a large score and which a side has to complete before it may go out.

terms.name: Canasta
terms.text: A meld of at least seven cards of one rank in the game of that name. A natural canasta, with no wild cards, scores more than a mixed one.

terms.name: Cannon
terms.text: A Chinese chess piece that moves along rank or file but can only capture by jumping over exactly one piece, called the screen.

terms.name: Capital riddle
terms.text: A riddle where the player who cannot answer loses their head, from the German word Halsrätsel. Huizinga says it turns up in Indian, Greek and Norse stories.

terms.name: Capture by landing
terms.text: Removing an enemy piece by moving a piece onto the space it stands on. The captured piece goes back to the start or off the board.

terms.name: Card drafting
terms.text: A way of dealing where players take a card from a hand and pass the rest on. Passing the hand can deny a card to the next player.

terms.name: Card play conflict resolution
terms.text: Players play one or more cards, together or one after another, to change the outcome of a conflict and to trigger special abilities.

terms.name: Card sleeve
terms.text: A thin plastic cover that protects a card from wear.

terms.name: Cardinal utility function
terms.text: A rule that gives each outcome a number, so that the size of a preference can be stated.

terms.name: Care ethics
terms.text: An approach, associated with Nel Noddings, that sets up conditions likely to encourage goodness, rather than teaching virtues directly (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Career
terms.text: In The Sims, a ladder of jobs, each with set requirements such as number of friends or points in creativity. When they are met the career ends and another begins.

terms.name: Carnival
terms.text: A short period of licence in which people wear masks and break the usual rules. Caillois calls it nearer to paidia than ludus.

terms.name: Carnivalesque
terms.text: Having the character of a festival in which rank is turned over, food is plentiful and laughter breaks into serious business. The book applies the word, from Bakhtin, to the shepherds' plays.

terms.name: Carom
terms.text: In billiards, a stroke where the cue ball hits both object balls, which scores a point.

terms.name: Carte blanche
terms.text: A hand with no king, queen or jack, shown at once for a score in Bezique.

terms.name: Cartesian coordinate space
terms.text: Space described by a grid with two straight axes, the usual way a board or screen is laid out. Koster notes it is only one of many shapes a game space can take.

terms.name: Cash
terms.text: To lead a card and win the trick with it.

terms.name: Caster
terms.text: The player who throws the dice in Hazard.

terms.name: Castle
terms.text: A marked square where a piece cannot be captured. In Pachisi a castle holding one player's piece is open to his partner and closed to the enemy.

terms.name: Castle (Beverley)
terms.text: A built structure for the Rogation Monday procession of the relics of Saint John of Beverley. It was a viewing stand with ample refreshment, where prominent guilds sat to watch, and guild members wore livery there.

terms.name: Castling
terms.text: A chess move where the king moves two squares towards a rook and the rook jumps to the square beside it. It is allowed once, and only if neither piece has moved.

terms.name: Castling
terms.text: A special chess move in which the king moves two squares toward a rook and the rook jumps over it. It counts as one move and can be done once a game.

terms.name: Casual game
terms.text: A short, easy-to-start game, often played online. Flanagan says such games are seen as the main product for women players.

terms.name: Casual game
terms.text: A game that is easy to learn, quick to play and light on computer power, often played in short bursts on a browser or phone. Bejeweled and Peggle are examples.

terms.name: Casual game
terms.text: A game with lesser commitment to play than hard-core play, usually played to relax, escape or fight boredom; there is no agreed meaning (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Casual social association
terms.text: The third step on Boyd's scale, covering activities such as group singing and equipment games like quoits, cards, board games and tennis.

terms.name: Cat and Rat
terms.text: A circle game used by Boyd as a teaching example. A Cat stands outside a ring of children holding hands, a Rat stands inside, and the children try to keep the Cat out.

terms.name: Catch-up event
terms.text: In the book's model, an event that makes the players' chances of winning more even, which reduces the variance of the state vector.

terms.name: Catch-up feature
terms.text: A rule meant to help players who are behind close the gap, such as the shells in Mario Kart.

terms.name: Category
terms.text: A named group such as birds or cities, used in word games to decide which words fit.

terms.name: Category (scoring)
terms.text: In Yacht and Yahtzee, one of the named scoring boxes on the pad. Each can be used once, and a player picks one after each turn.

terms.name: Cave-culture-game
terms.text: Travis's name for the contest in Plato's cave, where prisoners compete to predict what the shadows on the wall will do and win prizes and honours for it (chapter by Roger Travis).

terms.name: Center piles (Grabouche)
terms.text: Piles built up in the middle of the table from an Ace to a King, which any player may add to. A King finishes a pile and it is removed.

terms.name: Centrality measure
terms.text: A rule that scores how central a member is in a network, used to find who is at the centre when there is no top.

terms.name: Centre stack
terms.text: A pile in the middle that both players may add to, built up in order from an ace.

terms.name: Chain drawing (dessin successif)
terms.text: A game in which each player studies the last drawing for five seconds and redraws it from memory, so the first, middle and last drawings in the chain can be compared.

terms.name: Chain-question
terms.text: A riddle form in which one question leads on to the next.

terms.name: Challenge
terms.text: A player's call that the previous player's declared score is false. In Liar Dice the loser of the challenge loses a life.

terms.name: Challenge
terms.text: A chance for action in an activity that asks for skill. Someone without the right skill does not see it as a challenge at all.

terms.name: Challenge
terms.text: The way a game pushes back against the player. It can come from a hard skill, a hard goal or hard ideas in the content.

terms.name: Challenge
terms.text: A move in which a player says an opponent's answer or play is wrong and puts something at stake to prove it. It gives a game with little contact between players some interaction.

terms.name: Challenge
terms.text: A player's right to ask another to prove a claim. The challenger or the challenged takes the penalty, depending on who was right.

terms.name: Chance
terms.text: The use of randomness in a game. The more chance, the harder it is to plan ahead.

terms.name: Chance culture
terms.text: A group of people who openly accept that life depends on risk. The book gives colonial Southern planters and frontier adventurers as examples.

terms.name: Chance operation
terms.text: A rule that lets dice, sticks, spinners or other random means decide part of an outcome.

terms.name: Change request
terms.text: A form used to settle disputes over accuracy. Historians scored each fix for priority, developers scored it for difficulty, and the team compared the two scores (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Changed game
terms.text: DeKoven's definition is a variation that needs a new strategy. Swapping X and O for other marks changes the look and leaves the game as it was.

terms.name: Changing the game
terms.text: Challenging the rules and the status quo with the intent of altering them, whether or not the game ends up altered. The author treats it as a commitment to keep pushing, not as a result.

terms.name: Chaotic story
terms.text: A story cut into thousands of pieces and spread over many media, so that it does not exist until players assemble it.

terms.name: Character armor
terms.text: Ernest Becker's name, taken from Wilhelm Reich, for the personality a person builds as a defence against awareness of death. Hoffman links it to the hero a player builds in a game (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

terms.name: Character education
terms.text: An approach that builds moral behaviour through models and habits, for example inspirational stories, instruction and practice (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Character sheet
terms.text: A paper record of a role-playing character's name, class, numbers, spells and items.

terms.name: Character sheet
terms.text: A page that gives a player their goals and how their character sees the world. Balzac calls it the player's doorway into the game (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Characteristic
terms.text: A general feature that describes what sort of game it is, such as how many players it takes, how long it lasts or how much luck it has. It is the kind of thing a friend asks before agreeing to play.

terms.name: Charade (in the Cuban lottery)
terms.text: A deliberately ambiguous statement the banker reads before the draw, such as "A bird pecks and goes away", which players decode to pick a symbol.

terms.name: Charades
terms.text: A party game in which a player acts out a word, phrase or title without speaking, using no props.

terms.name: Chaturaji
terms.text: In Modern Chaturanga, the point scored for having the last raja still on the board.

terms.name: Cheat
terms.text: A player who breaks a rule while pretending to follow it. The cheat depends on other players keeping the rules.

terms.name: Cheat
terms.text: A player who breaks the rules in secret while still pretending to play. The cheat still accepts the game, so a group treats this person more gently than a spoil-sport.

terms.name: Cheat
terms.text: In Suits's words, a player who aims at the goal of a game but ignores its rules. Wark sets this against the trifler.

terms.name: Cheating
terms.text: Doing something to give yourself more than an even chance to win. DeKoven separates this from rule-breaking done to keep a game going.

terms.name: Cheating
terms.text: Breaking the rules to gain an advantage. How easy it is, how well it works and how it is punished differ between games.

terms.name: Cheating
terms.text: Acting outside the formal limits of a game in order to win. Koster treats it as lateral thinking that shows the player has understood the game.

terms.name: Cheating prevention by device
terms.text: A piece of equipment that stops a player from altering a throw, such as the straw ring for Nyout dice or the Roman dice tower.

terms.name: Check
terms.text: A threat to capture the king on the next move.

terms.name: Check
terms.text: In chess, a king under attack by an enemy piece. The attacked player has three replies: move the king, capture the attacker, or put a piece in between.

terms.name: Check
terms.text: To stay in without betting, allowed when no one before you has bet.

terms.name: Check
terms.text: A warning that a king could be captured on the next move. The player in check has to move the king, capture the attacker or block it.

terms.name: Check
terms.text: In poker, passing without betting while staying in the hand.

terms.name: Check (chess)
terms.text: A threat to capture the king on the next move.

terms.name: Check-in
terms.text: In Foursquare, telling the app where you are so friends are alerted and your visits are logged.

terms.name: Checkered Game of Life
terms.text: A board game by Milton Bradley, published in 1860, that taught moral habits as players moved through spaces for virtue and vice. Parker Brothers published a similar game, The Game of Christian Endeavor, in 1896.

terms.name: Checkless Chess
terms.text: A chess variant in which a player may not give check unless it is checkmate.

terms.name: Checkmate
terms.text: A position in which the king is in check and cannot escape, so the game is lost.

terms.name: Checkmate
terms.text: A chess position where the king is attacked and none of the three replies is possible. The game ends at once.

terms.name: Checkmate
terms.text: A check from which the king has no escape, which ends the game.

terms.name: Checkmate
terms.text: A position in which a king is in check and none of the three answers is possible. The game ends there.

terms.name: Chip-taking game
terms.text: A game where each turn a player may remove a resource from a chosen opponent and the last one left wins. Skill in the rest of the game hardly matters.

terms.name: Chips
terms.text: Tokens used in poker to stand for stakes. A business writer pictures the earth as a table with a fixed number of chips, where each player tries to pile up as many as he can.

terms.name: Chomp
terms.text: A taking-away game on a rectangular grid in which each move crosses out every square above and to the right of the chosen one, and whoever has to choose the bottom left corner loses.

terms.name: Chooser
terms.text: The player in Fictionary who picks the dictionary word and reads out all the definitions. The role passes round the table.

terms.name: Choosing by lot
terms.text: Picking officials by drawing lots. The Greek founders of democracy saw it as completely equal, since no one is favoured.

terms.name: Chorea (plural choreae)
terms.text: A song-dance, a dance performed to singing. Church rules listed it with wrestling among the games banned from churchyards on feast days.

terms.name: Choreopower
terms.text: A named strength, such as style, courage or humour, that viewers award to a dancer in Top Secret Dance-Off by adding one point to a video. Together the points make a profile of what each player is like.

terms.name: Chouette
terms.text: A way for three people to play a two-player game: one plays alone against two partners, and the roles rotate after each game.

terms.name: Chouette
terms.text: A form of backgammon for three or more in which one player in the box faces a team led by a captain.

terms.name: Chow
terms.text: In Ma-jong, a run of three consecutive numbers of one suit.

terms.name: Christmas Lord
terms.text: A figure chosen to rule the Christmas season in jest, also called a King of Fools. The book asks whether Herod in the Wakefield play is built as one, and the torturers call Christ King Copin.

terms.name: Chu Shogi
terms.text: A medieval Japanese chess variant on a 12x12 board with 92 pieces, in which nearly every piece can promote.

terms.name: Chunking
terms.text: The brain's habit of packing a set of steps or features into one unit that runs without thought, like the whole routine of getting dressed. Koster says learning a game means chunking its patterns.

terms.name: Circular causality
terms.text: A loop in which two things shape each other. The book uses it for the self directing attention while attention builds the self.

terms.name: Citadel
terms.text: In Circular chess, a fortified square on the board. A king that entered the opponent's citadel reached sanctuary and the game was drawn.

terms.name: Civil and military series
terms.text: In Chinese dice and dominoes, the two groups of throws or tiles. A throw by the banker names which group counts for that round.

terms.name: Clear goals
terms.text: Aims that a player always knows, such as returning the ball or mating the king. The book lists them among the conditions for flow.

terms.name: Cleared hand
terms.text: A Mahjong hand using one suit only, with or without Winds and Honors, which is harder to build and scores more.

terms.name: Clerkes play
terms.text: A play of clerks: a revel by clerics in minor orders and choirboys, with masks, torturers and ragged costumes, in the Christmas season and from Easter to Whitsuntide.

terms.name: Climber
terms.text: The author's name for a player who works up in an individual and opportunistic way, driven by ambition and mostly unconcerned with the wider group.

terms.name: Climbing the heuristics tree
terms.text: Learning more refined rules of thumb for a game over time. For serious players this learning is much of the pleasure.

terms.name: Clique network
terms.text: A tight group in which everyone knows everyone else. It brings high trust, but news and chances circulate inside it and do not leave.

terms.name: Closed ethical system
terms.text: A game whose ethical choices form a limited range that the designers set, so no choice outside that range can be made (chapter by Roger Travis).

terms.name: Closed poker
terms.text: A form of poker where every card a player holds is hidden from the others.

terms.name: Closeness centrality
terms.text: A score for how short the paths are from a member to all the others in a network.

terms.name: Closing
terms.text: In Sixty-Six, the leader turns down the trump card to stop all drawing, betting they can reach 66 points without it.

terms.name: Closing a number
terms.text: In Cricket darts, hitting a number three times so the team can score on it while the opponent has not closed it.

terms.name: Closing the stock
terms.text: Ending the drawing of cards by turning down the trump card, after which players have to follow suit and win if they can.

terms.name: Club-law
terms.text: An optional Division Loo rule that everyone has to play when Clubs are trump, and then there is no dummy.

terms.name: Clumping
terms.text: A catch-up effect that only reaches nearby players, so groups of close players keep hitting each other while far-off groups are not affected. The Green Shell in Mario Kart does this.

terms.name: Co-occurrence of mechanics
terms.text: How often two mechanics are tagged on the same game. The paper counts the pairs found together in more than 1% of its games, and notes that the most popular mechanics dominate the result simply because they are popular.

terms.name: Co-op mode
terms.text: A way of playing in which players work together against computer-controlled opponents rather than against each other. Rock Band and Left 4 Dead are examples.

terms.name: Co-play
terms.text: Parents and children playing a game together, which many mothers in the authors' data say they would like to do more with games made for it (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Coach
terms.text: A person who looks after the players' ability to play, including taking a player out when the game has become a matter of personal proof.

terms.name: Coarse-grained values
terms.text: Values with fewer and blunter distinctions, which result when simple measures replace a person's finer vocabulary for what matters.

terms.name: Cobra effect
terms.text: A situation where a rule meant to remove a problem makes it larger. In India a bounty on snakes led people to breed snakes for the bounty.

terms.name: Code duello
terms.text: The written rules of the duel, which gave the fight a formal order. John Hyde Wilson wrote them down in 1838, and many duels ended without blood.

terms.name: Code prototype
terms.text: A trial of technical matters, such as whether code runs on certain machines or a new device behaves as hoped. Also called a tech prototype.

terms.name: Code-switching
terms.text: Changing how you speak, such as accent or dialect, to suit the listeners. The author calls it one common kind of covering.

terms.name: Codemaker and codebreaker
terms.text: The two roles in MasterMind. One player hides a code and answers guesses with pegs, and the other tries to find the code.

terms.name: Coffee-housing
terms.text: Sharp practice at the table, such as misleading talk. It is considered unethical but is not cheating.

terms.name: Cognitive friction
terms.text: The breakdown of fit between what a player does and how the game shows it, which a player cannot repair by using what they know as a player or as a member of a culture (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Cognitive load
terms.text: The amount of mental effort a task puts on working memory. Khetrapal notes that extra load worsened task performance even in children as old as thirteen (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

terms.name: Collaboration
terms.text: Working together in three ways at once: cooperating toward a goal, coordinating effort and resources, and cocreating something new that none could make alone.

terms.name: Collaboration radar
terms.text: A sense of who would suit which task, built from a large social network and from tools that show what other people are doing and are skilled at.

terms.name: Collaborative creation system
terms.text: A part of a game where players build levels or content for one another and publish it. Little Big Planet's Popit is one.

terms.name: Collaborative filtering
terms.text: A recommendation method that suggests items liked by people who are similar to you, or by your friends.

terms.name: Collaborative yomi
terms.text: Naomi Clark's twist on yomi, where players guess each other's actions in order to help one another instead of to win.

terms.name: Collaboratory
terms.text: An online space where people from many places practise working together at a large scale.

terms.name: Collectible card game
terms.text: A card game whose cards are bought in random packs, so players start with unequal power and the number of cards keeps growing.

terms.name: Collective commitment
terms.text: Each player's reliance on the others to see a game through to its end, even when the result is going against them.

terms.name: Collective context
terms.text: A story shared by many players, each acting inside it and talking to the others on forums and wikis.

terms.name: Collective effervescence
terms.text: Durkheim's phrase for the sense of belonging to a real group when many people think and feel the same thing together, as at a concert.

terms.name: Collective intelligence
terms.text: Knowledge gathered from many people's experience into one shared resource, such as a strategy wiki.

terms.name: Collective reward
terms.text: A prize shared by all players, not kept by one. In Club Penguin's Coins for Change, players give their points to a common pool that decides how real money goes to charities (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Collectivism
terms.text: In Boyd's scale of groups, the end where members are interested mainly in one another as persons and not only in the activity.

terms.name: Collision
terms.text: An operational logic that decides when two things count as touching. In Pong it means a ball is deflected; in Pac-Man it means a pellet is eaten.

terms.name: Combat results table
terms.text: A table in hex wargames where a dice roll and the odds are looked up to find the outcome of an attack.
