terms.name: Combinatorial game theory
terms.text: Maths of two-player games with alternating moves, no luck and no hidden information, built by John Conway. It treats positions as a kind of number.

terms.name: Combining
terms.text: Capturing two or more table cards whose values add up to the value of a card in your hand.

terms.name: Combining
terms.text: In Casino, capturing two or more table cards whose values add up to the value of the card played.

terms.name: Combo
terms.text: A chain of moves where each leads into the next, often playing out by itself once the first hits.

terms.name: Combo
terms.text: A scored or rewarded sequence of moves performed in the right order. Koster lists it among the few real advances in fighting games.

terms.name: Comforter
terms.text: An object a child clings to that does not quite do the work of a transitional object, because the child needs the actual person more. The example is a boy's rabbit, kept until age five or six.

terms.name: Commensurable goals
terms.text: Goals that can be measured on one common scale. A game with victory points gives each kind of achievement a stated rate, such as four points per sheep.

terms.name: Commensuration
terms.text: Turning different qualities into numbers on one scale so they can be compared. It also decides what people attend to, since what is not turned into a number drops out.

terms.name: Common denominator
terms.text: In Boyd's use, what a group can agree on and do together. Games, folk dances and clubs that need co-operation depend on a right estimate of it.

terms.name: Common failure
terms.text: An everyday slip such as missing a deadline.

terms.name: Common ground
terms.text: The agreement every multiplayer game starts from: the players accept the same rules and value the same goal.

terms.name: Communal model
terms.text: A pattern of ethical thinking in which a player considers the wider game community and its stakeholders, and applies the spirit of the rules to new situations (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Communitas
terms.text: An idea from Victor Turner: a situation outside the usual social structure in which people are more equal than normal, and which renews the society it briefly leaves. The author applies it to parish ales and games.

terms.name: Communitas
terms.text: An anthropologist's word for an intense feeling of togetherness and solidarity among a group.

terms.name: Community card poker
terms.text: A form of poker in which players combine their own hidden cards with shared cards laid in the middle, as in Texas Hold'em.

terms.name: Community cards
terms.text: Cards in poker that all players can use to make their hand, as in Texas Hold 'Em.

terms.name: Community cards
terms.text: Cards placed face up in the middle that every player may use as part of his own hand.

terms.name: Community evolution game
terms.text: A game, such as Magic: The Gathering or Android: Netrunner, whose play depends on a player community that keeps changing which decks and strategies are common.

terms.name: Community of practice
terms.text: The shared activities around a game, such as FAQs, strategy guides, forums and other players, which Gee calls gaming as against the game itself (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Compensation
terms.text: A payment made to the side that held less powerful cards, equal to what the more powerful side could typically have expected to win, so that luck of the deal is reduced.

terms.name: Competition
terms.text: A contest between players, which Boyd treated as part of many games. In her account it has no jealousy or injustice, and winning is the final step in solving the game's problem.

terms.name: Competition
terms.text: From the Latin for seeking together. The book says it helps only while attention stays on the activity, not on beating the other person.

terms.name: Competition against the machine
terms.text: A player pits themselves against the challenge of the game itself, as in Desert Golfing.

terms.name: Competitive and collaborative interaction
terms.text: The paper scores interaction on two separate scales, one for competition and one for collaboration, instead of one scale running from one to the other. A game can be high on both, as in Tichu, where partners cooperate in order to compete against the other team.

terms.name: Competitive examination
terms.text: A test used to choose officials by ability and not by birth. Caillois counts it as agon spreading from games into the state.

terms.name: Competitive play
terms.text: Play in which some players win and others lose, and players or teams try to come out ahead of an opponent.

terms.name: Competitive-cooperative game
terms.text: A game where either one player wins or all lose, so some teamwork is needed to avoid shared failure.

terms.name: Compilation
terms.text: A volume made by gathering plays of separate origin and joining them. The N-Town manuscript is one: whole sequences existed on their own before the scribe joined them.

terms.name: Complete game prototype
terms.text: A prototype with every part in place, including menus, start screens, all actions and objects, playable from start to finish.

terms.name: Complete information
terms.text: A state where all players know the rules, but not everything about the current position.

terms.name: Completion
terms.text: The sense of a game being finished. DeKoven says winning ends a game but does not give completion.

terms.name: Complexity
terms.text: In this book, a self that is both differentiated and integrated. Flow makes the self more complex.

terms.name: Complexity rating
terms.text: The average score from 1 to 5 that BoardGameGeek users give for how hard a game is to understand. It takes in the rulebook, the play time, the technical skill needed and how much time goes on planning rather than acting.

terms.name: Compliance
terms.text: Going along with other people's pattern or game without adding anything of one's own. It looks like taking part, but the player is absent.

terms.name: Compliance (as a way of living)
terms.text: A relationship to the world where its details are noticed only as things to fit in with. The book links it to a sense that nothing matters.

terms.name: Component
terms.text: Any physical part of a game: board, token, card, die, miniature or rulebook. The book also treats the players as parts of the game while it is being played.

terms.name: Component-of-self
terms.text: Järvinen's name for a token that stands in for the player, so that the player's own skills and body become part of what the game has to take into account.

terms.name: Compound mechanics
terms.text: Sicart's name for a set of related mechanics that work together inside one limited mode of interaction. Driving is his example, made up of several mechanics that together model driving.

terms.name: Comprehensive and heterogeneous
terms.text: Two aims of a ranking. Comprehensive means it covers nearly every aspect of the thing, heterogeneous means it tries to compare things of very different kinds. The book says the two pull against each other.

terms.name: Compulsory capture
terms.text: A rule that a player has to take a piece when one is on offer. Fighting Serpents and Alquerque both use it.

terms.name: Compulsory capture
terms.text: A rule that a player has to take an enemy piece when one can be taken. Checkers keeps it by letting the opponent punish a missed capture.

terms.name: Compulsory capture
terms.text: A rule that a player who can capture has to do so and may not make another move.

terms.name: Compulsory capture
terms.text: A rule that a player who can capture has to do so. Versions differ on whether the player has to choose the capture that takes the most pieces.

terms.name: Computable morality system
terms.text: A meter or score in a game that measures a player's choices on a fixed scale running from one pole to another, such as 'good' to 'evil' and shows the result, whatever the player thinks of those choices (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Con game
terms.text: A fairground gambling game where the operator's skill or hidden advantage means the player is likely to lose. The player who keeps betting is called a sucker.

terms.name: Concealed set
terms.text: A set whose tiles were never shown, which scores higher in Ma-jong than the same set shown.

terms.name: Conceit
terms.text: An extended metaphor a game is about, such as medieval warfare in chess or science fiction war in Starcraft. It is close to theme or motif.

terms.name: Concentration (memory)
terms.text: A game in which all cards lie face down and players turn two at a time to find pairs, which rewards remembering where cards are.

terms.name: Concept
terms.text: An idea or theory about what could make a game. It becomes a design once structured so prototypes can be made from it.

terms.name: Concept ARG
terms.text: An alternate reality game spread as an idea and rule set that players adapt for their own lives. The author's 'SuperBetter' is one.

terms.name: Conception-perception gap
terms.text: The gap between a baby's early world of what it conceives and the later world of what it perceives. The book says a paradox over this gap has to be allowed to stand.

terms.name: Conceptual relationship model
terms.text: The authors' model of how the parts of game design relate. General patterns are instantiated through contextualization, which is broken down into mechanics, which developers turn into code. Players then read the finished code through the patterns they already know.

terms.name: Conceptualize
terms.text: The first step of the game design cycle: forming an idea for the game and its play experience.

terms.name: Concession
terms.text: Giving up a hand before it is played, paying a smaller loss than failing in play.

terms.name: Concourse of shipping
terms.text: In Shaturanga, three ships on adjacent squares joined by a fourth, which lets the player capture two enemy ships.

terms.name: Conditional necessity
terms.text: The idea that you cannot change your situation but can still choose to will it. The book says Ahab keeps the cards he was dealt and plays them actively, where Stubb only gives in.

terms.name: Condorcet cycle
terms.text: A result of pairwise majority votes where A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, though each voter has a consistent order.

terms.name: Confirmation bias
terms.text: Taking in information in a way that keeps existing beliefs whole and setting aside what conflicts with them.

terms.name: Confirmation trap
terms.text: The habit of seeking evidence for what one already believes and ignoring evidence against it (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Conflict (in Crawford's sense)
terms.text: A goal plus obstacles that answer back to the player. If the obstacles stay passive the challenge is a puzzle; if an intelligent agent blocks the player on purpose it is a game.

terms.name: Conflicting patterns
terms.text: One of the three kinds of relation a pattern can have, the other two being superior patterns and subpatterns. A conflicting pattern is one that is difficult to put into a game together with the given pattern.

terms.name: Confrontation
terms.text: A grown-up standing up, claiming a personal view, and meeting a young person's challenge without anger or revenge. The book sets it against explaining at length.

terms.name: Connection game
terms.text: A game in which players try to link two sides of the board with an unbroken chain of their pieces. Hex is the example.

terms.name: Consciousness
terms.text: Information that a person is aware of and can direct on purpose, such as sensations, feelings and thoughts. The book calls it intentionally ordered information.

terms.name: Consensus
terms.text: Agreement reached by members freely stating their differences. Boyd held this is the only way to it.

terms.name: Consensus decision-making
terms.text: Deciding as a whole team so that everyone buys in. It differs from simple agreement, where people may go along without consenting.

terms.name: Consequence
terms.text: One of Simkins's four design principles: the player, through the character, can change the game world by actions taken in the game (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Consequence-based thinking
terms.text: Weighing the effects of one's actions on oneself, other people, groups and the wider game community (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Consistency
terms.text: A game answering the same action in the same way each time, so players can learn from its feedback.

terms.name: Consolidated pattern template
terms.text: The paper's proposed set of required fields: name, keywords, description, related patterns and reference. Any other fields, such as an image, a confidence level or an example, are optional, so a pattern from any of the six collections can be fitted to it without losing information.

terms.name: Constitutive rules
terms.text: Rules that forbid the most efficient route to the pre-lusory goal and so create the game. Dribbling in basketball is one.

terms.name: Constraint
terms.text: A limit placed on what players can do with objects, other players or the playspace, put there to shape the play.

terms.name: Constructed situation
terms.text: The Situationists' name for a short moment of life set up on purpose, by changing a place and what people do in it, to break up boredom.

terms.name: Constructed, sealed, draft
terms.text: Three ways to build a Magic deck: from any allowed cards you own, from a few random packs you are given, or by picking cards in turn from a shared pool.

terms.name: Content multiplier
terms.text: A feature such as character classes, difficulty levels or customisation that lets existing content be played again in a new way.

terms.name: Content versus cohorts
terms.text: A way to change who a programme is for. It is open to anyone with a stated interest, such as a commitment to racial equity, and is not limited to members of one group.

terms.name: Content-based filtering
terms.text: A recommendation method that suggests items like those you liked in the past.

terms.name: Contest
terms.text: A puzzle that several agents race to solve, where only one can reach the solution first. Weightlifting, an arm-wrestling match and a hot-dog eating race are his examples.

terms.name: Contest
terms.text: One of two basic functions of play: a struggle for something, such as a prize or the first place.

terms.name: Context of play
terms.text: When, where and with whom a game is played, and on what device or in what setting.

terms.name: Contextualization layer
terms.text: The layer the authors add between patterns and mechanics. It holds scenarios that show how a pattern is meant to be used in a particular design and why that is a sound idea for the game.

terms.name: Continuous space
terms.text: A space where exact position matters, so a very small difference changes the outcome, as with where a rocket lands in Quake. Burgun notes every game still ends in some discrete condition.

terms.name: Contract
terms.text: The promise made at the end of an auction, such as winning a stated number of tricks. Meeting it or failing it decides how points are scored.

terms.name: Contract
terms.text: The final bid in Bridge, which the declarer's side has to fulfil to score.

terms.name: Contract (in Rummy)
terms.text: A set of sets that a player has to show in a first meld, which changes from deal to deal.

terms.name: Control feel
terms.text: How a player's input becomes action in the game, from the heft of a chess piece to the bounce of Q*bert. Physics games have a pronounced feel.

terms.name: Convention
terms.text: A general rule that holds across many games, such as taking turns or playing a game to its end. Breaking a convention usually costs more than breaking one rule of one game.

terms.name: Convention
terms.text: An agreed meaning for a call that has no natural meaning, such as a bid that asks the partner how many aces he holds.

terms.name: Convention (ethics)
terms.text: An agreed meaning for calls between partners, which is not unethical if the opponents are also told what it means.

terms.name: Converting
terms.text: Customising a miniature by joining parts from different figures, such as a head or a weapon bought separately.

terms.name: Cooldown
terms.text: A wait after using a move before it can be used again, or while the user is open to attack. Designers use it to balance a powerful move.

terms.name: Cooperative game
terms.text: A game where several players work together against the game system, which takes the role of opponent through cards or dice.

terms.name: Cooperative game
terms.text: A game that ends when all players have reached the goal or all have given up. Building a human pyramid is the example.

terms.name: Cooperative game
terms.text: A game where all players are on one team and win or lose together. The book treats it as a mix of a single-player game and a team game.

terms.name: Cooperative game
terms.text: A game where players win or lose together against the game itself. Pandemic is the example.

terms.name: Cooperative game
terms.text: A game where players share a goal and usually hold different complementary roles, such as Pandemic, Hanabi or Space Alert.

terms.name: Cooperative interaction
terms.text: How much team members can affect each other's performance. A swim relay team has little, a football pass has a lot.

terms.name: Cooperative play
terms.text: Play in which players work together to reach the game's goals.

terms.name: Cooperative play
terms.text: A way of playing a game with one list and no rivalry, offered for the sibling game From A to Z and the travelling scavenger hunt.

terms.name: Core game prototype
terms.text: A prototype that brings all the core parts of the game together, with rough placeholders for content and basic art and sound.

terms.name: Core mechanic
terms.text: The small central rule set at a game's heart, into which content is poured. Moving a piece in chess is Koster's example.

terms.name: Core mechanic
terms.text: The basic loop found in every game: the player makes a choice, the system responds, and this repeats (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Core mechanism
terms.text: The simple central action a game is built around, such as jumping, bidding, deduction, pushing or aiming. Everything else is meant to support it.

terms.name: Core mechanism and auxiliary mechanism
terms.text: A core mechanism is what the players activate directly, as their main action in the game. Auxiliary mechanisms are the others, which set the system in motion and help the game progress.

terms.name: Corn husking
terms.text: A community work event run as a contest, where neighbours race or compete at a chore. Barn raisings and stump clearings were treated the same way.

terms.name: Corner
terms.text: Buying up all of one commodity, such as wheat, so that anyone who needs it has to pay your price. In the novels the book discusses, a corner is the prize that shows total control of a market.

terms.name: Corpus Christi
terms.text: A church feast day on which the northern cities held processions and plays. York was asked in 1426 to move its play to the day after.

terms.name: Correct rejection
terms.text: Judging correctly what a thing is not for, such as seeing that a pillow will not work as a hammer.

terms.name: Corrective recategorization
terms.text: When a high-status person from a low-status group answers a remark such as you are not like the others by stating that they belong with the group.

terms.name: Corruption of a game
terms.text: What Caillois calls the loss of a game's closed frame when its pull spreads into ordinary life. Each of the four kinds corrupts in its own way.

terms.name: Cost (to the player)
terms.text: Anything that stands in the way of playing, including money, time to learn, time to play, space, injury risk and equipment.

terms.name: Couleur
terms.text: In Solo, the suit chosen as the premium suit, in which bids are worth twice as much.

terms.name: Counterfeit
terms.text: To act a sacred rite so closely that it could be taken for the real one. A 1576 order to Wakefield forbade plays in which the sacraments were counterfeited.

terms.name: Counting cards
terms.text: Cards that carry points when won in tricks, such as aces and tens, as against cards that carry none.

terms.name: Counting out
terms.text: Claiming during play that your captured cards already reach the winning score. A wrong claim loses the game.

terms.name: Counting tiles
terms.text: In Forty-two, tiles whose pips total 5 or 10, which score extra points when won in a trick.

terms.name: Counting-out rhyme
terms.text: A chanted verse children use to pick one of them by chance, such as who is "it". Caillois places it among chance games with little structure.

terms.name: Coup
terms.text: In Baccarat, one deal and the decision that settles the bets on it.

terms.name: Covenant
terms.text: In Puritan teaching, an agreement with obligations on both sides. Oriard notes that God was understood to bind himself to a covenant like a business contract, and compares it with the rules of a game.

terms.name: Covering
terms.text: Toning down a disfavoured part of your identity so as to fit the mainstream. The term comes from the law professor Kenji Yoshino.

terms.name: Cow
terms.text: In Pallanguli, a hole holding four seeds. It goes to the owner of the hole and is put at once into his store.

terms.name: Cowbell dance
terms.text: A small act that tells others you are not a threat, named after the bell a hiker wears in bear country. The example is a man whistling classical tunes on a night street so that strangers relax.

terms.name: Cowrie shells
terms.text: Small sea shells with a slit mouth, thrown as dice. The number of mouths facing up gives the score, as in Pachisi and Thaayam.

terms.name: Cows and leopards
terms.text: A south Asian game in which two leopards try to kill cows by jumping, and twenty-four cows try to trap the leopards.

terms.name: Crabs
terms.text: A throw of 2 or 3 at Hazard, which loses the stakes when the caster is throwing for the chance.

terms.name: Craps
terms.text: The American form of Hazard, reduced to simpler rules and odds, and played in a street or army camp with no equipment but dice.

terms.name: Crash
terms.text: In the word game Crash, a letter of a guess that sits in the same position as in the hidden target word.

terms.name: Creative apperception
terms.text: A way of seeing the outside world as something one meets and shapes, not only something one fits into. The book says it is what makes a person feel life is worth living.

terms.name: Creative work
terms.text: Play in which a player makes decisions that matter and feels pride in what was made, such as designing a house in The Sims.

terms.name: Credit rating
terms.text: A grade given to a company or government for how likely it is to repay debt. Credit scores are for individuals, credit ratings for firms and governments.

terms.name: Credit score
terms.text: A single number computed from a person's credit record to show how likely they are to repay a loan. The FICO score runs from 300 to 850.

terms.name: Crib
terms.text: In Domino Crib, a set of tiles put aside by the players and counted for the dealer.

terms.name: Crib
terms.text: In cribbage, the cards discarded by the players that score for the dealer.

terms.name: Crib
terms.text: In Cribbage, a hand of four cards made from two discards by each player. It scores for the dealer.

terms.name: Crib
terms.text: An extra hand in Cribbage made of cards put away by every player, which belongs to the dealer and is counted at the end.

terms.name: Crib
terms.text: In cribbage, an extra hand made from cards each player sets aside. It belongs to the dealer and is counted at the end of the hand.

terms.name: Cribbage board
terms.text: A board of holes and pegs used to keep score where points come in small quick amounts.

terms.name: Criss-cross
terms.text: A trap in a solitaire layout where two piles each hold a card the other needs, so neither can be freed.

terms.name: Criterion of comparability
terms.text: Jánossy's idea that the more two things differ in kind, the bigger the difference in size has to be before a ranking of them can be relied on.

terms.name: Criterion of comparison
terms.text: The property used to put items in order, such as height, price or population. A list needs a set of items and one of these.

terms.name: Critical ethics
terms.text: An ethics whose principles and traditions are open to debate and adjustment even while they are being applied (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Critical mass
terms.text: Enough players in one place and time for a game to work. Games like the Comfort of Strangers announce a time and area for this reason.

terms.name: Critical play
terms.text: Making or taking part in play that asks a question about some part of human life, such as what winning, losing or cooperating means. The question can be abstract or tied to a real event.

terms.name: Critical play method
terms.text: Flanagan's version of iterative design with added steps: set values goals, build rules that support them, allow many play styles, test with varied players, and check the values appear in play.

terms.name: Croquet
terms.text: A lawn game in which players hit balls through wickets and may knock an opponent's ball away. In Stowe's novel the characters use it to describe how a person manages friends and enemies.

terms.name: Croquet (stroke)
terms.text: In the game of croquet, placing your ball against the ball you hit and striking so that one or both move.

terms.name: Cross and circle game
terms.text: A race board made of a circle of marks with a cross of paths through it, like the Korean game Nyout. A piece landing on a cardinal mark can take a short cut along an arm of the cross.

terms.name: Cross-identification
terms.text: Putting oneself in another person's place and letting the other do the same. It first needs a self that stands on its own feet.

terms.name: Cross-ruff
terms.text: A run of plays in which two partners take turns winning tricks by trumping the suits the other leads.

terms.name: Crossword Squares
terms.text: A paper game in which every player draws a hidden 5x5 grid, each player in turn calls a letter, and all players write that letter in a square of their own grid. Words read across or down are scored.

terms.name: Croupier
terms.text: An employee of the house who runs or advises a banking game.

terms.name: Crowd game
terms.text: A game meant for very large face-to-face groups.

terms.name: Crowdsourcing
terms.text: Handing a large job to a big group of people, usually over the internet, so that many small contributions add up to something one organisation could not do alone. Wikipedia is the main example given.

terms.name: Crownhead
terms.text: The far back row of the board, where a draughtsman is crowned a king.

terms.name: Crowning
terms.text: In checkers, topping a piece that has reached the far row so that it can also move backward. It gives the piece a new power for the rest of the game.

terms.name: Crowning (king row)
terms.text: Reaching the far row, where a single man becomes a king and gains the power to move backward.

terms.name: Crunch time
terms.text: A stretch of long working hours in a game studio before a deadline. Wark describes it growing from eight hours a day to seven days a week.

terms.name: Cue ball
terms.text: The white ball in pool that the player hits with the cue to knock the other balls.

terms.name: Cueing
terms.text: Recognising from context which skill to use. For ethics it means noticing that a situation calls for ethical thought at all (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Cultural experience
terms.text: Experience of the inherited common pool of a people's art, tradition and ideas, and the pleasure of adding to it. The book counts it as a continuation of play.

terms.name: Cultural pool
terms.text: The common store of human tradition that people can add to and draw from, if they have somewhere to put what they find. Myths are an example.

terms.name: Cultural tool
terms.text: In Vygotsky's sense, something made by a culture, such as language, that a person uses to think. Khetrapal argues that games can act as such a tool for young children (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

terms.name: Culture as a game
terms.text: The author's comparison of a culture to a game, when its goals and rules fit its people so closely that they reach flow often. The Athenian city is his example.

terms.name: Cum decorem
terms.text: The opening words of Pope Innocent III's decree against ludi theatrales in churches. Later bishops copied or quoted it in their own statutes.

terms.name: Cup-and-ball
terms.text: A toy in which the player swings a ball on a string and catches it in a cup. Caillois uses it to show a game of solitary skill that turns into a contest.

terms.name: Cursus honorum
terms.text: The fixed ladder of offices a Roman official climbed. Caillois uses it as an example of agon entering administration.

terms.name: Cushion carom
terms.text: A billiards carom where the cue ball has to touch one or more cushions.

terms.name: Custodian capture
terms.text: Capturing an enemy piece by trapping it between two of your own pieces. The Zuni Stone Warriors game uses it.

terms.name: Cut
terms.text: Splitting the shuffled deck into two parts and swapping them, done by the player to the dealer's right.

terms.name: Cut scene
terms.text: A short film passage the game shows between periods of play, often as a reward for finishing a level.

terms.name: Cut-up
terms.text: Tzara's method of making a poem by cutting a newspaper article into single words, shaking them in a bag and copying them in the order they come out.

terms.name: Cutthroat
terms.text: Any game in which each person plays for himself, especially a three-player version of a four-player partnership game.

terms.name: Cycle (of plays)
terms.text: A series of biblical plays running from Creation to Doomsday. The author says full cycles were rare, and that Coventry and Chester before the sixteenth century probably covered only New Testament subjects.

terms.name: Cyclic dominance
terms.text: A set of items in which each one beats another in a loop, so that none can be placed at the top.

terms.name: Dame (common points)
terms.text: Empty points in Go that touch stones of both colours and belong to neither side.

terms.name: Damping factor
terms.text: In PageRank, the chance, set at 0.85, that a surfer follows a link instead of jumping to a random page. Changing it can change the order of results.

terms.name: Dance-off
terms.text: A team event in Top Secret Dance-Off where each member films a dance alone and the team scores a point for every member who submits one.

terms.name: Dancer's high
terms.text: The mix of excitement, flow and affection that comes from dancing with others, built from movement, touch, synchronised steps and a crowd moving together.

terms.name: Dangerous play
terms.text: Play that includes real physical risk. DeKoven says it is play only when every person involved knows the consequences and has chosen to be in it.

terms.name: Dark imagination
terms.text: Picturing the most severe outcomes of a scenario in detail before looking for ways through it.

terms.name: Data visualization (on a board)
terms.text: How a board shows numbers such as points, money or health: on tracks, cards, tokens or score pads. Each choice changes what players notice.

terms.name: Database
terms.text: In Wark's account, the stored collection of numbers and facts that a strategy game draws on. Playing it means moving through the collection, with no story to follow.

terms.name: Dead (card or hand)
terms.text: Out of play.

terms.name: Dead game sport
terms.text: A phrase from dime novels for a reckless adventurer ready to risk everything on one card and not troubled by the result. In Wharton's novel it is used as praise for Lily Bart.

terms.name: Dead hand
terms.text: In Mahjong, a hand that has not gone out when another player has, or one that is declared void after the wall runs out.

terms.name: Dead hand
terms.text: A hand that has been ruled out of winning the pot because of an error, though its owner may remain in the betting.

terms.name: Dead mass
terms.text: In Wei-ch'i, a group of pieces that will be captured whatever the owner does, so both players leave it and play elsewhere.

terms.name: Dead on a ball
terms.text: In croquet, having already roqueted a ball so that it cannot be hit again until the player has scored a wicket.

terms.name: Dead tile
terms.text: In Mahjong, a discarded tile that nobody claimed straight away, which cannot be used later.

terms.name: Dead wall
terms.text: In Ma-jong, the part of the wall kept aside, including the loose tiles, which cannot be drawn in ordinary play.

terms.name: Deadwood
terms.text: Cards in a Rummy-type hand that are not part of any set. Their total value is what a player tries to keep low.

terms.name: Deadwood
terms.text: In knock rummy and gin, the cards in a hand that are not part of any meld. Their total is what counts against a player.

terms.name: Dealer's choice
terms.text: A rule in poker where the dealer picks the variant for that hand. DeKoven adds that all players need to agree on the variant.

terms.name: Dealer's choice
terms.text: A way of playing in which each dealer, on his turn, picks which game is played and which cards are wild.

terms.name: Dealer's choice
terms.text: A way of playing in which each dealer picks the game variant for that hand.

terms.name: Dealer's choice
terms.text: A home rule that lets the dealer pick which poker game is played for that hand and which cards are wild.

terms.name: Dealer-critic system
terms.text: A market in which dealers and critics, rather than an academy's jury, build an artist's reputation through galleries and one-person shows.

terms.name: Debriefing
terms.text: The talk after a game where players review what they did and how it affected others. Balzac holds it back until the end, because comments during play change the game (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Debt of honour
terms.text: A bet that has to be paid at once and without argument, because refusing would ruin a gentleman's name. A Southern gentleman said a gambling debt was one, and a debt to a tradesman was not.

terms.name: Decathected
terms.text: Drained of its charge of feeling. The transitional object is not forgotten or mourned; it loses meaning as the same feeling spreads over play and culture.

terms.name: Decathlon (game events)
terms.text: A series of different games over one event, in which players earn points by finish position in each and the highest total wins.

terms.name: Decision-making
terms.text: The player's choosing of the next action from what the game state shows.

terms.name: Decisive randomness
terms.text: Randomness that makes the decision for the player. Rolling a die to move in Snakes and Ladders is the example, since the die settles where the piece goes.

terms.name: Deck-building game
terms.text: A game where each player starts with a small deck, buys cards to add to it, and draws from it in later turns.

terms.name: Declaration
terms.text: A statement of what the hidden dice show, which may be true or a bluff.

terms.name: Declaration
terms.text: Saying in advance which part of a split pot you are going for, such as high, low or both.

terms.name: Declaration (Bezique)
terms.text: A combination of cards shown face up on the table for points, the same as a meld in Pinochle.

terms.name: Declarer
terms.text: The player who made the highest bid and so has to carry out the promise. He plays his partner's cards as well as his own.

terms.name: Declarer
terms.text: In Bridge, the player who first named the trump suit of the final contract. This player plays both their own hand and the dummy.

terms.name: Declaring out
terms.text: Claiming at any moment that you have reached the target score, which ends play. If the claim is false, the opponent scores.

terms.name: Decorum
terms.text: Fitting conduct, in the Roman sense that John of Salisbury used: grave, restrained, and not drawing attention to oneself.

terms.name: Dedicated deck
terms.text: A deck made for one card game, such as Uno or Rook, as opposed to the standard fifty-two-card deck.

terms.name: Deductive game
terms.text: A game in which a player works out a hidden answer from replies to guesses, as in Jotto and MasterMind.

terms.name: Defense mechanisms
terms.text: The four habits used to protect a harmful habit from scrutiny: avoidance, denial, minimization and rationalization.

terms.name: Defer judgment
terms.text: A brainstorming rule: hold back from judging your own or others' ideas while ideas are being produced.

terms.name: Defining the win
terms.text: Agreeing in advance with the person who judges your work what counts as success. Carla Harris describes landing a hard-to-get client meeting that her manager did not count, because the manager only counted a sale.

terms.name: Degree centrality
terms.text: A score for a member of a network equal to how many direct links that member has. The members with the most links are called hubs or connectors.

terms.name: Delight
terms.text: Koster's word for the thrill of recognising a pattern and being surprised by it, as when the Statue of Liberty appears in Planet of the Apes. He says it rewards what is already learned and is not the same as fun.

terms.name: Demonstratio
terms.text: A Latin word used in records for a display, such as bear baits or ridings of Saint George, and not only for plays. A Shrewsbury entry shows why the book doubts it names a play.

terms.name: Den
terms.text: The goal square of each player in the Jungle game. Entering the enemy's den wins.

terms.name: Denial of separation
terms.text: Using a thing, such as string, to deny that two things are apart. It starts as communication and can turn into a fixed habit.

terms.name: Dependency
terms.text: A task that cannot be done until another task is finished.

terms.name: Dependent and independent variables
terms.text: Quantities in a model, some of which change because of the others. A player of Civilization III finds out which is which by trial and error.

terms.name: Depth
terms.text: The number of skill ranks that separate an average beginner from the world champion in a game of pure skill. The author gives chess as about 20 to 25 and Go and shogi as about 40.

terms.name: Descriptive and normative theory
terms.text: A descriptive theory asks how the world works. A normative theory asks how the world ought to work.

terms.name: Descriptive ethics
terms.text: In Simkins's account, ethics of practice: it asks what members of a culture tend to do and defends its claims by tradition (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Descriptive notation
terms.text: The older chess notation in which every square has two names, one for each player's view. It does not extend to variants or other games.

terms.name: Design
terms.text: A plan of an object made before it exists, showing its form, function or mechanics.

terms.name: Design document
terms.text: A record of the specific decisions made about a game, including its design values, that works as an overview for the whole team.

terms.name: Design ethnography
terms.text: A way of studying a design by taking part in its use and watching it over time. The researcher both joins in and observes from the edge (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

terms.name: Design goal (mission statement)
terms.text: The aim the designer sets at the start of a project, which later steps are checked against.

terms.name: Design language
terms.text: What a field of design uses to talk about its work. The paper, following Rheinfrank and Evenson, gives three parts: a collection of available design elements, information on how they can be used together, and descriptions of when elements or combinations suit or cause trouble.

terms.name: Design pattern
terms.text: In the sense taken from the architect Christopher Alexander, a description of a design problem followed by a description of its solution. The structure is plain: if problem A exists, solution B can be applied to solve it.

terms.name: Design stance
terms.text: Attending to the design of the game itself and how it supports many different playings, not to one session.

terms.name: Design values
terms.text: The qualities and characteristics a designer wants a game and its play to have, such as how it feels, who it is for and what it means.

terms.name: Designer board game
terms.text: A board game that carries the designer's name on the box, from the German-led revival since the 1990s.

terms.name: Designeritis
terms.text: Koster's name for the habit of designers who know so many games that they fall back on known solutions.

terms.name: Deuce
terms.text: A tied score near the end of a race to a set total, such as 10-10 in an 11-point game. In table tennis the order of serving changes after every point.

terms.name: Deviser
terms.text: The person who arranges a pageant, revel or play: its scenes, structures, costumes and materials. Richard Gibson devised court revels for forty years, and Gover Martin was deviser of the New Romney play of 1560.

terms.name: Diagnosis
terms.text: The authors' term for working out the underlying cause of what testers did or said, as a doctor does from reported symptoms.

terms.name: Diagonal move
terms.text: A move across the corners of squares, along a diagonal of the board.

terms.name: Dice rolling
terms.text: A die is used to bring randomness into the game.

terms.name: Dice simulation
terms.text: A way to get dice rolls in postal play from a number both players can look up, such as a stock index, by taking the remainder when divided by six.

terms.name: Dice sticks
terms.text: Flat sticks, round on one side and flat on the other, thrown in place of dice. The number of flat sides facing up gives the score, as in Zohn Ahl and Nyout.

terms.name: Dice-controlled movement
terms.text: A rule in which the number rolled decides which kind of piece may move, as in Modern Chaturanga, mixing chess-like strategy with chance.

terms.name: Diceless dice
terms.text: A system in which each player has a list of all possible rolls and crosses one off when he chooses it, so luck is replaced by planning.

terms.name: Dictionary odds
terms.text: A handicap in word games in which the less skilled player may consult the dictionary of record at any time during play.

terms.name: Dictionary of record
terms.text: The one word list a group agrees to check disputed words against. Serious Scrabble play depends on it.

terms.name: Diegetic component
terms.text: A part of a game that belongs to its imagined world, such as a miniature of a character, as against a part that only helps with running the game.

terms.name: Differentiation
terms.text: Movement towards being unique and separate, through gaining rarer skills.

terms.name: Difficulty (Burgun's sense)
terms.text: The size of the obstacle between a player and winning. He applies it to single-player systems, since in multiplayer games the opponent sets the difficulty.

terms.name: Digital
terms.text: Division of things by a line into either one side or the other, so that a ball is big enough or it is not.

terms.name: Digital game
terms.text: Burgun's name for a game played on a computer, kept apart from the wider phrase video game, which also covers puzzles and simulators.

terms.name: DIKW
terms.text: A model of how people make sense of things: data, then information, then knowledge, then wisdom.

terms.name: Dilemma
terms.text: A question built so that either answer works against the person answering. The opponent is forced to admit something not covered by the first point.

terms.name: Dilettante
terms.text: From the Latin for finding delight. Originally a person who enjoys an activity.

terms.name: Dimension (of a bid)
terms.text: The number of different things being weighed in a bid. An item with a single point of value gives an empty, one-sided contest.

terms.name: Dionysian society
terms.text: Caillois's name for societies held together by masks and possession, that is by mimicry and ilinx. He sets them against orderly societies built on rank and merit.

terms.name: Diorama
terms.text: A small scene of figures set in a landscape, built for display.

terms.name: Direct action
terms.text: An action where the player touches an object or the playspace straight away, such as hitting a pinball with a flipper.

terms.name: Direct and indirect capture
terms.text: In The Glass Bead Game, a last bead landing in a pit holding exactly one bead takes that bead if it is a gem, which is a direct capture. If it is a stone, the capturer takes any gem from the other side, which is an indirect capture.

terms.name: Direct reciprocity
terms.text: Helping someone because they helped you, or will.

terms.name: Directed graph
terms.text: A set of points joined by links that run one way only, as the chutes and ladders do on that board game. Distance on such a board is counted in moves, not in physical length.

terms.name: Directional heuristic
terms.text: A rule of thumb that tells a player what strategy or move to follow, such as control the centre squares.

terms.name: Disarming mechanisms
terms.text: Looks or habits that lower how threatening a powerful person seems to observers, such as code-switching or a baby-faced appearance.

terms.name: Discernment
terms.text: In Salen and Zimmerman's usage, whether a player can detect that a game action changed anything. A game with 'poor' discernment is hard to read (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Discovered life theme
terms.text: A life theme a person writes from their own experience. The opposite is an accepted theme, taken from a script written by others.

terms.name: Discovery work
terms.text: Play that rewards investigating unfamiliar places, objects and characters.

terms.name: Discrete space
terms.text: A space in which every point inside a region means the same to the rules. The hoop in basketball and each square of a chess board are examples.

terms.name: Discuss
terms.text: The playtest task of talking with testers afterwards, using open questions instead of yes-or-no or leading ones.

terms.name: Disguised lottery
terms.text: Caillois's name for a contest that looks like a test of talent or knowledge but works like a lottery, because few can win and the odds fall as the prize rises. A television quiz with "double or nothing" is his example.

terms.name: Disguising
terms.text: A court entertainment in which costumed figures arrive, perform a pageant and dance. Wolsey's household staged Schatew Vert as a banquet and pageant-disguising in 1522.

terms.name: Disillusionment
terms.text: The slow loss of that early feeling that the world answers wishes at once. The carer lessens her exact adaptation as the child becomes able to bear waiting and failure.

terms.name: Disinterested interestedness
terms.text: The author's description of aesthetic striving play: during the game the player is wholly interested in winning, while the reason for playing is to enjoy the struggle, whatever the result.

terms.name: Disinterestedness
terms.text: The quality of play that is not aimed at food, money or other material gain. A game is complete in itself.

terms.name: Display
terms.text: Playing to be seen, with the watchers' satisfaction counted ahead of the players' own. DeKoven sets it against play.

terms.name: Display
terms.text: Showing something out of the ordinary to an audience to win admiration, as a peacock does with its tail. With a dance added it becomes a performance.

terms.name: Disposable end
terms.text: A goal taken up for a short time and put down without harm to the player's lasting values. Collecting green tokens in one board game is the plainest case.

terms.name: Disruption
terms.text: A creative act that shifts the logic a field runs on; the book places it between subversion and intervention.

terms.name: Disruption
terms.text: In Travis's usage, interference from outside a mimesis, such as a play, film or game, that disturbs how it works and puts it in question (chapter by Roger Travis).

terms.name: Dissociation
terms.text: A state where part of a person carries on separately, for example someone who sits still and in her head paints a picture. The watcher sees nothing happen.

terms.name: Distributed computing
terms.text: Linking many separate computers over the internet so that each works on a small piece of one large calculation. Folding@home works this way.

terms.name: Distribution voting
terms.text: Giving each person a fixed number of votes, such as five, to spread over ideas as they wish.

terms.name: Diversion
terms.text: In Thoreau's use, play that only restores the energy that work used up. He kept the word apart from amusement.

terms.name: Divesting game
terms.text: A game in which the aim is to get rid of all your cards, or to avoid being the last with cards.

terms.name: Divination
terms.text: The practice of reading the future from cards, stars or omens. Caillois says it grows from the same attitude as games of chance.

terms.name: Divination
terms.text: The old practice of reading the future from objects such as bones, sticks or sacrificed birds. The book treats games of chance as its secular descendant.

terms.name: Divination
terms.text: Seeking guidance about the future by reading chance results; the book links it to the origin of games of chance and of Go.

terms.name: Dix
terms.text: The Nine of trumps in Pinochle. Its holder may swap it for the turned-up trump card and score 10 points.

terms.name: Dix
terms.text: The lowest trump (a nine or seven depending on the game). Its holder may swap it for the face-up trump card and score a few points.

terms.name: Dix
terms.text: In Pinochle, the nine of trumps. Swapping it for the turned-up trump card scores 10 points.

terms.name: DKP
terms.text: Dragon kill points, a guild's own point system for deciding which member gets valuable items, made by guilds and not by the game.

terms.name: Dodgeball
terms.text: A ball game that Boyd described being played with no sides chosen, at quick tempo and with players changing roles often.

terms.name: Dogleg
terms.text: A hole whose route bends round an obstacle, such as the corner of a house in Kickball Golf.

terms.name: Dogmatic ethics
terms.text: An ethics whose principles or traditions are not questioned, so debate is about what they mean (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Doing the dance
terms.text: Watching and adjusting your own behaviour, dress and speech in a setting where others wrote the rules, so that the people there feel at ease.

terms.name: Dolphin, ostrich and shark
terms.text: The author's three types for how a person relates to racial inequality: the dolphin holds fair values but does not change the system, the ostrich looks away to follow self-interest, and the shark wants a ladder with themselves on top.

terms.name: Domains
terms.text: The eight broad groups BoardGameGeek places games in: abstract, children's, customisable, family, party, strategy, thematic and war games. The paper uses them to see which mechanics turn up in which kinds of game.

terms.name: Dominance hierarchy
terms.text: A ranking inside a group of animals based on who wins encounters. It is found in insects, fish, birds and primates.

terms.name: Dominance strategy
terms.text: Reaching high rank by size, strength and the power to frighten others, so that the group accepts rank only because it is forced.

terms.name: Dominated strategy
terms.text: A choice that pays less than another for a player whatever the opponent does, so a clever player never takes it.

terms.name: Domineering
terms.text: A game where one player places dominoes vertically and the other horizontally on a grid, and whoever cannot move loses.

terms.name: Domino (tile)
terms.text: A tile, once ivory or bone, divided into two halves, each blank or with one to six spots. A full set is 28 tiles.

terms.name: Domino!
terms.text: The call a player makes after playing their last tile, which ends the hand.

terms.name: Dominoes
terms.text: A row of tiles stood on end so that pushing the first topples each of the rest in turn. In a late Twain story it pictures a life in which the first event settles everything after it.

terms.name: Dots-and-boxes
terms.text: A children's game in which players join neighbouring dots and take another turn whenever they complete a square.

terms.name: Double
terms.text: A call that raises the scoring value of an opponent's bid, so a failure costs more and a success pays more.

terms.name: Double airfield
terms.text: Two separate empty points inside a Wei-ch'i group. An enemy piece placed on either is captured at once, so the group stays safe.

terms.name: Double down
terms.text: Doubling a bet in return for taking just one more card.

terms.name: Double dribble
terms.text: In basketball, dribbling with both hands at once or starting to dribble again after stopping. It is a violation.

terms.name: Double dummy
terms.text: Playing with all hands face up.

terms.name: Double elimination
terms.text: A tournament format where a player is out after losing two matches.

terms.name: Double header
terms.text: In the Bergen game, a play that makes both ends of the line show the same number. A triple header makes three ends match.

terms.name: Double in / double out
terms.text: In darts, hitting the double ring to start scoring, and hitting a double that takes the score exactly to zero to finish.

terms.name: Double jeopardy
terms.text: The extra penalty that Black women leaders were found to receive for mistakes, because they match neither the White nor the male picture of a leader.

terms.name: Double-header
terms.text: In dominoes, a double placed at the open end of the row. A second double added at the other end makes a triple-header.

terms.name: Double-in
terms.text: A darts rule that a player has to hit a double before any score counts.

terms.name: Double-nine set
terms.text: A larger domino set used for games such as Matador, Cyprus and Tiddle-a-Wink.

terms.name: Double-out
terms.text: A darts rule that the last dart has to land in the double ring and bring the score to exactly zero.

terms.name: Double-six set
terms.text: The standard Western domino set of twenty-eight tiles, running from blank-blank to six-six.

terms.name: Doubled pawn
terms.text: Two pawns of the same side standing on the same file in chess.

terms.name: Doubles
terms.text: Rolling the same number on both dice. In backgammon the player then plays that number four times instead of twice.

terms.name: Doubles (dice)
terms.text: Two dice showing the same number. In backgammon the player moves that number four times instead of twice.

terms.name: Doublet
terms.text: A roll of two dice showing the same number, which is played four times.

terms.name: Doublet (domino)
terms.text: A domino with the same number at both ends.

terms.name: Doubleton
terms.text: A hand holding just two cards of a suit.

terms.name: Doubling combinations
terms.text: Hands in Mahjong that double the total points, such as holding all one suit or three Dragons.

terms.name: Doubling cube
terms.text: The backgammon device by which a player offers to double the stake in mid-game. The opponent either accepts and plays on at the higher stake, or refuses and loses the game.

terms.name: Doubling cube
terms.text: A backgammon device that lets a player who feels they are winning offer to double the stakes, which the other may refuse by conceding.

terms.name: Doubling cube
terms.text: A marker showing the current stake, which a player may offer to double. The other player either accepts or resigns the game.

terms.name: Doubling cube
terms.text: A die-sized cube marked 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 used in backgammon. A player offers it to double the stakes, and the opponent accepts or loses the game at the old stake.

terms.name: Doubling cube
terms.text: A die marked 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 that players use to raise the stakes in the middle of a game. The opponent has to accept the new stake or resign on the spot.

terms.name: Doubling down
terms.text: In blackjack, doubling the bet after seeing the first two cards, and taking only one more card.

terms.name: Doubling up
terms.text: Placing two pieces of one colour on one space. In some games this makes them a unit that is safe or can only be attacked by an equal or larger group.

terms.name: Down
terms.text: One try by the attacking team in touch football. After the first, a team has three more downs to reach the goal line before giving up the ball.

terms.name: Downtime
terms.text: Time when a player is not actively playing, for example waiting for a turn. Thinking during your own turn does not count.

terms.name: Downward comparison
terms.text: Comparing yourself with someone who is behind you. It can bring gratitude or a feeling of being above them.

terms.name: Drama (as the author uses it)
terms.text: An acted script that holds, or once held, a whole narrative, so that it is both a written text and a performance. The author uses it to tell a drama apart from a social event.

terms.name: Dramatic mode
terms.text: In medieval rhetoric, one of three ways of telling a story: the poet never speaks in his own voice and only the characters speak. It describes how a text is arranged, not whether anyone acts it out.

terms.name: Draughtsman
terms.text: A piece in draughts. It moves diagonally forwards one square and becomes a king on reaching the far side.

terms.name: Draw
terms.text: An outcome where the rules name no winner. Chess is the classic case, and some games add rules such as a penalty shootout to prevent it.

terms.name: Draw
terms.text: A game that ends with no winner. Chess lists several causes, among them stalemate, repeated moves and too few pieces to force a win.

terms.name: Draw
terms.text: In Poker, discarding some cards and taking the same number from the pack.

terms.name: Draw
terms.text: An exchange in which a player discards some cards and takes the same number of new ones from the pack.

terms.name: Draw
terms.text: A result in which neither player wins. A journalist quoted by Oriard calls flirtation a game played on top of the table between evenly matched players that ends in a draw.

terms.name: Draw game
terms.text: A domino game in which a player who cannot play has to draw from the boneyard until he can.

terms.name: Draw game and block game
terms.text: Two forms of dominoes. In the draw game a player who cannot play takes tiles from the boneyard. In the block game the player simply passes.

terms.name: Drawishness
terms.text: The tendency of a game to end in a tie. The author gives it as one reason Anglo-American Checkers is less interesting than other forms.

terms.name: Dressing
terms.text: The art, story, sound and setting wrapped around a game's rules. Koster says players see through it to the mechanics, but it still shapes how the game feels.

terms.name: Dressing up
terms.text: Wearing a mask or costume to play another being. Huizinga treats it as the clearest sign that play is set apart from ordinary life.

terms.name: Dromenon
terms.text: A Greek word for a ritual act, "something acted". It names a rite performed as a contest or show.

terms.name: Drop rule
terms.text: A shogi rule letting a captured piece be placed back on the board on the capturer's side.

terms.name: Drop rule
terms.text: In shogi, the rule that a captured piece joins the capturer's army and can be put back on any vacant square on a later turn.

terms.name: Dual-track point system
terms.text: A scoring design with one track that decides who wins and another that can be spent for power in the game, such as victory points and money in European boardgames.

terms.name: Duck
terms.text: To play a low card on purpose, giving up a trick you could have won.

terms.name: Dummy
terms.text: In bridge, the open hand of the winning bidder's partner, played by the declarer, which reduces hidden information.

terms.name: Dummy
terms.text: An extra hand dealt face down to the middle of the table that a player may take in place of their own.

terms.name: Dummy
terms.text: A hand laid face up on the table so everyone sees it. One player plays its cards while its owner takes no part in the choices.

terms.name: Dummy
terms.text: In bridge, the declarer's partner, whose cards are laid face up on the table and played by the declarer.

terms.name: Dummy
terms.text: In Bridge, the declarer's partner, who lays their hand face up and takes no further decisions.

terms.name: Dunbar's number
terms.text: The estimate by Robin Dunbar that a person can keep about 150 stable relationships, between 100 and 200.

terms.name: Dungeon Master
terms.text: The referee in Dungeons & Dragons who handles hidden information and rules decisions.

terms.name: Dungeon Master
terms.text: In Dungeons and Dragons, the player who describes the world and referees. The book also calls the role storyteller.

terms.name: Dunning-Kruger effect
terms.text: The finding that people with little knowledge of a task rate their own skill too highly, while skilled people tend to rate themselves lower.

terms.name: Duplicate
terms.text: A format in which several players or teams play the same deal or the same dice rolls and are compared by results, so that skill is separated from luck.

terms.name: Duplicate Bridge
terms.text: A way of playing Bridge in which different tables hold the same cards and compare the scores made on them.

terms.name: Duplicate cards
terms.text: Two identical cards in a pack. The one played first ranks higher when both fall in a trick.

terms.name: Dux
terms.text: In the suggested rules for Ludus Latrunculorum, a leader piece that can jump over an enemy piece to break into a defensive position.

terms.name: Dynamic difficulty adjustment
terms.text: A feature where the game changes its difficulty to suit the player as they go. Burgun says it rewards careless play and punishes skilled play.

terms.name: Dynamic difficulty adjustment
terms.text: A game quietly helping the player when behind and helping the computer when the player is ahead.

terms.name: Dynamics
terms.text: The shifting relationships between elements in a system, and the outcomes when players and objects interact in a game.

terms.name: Débat
terms.text: A staged argument between two sides, with a judge. The author finds it in court disguisings such as the Hertford mumming, where husbands and wives state their cases and the king decides.

terms.name: Dérive
terms.text: A drift: an unplanned walk through a city, taken to find new views of familiar streets.

terms.name: Earthball
terms.text: A six-foot ball painted like a globe, used in New Games events for games with large crowds.

terms.name: Ease of spirit
terms.text: Charles Blow's phrase for the calm of growing up where you are welcome, which the author links to his boyhood neighbourhood.

terms.name: East Wind
terms.text: The first dealer in Mahjong, who is the banker and chooses seats. Other players are named South, West and North by their seat.

terms.name: Easterlin paradox
terms.text: The claim that richer people within a country are happier than poorer ones, but richer countries are not clearly happier than poorer ones.

terms.name: Echo chamber
terms.text: A set of sources, often chosen by filters, that returns a person's own beliefs back to them and leaves out surprising news.

terms.name: Echo chamber
terms.text: A closed network where the same news passes round and round and goes no further. In the story, this is what happened to the news William Dawes carried.

terms.name: Ecosystems thinking
terms.text: Seeing a situation as a web of linked parts, and expecting a change in one part to reach others in surprising ways.

terms.name: Edutainment
terms.text: A label from the 1980s and 1990s for learning software that dropped lessons into popular game formats without checking that they fit the story, such as sums inside a Space Invaders clone (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Effective elimination
terms.text: Having a chance of winning that is very small but not zero, so the player feels out of it.

terms.name: Ego crutch
terms.text: Luck giving players something to blame for losses.

terms.name: Egocentric bias
terms.text: Overestimating your own share in a joint effort. Students in four-person groups reported contributions that added up to 130 to 170 percent.

terms.name: Eldest hand
terms.text: The player sitting to the left of the dealer, who normally plays or bids first.

terms.name: Eldest hand
terms.text: The player sitting to the dealer's left, who leads first.

terms.name: Elegance
terms.text: Doing a lot with a little. Burgun lists four marks of a sound design: useful, beautiful, easy to learn and efficient, and says elegance covers all four.

terms.name: Elimination
terms.text: A rule that a player who errs or loses a round leaves the game. The last player left wins.

terms.name: Elimination game
terms.text: A game where players who lose drop out and the rest play on, as in dodgeball, Simon says and musical chairs. Eliminated players wait on the side.

terms.name: Elo rating
terms.text: A rating system where the difference between two players' numbers gives the chance of each winning.

terms.name: Elo rating
terms.text: A number for each chess player that changes after every game. A win over a higher-rated player moves it more than a win over a lower-rated one.

terms.name: Emcee
terms.text: A person who runs a game without playing it, collecting the words and counting the clues.

terms.name: Emergence
terms.text: Patterns that arise from simple rules without being planned. Koster notes they often make games easier by opening loopholes.

terms.name: Emergensight
terms.text: The ability to work calmly in a large, disordered collaboration, filtering noise and watching for chances nobody planned.

terms.name: Emergent complexity
terms.text: The patterns and problems that appear only when people play the rules. Go has simpler rules than chess but more emergent complexity.

terms.name: Emergent play
terms.text: Play that arises when players bring their own strategies and read the rules in ways the designers did not plan (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Emotional content
terms.text: Chris Crawford's phrase: a game gives a simplified, deliberate picture of emotional reality.

terms.name: Emperor
terms.text: In medieval Tai Shogi and Emperor King Chess, a piece that can jump to any square on the board, with a ban on landing on an enemy emperor that is defended.

terms.name: Employee resource group
terms.text: A group inside a company where staff from a shared background meet for support, mentoring and a say. It is also called an affinity group.

terms.name: Emulation
terms.text: Doing an act in response to seeing another do it, with the aim of equalling or beating it. Boyd said it works when the model is playful and within the learner's reach, and differs from copying.

terms.name: En passant
terms.text: A chess capture. When a pawn moves two squares past an enemy pawn, that enemy pawn may take it as if it had moved one square, but only on the very next move.

terms.name: En passant
terms.text: A pawn capture made at once after an opposing pawn moves two squares forward and passes it, taking it as if it had moved one square.

terms.name: En passant
terms.text: A chess capture open for one move only. A pawn that has just moved two squares can be taken as if it had moved one.

terms.name: En prise
terms.text: Said of a piece that can be captured by the opponent on the next move.

terms.name: En prise
terms.text: A French chess phrase for a piece that is exposed to capture.

terms.name: Enabler
terms.text: The author's name for a player who keeps the existing system in place and seeks to fit in with the dominant group, often by denying that the problem exists.

terms.name: Endgame
terms.text: The stage at the highest level, where the hardest opponents and tasks are found.

terms.name: Ending condition
terms.text: An event that ends the game, such as the tiles running out or nine innings passing, after which the winner is worked out.

terms.name: Endless game
terms.text: A game with no boundary or end point that can be played anywhere and pulls others in. In Echo, a player repeats whatever the other says, and words cannot stop it.

terms.name: Endless runner
terms.text: A single-player game where a character keeps running and the player jumps obstacles until failing, with the score set by distance. Canabalt is the example.

terms.name: Endogenously meaningful
terms.text: Having an effect inside the game's own rules. Throwing a ball out of bounds forward, left or back counts as one possibility because all three mean the same thing in football.

terms.name: Engagement economy
terms.text: A setting in which projects compete for people's mental effort and active contribution, not only for their attention.

terms.name: Enjoyment
terms.text: A rewarding feeling that comes when a person goes beyond what they were already able to do and learns something new. It needs full attention and leaves the person changed.

terms.name: Enjoyment as duty
terms.text: A mid-century attitude that enjoying yourself is expected of everyone, so that enjoyment becomes an obligation. Wolfenstein gave it a name in 1955 that the book quotes.

terms.name: Entanglement
terms.text: The idea that players, pieces, rules and surroundings form one mixed-up whole in play, and cannot be pulled apart cleanly.

terms.name: Entering
terms.text: Putting a piece back on the board after it was hit. A backgammon player with a piece on the bar can make no other move first.

terms.name: Entering (Emergo)
terms.text: Placing a checker on a vacant cell at the start of the game. Entering takes precedence over moving when no capture is available.

terms.name: Entering a piece
terms.text: Bringing a piece from off the board onto the track. Often it needs a particular throw, such as a 1 in Thaayam or a 5 in the Sumerian game.

terms.name: Entry
terms.text: A card that lets a player win a trick and so gain the lead.

terms.name: Environmental design values
terms.text: One of Holm's kinds: values about the environment and sustainability.

terms.name: Ephemera
terms.text: Things made for the moment and not kept. Printers treated plays and royal entries this way, so most texts were never printed.

terms.name: Epic
terms.text: Something far beyond the ordinary in size, scale and intensity, of heroic proportions. The book uses it for games' stories, spaces and projects.

terms.name: Epic context for action
terms.text: A shared story that connects each player's play to a bigger mission.

terms.name: Epic environment
terms.text: A space whose scale provokes awe. A built one is the result of design and many people's work, like a cathedral or a game world.

terms.name: Epic project
terms.text: A cooperative effort by many players at large scale over months or years, such as writing a wiki.

terms.name: Epic win
terms.text: A big, usually surprising success, such as an underdog victory or a result the player did not think possible. It changes what the player expects from the next attempt.

terms.name: Epideixis
terms.text: The Greek word for a sophist's public performance of skill or knowledge.

terms.name: Epistemic game
terms.text: A game, in Shaffer's sense, whose rules teach the skills, knowledge, identities and values of a professional practice such as policing or medicine (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Equilibrium point
terms.text: A pair of strategies where neither player can gain more by changing alone.

terms.name: Erdős number
terms.text: The number of steps of co-authorship between a mathematician and Paul Erdős. His 512 direct co-authors have number 1, their co-authors number 2.

terms.name: Ergodic
terms.text: A word from Espen Aarseth for media where the order of what is shown changes according to the player's actions (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Essential game
terms.text: The simple abstract game a larger game is a disguised version of, such as a chip-taking game.

terms.name: Ethical cognitive dissonance
terms.text: A design method that puts the rules and the meaning of a game in conflict on purpose, so the player has to work out for themselves what their actions mean (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Ethical drift
terms.text: A slide from fair to unfair conduct in small steps, with each step excused by the last. Balzac saw it compressed into the span of a single game (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Ethical gameplay
terms.text: The moral experience of a game in which what the rules reward conflicts with what the story and setting suggest those actions mean (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Ethics
terms.text: A culture's system of choices and moral judgments thought to lead to the life of a 'good' person, and also the way an individual makes choices by their own idea of how to be a 'good' person.

terms.name: Euchred
terms.text: In Euchre, failing to win three tricks after naming trump. The other side scores two points.

terms.name: Euchred
terms.text: Failing, as the making side, to win a majority of tricks, which gives the opponents points.

terms.name: Euchred
terms.text: In Euchre, being the maker's side and failing to win three tricks. The other side then scores 2 points.

terms.name: Eurogame
terms.text: A board game, mostly from Germany, with a light theme such as farming or trade, little direct conflict and little luck.

terms.name: Eurogame
terms.text: A style of hobby board game in which the rules and mechanics stay visible and players are invited to try different strategies on each replay.

terms.name: Eustress
terms.text: Stress felt as a chosen challenge, with confidence that it can be met. The body reacts as it does to harmful stress, but the person feels motivated instead of afraid.

terms.name: Evaluate
terms.text: The step of reviewing playtest results to understand and strengthen the design.

terms.name: Events of Instruction
terms.text: Robert Gagne's sequence for teaching media: gain attention, state the objectives, then give chances to practise skills, among other steps (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Evolutionary thesis
terms.text: The story that medieval drama developed in steps from church liturgy to cycles to moralities to Elizabethan theatre. The book calls it still present in histories, courses and textbooks.

terms.name: Exact throw
terms.text: A throw that matches the number of spaces needed to bring a piece home or off the board. Anything higher is not allowed, so a piece may wait several turns.

terms.name: Exaggeration
terms.text: Making an idea as huge as possible, as a child says a carrot is as big as God. Huizinga calls it a typical play-function, found in myth and poetry too.

terms.name: The exchange
terms.text: In chess, winning or losing a rook in return for a minor piece.

terms.name: Execution barrier
terms.text: A physical skill, such as speed or exact button timing, that stands between a player's choice and its result. Burgun says it turns a game toward a contest.

terms.name: Executive attention
terms.text: Attention a person chooses to give, such as reading a sign or checking a health meter. Also called voluntary attention.

terms.name: Exemplum
terms.text: A short story or action offered as a pattern for the audience. Mannyng turns Christ's prayer in the garden into an exemplum for all Christians.

terms.name: Exhaustible content
terms.text: Game material that has little appeal once a player has experienced it, such as a crossword or the puzzles of Myst.

terms.name: Exhilaration
terms.text: A lift of feeling that Boyd said play needs in order to be play. It differs from plain excitement.

terms.name: Exit, voice and loyalty
terms.text: Albert Hirschman's three responses to a failing organisation: leave, speak up, or stay out of attachment. Exit is described as a last resort after voice has failed.

terms.name: Exotelic
terms.text: Describes an activity done only for outside reasons, such as money or approval. Most activities mix this with the autotelic kind.

terms.name: Exotic Chess
terms.text: A family of chess variants where checkers placed under pieces stand for special powers, each usable once in the game.

terms.name: Expanded deck
terms.text: Two or more decks mixed together to allow more players or bigger hands.

terms.name: Expected score
terms.text: In the Elo system, the chance of winning that the rating gap between two players predicts before the game. A 100-point gap predicts 64 percent for the higher player.

terms.name: Experience points
terms.text: Points a player earns for completing tasks, which add up to raise the level of their character.

terms.name: Experience Sampling Method
terms.text: A research method in which people carry a pager that goes off at random times in the day. Each time, they write down what they are doing and how they feel.

terms.name: Experience sampling method
terms.text: A research method that interrupts people at random times and asks what they are doing and how they feel.

terms.name: Experience-based play
terms.text: Play built around exploring, unfolding a story or being together, instead of beating a skill challenge.

terms.name: Experienced player playtest
terms.text: A test where players use a prototype over days or weeks so the team sees how skill and strategy develop and how changes affect them.

terms.name: Experiential, constructive, deconstructive
terms.text: Koster's three roles: taking in an experience, making it, or taking it apart to see how it works. Playing, modding and hacking a game fall in each.

terms.name: Experiments in living
terms.text: John Stuart Mill's term for small trials of other ways of life. The author calls games a quick rough-sketch version.

terms.name: Expertise exchange
terms.text: A shared profile page where students list what they do most skilfully, so teammates can find the right person.

terms.name: Explicit and implicit data
terms.text: Explicit data is what a person states, such as a thumbs-up. Implicit data is what their behaviour shows, such as watching a film twice in a week.

terms.name: Explicit costing system
terms.text: A rule making a player pay an in-game price to use an object, such as mana for a card or gold for a unit, so more powerful objects can cost more.

terms.name: Explicit ending
terms.text: A point where a game is finished, as in puzzles and single-player RPGs. It pushes against replay.

terms.name: Explicit rules
terms.text: Rules given in the instructions or score, such as "Make a sandwich" or "Follow a line".

terms.name: Explicit subgame
terms.text: A distinct game with its own rules inside a larger game, like the tactical map battle in Titan or the minigames in Mario Party.

terms.name: Exploit
terms.text: In a computer game, something the code lets you do that the designers did not intend, such as a button sequence that produces a million gold pieces.

terms.name: Exploit
terms.text: Using a loophole that sits inside the rules to skip the challenge a designer meant. Koster says players call it legal because the game allows it.

terms.name: Exploit
terms.text: A way in the rules that lets a player gain an advantage in an unintended way, which playtests often reveal.

terms.name: Exploration
