terms.text: In Burgun's use, the real activity of every game: testing the limits of a possibility space. It is not only a map hidden under fog.

terms.name: Explorer
terms.text: In Bartle's list, a player who wants to learn the full breadth of a game's space of possibility.

terms.name: Explosion (in dice)
terms.text: In Chaos in the Old World, a six on the die that grants an extra free attack.

terms.name: Exponential scoring
terms.text: A scale in which each extra unit of effort doubles the points. In the Big Boggle variation each added letter doubles a word's value.

terms.name: Expositor
terms.text: A figure who steps out of the action to explain what it means. In the Chester Abraham he closes each of three episodes with the meaning.

terms.name: Expressive play
terms.text: Play that expresses a feeling or an idea, whether the designer's or the player's.

terms.name: Expressive skills
terms.text: Skills that put inner experience into outward form, such as singing, dancing or telling a joke. They are set against instrumental skills.

terms.name: Expulsion
terms.text: In Eleusis, removal of a player from a round after an incorrect play once the layout has grown past a set length.

terms.name: Exquisite corpse (cadavre exquis)
terms.text: A Surrealist group word game in which each person adds a part of a sentence, knowing only the last contribution or following an agreed pattern such as adjective, noun, adverb, verb.

terms.name: Extended mind
terms.text: The thesis, from Clark and Chalmers, that thinking uses tools outside the skull, such as pen and paper or a screen. The authors apply it to games as aids for thinking about values (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: External playtest
terms.text: A test with people outside the team, such as friends, other designers or the target audience.

terms.name: Externalization
terms.text: A technique from narrative therapy that puts a problem outside the person. In a game, the character failed or erred, not the player, so feedback feels less like an attack (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Extinction
terms.text: A win condition in Extinction Chess. A player loses when the last piece of any one kind, such as the last knight or the queen, is captured.

terms.name: Extopia
terms.text: Wark's word for a state in which gamer and game cease to be separate terms and the limits of any place disappear.

terms.name: Extra turn
terms.text: A right to throw again, given for a high throw, a capture or landing on a marked point. It lets a player's luck run on within one turn.

terms.name: Extrinsic play
terms.text: Play for something it brings, such as fitness, fame or money. A professional sprinter and a person running for mental health both play this way.

terms.name: Extrinsic reward
terms.text: A reward from outside the activity, such as money, goods, status or praise.

terms.name: Eye
terms.text: A single empty point enclosed by stones of one colour. A group with two separate eyes cannot be captured.

terms.name: Eye
terms.text: In Go, an empty point surrounded by one player's stones. A group with two separate eyes cannot be captured.

terms.name: Facilitating environment
terms.text: The surroundings and people that make growth possible, studied by the book in human terms for a dependent child.

terms.name: Fade
terms.text: In Craps, to cover part of the shooter's bet by putting in an equal amount.

terms.name: Failure
terms.text: Falling short of an aim in a game. Juul sorts it by where players place the blame: themselves, the game or circumstances.

terms.name: Fair and foul
terms.text: The parts of a field where a hit ball counts and where it does not. Over-the-Line marks them with poles, shirts or parked cars.

terms.name: Fair play
terms.text: The shared idea that opponents meet on equal terms and win without cheating. Oriard shows that people in the same culture meant different things by it.

terms.name: Fair play system
terms.text: A real settlement in western Pennsylvania from 1769 to 1784 where elected fair play men settled disputes by what the community agreed was fair.

terms.name: Fair witness
terms.text: A person outside the contest, such as an umpire or referee, who is given power to stop the game and judge. Players hand over this duty so that they can play fully.

terms.name: Fairground
terms.text: A marked-off space of crowds, lights and machines where all four kinds of play sit together, with dizziness the main one.

terms.name: Fairness
terms.text: A game's promise that all players follow the same rules and have the same chance to win. Young children use the word to mean that they get the prize.

terms.name: Fairy chess
terms.text: Chess problems and games that use unorthodox pieces or rules.

terms.name: Fall on the grenade
terms.text: Making a sacrifice to stop the leader from winning. Players may argue that someone else ought to do it, or wait so that another player is forced to.

terms.name: False affordance
terms.text: A wrong guess about what a thing can do, such as a door in a 3D game that will not open.

terms.name: False choice
terms.text: A choice that only looks like one because one option is clearly ahead, as in "do X or die". Burgun says players see through it.

terms.name: False eye
terms.text: An empty point that looks like an eye but can be filled by the opponent, so it does not keep the group alive.

terms.name: Falsecard
terms.text: An intentionally misleading play, made to give the opponents wrong information.

terms.name: Familiarity
terms.text: How well players know a game and each other. It lets people trust each other's moves, and a variation of a known game can stay within it.

terms.name: Family (solitaire)
terms.text: A complete sequence built on a foundation, such as King down to Ace.

terms.name: Fantasy overlay
terms.text: A statement of how the game's world differs from the real one. Balzac holds that people stay the same in any setting; only the scenery changes (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Fantasying
terms.text: Daydreaming that runs on its own and takes up energy. It feeds nothing into dreaming, playing or living.

terms.name: Farced play
terms.text: Boyd's term for play pushed or forced, such as a game acted out without the players getting into it. She read it as a sign of limited ability to enter the game in mind.

terms.name: Fatigue system
terms.text: A rule that cuts the rewards of a player who has played for several hours in a row. Some games in South Korea and China use one.

terms.name: Fault
terms.text: An act that loses a rally, such as touching the net or hitting the shuttle before it crosses.

terms.name: Fayles
terms.text: The medieval backgammon variant in which a player who cannot use all three dice thrown loses the game at once.

terms.name: Federation of groups
terms.text: Several groups working on joint programmes while each keeps its own identity and its right to decide for itself. Boyd saw this as the highest stage of group growth.

terms.name: Feedback
terms.text: What the game does with a player's input: the result the rules return. A flying 100 on screen is only a picture of the actual feedback, the points scored.

terms.name: Feedback
terms.text: Information the game gives back about play, such as the number of seeds a player has collected.

terms.name: Feedback
terms.text: The information a game gives back about an action and its effect on the game state, such as a character moving when a stick is pushed.

terms.name: Feedback from testers
terms.text: What testers show about where the game falls short of what its maker intended, which the designer takes into account without necessarily acting on it.

terms.name: Feedback loop
terms.text: The cycle in which a player acts and the game answers. In video games the cycle is tight, so there is almost no gap between action and response.

terms.name: Feedback system
terms.text: Whatever tells players how close they are to the goal: points, levels, a score, a progress bar, or just knowing when the game ends.

terms.name: Feedback thermometer
terms.text: A gauge on screen that moves with the player's actions. In Peacemaker, very sensitive gauges show how delicate the Israeli-Palestinian situation is (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Feeding
terms.text: In Wari, putting seeds into the opponent's empty cups. A player has to do this if he can.

terms.name: Festival
terms.text: A time set apart from daily life with its own rules, mirth and limits of time and place. Huizinga says it shares nearly every mark of play.

terms.name: Fiction
terms.text: The story or setting a game puts over its rules. Koster compares it to the word problem in a maths class, which the player learns to look past.

terms.name: Fiero
terms.text: The triumph shown by a raised fist when a hard task is done. Koster counts it as a signal to others of your worth.

terms.name: Fiero
terms.text: An Italian word for pride, used by designers for the rush after beating a hard challenge. People tend to throw their arms over their heads and shout.

terms.name: Fight-or-frolic
terms.text: Oriard's name for a story pattern in which the same people fight in earnest and then play, so that violence and merriment sit side by side. A scout in a Simms novel turns playful before a duel, like a boy in a playground.

terms.name: Figurative game
terms.text: In Chateau's scheme, a game of imitation and illusion, such as playing shop or soldier. Caillois says it matches his mimicry.

terms.name: File and rank
terms.text: In a rectangular grid, files are the vertical columns, lettered from the left, and ranks are the horizontal rows, numbered from the first player's side.

terms.name: Finesse
terms.text: An attempt to avoid losing a high card to an opponent's higher card by playing in a way that depends on where that card is.

terms.name: Finite game
terms.text: A game played in order to win, after which it is over. The term comes from James P. Carse.

terms.name: First hand
terms.text: In Wei-ch'i, the initiative held by a player whose move forces the opponent to defend.

terms.name: First-move advantage
terms.text: The edge the player who moves first holds in some games. A game that cannot end in a draw always gives someone this edge in theory.

terms.name: First-order rule
terms.text: A rule everyone needs to know to play or follow the game, such as how pieces move in chess.

terms.name: First-past-the-post
terms.text: A voting system in which each voter picks one candidate and the candidate with the most votes wins. Also called plurality voting.

terms.name: First-person perspective
terms.text: A view from the eyes of the character, so the player feels inside the game space (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Fischer Random Chess
terms.text: A chess variant with randomly set starting positions of the pieces, used to stop play settling into memorised patterns.

terms.name: Fish pile
terms.text: The face-down pile that players draw from in Go Fish when an opponent says they do not hold the asked-for card.

terms.name: Fishing
terms.text: In Ma-jong, waiting for the one tile that completes the hand. Once declared, the player cannot change his hand.

terms.name: Fitness
terms.text: In Barabási's model of success, a quality of a work that lets a late arrival still gather attention against earlier ones.

terms.name: Five pillars
terms.text: The author's five areas for breaking systemic racism into parts: economic, civic, health, justice and education.

terms.name: Five practices of organising
terms.text: Ganz's list: relationships, storytelling, action, structure and leadership, and strategy.

terms.name: Five-in-a-row
terms.text: A winning shape of five pieces on a row, column or diagonal, as in Go-Bang.

terms.name: Five-in-a-row
terms.text: A family of games where players place stones to make a line of five, including Go-Moku, Renju and Pente without captures.

terms.name: Fixed game
terms.text: A game arranged beforehand so that one side always comes out ahead. Himes's novel pictures a crap game run by whites in which Black players cannot win.

terms.name: Fixed justice scenario
terms.text: A design where the game requires a player to carry out acts that might seem wrong, because the story justifies them, such as shooting monsters in Doom (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Fixed stage
terms.text: A play given at one place with its stages built there, indoors or outdoors, instead of moving from stop to stop. Most plays in East Anglia and the south-east worked this way.

terms.name: Flag falling
terms.text: Running out of time on a chess clock, which loses the game.

terms.name: Flash
terms.text: A climbing word for completing a hard problem on the first attempt.

terms.name: Flexible optimism
terms.text: Martin Seligman's term for checking your chances honestly and raising or lowering your effort to match.

terms.name: Flipping capture
terms.text: Capture by turning the enemy piece over to your colour instead of removing it, as in Reversi, Othello, Lotus and Modern Ming-Mang.

terms.name: Floating combat text
terms.text: Damage numbers that rise from a target's head in a computer game. The book treats them as the screen's version of watching dice roll.

terms.name: Flop
terms.text: The three community cards turned over at once after the first round of betting.

terms.name: Flop, turn and river
terms.text: In Texas Hold'em, the three shared cards laid first, then the fourth, then the fifth, with a round of betting after each.

terms.name: Flow
terms.text: The state in which a person is so involved in an activity that nothing else seems to matter. People do the activity for its own sake, even when it is hard or tiring.

terms.name: Flow
terms.text: A state in which a person is so absorbed in an activity that self-consciousness drops away and the activity shapes its own direction.

terms.name: Flow
terms.text: A state of full concentration, named by Csikszentmihalyi, where challenge matches skill. Koster says it is not the same as fun, because flow can come from using a skill already mastered.

terms.name: Flow
terms.text: The state of working at the very edge of your ability. In it, both quitting and winning feel like a loss.

terms.name: Flow activity
terms.text: An activity built mainly to give enjoyable experience, such as play, art, ritual or sport. It has rules, goals and feedback and is set apart from daily life.

terms.name: Flow channel
terms.text: The band between boredom and anxiety where a person's skills match the challenges. The diagram of Alex learning tennis shows him leaving and re-entering it.

terms.name: Flow state
terms.text: Csikszentmihalyi's name for deep focus and enjoyment, reached when the challenge matches the skill of the person.

terms.name: Flowers and seasons
terms.text: Eight extra tiles in some Ma-jong sets, rarely used.

terms.name: Flowers and seasons
terms.text: Eight extra Mahjong tiles that score points when drawn, are shown to all, and are replaced by a loose tile.

terms.name: Fluff
terms.text: The background story a company writes to go with a game world. Some players ignore it and play only for the rules.

terms.name: Flush
terms.text: Five cards of one suit in Poker. It beats a straight.

terms.name: Fluxkit
terms.text: A box of inexpensive play items and instructions made by Fluxus artists, often with no predictable way to play it.

terms.name: Fly ball
terms.text: A batted or thrown ball caught before it touches the ground. In Flies Are Up, catching it earns the fielder a turn at bat.

terms.name: Flâneur
terms.text: A stroller who walks city streets to watch and be seen. The figure began as a leisured European man who could walk wherever he liked.

terms.name: Fog of war
terms.text: A rule that hides parts of the map outside your units' view. It turns open information into hidden information.

terms.name: Fog of war
terms.text: Hiding parts of the map so players do not know what the other side has done, which makes choices like a simultaneous guess.

terms.name: Fold
terms.text: Leaving a round of poker when the chance of winning looks too low to match the stake. DeKoven counts it as a way to quit with honour.

terms.name: Fold
terms.text: In poker, dropping out of the current hand and giving up what has been put in the pot.

terms.name: Folk dance
terms.text: A dance made by common people and danced for the dancers' own pleasure. Boyd called it close kin to the game.

terms.name: Folk game
terms.text: A traditional group game passed from one generation to the next, like other folkways. Boyd noted that many are taken up by other cultures.

terms.name: Folk hero-combat play
terms.text: A traditional play in which England's champion fights a motley crew of clowns and Turks. Saint George appears in some of these.

terms.name: Follow suit
terms.text: A rule that a player puts down a tile of the suit that was led if he can.

terms.name: Follow suit
terms.text: The rule that a player has to play a card of the suit led when they hold one.

terms.name: Follow suit
terms.text: A rule that a player who holds a card of the suit that was led has to play one of that suit. A player with none may play anything.

terms.name: Follow suit
terms.text: To play a card of the same suit as the one led. A player with none can play a trump or discard.

terms.name: Foot spot
terms.text: The marked place on a pool table where the apex ball of the triangle sits, and where pocketed balls are put back.

terms.name: Foot-fault line
terms.text: A line behind which a player has to stand when throwing. Stepping over it makes the throw illegal.

terms.name: Footbridge dilemma
terms.text: A variant of the trolley dilemma where the only way to save five people is to push a stranger onto the tracks. Most people refuse, though the number of deaths is the same (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Forced move
terms.text: A turn where a player has only one legal move to make.

terms.name: Forced ranking
terms.text: A review rule that fixes how many people have to fall in each grade whatever their actual results. At Enron 15 percent had to be graded lowest.

terms.name: Forced simple
terms.text: In Solo, when everyone passes, the holder of Spadilla has to call an Ace and play with its holder.

terms.name: Forcing bid
terms.text: A call that obliges the partner to speak again, so the auction cannot stop yet.

terms.name: Forecasting game
terms.text: A game in which many people imagine and test possible futures together and record what they find. World Without Oil and Superstruct are examples.

terms.name: Forehand, middlehand, endhand
terms.text: The names Skat gives the three seats in order from the dealer's left, which decide who bids first and who may defend a bid.

terms.name: Forfeit
terms.text: A payment of a counter or other token made when a player lands on a penalty space or cannot move.

terms.name: Forfeit
terms.text: A fixed payment into the pool by a player who passes or breaks a rule.

terms.name: Forgetting curve
terms.text: Ebbinghaus's finding that memory of a list decays quickly at first and then more slowly, and that long lists are harder than short ones.

terms.name: Fork, bridge and ring
terms.text: The three winning formations in Havannah. A fork joins three edges, a bridge joins two corners, and a ring is a closed loop around at least one point.

terms.name: Formal Abstract Design Tools
terms.text: Doug Church's short descriptions of design tools, each with a name and a brief description, kept as a list. They describe how elements of a game interact, not what elements a game has.

terms.name: Formal Abstract Design Tools
terms.text: Doug Church's attempt at a shared design vocabulary for designers. Each tool is a one-sentence description, for example Perceivable Consequences, a clear reaction from the game world to what the player does.

terms.name: Formal system
terms.text: A set of explicit rules, usually mathematical, that leaves out the loose details of real life. Koster says most games are formal systems, which makes them clear to learn from and also limited.

terms.name: Format
terms.text: A fixed way to play a game, such as sealed or constructed Magic, or a game speed setting in a strategy game.

terms.name: Formlessness
terms.text: The state of material before it is cut, shaped and put together. A person needs to be allowed to begin there.

terms.name: Fortress
terms.text: In Chinese chess, the square of nine points where the general and the mandarins stay. Taking the enemy fortress by storm wins the game.

terms.name: Fortress
terms.text: A group of pieces placed where they cannot be captured, such as a few pieces in a corner. It lets a player avoid defeat in a game where the aim is to capture everything.

terms.name: Fortuna
terms.text: Chance or luck. In Isidore's account of games, chance appears in war and in the arena, and his list of games ends with games of chance.

terms.name: Fortune's football
terms.text: A person kicked from one event to the next by luck, with no say in where they land. James Butler's 1797 novel takes its title from the idea: its hero is captured, rescued and carried across Europe by chance.

terms.name: Foul (ball games)
terms.text: A play against the rules, such as stopping a ball before hitting it. Each foul scores a point for the other side.

terms.name: Foul (in word games)
terms.text: Calling a word when the letters needed are not all available, which costs the caller his last word.

terms.name: Foul and violation
terms.text: In basketball, a foul is rough contact such as blocking or hacking, and a violation is a breach of ball-handling rules. Both hand the ball to the other side.

terms.name: Foul throw
terms.text: A dice throw that does not count, such as a die falling off the table, tilted on another die, or touched while rolling.

terms.name: Found object
terms.text: An object a baby adopts as if it were made up on the spot, though it was in the room before. Every object in the early world has this quality.

terms.name: Foundation
terms.text: A card or row of cards where a solitaire family is built up.

terms.name: Foundation
terms.text: In solitaire, a card or pile on which the whole pack is built up in order. Getting all cards onto the foundations wins the game.

terms.name: Four axes of covering
terms.text: Yoshino's four areas where people tone themselves down: appearance, affiliation, activism and association. An example of association is not being seen with friends from your own group.

terms.name: Four Component Model of Moral Functioning
terms.text: A model by James Rest and Darcia Narvaez that splits moral ability into moral sensitivity, moral judgment, moral motivation and moral action (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Fourth highest
terms.text: In Whist, leading the fourth highest card of a suit. It tells the partner that exactly three cards of the suit are higher.

terms.name: Fourth wall
terms.text: The invisible barrier between a performance and its audience. Boal worked to break it down.

terms.name: Fox and Geese
terms.text: A Scandinavian game in which one fox captures by jumping and several geese try to trap it. The two sides move and win differently.

terms.name: Fox game
terms.text: A game with unequal sides, in which one player is the fox and the others play many geese or sheep; the goals of the two sides differ.

terms.name: Fragmentation of pattern collections
terms.text: The state of game design patterns where each collection uses its own template and conventions, so patterns overlap or contradict across collections and cannot be used as one language.

terms.name: Frame
terms.text: One round of play. In bowling it is a turn of up to two rolls, and in bocce it is the playing of all eight balls.

terms.name: Frame layer
terms.text: The player's earlier experience of games, life, films and culture, which shapes what they expect from a game.

terms.name: Frame of reference
terms.text: The general pattern and requirements that a play activity sets, such as a game's rules and purpose. Boyd said players can act in their own way inside it.

terms.name: Framing effect
terms.text: People accept an option when it is stated as a chance of living and refuse the same option when it is stated as a chance of dying.

terms.name: Free bid
terms.text: A bid made only on the bidder's own strength, not because he was pushed to bid.

terms.name: Free four
terms.text: A row of four stones with an empty point at each end, which can become five in two different ways and so cannot be blocked.

terms.name: Free time
terms.text: Leisure that no duty claims. Huizinga says play is done in it, and is never imposed by need or obligation.

terms.name: Free will setting
terms.text: An option in The Sims. When it is on, characters act on their own; when it is off, their actions follow the player's plan.

terms.name: Freedom
terms.text: One of Simkins's four design principles: the player can have the character take the actions the player wants within the game's social setting (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Freeze
terms.text: In Freeze Tag, a tagged player stands still like a statue until another player touches them.

terms.name: Freeze-out
terms.text: A betting rule that sends a player out of the game when he has lost his original stake.

terms.name: Fresh deal
terms.text: A new hand of cards dealt to everyone, so the earlier luck no longer counts. In a story a miners' camp names a baby Luck to give him a fresh deal at life.

terms.name: Friend and family playtest
terms.text: A test with people close to the team, where what they do tells more than what they say.

terms.name: Friendly local game store
terms.text: A neighbourhood shop that sells games and gives its tables to players. Shortened to FLGS.

terms.name: Fritillus
terms.text: A wooden dice box or tower with an inside track, used in Roman times so that dice could not be palmed or switched.

terms.name: Frontierism
terms.text: A theme in many games and software: conquest, survival and rule over local people and land.

terms.name: Frozen discard pile
terms.text: In Canasta, a discard pile that can be taken only with two natural cards of the same rank as the top card. A wild card or black three discarded on it freezes it.

terms.name: Frozen pile
terms.text: A discard pile that may be taken only by matching its top card with a natural pair from the hand, so it is harder to claim.

terms.name: Full house
terms.text: In Indian Dice, three of a kind and a pair together.

terms.name: Full house
terms.text: Three of a kind plus a pair in Poker. It beats a flush.

terms.name: Full information
terms.text: A situation where every element of the game state is visible to every player, as with the pieces in chess.

terms.name: Fully cooperative game
terms.text: A game with no traitor mechanic where everybody wins or everybody loses, so every interaction is aimed at the shared result. Pandemic and ...and then we held hands are the examples.

terms.name: Fumage
terms.text: Making marks on paper or canvas with the smoke of a candle or lamp, then reading the shapes, as in fortune-telling or inkblot tests.

terms.name: Fun
terms.text: Koster's narrow meaning: the pleasure the brain gives when it masters a problem or takes in a new pattern. He separates it from delight, physical thrill and social pleasure.

terms.name: Fun failure
terms.text: Failing in a way that the player finds exciting and interesting and that makes them want another try.

terms.name: Fundamental attribution error
terms.text: Explaining someone's poor performance by their character, not their situation. Balzac says people apply the reverse to themselves and assume they would act rightly (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Gallery game
terms.text: Brathwaite's name for a game made as an artwork to be shown in a gallery, such as her handmade non-digital series The Mechanic is the Message (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

terms.name: Gallows (Hangman)
terms.text: The drawing of a gallows and noose where each wrong letter adds a body part. The word is guessed before the figure is complete.

terms.name: Gambit
terms.text: A chess opening where the first player gives up a pawn on purpose to get an attack.

terms.name: Gambit
terms.text: In chess, the deliberate loss of a pawn or piece in return for some other advantage.

terms.name: Gambling
terms.text: Playing a game to win the opponent's money. Boyd said the gambler cares about the stakes and not about the game itself.

terms.name: Game
terms.text: An activity that gives the players a common goal whose result has no bearing on anything outside the game. DeKoven treats a game as a social performance that exists only while the players keep making it.

terms.name: Game (Burgun's definition)
terms.text: A system of rules in which agents compete by making ambiguous decisions. Burgun offers this as a tight working meaning for designers, and says other uses of the word are not wrong, only wider.

terms.name: Game (unit of play)
terms.text: The standard full round of play, usually from a set starting position to the point where a winner is decided.

terms.name: Game arc
terms.text: How the number of choices rises and falls over a game. The usual shape starts sparse, becomes bushy and ends sparse, like a story with a climax.

terms.name: Game as technology
terms.text: Flanagan's view that a game is an ordering device: its rules and conventions set up timed, patterned relationships between players, even without gadgets.

terms.name: Game balance
terms.text: The state where a game's choices are all worth taking, so that the tree of choices is as bushy as intended and not cut down by a few much more powerful options.

terms.name: Game board
terms.text: The surface a game is played on. It shows where pieces stand. It also seats players in relation to each other and sets the order of turns.

terms.name: Game board
terms.text: The marked surface that lays out the route players follow. A 1968 parody of Monopoly marked a route from the ghetto to the White House, with a square telling the player to choose George Wallace as running mate.

terms.name: Game butcher
terms.text: Roosevelt's name for a hunter who killed animals only for hides or numbers, against the hunters' code of killing for meat or for sport.

terms.name: Game community
terms.text: A group that has come together for one game, such as a bowling league or a bridge club, and judges itself by winning at that game. DeKoven sets it against the play community.

terms.name: Game conversion
terms.text: A kit that changes the pictures and theme of an existing arcade or pinball machine without changing its working parts, sold in wartime to make old games carry new themes.

terms.name: Game customization
terms.text: Players changing a game to suit themselves, by personal style, house rules or choices built into the game.

terms.name: Game design
terms.text: The work of planning how a game runs: its core actions, themes and, above all, the play it gives the people who take part.

terms.name: Game design pattern
terms.text: A description of interaction that keeps coming up in game play. The authors build their model on such patterns, and use them to design, analyse and compare games.

terms.name: Game design patterns
terms.text: In this paper, semi-formal, linked descriptions of parts of a game's design that keep coming up and that concern game play, with alarms, fog of war and grinding as examples.

terms.name: Game developer playtest
terms.text: A test with fellow game makers, who give detailed feedback but may describe the game they would make.

terms.name: Game development
terms.text: The whole job of making a game: design, programming, art, writing, sound, testing, selling and more. Design is one part of it.

terms.name: Game engine
terms.text: The software that builds a game's world and fixes what the player can do in it. Wark says it makes worlds that seem made for the player to act upon.

terms.name: Game for change
terms.text: A game that takes on social concerns such as poverty, racism, war or human rights, often through education and outreach. Also called a social impact game.

terms.name: Game for change
terms.text: A serious game whose aim is lasting change in the world, whether physical, political, economic or otherwise (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Game format
terms.text: The third element of family game design: deciding what kind of game it is, such as physical, thinking, creative or social play, solo or shared, and what roles players can take (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Game journal
terms.text: A log in which the player explains why they chose as they did. In Knights of Astrus it doubled as a way to assess the player (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Game master
terms.text: In a tabletop role-playing game, the person who runs the opposing forces, sets scenes and picks the campaign. Burgun calls the job a real-time game designer.

terms.name: Game mechanic
terms.text: A part of a game's rule system that covers one general or specific aspect of the game. Roll and move is the example given: it says a die is rolled and something is moved by the result, but not how it moves or why.

terms.name: Game modification
terms.text: Changing an existing game's art, story or code to make a new version. Bilal hacked a game to make The Night of Bush Capturing: A Virtual Jihadi.

terms.name: Game of Goose
terms.text: A race game first published in England in 1597, in which players move along a board by the roll of dice toward a goal. Oriard calls it the prototype for most English and American board games, with ancestors at least four thousand years old.

terms.name: Game of life
terms.text: The picture of life as a game in which a person freely competes for a prize that can be spiritual, such as salvation, or worldly, such as wealth.

terms.name: Game of life
terms.text: The saying that life is played by rules like a game. The book shows it used by an adult to teach a boy, and rejected by the boy.

terms.name: Game of patience
terms.text: A solitary card game such as solitaire, where skill has little effect on the result. Caillois places it where ludus meets alea.

terms.name: Game of strategy (theory of)
terms.text: A branch of mathematics that studies opponents who have to choose among moves in turn, starting from heads or tails, paper-rock-scissors and simplified poker.

terms.name: Game of superlatives
terms.text: A question game in which each answer outdoes the last, as in "What is sweeter than honey?".

terms.name: Game performance
terms.text: One actual playing of a game, at a particular time and place, as opposed to the game as a set of rules and parts on a shelf.

terms.name: Game production
terms.text: Building the game that a finished design describes. The authors compare design to an architect's plans and production to the building crew.

terms.name: Game purism
terms.text: The view that a person only plays a game if they do it purely for the pleasure of playing. The author says Suits did not hold this view.

terms.name: Game state
terms.text: The condition of a game at one moment: where the pieces are, what the scores are, whose turn it is. Components record it as play goes on.

terms.name: Game state
terms.text: A snapshot of one moment in a game: where players and objects are, the score, and how far the players have got towards the goal.

terms.name: Game system
terms.text: The rules and components of a game taken apart from any single playing of it.

terms.name: Game theory
terms.text: A branch of mathematics about how competitors choose when each has a formal model of the choices. Koster notes it describes why people choose as they do in a game but does not help a designer make a game.

terms.name: Game theory
terms.text: The mathematical study of choices made by separate agents who calculate their own interest, as in the prisoner's dilemma. Wark contrasts it with gamer theory.

terms.name: Game tree
terms.text: The branching set of choices a game offers over time.

terms.name: Gamer regret
terms.text: The worry a player feels about what else could have been done with the hours spent playing.

terms.name: Games of chance
terms.text: In church law, games the clergy and laity were told to avoid. The term could cover anything from gambling to martial contests.

terms.name: Games of chance
terms.text: Games where luck decides a single turn, such as dice rolls. Koster argues they still teach about odds because players return to them turn after turn.

terms.name: Games of emergence
terms.text: Jesper Juul's name for games whose possibilities come largely from how players use the actions, objects and playspace, such as story-making games.

terms.name: Games of progression
terms.text: Jesper Juul's name for games where the player makes decisions but every outcome was written in advance by the makers.

terms.name: Games preserve
terms.text: A place built for play communities, with many kinds of games, quiet and active areas, and care for the pieces. DeKoven built one in a barn on a farm.

terms.name: Gamesmanship
terms.text: A way of playing that accepts the written rules but recognises no code beyond them, so finding a loophole counts as skill.

terms.name: GamesMaster
terms.text: A person who runs a live game: settles rules disputes, helps stuck players and links the game to the outside. Typical games use three to five (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: GamesMother
terms.text: A helper with no power to make rulings and little knowledge of the plot, who aids upset players and can take small roles (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Gamespace
terms.text: Wark's name for a world in which work, politics, school and leisure are all arranged as games, with ranks, scores and winners. It has no outside to step into.

terms.name: Gamification
terms.text: Putting game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards into non-game activities in order to change motivation.

terms.name: Gaming mind
terms.text: The side of a player that is concentrated and set on the goal. DeKoven says a game stays well played while it keeps a dialogue with the playing mind.

terms.name: Gaming the system
terms.text: Using a system's rules for personal gain in a way they were not meant to be used. The phrase shows how wary people are of games.

terms.name: Gaming the system
terms.text: Choosing actions to move an outside measure and not the thing it measures, such as picking easy courses to raise a grade average.

terms.name: Gaming the system
terms.text: Treating a game purely as its rules, and ignoring its story and pictures, in order to win (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Gammon
terms.text: A double win in backgammon, scored when the loser has borne off no piece. A backgammon is a triple win, when the loser also has a piece on the bar or in the winner's inner table.

terms.name: Gammon
terms.text: A double win in backgammon, scored when the loser has not borne off a single piece. Backgammon proper is a triple win or more.

terms.name: Gammon
terms.text: A win in backgammon in which the loser has not borne off any piece. It doubles the value showing on the cube.

terms.name: Gammon
terms.text: A loss in which the loser has taken no pieces off the board. It counts double.

terms.name: Gammon and backgammon
terms.text: A loss counted double if the loser has borne off no stone, and triple if he also has a stone in the winner's home table or on the bar.

terms.name: Gated storyline
terms.text: A plot built so that every player passes the same points, and so reaches the same ending even when routes differ. Knights of Astrus used this to be sure all dilemmas were met (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Gender-based design values
terms.text: One of Holm's kinds: values that bring ideas of gender equality into the design.

terms.name: General prescription
terms.text: The author's rule for aesthetic striving games: play following the rules and aiming at the goal, then appreciate the activity that results.

terms.name: Generative participatory art
terms.text: A participatory work where the audience's activity produces the thing they then attend to.

terms.name: Genre
terms.text: A group of similar games, at any level from boardgames down to real-time strategy, whose shared features are standards for those who know the group.

terms.name: Genre
terms.text: A label such as shooter or platformer that groups games by convention. The authors think it limits design, since it points a maker at other games instead of at the play they want to give.

terms.name: Genuine situation
terms.text: An everyday, real-life setting where results are not pretend. Boyd used the term for work.

terms.name: Ghost
terms.text: A spoken word game in which players add letters in turn and are penalised for completing a word. A player who doubts that any word starts with the letters given may challenge.

terms.name: Ghosting
terms.text: A way of playing the Thief games in which the player gives up all violence, partly for difficulty and partly to stay in character as a thief with a code (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Gift (in Seven-Up)
terms.text: A point scored when the dealer accepts a trump the opponent has begged.

terms.name: Gimme lief
terms.text: A boys' game in which one asks another's permission to take a single blow with an agreed object, and then the other takes the same kind of blow back. Consent and equal exchange are the rule.

terms.name: Gin
terms.text: A Rummy game where sets are kept in the hand. A player who forms sets with all cards but one discards the last and says "Gin" to end the hand.

terms.name: Gin
terms.text: A hand in which every card belongs to a set, with no deadwood. It earns a bonus.

terms.name: Gini coefficient
terms.text: A measure of inequality from 0, where everyone has the same income, to 1, where one person has all of it.

terms.name: Giving up
terms.text: Letting yourself lose so that the other players can carry on. It is a further step than quitting, used when the game has no way out.

terms.name: Glad Game
terms.text: The game Pollyanna teaches a whole town in a 1913 novel, in which the object is to find something to be glad about in every person and event. It replaces moral striving with feeling content.

terms.name: Glass cliff
terms.text: A pattern in which women and people of colour are promoted mainly when an organisation is close to disaster.

terms.name: Glicko system
terms.text: An extension of Elo by Mark Glickman that gives each player a rating and also a ratings deviation, a number for how uncertain that rating is.

terms.name: Glorious failure
terms.text: A large failure from aiming high, which still gives valuable lessons or a notable moment.

terms.name: Go
terms.text: In Cribbage, the call of a player who cannot play without taking the running total over thirty-one. The other player scores a point.

terms.name: Go
terms.text: In cribbage, a call saying that you cannot play a card without going over 31. The other player then plays on if they can.

terms.name: Go (cribbage)
terms.text: Said by a player who cannot play a card without passing 31. The other player may play on and scores for the last card.

terms.name: Go fish
terms.text: The call made when a player asked for a rank does not have it. The asker has to draw from the stock.

terms.name: Goal
terms.text: What the players try to reach while playing. It can be a score to beat or just an experience to have.

terms.name: Goal
terms.text: The specific outcome players work to reach. It holds their attention and gives them a sense of purpose.

terms.name: Goal chunking
terms.text: Grouping a fine scale of scores or ratings into coarse steps players care about, such as letter grades in Dance Dance Revolution or breaking four hours in a marathon.

terms.name: Goal of a game
terms.text: The target a player aims at during play, such as crossing the finish line first or scoring more points. It is separate from the player's reason for playing.

terms.name: Goban
terms.text: The Go board, a grid of 19 by 19 lines whose crossings are the places where stones are put.

terms.name: God game
terms.text: A game that lets one player shape a whole world, a people or a life over a long span. The Sims, Civilization and Black & White are examples.

terms.name: Going alone
terms.text: In Euchre, a player plays without their partner, whose cards are put face down. Winning all five tricks then scores four points.

terms.name: Going gin
terms.text: In gin rummy, laying down all ten cards in melds. It earns a 25-point bonus.

terms.name: Going ma-jong
terms.text: Completing a winning hand of four sets and a pair, and calling the win.

terms.name: Going on each
terms.text: In Twenty-One, splitting a dealt pair into two hands with a stake on each.

terms.name: Going out
terms.text: Getting rid of all your cards by forming sets, which ends the hand in Rummy.

terms.name: Going out
terms.text: Getting rid of all the cards in your hand and so ending the deal.

terms.name: Going over the top
terms.text: Passing the target total in Thirty-six and being put out of the game.

terms.name: Going rummy
terms.text: Melding your entire hand in a single turn, without any earlier meld, which pays double.

terms.name: Going rummy
terms.text: In basic rummy, laying down all your cards in melds in a single turn. It earns double points.

terms.name: Goodhart's law
terms.text: The claim that an indicator loses the information that made it useful once it becomes a target for policy.

terms.name: Grand (Skat)
terms.text: A Skat bid where only the four Jacks are trumps and all four suits are equal.

terms.name: Grand slam
terms.text: In Wari, a move that captures every seed on the opponent's side. The basic rules forbid picking them up. The variation allows it.

terms.name: Graph theory
terms.text: The mathematics of points joined by links. Koster says many board games can be read as graphs, which is what players meant when they called a game about vertices.

terms.name: Grasshopper
terms.text: A piece that moves like a queen but only by jumping over exactly one piece of either side and landing on the very next square.

terms.name: Grassroots and grasstops
terms.text: Two levels at which a change is pushed. Grassroots work moves individual people, and grasstops work moves leaders and institutions so the change is fixed in place.

terms.name: Gratuitous difficulty
terms.text: Caillois's phrase for the taste, shown in puzzles and strategy games, for taking on a hard task for its own sake and finishing it.

terms.name: Great escape
terms.text: In 'SuperBetter', the author's recovery game, noticing a trigger and stepping away before it does damage, counted as a win.

terms.name: Greek Chorus
terms.text: Balzac's untested idea of teams who follow game groups and, when called, discuss aloud what they see, written into the story as gods or an artificial intelligence (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Greimas square
terms.text: A diagram of four terms: two that oppose each other and two that are each the other side of the first pair. Wark uses it to lay out the four endings of Deus Ex.

terms.name: Griefer
terms.text: A player who tries to spoil a game for others.

terms.name: Griefing
terms.text: Behaviour in a game that does not help the player's own position but only makes another player miserable. It is called kingmaking's evil twin.

terms.name: Griefing
terms.text: Harassing or bullying other players in an online game (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Grind level
terms.text: A stage of a game that takes repeated effort and can be dull, which a player gets through by starting again after each defeat.

terms.name: Grinding
terms.text: Any action a player can repeat with little or no risk to gain a reward, such as fighting low-level monsters again and again for experience points.

terms.name: Griphos
terms.text: A Greek riddle or joke question played for rewards or forfeits.

terms.name: Grognard capture
terms.text: Lower-skilled players leaving a game and new versions being made for the remaining expert players, so the audience shrinks to ever more skilled players.

terms.name: Grok
terms.text: To understand something so completely that it becomes automatic and part of you. Koster takes the word from Heinlein and says a player who has groked a game's patterns stops finding it new.

terms.name: Grotesque realism
terms.text: Bakhtin's name for festival humour that dwells on the body, food and death. The book finds it in the shepherds' feast and in Herod's slaughter scene.

terms.name: Group (set)
terms.text: In Rummy, three or more cards of the same rank.

terms.name: Group movement
terms.text: In Wari, advancing a falling sequence of seeds in neighbouring cups as a block when empty cups lie ahead.

terms.name: Group movement (Medusa)
terms.text: A rule in Medusa letting a player move one stone from each group of two or more over friendly stones to the first empty space beyond, in the same turn as placing a stone.

terms.name: Guard
terms.text: A small card kept with a higher card of its suit so that the high card is not captured.

terms.name: Guessing game
terms.text: Any game where one player holds information and another tries to reach it. The kinds of clue allowed decide which guessing game it is.

terms.name: Guided Experiential Learning
terms.text: Richard Clark's model of teaching with four needs: real problems, a shown way to solve them, practice with feedback, and links to what the learner already knows (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Guideline
terms.text: A rule of thumb for playing a game that holds usually but not always, such as keeping away from the Heavy in Team Fortress 2. Burgun says skilled play means knowing when to drop one.

terms.name: Guignol
terms.text: A French glove puppet show, like Punch and Judy, where a rude puppet breaks every rule and the crowd cheers.

terms.name: Guild
terms.text: A trade body of a town, such as the Smiths or the Bakers. In the northern cities each guild owned, paid for and acted one play of the series.

terms.name: Guild
terms.text: A long-term alliance of players who take on the hardest raids together.

terms.name: Guild
terms.text: A formally recognised, long-lasting group within an online game whose members support each other, socialise and work together (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Guild ascription
terms.text: A note in a manuscript saying which guild played which pageant. Towneley has only five, added in the sixteenth century.

terms.name: Gunner
terms.text: A basketball player who takes many shots and scores a lot, but does not play defence.

terms.name: h-index
terms.text: A number for a researcher: the largest H such that H of their papers have at least H citations each. With 10 papers cited at least 10 times each but no 11 cited 11 times, the h-index is 10.

terms.name: Hackenbush
terms.text: A two-player game of removing coloured edges from a drawing connected to the ground, used to show how game positions behave like numbers.

terms.name: Hacker
terms.text: Someone whose free, self-directed activity makes its own rules and its own measure of success. Wark places the hacker outside work and outside play.

terms.name: Half-real
terms.text: Jesper Juul's description of games as having real rules that are communicated to the player through a fictional world (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Halma
terms.text: A Victorian-English race game on a square grid that inspired Chinese Checkers. Pieces step or jump in eight directions and none are captured.

terms.name: Halo effect
terms.text: A bias where the overall impression of a person decides how each separate trait or performance is scored.

terms.name: Hand management
terms.text: Use of cards in which players are rewarded for playing them in certain sequences set by the rules.

terms.name: Hand ranking
terms.text: The fixed order of card combinations, from five in a row of one suit down to a single high card, used to decide who wins.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: Pieces given in advance to the lower-ranked player so a game is more even. In Wei-ch'i, the lower-ranked player takes Black and receives stones on set points.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: A built-in advantage given to the weaker player so a match stays close. Go has used handicaps for thousands of years.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: An advantage given to a weaker player so that the chances of both sides stay equal. In chess, the weaker player may start with an extra pawn.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: A rule that makes the challenge more even when players differ in skill. Examples are starting with fewer pieces, playing blindfolded or using the wrong hand.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: A rule variant meant to make an uneven match even, such as extra stones in go or weights on a racehorse.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: In Go, a way to match players of different skill by shrinking the board or giving the weaker player more moves or pieces.

terms.name: Handicap
terms.text: A change made to help the less skilled player so that the two have about equal chances, such as moving a net closer to the more skilled player.

terms.name: Handicap category
terms.text: In Trivial Pursuit with handicaps, a category in which a player who has won before has to answer two questions in a row to earn a wedge.

terms.name: Handicap points
terms.text: Marked points on a Go board where extra stones may be placed to even out a game between players of different strength.

terms.name: Handicap stones
terms.text: Stones the less powerful Go player places on the board before play begins, one for each rank of difference, usually on the star points.

terms.name: Handplay
terms.text: Playing a hand without taking up the widow, in return for a higher score.

terms.name: Happening
terms.text: A staged event or performance, often with audience participation, from which many Fluxus games came.

terms.name: Happiness activity
terms.text: A short habit shown by studies to raise well-being, such as acts of kindness or daily thanks.

terms.name: Happiness engineer
terms.text: The book's name for a game designer who applies research on emotion to shape how players feel.

terms.name: Happiness hack
terms.text: A small game or activity made to bring about one positive feeling or habit in everyday life, tested with real people and then shared freely so that others can copy it.

terms.name: Happiness hacking
terms.text: The author's term for designing light, free, shared games that get many people to try a happiness activity.

terms.name: Happy embarrassment
terms.text: The pleasant feeling of being teased by someone you trust, or of acting silly in front of them.

terms.name: Hard fun
terms.text: Lazzaro's name for the pleasure of meeting a challenge that tests the player's skill. Koster ties it to the state of flow.

terms.name: Hard fun
terms.text: Hard work that a person chooses and enjoys, as opposed to easy relaxing pastimes such as watching television.

terms.name: Hardball
terms.text: Baseball played in a hard-edged way, used for politics played with no softness. The word carries the idea that the game is about getting power and that players who hold back are not wanted.

terms.name: Harmony of action
terms.text: The sense, available to the player, that their own deciding and acting fitted what the situation asked, such as timing a jump in Super Mario just so.

terms.name: Harmony of capacity
terms.text: The sense that all of one's abilities are working at their limit and only just enough for the task. It appears only in demanding play.

terms.name: Harmony of solution
terms.text: The fit between a move and the problem it answers, such as a chess move that escapes a trap. A spectator can see it as well as the player.

terms.name: Harvesting patterns
terms.text: The authors' way of finding patterns by analysing existing games and other fields: recognise a candidate, analyse it in example games, describe it, test it in a small prototype, and evaluate it. In practice the steps became loose and repeated, with candidates fusing, changing and being created at almost any stage.

terms.name: Having the move
terms.text: In checkers, holding the position that lets you force the opponent into a cramped spot and make the last move. It is not the same as it being your turn.

terms.name: Having to win
terms.text: A condition where a player cannot leave the game and will bend any rule or ignore any person to win. The game's rules are unchanged but it no longer feels like play.

terms.name: Hawks and Doves
terms.text: A game where being aggressive pays against someone who gives way and is a disaster against another aggressor. It is also called chicken.

terms.name: Head table
terms.text: In Bunco, the table where winners stay while winners and losers at the other tables move.

terms.name: Head-to-head competition
terms.text: Players face each other directly, so each has to think about the other's choices as well as their own.

terms.name: Heads and tails
terms.text: A coin game in which one player tosses and the other calls the side while the coin is in the air.

terms.name: Heads-up display
terms.text: The on-screen panel that shows a player's points and traits changing as they play.

terms.name: Health bar
terms.text: A shown meter of a character's remaining health, where only empty or not empty changes the game.

terms.name: Heavy strategy game
terms.text: A game whose central features only show after repeated plays and real skill, such as 1830 or Dream Quest.

terms.name: Heavy-tail distribution
terms.text: A spread of values that is lopsided, with many small items and a few very large ones, unlike the symmetrical bell curve. Also called a long-tail distribution.

terms.name: Hedonic adaptation
terms.text: The way a person gets used to a pleasure, so that a larger amount is needed for the same feeling.

terms.name: Hedonic resilience
terms.text: A steadier mood built by repeating activities that reward themselves, so that outside events matter less.

terms.name: Heinz Dilemma
terms.text: Lawrence Kohlberg's most cited story: a man cannot afford a medicine his wife needs and the druggist will not lower the price. Listeners' reasoning about what he ought to do placed them on a six-point scale of moral development (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Heterocosm
terms.text: An "other world" that a game builds, with its settings, characters and events. It can be carried from one game to another.

terms.name: Heterotopia
terms.text: A place set apart with its own rules, such as a stadium, gallery or court. Foucault's term, which Wark uses for the fields where games used to stay.

terms.name: Heuristic
terms.text: A rule of thumb that helps a player play, such as develop your pieces in chess. Players talk about heuristics after a game more than about rules.

terms.name: Heuristic
terms.text: A mental shortcut used to decide fast when there is too much information to weigh.

terms.name: Heuristic drift
terms.text: A shift in the daily rule of thumb a person uses for a value, caused by the pleasure of a clear measure, so the rule of thumb stops tracking the value.

terms.name: Hex grid
terms.text: A map divided into hexagons, a layout that came into hobby games from wargames.

terms.name: Hex wargame
terms.text: A wargame played on a map of hexagons with units on them, with long complex rules.

terms.name: Hidden affordance
terms.text: Something a thing can do that its look does not show, such as rewinding time in Braid.

terms.name: Hidden role
terms.text: A job or side that a player is given in secret, such as Killer or Mafia. Other players have to guess it from behaviour.

terms.name: Hidden spectator
terms.text: A design where the game appears not to be watching a player's acts and later shows the consequences, for example the ghosts of everyone the player killed in Metal Gear Solid 3 (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Hidden transcript
terms.text: James C. Scott's term for the account that people under power share among themselves, which runs against the official account. Flanagan links it to unplaying.

terms.name: High count
terms.text: In Eleusis scoring, the largest number of cards held by any player, from which each player's own card count is subtracted.

terms.name: High Jump
terms.text: A Somali game on the Seega board, with jump capture instead of custodian capture.

terms.name: High score
terms.text: The ranked list of top results kept for a game. Wark says every game, inside and outside the cave, has its own such ranking.

terms.name: High, low, jack and game
terms.text: Four scoring prizes in the All Fours family: the highest trump, the lowest trump, the jack of trumps, and the most points in tricks.

terms.name: High-card points
terms.text: A count in bridge giving ace 4, king 3, queen 2 and jack 1, used to judge how much a hand is worth.

terms.name: High-low
terms.text: A poker form in which the pot is shared between the highest and the lowest hand. Players declare before the showdown which they are aiming for.

terms.name: High-low poker
terms.text: A form of poker where the pot is split between the highest and the lowest hand.

terms.name: High-stakes work
terms.text: Fast, action-based play with a real chance of spectacular failure, such as racing at top speed or fighting zombies.

terms.name: Hindsight bias
terms.text: Believing after an outcome that you had predicted it.

terms.name: Hint rule
terms.text: An agreement made before play about when a stuck player may ask for a clue and how the clue-giver answers. It can be written into the rules, such as allowing a hint after the fifth guess.

terms.name: Historical empathy
terms.text: Understanding why people in the past acted as they did by rebuilding their beliefs, values, goals and feelings, without assuming they were foolish (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Historical thinking
terms.text: Treating history as a way of knowing, not a list of names and dates: weighing evidence, finding causes and spotting change over time (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Hit
terms.text: In Twenty-One, a request for another card. "Stay" means the player keeps the cards they have.

terms.name: Hit
terms.text: Landing on a blot, which sends the stone to the bar.

terms.name: Hit and stand
terms.text: In Blackjack, taking another card is a hit and stopping is a stand.

terms.name: Hit and stand
terms.text: In blackjack, a player asks for another card by saying hit me, or keeps the current hand by saying stand.

terms.name: Hitting
terms.text: Landing on an opponent's lone piece so it is taken off the board. In backgammon the hit piece goes on the bar and has to re-enter.

terms.name: Hnefatafl
terms.text: The Saxon form of tafl, with a king or hnefi in the middle and a smaller force defending. Its pieces are called hunns.

terms.name: Hobby
terms.text: Caillois's word for a side activity done for pleasure, such as collecting or building scale models. He says it grows in factory societies as a reply to repetitive work.

terms.name: Hocktide
terms.text: A spring custom after Easter used by parishes to raise money. On Hock Monday women captured and bound men for ransom; on Hock Tuesday men captured women.

terms.name: Hole cam
terms.text: A small camera that shows a poker player's hidden cards to the television audience.

terms.name: Hole card
terms.text: A card dealt face down and seen only by its owner.

terms.name: Hole card
terms.text: A card dealt face down in stud poker, hidden from the other players.

terms.name: Hole card
terms.text: In poker, a card dealt face down that only its owner can see.

terms.name: Home base
terms.text: The place in hide-and-seek and tag where a player is safe or from which the search begins.

terms.name: Home base
terms.text: A place on the playing area where a player is safe, or where captured players wait.

terms.name: Home field
terms.text: The last stretch of a track, where a player has to bring all of their pieces before they may start taking them off the board.

terms.name: Homebrew
terms.text: Game material that players make themselves, outside the official scenarios.

terms.name: Homeostatic experience
terms.text: An experience such as sleep, rest or food that returns the body to balance. It restores order but adds no new skill.

terms.name: Homo economicus
terms.text: The imagined person of rational choice theory, who calculates gain without error or feeling.

terms.name: Homophily
terms.text: The tendency to spend more time with people who are like ourselves.

terms.name: Honors
terms.text: In Whist, the Ace, King, Queen and Jack of trumps. Holding them scores extra points.

terms.name: Honours
terms.text: The highest cards of a suit. Holding several of them scores a bonus whether or not the holder wins the hand.

terms.name: Hook mover
terms.text: A piece that can make two perpendicular moves in one turn. 3D Hook-Move Chess uses it so that a king and rook can again force mate in three dimensions.

terms.name: Hoop (Arithmetic Croquet)
terms.text: A multiple of ten that a player has to pass by a rule of equal steps on either side in Lewis Carroll's number game.

terms.name: Horse swap
terms.text: A trade of horses done as a public contest of wit, with each side hiding the faults of its animal.

terms.name: Hot Cockles
terms.text: A game named in the Coliphizacio, where the torturers say they will teach Christ a new play of it. The book takes their talk as the language of a Christmas game.

terms.name: Hotter and colder
terms.text: Calls by those who know where an object is hidden to tell a seeker how near he is.

terms.name: House (mancala)
terms.text: A pit allowed to grow large so that, when finally played, it laps the board more than once and sets up a multiple capture.

terms.name: House edge
terms.text: The percentage by which the dealer or bank is ahead of the players over many rounds. A gambler in Harte's story accepts fate because he knows the usual percentage favours the dealer.

terms.name: House percentage
terms.text: The share of all money bet that the house keeps over a long run because of how payouts are set.

terms.name: House rule
terms.text: A variant a group makes up and plays by, such as money going to the player who lands on Free Parking in Monopoly.

terms.name: House rule
terms.text: A change to a game's printed rules that a group of players agrees on and uses at its own table.

terms.name: How might we question
terms.text: A question starting with those words, borrowed from IDEO, that opens a design project, such as how might we share the feeling of the first snow of the year.

terms.name: Hubris
terms.text: Pride that leads a person to take on forces far above them. The book says Magnus Derrick's flaw in Norris's The Octopus is hubris, not greed.

terms.name: Huff
terms.text: Taking away a piece from a player who did not make a capture he was able to make. In Alquerque a piece that could capture and did not was huffed.

terms.name: Huff or blow
terms.text: The old rule that a player who failed to capture when able lost the piece that had been able to capture.

terms.name: Huffing
terms.text: A penalty in checkers. A player who skips a capture they were able to make can have the piece that could have captured removed by the opponent, who then takes their own move as well.

terms.name: Hug tag
terms.text: A tag game where a player is safe while hugging someone. The length of a hug is not fixed, and a rule such as no repeat hugs was tried by the group.

terms.name: Human intelligence task
terms.text: A small job that a computer cannot do but a person can, such as labelling a picture. Amazon Mechanical Turk pays a few cents for each one.

terms.name: Human shogi (ningen shogi)
terms.text: A festival version of the Japanese chess game shogi, played on a human-sized board with people as the pieces.

terms.name: Humanistic Ethos
terms.text: Phelps's set of four observable qualities for judging an activity: poetic imagination, dialogic relations, systemic thinking and existential vigor (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Hybrid play
terms.text: Play that blends public space with online game space.

terms.name: Hypocrita
terms.text: The Latin word for actor or mime. It carried the charge that the actor puts on a mask and shows emotion that is not his own.

terms.name: Hypocrite
terms.text: A tic-tac-toe variant DeKoven names, where either player may place either mark as long as the move finishes three in a row.

terms.name: Hypodescent
terms.text: The rule that a person with any Black ancestor counts as Black, also called the one-drop rule. Brazil and Jamaica historically drew the line differently.

terms.name: Idea speed-dating
terms.text: A group exercise where each person writes a game idea, pairs swap and merge two ideas into one, and the group votes on the results.

terms.name: Idealizers
terms.text: Sutton-Smith's name for play scholars, such as Huizinga and Caillois, who treat play as free, voluntary and tied to leisure and class.

terms.name: Ideational culture
terms.text: Sorokin's name for a culture that organises goals around spiritual or abstract principles and looks down on material concerns.

terms.name: Ideational organisation
terms.text: A way of organising pretend play by adding ideas that fit within a concept, such as a school or factory in a town. Boyd set it against organising by a leader's authority.

terms.name: Identification (with a champion)
terms.text: Caillois's word for a diluted form of mimicry, where fans share in the success of a star or athlete by imagining themselves in their place.

terms.name: Igui
terms.text: In Chu Shogi, a lion's capture of a piece on an adjacent square without moving, which counts as a turn.

terms.name: Il piu col piu
terms.text: Italian draughts rule that when a player has a choice of capture he is required to take the greater number, or if the numbers are equal, the more valuable pieces.

terms.name: Ilinx
terms.text: Caillois's word for games that seek dizziness, a brief loss of steady perception. Whirling in circles and swinging are examples.

terms.name: Ilinx
terms.text: In Caillois's scheme, activities that scramble ordinary perception, such as spinning, a merry-go-round or skydiving. Also called vertigo.

terms.name: Ilinx
terms.text: Play that seeks dizziness or a shaken sense of balance and order. Caillois names it as one of four kinds of play, alongside agon, alea and mimesis.

terms.name: Illusion
terms.text: A word from the Latin for "in play". It names the shared pretence that a game is real while it lasts.

terms.name: Illusion
terms.text: The experience, given to a baby by close care, that what is wanted appears just where the baby is ready to find it. It is the early form of the make-believe that later shows up in games and the arts.

terms.name: Illusion of choice
terms.text: A technique where a game lets a player try an action that cannot succeed, or seems to offer a choice that makes no difference to the game (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Illusion of control
terms.text: A belief that your actions, such as picking lottery numbers or breathing on dice, change a random result.

terms.name: Imaginary runner
terms.text: A runner who is not played by anyone but counted when a ball passes a line. It lets a small team play baseball without bases.

terms.name: Imaginary runner
terms.text: In Wiffle Ball, a runner who is counted but not played. A single puts one on first, and later hits push earlier runners along.

terms.name: Immediate feedback
terms.text: Information that tells a person right away whether the last action moved them towards the goal. A climber learns it every second.

terms.name: Immediate task
terms.text: A quick task done in a short time, such as fixing a known bug. It is the most common kind.

terms.name: Impact factor
terms.text: The average number of citations received this year by a journal's articles from the previous two years. It is used to compare journals within one subject.

terms.name: Impartial game
terms.text: A game where both players have the same options at every step, such as Nim.

terms.name: Impasse
terms.text: In Wei-ch'i, an empty space bordered by both colours where whoever enters first would be captured, so both leave it alone.

terms.name: Imperfect information
terms.text: A situation where some of the game state is hidden from players, as with face-down cards.

terms.name: Implicit rules
terms.text: Rules about how a game is really played, such as shaking hands afterwards or not gloating, which players settle among themselves.

terms.name: Implicit subgame
terms.text: A hidden rock-paper-scissors relationship among game elements, such as melee beating ranged, ranged beating flying, and flying beating melee.

terms.name: Impressionable years hypothesis
terms.text: The idea that people change their beliefs most readily before adulthood. The authors use it to focus on childhood and early adolescence (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: In the hole
terms.text: Having a score below zero.

terms.name: Incidental learning
terms.text: What people pick up from the messages built into media without being taught them. The Sims is said to teach spending, because players have to earn money to buy things.

terms.name: Incommensurable
terms.text: Not measurable on one common scale, as in comparing apples and oranges.

terms.name: Incomprehensible busywork
terms.text: Game choices so opaque to the player that they are made at random and cannot be done well or badly, so they feel like unrelated work.

terms.name: Incubate
terms.text: The step in evaluation where team members mull a problem alone, for 10 minutes or a few days, before gathering ideas.

terms.name: Incubation versus segregation
terms.text: Two separations that look alike. Incubation is a protective space for a group with a safe purpose, and segregation is a rule that keeps one group on top.

terms.name: Independence of irrelevant alternatives
terms.text: The condition that adding or removing a third option is expected to leave unchanged how two other options rank against each other.

terms.name: Independent game
terms.text: A game developed and published by an individual or a small team.

terms.name: Index
terms.text: The small number and suit symbol printed in the corner of a card, so that it can be read when held in a fan.

terms.name: Indian poker
terms.text: A poker variant where each player holds one card on the forehead, so everyone sees everyone's card except their own.

terms.name: Indicator
terms.text: A single number that stands for a complicated state of affairs and hides the negotiation behind it, such as the Human Development Index.

terms.name: Indirect action
terms.text: An effect that happens without the player touching the thing itself, such as the ball setting off a bumper after the flipper hits it.

terms.name: Indirect reciprocity
terms.text: Helping someone who cannot repay you, because others see it and your reputation for helping brings you help later.

terms.name: Individualistic model
terms.text: A pattern of ethical thinking in which a player judges actions by personal consequences and considers rules mainly to avoid punishment (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Individuated participation
terms.text: The second step on Boyd's scale, in which a person takes part in a group activity somewhat alone, as in crafts, skating or playing an instrument.

terms.name: Individuation
terms.text: In Boyd's scale of groups, the end where each member acts largely alone and has little interest in the others.

terms.name: Induction and deduction in games
terms.text: Clint Hocking's pair. In film or books, the audience induces a meaning from one case; in a game, the player can deduce meaning from a whole system of rules (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Infinite game
terms.text: A game played in order to keep playing for as long as possible. Tetris is the book's example.

terms.name: Informal rule set
terms.text: Unwritten rules that players share but never state, such as the assumptions of a tea party. Koster says a child who cries foul when one is broken shows the rules were there.

terms.name: Information space
terms.text: The set of meanings a player can draw from a game, shaped by what is visible, hidden, clear or vague.

terms.name: Inherent complexity
terms.text: The complexity written into the rule set itself, such as the number of piece types and special moves.

terms.name: Inhibition
terms.text: An official order stopping a performance. In 1572 the archbishop of York sent one to Chester, and the mayor later claimed it arrived too late.

terms.name: Initial meld requirement
terms.text: A minimum total of points a first meld has to reach before a side may start melding. It rises with the side's score.

terms.name: Initial meld requirement
terms.text: In Canasta, the minimum points a side's first meld has to add up to before it may play, set by the side's score so far.

terms.name: Inner table
terms.text: The home quarter of a backgammon board, where a player gathers pieces before bearing them off.

terms.name: Inner table
terms.text: The last six points a backgammon piece has to pass before bearing off.

terms.name: Inning
terms.text: One round of baseball in which each team has a turn to bat. A game is played over an agreed number of innings.

terms.name: Input
terms.text: Suggestions from players about how to change a game, which a designer may act on. The authors set it against feedback.

terms.name: Input measure
terms.text: A count of what goes into an effort, such as library volumes or the number of students per teacher.

terms.name: Input resolution
terms.text: How much information a player can send the game at one moment or turn. A chess move has a low resolution (one piece, one destination); a Quake player can run, turn and fire at once.

terms.name: Instruction painting
terms.text: Ono's card or work that gives the viewer instructions to complete the piece, so the viewer makes the work.

terms.name: Instrumental play
terms.text: Play that is valued because it serves something else, such as work done faster, health or a steadier town, and not for itself.

terms.name: Instrumental skills
terms.text: Skills learned to deal with the surroundings or earn a living. People often feel them as imposed from outside.

terms.name: Instrumentalization
terms.text: Treating games as tools for goals outside play, such as teaching or health. Zimmerman uses the word to name what DeKoven's book resists.

terms.name: Integrated group
terms.text: A group with a sense of belonging, shared effort, and joint and personal responsibility. Boyd held that not every group reaches this, and that a group needs shared work to get there.

terms.name: Integration
terms.text: Movement towards union with other people, ideas and things beyond the self.

terms.name: Integration
terms.text: In Salen and Zimmerman's usage, whether a player can see how a change affects their later goals in the game (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Integrative Ethical Education
terms.text: Darcia Narvaez's approach to teaching morals by building four kinds of knowledge: identification, declarative, procedural and execution (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Intellectual property (IP)
terms.text: In this book, the ownable part of a game's conceit, such as Star Wars in a Star Wars game. Chess has none because its conceit is public.
