terms.name: Intended strength
terms.text: A part of the game that works as the designer meant.

terms.name: Intensive interaction
terms.text: The fourth step on Boyd's scale, covering group games, country dancing and dramatics, where co-operation is needed while the activity lasts.

terms.name: Intention
terms.text: A wish to get or do something, which keeps awareness arranged and pulls attention towards some things and away from others.

terms.name: Intention of playing well together
terms.text: The shared aim that sits above any game or score. Players have to renew it again and again, because it does not stay fixed once stated.

terms.name: Intentionality
terms.text: The direction of meaning in what someone does. The paper separates original intentionality, when a person means something by an action, from derived intentionality, which is another person's reading of that action. It uses the idea to explain why design decisions are hard for others to read.

terms.name: Interaction level
terms.text: A game's level of conflict between players, scored in the paper as direct conflict, low conflict or no conflict. It is read together with whether a player can be eliminated.

terms.name: Interactive fiction
terms.text: A playable story told mostly in text, in the line of early text adventures like Zork. Alabaster is an example.

terms.name: Interactive system
terms.text: A space of possibilities set by explicit rules that a person can act inside. Puzzles, contests and games are all kinds of interactive system, as are toys and simulators.

terms.name: Interactivity
terms.text: The ability of players to influence the progress of other players. A boxing match or chess is highly interactive, a footrace almost not at all.

terms.name: Interface
terms.text: All the ways a game sends information to a player and takes the player's choices back. Every game has one, from a chess piece to a mouse click.

terms.name: Interface prototype
terms.text: A trial of how the player engages with the game: a heads-up display, a custom controller, or screen layouts, which can be done in image or presentation software with no code.

terms.name: Interference
terms.text: A call that something from outside the game, such as a pole or a stranger, has spoiled the last play so that it does not count.

terms.name: Interlude
terms.text: In some town records, a musical performance with something to look at, such as a pageant. The word did not always mean a short acted piece.

terms.name: Interlude
terms.text: A planned break, such as halftime or a huddle, that suspends the game without ending it. Rituals like a handshake or a bow can serve the same purpose.

terms.name: Interlude
terms.text: A pause in daily life that is satisfying in itself and ends when it ends. It is how play first appears, before it becomes a regular part of life.

terms.name: Intermediate area of experience
terms.text: A third part of life, besides inner life and the outside world, where both contribute and no one asks which is which. Play, art and religion take place there.

terms.name: Internal object
terms.text: A mental picture of a person that lives in the mind and can feel alive, dead or threatening. The transitional object is not this, because it is a thing that can be held.

terms.name: Internal playtest
terms.text: A test among the people making the game, usually the team's first.

terms.name: Interpersonal model
terms.text: A pattern of ethical thinking in which a player considers people close or similar to themselves and follows rules to promote fairness and reciprocity (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Interrogative discourse
terms.text: A dialogue in which one sage questions another in turn, and the roles can swap. Huizinga treats it as a descendant of the riddle-contest.

terms.name: Intersectionality
terms.text: Kimberlé Crenshaw's word for the way several social categories overlap, so that a Black woman faces different treatment from a Black man or a White woman.

terms.name: Intersubjectivity
terms.text: Schutz's name for shared meaning, which has two parts: the medium used to communicate, such as scenarios, prototypes, speech, writing or drawing, and the shared ways of using that medium that grow up during communication.

terms.name: Interval scale
terms.text: A scale where the gaps between values mean something but zero is a convention. Celsius is the example: 20 degrees is not twice as hot as 10.

terms.name: Intervention
terms.text: A kind of subversion that steps into a social or political matter directly to change its course, for instance by putting art or play into a public street.

terms.name: Intra-action
terms.text: Karen Barad's term for the way things shape each other by acting together, instead of acting on each other from outside.

terms.name: Intrinsic play
terms.text: Play for the value of the activity itself. Intrinsic and extrinsic play is a different split from achievement and striving play.

terms.name: Intrinsic reward
terms.text: A reward that comes from the activity itself: pleasant feelings, personal strengths and bonds with other people.

terms.name: Intrinsic satisfaction
terms.text: The pleasure a player takes in playing itself, with no reward from outside. Boyd's definition of play rests on it.

terms.name: Intrinsic variability
terms.text: Play that differs from session to session without the designer making new material, usually because of other players.

terms.name: Introduce
terms.text: The first playtest task: telling testers the state of the prototype, such as that the art or win condition is unfinished, so they know what to comment on.

terms.name: Introspection
terms.text: Looking inward to judge one's own play while it goes on. Boyd said it breaks the spirit of play.

terms.name: Intuitiveness
terms.text: How little effort a player needs to carry out the basic actions, which grows with repeated play.

terms.name: Invisible tutorial
terms.text: Teaching a game's rules through its design, such as level layout and picture cues, so that no separate lesson is needed.

terms.name: Irony (in games)
terms.text: A deliberate gap between what a game shows or says and what it asks the player to do, which leaves room for the player to think about it.

terms.name: Irrisiones
terms.text: Latin for derision or mockery. Church writers used it for games that jested with holy things, such as a summer game that mocked the Crucifixion.

terms.name: Isolated pawn
terms.text: A chess pawn with no friendly pawns beside it to support it.

terms.name: Isolated piece
terms.text: In Fields of Action, a piece with no neighbours. It may move any distance, but cannot capture and has to end next to at least two pieces.

terms.name: It
terms.text: The player in a chasing or searching game who has to tag or find the others.

terms.name: It
terms.text: The player in a game who has a special job, such as seeking, guessing or chasing. Who is It changes during play.

terms.name: Iteration
terms.text: One trip round the cycle of concept, prototype, playtest and evaluation.

terms.name: Iterative design
terms.text: A cycle of setting a goal, making the minimum rules and pieces, building a prototype, play testing, revising and repeating.

terms.name: Iterative design
terms.text: A cycle of imagining, making, testing and judging a design, repeated until the design is understood.

terms.name: Iterative design
terms.text: A cycle of designing, playtesting and redesigning that depends on reading closely how players handle the rules, setting and goals (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Iterative game design process
terms.text: A cycle of imagining an idea, building a rough version, testing it with players and judging the results, repeated several times.

terms.name: J'adoube
terms.text: A chess phrase, French for "I adjust". A player says it before touching a piece only to straighten it, so the touch does not force a move.

terms.name: Jack (bowls)
terms.text: A target ball thrown first in games like Bowling for the Jack. Players then try to land their balls near it.

terms.name: Jackpot (Poker)
terms.text: A Poker variant where a player may only open the betting with a pair of Jacks or higher. If nobody can, everyone adds to the pot and a new hand is dealt.

terms.name: Jacks (game)
terms.text: A game of tossing small metal or plastic pieces and picking them up while a small ball bounces.

terms.name: Jail
terms.text: A marked spot where captured players wait. A teammate can free them by touching them.

terms.name: Jailbreak
terms.text: A move that frees captured players, such as kicking the can in Kick the Can. It can make a game of capture go on for a long time.

terms.name: Jambone
terms.text: A Euchre play where a player goes alone with their cards face up on the table, and an opponent picks the card for the first lead.

terms.name: Jamboree
terms.text: A Euchre hand made of the five top trumps, which scores 16 points at once and needs no play.

terms.name: Jargon factor
terms.text: The rise of specialist terms as a form matures, until newcomers cannot enter. Koster says it marks games that grow ever more complex.

terms.name: Jen ratio
terms.text: Dacher Keltner's measure of a shared place: positive contacts between strangers divided by negative ones over a fixed time, such as an hour.

terms.name: Jeu forcé
terms.text: The draughts form in which capture is compulsory, as opposed to the earlier game with no compulsion. English draughts descends from it.

terms.name: Jeux de regle
terms.text: In Ecarte, hands that the book says are played without asking for a swap, worked out from the odds.

terms.name: Jink
terms.text: In Spoil Five, winning all five tricks, paid extra by agreement.

terms.name: Joculator
terms.text: A medieval entertainer who sang the deeds of princes and the lives of saints. One bishop's sorting of performers allowed this kind and condemned entertainers who used lewd movement, masks or wanton songs.

terms.name: Jogo do Bicho
terms.text: The Brazilian "animal game", a street lottery where the first hundred numbers are grouped into twenty-five animals and bettors choose an animal, often from a dream.

terms.name: Joker (as top trump)
terms.text: An added card that outranks every trump, used in Five Hundred and Hasenpfeffer.

terms.name: Joker (wild trump)
terms.text: An extra card added to a pack that is always a trump. In Railroad Euchre it beats even the right bower.

terms.name: Jollying
terms.text: Boyd's word for cheering players on, in the spirit of play, to make finishing a slow game something of a challenge.

terms.name: Joseki
terms.text: A set sequence of moves in Go that is known to be safe for both sides, usually in the opening stage.

terms.name: Joy-leap
terms.text: In Courier chess, the opening jump of the queen to the third square, and a pawn's jumps in a variant, used to speed up a slow opening.

terms.name: Jump cut
terms.text: A sudden switch from one view to another, which can catch the player's reflexive attention.

terms.name: Jury theorem
terms.text: Condorcet's result that if each juror is independently more likely right than wrong, a bigger jury is more likely to reach the right verdict. It applies only where a correct answer exists.

terms.name: Just community
terms.text: Lawrence Kohlberg's idea of a group where people debate, discuss and settle real moral issues that concern them (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Kairos
terms.text: A Greek word for the right moment, an occasion that cannot be repeated. Caillois places it among the Greek ideas of luck.

terms.name: Karma points
terms.text: A score that some role-playing games raise or lower according to a player's choices, so that moral behaviour becomes a number that changes the character (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Keeping score
terms.text: Recording who is ahead as play goes on. One investment writer claimed that players would play for plastic beads instead of money, as long as there was a way to keep score.

terms.name: Key word
terms.text: In Guggenheim, a five-letter word whose letters give the starting letters for each column of the grid.

terms.name: Keywords
terms.text: Short labels on a pattern for the parts of a game it relates to, used to find it. The paper treats the domains of The 400 Project as the same thing as keywords.

terms.name: Kicker
terms.text: An extra high card kept in the hand beside a pair when drawing.

terms.name: Killer
terms.text: In Bartle's list, a player who likes to impose their will on others, by attacking, blocking or dominating them.

terms.name: Killer (Assassin)
terms.text: A live game where each player has one target to eliminate and inherits the victim's target, and the last player left wins.

terms.name: Killer (darts)
terms.text: A darts player who has hit their own number five times and can now take hits off opponents.

terms.name: Kim's Game
terms.text: A memory game from Kipling's novel Kim. Objects are laid on a tray, looked at for a minute, covered, and the player writes down all that can be recalled.

terms.name: Kinds of play
terms.text: The authors' way of sorting games by what players do, such as compete, cooperate, perform or simulate, instead of by genre. The kinds can be blended.

terms.name: King
terms.text: A piece promoted from an ordinary piece in draughts, able to move backwards as well as forwards.

terms.name: King (checkers)
terms.text: A checkers piece that has reached the far row and is marked by a second piece stacked on it. It can then move both forwards and backwards.

terms.name: King game
terms.text: A parish game, often at Whitsun, in which locals chose a king, sometimes a queen too, to preside over feasts and entertainments. The king could be a fool figure, and bowers were built in the fields.

terms.name: King of the castle
terms.text: A children's game in which one child stands on top and claims the place and another knocks the king off and takes it. The book treats it as a very old game that at puberty turns into a life situation.

terms.name: King's row
terms.text: The far row of a checkers board, which a piece has to reach to be crowned.

terms.name: Kinger
terms.text: A special piece in Parton's game Kinger. It can be captured only by an enemy kinger, and it may not end a capture on the edge of the board.

terms.name: Kingmaking
terms.text: A player with no chance of winning choosing which of two contenders will win, by choosing whom to affect. It needs targeted interaction and a player who is logically eliminated.

terms.name: Kitty
terms.text: A common pool of chips that collects payments on certain bids and is shared out when the session ends.

terms.name: Knock
terms.text: To end a hand by declaring it over, usually with a rap on the table, so that all hands are shown and counted.

terms.name: Knocking
terms.text: Signalling you are satisfied with your hand by knocking on the table, after which the others get one last draw.

terms.name: Knocking
terms.text: In knock rummy and gin, ending the hand by laying down ten cards and showing a low deadwood total.

terms.name: Know-your-place aggression
terms.text: Koritha Mitchell's phrase for the hostility that meets people from marginalized groups when they win or succeed.

terms.name: Knowledge-based recommendation
terms.text: A recommendation method that suggests items matching needs the user has stated.

terms.name: Knuckling down
terms.text: The marbles stance in which a player rests a knuckle on the ground and flicks the shooter with the thumb, instead of pushing with the hand.

terms.name: Ko fight
terms.text: A struggle in which each player makes forcing threats elsewhere to be allowed to repeat the move the ko rule forbids. It goes on until one player runs out of threats.

terms.name: Ko rule
terms.text: A rule that stops a move from recreating a board position that has appeared before, so play cannot repeat forever. The superko rule covers repeats across the whole board.

terms.name: Ko rule
terms.text: A Go rule that bans a move which would bring back the board as it stood after the same player's last turn. It stops endless repeating.

terms.name: Ko threat
terms.text: In a ko fight, a move elsewhere on the board that the opponent has to answer, which changes the position so that the forbidden reply becomes legal.

terms.name: Komi
terms.text: A point bonus given to one player in go, usually 7 and a half to white, to offset black's advantage of moving first. The half point stops ties.

terms.name: Komi
terms.text: Points added to the second player's score in Go to make up for the first player's advantage.

terms.name: Komos
terms.text: A noisy festive procession at the feast of Dionysus. Huizinga says Greek comedy grew out of it.

terms.name: Konakis
terms.text: The central square or throne in the Lapp game Tablut. Only the king may stand on it.

terms.name: Koyemshis
terms.text: Clown figures of the Zuni who tease the audience, mock the other spirits and are rewarded with gifts at the end of the festival. Their behaviour follows ritual.

terms.name: Kredati
terms.text: A Sanskrit word for play that covers adults, children and animals, and especially sudden, lively movement. Caillois compares it to paidia.

terms.name: Kvell
terms.text: The glow of boasting about someone you mentor.

terms.name: Kyu
terms.text: A rank in Go for amateur players. The difference in kyu between two players sets how many handicap stones the less powerful one gets.

terms.name: La perruque
terms.text: De Certeau's term for doing your own work while on someone else's time.

terms.name: Labile
terms.text: Easily changed or upset. Huizinga uses it of the play-mood, which can collapse when real life breaks in.

terms.name: Ladder
terms.text: In Halma, a line of pieces set up so that a moving piece can leap along it several times in one turn.

terms.name: Lag
terms.text: A way of deciding who goes first in marbles. Each player shoots a marble toward a line, and the one that ends up closest goes first.

terms.name: Language game (secret language)
terms.text: Play that changes ordinary speech by a rule, such as pig latin, Verlan or invented gibberish, often passed on by word of mouth.

terms.name: Lap
terms.text: One circuit of sowing. In Chisolo a move may consist of several laps.

terms.name: Lap game
terms.text: A Euchre variant where points scored beyond the five needed for a win carry over to the next game.

terms.name: Larvae
terms.text: Latin for distorted or monstrous masks. Church rules told clerics not to wear them, and Innocent III objected to "masks of monsters" in churches.

terms.name: Last licks
terms.text: A final turn given to players who have had one turn fewer than the player who finished first, so that going first is not a built-in gain.

terms.name: Lasting interest test
terms.text: The author's measure of a game: whether players become more or less eager to play again after playing it many times.

terms.name: Lateral thinking
terms.text: Reaching a goal by a route outside the obvious one. Koster sees it in the cheat who chooses a wider battlefield than the game offers.

terms.name: Law (head start)
terms.text: In fox hunting, the advantage given to the quarry before the chase begins. A fox hunter said the quarry be given considerable law, so the contest would be fair.

terms.name: Lay
terms.text: Three or more cards of the same rank in Rummy.

terms.name: Layers of player experience
terms.text: Five stages through which a player meets a game: sensory, information, interaction, frame and purpose.

terms.name: Laying off
terms.text: Adding a card from your hand to a set already on the table, your own or an opponent's.

terms.name: Laying off
terms.text: In rummy, adding a card to a meld already on the table, including an opponent's.

terms.name: Layout
terms.text: Markings on a table for placing bets, or the array of cards first dealt out in solitaire.

terms.name: Layout
terms.text: The line of dominoes growing on the table. Players add to its open ends.

terms.name: Layout
terms.text: In solitaire, the arrangement of cards on the table that the player works from. Klondike's layout is seven columns of 1 to 7 cards.

terms.name: Lead
terms.text: To play the first card of a trick. The card led sets the suit the others have to follow.

terms.name: Lead
terms.text: Playing the first card of a trick or hand. The player to the dealer's left usually leads first.

terms.name: Lead object and release object
terms.text: In Chain Reaction, a lead object (a Starbucks cup) sends the walker off in the direction it is moving. A release object (an independent bookshop) lets the walker stop.

terms.name: Leaner
terms.text: In horseshoes, a shoe resting against the stake. It scores in home play but not in official play.

terms.name: Learner testing
terms.text: Lewis Johnson's name for playtesting that checks whether players learn what the game was meant to teach, not only whether they enjoy it (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Learning curve
terms.text: How the difficulty of a game rises as the player gets more skilled.

terms.name: Learning objective
terms.text: A sentence saying what players are meant to be able to do or understand after playing. Swain advises writing these first and ranking them so each rule can be tuned to them (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Left-digit effect
terms.text: Reading numbers from the left, so that $19.99 looks clearly smaller than $20.00.

terms.name: Leg
terms.text: A single round of a dice game like Indian Dice. Two players play to two legs out of three.

terms.name: Legacy game
terms.text: A game whose components are permanently changed by play, so that the next session starts from a different board.

terms.name: Leisure
terms.text: Free time spent on chosen, active pursuits, which the book treats as an invention of the industrial age as much as a goal in itself.

terms.name: Lemonade
terms.text: A children's game where one team mimes a trade and the other guesses it, then the guessers chase the miming team to a base line. DeKoven calls the miming part a prelude to tag.

terms.name: Lens
terms.text: Jesse Schell's form of a design tool: a numbered title, a description and a set of questions the designer asks about their game from one point of view. His book has 113 lenses.

terms.name: Leopard
terms.text: In Cows and Leopards, one of the two pieces that kill cows by jumping over them.

terms.name: Let
terms.text: A serve in table tennis that touches the net and still lands on the other side. It is replayed with no limit on the number of lets.

terms.name: Levees
terms.text: The old name for tricks, used in French Boston, where bids are counted in levees.

terms.name: Level
terms.text: A stage in a game with a set threshold. Wark says that a higher level is only more of the same quantity as a lower one, whatever name it is given.

terms.name: Level playing field
terms.text: A contest in which the ground gives no side an advantage. The book says American belief that life is a game rests on a field that may or may not be level.

terms.name: Level playing field
terms.text: A phrase for a world where everyone starts equal and the rules are the same for all. Wark notes that the phrase hides who owns the teams and who writes the rules.

terms.name: Level up
terms.text: To move on to a higher level in a game after meeting its demands.

terms.name: Leveling up
terms.text: Earning points that raise a character's level, which then opens harder work.

terms.name: Leveling versus lifting
terms.text: A way to change the wording of a goal. It aims at an even field for all groups, such as checking pay for gaps, in place of help for one group.

terms.name: Liberty
terms.text: In Go, an empty point next to a stone or group. A group with no liberties is captured.

terms.name: Liberty
terms.text: An empty point next to a stone in Go. A stone or group with no liberties left is captured.

terms.name: Liberty (breathing space)
terms.text: An empty point next to a stone or group of stones in Go. A group with none is captured.

terms.name: Library of agencies
terms.text: The idea that the games people have made form a store of recorded ways of acting, which later players can enter and learn from.

terms.name: Library of socialities
terms.text: The idea that multiplayer games store many social arrangements, such as a team, shifting alliances or uneven powers, which players can step into and try.

terms.name: Licence
terms.text: Written permission to stage a play. Elizabeth's proclamation of 1559 banned interludes unless notice was given beforehand and a licence issued.

terms.name: Licensed game
terms.text: A game whose conceit is an intellectual property rented from someone else, such as a game of a television series.

terms.name: Life
terms.text: A token a player loses when wrong in Liar Dice. A player with no lives is out.

terms.name: Life hacking
terms.text: Looking for simple tips and tricks to improve everyday productivity, such as working ten minutes then resting two.

terms.name: Life theme
terms.text: A set of goals tied to one ultimate goal that gives meaning to what a person does. The book compares it to the rules of a game.

terms.name: Life-management ARG
terms.text: An alternate reality game that is software or a service for managing real life like a game, such as Chore Wars.

terms.name: Lifeboat dilemma
terms.text: A classic ethics puzzle in which not everyone can be saved. In Knights of Astrus, escape pods fit twelve but need eight people to launch, and a stroke victim needs a seat (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Lifter
terms.text: The author's name for a player who uses an insider position to open chances for others as well, even when it is awkward or unpopular.

terms.name: Lightweight asynchronous collaboration
terms.text: Working together without being online at the same moment, by sharing creations that others later pick up.

terms.name: Likert scale
terms.text: A rating scale of statements answered from strongly disagree to strongly agree, with the five answers scored 1 to 5.

terms.name: Lily pads
terms.text: A picture for how some people advance, by hopping between organisations, in place of climbing a ladder inside one. The author says it fits women and people of colour more than White men.

terms.name: Liminal
terms.text: Turner's word for a threshold period in which a group of players may rework the usual conventions of their culture.

terms.name: Limit
terms.text: A top amount a player can win in one hand, so one lucky hand does not break a table.

terms.name: Limit (betting)
terms.text: The largest amount any one bet or raise may be in a game of Poker, agreed before play.

terms.name: Line (box) bonus
terms.text: A fixed bonus added for each hand a player won during a game, counted after the game ends.

terms.name: Line of scrimmage
terms.text: The spot where the last runner was tagged, from which the next play starts.

terms.name: List and network collections
terms.text: A list is a plain set of patterns. A network is a set in which patterns have relationships to each other, such as parent, child or related.

terms.name: Listen
terms.text: The playtest task of hearing players talk through what they do, why they choose and how they feel.

terms.name: Listicle
terms.text: An article built as a numbered list. The number in the title tells the reader how many items and so how much time to spend.

terms.name: Literalism
terms.text: Showing a story exactly as written so that gaps and puzzles in it show too. The book argues that playing a text on stage forced out questions that a commentary would have settled.

terms.name: Liturgical parody
terms.text: A mocking copy of church ritual, usually by choirboys or lower clergy in the days after Christmas. An example is the Padua Herod, who bursts into the choir in an untidy tunic and strikes people with an inflated bladder.

terms.name: Live coding
terms.text: The authors' term for changing a game's code and testing straight away, to see how the change alters play.

terms.name: Live event ARG
terms.text: An alternate reality game that gathers players at physical places for a game of an hour or a day.

terms.name: Live-action roleplaying
terms.text: A game in which participants take on the roles of people in a complex situation and act out their decisions in person (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Liveness (of an object)
terms.text: Höch-style objects carry a look of wanting to be acted on, shown by signs of past collision and by shapes that invite handling.

terms.name: Living document
terms.text: A document updated every time the team goes round the design cycle, so it always shows the current understanding of the game.

terms.name: Loaded dice
terms.text: Dice weighted so they land the way their owner wants. A 1904 magazine writer used the phrase for the inside information that bankers hold and others lack.

terms.name: Loading
terms.text: In Russian Bank, placing your spare cards on the opponent's piles to get rid of them.

terms.name: Local champion
terms.text: The person in a community who wins at every kind of contest, such as Billy Kirby in Cooper's The Pioneers. The type returns in later Westerns.

terms.name: Local multiplayer game
terms.text: A videogame played by two or more people in the same room in front of one screen.

terms.name: Located media
terms.text: Flanagan's term for everyday media tied to a place and the people in it, such as community and grassroots projects, set against high-technology locative media.

terms.name: Location-based game
terms.text: A game that uses a phone's GPS and can be played only in a certain place.

terms.name: Locative game
terms.text: A game played in real places, where the spot a player stands on changes what the rules give them. Phones, GPS or paper maps often track where players are.

terms.name: Locative media
terms.text: Art and games made with GPS, mobile phones and maps, so that position in a city becomes part of the work.

terms.name: Logic of iteration
terms.text: Meeting a problem in a story by repeating the main pattern again instead of explaining it. Towneley repeats the plan of providence after Christ's prayer in the garden.

terms.name: Logical elimination
terms.text: Having no chance of winning but still having to play, which sports call mathematical elimination.

terms.name: London aesthetic
terms.text: The taste of London's court and ruling guilds for elaborate display and formal speech, not narrative scenes with dialogue. Fully acted biblical or moral scripts were not given in London proper until well into the sixteenth century.

terms.name: Lone hand
terms.text: Playing a hand without a partner in return for a larger score.

terms.name: Long die
terms.text: A four-sided die, shaped like a long stick, used in Egyptian games.

terms.name: Long die
terms.text: A four-sided die marked 2, 3, 4 and 5, used in Shaturanga to decide which piece moves.

terms.name: Long leap
terms.text: A jump over an enemy piece to land beyond it, where empty spaces may lie on either side of the captured piece.

terms.name: Long-range task
terms.text: A guidepost of the whole design, such as reaching a first core prototype.

terms.name: Looed
terms.text: Taking no trick in a round of Loo, which sets a player back five points or makes them add to the next pool.

terms.name: Loophole
terms.text: A gap in the wording of a rule that lets a player gain an advantage without breaking the rule. American football coaches in the 1890s looked for them and then new rules were written to close them.

terms.name: Loose tiles
terms.text: The two tiles at the end of the Mahjong wall used to replace tiles drawn to complete a hand.

terms.name: Lord of Misrule
terms.text: A Christmas ruler of revels chosen in colleges. Cambridge used the figure to channel rowdiness, and in 1548 the university ordered that no one be lord of games at Christmas under any name.

terms.name: Lose condition
terms.text: A rule that ends play in a loss. Burgun says permanent death in a roguelike is only this, not proof that the player has been cheated.

terms.name: Loss aversion
terms.text: The tendency to feel a loss about twice as strongly as a gain of the same size, from prospect theory.

terms.name: Loss of self-consciousness
terms.text: Not worrying about how one looks or who one is while absorbed in an activity. The person is still aware, but not of the self.

terms.name: Lot
terms.text: A method of choosing by chance, such as drawing marked stones or dice, used in the Bible to divide land or choose a replacement apostle. Believers read the result as God's choice, not as luck.

terms.name: Lottery (simple, complex, continuing)
terms.text: A simple lottery has one draw; a complex lottery has many possible combinations; a continuing lottery has two or more stages, the first winner entering a second draw.

terms.name: Lotus
terms.text: In the game Lotus, the six points around one of the seven hexagons on the board. A group holding a lotus can never be captured.

terms.name: Low poker (lowball)
terms.text: A form of poker where the lowest hand wins.

terms.name: Lowest common gaming denominator
terms.text: The skill level of the least experienced player in a group. A family game is built so that this player can take part (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Luck and pluck
terms.text: Two ingredients thought to make success: luck is chance and pluck is determined effort. Nineteenth-century writers on success agreed that both were needed and argued over how much each counted.

terms.name: Ludeme
terms.text: Ben Cousins's name for a basic unit of play, such as get to the other side or visit every location. Koster says checkers has just two.

terms.name: Ludeme
terms.text: A conceptual element of a game, usually a rule rather than a physical component. The paper adopts Browne's wording: a unit of information that can be moved from one game to another and changes how the game works in at least one plausible case.

terms.name: Ludi inhonesti
terms.text: Latin for dishonourable games: the rowdy, immoral pastimes that church writers tried to stop, as against religious plays.

terms.name: Ludi theatrales
terms.text: A label Pope Innocent III gave to disorderly games held inside churches and monasteries at certain times of year. The word "theatrical" here meant improper, not staged.

terms.name: Ludic imperative
terms.text: Olli Leino's name for the assumption that to study a game one has to play it in the spirit its designer intended. Leino objects to it; the author does not.

terms.name: Ludic loop
terms.text: The anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll's name for a steady stream of small challenges and rewards at a set pace, as in video slot machines, which keeps people playing without the play being interesting.

terms.name: Ludimagister
terms.text: The Latin word for a school's master of games, a schoolmaster who writes and stages plays. The book wonders whether the Wakefield Master was one.

terms.name: Ludo-textual analysis
terms.text: Booth's method of reading a game as both a made object and an experience of play, looking at how players actually use the objects.

terms.name: Ludonarrative dissonance
terms.text: A clash between what a game's story says and what its play asks the player to do; Travis argues that Bioshock uses it to comment on its own ethics (chapter by Roger Travis).

terms.name: Ludum Dare
terms.text: A 48-hour game jam built around a theme. A call for 10-second games inspired Queers in Love at the End of the World.

terms.name: Ludus
terms.text: The pole of play marked by arbitrary rules, effort and skill, where difficulty is added on purpose. A crossword puzzle sits at this end.

terms.name: Ludus
terms.text: Caillois's name for structured play held in place by rules, such as a tournament game played with miniatures.

terms.name: Ludus (plural ludi)
terms.text: The Latin word for play. It covered games, sports, music-making and acted scripts, so the word alone does not say which of these a record means.

terms.name: Lurched
terms.text: Losing a game of Cribbage before the loser passes the halfway mark, which counts as a double loss.

terms.name: Lusory attitude
terms.text: Bernard Suits's name for the willingness to follow a game's rules, since the game cannot happen unless players go along with them.

terms.name: Lusory attitude
terms.text: Bernard Suits' name for players' willingness to accept a harder or less direct way of doing something for the sake of the play it brings.

terms.name: Lusory attitude
terms.text: The state of mind in which a person accepts the goal and the rules for the sake of the activity they make possible.

terms.name: Lusory goal
terms.text: Reaching the pre-lusory goal while obeying the rules. In basketball this is making a basket, not merely getting the ball through the hoop.

terms.name: Lusory lots
terms.text: Increase Mather's name for gambling with dice and cards. He forbade it as blasphemy because the lot belonged to God.

terms.name: Lynching
terms.text: In Mafia, the group vote that removes one player from the game each day.

terms.name: Machine zone
terms.text: The state described by long-time slot machine gamblers in which awareness of the world, time and self falls away.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: Huizinga's name for the marked-off space and time in which play happens, set apart from everyday surroundings, whether by a drawn line or by agreement.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: Huizinga's idea of a marked-off space, such as a card table, a stage or a tennis court, inside which special rules apply while people play.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: The bounded space in which play happens, set apart from everyday life. Inside it ordinary customs stop counting and special rules apply.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: The idea, from Huizinga, that a game is a protected space cut off from ordinary life, where its rules hold and outside actions do not count. Koster uses it to separate moves inside a game from cheating that reaches beyond it.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: The social space of a game inside which players agree to act outside ordinary habits. A crowd playing together makes the circle feel safer.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: Huizinga's idea of a bounded space and time for play that is set apart from ordinary life, with its own rules. Later writers argue about how sealed it is.

terms.name: Magic circle
terms.text: Huizinga's name for the invisible edge between a game and ordinary life. Macklin notes that in a street game it blurs, because passers-by are drawn into play (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Mahjong (going out)
terms.text: Completing a hand of 14 tiles in the game of Mahjong, made of groups and a pair, which ends the round.

terms.name: Maieutic end
terms.text: An end that is reached by coming to have other ends, such as settling on a career. Once the new end is found, it stands on its own.

terms.name: Main and chance
terms.text: In Hazard, the two numbers set by throws. The caster wins by repeating the chance before throwing the main, and loses if he throws the main first.

terms.name: Main chance
terms.text: An opening that a person can seize, as against luck that simply happens to them. The book says the naturalist writers moved chance from a check on effort to a source of openings.

terms.name: Mainline and sideline
terms.text: In Eleusis, the row of accepted cards and the columns of rejected cards beneath it that together show the pattern players have to infer.

terms.name: Mais d'or
terms.text: A Haitian children's game in which two children hold hands, lean back and turn until breathless, then stagger about. It is a game of dizziness.

terms.name: Majority judgment
terms.text: A method of Balinski and Laraki in which each voter grades each candidate and the candidate with the highest median grade wins.

terms.name: Make-believe
terms.text: Knowing that a thing is only pretended while still playing it fully. Huizinga finds this double awareness in children, actors and ritual.

terms.name: Make-believe
terms.text: Play in which the players agree to treat things as something else, such as lath swords or a Sunday School outing as an army. It works only while everyone shares the pretence.

terms.name: Maker
terms.text: The player who decides the trump suit and so takes on the risk of the hand.

terms.name: Maker
terms.text: In Euchre, the player who accepts or names the trump suit. The maker's side has to win three tricks of five.

terms.name: Making a point
terms.text: Putting two or more pieces on one point so that the opponent cannot land there.

terms.name: Man and king (checkers)
terms.text: Unpromoted pieces are men and promoted ones are kings. Kings in International Checkers move any distance along a diagonal and capture from afar.

terms.name: Man in the box
terms.text: In Chouette, the single player who plays against a team led by a captain.

terms.name: Mancala
terms.text: A word for all the games in which seeds or stones are lifted from pits and dropped one by one into the pits beyond. Taken from the Arabic Mankala'h.

terms.name: Mancala
terms.text: A family of counting, sowing and capture games played on rows of hollows with seeds or stones, found across Africa, the Middle East and South India under many names.

terms.name: Mancala
terms.text: The oldest known game, a counting game played in Egypt between about the fifteenth and eleventh centuries BC.

terms.name: Mancala
terms.text: A family of games from Africa, Asia and South America played by moving seeds or pebbles round rows of pits.

terms.name: Mancala
terms.text: A family of ancient African seed-sowing games played on rows of pits or bowls. Wari is the simplest of them.

terms.name: Mancala game
terms.text: One of R. C. Bell's six ancient groups, also called sowing or count-and-capture games.

terms.name: Mandatory capture
terms.text: A rule that a player has to jump an enemy piece whenever a jump is possible. It takes some choice away from the player and makes moves easier to predict.

terms.name: Manilla
terms.text: In Solo, the Seven of whichever suit is trump, ranking second.

terms.name: Map hack
terms.text: A program that shows the parts of a Starcraft map hidden by fog of war.

terms.name: Map-colouring game
terms.text: A paper game in which players colour regions of a drawn map under rules about which neighbouring regions may share a colour.

terms.name: Marbles (as currency)
terms.text: Small balls children win and lose, which also buy sweets, knives and help with homework. Caillois says they quickly form a true money system.

terms.name: March
terms.text: In Euchre, winning all five tricks, which scores two points.

terms.name: March
terms.text: Winning all five tricks in a hand of Euchre.

terms.name: March
terms.text: In Euchre, winning all five tricks in a hand.

terms.name: Marker track
terms.text: A strip of spaces on paper with a marker. In Lotus and Medusa a pass moves the marker toward the passer, and the position at the end gives points. It works as komi and as a handicap.

terms.name: Marriage
terms.text: In Pinochle, a King and Queen of the same suit, melded for 20 points, or 40 in the trump suit.

terms.name: Marriage
terms.text: A king and queen of one suit shown together to score points.

terms.name: Marriage
terms.text: In Pinochle, a king and queen of one suit. It scores 20 points, or 40 in the trump suit.

terms.name: Marshall and cardinal
terms.text: In Grand Chess, a marshall moves as a rook or knight and a cardinal as a bishop or knight.

terms.name: Mask (as play)
terms.text: A disguise worn in play to change who the wearer seems to be. At a carnival the masked person does not claim to be the character, only enjoys the freedom the disguise gives.

terms.name: Massively multiplayer game
terms.text: A game where the number of people a player deals with is much smaller than the number playing, such as World of Warcraft or pari-mutuel betting.

terms.name: Massively multiplayer online game
terms.text: A game on a remote server where thousands of players share one world at once. World of Warcraft is the example.

terms.name: Massively single-player online game
terms.text: Will Wright's name for a game played alone in which much of the world is made by other players and downloaded into each person's copy. Spore is the example.

terms.name: The master's house
terms.text: David Thomas's name for both the mental and the material space built by those in power. Part of leaving it in your mind is knowing it is not your only source of support.

terms.name: The master's tools
terms.text: Audre Lorde's phrase, which the author takes to mean that the owner's tools may win a round but will not rebuild the house. He reads it as asking you not to depend on those tools, and not as a ban on using them.

terms.name: Mastermind
terms.text: A code game where one player sets a hidden row of coloured pegs and the other guesses it. The setter replies with pegs that show how many colours and positions are right.

terms.name: Mastery
terms.text: Having worked a game out so fully that no choice is left to explore. Burgun wants it to stay out of reach even for a very long-time player.

terms.name: Mastery goals
terms.text: Goals of learning as much as possible about a subject, driven by a wish to know.

terms.name: Mastery Problem
terms.text: The trap where skilled players keep winning, while beginners are knocked out in the first match before they can learn.

terms.name: Matador
terms.text: In the Matador game, a tile that can be played anywhere, since its ends add to ten with a neighbouring end.

terms.name: Matador
terms.text: In the domino game of that name, a tile that may be played anywhere without matching, since ends are matched by totalling seven.

terms.name: Matador
terms.text: In the domino game of that name, a tile whose halves add up to seven, or the double blank. It can be placed where no other tile fits.

terms.name: Matador (domino)
terms.text: In the domino game of Matador, a tile that can be played anywhere, because the usual matching rule is to make seven.

terms.name: Matadores
terms.text: The four Jacks in Skat, which are the highest trumps. Holding or lacking them in unbroken order raises or lowers the value of a bid.

terms.name: Matadors
terms.text: The top trumps held in unbroken order from the jack of clubs. Counting how many a hand has or lacks raises or lowers the value of the game.

terms.name: Match
terms.text: One session of play of a game. The game as a rule set only happens when somebody plays a match.

terms.name: Match
terms.text: A series of games agreed on as enough play to settle who the winner is, often a win of two games out of three.

terms.name: Match by suit or rank
terms.text: A rule in which a played card has to share either the suit or the number of the card before it.

terms.name: Matching pennies
terms.text: A two-player simultaneous game where one player wins if two secret choices of heads or tails match and the other wins if they differ. Move and countermove fights often work this way.

terms.name: Matchpoint
terms.text: In duplicate bridge, a point earned for each rival you outscore on the same deal, and half a point for each tie.

terms.name: Material basis
terms.text: The physical or coded stuff of a work, which anyone may handle in any way, as opposed to the work itself, which is met by following the prescriptions.

terms.name: Matthew effect
terms.text: Robert Merton's name for the way small differences are enlarged because those who start ahead receive more resources and so move further ahead.

terms.name: Maximizer
terms.text: A person who searches for the highest-valued option among those on offer.

terms.name: Maximum capture rule
terms.text: A rule that when there is a choice of captures, the player has to take the route that removes the most pieces.

terms.name: Maximum-capture rule
terms.text: A rule that forces the player to pick the jump sequence that captures the most pieces, as in International Checkers.

terms.name: Mayor
terms.text: In Foursquare, the title held by whoever has checked in most often at a place, which another player can take away.

terms.name: MDA framework
terms.text: A way of analysing games in layers, set out by Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek. The chapter uses it as rules, mechanics and aesthetics.

terms.name: Meaning
terms.text: The feeling of being part of something bigger than yourself, so that your actions matter beyond your own life. The book separates it from value.

terms.name: Meaningful choice
terms.text: A choice a player in fact weighs. It depends on skill, since the same position may give a beginner no meaningful choices and an expert only a few.

terms.name: Meaningful choice
terms.text: Letting each player pick their own task from a pool, so that nobody is assigned a job and every task is taken voluntarily.

terms.name: Meaningful decision
terms.text: A choice whose effects spread through the system and change later play. Burgun contrasts it with a choice that only carries emotional meaning from the theme.

terms.name: Meaningful play
terms.text: Salen and Zimmerman's name for the designer's work of building situations in which a player's choices carry weight in the game.

terms.name: Meaningful possibilities
terms.text: Moves that differ in what they mean inside the rules. Go has many more of these than raw moves counted by ignoring their effects.

terms.name: Mechanic
terms.text: An action players take in a game, such as move, build, trade or treat. The book follows Sicart: methods players use to act on the game state.

terms.name: Mechanic
terms.text: A feature of a board game, as tagged on BoardGameGeek, that captures one side of how the game works: how it is set up, how resources and powers are shared out, what triggers a win, how turns run, or how actions are carried out. The paper works with 182 of these tags.

terms.name: Mechanic
terms.text: In Swain's use, both what a player does in a game (run, jump, negotiate) and how the game responds. The mechanics are where the player meets the game (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Mechanism and mechanic
terms.text: The paper treats a mechanism as the smallest mechanical element of a game, and a mechanic as a combination of mechanisms in motion. It says the literature often uses the two words as if they meant the same.

terms.name: Mechanistic fallacy
terms.text: The mistake of expecting that joining a flow activity guarantees the experience. What counts is the challenge and skill the person perceives.

terms.name: Media effects
terms.text: A way of talking about games that asks what a game does to the player.

terms.name: Media ethics
terms.text: A way of talking about games that asks what the player does with the game.

terms.name: Median
terms.text: The value that splits a set of numbers into a higher half and a lower half.

terms.name: Medium
terms.text: A channel for conveying patterns. Koster says game is not a medium but one use of one, which he calls formal abstract models for teaching patterns.

terms.name: Medium of sociality
terms.text: The social relationships between players, which a multiplayer designer shapes by giving each player a goal, abilities and obstacles.

terms.name: Meld
terms.text: A set of cards in a particular combination shown face up to score points, as in Pinochle.

terms.name: Meld
terms.text: To put a set of cards face up on the table so that it counts for scoring or for going out.

terms.name: Meld
terms.text: A group of cards laid on the table for points, such as a marriage in Pinochle, or a set or sequence in rummy.

terms.name: Meld (scoring combination)
terms.text: In Pinochle, a named combination of cards, such as a marriage or four aces, shown for points before or during play.

terms.name: Melding
terms.text: Laying down certain combinations of cards from the hand for points, as in pinochle.

terms.name: Meme
terms.text: A story or idea that passes between people and cultures and survives or fades by a kind of selection. The authors use it to explain why some tales last for centuries (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Memento mori game
terms.text: A game that reminds the player they are mortal, through features such as one life, fixed endings and slow movement, as Jason Rohrer calls his game Passage (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Mental model
terms.text: A player's picture of how a game works, which can differ from how it actually works and which grows as they play.

terms.name: Mental skill
terms.text: Skill in thinking, such as remembering a path and tracing its mirror image in The Witness.

terms.name: Mental work
terms.text: Play that exercises thinking, either in short bursts like timed sums or over long campaigns like a ten-thousand-year strategy game.

terms.name: Merci
terms.text: An extra move allowed once a solitaire has stalled, such as dealing the last cards or pulling out one card, to give the player a last chance.

terms.name: Merging of action and awareness
terms.text: The experience of being so absorbed that the person stops noticing themselves apart from what they are doing.

terms.name: Message Model of Meaning
terms.text: Frank Lantz's phrase for the view that an author puts a message into a work and the audience receives it intact. Sharp says games fit it badly (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

terms.name: The meta
terms.text: The shifting set of popular decks and strategies among a game's players, which each player has to respond to when building a deck.

terms.name: Meta-gaming
terms.text: Finding one's own goals in a game that its designers did not intend, or playing with the system, such as competing to run over the most pedestrians (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Metagame
terms.text: A game wrapped round another game, such as unlockables, high-score boards or customisation. Burgun says it can lower the weight of choices in the main game.

terms.name: Metagame
terms.text: The game outside the game: preparation, forums, tournaments, stories and other activities around a game that are not the play itself. Hardcore players also use the word for the current mix of decks or strategies in use.

terms.name: Meter
terms.text: A bar graph on screen that shows how a character is doing, such as hunger or sleep. In The Sims the bars drift toward empty unless the player acts.

terms.name: Methectic
terms.text: A Greek word meaning taking part. Huizinga says a rite is methectic rather than mimetic, because the people join in the event itself instead of only copying it.

terms.name: Microflow
terms.text: A small patterned action, such as doodling or humming, that people use to fill dull gaps. It lowers boredom but adds little.

terms.name: Microgame
terms.text: A very short game of a few seconds. WarioWare: Smooth Moves has over two hundred, each asking for a quick silly movement.

terms.name: Microinteraction
terms.text: A small contact between strangers, such as a smile, a thank-you, an eye roll or a bump, counted in the jen ratio.

terms.name: Micropayment
terms.text: A very small sum of money paid for one small contribution to a crowd project.

terms.name: Mid-range task
terms.text: A significant milestone, such as finishing a prototype or the art direction. Long-range tasks are made of these.

terms.name: Might-do list
terms.text: A list of possible tasks from which one big thing is chosen for the day, so that planning and doing are kept as two separate stages.

terms.name: Mill
terms.text: In Nine Men's Morris, a row of three pieces along a line. Forming one lets a player remove an enemy piece.

terms.name: Mill (morris)
terms.text: Three pieces of one colour in a line, which allows the owner to remove an opposing piece.

terms.name: Mimesis
terms.text: The Greek idea of imitation, central to Aristotle on tragedy. Medieval readers working from Arabic commentary replaced it with "likening", a kind of picture that stirs feeling towards virtue.

terms.name: Mimesis
terms.text: In Roger Travis's usage, identificative performance: pretending to be somebody else, as in acting in a tragedy, reading a dialogue or playing a video game (chapter by Roger Travis).

terms.name: Mimesis
terms.text: Play of pretending, imitation and show. It is Caillois's name for the kind of play built on make-believe and spectacle.

terms.name: Mimetic
terms.text: Imitating or copying something. Huizinga contrasts it with taking real part in a sacred event.

terms.name: Mimicry
terms.text: Caillois's word for games of make-believe, where a player takes on another character or a pretend world. A child playing train and an actor on stage are examples.

terms.name: Mimicry
terms.text: In Caillois's scheme, activities that make an alternative reality by pretending, such as dance, theatre and children's make-believe.

terms.name: Miming
terms.text: Acting out a word or phrase in silence so that others can guess it.

terms.name: Mimis
terms.text: The author's shorthand for canon 16 of the Fourth Lateran Council (1215). It told clerics not to watch mimes, entertainers and actors, to avoid taverns, and not to play or watch dice and games of chance.

terms.name: Mini
terms.text: In Nike+, a small avatar that looks like the runner and reacts to how often and how far they run.

terms.name: Mini-game
terms.text: A small, short game. Bookchin's The Intruder links ten arcade-style mini-games along one story.

terms.name: Miniature
terms.text: A scaled-down figure of a character, creature or object, used for play and display. Its size is given as the height of a human figure in millimetres.

terms.name: Miniatures game (minis game)
terms.text: A wargame played with figures on a table, where units move a measured distance and not from space to space.

terms.name: Miniaturing
terms.text: The whole pastime built around miniatures: painting, converting, gaming, collecting, storytelling and showing them.

terms.name: Minimalism
terms.text: The principle that a work contains only as many strokes, words or rules as it needs. A thick rule book can still be minimal if each rule is needed.

terms.name: Minor pieces
terms.text: The knights and bishops in chess, named to tell them apart from queens and rooks.

terms.name: Miracula
terms.text: In English church records and preaching manuals, a word for rowdy activities like Innocent's ludi theatrales. It comes from an old Latin sense of "monstrosity" and did not mean miracle plays.

terms.name: Mirror match
terms.text: A game between two sides with the same character or set-up. Burgun says a sound design keeps these interesting.

terms.name: Mirror strategy
terms.text: Replying to every move with the move that is symmetrical about the centre of the board. In Epaminondas it makes the second player draw, so a rule bans moves that create left-to-right symmetry on the far row.

terms.name: Mirror-role
terms.text: The part a carer's face plays for a baby: the baby looks and sees itself, because the carer looks at the baby and her look is shaped by what she sees.

terms.name: Mirroring
terms.text: One of Simkins's four design principles: the game world and its characters reflect back the actions the player has taken (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Misdeal
terms.text: A dealing error, such as too many cards or an exposed card, that makes the deal start again.

terms.name: Misdeal
terms.text: A deal done wrongly, for example with a card shown or a wrong count of cards. The cards are thrown in and dealt again.

terms.name: Misdeal
terms.text: A dealing mistake that can be called before the first round of play. The cards are collected and dealt again.

terms.name: Misere
terms.text: A bid to win as few tricks as possible, in fact none. There is no trump in a misere hand.

terms.name: Misere
terms.text: A bid to take no counting cards at all.

terms.name: Misere
terms.text: A reversed form of a game in which the player who makes the last move or takes the last object loses.

terms.name: Misfire
terms.text: In Cruel 2 B Kind, a kind gesture aimed at someone who is not playing. The designers count it as a gain.

terms.name: Miss
terms.text: An extra hand dealt to the table in Loo that a player may swap for their own.

terms.name: Missile (Missile Chess)
terms.text: A checker under a piece that lets it capture a piece on a square it could move to without moving there. It can be used once.

terms.name: Mission
terms.text: A set task in a game with a clear reward. In Vice City each mission pays a fixed sum of money.

terms.name: Mistigris
terms.text: A Joker added to a Poker pack that its holder may name as any card not already in their hand.

terms.name: Mixed strategy
terms.text: A set of probabilities for playing each choice, such as one third each of rock, paper and scissors.

terms.name: Mixed strategy
terms.text: A way of playing in which choices are made at random in set proportions so that an opponent cannot predict them.

terms.name: MMORPG
terms.text: A massively multiplayer online role-playing game, in which very large numbers of players share one online world. EverQuest and World of Warcraft are examples.

terms.name: Mock battle
terms.text: A pretend fight put on inside a procession. Bristol in 1461 and Norwich in 1471 staged one for Saint George.

terms.name: Mod
terms.text: A player-made change to a computer game, from a small tweak to a total conversion.

terms.name: Mod
terms.text: A player-made change to a game's rules, art or content. Koster likens it to house rules in board games.

terms.name: Mod
terms.text: A change a player makes to a game's own files or contents so it plays differently. Wark says a theorist who mods does it to play more closely inside the game.

terms.name: Moderator
terms.text: A person who runs a hidden-role game such as Mafia. They know every role, announce what happens and settle disputes.

terms.name: Modern board games
terms.text: The recent hobby games that the paper studies. They can contain cards, boards, dice, pawns, miniatures and even electronic devices, and they centre on the players and their face-to-face decisions.

terms.name: Modular design
terms.text: A design where the core play can take in new elements such as extra characters, places or modes. Booth finds that crowdfunding favours it.

terms.name: Moira
terms.text: A Greek word for the portion each person is given by fate. Caillois uses it with tyche, luck, to describe birth as a kind of lottery.

terms.name: Moodboard
terms.text: A collection of images from comics, film, art and photographs used as reference points for how a game is meant to look. A sound version can be made from existing music.

terms.name: Moral action
terms.text: The ability to carry out a moral decision and see it through (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Moral competence and moral performance
terms.text: Bandura's split between knowing how to reason about right and wrong and actually behaving that way. A person can have the first and still not show the second (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Moral dilemma
terms.text: A choice between two or more claims that each carry real moral weight, as in the abortion or euthanasia debates (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Moral disengagement
terms.text: Bandura's term for the ways people switch off their sense of right and wrong, such as justifying an act, using soft labels, ignoring harm or treating victims as less than human (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Moral education
terms.text: An approach that builds moral behaviour through reasoning and reflection, for example by discussing dilemmas (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Moral engagement
terms.text: A player feeling a real moral emotion, such as guilt, about something that happens in the fiction of a game because of what the player did (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Moral improvement game
terms.text: A nineteenth-century board game meant to teach young people proper Christian living, such as The Mansion of Happiness (1800) and Virtue Rewarded and Vice Punished (1818). Players are rewarded or sent back by their conduct.

terms.name: Moral judgment
terms.text: The ability to reason about a moral question and make a moral choice (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Moral motivation
terms.text: The wish to act on a moral decision and to put it ahead of other concerns (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Moral sensitivity
terms.text: The ability to notice moral features of a situation and respond to them (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Moral temptation
terms.text: A situation where a person may feel excused in doing something plainly wrong, such as copying pirated music. It differs from a dilemma because only one side has a moral claim (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Morality game
terms.text: A game whose spaces and rules reward some behaviours and punish others, as in Mansion of Happiness, where idleness sends a player back to poverty.

terms.name: Morality play
terms.text: A play whose characters stand for qualities, such as World, Flesh and Devil, and which follows a person's fall and return through penance. The book treats the label as a loose one covering plays that differ in length, staging and action.

terms.name: Morality play
terms.text: A story in which characters stand for qualities and a central figure has to choose between them. The book reads Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises as one, with a true player, a false player and an Everyman in between.

terms.name: Morality scale
terms.text: A single sliding measure running from 'good' to 'evil' that a game moves according to a player's actions and which may change how characters treat the player (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Morally transformative technology
terms.text: The author's description of a game that turns an act that would hurt outside play, such as blocking or attacking, into an experience both players value.

terms.name: Morphology of conversion
terms.text: The fixed sequence of stages, each with signs a believer could check, that Puritan teachers said a saved soul passed through. Oriard compares it to the squares on a board game.

terms.name: Morra
terms.text: A children's and gamblers' guessing game on odd and even, played with marbles or fingers. Caillois uses it to show chance among children.

terms.name: Morris game
terms.text: A game played on a board of lines and points on which pieces are placed and then moved to make rows of three.

terms.name: Mortgage value
terms.text: In Monopoly, the sum the bank pays when a property is mortgaged. In Auction Monopoly it is the lowest allowed opening bid.

terms.name: Motivation
terms.text: The angle a designer takes on a game, such as what the player does, a constraint, a story or a personal experience.

terms.name: Motivational inversion
terms.text: In ordinary life people pursue means for the sake of ends. In a game a player takes up an end, such as getting a ball in a net, for the sake of the activity of pursuing it.

terms.name: MUD
terms.text: A text-based multiuser dungeon, an early online world run by typed commands. The authors trace today's online role-playing games back to MUDs and their object-oriented cousins, MOOs (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Muggins
terms.text: A rule that lets an opponent claim any score you missed in counting.

terms.name: Muggins points (dominoes)
terms.text: Points scored by a play that makes the total of the open ends a multiple of five.

terms.name: Multiplayer game
terms.text: In this book, a game with at least three sides. Two-player games and two-team games are not counted.

terms.name: Multiplayer solitaire
terms.text: Games where players can do very little to each other through the rules, so each plays almost alone, and the scores are compared at the end.

terms.name: Multiple capture
terms.text: Capturing more than one piece in one move by a chain of jumps, with a change of direction allowed.

terms.name: Multiple intelligences
terms.text: Howard Gardner's list of seven kinds of ability, including spatial, musical and interpersonal. Koster uses it to say different people take to different games.

terms.name: Multiple jump
terms.text: Capturing several pieces in one turn by jumping again from the square landed on.

terms.name: Multiple jump
terms.text: Several jumps made in one turn by the same piece. In checkers the player has to keep jumping as long as another jump is open.

terms.name: Multiple victory conditions
terms.text: Several different ways to win in one game, such as reducing life to zero or emptying the deck in Magic.

terms.name: Multiple-criteria decision making
terms.text: Ordering choices when each choice has several properties that pull in different directions, such as price and quality.

terms.name: Mumming
terms.text: An entertainment in which disguised figures arrive at a feast, typically introduced by a presenter, and end with a gift, a song or a dance. Lydgate wrote mummings for London guilds and for the court.

terms.name: Muscle memory
terms.text: The common name for skills done without conscious thought. Koster says the work is really done by nerves and brain, which is why practice can even be mental.

terms.name: Muscular Christianity
terms.text: A mid-nineteenth-century belief, brought from England, that team sport builds both the body and moral character.

terms.name: Mutual information between mechanics
terms.text: A score from -1 to 1 for how much seeing one mechanic in a game tells you about another, with the popularity of each taken out. The paper looks at pairs scoring above 0.65, which it reads as mechanics that turn up together because of something they share.

terms.name: Mutual regard
terms.text: Players trying hard because each expects a worthy partner or opponent, which makes the game itself possible.

terms.name: Mutual-participant group
terms.text: Boyd's name for a group where members take part together in feeling, thinking and acting on interests they share.

terms.name: Naches
terms.text: The pride felt when someone you mentor succeeds. Koster counts it as a feedback signal that keeps a group going.

terms.name: Naches
terms.text: A Yiddish word for the pride felt when someone you taught or helped succeeds. Called vicarious pride in the book.

terms.name: Napoleon
terms.text: A bid in the card game of that name to win all five tricks, paid at ten chips.

terms.name: Narrative ARG
terms.text: An alternate reality game that uses video, text, photographs and audio to weave real missions into a story lasting weeks, months or years.

terms.name: Narrative design
terms.text: Making a game's storyworld: backstory, characters, dialogue and scenarios joining levels or scenes.

terms.name: Nash equilibrium
terms.text: An outcome where neither player can gain more by changing strategy alone.

terms.name: Natural
terms.text: In blackjack, an ace together with a face card or a ten as the first two cards. It pays double in most home games.

terms.name: Natural (blackjack)
terms.text: An ace with a ten-value card as the first two cards, which wins at once at higher odds.

terms.name: Natural and craps
terms.text: In Craps, a first roll of 7 or 11 wins, and a first roll of 2, 3 or 12 loses.

terms.name: Natural card
terms.text: In a game with wild cards, a card that stands for itself. A set made only of natural cards is called pure.

terms.name: Natural play
terms.text: A move in solitaire that builds on a card of the same suit. It is often preferred to a move that does not.

terms.name: Natural twenty-one
terms.text: An Ace and a ten-value card dealt as the first two cards, which pays double.

terms.name: Navigability
terms.text: Whether a player knows how to move through the playspace and the game as a whole, including the menus, options and long-term goal.

terms.name: Needs analysis
terms.text: A study, done with subject experts, of the skills and concepts players need to master a topic. Its list becomes the learning objectives (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Negative space
terms.text: In art, the meaning carried by what surrounds a hidden subject. Koster's example is Minesweeper, where the unseen mines are understood from the numbers around them.

terms.name: Negentropy
terms.text: The opposite of psychic entropy, a state in which attention runs freely towards chosen goals. Flow is one name for it.

terms.name: Nemesis
terms.text: The force that pays back a player who goes too far. A novel's narrator uses the word for the swing that brings down a speculator after a long run of wins.

terms.name: Neutral point
terms.text: A vacant point between two Wei-ch'i formations that belongs to neither player and does not count in the score.

terms.name: New Games
terms.text: A movement and set of games in which rules are a starting point and players adjust them. The games are called new because they are kept new by how people play them.

terms.name: New Games movement
terms.text: A movement from the early 1970s that invented cooperative and inclusive sports, such as earth ball and parachute games.

terms.name: New player playtest
terms.text: A test with people who have never played the game, used to see how people learn it. The authors suggest five to seven.

terms.name: Nick
terms.text: A throw in Hazard that wins the stakes at once, such as repeating the main point.

terms.name: Night and Day
terms.text: The two phases of Mafia. At night the Mafia choose a victim in secret. By day everyone talks and votes.

terms.name: Nil bid
terms.text: A promise to win no tricks at all. It scores a bonus if kept and a loss of the same size if broken.

terms.name: Nim
terms.text: A two-player game of piles of pebbles where you take any number from one pile and the player with no pebbles to take loses.

terms.name: Nim
terms.text: A taking-away game in which players remove any number of objects from one pile in turn. The player who takes the last object wins.

terms.name: Nim-sum
terms.text: The total of the pile sizes written in binary and added with the rule 1+1=0. A player to move when the nim-sum is zero loses against error-free play.

terms.name: No takebacks
terms.text: A convention that once a move is made it stands. It slows a player's thinking less, because the other player does not have to plan for a move being undone.

terms.name: No-passing rule
terms.text: A rule forbidding a player to pass. In One-Capture Go it forces players to keep making moves even when nothing useful is left.

terms.name: Noise
terms.text: In Koster's use, any pattern we do not yet understand. A game that shows a player no pattern they can follow reads to them as noise.

terms.name: Nomic
terms.text: A game in which changing the rules is itself part of play. Koster says even it has limits, since a rule cannot alter physics.

terms.name: Nominal scale
terms.text: A scale that only uses names or labels, with no order between them.

terms.name: Non-player character
terms.text: A character in a game controlled by the game, not a player. In Tactical Iraqi, these characters speak no English, so the player has to use Arabic (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Non-player character
terms.text: A character in a game that the game controls and the player does not.

terms.name: Non-player character (NPC)
terms.text: A character in a game that no player controls. In street games, passers-by who do not know about the game can end up in this role.

terms.name: Non-purposive state
terms.text: A resting state with no aim, a kind of ticking over, from which a creative reaching-out can start. It differs from rest taken after work.

terms.name: Non-transitivity
terms.text: The logic behind Paper Rock Scissors: even if A beats B and B beats C, A does not beat C. The authors say designers sometimes call this triangularity.

terms.name: Nonlinear
terms.text: Having no single order in which events or ideas come. A game is a web of possibilities, so its rule book and design document keep pointing forward to things not yet explained.

terms.name: Nonorthogame
terms.text: A game with no formally defined winners and losers, where players set their own goals, such as an MMO or a sandbox game.

terms.name: Nonplayer character
terms.text: A character in a game that the computer controls instead of a player.

terms.name: Normal science
terms.text: Kuhn's term for research that solves puzzles inside an accepted framework. The rules limit which answers count, and the challenge is reaching a known kind of result in a new way.

terms.name: Normative attachment
terms.text: A goal depends for its worth on another goal. In play the game goals stay attached to the player's wider wish for an interesting struggle, so the player can leave the game if it fails that wish.

terms.name: Normative ethics
terms.text: In Simkins's account, ethics of principle: it asks what one ought to do and defends its claims by principle (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Not-me possession
terms.text: The first thing an infant owns that is plainly other than the infant's own body. The book studies it as a possession, not as a stand-in for a person.

terms.name: Notation
terms.text: A written way of recording each move of a game, such as naming the piece and the square it goes to.

terms.name: Noun-verb-adjective brainstorming
terms.text: Writing nouns, verbs and adjectives on index cards, then shuffling them to form a how might we question.

terms.name: Nudge
terms.text: A change in how a choice is presented that steers people toward one option without forbidding the others.

terms.name: Null
terms.text: A Skat bid to take no tricks at all. The lone player loses if they take even one.

terms.name: Null
terms.text: A game in which the player tries to take no trick, with no trumps. In the open version his hand is shown face up.

terms.name: Nullo
terms.text: Play whose only aim is to win no tricks, or only harmless ones.

terms.name: Nullo bid
terms.text: A bid in Five Hundred to lose every trick at no-trump.

terms.name: Oasis of play
terms.text: A short stretch of playing set inside a hard life, such as a swim, a fishing trip or a centre-field afternoon, remembered as free.

terms.name: Object
terms.text: A thing players handle during play, such as a ball, a net, money or a character's health.

terms.name: Object art
terms.text: An art made for the qualities of the finished object, such as a painting.

terms.name: Object model
terms.text: A way of making money where the game needs many objects, possibly used up, as in Magic cards or auto racing.

terms.name: Object-presenting
terms.text: One of three early functions of the environment: offering the infant a thing in such a way that the infant feels it was made by the infant.

terms.name: Object-relating
terms.text: Dealing with an object in a way that can be described from the subject's side alone, with feeling and projection placed on it. The object has become 'meaningful' to the subject.

terms.name: Object-usage
terms.text: Dealing with an object as a real thing in its own right, with its own properties, which was there all along. It is a later and harder capacity than relating.

terms.name: Objective dangers
terms.text: In climbing, the risks nobody can fully foresee, such as storms or falling rock. They are set against the subjective dangers.

terms.name: Objective game
terms.text: In Chateau's scheme, a game of construction and work, which looks ahead to adult labour.

terms.name: Observe
terms.text: The playtest task of watching body language, onscreen action, remarks and eagerness to play, without helping, talking or coaching.

terms.name: Obstacle (in ludus)
