terms.text: The difficulty a ludus player works against. Caillois says the conflict is with the obstacle and not with a rival.

terms.name: Oche
terms.text: The line a darts player stands behind to throw. Its name has no sure origin.

terms.name: Odd trick
terms.text: In Bridge or Whist, a trick won beyond six.

terms.name: Odds (payout)
terms.text: The ratio at which a winning bet is paid, such as 35 to 1 for a single number in Roulette.

terms.name: Officer
terms.text: A promoted piece in Lasca, shown by flipping a marked piece over. It moves and jumps in both directions.

terms.name: Officia scenica
terms.text: Isidore's name for the six kinds of stage performer: tragedians, comedians, thymelici, histriones, mimes and dancers.

terms.name: Old Maid
terms.text: The single unpaired card left at the end of the card game of that name. Whoever is holding it loses.

terms.name: Old Nick
terms.text: A character in a tic-tac-toe variant called tit-tat-toe. Points from tied games go to him, and the next player to win takes them all.

terms.name: Omino Go
terms.text: A Go variation in which a player may place up to four connected stones in one of the shapes of the tetromino family in a single turn. Two stones would make Domino Go and five Pentomino Go.

terms.name: Omnipotence
terms.text: The feeling of controlling the world by wishing. A baby gets a taste of it when care fits needs almost exactly, and play keeps a trace of it.

terms.name: On his honour
terms.text: Continuing to play after losing all chips, with one more loss putting you out.

terms.name: On the parish
terms.text: In Liar Dice, the extra life granted to the first player to lose three.

terms.name: One and a half player game
terms.text: A game where one human plays and the computer plays simulated opponents, as when playing Starcraft against the AI.

terms.name: One-Capture Go
terms.text: A Go variation in which the first player to capture a single stone wins and nobody may pass.

terms.name: One-shot and two-shot decision
terms.text: In Barbudi, a bet decided by one decisive roll, or one in which some rolls win or lose only half the bet.

terms.name: One-sided team game
terms.text: A game where one side of several players plays against the rules or an AI. It is usually called a cooperative game.

terms.name: Open end
terms.text: An end of the domino layout where a matching tile can legally be played.

terms.name: Open poker (stud)
terms.text: A form of poker where some of each player's cards are face up and some face down.

terms.name: Open question
terms.text: A question that asks for the tester's own words, such as how did playing make you feel, instead of did it feel enjoyable.

terms.name: Open Scrabble
terms.text: A Scrabble form in which all tiles are laid face up in a string and each player draws from either end, so no luck is involved in drawing.

terms.name: Openers
terms.text: The minimum hand a rule demands before a player is allowed to start the betting, such as a pair of jacks.

terms.name: Opening
terms.text: A known start of play, a few first moves treated as settled. Chess has many solved openings, and Go has joseki.

terms.name: Opening setup
terms.text: The arrangement of pieces at the start. Changing it makes memorised openings useless.

terms.name: Operational environment
terms.text: The rule-governed space in which moving pieces changes the state of the game world.

terms.name: Operational glance
terms.text: Lee's term for the quick look over a board to find openings, much as a tactician scans a map.

terms.name: Operational logic
terms.text: Wardrip-Fruin's name for a basic process in a game, such as chance, collision or resource, that both works as a calculation and tells the player what something means.

terms.name: Opportunities for action
terms.text: The things an activity lets a person try. These are what the book also calls its challenges.

terms.name: Opportunity cost
terms.text: The price of a choice that cannot be undone because the other option is now gone. Koster says a game needs failure to cost something.

terms.name: Oppositional game
terms.text: A game where players act against each other. The author notes that a game can be competitive without being oppositional, as when people race to solve the same puzzle.

terms.name: Optimal experience
terms.text: The author's name for the most rewarding moments of life. They come when body or mind is stretched towards something difficult that the person chose to try.

terms.name: Optimal experience design
terms.text: Giving a game compelling goals, interesting obstacles and well-built feedback so that players join in fully.

terms.name: Optimal stopping problem
terms.text: A problem of when to stop looking through options that arrive one at a time and cannot be recalled. Also called the secretary problem.

terms.name: Ordering up
terms.text: In Euchre, a player agrees to the turned-up card as trump and makes the dealer take it.

terms.name: Ordinal scale
terms.text: A scale that gives order such as first and second but not how big the gap between the places is.

terms.name: Ordinal utility function
terms.text: A rule that lets a person order all outcomes from most to least wanted, without saying how much more one is wanted than another.

terms.name: Ordinary life
terms.text: Huizinga's name for everyday existence outside the game. Play is a temporary step out of it into a separate sphere with its own mood.

terms.name: Organised nonsense
terms.text: Nonsense that a person has arranged so as to communicate it. The book calls it already a defence, as organised chaos is a denial of chaos.

terms.name: Organised play
terms.text: Play whose teams, leagues, times and aims are set by someone outside the players. The book says the organising brings in objectives beyond the activity itself.

terms.name: Organizational ARG
terms.text: An alternate reality game that uses game design as the guiding idea for a new institution, such as Quest to Learn.

terms.name: Orthogame
terms.text: A game for two or more players, with rules that rank or weigh the players, played for entertainment. Winners and losers, scores or finishing times all count as ranking.

terms.name: Orthogonal move
terms.text: A move along a rank or file, in a straight line along the squares.

terms.name: Out-of-place principle
terms.text: The finding that members of a lower-status group who rise to high positions meet more hostility, because they are above the place others have set for them.

terms.name: Output measure
terms.text: A count of what comes out of an effort, such as how well graduates do in later life.

terms.name: Ouverte
terms.text: A bid played with the lone player's cards face up on the table, which raises its value.

terms.name: Over-catch-up
terms.text: Catch-up so powerful that being first does not help or even pays less than second, so players hold back and play only the end.

terms.name: Overcall by announcement
terms.text: Raising a previous bid by announcing the value of your melds, ten points for each hundred, without naming a suit.

terms.name: Overlap of two play areas
terms.text: The shared patch that opens when two people each bring their own playing and let the two meet. Talk with a therapist, or a game played together, happens there.

terms.name: Overline
terms.text: In Renju, a row of six or more stones. Black may not make one, while White wins if he does.

terms.name: Overthrown
terms.text: In Eleusis, removed from the Prophet's role after an incorrect call, with five cards added to his hand.

terms.name: Overtime
terms.text: An added period of play agreed so that a game can reach a result when time has run out. DeKoven uses it to show that agreements about ending can be changed.

terms.name: Overtrick
terms.text: A trick won beyond what the contract promised. It earns a little extra but does not count towards winning the game.

terms.name: Overtrick and undertrick
terms.text: A trick won beyond the contract, or a trick short of it. Overtricks add bonus points and undertricks give points to the other side.

terms.name: Pachinko
terms.text: A Japanese upright pinball game where steel balls fall through pins. Caillois quotes a report of 600,000 machines in Japan.

terms.name: Packing and cracking
terms.text: Two redistricting tricks. Packing crowds like-minded voters into one district; cracking spreads them across many districts to thin their weight. Players of The Redistricting Game found both unaided (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Pageant
terms.text: Originally a "show", especially something painted or ornamented. In records it can mean a decorated wheeled object, a living picture in a painted set, a carried effigy or shrine, or a painted cloth; at court it also covered built structures such as a pageant castle and dungeon that Henry VIII and five lords assaulted.

terms.name: Pageant car
terms.text: A wheeled pageant used in court revels. At Greenwich in 1514 one held a castle, a rock, and a gilded cave with silk curtains, with musicians hidden in the rock and a presenter reading its meaning.

terms.name: Pageant wagon
terms.text: A wheeled stage on which one guild's play was performed. In York, Coventry and Chester the wagons moved through the town and stopped at set places in turn.

terms.name: PageRank
terms.text: The algorithm of Google's founders that ranks web pages by how relevant they are to a query and how important the pages linking to them are.

terms.name: Paidia
terms.text: The pole of play marked by free improvisation, noise and carefree high spirits, with few or no rules. A small child banging on a drum plays at this end.

terms.name: Paidia
terms.text: Caillois's name for free, improvised play with no fixed rules, such as moving toy figures about and giving them voices.

terms.name: Pair (domino)
terms.text: Two tiles that go together because they match or because their spots add up to a set count.

terms.name: Pair royal
terms.text: Three cards of the same rank played in a row in Cribbage, scoring six.

terms.name: Pairing
terms.text: Capturing table cards by playing a card from your hand with the same rank.

terms.name: Pairing
terms.text: In Casino, capturing table cards of the same rank as the card played from the hand. It is the only way to pick up a face card.

terms.name: Pairwise comparison
terms.text: Judging two people or things against each other on one property, such as who is taller or who is stronger. Boxing is the plain example.

terms.name: Palindrome
terms.text: A word or phrase that reads the same forward and backward, used as a puzzle form by Jarry, Poe and others.

terms.name: Pallino
terms.text: The small target ball in bocce. Teams score by getting their balls closer to it than the other team's closest ball.

terms.name: Palm Sunday prophets
terms.text: A custom in which children in beards sang or read prophecies from a frame or scaffold over a church porch. At Saint Mary Magdalen Milk the prophets then rode in procession.

terms.name: Pantomime (in Augustine)
terms.text: An ancient stage performer who danced to a song sung by others, with music. Augustine counted him with the mime and the actor as the three kinds of performer in the theatrum.

terms.name: Paper prototype
terms.text: A rough version of a game made on paper and cards to test ideas before building a finished or digital version.

terms.name: Paper prototype
terms.text: A rough, simplified version of a game made from paper cut-outs, drawings, tokens and small objects, made to start seeing the game before it is playable.

terms.name: Paper prototype
terms.text: A rough model of a game made from paper, cards or a poster board, used to test an idea before building the real thing. Peacemaker and SurgeWorld both started as board games (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Paper Rock Scissors
terms.text: A pattern taken from the children's game, where players try to outwit each other by guessing what the other will do. There is no winning strategy, and that is the point of the pattern.

terms.name: Paper-rock-scissors
terms.text: A hand game where paper wraps rock, rock breaks scissors and scissors cut paper. Caillois uses it as a simple case in the mathematics of strategy.

terms.name: Par
terms.text: The number of strokes an expert is expected to need for a hole. The author sets a par for each hole in his kickball course and changes it as he improves.

terms.name: Parabasis
terms.text: A moment in old Greek comedy when the chorus faces the audience and mocks named targets.

terms.name: Paradox of control
terms.text: The finding that people enjoy exercising control in an uncertain situation, not simply having control. A safe routine gives no sense of it.

terms.name: Paramount reality
terms.text: The ordinary world of common sense. Games separate players from it with uniforms, special places and their own rules.

terms.name: Paranoiac-critical method
terms.text: Dali's method of reading new, unexpected links between signs, by playing with the relation between a sign and what it stands for.

terms.name: Paratext
terms.text: Material that comes with a game but is not part of play, such as an art book, a signed print or a wine glass sold with a game about wine.

terms.name: Pareto optimality
terms.text: A state of sharing out resources in which nobody's utility can be raised without lowering someone else's.

terms.name: Pari-mutuel betting
terms.text: Betting where all bets go into one pool and payouts depend on how much was bet on each racer, so the odds are set by the bettors.

terms.name: Parish ale
terms.text: A feast-day gathering held by a parish to raise money for its church, with drinking, games, wrestling matches and tilts. It was the most common kind of ludus in late medieval England and is often mistaken for a saint play.

terms.name: Parity
terms.text: Equal outcomes and positions, as against egalitarianism, which is about equal kindness in process. The author says one can favour the second without the first.

terms.name: Parlor game
terms.text: A social game played at gatherings, often with no equipment beyond pencil and paper, and sometimes just a stunt.

terms.name: Parochial altruism
terms.text: Helping those inside your own group while being hostile to those outside it. The book links it to the slogan 'cooperate to compete'.

terms.name: Part-score
terms.text: Points scored towards a game that fall short of the amount needed to win it. They stay on the sheet and add to later scores.

terms.name: Participation architect
terms.text: A role on a project team whose job is to make sure every player finds a way to contribute.

terms.name: Participation bandwidth
terms.text: The total amount of effort and attention that people can give to the collective projects they join, alone and together.

terms.name: Participation spam
terms.text: Unrequested invitations to join someone else's group or project, which pile up until a person can answer few of them.

terms.name: Participatory art
terms.text: A work whose audience has to take some action, such as a choice, in order to experience it.

terms.name: Partner call
terms.text: In French Boston, the top bidder may ask another player to join them and share the win or loss.

terms.name: Partners
terms.text: Two players on the same side who win or lose together, as when players sitting opposite each other in Pachisi share a result.

terms.name: Partnership
terms.text: Two players who score as one unit. Their separate hands are hidden from each other.

terms.name: Party game
terms.text: A light game whose mechanisms stay simple so they do not get in the way of the social play.

terms.name: Party game
terms.text: A game meant to be played face to face with others and easy to pick up on the first try, such as WarioWare: Smooth Moves.

terms.name: Party game
terms.text: A game whose practice discourages skill building, such as Cards Against Humanity, where the winner is picked by a judge's taste.

terms.name: Pass (of cards)
terms.text: Giving cards from your own hand to a neighbour, chosen before you see what you receive.

terms.name: Pass and don't pass
terms.text: Bets that the shooter will win or lose.

terms.name: Passed pawn
terms.text: A chess pawn with no enemy pawns ahead of it or on the files next to it, so nothing blocks its march to the far row.

terms.name: Passed pawn
terms.text: A pawn with no enemy pawn left in front of it on its file or the files beside it, so nothing can stop it by pawns alone.

terms.name: Passing
terms.text: Hiding a part of your identity completely, such as a light-skinned person being taken for White. The book separates it from covering, which dials a trait down but does not hide it.

terms.name: Pasted-on theme
terms.text: A theme added late in development that has almost no effect on how the game plays.

terms.name: Pat hand
terms.text: A hand in poker to which no cards are drawn.

terms.name: Pater Noster play
terms.text: A guild-sponsored play built on the Lord's Prayer, whose seven petitions were linked to the seven Deadly Sins. At Beverley each sin was assigned to a group of guilds, and an eighth pageant, Vicious, to the gentlemen.

terms.name: Path of the puzzle
terms.text: One way of crossing agential distance: allow only a narrow set of solutions so players' experiences stay close. Text adventures and Myst did this.

terms.name: Patience game
terms.text: A game for one player, such as Solitaire, in which the aim is to solve a problem.

terms.name: Pattern
terms.text: A regularity the brain can notice and store, such as the way a tic-tac-toe line wins or how cars move forward. Koster treats a game as a pattern the player learns.

terms.name: Pattern consolidation
terms.text: A process in which different pattern collections are joined into a single one with a consistent template, naming and structure. The paper says it is hard because templates differ, patterns can overlap or contradict, and a joined collection might be too large to move around in.

terms.name: Pattern language
terms.text: A set of patterns joined in a network, where each pattern points to others that complement it. Alexander held that this lets a user see the language as a whole.

terms.name: Pattern movement
terms.text: Pieces that can move only in a set pattern on the board.

terms.name: Pattern template
terms.text: The fixed headings each pattern is written under: name, description, consequences, using the pattern, and relations. The description can note the game where it was found and examples of games that show it.

terms.name: Patterned family interaction
terms.text: A small, regular family event such as dinner time or planned viewing of a programme; Bryant and Drell treat regular family game play as this kind of ritual (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Pawn promotion
terms.text: The chess rule by which a pawn that reaches the far side becomes another piece.

terms.name: Pay-off
terms.text: The advantage or loss that comes to a player out of a situation and its results. In Boyd's account it is part of the situation itself and does not need a separate prize.

terms.name: Pay-off pile
terms.text: A private pile each player is trying to empty. The first to empty it wins.

terms.name: Payoff matrix
terms.text: A table showing what each player gets for every pair of simultaneous moves, used in von Neumann game theory.

terms.name: Peak performance
terms.text: A New Age idea that people do their most successful work when the work feels like play.

terms.name: Pecking order
terms.text: The rank order among chickens in one run, first described by Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe, in which each bird gives way to those above it. It sets who gets food and mates first.

terms.name: Peer review
terms.text: A process in which an editor sends a submitted paper to other experts, who advise accepting, revising or rejecting it.

terms.name: Peer sanctioned play
terms.text: Behaviour that the written rules do not forbid but the players accept, such as distracting a hopscotch player in the queue.

terms.name: Peg (staking)
terms.text: Striking the turning stake in croquet after going through the arches.

terms.name: Pegging
terms.text: Scoring in Cribbage by moving pegs along a board with holes. The score is kept on the board and not on paper.

terms.name: Pegging
terms.text: Moving a peg forward on the cribbage board to record points as they are scored.

terms.name: Penalty card
terms.text: A card shown by accident that stays face up on the table until it is played. Everyone now knows something about that hand.

terms.name: Penalty space
terms.text: A space on the track that costs the player who lands on it a turn, a payment or a move back. Bell suggests that the marked squares of Patolli were of this kind.

terms.name: Perceptible affordance
terms.text: What a thing visibly invites you to do, such as a keyhole inviting a key.

terms.name: Perfect information
terms.text: A game in which everything about the state of play is visible on the board to all players at all times, as in Go, chess and the more complex forms of mancala.

terms.name: Performance
terms.text: Display carried into movement or acting, a step out of common reality.

terms.name: Performance currency
terms.text: The reputation you earn by delivering results, which can be traded for a raise, a hearing, an introduction or a second chance after a mistake.

terms.name: Performance goals
terms.text: Goals of showing skill through tasks and results, such as a grade, driven by reward, rank or status.

terms.name: Performance-reward bias
terms.text: The finding that equal performance earns different rewards for different groups. In one study, teams of women founders raised about half the money of teams of men while earning more revenue.

terms.name: Performative game
terms.text: A game that works through acting and staged participation, aiming to influence society or to show a playful picture of how the world could be.

terms.name: Performative play
terms.text: Play whose core is performance, so it is dramatic to watch as well as to take part in. Charades and Twister are examples.

terms.name: Performativity
terms.text: Butler's idea that an identity such as gender is produced by repeated performance and not by the body alone, so performing differently opens a way to resist fixed categories.

terms.name: Peripheral controller
terms.text: An extra device sold with a game to make it easier to play, such as the dance pad for Dance Dance Revolution. It adds cost but can set a game apart (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Permadeath
terms.text: A rule where a lost character is gone for ever. In a score-based roguelike it ends one run, not the game.

terms.name: Permadeath
terms.text: The permanent end of a player's character in an online game, even after months or years of play, which a small group of players ask for so the game feels serious (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

terms.name: Permanent beta
terms.text: A state in which software stays in its test stage and is changed continuously instead of being finished and released once.

terms.name: Permanent trump
terms.text: A card that is always a trump, whatever suit has been named, such as the black queens in Solo.

terms.name: Permanent trumps
terms.text: Cards that are trumps in every deal whatever suit is named, such as the four jacks in Skat.

terms.name: Perpetual attack
terms.text: In Wei-ch'i, a repeating capture and recapture on the same point. The rule bars the recapture until another move has been made elsewhere.

terms.name: Perpetual check
terms.text: A repeated sequence of checks that cannot be stopped; Shatranj counted it as a draw.

terms.name: Perpetual check
terms.text: A chess situation where one side can keep giving check again and again and the other cannot escape. The game is counted as a draw.

terms.name: Perpetual check
terms.text: A draw when one player can give check without stopping.

terms.name: Persistent world
terms.text: An online game that continues running and keeps each player's character for weeks, months or years, unlike a game finished in a single sitting (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

terms.name: Persona
terms.text: An invented player described with a name, age, job, history and tastes, used to keep a real audience in mind. Teams often make two or three.

terms.name: Personal service record
terms.text: A public page listing everything a player has done in Halo, with charts and a play-by-play of every match.

terms.name: Personalized ranking
terms.text: A ranking where each user sets their own weights for the factors, for example with sliders, and sees an order made for their priorities.

terms.name: Personification
terms.text: Giving a quality a person's body and voice on stage. Caro, who stands for the flesh, is huge, sits in a tower and wears a costume of flowers.

terms.name: Personification
terms.text: Treating a lifeless thing or an idea as a living person. Huizinga says it comes from the same play attitude, as when someone scolds a stubborn collar-stud.

terms.name: Perspective-taking
terms.text: Using social cues, past experience and imagination to understand the motivations and needs of other players, one of three skills Gilbert finds in young gamers' ethical thinking (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Persuasive game
terms.text: Ian Bogost's term for a game that teaches or argues a point of view through the way it is played.

terms.name: Perverse incentive
terms.text: A reward that works against its makers' purpose, such as paying teachers for test scores and getting teaching to the test. It differs from value capture because the person's values do not change.

terms.name: Pet-to-threat effect
terms.text: A change in how a new arrival is seen. At first she is welcomed and treated kindly, then, as she rises, she is treated as a danger to the existing order.

terms.name: Petty diplomacy
terms.text: In a competitive game for three players with interaction, the two trailing players always pull down the leader, which can produce a never-ending stalemate. Race games, where players can do little to each other, do not have this.

terms.name: Petty diplomacy
terms.text: The problem in three-player pure strategy games where players spend their effort persuading each other who to attack instead of playing the game.

terms.name: Phalanx
terms.text: A tight block of soldiers moving together. Epaminondas is named after a general who used one.

terms.name: Phalanx (Epaminondas)
terms.text: An unbroken line of two or more same-coloured pieces along a row, column or diagonal. It moves as a unit a number of squares up to the number of pieces in it, and captures a smaller phalanx when its head lands on the other's head.

terms.name: Phantasy
terms.text: Phelps's spelling for a made world that shows the sorrowful absence of something real, such as a world without laughter, as against fantasy, which is the playful presence of something unreal such as dragons (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Phasing
terms.text: A display effect in which the server shows each player a different version of the world, depending on what that player has done.

terms.name: Photo collage
terms.text: A picture made by cutting and combining photographs and printed material, developed by Höch and Hausmann.

terms.name: Photoplay
terms.text: Taking photographs that tell a story with toys or figures.

terms.name: Physical prototype
terms.text: A prototype that tries out how the game's actions feel by doing them with bodies and objects, such as a field game version of a videogame.

terms.name: Physical work
terms.text: Play that makes the body tired, such as virtual boxing or dancing to a screen.

terms.name: Pick on the leader
terms.text: A common move in political games where the other players all attack whoever is ahead. It works as a catch-up feature.

terms.name: Pick-up
terms.text: A game object that gives the player a new ability when collected. The large dots in Pac-Man are the example Koster gives.

terms.name: Pickle jar
terms.text: In Duck Duck Goose, the middle of the circle where a caught player waits until another player is caught.

terms.name: Pie rule
terms.text: A balancing rule. One player sets up the starting position, and the other chooses which side to play. Because the first player does not know which side the opponent will take, he tries to make both sides equal.

terms.name: Pile of shame
terms.text: The heap of unpainted or unfinished miniatures that a hobbyist has bought and not yet used.

terms.name: Pile of twenty
terms.text: A stack of twenty cards given to each team in Grabouche, with the top card face up. The first team to play all of them wins.

terms.name: Pilot experimentation
terms.text: Running many small tests of different strategies, then enlarging the ones that work.

terms.name: Pinball
terms.text: A table game of launching a steel ball against bumpers for a score. A cited writer says the player feels he is pitting his own skill against industry.

terms.name: Ping quotient
terms.text: How readily a person reaches out over electronic networks to ask others to take part, and answers when asked.

terms.name: Pinned piece
terms.text: In Plakato, a blot that stays where it is when hit and cannot move until the hitting piece moves off.

terms.name: Pinochle (meld)
terms.text: The Queen of Spades with the Jack of Diamonds in Pinochle, melded for 40 points.

terms.name: Pip
terms.text: A spot on a card, die or domino.

terms.name: Pitcher
terms.text: The high bidder in Pitch, who leads first and whose lead names the trump suit.

terms.name: Pitfall
terms.text: A random unlucky event for a player. Windfalls and pitfalls cut the link between what a player chose and how the game went.

terms.name: Place
terms.text: The open ground in the middle of a fixed-stage play, around which the scaffolds stood. Crowds, battles and crucifixions were played there.

terms.name: Plain suit
terms.text: A suit that is not trumps.

terms.name: Plan-Do-Study-Act
terms.text: Walter Shewhart's cycle at Bell Labs: find a problem, design a fix, study the results with statistics, and repeat if problems remain.

terms.name: Plane of movement
terms.text: In 3D Hook-Move Chess, one of the flat slices of the 8x8x3 block of squares. A piece's move has to stay inside a single plane.

terms.name: Planet craft
terms.text: Stewart Brand's term for the skill and cunning needed to change how the earth's systems work on purpose.

terms.name: Platform
terms.text: The machine a computer game runs on, such as a PC, console or handheld. It is a cost spread over many games.

terms.name: Platform choice
terms.text: The second element of family game design: deciding where the game will be played, meaning which device, in which part of the home, and with what way for players to talk (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Platform game
terms.text: A game in which the player crosses a landscape, either reaching the other side or touching every location. Koster uses the family to show how designers change a game by adding dimensions.

terms.name: Platform studies
terms.text: The study of how the technology something is made on limits and shapes what gets made. Booth applies it to Kickstarter.

terms.name: Platformer
terms.text: A single-player game where the player moves through a map by jumping, climbing and avoiding obstacles.

terms.name: Plausible deniability
terms.text: In play, the freedom to say that one's character, not oneself, did something. It lets players hear feedback without losing face (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Plausible deniability of failure
terms.text: Juul's name for the habit of treating a game as important when winning and as unimportant when losing.

terms.name: Play
terms.text: Acting out anything that is not for real, so that nothing carries over as a consequence. A play fight leaves nobody hurt.

terms.name: Play
terms.text: The thinking and doing that happen when people take part in a game, including how they deal with each other through its rules.

terms.name: Play (Caillois's definition)
terms.text: An activity that is free, separate in time and place, uncertain in outcome, unproductive, governed by rules or by make-believe. Caillois lists these six qualities as the common core of all games.

terms.name: Play behaviour
terms.text: Boyd's name for conduct that has nothing to do with routine living and is done for its own immediate satisfaction. Games, dances, drama and sports are patterns produced from it.

terms.name: Play community
terms.text: The group of people who play together and take each other's safety, willingness and trust as more important than any one game. The group decides whether a game suits it.

terms.name: Play interaction
terms.text: In Hoffman's usage, one round of the hypothesise-and-test loop, such as swapping money tokens for property tokens in Monopoly. A game is the set of play interactions held in by a rule set (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

terms.name: Play leader
terms.text: An adult who joins a group's play in mind and body in order to guide it. Boyd's leader steers the process and does not stop members from contributing.

terms.name: Play lifetime
terms.text: How long players keep playing a game, from a few hours to a whole life.

terms.name: Play money
terms.text: Tokens or paper that stand for money inside a game and have no worth outside it. In Gaddis's novel J R a boy's game money is also real corporate money, so the line between them breaks down.

terms.name: Play movement
terms.text: A reform effort from the 1880s in which towns and reformers organised play for children and adults, for the sake of health, citizenship and less crime.

terms.name: Play offered for acting
terms.text: A printed play written for small groups, with few props and costumes and parts that one actor can double. Four to eight men are enough for the ones the book lists.

terms.name: Play power
terms.text: The 1960s idea that playing, with pranks and costume, could change politics as well as protest could.

terms.name: Play stance
terms.text: Taking part in a game directly, in the practical activity of play.

terms.name: Play test
terms.text: A session where players try a game while the designers look for dead ends, dull stretches and the difficulty of each task.

terms.name: Play values
terms.text: Eric Zimmerman's name for the abstract principles a design is meant to embody. The authors' design values are based on this idea.

terms.name: Play versus recreation
terms.text: Boyd's distinction. Play needs self-started, spontaneous activity, even in its most passive forms, while recreation may need no more than passive reception of entertainment produced by others.

terms.name: Play-centric
terms.text: A way of designing games that puts first the experiences players have.

terms.name: Play-community
terms.text: The group of people who share a game and feel set apart together by it. It can carry on as a club after the game is over.

terms.name: Play-ground
terms.text: Any space marked off beforehand, in fact or in the mind, where a game or ritual takes place and its own rules apply. The arena, card table, tennis court, stage and chessboard are all examples.

terms.name: Play-mood
terms.text: The feeling of playing, which sits between light-heartedness and rapture. It can break at any moment if something outside intrudes or the players lose interest.

terms.name: Playable model
terms.text: A set of operational logics working together to stand for something players can learn and act on, such as exploring a haunted mansion in Betrayal at House on the Hill.

terms.name: Playable prototype
terms.text: A rough version of a game, made on paper or by acting it out, so the idea can be tried early.

terms.name: Playable prototype
terms.text: Usually the first digital prototype, built to model the core activity players do. It is kept rough, with simple shapes and colours.

terms.name: Playbook
terms.text: The written text of a town's play, kept safe by an official. At New Romney the book was held by the clerk of the Commonalty and later passed to a craftsman who built parts of the play.

terms.name: Playcentric design
terms.text: A method that puts the player at the middle of design: build a quick prototype, let real players try it, change it, and repeat (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Playculture
terms.text: The wider culture of play around a game, in which players mix play with daily life, share, change and comment on what they play.

terms.name: Player
terms.text: Someone who takes part in any ludus: an athlete, a musician, or a dice or card player, as well as an actor.

terms.name: Player agency
terms.text: The player's ability to make choices that mean something to that player.

terms.name: Player character
terms.text: The onscreen figure that represents the player.

terms.name: Player investment design
terms.text: The work of building rewards and long-term goals so that players feel tied to their character and to the world, and contribute because taking part is itself rewarding.

terms.name: Player matching
terms.text: Putting players against others of similar skill or willingness to invest, through friends, local groups, leagues or ratings.

terms.name: Player microclimate
terms.text: A local community of players whose habits and style make a game feel different from the same game elsewhere.

terms.name: Player model
terms.text: An idealised picture of the person who deals with one level of a game, used by a designer to decide whom that level is meant to appeal to, inform and engage (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Player profiles Timmy Johnny Spike
terms.text: Magic designer Mark Rosewater's three kinds of player: one who wants a feeling, one who wants to express something, one who wants to prove something.

terms.name: Player reliance
terms.text: How far a game needs input from the players that the game itself does not supply, such as conversation, a hint, a story or earned trust. A game where players choose from a set of options has low player reliance.

terms.name: Player-centered design
terms.text: Designing with the limits and habits of people in mind: how they see the playspace, how much information they can handle, and where and with whom they play.

terms.name: Players
terms.text: The people who set the game going by using actions and objects in the playspace under the rules. The authors count them as one of the six elements of a game.

terms.name: Playground
terms.text: The middle area where play starts, between the carer and the baby, built on the baby's confidence that the carer is reliable.

terms.name: Playing a game
terms.text: The special case where play and game are both present. The game is the script, and the players choose how to act it out.

terms.name: Playing and play
terms.text: The book separates two words. Playing, the verbal noun, is the act and the experience. Play, the noun, is the content or material a watcher can describe.

terms.name: Playing for keeps
terms.text: Playing with real consequences, such as money, outside the game.

terms.name: Playing for points
terms.text: Playing to score as much as possible, or for second place, after having no chance to win.

terms.name: Playing mind
terms.text: The side of a player that is inventive and loose and follows the moment. It works together with the gaming mind.

terms.name: Playing on / playing off
terms.text: In Cribbage, playing on means taking risks to catch up when behind. Playing off means refusing pairs and fifteens to keep a lead.

terms.name: Playing the game
terms.text: Working inside the existing rules and systems of a workplace or society to get on, or to reach a position from which others can be helped. The author says everybody does this to some extent, because everybody has to live in a world whose rules were written by others.

terms.name: Playing to win
terms.text: Accepting the conditions of the game and judging your moves by how they reach its goal, while staying inside its rules.

terms.name: Playspace
terms.text: The area in which a game takes place and where its objects sit, such as a field, a board or a sheet of graph paper.

terms.name: Playtest
terms.text: A session where players try a prototype and the designer watches what experience they have.

terms.name: Playtest
terms.text: Letting the intended audience play a game before it is finished. The authors advise doing it early and often, and noting both what players enjoy and what they learn (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Playtest plan
terms.text: A prepared outline of how to introduce the game, what testers need to know, what the team wants to learn and how feedback will be captured.

terms.name: Pleasure
terms.text: A comfortable feeling that comes when a bodily or social expectation is met, such as eating when hungry. It needs no effort and does not make a person more skilled.

terms.name: Plot hook
terms.text: A personal goal or lead given to a player so they still have something to do if their group fails (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Plough play
terms.text: A folk play of the farming year whose players collect money. The book thinks the Mactacio Abel may be one that has been given a parody of the mass.

terms.name: Plums (marbles)
terms.text: The marbles set in a row to be shot at in a marble game, which the shooter keeps if hit.

terms.name: Plus-one
terms.text: A small message that credits a named strength to a person, with a reason, and adds up over time. Plusoneme is the site.

terms.name: Pocket piece
terms.text: A piece held off the board at the start that a player can drop onto an empty square on a later turn, as in Pocket Knight Chess.

terms.name: Point
terms.text: In backgammon and tabula, one of the twenty-four triangular spaces on which pieces rest.

terms.name: Point (backgammon)
terms.text: One of the 24 narrow spaces on a backgammon board. A player who puts two or more pieces on a point is said to make it, and the opponent cannot land there.

terms.name: Point (backgammon)
terms.text: One of the 24 triangular spaces on a backgammon board. Pieces sit on points, and a point holding two or more pieces of one colour cannot be landed on by the opponent.

terms.name: Point (craps)
terms.text: A first roll of 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10, which the shooter has to roll again before a 7 to win.

terms.name: Point count
terms.text: A way of valuing a hand by giving each high card a fixed number of points and adding them up. It lets players compare hands with a single number.

terms.name: Point number
terms.text: In Buck Dice, a number set by one die, and every die matching it scores a point for the thrower.

terms.name: Points
terms.text: Numerical scores given to each player, usually with the highest score winning, though the lowest wins in golf and hearts.

terms.name: Poison (croquet)
terms.text: A variation in which a ball that has passed the last wicket becomes poison. It eliminates any ball it hits, and hitting the stake eliminates it.

terms.name: Poker dice
terms.text: Dice marked with Ace, King, Queen, Jack, Ten and Nine in place of pips.

terms.name: Poker face
terms.text: An expression that gives away nothing about one's hand. It lets a player take part in something outside their control.

terms.name: Poker face
terms.text: A face that shows nothing about the cards in the hand. A character who cannot keep one grins at a high hand.

terms.name: Pole position
terms.text: The preferred starting place in a race, named in auto racing.

terms.name: Polemical drama
terms.text: A play written to push one side of a religious or political dispute. John Bale wrote several for the king's side against the Catholic church.

terms.name: Political allegory
terms.text: A story from one setting that stands for people and events in another. In Godly Queen Hester, Aman stands for Cardinal Wolsey and the Jews for English monks.

terms.name: Politics
terms.text: In this book, players choosing others to target in arbitrary ways that affect their positions differently. It grows with both the amount of interaction and the freedom to choose targets.

terms.name: Pool
terms.text: A common store of stakes or forfeits, which the winner takes at the end of the game.

terms.name: Pool
terms.text: Chips put in by players that go to the winner of a later bid. If everyone passes, each player adds to it again.

terms.name: Pool
terms.text: The pile of chips or stakes that the winner of a hand collects. If nobody qualifies it can stay on the table and grow.

terms.name: Pool (dominoes)
terms.text: The face-down tiles left after players draw their hands, from which players draw when they cannot play.

terms.name: Pool (marbles)
terms.text: The marbles put in a ring by all players at the start of a marble game, from which the shooter takes what is knocked out.

terms.name: Positional asymmetry
terms.text: A difference in the starting state of players, such as moving first, a different character class or seat order, that could change the likely result if two equally skilled players swapped.

terms.name: Positional heuristic
terms.text: A rule of thumb for judging the state of the game and telling who is ahead, such as counting piece values in chess.

terms.name: Positive failure feedback
terms.text: A response to a mistake that is vivid or funny and shows the player their own effect on the game, such as the monkey flying off the lane in Super Monkey Ball 2.

terms.name: Positive feedback
terms.text: A loop in which a result strengthens the cause that produced it, so a small lead grows.

terms.name: Positive participation
terms.text: Active, willing contribution from everyone in a group, which the book says a community needs.

terms.name: Positive psychology
terms.text: The field that studies how people flourish and which activities make them content.

terms.name: Posse
terms.text: A group of about ten students from similar backgrounds placed together at one university. About 90 percent of the programme's alumni graduate.

terms.name: Possession
terms.text: Having the ball and the right to try to score. In half-court basketball the last player to score keeps possession.

terms.name: Possession (trance)
terms.text: A state in which a person acts out the character of a god or spirit while losing awareness of himself. Caillois treats it as mimicry joined to ilinx.

terms.name: Possibility space
terms.text: The full set of situations and moves a rule set allows. Burgun treats exploring it as what playing a game is.

terms.name: Possibility space
terms.text: The full range of states a game can reach, such as the values one to six on a die. The only way to learn one, Koster says, is to explore it by playing.

terms.name: Possibility space
terms.text: All the positions and moves that a game or problem allows. Chess has more possible games than a person can explore in a lifetime.

terms.name: Possibility space
terms.text: The range of actions a game makes available to a player.

terms.name: Postal play
terms.text: Playing a game by sending each move through the mail, usually on a postcard, using as brief and clear a notation as possible.

terms.name: Postlude
terms.text: A shared ending after play, such as golf's nineteenth hole, or beer and pizza, where players review moments of the game and rejoin each other.

terms.name: Posttraumatic bliss
terms.text: A term from Jennifer Michael Hecht for the shift in attention that follows a near-death event or a terminal diagnosis, when a person enjoys the present more and cares less about trivial things.

terms.name: Pot
terms.text: In poker, all the money bet during a hand, won by the player with the highest-ranking hand.

terms.name: Pot
terms.text: The pile of all bets in a betting game. The aim is to win it.

terms.name: Pot game
terms.text: A marbles game played around a hole in the ground, where players try to get close to the hole or knock marbles into it.

terms.name: Pot limit
terms.text: A betting limit where the most you may bet equals the number of chips already in the pot.

terms.name: Pot odds
terms.text: The comparison between the chance of completing a hand and how much the pot pays for taking the risk.

terms.name: Pot-hunter
terms.text: A hunter who is only after the kill. The Southern gentleman's code separated him from the true sportsman, for whom the chase mattered more.

terms.name: Potential space
terms.text: The gap between baby and carer that is neither inside the child nor outside in the world. The book gives play a place there.

terms.name: Potsie
terms.text: The small object, such as a stone or beanbag, thrown into the boxes in Hopscotch.

terms.name: Potting
terms.text: Landing a disc in the cup. In tiddlywinks a successful pot earns another turn.

terms.name: Power law
terms.text: A pattern where the number of items of a given size falls steeply as the size grows. City sizes, word counts and links in networks follow it.

terms.name: Power song
terms.text: In Nike+, a preset song the runner can call up with one button press, like a power-up.

terms.name: Power with and power over
terms.text: Ganz's distinction between power built together with others in a movement and power exercised over others in oppression.

terms.name: Power-up
terms.text: A pick-up that temporarily raises what the player can do. Galaga, Koster says, made it a standard part of shooters.

terms.name: Power-up
terms.text: In 'SuperBetter', the author's recovery game, a small action you can do at any moment to feel less unwell, listed in advance.

terms.name: Practical environment
terms.text: The surroundings of a game seen as something that stands against the player's goals and abilities, such as the walls of a climb or the settings of a software level.

terms.name: Practice
terms.text: Building a library of chunked knowledge that can be reused on new tasks. Koster's example is how years of guitar made the mandolin quick to pick up.

terms.name: Practice game
terms.text: A game declared void before it starts, so that everyone can learn the rules. It can begin with a few rules and add more in later rounds.

terms.name: Pre-Chess
terms.text: A chess variant in which players take turns placing their eight back-row pieces on their first rank before play starts.

terms.name: Pre-lusory goal
terms.text: In Suits's account, the state of affairs a player tries to bring about, described without the rules, such as getting the ball through the hoop.

terms.name: Preconventional, conventional and postconventional morality
terms.text: Kohlberg's three levels of moral reasoning: judging by consequences to oneself, judging by approval and law, and judging by agreed rights and self-chosen principles. Each level holds two of his six stages (chapter by Dan Staines).

terms.name: Predicted failure
terms.text: A failure the team expects a prototype to show in testing. It is the kind iterative design relies on.

terms.name: Predictive process
terms.text: A way of working that assumes the end product is understood in advance and can be built without changes to the design.

terms.name: Predictive scenario
terms.text: Balzac's name for a live-action game that simulates skills such as ethical decision-making so people act as they would in real life (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Preemptive bid
terms.text: A high bid made early on a hand low in card value to shut the opponents out of the auction.

terms.name: Preference (trump rank)
terms.text: In Boston, the suit turned up is first preference, the other suit of the same colour is second preference, and the two others are common suits.

terms.name: Prelude
terms.text: A ritual or set-up before the main action. In the children's game lemonade, the chanting and miming lead into the chase that players actually want.

terms.name: Preoccupation
terms.text: The near-withdrawn, absorbed state of a young child at play, close to the concentration of older children and adults. It cannot easily be broken into.

terms.name: Preparation
terms.text: The choices a player makes before a challenge that change their odds, such as healing before a fight or building a hand of cards.

terms.name: Prescriptive frame
terms.text: The set of norms telling an audience how to encounter a work and what to attend to. A painting is looked at from the front; a game is played by its rules toward its goal.

terms.name: Prescriptive ontology
terms.text: The view that a work is not just its material but the material as met under the right prescriptions. Reading Moby Dick's words in random order is not reading Moby Dick.

terms.name: Presence
terms.text: The feeling that the game world has replaced the real one as the place one is in. The authors ask whether strong presence lets a virtual self touch the real self (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Presentational (against representational)
terms.text: A style in which figures do not speak in their own voices but are introduced and "read" by a presenter, with little talk between participants. The author uses it for Lydgate's mummings and court pageants, as against plays where actors take on characters and speak to one another.

terms.name: Presentism
terms.text: Judging people of the past by the standards of today. Wineburg, cited by the authors, calls it the usual state of affairs for students (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: PRESS model
terms.text: The author's earlier plan for change: Problem awareness, Root cause analysis, Empathy, Strategy and Sacrifice. He says he found empathy the step most often missing.

terms.name: Press-your-luck strategy
terms.text: A reaction to a race where a player who is ahead plays safe and a player who is behind takes bigger risks. Yahtzee and Can't Stop have it.

terms.name: Prestige strategy
terms.text: Reaching high rank by skill and knowledge that the group values, so that the group gives rank freely.

terms.name: Prevailing wind
terms.text: In Ma-jong, the wind that names the current round. A pung of it doubles the player's score.

terms.name: Primary win condition
terms.text: The supergoal of a game, the achievement that stands above all smaller goals. In Spore it is reaching the black hole at the centre of the galaxy.

terms.name: Prime
terms.text: Six closed points in a row, which an opposing stone cannot jump over.

terms.name: Prisoner's dilemma
terms.text: A game-theory puzzle in which two people choose to cooperate or betray and the pay-off table shows each outcome. Burgun suggests such tables as a tool for balancing moves.

terms.name: Prisoner's dilemma
terms.text: A game where each of two players gains more by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end with less than if both kept quiet.

terms.name: Prisoners
terms.text: Stones captured in Go, which are kept by the capturer and subtracted from the score of the other.

terms.name: Private information
terms.text: Facts about the game state that one player knows and others do not, such as a card in a hand or a fogged-out part of a map.

terms.name: Privileged pawn
terms.text: In Shaturanga, a pawn belonging to a player who had only a ship and the pawn left. It could be promoted to any piece he chose.

terms.name: Probability space
terms.text: The likelihood that a player will pick one available option over another, which a designer can shape much as a magician forces a card.

terms.name: Probe, hypothesize, reprobe, rethink cycle
terms.text: James Paul Gee's four-step account of play: the player tries something in the game world, guesses what it means, tries again with that guess, and then keeps or changes the guess (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

terms.name: Problem situation
terms.text: Boyd's description of a game: a situation set up for a time in the imagination, which players solve by playing.

terms.name: Problema
terms.text: The Greek word behind "problem". It meant something thrown down as a challenge or held up as a shield.

terms.name: Procedural conflict
terms.text: A team disagreement about how the team works, such as meeting style, schedule or who does what.

terms.name: Procedural generation
terms.text: Making game content, such as golf holes, from rules run by code instead of drawing each one by hand.

terms.name: Procedural level
terms.text: The part of a game made of its rules and mechanics: the formal system that takes inputs and gives outputs (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Procedural rhetoric
terms.text: Bogost's term for the way a game makes meaning through the actions its rules invite players to take.

terms.name: Procedural rhetoric
terms.text: Ian Bogost's name for making an argument by modelling a causal system, so that the player finds the argument by playing. McDonald's Video Game is the standing example.

terms.name: Procedural rhetoric
terms.text: Ian Bogost's name for the way a game's rules and its content together make a claim about how some part of the world works (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Process art
terms.text: An art made so that the audience appreciates the qualities of its own activity. The author lists games, social dances, cooking and fondue as examples.

terms.name: Processional staging
terms.text: Playing a series of plays one after another at several stops in a town, so each audience waits at its own stop while the wagons come to it. The book sets it against plays given on a fixed stage.

terms.name: Production blueprint
terms.text: A detailed drawing of dimensions and specifications, such as paddle and ball sizes and bounce angles in Pong.

terms.name: Production plan
terms.text: A list of who does what by when once design is complete, usually kept as a new version of the tracking spreadsheet.

terms.name: Productive randomness
terms.text: Randomness that hands the player a set of options to choose from. The paper's example is rolling three dice and choosing which one to use for the move.

terms.name: Progression
terms.text: The rule by which winners and losers move between tables after each round, so everyone meets new partners and opponents.

terms.name: Progression as growth or movement
terms.text: The paper groups the ways its games show progress into two kinds: growth or accumulation, where pieces are added to fill adjacent spaces, and moving or advancing, where pieces are added and removed to show movement. Both depend on a board divided into connected sections.

terms.name: Prohibited move
terms.text: In Renju, a move forbidden only to Black, such as a double three or a double four, that makes the first player's side give up some of its advantage.

terms.name: Projective identity
terms.text: The character a player takes on in a game. The player projects part of themselves onto it, and also takes on its project, meaning the goals and roles the game gives it (foreword by Henry Jenkins, after James Paul Gee).

terms.name: Prolocutor
terms.text: A speaker who opens and closes a play and talks to the audience. In Bale's Enterlude the Prolocutor tells the people where they stand between the old law and the new.

terms.name: Promotion
terms.text: A change of a piece into a piece with wider moves, usually on reaching the far side of the board. In Shatranj a pawn became a prime minister.

terms.name: Promotion
terms.text: A pawn that reaches the far side of the chessboard is swapped for a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Most players pick a queen.

terms.name: Promotion (queening)
terms.text: When a chess pawn reaches the far row, its owner swaps it for a queen, rook, bishop or knight.

terms.name: Promotion (shogi)
terms.text: Flipping a shogi piece over so it moves with new powers. Pieces are flat and single-coloured so they can be flipped and can change sides.

terms.name: Promotion zone
terms.text: The far ranks of a shogi board in which a piece may be turned over to its promoted value.

terms.name: Prop
terms.text: An object that prompts or fixes what players imagine. A wooden figure on a tower makes players imagine a superhero climbing it. The word comes from theatre.

terms.name: Prophet
terms.text: In Eleusis, a player who thinks he knows the secret rule and takes over calling cards right or wrong. If he calls wrongly he is overthrown.

terms.name: Proposal (Solo Whist)
terms.text: In Solo Whist, a bid asking for a partner to take eight of thirteen tricks together.

terms.name: Propose
terms.text: In Ecarte, the non-dealer's request to swap cards. The dealer may accept or refuse.

terms.name: Prosocial emotions
terms.text: Feelings directed at other people, such as love, compassion, admiration and devotion, which build lasting bonds.

terms.name: Prosocial learning
terms.text: A word for any learning that deepens a person's ability to act in moral, ethical and civil ways, covering both moral education and character education (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

terms.name: Protected lion
terms.text: A lion that another piece defends. A lion may take an opposing lion two squares away only if it is unprotected.

terms.name: Protocol
terms.text: A set of rules saying which points in a network may open to which others. Wark treats the structure of a game's world as this kind of rule.

terms.name: Prototype
terms.text: A playable form of some or all of a game's design, made to work through a design question.

terms.name: Pruning
terms.text: Players cutting down the tree by dropping duplicate or obviously losing moves, or by treating nearly equal moves as one.

terms.name: Pseudocode
terms.text: Code written in no particular syntax, which sets out the logic of a program in plain steps.

terms.name: Pseudosymbol
terms.text: A symbol reduced to a trademark or political badge that only identifies a group, as Thomas Merton uses the word, in contrast to a symbol that invites feeling for others (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Psychic bid
terms.text: A bid not justified by the cards held, made to deceive the opponents.

terms.name: Psychic energy
terms.text: The author's name for attention, seen as a limited supply. Nothing is thought, remembered or decided without spending it.

terms.name: Psychic entropy
terms.text: Disorder in awareness, which appears when information clashes with a person's goals. Worry, fear and anxiety pull attention away from what the person wants to do.

terms.name: Psychic offloading
terms.text: Trusting the game and the match to turn a fierce contest into something useful for both, so a player need not keep the opponent's wellbeing in mind during play.

terms.name: Psychogeography
terms.text: Debord's method of walking a city to notice how streets and places change the feelings, thoughts and behaviour of the walker.

terms.name: Psychological group
terms.text: A set of people who share a sense of identity and purpose, as against a collection of people who merely happen to be in one place. In the research cited, the first kind solved puzzles faster.

terms.name: Psychological intimacy
terms.text: The close sharing among members of a small group that Boyd saw as the core of group experience. She said arts and play create it as well as express it.

terms.name: Psychomachia
terms.text: A battle of virtues and vices for a person's soul. In the Castle of Perseverance the Virtues fight the Sins with roses as weapons until Humanum Genus gives way to Covetise.

terms.name: Psychosocial moratorium
terms.text: A term Gee borrows from Erik Erikson for a setting where the cost of taking risks is low. Games offer one, so players can try acts they would avoid in real life (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Public information
terms.text: Facts about the game state that every player knows.

terms.name: Pun
terms.text: A word or sign used for two or more meanings at once, as when the Chinese word for fish sounds the same as the word for abundance.

terms.name: Pung
terms.text: In Ma-jong, three identical tiles. It may be made by taking a tile just discarded.

terms.name: Punter
terms.text: A player who bets against the bank.

terms.name: Pure busywork
terms.text: Mechanical steps that follow a fixed procedure with no choices, such as dealing cards or making change.

terms.name: Pure one-player game
terms.text: A game where the player plays against the system and not against an imagined opponent. Crossword puzzles, Tetris and card solitaire are examples.

terms.name: Pure strategy
terms.text: One definite choice in a game's grid, as opposed to a mixed strategy.

terms.name: Pure strategy game
terms.text: A game with no hidden information and no chance element, such as chess.

terms.name: Purpose layer
terms.text: The reasons a player has for playing and what they hope to get from it, which can differ from the designer's goals.

terms.name: Purpose, resolution, harmony
terms.text: The three senses of meaning in the last chapter. A person has a goal, works at it with effort, and feels thoughts, feelings and actions agree.

terms.name: Purposelessness
terms.text: Play without an aim beyond itself. DeKoven says a goal inside a game lets people reach it, and that play itself has no purpose.

terms.name: Put in
terms.text: In Boston, taking fewer tricks than you bid. A player put in for two tricks pays chips to each opponent.

terms.name: Puzzle
terms.text: An interactive system that adds a problem with a solution. Once the solution is known, the puzzle usually stops holding interest, like a riddle whose answer you have heard.

terms.name: Puzzle
terms.text: In Crawford's use, a challenge that stays fixed and is solved with clues, unlike a game, where rules and situations can shift with what players do.

terms.name: Puzzlelike hidden information
terms.text: Something the game knows and the player has to work out from clues and experiments, such as the weakness of a boss or the answer to a crossword.

terms.name: Pwn
terms.text: Gamer slang for a victory big enough to gloat about. It began as a typing slip for own.

terms.name: Pyramidal die
terms.text: A four-sided die shaped like a pyramid, as found in the Sumerian boards of Ur.

terms.name: Qualifier
terms.text: A tournament or race meant to pick a group who go on to another, where entrants care only about getting in and not about the final place.

terms.name: Quantitative benchmark
terms.text: A specific number a person aims for, used to focus effort.

terms.name: Quantity over quality
terms.text: The first brainstorming rule: produce as many ideas as possible whatever their worth.

terms.name: Quantized
terms.text: Forced onto a fixed set of values, as a grey picture is reduced to 256 shades. Games, Koster says, tend to be quantized models of real things.

terms.name: Queening (promotion)
terms.text: When a pawn reaches the far edge it is replaced by a more powerful piece, usually a queen.

terms.name: Query game
terms.text: A game in which players find a hidden subject by asking questions answered with yes or no.

terms.name: Quest
terms.text: A task given to a player with a goal, a reason, where to go, what to do and a proof of completion.

terms.name: Quiniela
terms.text: A pari-mutuel bet on the winning numbers of a state lottery. The Jogo do Bicho was tied to one in Brazil.

terms.name: Quitting
terms.text: Leaving a game for any reason without the leaving meaning anything about the player. DeKoven treats the freedom to quit as the partner of the freedom to play.

terms.name: Quong
terms.text: In Ma-jong, four identical tiles.

terms.name: Quota
terms.text: In Beggar-Your-Neighbor, the number of cards a player has to put down on an ace or face card: four, three, two or one.

terms.name: Quête
terms.text: A collecting round made by a costumed group, such as a boy bishop, mummers, disguisers or plough boys. The author places it between asking for donations and holding people to ransom.

terms.name: Race
terms.text: A multiplayer game built from several copies of a one-player game, one for each player, such as a footrace, golf or Scrabble.

terms.name: Race game
terms.text: A game, usually decided by luck, where players move round a track to finish first. Pachisi, Ludo and Sorry! belong here.

terms.name: Race game
terms.text: A boardgame where players move pieces along a track to the end first, usually with dice, such as Chutes and Ladders, Candy Land and Parcheesi.

terms.name: Race game
terms.text: A board game in which the aim is to be first to cross the board and reach the goal. The result depends on chance, as in the Game of Goose, where the dice decide.

terms.name: Race game
terms.text: A game won by being first to bring all your pieces home, such as backgammon, Sorry! and Parcheesi.

terms.name: Race mechanic
terms.text: A core mechanic in which players hurry to reach places or goals first. Re:Activism used it to bound time and space, and found it crowded out lingering at sites (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Rack (frame)
terms.text: The triangular frame that holds the balls together at the start of a pool game.

terms.name: Raichi and Tuichi
terms.text: The words a Tablut player had to call when the king had one clear route (Raichi) or two (Tuichi) to the edge. Two routes could not be blocked at once.

terms.name: Raid
terms.text: A mission that only a group of players can finish, which needs roles to be planned and rehearsed.

terms.name: Railroading
terms.text: Steering a player along a fixed track of plot, so the player has little say over how the story or characters develop (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Raise
terms.text: Increasing a bet in Poker, within the agreed limit. Everyone still in has to match it or drop out.

terms.name: Raise
terms.text: To put in more than a call needs, which forces every later player to match the extra amount or give up.

terms.name: Raise
terms.text: In poker, matching the current bet and adding more, which forces the later players to match the higher amount.

terms.name: Raja
terms.text: The king in Chaturanga, the old Indian ancestor of chess. A raja starts on a throne and the game is scored by what rajas do.

terms.name: Rally point scoring
terms.text: A way of scoring in which the team that wins the rally gets the point, whether or not it was serving.

terms.name: Random element
terms.text: A game feature that moves the game to a new state unpredictably, such as dice, cards, weather or a random number generator.

terms.name: Randomness
terms.text: Results that players cannot predict, from dice, shuffled cards or generators. Burgun counts effective unpredictability as enough, since no dice or computer are truly random.

terms.name: Randomness (luck)
terms.text: Uncertainty in outcome. It is not the same as dice or cards, since rock-paper-scissors and chess have uncertainty without them.

terms.name: Range of challenges
terms.text: The different situations a game's rules can produce, which keep the rules from being used up quickly.

terms.name: Range of competition
terms.text: The spread of opponents with whom a player can have a game where both have a real chance of winning. Luck widens it.

terms.name: Rank
terms.text: A row of squares on a chessboard, running across between the two players.

terms.name: Rank and yank
terms.text: A yearly review in which a company ranks all employees against each other and dismisses those at the bottom, such as the lowest 10 percent.

terms.name: Rank of pits
terms.text: A row of holes on a mancala board. Two-rank boards have two rows, four-rank boards have four.

terms.name: Rank reversal
terms.text: A change in the order of items caused by a factor that has little to do with the items, such as a setting in the method.

terms.name: Ranked-choice voting
terms.text: A voting system where voters rank candidates and, if no one has a majority, the last-placed candidate is dropped each round and votes pass to next choices.

terms.name: Ranking
terms.text: Putting a set of items in order by a criterion, by comparing them directly with one another.

terms.name: Rant
terms.text: A loud boasting speech by a ruler or tyrant, usually at the start of a play. The Wakefield Master wrote several, for Pilate, Herod's messenger and others.

terms.name: Rare card
terms.text: A card that is more powerful than others and harder to find, used in collectible card games.

terms.name: Rating
terms.text: Giving each item its own score on a common scale, so that the items can be put in order afterwards.

terms.name: Rating system
terms.text: A set of numbers for each player showing skill. Point accumulation depends on how often you play. Systems like Elo add and subtract points by expected result.

terms.name: Ratings deviation
terms.text: In the Glicko system, a number that measures how unreliable a rating is. It is high for a player who has not played for a long time.

terms.name: Ratio scale
terms.text: A scale with a true zero, so that one value can be twice another. Length, mass and duration are examples.

terms.name: Rational choice theory
terms.text: A theory that assumes people have fixed preferences, full information, and no emotions, and so pick the option with the greatest expected gain.

terms.name: Re-skin
terms.text: A version of a game with a new theme but the same rules. The Mario editions of Monopoly play like Monopoly.

terms.name: Reactive agent
terms.text: The kind of player who deals with the rules as inputs and outputs, works out strategy, and does not ask what the actions mean. Also called the mechanical player (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Reading out
terms.text: Following a sequence of moves and replies ahead in your head, as in if she goes there, I go there and she takes my rook.

terms.name: Readymade
terms.text: An ordinary manufactured object that an artist picks and presents as art, sometimes with a small change such as a signature or a joke in the title.

terms.name: Real time
terms.text: Play in which the exact moment of an action matters. It is the opposite of turn-based play, where only the order of turns matters.

terms.name: Real-time coordination tool
terms.text: A feature that shows who is online, what they are playing and what they have achieved, so that players can find the right partner at the right moment.

terms.name: Real-time game
terms.text: A game where everything moves at once and the state keeps changing, so players have little time to read it.

terms.name: Real-time strategy (RTS)
terms.text: A computer strategy game played in continuous time where players gather resources, build bases and armies, and fight.

terms.name: Reassembly
terms.text: Making a picture by breaking found images into fragments and putting them together again, the method behind Dada and Surrealist collage.

terms.name: Recalcitrance of a medium
terms.text: The built-in difficulty of working in a medium that cannot be settled by thinking beforehand, such as the slowness of oil paint. For games the author names it agential distance.

terms.name: Reciprocal rewards
terms.text: The shared enjoyment that players produce for each other by acting as if the game matters.

terms.name: Recognizance (cast list)
terms.text: A written record of who is to play which part. Three survive for New Romney's Passion play of 1555 and list the disciples, Pilate, Herod, and tormentors with names like Mischance and Untrust.

terms.name: Recreationist
terms.text: A trained person who teaches others how to use free time, including skills of play.

terms.name: Red Queen's Race
terms.text: Running hard just to stay in place. Koster uses it for designers who keep having to add challenges because players keep mastering them.

terms.name: Redactor
terms.text: A later reviser who edits and adds to an existing text. The book asks whether the second Pilate rant in Towneley was written by one.

terms.name: Redeal
terms.text: Gathering the unplaced cards, shuffling them and laying them out again, allowed a fixed number of times in some solitaires.

terms.name: Redlining
terms.text: The historic practice of marking some neighbourhoods as unfit for loans or housing, which keeps areas separated. An address can still stand in for this in a model.

terms.name: Redouble
terms.text: Offering the cube back at twice the current value after accepting a double. The new owner of the cube may do so at any time.

terms.name: Referee
terms.text: A person who sits out of the game to prepare topics, settle disputes and keep time, as in Charades.

terms.name: Referee (in Kriegspiel)
terms.text: A third person who sees both boards, says whether a move is allowed and announces captures and checks without naming the pieces.

terms.name: Reflecting back
terms.text: What a trusted person does when they receive someone's indirect communication and give it back, so that it adds up into a sense of self. Talking to oneself does not do this unless it was once done by someone else.

terms.name: Reflecting team
terms.text: A group in family therapy that sits behind a one-way mirror and talks among themselves about what they see, without telling anyone what to do (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Reflective agent
terms.text: The kind of player who reads the story, setting and signs of a game and puts what they are doing into a wider personal and cultural picture (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Reflective practice
terms.text: Donald Schön's way of working in which makers step back from the work to see the whole and change their priorities as they learn.

terms.name: Reflexive attention
terms.text: Attention pulled involuntarily by something loud, fast-moving or new.

terms.name: Refrain
terms.text: A line or pattern that returns inside a song or game. Huizinga uses it as an example of the repetition and alternation that run through play.

terms.name: Regenall
terms.text: The Chester name for the city's master set of play texts, apparently like York's register. Later copies show it was a body of texts from which a cycle could be put together each year.

terms.name: Regimentation
terms.text: Telling players how to play, how to solve the problem and how to act as they play. Boyd set it against spontaneity.

terms.name: Register
terms.text: The city's own copy of the guilds' play texts, kept so the clerk could check what was spoken. At York some guilds never registered their texts and others played different words.

terms.name: Regressive coping
terms.text: A response to stress that withdraws, denies or lashes out. Also called an immature or neurotic defence.

terms.name: Regulations
terms.text: Rules that have grown into an official code kept by officials, so that players no longer own them. DeKoven says this moves a community towards being a game community.

terms.name: Related patterns field
terms.text: A field in a pattern's description that lists other patterns it contradicts or complements. The paper recommends it for consolidated collections, following the network structure of Alexander.

terms.name: Relative and absolute winning
terms.text: Winning relative to others means having more than they have. Winning in absolute terms means having enough for yourself. The author says relative winning leaves no way to get both sides to work on equality.

terms.name: Relay (Knight Relay)
terms.text: The rule that pieces a knight's move from their own knight gain the power to move like a knight.

terms.name: Remediation
terms.text: Taking images, stories and characters from older media, such as films and novels, and reusing them inside a new medium such as a game.

terms.name: Rendezvous
terms.text: The yearly gathering of fur trappers in the mountains, a holiday of drinking, storytelling, brawling and gambling after the hunting season.

terms.name: Reneging privilege
terms.text: A rule that lets a holder of the top trumps keep them back when a lower trump is led.

terms.name: Repetition
