terms.text: The ability of a game to be played again from the start, as with a game of chess or a yearly festival. Huizinga counts it among the most important features of play, within games too, as in the refrain.

terms.name: Replacement capture
terms.text: A capture made by moving onto the square held by an enemy piece and taking it off the board.

terms.name: Replacement game
terms.text: A game won by moving all your pieces into the places the opponent's pieces started in, as in Five Field Kono and Halma.

terms.name: Replayability
terms.text: How well a game holds up when played again. Single-player games tend to use up their content faster than multiplayer ones.

terms.name: Replayability
terms.text: The chance to play the same game again and try a different approach each time.

terms.name: Representatio
terms.text: A Latin word for a liturgical re-enactment, such as the visit to the tomb at Easter or Herod's rage at Christmas. Writers used it for devotional pieces in church and kept it apart from words for theatrical show.

terms.name: Representation
terms.text: The other basic function of play: showing or acting out something, such as a prince, an animal or a season. A game can combine the two and represent a contest.

terms.name: Representational space
terms.text: Lefebvre's name for space as people live it, tied to the history of a group or a site. It need not be tidy or consistent.

terms.name: Reputation
terms.text: Social information about the value of a person and their acts, which others use to decide whether to trust, buy from or help them.

terms.name: Reputation points
terms.text: Points earned by finishing tasks for others. In Groundcrew they open access to harder tasks and can be spent to ask others for help.

terms.name: Reserving (reneging)
terms.text: In Solo, the right of a player to hold back a high Matadore instead of following when a lower trump is led.

terms.name: Reskinning
terms.text: Changing the look of a play object or game, by costume, mask, make-up or new art, so that it can enter a scene it was not made for.

terms.name: Resource allocation
terms.text: Choosing how to spend limited supplies among uses. In SimEarth the player divides energy among agriculture, science, medicine and the arts.

terms.name: Resource commitment game
terms.text: A subgame where players secretly split a fixed number of points across several areas and compare, winning the areas where they have more.

terms.name: Resources and power
terms.text: Marshall Ganz's two words. Power is formal authority and rank, and resources are the means people hold that can be turned into power. The Black residents of Montgomery had no power over the buses but had their feet.

terms.name: Respawn
terms.text: Returning to play after being killed in a computer game.

terms.name: Respot
terms.text: Putting knocked-down pins back in place after a foul or a ball that went into the gutter, so that the roll scores nothing from them.

terms.name: Resting bonus
terms.text: A rule that raises the rewards of a player who has spent time away from the game. World of Warcraft uses one.

terms.name: Restriction play
terms.text: A tournament rule that forces the first moves of a game to be drawn by chance, to avoid the draws that follow well-known openings.

terms.name: Rethrow option
terms.text: A limited number of times a player may throw the dice again if he dislikes the first result.

terms.name: Retired side
terms.text: A team that has made three outs. It leaves the field of attack and the teams swap roles.

terms.name: Rettah
terms.text: In Rettah chess, a king that moves as a queen or a knight and, when checked, has to capture the checking piece.

terms.name: Returns to effort
terms.text: How the reward grows as a player puts in more effort. It usually rises but at a slowing rate.

terms.name: Returns to skill
terms.text: How much a skilled player can win by using skill. Luck lowers the returns without changing the amount of skill.

terms.name: Revels
terms.text: The court entertainments of banquets, masks, plays and tournaments. Wolsey used them to flatter and manage the king and foreign ambassadors.

terms.name: Reverse migration
terms.text: The return of Black families to the American South, which began in the 1970s. Charles Blow proposes moving in numbers to states where they could become a voting majority.

terms.name: Reversi
terms.text: A public-domain Victorian game that differs from Othello mainly in its opening: players place the first four centre pieces however they like instead of crossing the colours.

terms.name: Review
terms.text: The first evaluation step: checking that the team agrees on the playtest's strengths and weaknesses and then revisiting the design values.

terms.name: Revoke
terms.text: Failing to follow suit when you could have. Card games punish it, often by giving points to the opponents.

terms.name: Revoke
terms.text: Playing a card of another suit when the player could have followed suit. Each game states what it costs.

terms.name: Revolution
terms.text: A Skat game in which all three hands are face up, and the opponents may swap cards and talk to each other.

terms.name: Revolutionary carnival
terms.text: A protest staged as a festival, with costume, music and jokes. The book gives it as Roszak's name for the Yippies' methods.

terms.name: Reward
terms.text: What a player gets from playing, such as the pleasure of winning, satisfaction from playing well, challenge, aesthetic pleasure, excitement, escape and social time.

terms.name: Reward structure
terms.text: The fourth element of family game design: what actions the game rewards, who is rewarded (one player or a team) and how, for example with points (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Reward/effort ratio
terms.text: How much a player gains in winning chances or other rewards for the effort put in, whether in play or in preparation.

terms.name: Rewriting
terms.text: Changing the stories told around a game or toy, for example doll stories written as if by the dolls, so that the accepted ways of playing widen.

terms.name: Rhetoric of abuse
terms.text: A way of speaking in which old complaints against the Roman theatrum were aimed at activities that had nothing to do with a stage.

terms.name: Rhetorical ideology
terms.text: An unquestioned prejudice or value system; Phelps says a game can help players see it without being able to remove it for them (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Rhythm game
terms.text: A game in which the player has to press keys at timed moments. In Hush the player types falling letters at the instant they are brightest.

terms.name: Rhythm game
terms.text: A game in which the player presses buttons or sings to cues in time with a song. Rock Band is the book's example.

terms.name: Ricochet (Kickball)
terms.text: A continuous route in which each shot begins where the previous one ended and the ball is bounced off the target toward the next hole.

terms.name: Riddle
terms.text: A set question that has one answer found by knowing the rules or the secret names involved. Huizinga says riddle-contests were once sacred games.

terms.name: Riddle contest
terms.text: An old contest in which one person sings a text with hidden meaning and the other has to decode it. The author sees it as a root of logic and knowledge.

terms.name: Riddle-contest
terms.text: A match in which two players ask each other riddles in turn. In old stories the loser could be punished or lose a prize.

terms.name: Riders and leapers
terms.text: Riders move any distance along open lines, as rooks and bishops do. Leapers jump straight to a square at a fixed distance, as knights do.

terms.name: Riding
terms.text: A yearly show in which a figure such as Saint George, or the months of the year, was ridden through the town, done for the wealth of the church.

terms.name: Riding of the banns
terms.text: A procession through a town announcing a coming play. At Chester it followed a route that touched every seat of secular power, so that it announced the city's jurisdiction.

terms.name: Ring tournament
terms.text: A mounted contest in which knights wearing their ladies' colours compete for rings, used by Southern writers to link gentlemen's sport to medieval chivalry.

terms.name: Ringed piece
terms.text: A chess handicap in which the less skilled player names one of the more skilled player's pieces, and the more skilled player has to give checkmate with that piece or lose.

terms.name: Ringer
terms.text: In horseshoes, a shoe that lands around the stake.

terms.name: Ringer
terms.text: In horseshoes, a shoe that completely surrounds the stake. A straightedge across the open end settles doubtful cases.

terms.name: Ritualized play
terms.text: Play that a group repeats, sometimes at set times, until it becomes a habit of the group. A game that takes long to set up is less likely to become one (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: River
terms.text: In Chinese chess, the one-square gap between the two halves of the board. Elephants cannot cross it, other pieces can.

terms.name: Rob the pack
terms.text: To search the stock for the cards one wants to replace the ones discarded.

terms.name: Robbing
terms.text: In Spoil Five, swapping a card from your hand for the turned-up trump card. A player who holds the Ace of trumps has to do it.

terms.name: Robin Hood game
terms.text: A parish fund-raiser in which young men dressed as Robin Hood and his band and went about collecting alms. It is not usually a script.

terms.name: Rock, paper, scissors
terms.text: A two-player hand game where rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper and paper beats rock, so no choice beats all others.

terms.name: Rock-paper-scissors (RPS)
terms.text: A balanced three-way relation where each choice beats one and loses to another. It cannot collapse because all three stay worth choosing.

terms.name: Rogation Day procession
terms.text: A walk marking the bounds of a town and its fields. It gave Christian meaning to an older spring fertility ritual.

terms.name: Rogue-like
terms.text: A computer game where each playing has a freshly generated map and a character who dies permanently.

terms.name: Roguelike
terms.text: A game in Rogue's line, with random maps, turns, a single character, score-based play and permanent death.

terms.name: Role
terms.text: A part in a game such as pitcher, catcher, fox or hen. Boyd said players take the part and act as themselves, which differs from acting a character in a play.

terms.name: Role (team)
terms.text: The part a game gives a team member, which sets how that player can contribute. Roles can be written in the rules or only a habit of play.

terms.name: Role selection
terms.text: A mechanism where on a turn you pick a role card that gives an action, and others cannot take it that turn.

terms.name: Role usurpation
terms.text: A teammate telling another exactly what to do, so that the second player's part is taken over. Turn-based cooperative games are open to it.

terms.name: Role-playing
terms.text: Play in which stories come out of players taking on roles under a loose set of rules.

terms.name: Role-playing game (RPG)
terms.text: A game where each player plays one character with special attributes who gains power and equipment as play goes on.

terms.name: Role-playing mat
terms.text: A vinyl sheet with a grid, drawn on in marker pen to show the scene where miniatures stand.

terms.name: Roll-and-move
terms.text: A game where you roll dice and move your piece that many spaces along a path, and the space you land on tells you what happens next. Snakes and Ladders is the example given.

terms.name: Roll-off
terms.text: An extra round of rolling used to break a tie.

terms.name: Roquet
terms.text: In croquet, hitting another ball with your own ball, which earns an extra stroke.

terms.name: Roqueting
terms.text: In croquet, hitting another player's ball with your own. It earns two bonus strokes with several choices for taking them.

terms.name: Rosette
terms.text: A ring of six stones around a hexagon on a hexagonal Go grid. Under Rosette's special rule a group holding one cannot be captured.

terms.name: Rote training
terms.text: Learning by repeating a task until it runs on reflex. Koster compares the practice of an arcade game to military drill.

terms.name: Rough-and-tumble
terms.text: A frontier fight with almost no limits, in which biting and gouging were common. Visitors took it as a sign of how little restraint the frontier had.

terms.name: Rounced
terms.text: In Rounce, entering a hand and taking no trick, which adds five points to a player's score.

terms.name: Round
terms.text: One complete play of a mancala game, after which seeds are counted and a new round starts.

terms.name: Round robin
terms.text: A tournament format where every player plays every other, and the top record wins. It suits small numbers of players.

terms.name: Round the corner
terms.text: Treating king, ace and two as a sequence, so that the order of ranks forms a loop.

terms.name: Roundelay
terms.text: A children's circle song with actions, such as "Old Rogers" or "Jenny Jones". Caillois reads some as the leftover scripts of old rituals.

terms.name: Roundhouse
terms.text: A king and queen of every suit held together, a meld worth a large number of points in three-hand Pinochle.

terms.name: Rover
terms.text: In croquet, a player who has gone through all arches and may roam the lawn helping partners or harming opponents.

terms.name: Royal entry
terms.text: A staged welcome with speeches and displays when a ruler visited a town. The expense was large, but the texts were seldom printed because the show was thought finished once seen.

terms.name: Rubber
terms.text: In Whist, a match won by the first side to win two games.

terms.name: Rubber
terms.text: A match won by the first side to win two of three games.

terms.name: Rubber
terms.text: A series of Bridge games won by the first side to win two.

terms.name: Rubberbanding
terms.text: A feature that slows the leader and speeds up those behind in a race so the finish stays close.

terms.name: Rubbish hole
terms.text: In Pallanguli, a hole the losing player cannot fill at the start of a new round, marked with a little stick and left out of play.

terms.name: Rubicon
terms.text: A situation in which the loser's score is under a fixed line, so the winner scores the total of both scores and a larger bonus.

terms.name: Rubric
terms.text: A heading or note written into a manuscript, often in a different ink. In Towneley, two plays carry a rubric naming Wakefield.

terms.name: Rule
terms.text: An instruction that says what players can and cannot do. Rules allow some actions and block others.

terms.name: Rule complexity
terms.text: The length, difficulty and intricacy of a game's rules, which sets how much time and effort a player puts in before they can play. Mage Knight, with two 20-page rulebooks, is high, and Dixit, with a two-page rulebook, is low.

terms.name: Rule lawyering
terms.text: Using little-known rules of a complex game to one's advantage, often only when it helps.

terms.name: Rule-based thinking
terms.text: Interpreting the rules of a game and judging actions by whether the official or agreed rules allow them. Gilbert notes online games often lack clear rule sets, so disputes remain (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

terms.name: Rule-governed play
terms.text: Play in which the rules are fixed and shared, as children keep them, and the players take it seriously. The book sets it against spontaneous play.

terms.name: Rules
terms.text: The agreed limits that decide what counts inside the play-world. Huizinga says they bind absolutely, and if they are broken the game ends.

terms.name: Rules
terms.text: Limits on how players may reach the goal. They close off the obvious routes, so players try routes they had not explored.

terms.name: Rules (as against mechanics)
terms.text: In Germaine's chapter, the rules are the system fixed in advance, and the mechanics are what players actually do inside that system.

terms.name: Rules lawyering
terms.text: The moment when a player grabs the rule book to check a ruling. Train is built to provoke it, since several of its rules are open to more than one reading (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

terms.name: Rules of irrelevance
terms.text: Goffman's idea that the look of a game piece does not matter to the game. A chess piece can be carved ivory or a stone from your shoe.

terms.name: Rules-free view of autonomy
terms.text: The view that the fewer the rules, the freer the person. The author argues against it.

terms.name: Run (Rummy)
terms.text: Three or more cards of the same suit in order of rank.

terms.name: Ruse and bluff
terms.text: In game theory, ruse is a player's skill in predicting an opponent, and bluff is the answer to it, hiding information or hiding ability.

terms.name: Rush-eco-turtle
terms.text: A strategy-game triangle where a fast attack beats an economic buildup, the buildup beats a defensive posture, and the defence beats the attack.

terms.name: Safe area
terms.text: In DeKoven's classroom, a place set aside where anyone could sit out for any length of time without being asked to join. One girl stayed there for weeks before she played.

terms.name: Safe base
terms.text: A spot where a runner cannot be tagged, such as a base in Pickle. A runner who leaves it can be tagged.

terms.name: Safe pattern
terms.text: In Tsianshidsi, a pair of pile sizes such as 1 and 2, 3 and 5 or 4 and 7 that always lets the player who made it reach another safe pattern next turn and so win.

terms.name: Safe space and brave space
terms.text: The author's names for two kinds of place. The enclave of your own group protects your wellbeing, and the wider mainstream is where more openings are found.

terms.name: Safe square
terms.text: A square on which a piece cannot be captured. Thaayam calls its safe squares havens, as a guest is safe in the host's house.

terms.name: Saint play
terms.text: An enactment that shows the life of a saint, or a major event in it, usually with a spoken script. The author argues that most records called "play of Saint X" show something else.

terms.name: Salon des Refusés
terms.text: The Exhibition of Rejected Art, set up in Paris in 1863 as another route to exhibition for artists the official Salon jury turned down.

terms.name: Salting
terms.text: Discarding useful cards early so that a later player's capture of the discard pile will pay off for you.

terms.name: Salvo
terms.text: In Battleship, a set of shots fired together before the opponent answers.

terms.name: Salvo
terms.text: In Crash, a set of one or more five-letter guesses made in a single turn.

terms.name: Sandbagging
terms.text: Opening with a check in poker while holding a very high-ranking hand. It is allowed and was once seen as slightly shady.

terms.name: Sandbox game
terms.text: A game with no set objectives where the player tries actions and sees the results, such as SimCity.

terms.name: Sandbox game
terms.text: A game that gives a setting and wide freedom, without fixing what the player does in it (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Satisficer
terms.text: A person who stops at an option that meets a set level.

terms.name: Satisficing
terms.text: Choosing the first option that meets a set level, from satisfy and suffice, instead of searching for the top option.

terms.name: Saturation point of play
terms.text: The limit on how much a person can hold in play. Past it, excitement ends in a climax, a failed climax, or a provoked reaction from others.

terms.name: Saturnalia
terms.text: A festival period when ordinary rules are suspended. Huizinga links it to carnival and to student ragging as survivals of a sacred play-season.

terms.name: Save
terms.text: Storing the state of a game so the player can go back to it after a failure. Wark ties it to the way a game can undo time.

terms.name: Save-and-exit
terms.text: A way to pause a game and continue later with no ability to reload an earlier position.

terms.name: Saving and loading
terms.text: A feature that lets a player reload an earlier position. Burgun says it turns every decision into a false one, since any result can be undone.

terms.name: Scaffold
terms.text: A raised platform built for one group or place in a play, such as Herod, hell or heaven. New Romney paid for eight in its Passion.

terms.name: Scale (of a miniature)
terms.text: The size class of a miniature. Gaming figures mostly fall between 28 and 32 mm; larger ones of 54 or 75 mm are mostly for display.

terms.name: Scaled performance
terms.text: An outcome where the game gives each player a score, as points or as time, and not only a win or loss.

terms.name: Scena
terms.text: In Isidore's account, a part of the ancient theatre where performers played. Later medieval readers took it to be a tent where mimes changed costume before coming out to perform.

terms.name: Schadenfreude
terms.text: The pleased feeling when a rival fails. Koster counts it as a social signal of pushing someone down.

terms.name: Schema
terms.text: A mental structure that holds a pattern of knowledge, such as what a doctor does. Schemata link up in layers and change when new events fail to fit them (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Schematic
terms.text: A blueprint-like picture of how a game looks onscreen, made to explain what play will be like and what needs building.

terms.name: Schmeiss
terms.text: In Klaberjass, a proposal to throw in the deal. If refused, the proposer has to take the trump suit shown.

terms.name: Schneider
terms.text: In Skat, a result where the losing side scores fewer than 31 points (or the lone player loses with the other side at 91). It raises the payment.

terms.name: Schneider
terms.text: A big win, in which the loser has taken under half the points needed, or the winner declared he would take at least 91. It doubles or raises the score.

terms.name: Schwartz
terms.text: In Skat, winning every trick, or losing the lone player's every trick. It raises the payment further than Schneider.

terms.name: Schwarz
terms.text: The biggest win, in which one side takes every trick.

terms.name: Scientific football
terms.text: A name used from the 1880s for football played as a contest of planned tactics and technical inventions rather than plain strength.

terms.name: SCImago Journal Rank
terms.text: A journal score, like PageRank, in which a citation from a more important journal counts for more.

terms.name: Score
terms.text: A system of points that rewards chosen things. Giving points for bravery, grace or keeping a rally going instead of for winning shots makes a different game.

terms.name: Score
terms.text: The number a game gives back to a player for what they did. Wark says in gamespace the score is the main thing and needs fall away.

terms.name: Score (event score)
terms.text: A short written instruction for an action, used by Fluxus artists as a game or artwork, such as "Make a salad".

terms.name: Score card
terms.text: A sheet on which a player marks results to see progress. Franklin kept a little book with a column for each virtue and marked his faults every day.

terms.name: Score card
terms.text: A sheet on which a player records progress. A self-help book of 1981 asked readers to tally their results on score cards at the end of each chapter.

terms.name: Score-based game
terms.text: A game where the goal is to beat a stored score, usually your own earlier one, so it works as a game played by turns across time.

terms.name: Scoring system
terms.text: The part of a game that says what to care about and whether players compete or cooperate. The board game designer Reiner Knizia called it his main tool.

terms.name: Scrapbook house
terms.text: A paper dollhouse made in an old ledger, one room to a page, from catalogue and magazine cut-outs, with paper family and servants.

terms.name: Scratch (pool)
terms.text: A foul in pool, such as the cue ball dropping in a pocket. It costs the player a ball.

terms.name: Screen
terms.text: The single piece of either side that a cannon jumps over to capture.

terms.name: Screen chess
terms.text: A chess variant in which a screen hides each player's setup, which is made anywhere on his own half. The hidden setup removes opening theory.

terms.name: Screenworld
terms.text: David Phelps's word for the world of interactive screen technology and online worlds, as distinct from the structure of the physical world (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Search engine optimization
terms.text: Work to raise a website's place in search results. White-hat optimizers keep to the search engine's rules and black-hat optimizers try to trick its algorithm.

terms.name: Second-order design
terms.text: Design where the maker shapes the game and the players then decide how, when and why to play it, so the play is shaped only indirectly.

terms.name: Second-order design problem
terms.text: Eric Zimmerman's description of game design: a designer cannot design play directly but only the rules that then produce play (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Second-order rule
terms.text: A rule that needs to be known for the game to happen but that a player may not need to know, such as the fine punishments for breaking rules in a chess tournament.

terms.name: Secrecy
terms.text: The habit of play to wrap itself in a secret, as in "this is for us, not for the others". It marks the difference between those inside the game and those outside.

terms.name: Secret ally
terms.text: A guest who visits a school or game and later coaches players in a boss level.

terms.name: Secret information sheet
terms.text: In Haggle, a slip given to a player that states part of the scoring rules, so that the full scoring is known only by gathering many sheets.

terms.name: Secret mission
terms.text: An optional task hidden somewhere that a student has to find before they can attempt it.

terms.name: Secret rule
terms.text: In Eleusis, the hidden rule the dealer makes up for a round, which decides which cards may be added to the main line. Players try to work it out from what is accepted and refused.

terms.name: Secret weapon
terms.text: In Cruel 2 B Kind, a kind gesture assigned to a player, such as a compliment or a wink, used to knock out other players.

terms.name: Secrets
terms.text: Hidden objects scattered through a level to reward players who search it fully. In Koster's account they teach thoroughness.

terms.name: Seeding
terms.text: Assigning tournament pairings from existing rankings and not at random.

terms.name: Seega
terms.text: A north-east African game on 5 by 5 squares, in which players place twelve stones each and then capture by custodian capture.

terms.name: Seidhr
terms.text: A Norse trance ritual of music, costume and travel to the other world. Caillois uses it to show the Germanic preference for vertigo.

terms.name: Seki
terms.text: In Go, a local standoff in which neither side can safely play at a point, so the point counts for nobody.

terms.name: Self
terms.text: The picture a person holds of their own goals and everything they have lived through. It steers attention, and attention in turn shapes it.

terms.name: Self-determinism
terms.text: Acting by rules the group made, including rules one helped to make and applies to oneself. Boyd used the word for what a game builds in a child.

terms.name: Self-effacing end
terms.text: An aim that cannot be reached by aiming at it directly. Absorption in a climb, or relaxation, only arrive when the person aims at something else, such as reaching the top.

terms.name: Self-efficacy
terms.text: A person's belief that their actions can produce the results they want. Bandura links it to whether people choose to act and whether they resist pressure to go along (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
terms.text: A process where a small difference in rank leads to changes, such as the quality of applicants, that widen the difference next year.

terms.name: Self-gratification
terms.text: Getting what one wants when one wants it, as a baby does. Boyd saw games as the place where a child moves from this to following shared rules.

terms.name: Self-help paradox
terms.text: The point that happiness is mostly social, yet self-help is private.

terms.name: Self-serving bias
terms.text: Taking credit for success and denying blame for failure or anything uncomfortable (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Self-validating rules
terms.text: Rules that count as correct only because the game uses them, with no outside test of whether they are right. The book says a businessman can treat business as a game of this kind, cut off from the rest of society.

terms.name: Selling the pitch
terms.text: In Auction Pitch, the right to name trump is offered for sale to the highest bidder.

terms.name: Semantic level
terms.text: The part of a game that needs a person to interpret it: the pictures, sounds, story and setting that tell the player what state the game is in (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

terms.name: Semi-cooperative game
terms.text: A game in which players work together for nearly the whole game, usually to stop a condition that makes everyone lose, but only one player wins at the end. Archipelago and CO2 are examples, and they tend to give each player a secret winning objective.

terms.name: Sensate culture
terms.text: Sorokin's name for a culture that organises goals around pleasure and practical needs.

terms.name: Sense of space
terms.text: The area or network in which a challenge takes place, such as a chess board or the web of relations at a bridge table.

terms.name: Sensory overload
terms.text: The state where there is more information than the player can turn into meaning. Koster pairs it with deprivation, as the two edges a game moves between.

terms.name: Sequence (run)
terms.text: In Rummy, three or more cards of the same suit in order of rank.

terms.name: Sequence (scoring)
terms.text: In Klaberjass, three or more cards of one suit in order, held in the hand, which score points for one player only.

terms.name: Serious game
terms.text: A game made for education or training, such as disaster relief, hazardous work, military use or redesigning parks and transit.

terms.name: Serious game
terms.text: Mary Flanagan's name for a game that delivers social or political criticism, such as September 12th.

terms.name: Service
terms.text: The idea that each player's effort adds to something that benefits all other players.

terms.name: Service line
terms.text: A line on a court that a serve has to land beyond, or inside of, to count. Badminton has a short and a long one.

terms.name: Session
terms.text: One continuous period of play, such as an evening.

terms.name: Set (Bunco)
terms.text: Six rounds of Bunco, one for each number on the die. Groups usually play four sets in an evening.

terms.name: Set and sequence
terms.text: The two kinds of meld in rummy. A set is three or four cards of one rank and a sequence is three or four cards of one suit in order.

terms.name: Set back
terms.text: A penalty where points are added to a player who bid for a privilege and failed.

terms.name: Set back
terms.text: In Pitch, to lose the amount of your bid from your score because you won fewer points than you bid.

terms.name: Shadow
terms.text: An observer who follows a group or person, takes notes, has no power in the game and later shares an outside view in the debrief (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Shadow piece
terms.text: In Emergo, the last checkers of a player stacked together and entered as one piece, which can be tall and so a target or a force.

terms.name: Shanghai
terms.text: In darts, hitting the single, double and triple of one number in a turn, which wins at once in some versions.

terms.name: Shared intentionality
terms.text: Michael Tomasello's name for the human ability to take part with others in an activity that has a shared goal and a shared understanding of who does what.

terms.name: Shared reality
terms.text: The world that other people perceive in common with oneself, as against the private inner world. An object that is used has to belong to it.

terms.name: Sharp play
terms.text: A move within the rules that some players still see as taking advantage, such as sandbagging in poker or bringing a tournament deck to a casual game.

terms.name: Shatranj
terms.text: A chess form played for about a thousand years in Islamic countries, with less powerful pieces and a bare-king win. It led to modern chess.

terms.name: Shelter
terms.text: In Conspirators, one of the edge points that holds only one piece. There are not enough for every piece, so one player is left out.

terms.name: Shoe
terms.text: A box holding several packs, from which cards are slid out one at a time.

terms.name: Shooter
terms.text: The player who rolls the dice in Craps.

terms.name: Shooter
terms.text: In marbles, the larger marble a player flicks at the target marbles.

terms.name: Shooter and fader
terms.text: In Barbudi, the shooter rolls the dice and the fader bets that the shooter will not win.

terms.name: Shooting a marble
terms.text: Flicking a marble with the thumb, held back by the middle finger, to hit another marble.

terms.name: Shooting at a mark
terms.text: A frontier contest in which each shooter fires at a target and the most accurate aim wins. It made a game out of a skill needed for hunting and survival.

terms.name: Shooting match
terms.text: A contest in which men shoot at a target for a prize, such as a turkey. In Kirkland's writing a version with a live turkey tied to a post is called cruel.

terms.name: Shooting the moon
terms.text: In hearts, taking all the hearts and the queen of spades, which turns a big penalty into a big gain at a risk.

terms.name: Shooting the moon
terms.text: In hearts, taking all the penalty cards in one hand, which swaps the largest penalty for the largest reward.

terms.name: Shooting the moon
terms.text: In Hearts, one player taking every heart and the queen of spades. The penalty flips into a bonus.

terms.name: Short game
terms.text: A game in which not all the pack is in play.

terms.name: Short leap
terms.text: A capture made by jumping over an enemy piece on the next space and landing on the space just beyond it.

terms.name: Short-range task
terms.text: A substantial task measured in days and finished within a week or two, such as implementing a new mechanic for a playtest.

terms.name: Short-term memory limit
terms.text: The finding that people hold about seven units at once. Koster says it explains why adding too many numbers to track makes a game hard fast.

terms.name: Show
terms.text: In cribbage, the counting of hands after all the cards have been played. The nondealer counts first.

terms.name: Showdown
terms.text: The moment when players reveal their hands and the highest-ranking hand takes the pot.

terms.name: Showdown
terms.text: In poker, the end of the hand when players still in turn up their cards and the highest-ranking hand wins the pot.

terms.name: Showing
terms.text: Counting and scoring the cards in a hand, at the end of a round, in a fixed order.

terms.name: Shrovetide
terms.text: The days of festival just before Lent. A reference to February suggests Mankind may have been played then.

terms.name: Shutout
terms.text: A game won while the loser has won no hand, which doubles the winner's score.

terms.name: Shutout (backgammon)
terms.text: A home table where all six points are closed, so a stone on the bar cannot enter.

terms.name: Shuttlecock
terms.text: The feathered or plastic projectile hit over the net in badminton. It is also called a shuttle or birdie.

terms.name: Side hustle
terms.text: A small business run beside a main job, such as selling a product for a company, baking, or reselling candy.

terms.name: Side pot
terms.text: A separate pile of chips formed when one player cannot match a bet, so the extra goes to whoever holds the higher-ranking hand among those who put it up.

terms.name: Side stack
terms.text: A pile belonging to one player, used to park cards, which only that player may add to.

terms.name: Side-out / serve change
terms.text: In badminton, the serve passes to the other team when the serving team loses a point.

terms.name: Sideout
terms.text: In volleyball, losing a rally on the other team's serve. The serve changes sides and no point is scored.

terms.name: Signature strength
terms.text: A personal quality, such as courage or wisdom, that a person can bring to a group. The Lost Ring gave each player one of six, and tasks to match.

terms.name: Silent brainstorm
terms.text: A timed exercise where everyone writes one idea per sticky note without talking, then the notes are put on a wall and grouped.

terms.name: Simulation
terms.text: A game that tries to model its conceit, such as PanzerBlitz or Counter-Strike.

terms.name: Simulation
terms.text: A model of a real situation that players can act on, with clear cause and effect. September 12th shows a town where each missile has set results.

terms.name: Simulation-based play
terms.text: Play inside a simplified model of a real system, which also puts forward a point of view on that system.

terms.name: Simultaneous double game
terms.text: Two copies of a game played side by side, with each player taking opposite sides on the two boards.

terms.name: Simultaneous movement
terms.text: A turn structure in which all players write their moves in secret and carry them out at the same time.

terms.name: Simultanism
terms.text: Apollinaire's name for putting unrelated pieces of one moment side by side in a poem so that the passage of time while reading is neutralised.

terms.name: Single (pool)
terms.text: The three chips a Division Loo dealer puts in before each deal. The pool is split into thirds, one per trick.

terms.name: Single and double bete
terms.text: The loss for a bidder who gives up before leading (single) or who plays and fails (double, which costs twice as much).

terms.name: Single elimination
terms.text: A tournament format where a player is out as soon as they lose a match, and the last one left wins.

terms.name: Single man
terms.text: An ordinary piece in Checkers before it becomes a king.

terms.name: Single player
terms.text: In Calabrasella, the one person who plays alone against the other two, who become allies.

terms.name: Single-player game
terms.text: A game played alone against the machine, not through a network of other people. Wark wonders if it will become a vanished form, like silent film.

terms.name: Singleton
terms.text: A hand holding just one card of a suit.

terms.name: Site-specific game
terms.text: A game whose pieces come from a particular kind of place, so it cannot be played the same way elsewhere. Tombstone Hold 'Em uses gravestones as its playing cards.

terms.name: Site-specific work
terms.text: Art tied to one place, so that the viewer has to be there for the work to be complete.

terms.name: Situated learning
terms.text: Learning that takes place inside a realistic setting, where the student handles real tasks, people and ideas (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Situational awareness
terms.text: Perceiving what is around you, understanding what it means and projecting what happens next. Air traffic controllers and drivers use it.

terms.name: Six degrees of separation
terms.text: The result of Stanley Milgram's letter study, in which a letter took about six hand-overs to reach a stranger in Boston. About half the letters went through the same four people.

terms.name: Skat (cards)
terms.text: In the game of Skat, the two cards dealt face down to the table. They belong to the lone player, who may swap them for cards in hand.

terms.name: Skill
terms.text: An ability to meet the challenges of an activity. The book counts reading, calculating and joking with friends as skills as well as bodily ones.

terms.name: Skill
terms.text: How well a player has mastered an action in a game.

terms.name: Skill chain
terms.text: A line of players each beating the next about 60 percent of the time. Its length measures returns to skill.

terms.name: Skill-based play
terms.text: Play that asks players to build skill at the game's actions in pursuit of its goal.

terms.name: Skilled control
terms.text: A physical skill such as aiming or jumping that an adviser cannot simply tell someone to do. It stops an expert from playing for a beginner.

terms.name: Skills-first hiring
terms.text: Hiring on what a person can do in place of what degree they hold. OneTen found about 88 percent of its member firms' middle-skill jobs asked for a four-year degree.

terms.name: Skin
terms.text: The outward look of a character: colour, hair, clothes. In The Sims it has no effect on play, while the hidden numbers underneath do.

terms.name: Skinner box
terms.text: A game that rewards repeated clicks with small prizes, in the manner of behaviourist B. F. Skinner's box for rats, to hold players by habit.

terms.name: Skunk
terms.text: In cribbage, winning before the loser has reached the final leg of the board.

terms.name: Slam
terms.text: A promise to win nearly all tricks: twelve for a little slam, all thirteen for a grand slam. It carries a large bonus.

terms.name: Slam
terms.text: A bridge contract for twelve tricks (small slam) or all thirteen (grand slam). It carries a large bonus.

terms.name: Slam (Euchre)
terms.text: Winning a Euchre game before the other side has scored a point. It counts as two games.

terms.name: Slobberhannes
terms.text: A four-player game where nobody wants tricks, and a player who takes the Queen of Clubs, the last trick and the first trick scores extra penalty points.

terms.name: Slot machine
terms.text: A coin-operated machine where the player starts a ball or reels and waits for a result. Caillois places it where skill and chance meet, with chance deciding.

terms.name: Slow tempo game
terms.text: A game, such as I Spy, in which little happens to hold interest and the climax comes late. Boyd saw it as a risk to the spirit of play.

terms.name: Small wins
terms.text: Modest changes made one after another, which the organisation does not resist as it would resist one large change. One example is asking first for flexible hours and then for child care on site.

terms.name: Smear (schmier)
terms.text: Giving a high-value card to your partner's trick.

terms.name: Smudge
terms.text: A bid of four in Pitch which wins the game at once, as long as the bidder's score is not below zero.

terms.name: Smurfing
terms.text: An experienced player making a new low-rated account to be matched with beginners and win more often.

terms.name: Snake and ladder line
terms.text: A line drawn between two points of a track so that a piece landing on one end moves to the other, moving forward or back. Bell finds this in the Egyptian Palm Tree game.

terms.name: Snip, snap, snorem
terms.text: Payments of one, two or three chips made by the player whose card is matched by a second, third or fourth card of the same rank.

terms.name: Snowball
terms.text: A game tendency where the player who gets ahead wins more and more because of the lead, such as a Monopoly player using money to buy more.

terms.name: Snowball event
terms.text: In the book's model, an event that makes chances of winning less even, which raises the variance of the state vector.

terms.name: Social comparison theory
terms.text: The theory, from Leon Festinger in 1954, that people judge their own abilities, beliefs and attitudes by comparing themselves with other people.

terms.name: Social context
terms.text: One of Simkins's four design principles: the in-game social setting gives meaning to the character's actions (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Social design values
terms.text: One of Holm's kinds: values about social change and the betterment of society.

terms.name: Social dynamics engine
terms.text: A system where non-player characters react to the player's morally relevant acts and pass their judgment to each other, so the game world reacts as a community (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Social education
terms.text: Boyd's name for what directed play and group life give a child: sharing in a group, taking on values, and learning to meet problems with others.

terms.name: Social loafing
terms.text: The tendency to put in less effort when others seem to be doing the work. It fades when each person's duty is clear and visible.

terms.name: Social narrative
terms.text: A meaningful sequence of people's actions, thoughts, feelings and their causes. It covers stories in books and also the patterns inside everyday dealings with others (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Social narrative play
terms.text: Play in which a person acts out, rehearses or changes a social narrative while thinking critically about it. It can happen alone, for example in an adventure game (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Social network game
terms.text: A game played inside an online social network against, or alongside, people the player already knows.

terms.name: Social norm
terms.text: An unwritten expectation of how members of a group behave. Breaking one brings correction or exclusion, and norms can push people toward harmful conduct as easily as toward kind conduct (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

terms.name: Social participation game
terms.text: A game that gives players real-world volunteer tasks written to feel as clear and doable as quests in a role-playing game.

terms.name: Social participation task
terms.text: A small task, done with other people or for them, that draws on feelings and social ability as well as thinking. Writing a message of luck to a child before a test is one.

terms.name: Social presence
terms.text: The sensation of sharing a space with other people.

terms.name: Social welfare function
terms.text: A rule that combines the utilities of all individuals into one score for a society. It can be their sum, their average, or the utility of the person with the lowest utility.

terms.name: Social work
terms.text: A work whose medium includes the social relationships among its participants.

terms.name: Socializer
terms.text: In Bartle's list, a player who plays mostly to deal with other players.

terms.name: Society of the spectacle
terms.text: Debord's phrase for a society in which people watch and buy images of life instead of acting for themselves.

terms.name: Soft war
terms.text: A form of fighting game, such as with styrofoam swords, where no one is hurt. DeKoven credits the idea to Stewart Brand.

terms.name: Softwar
terms.text: Stewart Brand's idea of conflict designed to suit everyone: kept to a region, refereed so a win or loss is certain, and cushioned so that harm is limited.

terms.name: Software requirement specification
terms.text: A technical document saying how software will work and be used. A game design document may include or sit beside one.

terms.name: Software toy
terms.text: A video game with no goal to reach.

terms.name: Solids and stripes
terms.text: The two groups of numbered balls in Eight Ball, assigned to the two players or teams.

terms.name: Solitaire
terms.text: A one-player game of position in which pegs jump over each other and are removed.

terms.name: Solitaire
terms.text: A game played by one person, building sequences called families on foundations.

terms.name: Solo, collaborative, competitive
terms.text: Koster's three ways to take part in an activity: alone, with others, or against them. He lays them across a grid for each medium.

terms.name: Solved game
terms.text: A game for which the winning strategy is known, so play has no open choices left. Tic-tac-toe is solved for most adults and unsolved for small children.

terms.name: Solved game
terms.text: A game where the rules of thumb are so complete that a player can never miss the winning move, as in tic-tac-toe or Nim.

terms.name: Somergame (summer game)
terms.text: A lay game held in summer, often in a churchyard or beside it. One 1469 Yorkshire example chose a village king and queen and led them with a minstrel in procession to a "somer house" by the church.

terms.name: Soother
terms.text: An object that always calms the child and brings sleep within minutes. A boy's blanket end and later a green jersey are the example.

terms.name: Sophist
terms.text: A travelling Greek teacher who gave paid shows of argument and cleverness and challenged rivals in public. Huizinga treats the sophist as a player in a contest of wits.

terms.name: Sore loser
terms.text: A player who fails to put down game goals when the game ends.

terms.name: Sorites
terms.text: A chain-question that moves one step at a time, such as asking which grain of a spilled sack makes the noise.

terms.name: Sound prototype
terms.text: A trial of a game's sound and music, often made at the same time as a playable prototype by other team members.

terms.name: Sounds-like
terms.text: In Charades, a gesture of a hand cupped at the ear to show that the guess has to sound like the word.

terms.name: Sourcing versus selecting
terms.text: Recruiting from a pool that is varied by design, for example from historically Black colleges, without choosing a person because of their group.

terms.name: Sowing
terms.text: Lifting all the seeds out of a pit and dropping one into each following pit.

terms.name: Sowing
terms.text: Moving pieces from a pit around a track of pits one at a time, as in mancala games.

terms.name: Sowing
terms.text: Taking all the seeds from one hollow and dropping them one by one into the following hollows, the basic move in mancala games.

terms.name: Sowing
terms.text: In mancala, picking up all the pieces in a pit and dropping them one at a time into the following pits.

terms.name: Sowing
terms.text: Picking up all the seeds from one pit and dropping them one at a time into the pits that follow.

terms.name: Space
terms.text: An empty place in a solitaire layout made by moving a pile away. It can be used to rearrange cards.

terms.name: Space of possibility
terms.text: All the different play experiences a game can give, set by how its actions, rules, goals, objects and playspace fit together.

terms.name: Spaced repetition
terms.text: Learning by repeating an item at growing gaps, such as after five minutes, 30 minutes and two hours, instead of cramming it all at once.

terms.name: Spadilla
terms.text: In Solo, the Queen of Clubs, which is always the top trump.

terms.name: Spare
terms.text: Knocking down all the pins with the two balls of a frame. The next roll is added to its score.

terms.name: Sparse game tree
terms.text: A game tree with few choices at a point.

terms.name: Special dice
terms.text: Dice with faces other than the usual one to six pips, such as the Bell and Hammer dice, Crown and Anchor dice or poker dice.

terms.name: Special role
terms.text: A job with its own power added to a hidden-role game, such as the Doctor who can save a person or the Sheriff who can investigate one.

terms.name: Specialist and maximalist profiles
terms.text: A specialist game concentrates on a few traits, as The Resistance does on player reliance and interaction. A maximalist game pushes all its traits high, as Mage Knight Board Game does.

terms.name: Spectacula
terms.text: Latin for public shows. The early church wrote against three kinds: chariot races in the circus, gladiator fights in the amphitheatre, and mimes and actors in the theatrum.

terms.name: Spectation
terms.text: How well a game suits being watched, whether by a stadium crowd, people at a bar or family sitting out a game of Monopoly.

terms.name: Spectator
terms.text: A person who watches and does not play. Watchers can push the players to put on a display instead of playing.

terms.name: Spectator effect
terms.text: A change in what a player does because someone else is watching, such as a child asking a parent whether he is stealing cars (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Spectator sport
terms.text: A game that many watch while a few play. The book calls politics the premier one in America, because the shrewd few play and the many follow.

terms.name: Spectator stance
terms.text: Watching part or all of a game session without taking part in it.

terms.name: Speech tag
terms.text: A label naming the speaker in front of each speech. Readers keep seeing the abstract name, while a viewer sees a person acting.

terms.name: Speedrun
terms.text: An attempt to finish a game with no random parts in the least possible time, often with software that enters the moves for the player. Burgun uses it to show that such a game has one fastest route.

terms.name: Speedrunning
terms.text: A way of playing a game where the goal is changed to finishing as fast as possible, sometimes by using glitches. The author counts it as a different game on the same materials.

terms.name: Spiral race game
terms.text: A race game whose track winds in a spiral towards a centre, such as the Hyena game or the Royal Game of Goose.

terms.name: Spit pile
terms.text: In Spit, a pile in the middle of the table where both players race to put cards in sequence up or down from the top card.

terms.name: Split
terms.text: Playing a pair of equal cards as two separate hands, each with its own bet.

terms.name: Split (in Stuss and Faro)
terms.text: When two cards of the same rank come up in one turn, so a bet on that rank both wins and loses. The dealer takes it, which is the dealer's only edge.

terms.name: Splitting pairs
terms.text: In blackjack, treating a pair of equal cards as two separate hands, each with its own bet.

terms.name: Spoil
terms.text: In Spoil Five, a hand in which nobody wins three tricks. The pool stays and players add to it.

terms.name: Spoil-sport
terms.text: A player who breaks the rules or walks out of a game, so that the shared play-world falls apart. The group usually sends this person away.

terms.name: Spoiler
terms.text: A detail that, once told, spoils an experience. Jason Rohrer, quoted by Sharp, said games do not have spoilers, since the experience is in the playing (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

terms.name: Spoilsport (the nihilist)
terms.text: A person who refuses to play because the rules have no reason behind them. Caillois says this person ends the game, where a cheat does not.

terms.name: Sponsor
terms.text: Usually a senior person who puts their own reputation behind you, speaks for you when you are not present and pushes for your promotion.

terms.name: Spontaneity
terms.text: In Boyd's use, free action by the whole person in response to a situation, where meaning and impulse come together. She set it apart from the rush of a mob, which gives no room to think.

terms.name: Spontaneous and instrumental networking
terms.text: Two ways of making contacts. Spontaneous contact has no planned purpose, and instrumental contact is sought out to reach a goal. The second can feel selfish, and people who feel that tend to do it less.

terms.name: Sport (a gambler)
terms.text: In Western novels the word for a gambler who was also a dandy and a gunman. It was a different meaning from sport as athletic contest.

terms.name: Sport of the gods
terms.text: A phrase for the view that humans are playthings of a power that decides everything. Oriard also lists the forms sport of fate and sport of chance.

terms.name: Sportsmanlike player
terms.text: A person who plays hard during the game but cares afterwards only that everyone had an interesting match. The author uses this person to show the all-consuming attitude can be kept inside a game.

terms.name: Sportsmanship
terms.text: A way of playing that accepts both the written rules and a code of conduct about how to behave, such as winning and losing gracefully. Oriard takes the word from the historian John Dizikes.

terms.name: Spot of indeterminacy
terms.text: A point in a game's design that is left open, so that each playing can turn out differently. The book takes the phrase from Roman Ingarden, who wrote about literature.

terms.name: Sprouts
terms.text: A paper game in which players join dots with lines and add a new dot on each line. No line may cross another and no dot may have more than three lines.

terms.name: Sputnik piece
terms.text: In Sputnik Chess, a rook, bishop or knight that has crossed the centre line and may then move in addition to the one normal piece moved each turn.

terms.name: Square deal
terms.text: Roosevelt's phrase for fair dealing with everyone. Oriard notes it points to the poker table, where tricks are part of play, rather than to the gentleman's playing field.

terms.name: Squeeze
terms.text: A series of plays that forces an opponent to throw away a card he needs.

terms.name: Squiggle game
terms.text: A two-person drawing game: one person makes an impulsive line, the other turns it into something, then they swap. The author uses it with children.

terms.name: Squop
terms.text: In tiddlywinks, to cover another disc, even slightly. A covered disc cannot be played until it is freed.

terms.name: Stack
terms.text: In Puluc, a conqueror piece with its prisoner underneath, which carries the prisoner back along the track.

terms.name: Stack
terms.text: In Stack-Up Checkers, a pile of captured pieces that moves as one piece and belongs to the colour on top.

terms.name: Stack (Lasca and Emergo)
terms.text: A column of captured pieces kept under the capturer. The player whose piece is on top controls the whole stack.

terms.name: Stacked deck
terms.text: A deck arranged beforehand so that one player wins whatever the others do. Hank Morgan in Twain's A Connecticut Yankee plays with one, since he has thirteen centuries of knowledge that his opponents lack.

terms.name: Stage (a station in a play)
terms.text: In the 1560 New Romney accounts, a separate built place for one party in the action: Pilate's stage, Herod's stage, the Tormentors' stage, heaven, the cave and hell.

terms.name: Stage direction
terms.text: A note in a script telling what is to be done, such as which persons descend with beams of light. N-Town directs three beams passing from Holy Ghost to the Son to the Father.

terms.name: Stage plan
terms.text: A drawing of where each scaffold and structure stands. The text of the Castle of Perseverance is followed by one, showing a castle in the centre with scaffolds around it.

terms.name: Stage play
terms.text: A phrase in English parish and city records that looks like acted drama but often meant king games and other folk activities, sometimes mocking or parodying.

terms.name: Staged game
terms.text: A game with stages so distinct they are almost separate games, such as bidding then play in bridge or drafting then play in Magic.

terms.name: Staggered start
terms.text: A setup in which players begin on different squares instead of all on the first one, so that later movers are not left with the smallest chances. In Monopoly the second player starts on Just Visiting and the third on Free Parking.

terms.name: Stakes
terms.text: What the players put at risk or play for, such as money, meaning, learning or dignity. DeKoven says stakes help give a game focus, as a score does.

terms.name: Stalemate
terms.text: A position where a player has no legal move. In Shatranj a stalemated king could exchange places with another piece, and otherwise the player lost.

terms.name: Stalemate
terms.text: A position in which neither side can make progress. Burgun says simple capture-for-capture area games drift toward it.

terms.name: Stalemate
terms.text: A chess position where the player to move is not in check but has no legal move. The game is a draw.

terms.name: Stalemate
terms.text: A position where the player to move has no legal move but is not in check, which is a draw.

terms.name: Stalemate
terms.text: A position in which the player to move has no legal move though not in check. Chess draws it, but Shatranj and the author's rules count it as a loss for that player.

terms.name: Stalemate
terms.text: A position in which the king is not in check but every move open to the player would put it in check. The game is a draw.

terms.name: Stand pat
terms.text: To keep your hand as dealt without exchanging any cards.

terms.name: Standard
terms.text: A commonly accepted pattern players already know, such as the fifty-two-card deck, taking turns, or the WASD keys. It can be a small detail or a whole genre.

terms.name: Standing pat
terms.text: In draw poker, choosing not to replace any cards. It can be shown by knocking on the table.

terms.name: Standing play
terms.text: A play kept at one site and given over several days. Lincoln held a standing play of Tobit over two days in the summer in the 1560s.

terms.name: Standoff
terms.text: A tie.

terms.name: Star-like organization
terms.text: A network in which one member is linked to nearly everyone and the others are linked mainly to that member. A class where 37 of 40 boys name the same friend is one.

terms.name: Start card
terms.text: In Cribbage, the top card turned up after the crib is laid out. Both hands and the crib count it as part of the hand.

terms.name: Starter
terms.text: In Domino Crib, a tile turned up from the stock and counted with each player's hand and the crib.

terms.name: Starter
terms.text: In Cribbage, the card turned up from the pack that counts as a fifth card in every hand.

terms.name: Starter
terms.text: In cribbage, the card turned up after the cut. Every hand and the crib are counted together with it.

terms.name: State vector
terms.text: A list of every player's current chance of winning, adding up to one. Its spread shows whether the game is snowballing or catching up.

terms.name: Static capture
terms.text: A piece is captured by another piece passing over it or landing on its space. The paper points out that this only works if the pieces have some pattern of movement.

terms.name: Status-size hypothesis
terms.text: The claim that physical size and social status go together, and that people judge higher-status people to be taller.

terms.name: Steal (word game)
terms.text: In Anagrams, taking another player's word by adding at least one tile from the pile and rearranging into a new word. A suffix alone does not count.

terms.name: Stealing a base
terms.text: Running to the next base while a pitch is being thrown, instead of waiting for the batter to hit.

terms.name: Stealing a word
terms.text: In Anagrams, using a word another player has made, with at least one more tile, to make a new word of your own.

terms.name: Stealth
terms.text: A way of playing in which the aim is to avoid being targeted. In Deus Ex it is one of three ways through the game.

terms.name: Step mover and ranging piece
terms.text: In Chu Shogi, a step mover goes one square at a time in set directions and a ranging piece goes any distance along open lines in some directions.

terms.name: Steracle (plural steraclis)
terms.text: A rare Middle English word for a show or sight, probably from the same idea as "spectacle". Around 1410 to 1420 a Norfolk witness listed as steracles the shooting, wrestling, stone-putting, running for a spear and football for cakes at a gathering.

terms.name: Stick-the-dealer
terms.text: A Euchre variation in which a dealer has to name a trump suit if everyone passes in the second round, so no hand is thrown in.

terms.name: Stigmatization, marginalization, subordination
terms.text: Three kinds of disadvantage the author and a colleague describe. Stigmatized people draw close watching and fear, marginalized people are mostly overlooked, and subordinated people are watched and liked but kept below others in power.

terms.name: Stimulus overinclusion
terms.text: The inability to keep irrelevant information out of awareness. The book links it to attentional disorders and to the loss of enjoyment.

terms.name: Stimulus pattern
terms.text: An example of play, such as a rope-jumping rhyme or a challenge to chase, that sets off a matching response in other players.

terms.name: Stock
terms.text: The cards left undealt, kept face down (or face up in some games) to be drawn from later.

terms.name: Stock
terms.text: The face-down pile of unused cards from which players draw.

terms.name: Stock
terms.text: The pile of cards left face down from which players draw.

terms.name: Stock and discard pile
terms.text: In rummy, the face-down pile that players draw from, and the face-up pile where they throw unwanted cards.

terms.name: Stock figure
terms.text: A familiar type that playwrights and audiences both know, such as the tyrant or the disobedient servant. The same types speak in the same voices in biblical, saint and morality plays.

terms.name: Stone
terms.text: The name Backgammon uses for a playing piece.

terms.name: Stones and gems
terms.text: The two kinds of bead in The Glass Bead Game. Plain stones have no value and coloured gems are worth from 1 to 5 points.

terms.name: Stoop
terms.text: In New York, the steps leading up to an apartment building, used as a bouncing wall in Stoopball.

terms.name: Stop (call)
terms.text: A call by a player who thinks the opponent broke the order of moves, which ends that player's turn if the charge is true.

terms.name: Stop card
terms.text: A card whose discard blocks the next player from taking the discard pile, so they have to draw from the stock.

terms.name: Stop card
terms.text: A card that, when discarded, stops the next player from taking the pile. In Canasta, a black three does this.

terms.name: Stop-and-draw penalty
terms.text: In Crazy Eights variations, a rule that makes the next player draw cards unless they can answer with the same rank, such as a run of twos.

terms.name: Stopper
terms.text: A card that will win a trick in a suit the opponents are running, and so halts them.

terms.name: Stops
terms.text: A family of games where a turn is blocked when the player lacks the next card in a sequence.

terms.name: Store
terms.text: The place where captured seeds are kept, either a special hole or a heap beside the board.

terms.name: Storehouse
terms.text: A larger pit at the end of a mancala board in which captured or scored pieces are kept.

terms.name: Story (narrative)
terms.text: A conceit that is told as a fixed series of events. Chess has a conceit but no story.

terms.name: Story beat
terms.text: A major moment in a story, which a game may mark with an image or a scene change.

terms.name: Storyboard
terms.text: A sequence of drawings showing how a scene is framed and what happens in it. In games it makes sure everyone understands how the screen will look.

terms.name: Storytelling
terms.text: Using story ways of shaping experience inside a game, such as text, scenes or the order in which things are found.

terms.name: Storyworld
terms.text: An invented world in which players act as characters, and whose events unfold from what those characters do.

terms.name: Straddle
terms.text: A Poker bet that doubles the blind before the cards are cut, giving the player the last say before the draw.

terms.name: Straight
terms.text: Five cards in order of rank in Poker. It beats three of a kind.

terms.name: Straight flush
terms.text: Five cards in order and all of one suit in Poker. It is the highest hand when straights are allowed.

terms.name: Strategic authenticity
terms.text: The idea that choosing how you present yourself and being authentic can both be true. The author asks you to know why you are doing each thing, whether to connect, to express yourself or to steer others' reactions.

terms.name: Strategic collapse
terms.text: When the real choices in a game shrink to a few because some options are far more effective than the rest.

terms.name: Strategic perception
terms.text: Simon Dor's term for how experienced players see a game differently, such as a chess player seeing lines of movement and not the figure of a rook.

terms.name: Strategy
terms.text: A plan of behaviour chosen in advance for a game, which says what a player will do in each circumstance that may arise. What arises depends on the plans the other side has chosen.

terms.name: Strategy
terms.text: A player's ability to work out the ways of acting that lead to the goal.

terms.name: Strategy game
terms.text: A game that asks for complex problem solving, as against games that ask for fast reactions. Khetrapal reports that most computer games used in schools were this kind or simulations, such as SimCity (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

terms.name: Strategy game
terms.text: A genre where the player manages resources over time and moves among many variables, such as Civilization III.

terms.name: Strategy guide
terms.text: A printed or online book that tells players how to raise their score or finish a game. Wark says his book is not one.

terms.name: Stretch goal
terms.text: On a crowdfunding page, an extra reward unlocked for all backers once total pledges pass a set amount. Anachrony's first campaign had fifteen.

terms.name: Strict elimination
terms.text: Being completely out of the game while the game goes on for others.

terms.name: Strike
terms.text: In baseball, a pitch the batter misses or a foul ball. Three strikes put the batter out.

terms.name: Strike (bowling)
terms.text: Knocking down all ten pins with the first ball of a frame. The next two rolls are added to its score.

terms.name: String line
terms.text: A line on a billiards or pool table behind which a ball is played from at the start of a stroke.

terms.name: Striving play
terms.text: Playing for the sake of the struggle to win. The player cares about winning only while the game lasts, and drops that care afterwards.

terms.name: Structural failure
terms.text: A failure that is often technical, such as bugs that stop the game being played.

terms.name: Structural framework
terms.text: The companion half of the model, which describes the parts of a game. At the top it separates a game instance, a game session and a play session, and below that it sorts the parts of a game into bounding, temporal and objective components.

terms.name: Structured goal
terms.text: A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, personally relevant and time-bound. Balzac says such goals raise commitment, enjoyment and learning in games (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Stud poker
terms.text: A form of poker in which some of each player's cards are dealt face down and some face up, so that other players can see part of the hand.

terms.name: Stupid game
terms.text: A game that only works if players try to win, yet whose memorable moments are the failures, such as the pile-up in Twister or the garbled message at the end of Telephone.

terms.name: Style frame
terms.text: A single image showing what the game will look like.

terms.name: Stymie
terms.text: Being blocked by another player's ball lying in your path. Modern golf lets a player mark the ball and lift it.

terms.name: Subgoals
terms.text: Smaller aims set inside a larger goal so that progress can be measured. The book lists them as a step in turning any action into flow.

terms.name: Subject matter expert
terms.text: A person with deep knowledge of the real topic a game models. They advise the design team and test the game; they are not asked to design it (chapter by Chris Swain).

terms.name: Subjective dangers
terms.text: In climbing, the risks that come from the climber's own lack of skill, including misjudging how hard a climb is.

terms.name: Subjective object
terms.text: The first object, before the baby has pushed it away as not-me. It prepares the way for objects that are perceived as separate.

terms.name: Subjunctive
terms.text: The quality of a story or game that lets the player project their identity onto a character inside it and take part in what follows, after Jerome Bruner (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Submersion
terms.text: Letting a temporary goal fill one's mind so that it feels like a final aim, while the reasons for playing drop out of sight.

terms.name: Subscendence
terms.text: Timothy Morton's word for thinking downward into many small connected things, as against viewing a whole from above.

terms.name: Substance and accident
terms.text: Substance is what all things of a kind share, such as chairness. Accidents are the particular marks that differ, such as colour or number of legs, and show the substance to us.

terms.name: Substantive conflict
terms.text: A team disagreement about the game itself, such as what kind of game it is or what experience to give.

terms.name: Subtle value game
terms.text: A game with goals that are unclear to apply, plural, and hard to rank, such as informal skateboarding or improv comedy.

terms.name: Subtractive pattern
terms.text: Barney's name for a pattern that mitigates or weakens the effect of another pattern. The paper takes it as the same idea as the conflicting patterns of Björk and Holopainen.

terms.name: Subversion
terms.text: An action that turns a rule, system or institution upside down from inside, in this book a creative act more than a destructive one.

terms.name: Sudden death
terms.text: A tiebreak in which tied players each try one more task, and anyone who fails while another succeeds is out. It repeats until one player is left.

terms.name: Suerte
terms.text: A Spanish word for one's luck and lot. Some Central American groups believe each person is born with a fixed suerte that decides character and fortune.

terms.name: Sufficient mothering
terms.text: The book's idea of a carer who adapts almost completely at the start and then adapts less and less as the child can cope. The carer need not be the mother, and need not be clever, only devoted.

terms.name: Sugoroku
terms.text: A Japanese roll-and-move board game, later printed as a picture sheet, with themes such as religion, travel, poetry or everyday life.

terms.name: Super Ghost
terms.text: A form of Ghost in which a letter may be added at either the beginning or the end of the sequence.

terms.name: Super-empowered hopeful individual
terms.text: A person who feels both hopeful about the future and personally able to change it, helped by networked tools. Shortened to SEHI.

terms.name: Superior patterns and subpatterns
terms.text: A superior pattern describes a more abstract characteristic and can be brought about by applying the given pattern. A subpattern is a more specific pattern that can be used to bring the given one about.

terms.name: Superstructure
terms.text: In Superstruct, a network built on top of existing groups that joins communities which do not yet work together, to solve a problem none could solve alone.

terms.name: Supporting mechanism
terms.text: A rule that exists to serve the core mechanism. Burgun asks of Cranium what rolling and moving have to do with answering trivia.

terms.name: Surround capture
terms.text: A capture made by filling every square next to a piece. In Tablut and Hnefatafl the king is captured this way.

terms.name: Survivability score
terms.text: A number from 0 to 100 in Superstruct that showed one player's progress. It was not made for ranking players against each other.

terms.name: Survival (of a game)
terms.text: A game that stays in use after the belief or ritual behind it has been lost. Caillois says many children's games began as ceremonies.

terms.name: Survival of the object
terms.text: An object survives when it comes through the subject's attacks without changing its quality or hitting back. The book says this is what places it outside the subject's control.

terms.name: Sustainable engagement economy
terms.text: An engagement economy that rewards contributors with feelings and experiences that can be produced again and again, instead of money or prizes, which run out.

terms.name: Swarm intelligence
terms.text: The skill of improvising with strangers toward a shared goal, which makes people more likely to band together.

terms.name: Sweat equity
terms.text: Work put into a project in the hope of later returns instead of payment.

terms.name: Sweep
terms.text: In Casino, taking every card on the table with one play. It scores a point.

terms.name: Sweep
terms.text: Taking every card on the table at once, which scores a point in Casino.

terms.name: Sweep
terms.text: In Casino, capturing every card on the table in one turn. It scores an extra point.

terms.name: Sweepstakes
terms.text: A lottery in which a large prize is drawn among many small ticket buyers. Caillois cites the Sweepstakes of the Grand Prix de Paris.

terms.name: Sweet spot
terms.text: The number of players that most often suits a game that allows a range of player counts.

terms.name: Swiss
terms.text: A tournament format where after each round, players with the same record are paired against each other.

terms.name: Swiss system
terms.text: A tournament format in which players with similar records are paired against each other each round.

terms.name: Symbiotic cooperation
terms.text: Cooperation where players depend on each other to play at all. In Way, one player cannot see what the other sees.

terms.name: Symbolic system
terms.text: A set of signs with its own rules, such as a language, mathematics or notation. The book compares it to a game with a separate reality.

terms.name: Symmetric game
terms.text: A game where each player has the same options as the other.

terms.name: Symmetric play
terms.text: Play in which every player has the same rules and the same strategy open to them, as in most mancala games.

terms.name: Symmetrical competition
terms.text: Competition where all players have the same actions and aim at the same goal.

terms.name: Symmetrical cooperative play
terms.text: Cooperation where all players have the same actions and attributes, so the players themselves work out who does what.

terms.name: Symmetrical forces
terms.text: A set-up where all sides start with the same pieces and powers, as in chess.

terms.name: Symmetrical information space
terms.text: A game where all players can see the same information about the state of play, as in basketball.

terms.name: Synaesthesia
terms.text: A blending of the senses. Rez joins colour, shape, beat, sound and controller vibration so that they pulse together.

terms.name: Synchronic reading
terms.text: Reading works side by side as if from the same moment, instead of in order of date. The book reads Bale's Baptism play beside the three older ones, which may have been played in the same year.

terms.name: Synthesizing medium
terms.text: A game, story or similar form that pulls scattered impulses and experiences into one organised whole for the player.

terms.name: Systematizing brain
terms.text: In Baron-Cohen's theory, a mind that favours rules and systems. Koster suggests formal game systems suit such minds, and contrasts them with empathizing minds.

terms.name: Systemic
terms.text: Describes a characteristic that depends mainly on the game as a system, for example on its rules.

terms.name: Systems dynamics
terms.text: A way of looking at a game as a set of linked parts, watching what the parts do to one another, not just listing them.

terms.name: T-chart
terms.text: A two- or three-column chart on which students sort items. Mission US teachers used one with the columns Patriot, Loyalist and Undecided (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Table card
