terms.text: A card a player puts face up in front of them in Grabouche when they cannot or choose not to play to the centre. At most four piles are allowed.

terms.name: Table stakes
terms.text: A betting limit where each player may bet only as many chips as he has on the table when the deal starts, with a side pot for the extra chips of others.

terms.name: Tableau
terms.text: The pattern of cards laid out on the table in solitaire games, from which cards are cleared by matching rules.

terms.name: Tableau
terms.text: The original layout of cards on the table in a solitaire game, from which cards are moved in order.

terms.name: Tableau vivant
terms.text: A living picture: people posed in a painted set, shown in a procession or royal entry without acting out a story.

terms.name: Tables
terms.text: The medieval name for the family of backgammon-like games. By the sixteenth century it meant any game played on a flat board.

terms.name: Tabletop role-playing game
terms.text: A game played around a table where each player speaks as a character and one person describes the world and referees.

terms.name: Tablut
terms.text: A Lapland game related to hnefatafl, played on 9 by 9 squares with a king and eight defenders against sixteen attackers.

terms.name: Tabula
terms.text: The Roman forerunner of backgammon, with 15 pieces each starting off the board, three dice and both players moving the same way.

terms.name: Tactic
terms.text: De Certeau's word for a small everyday move by someone with little power, made inside a system they did not set up. Tricking a game administrator or reskinning a character are tactics of this kind.

terms.name: Tafl
terms.text: A family of northern European games in which a smaller force with a special piece tries to break out while a larger force tries to hem it in.

terms.name: Tafl
terms.text: An Old Norse family of two-player strategy games with no chance, on a checkered or cross-shaped board, where a king and his smaller team are surrounded by a larger one.

terms.name: Tagging back
terms.text: Tagging the player who has just tagged you. Tag players decide before starting whether it is allowed.

terms.name: Takeaway
terms.text: A specific, agreed statement of what a playtest shows about the design, such as the paddle controls are too loose.

terms.name: Takeback
terms.text: A handicap that lets the less skilled player undo his last move once per turn after seeing the reply.

terms.name: Takeout (informatory) double
terms.text: A double that asks the partner to name a suit, instead of penalising the opponents.

terms.name: Taking all (shooting the moon)
terms.text: Winning every penalty card in a hand. The game then turns the penalty into a gain or cancels the hand.

terms.name: Taking-away game
terms.text: A game in which players remove items from a pile or array, such as Nim, Tsianshidsi and Chomp.

terms.name: Talking rights
terms.text: A meeting protocol for who speaks when, set so quiet people are heard and loud ones do not win by volume.

terms.name: Tally card
terms.text: A card handed to each guest at a party game that shows the starting table and records points scored in each round.

terms.name: Talon
terms.text: A pile of cards turned from the hand that cannot be placed at once, in solitaire.

terms.name: Tap
terms.text: To bet against another player the whole of his chips.

terms.name: Target audience
terms.text: The first of five elements of family game design: deciding who the game is for. A family can mean a parent and one child, a whole household, or relatives in different places (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Target audience playtest
terms.text: A test with people who enjoy the kind of play the game offers, usually at core or complete prototype stage.

terms.name: Target game
terms.text: A game where players aim at a mark and add their points to a team score, taking turns with no contact. Boyd's leader used them to settle an unsteady group.

terms.name: Targeted interaction
terms.text: An interaction where the acting player chooses which other player it lands on. The effect can help the target, as in trading, and not only harm.

terms.name: Targeting
terms.text: Picking out one thing among many as the object of an action. In Rez the player holds the trigger to select and lets go to fire.

terms.name: Taste cluster
terms.text: A group of users put together by what they watch and not by where they live. Netflix sorts its users into about 2,000 of them.

terms.name: Taw line
terms.text: The line from which players shoot in a marble ring game.

terms.name: Teachable agent
terms.text: A software character that knows less than the student, who teaches it a skill. It replaces a quiz.

terms.name: Team agreement
terms.text: A written understanding of a team's goal, member status, ownership, expected effort, roles, decision-making and length of working together.

terms.name: Team captain
terms.text: The member of a team who makes the final decision when teammates disagree.

terms.name: Teamwork
terms.text: Play built on cooperation, where each player has a role in a larger effort, such as a twenty-five-player raid.

terms.name: Technical activity
terms.text: Suits's name for an activity done to reach an end that is valued for itself, so the person takes the most efficient route. A game is the opposite, because the player accepts less efficient routes on purpose.

terms.name: Teddy-bear effect
terms.text: In one study, the Black chief executives of the largest companies had more baby-faced features than Black people lower down, while the White chief executives of the largest companies had less.

terms.name: Teetotum
terms.text: A small spinning top with numbered or marked sides, used in place of a die. Put and Take uses a six-sided one.

terms.name: Teetotum
terms.text: A children's game in which the player spins on one foot as fast as possible. It is Caillois's example of a game that seeks dizziness.

terms.name: Teetotum
terms.text: A spinning top marked with numbers, used in place of dice so that a children's game did not recall gambling.

terms.name: Teleportation
terms.text: A one-time move in Teleportation Chess by which a piece goes to any vacant square. Since the square has to be empty, it cannot capture.

terms.name: Telesthesia
terms.text: Wark's word for sensing and acting at a distance, through the telegraph, telephone, television and networks.

terms.name: Tempered radical
terms.text: A person from a stigmatized group who gets inside a mainstream organisation and uses that position to push for change that helps others in the group. The term is from Debra Meyerson and Maureen Scully.

terms.name: Temporary autonomous zone
terms.text: Hakim Bey's idea of a short-lived space that slips outside formal control. Souzis made one in which people agreed not to use their phones.

terms.name: Tenace
terms.text: Two cards of one suit that are close but not next to each other in rank, such as ace and queen.

terms.name: Tension
terms.text: The uncertainty in play, as the player tries to make something come off and so end the strain. Puzzles, target-shooting, gambling and sport all rest on it.

terms.name: Tension and release
terms.text: The pattern in a platformer jump: unease while the outcome is unknown, relief when you land.

terms.name: Tentative Black
terms.text: In Renju, the player who places the first stone but may be forced to become White if the opponent chooses to switch after the third stone.

terms.name: Tenth cards
terms.text: In Cribbage, the Ten, Jack, Queen and King, which all count as ten.

terms.name: Territorial possession
terms.text: A group of games, including Wei-ch'i, in which players win by controlling more of the board than the opponent.

terms.name: Territory
terms.text: A zone of the board set aside for play, one of the five parts Flanagan finds in an early mancala board.

terms.name: Territory
terms.text: In Go, the empty points a player's stones surround, which count towards his score.

terms.name: Territory
terms.text: In Go, the empty points and stones a player surrounds, which are counted at the end to find the winner.

terms.name: Territory
terms.text: In Go, the empty points a player has surrounded. The player with more territory wins.

terms.name: Thar's a bar
terms.text: A silly line game where each player points at an imaginary bear with a growing set of body parts, until everyone leans and falls. Nobody can succeed at it.

terms.name: Theatrical metaphor
terms.text: Calling something "theatrical" to condemn it. Medieval writers used it for any activity they judged indecorous, worldly or outside the church's own ritual, whether or not any acting was involved.

terms.name: Theatrum
terms.text: In medieval writing, the Latin word for a place of spectacle that was linked with obscene and immodest behaviour. It did not mean a building where dramas were staged, as "theatre" does now.

terms.name: Thematic
terms.text: The layer of story, pictures and setting laid over the rules, such as calling a token a soldier. Burgun separates it from the mechanisms, which are the game itself.

terms.name: Theme
terms.text: The framework a game uses to represent itself, which helps players grasp how its world works.

terms.name: Theme (as a layer)
terms.text: A literal layer of story and picture over the mechanisms. Burgun says it helps players learn what verbs mean, as bombs and arrows do in Zelda.

terms.name: Theme synergy
terms.text: How closely a game's theme, aesthetics and mechanics fit together. When it is high, taking the theme away leaves the mechanics without meaning, and when it is low the game would play much the same without it.

terms.name: Theriomorphic
terms.text: Shaped like an animal. Huizinga uses it of gods, spirits and masks that take animal form.

terms.name: Thick description
terms.text: A detailed account of events with their setting, so the reader sees what happened in context. Macklin uses it to describe the first play of Re:Activism (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Third area
terms.text: The part of life that is neither inner psychic reality nor the shared outside world. It contains play and cultural experience.

terms.name: Third place
terms.text: A play space that is neither work or school nor home, where a community can form across differences of opinion (chapter by David Simkins).

terms.name: Thirdspace
terms.text: Soja's word for lived and imagined space that sits between physical places and abstract ideas of space. Flanagan treats games as one such space.

terms.name: Thoughtful design
terms.text: Löwgren and Stolterman's name for design done with awareness that every choice affects people's lives and carries values (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

terms.name: Threat
terms.text: In Wari, a cup with one or two seeds that an enemy cup can reach with its last seed, so as to make a capturing count of two or three.

terms.name: Three E's
terms.text: Entrepreneurship, enclaves and exodus: the three routes the book gives for leaving the game.

terms.name: Three-in-a-row
terms.text: A winning shape of three pieces in a straight line, as in Noughts and Crosses, Three Men's Morris and Dara.

terms.name: Throne
terms.text: In Shaturanga, a marked square where a rajah starts. A rajah who lands on an enemy throne wins a stake.

terms.name: Throne
terms.text: The central square in Tablut, which only the king may occupy.

terms.name: Throw your hat in the ring
terms.text: To enter a contest openly. The book says the phrase began as a way of challenging a boxer.

terms.name: Thymelicus (plural thymelici)
terms.text: In Isidore's account, a musician who played organs, lyres and cytharas, named after the platform, the thymele, where he once stood. A church canon told clergy to leave a feast before these performers came in.

terms.name: Tiebreaker (tennis)
terms.text: A game of first to seven points, at least two ahead, with serve changing after the first point and every two points after.

terms.name: Tier
terms.text: A pledge level on a crowdfunding campaign. Each tier gives a different reward, such as the base game or a deluxe edition.

terms.name: Tier list
terms.text: A ranking of characters or units by power, made by players when a game with many asymmetric parts is not balanced.

terms.name: Tight and loose culture
terms.text: A tight culture sets the rules and materials for everyone, and a loose culture gives people room to design their own work. The author compares a business school with preset course readings to a public policy school where he could design his own courses.

terms.name: Tightrope (as ilinx)
terms.text: The profession of crossing a high wire. Caillois says the performer's aim is to master dizziness, and that thinking about the danger at the wrong moment is fatal.

terms.name: Tile-based
terms.text: A way of building a game space from equal squares, each holding one picture, so nothing can sit across two tiles. Koster notes early games moved piece by piece in this way.

terms.name: Time attack
terms.text: A mode that asks the player to repeat a familiar task within tighter time limits. Koster says it trains speed and reflex, so it suits action games and not strategy games.

terms.name: Time out
terms.text: A call that suspends a game without ending it, so that a player can ask for a rule to be explained. It is not part of the play itself.

terms.name: Time-Travelers' Potlatch
terms.text: A Surrealist group game in which players name historical figures and think of gifts they would give each one.

terms.name: Timekeeper
terms.text: A person who times each turn in Charades and adds up the minutes at the end.

terms.name: Token
terms.text: A piece that stands for the player, the player's team or some other position in the game.

terms.name: Token
terms.text: A small piece that stands for a player or a thing in the game, such as a wooden pawn, a hat or a boot on a board.

terms.name: Tombstone Hold 'Em
terms.text: A poker variant played in cemeteries, in which tombstone shapes give the suit and names and dates give the face value.

terms.name: Tool stick (Pickup Sticks)
terms.text: The one stick that differs from the rest and may be used to lift other sticks without disturbing them.

terms.name: Top-down simulation
terms.text: A model that shows a whole system from above, taking in many factors in simple form, as The McDonald's Videogame does.

terms.name: Topic
terms.text: In Wark's usage, a place that exists both on the ground and in language, such as a settlement known by name, before maps join places together.

terms.name: Topography
terms.text: Space that is charted by maps and lines, with fixed shapes and boundaries between what is mapped and what is not.

terms.name: Topology
terms.text: The study of what stays the same when a shape is squashed or stretched. Koster uses it to compare games: two games share a topology when one can be reshaped into the other without adding a hole.

terms.name: Topology
terms.text: Space as a network of lines in which any point can be linked to any other and shapes change into one another without breaking. Wark says games are the form that fits it.

terms.name: Topsy-turveydom
terms.text: A reversal in which the low overturn the high. In the Chester Shepherds play the apprentice wins the wrestling match against his masters.

terms.name: Tormentor
terms.text: The stock role of the people who beat and nail Christ, usually played as noisy and crude. New Romney named its tormentors Mischaunce, Untrust and Unhap.

terms.name: Torus
terms.text: A doughnut shape. A toric board is one whose top joins its bottom and whose left edge joins its right edge, so pieces and words run off one side and appear on the other.

terms.name: Total information
terms.text: A situation in which a player knows every relevant fact. Caillois says mathematical game theory assumes this, which real play rarely gives.

terms.name: Totemism
terms.text: A way of life in which groups of people identify with an animal, such as the kangaroo or tortoise. Huizinga reads this as a serious form of play.

terms.name: Touch
terms.text: A player's feel for the ball, shown in shooting that comes by instinct and cannot be switched on by will.

terms.name: Tournament
terms.text: A regulated combat in an enclosed field, with limits and no consequence outside it. Caillois sets it against war, which has no such frame.

terms.name: Tournamentality
terms.text: A state of mind where each game is a chance to get even for earlier losses. DeKoven says it removes the freedom to quit and to change the game.

terms.name: Tournee
terms.text: A Skat bid where trump is decided by turning up one of the two Skat cards.

terms.name: Tout
terms.text: In Solo, a bid to take all the tricks.

terms.name: Toy
terms.text: An interactive system with no problem to solve and no contest to win. Burgun puts a sandbox, a flight simulator and an unmodified Minecraft in this group.

terms.name: Toy-centric design
terms.text: Douglas Wilson's name for starting from a plaything, such as a new controller, and exploring what is enjoyable about it before building a game around it.

terms.name: Tracking spreadsheet
terms.text: A to-do list in spreadsheet form that guides a team through the tasks of making prototypes and running playtests.

terms.name: Trading card game
terms.text: A game where each player builds their own deck from cards collected or bought, such as Magic.

terms.name: Trading game
terms.text: A game in which the main activity is exchanging cards or information with other players, such as Haggle and Super Babel.

terms.name: Traditional design values
terms.text: One of Holm's kinds: values that use history and region for inspiration, such as working in a genre or reviving an old game.

terms.name: Tragedy of the commons
terms.text: The many-player version of the dilemma, where each user of a shared resource gains by overusing it and the resource is destroyed.

terms.name: Trailing
terms.text: In Casino, putting a card on the table without capturing anything.

terms.name: Trailing
terms.text: In Casino, discarding a card to the table because it cannot capture anything.

terms.name: Traitor mechanic
terms.text: A rule that gives one player a secret role so that they deceive the others.

terms.name: Traitor mechanism
terms.text: A rule where one player may secretly work against the group, as in The Resistance. It gives a reason to hide information.

terms.name: Transfer test
terms.text: A test that asks learners to use what they learned in a new situation they did not meet while learning. It shows understanding, not only skill at the game (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

terms.name: Transformation
terms.text: Boyd's word for how values and habits from play carry into wider life. She described a two-way flow, where children turn life into play and turn play back into life, with no direct copying of one behaviour.

terms.name: Transformation of time
terms.text: The change in how long time seems to last during flow. Hours often pass like minutes, and a short turn in dance can seem long.

terms.name: Transformational coping
terms.text: A response to stress in which a person stays calm, restates the problem and finds a new goal. Also called mature defence.

terms.name: Transformational play
terms.text: Sasha Barab's name for a game's ability to work upon the player and change them while the player acts in it (chapter by David Phelps).

terms.name: Transitional object
terms.text: A first possession, such as the corner of a blanket or a soft toy, that the baby treats as neither part of the self nor fully part of the outside world. The baby uses it to settle at sleep and at lonely times.

terms.name: Transitional phenomena
terms.text: The wider set of habits that work like the transitional object: babbling, a tune sung before sleep, a mannerism, a word. They belong to the middle ground between the self and the shared world.

terms.name: Transitivity
terms.text: The property of an order where if A is ranked above B and B above C then A is ranked above C. When it fails, no single ranked list can be made.

terms.name: Transitory public sociality
terms.text: Brief, anonymous, friendly contact between strangers in public places, such as a smile, holding a door or picking up a dropped item.

terms.name: Trap square
terms.text: In the Jungle game, a square beside a den. An enemy animal on it loses its power and can be captured by any defender.

terms.name: Trappers' rendezvous
terms.text: The yearly gathering of fur trappers, with wrestling, fights and heavy gambling. Writers used it to show how far play went outside towns.

terms.name: Trash-talking
terms.text: Playful insulting of an opponent during a game. The book argues it signals trust between friends.

terms.name: Travelling
terms.text: In basketball, taking steps with the ball without dribbling. The other player then takes the ball.

terms.name: Tretise of Miraclis Pleyinge
terms.text: A Middle English tract from around 1380 to 1414 against "miracle playing". Scholars have read it as an attack on religious drama; the author reads it as an attack on rowdy clerical games and their consequences.

terms.name: Trick
terms.text: One round of a card game in which each player plays a card in turn and the highest card wins the cards played.

terms.name: Trick
terms.text: One round of play in a card game in which each player puts down one card, and the highest card of the right kind takes all of them.

terms.name: Trick
terms.text: The cards played in one round of a card game, one from each player. The highest card wins it, or the highest trump.

terms.name: Tricon
terms.text: In Commerce, three cards of the same rank, the top hand in the three-card game.

terms.name: Trifler
terms.text: In Bernard Suits's words, a player who accepts the rules of a game but ignores its goal, for example someone who plays The Sims to arrange furniture and not to rise through careers.

terms.name: Trolley dilemma
terms.text: A thought experiment where a runaway trolley will kill five people unless a switch sends it to a track where it kills one. Most people say they would flip the switch (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

terms.name: Troops-on-a-map game
terms.text: A game where armies are placed and moved across a map divided into territories. RISK is the example.

terms.name: Truce
terms.text: A pause in feuds and revenge during a sacred feast. The ordinary laws of the tribe are put aside for the length of the festival.

terms.name: Truco
terms.text: An Argentine card game in which partners signal their cards to each other with set faces, winks and pouts without letting opponents read them. The signals are part of the rules.

terms.name: Trump
terms.text: In Forty-two, the suit named by the highest bidder. A trump tile beats the other suits.

terms.name: Trump
terms.text: A suit named as ranking above the others for a hand. A trump card beats any card of the other suits.

terms.name: Trump
terms.text: A suit that, for one hand or one game, beats every card of the other suits. Naming or revealing the trump suit changes which cards matter.

terms.name: Trump
terms.text: A suit that outranks the other suits for the hand. A player with no cards in the suit led may play a trump.

terms.name: Tug of war
terms.text: A sliding marker on a track decides who wins.

terms.name: Turn
terms.text: A block of game time during which one player acts, so that taking two seconds or two minutes makes no difference to the rules.

terms.name: Turn-based game
terms.text: A game where players act one after another, which leaves time to think about the game state.

terms.name: Turn-up
terms.text: A card turned over from the pack that proposes the trump suit, for acceptance or refusal.

terms.name: Turn-up (Speculation)
terms.text: The card turned to show trump in Speculation, which can be bought and sold before or after it is shown.

terms.name: Turning down
terms.text: In Euchre, the dealer refuses the turned-up trump and puts the card face up under the stock, so the next player may name a different suit.

terms.name: Turnover
terms.text: The other team gaining possession because a pass was incomplete, intercepted or dropped, or because a player took a step in Ultimate.

terms.name: Tutorial level
terms.text: An opening level that teaches the controls. Knights of Astrus did not announce it; the player learned by moving around, picking up items and opening the quest log (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Twenty questions
terms.text: A guessing game with three limits: only yes or no answers, a fixed number of questions, and a free category clue at the start such as animal, vegetable or mineral.

terms.name: Twenty Questions
terms.text: A guessing game where one player thinks of something and others find it with twenty yes-or-no questions.

terms.name: Twin
terms.text: In Thaayam, two pieces of one player placed together on a square. A twin moves at half the thrown distance and can only be hit by another twin.

terms.name: Twine
terms.text: A free tool for making branching text games that needs no programming or visual design, which made it attractive to anna anthropy as a model for new makers.

terms.name: Twitch game
terms.text: A game that depends at least partly on reflexes and eye-hand coordination, such as Quake or Starcraft.

terms.name: Two-phase game
terms.text: A game with a first stage in which pieces are placed on the board and a second stage in which they move and fight, as in Seega.

terms.name: Two-sided team game
terms.text: A game with two teams, each acting as one side that wins or loses together, such as football or bridge. It behaves much like a two-player game.

terms.name: Tychism
terms.text: Charles Peirce's view that chance is a real part of the universe, which moves from randomness towards order. The book offers it as an early philosophical case for taking chance seriously.

terms.name: Typology
terms.text: Reading a person or event as a forerunner of a later one, such as Isaac standing for Christ. The book says the plays use only the simplest sort.

terms.name: Tyranny of structurelessness
terms.text: Jo Freeman's phrase for a group with no formal structure, where informal and unaccountable structure appears and hides who holds the power.

terms.name: Tze
terms.text: The name of a playing piece in Wei-ch'i, a disc placed on a point of the board and never moved afterwards.

terms.name: Ultimatum Game
terms.text: A two-player game in which a proposer offers a split of a sum and the responder accepts or rejects it. If the responder rejects, both get nothing.

terms.name: Umpire
terms.text: A person who settles disputes about the rules in a game. In chess the umpire rules only when asked and cannot change the rules.

terms.name: Umpire
terms.text: The person on the field who applies the rules and sends offenders off. Roosevelt pictured government as an umpire, and Oriard asks who gets to be umpire.

terms.name: Unaware participant
terms.text: A person drawn into a pervasive game without knowing a game is going on.

terms.name: Uncanny
terms.text: Freud's term for the unease when something familiar shows a small oddness, as with a doll that seems nearly alive.

terms.name: Uncertainty
terms.text: Not knowing what will happen next. It can exist with no chance at all, as when you cannot tell where an opponent will throw.

terms.name: Under the guns
terms.text: Being first to bet in a round of poker.

terms.name: Under-promise and over-deliver
terms.text: A habit of handing in more than was asked, earlier than asked. The example given is finishing at 11 a.m. a task due at 2 p.m. and adding a note on the main competitor.

terms.name: Undercut
terms.text: The case where a player who did not knock holds an equal or lower deadwood count than the knocker, and so takes the hand and a bonus.

terms.name: Undertrick
terms.text: A trick by which the declarer falls short of the promise. The other side scores for each one.

terms.name: Undue advantage
terms.text: A gain from a method that removes the other side's chance, such as firing on an unarmed opponent. In Cooper's novels the hero refuses it even in war.

terms.name: Uniform
terms.text: A permanent, official costume that leaves the face bare. Caillois sets it against the mask, which hides the face and stands for sudden, frightening power.

terms.name: Unintended strength
terms.text: A part of the game that works in a way the designer did not plan.

terms.name: Unique loser
terms.text: An outcome where one player loses and everyone else counts as a winner, as in Old Maid.

terms.name: Unit of transposition
terms.text: The part of the original work that an adaptation carries across: its story, its world, its mechanics or its logics.

terms.name: Unit status
terms.text: The state of being one whole self that holds everything together, as against parts left in compartments or lying about.

terms.name: Unnecessary obstacle
terms.text: A difficulty that players take on although an easier route exists, such as swinging a club at a golf ball instead of dropping it in the hole by hand.

terms.name: Unplaying
terms.text: Acting out the forbidden, unexpected or unhappy version of a play script, such as a child holding a doll's funeral instead of tending it.

terms.name: Untempered radical
terms.text: An outsider who confronts the system directly and does not work inside it.

terms.name: Unverbalizable level
terms.text: Boyd's phrase, taken from Korzybski, for learning that happens by doing and cannot be put into words. She said games give unusual experience at this level.

terms.name: Upcard
terms.text: The top card of the discard pile, face up and available to take.

terms.name: Upcard
terms.text: In Euchre, the card turned face up after the deal. Its suit becomes trump if a player orders it up.

terms.name: Upward comparison
terms.text: Comparing yourself with someone who is ahead of you. It can bring hope and a push to do more, or it can bring envy.

terms.name: Urgent optimism
terms.text: The moment of hope just before success, when a player is eager to try as hard as possible.

terms.name: User-generated content
terms.text: Material made by players and added to a game, such as maps, dialogue or new dilemmas. Knights of Astrus was built with a map editor and XML files so students could add their own (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

terms.name: Utility function
terms.text: A rule that gives a number to how much a person wants each possible outcome, so that choices can be compared by that number.

terms.name: Utopia
terms.text: An imagined ideal place described on a page, separated from the world by a barrier of distance or time.

terms.name: Value capture
terms.text: What happens when a person with rich values meets a simplified, often numbered version of them, adopts it in place of the rich one, and finds their life has narrowed.

terms.name: Value clarity
terms.text: The author's name for the three traits that make game goals easy to live by: they are obvious to apply, easy to compare on one scale and easy to rank.

terms.name: Values at Play
terms.text: A research project that helps game designers take human values into account. It uses an exercise called Grow a Game.

terms.name: Values discourse
terms.text: The spoken or unspoken expression of personal or social beliefs within a social practice such as classroom teaching or family meals (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

terms.name: Values goal
terms.text: A human concern, such as equity or diversity, set at the start with the same weight as the design goal.

terms.name: Variable feedback
terms.text: A result that is not fully predictable and rewards greater skill with a larger return. In chess it is the opponent's reply to your move.

terms.name: Variable painting
terms.text: Fahlström's painting made of loose magnetic pieces on a metal board, played by rules written on it, so players can rearrange the picture.

terms.name: Variable player powers
terms.text: Each player has a special action only they can take, or a power that changes one of the standard actions.

terms.name: Vates
terms.text: An old word for the seer, prophet and poet who stands at the centre of early culture. Huizinga says the sophist took over this figure's role.

terms.name: Verb
terms.text: An action a player can take in a game, such as place, jump or bid. Themes help players remember what each verb does.

terms.name: Version control
terms.text: Software that lets a team share a store of code or art files and check files out so that one person does not write over another's work.

terms.name: Version failure
terms.text: Bugs that lead to small improvements in later releases.

terms.name: Vertex
terms.text: A point in a graph, such as a square on a board or a person in a social network. In Koster's note, each link between two vertices is called an edge.

terms.name: Vice
terms.text: A comic evil character in a morality play. In Mankind the vices are called Nought, New Guise and Nowadays, and they lead Mankind into the frivolity of the season.

terms.name: Victory condition
terms.text: What a player needs to do to win. Either achieving it ends the game, or an independent end condition occurs and the winner is whoever is in the right state then.

terms.name: Victory point track
terms.text: A scale printed on the board that shows every player's score at once.

terms.name: Victory points
terms.text: A shared currency a game uses to convert different achievements into one score.

terms.name: Vignette approach
terms.text: A scene design in Mission US where each player sees a random pick of short animations, so no two players see the same version of the Boston Massacre (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

terms.name: Vigorish
terms.text: The percentage of the money that goes to the banker of a game.

terms.name: Visceral reaction
terms.text: A physical thrill, such as the stretch and smash of a table-tennis stroke. Koster says it belongs to physical mastery and is not fun in his strict sense.

terms.name: Visitor participation rate
terms.text: The share of people who visit a crowd project and then sign up and add something. The Guardian expenses game reached 56 percent, against about 4.6 percent for Wikipedia.

terms.name: Visus
terms.text: A mechanical show of a scene. At Lincoln the cathedral's visus showed the Assumption and Coronation of the Virgin and was the main sight of the Saint Anne procession.

terms.name: Vita activa
terms.text: The life of action, in which a person reaches order by pouring effort into outside challenges. The book pairs it with the vita contemplativa.

terms.name: Vita contemplativa
terms.text: The life of reflection, in which a person sorts competing wishes by thinking about experience.

terms.name: Void
terms.text: Holding no cards of a suit. Such a hand may play any card when that suit is led.

terms.name: Void
terms.text: The blank page at the start of designing a game: every plot, character and event that could possibly go in (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Void, singleton, doubleton
terms.text: A suit in which a hand holds no cards, one card or two. Bridge players count them as points when deciding how to bid.

terms.name: Volador
terms.text: A Mexican ritual in which men in eagle costume hang by ropes from a high mast and spiral head down to the ground. Caillois uses it to show vertigo at its most extreme.

terms.name: Vole
terms.text: In Ecarte, winning all five tricks, which scores two points instead of one.

terms.name: Volley
terms.text: Hitting a ball back and forth to keep it in play, with no points. In Ping-Pong it can serve as a game of its own.

terms.name: Volley
terms.text: In badminton, the exchange of hits between teams until the birdie falls or goes out.

terms.name: Voluntarism about moral transformation
terms.text: The view that play turns hostile acts into friendly ones only because players decide to read them that way. The author argues that game design does part of the work.

terms.name: Voluntary participation
terms.text: Everyone playing knows and accepts the goal, rules and feedback, and may enter or leave freely.

terms.name: Von Neumann game
terms.text: A game where players make simultaneous choices and then the outcome is worked out, as in rock-paper-scissors or fog of war.

terms.name: Vortex
terms.text: The set of ideas, plots and characters actually in the game, joined so that any player could in theory meet any other (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

terms.name: Voting game
terms.text: A game with so much politics that the players are in effect electing the winner by choosing who to hurt, whatever the rules say about skill.

terms.name: Vulnerability
terms.text: In bridge, a state that raises both the bonuses and the penalties for a side.

terms.name: Vulnerable
terms.text: A condition of a side that has already won a game towards the match. Its risks and rewards on later hands are raised.

terms.name: Vulnerable
terms.text: In Bridge, a side that has already won a game, so that bonuses and penalties are higher for it.

terms.name: Wager
terms.text: Money or stakes put on the result of a play. In the Royal Game of Ur, landing on certain squares forced a player to raise their wager.

terms.name: Wager
terms.text: A bet placed on an outcome the bettor cannot control. Competitive matches can also become the object of wagers.

terms.name: Wager
terms.text: A bet on the outcome of a contest of wits or strength. Huizinga lists it, with the oracle, the lawsuit and the vow, among the forms competition can take.

terms.name: Waits
terms.text: Musicians hired by a town to play on a regular schedule and to attend the town's officials at feasts and on walks through the streets.

terms.name: Walk
terms.text: In baseball, the right to go to first base after four pitches that were not hittable.

terms.name: Wall (Mahjong)
terms.text: Four rows of tiles, 17 long and two high, built by each player and pushed together to form a square.

terms.name: Wall (territory game)
terms.text: A line of pieces that no enemy move can ever capture. In Modern Ming-Mang, walling off more than half the board wins.

terms.name: Wan
terms.text: A Chinese word for relaxed play: handling a jade piece, chess, collecting, enjoying a view. Caillois says it leaves out contests, dice and acting, and points the energy of paidia toward calm and slow thought.

terms.name: War (in cards)
terms.text: A tie in the game of that name, settled by each player adding cards and turning another, with the winner taking everything.

terms.name: Waste pile
terms.text: In solitaire, a pile for turned-up cards that cannot be played yet, whose top card stays available.

terms.name: Weathering
terms.text: Arline Geronimus's word for the slow wear on health and ageing caused by living under social marginalization.

terms.name: Weenie
terms.text: A large, visible landmark placed to draw people towards it. Theme parks use castles, and Journey uses a distant mountain.

terms.name: Weight
terms.text: A number that says how much one criterion counts against the others when several are added into one score.

terms.name: Well-played game
terms.text: A game that reaches a high point of skill and ease because of the way everyone in it plays. It is judged by the quality of the playing together, not by the score or the winner.

terms.name: Well-struck bargain
terms.text: A haggle where both sides reach a price and each leaves thinking they got the larger share. DeKoven reads the haggling itself as a form of play.

terms.name: Well-timed cheat
terms.text: Breaking a rule at a moment when the game is stalling and everyone takes the break as a way back into play. In musical chairs, a child carried his chair along and the group laughed and joined in.

terms.name: Werewolf (Mafia)
terms.text: A group game where secretly chosen werewolves kill townsfolk by night, and everyone votes to kill one suspect by day. A moderator coordinates.

terms.name: Wheel of Fortune
terms.text: The image of a goddess turning a wheel that lifts some people up and drops others, and who tells them not to complain when she plays.

terms.name: Wheel of Fortune
terms.text: An old picture of luck as a wheel that lifts the lowly and drops the high at random. The book names it as the older view that stayed alive alongside newer ones.

terms.name: Whimsical play
terms.text: Play of silly actions and unexpected results that gives a dizzy, amusement-ride feeling. Hit Me and QWOP are examples.

terms.name: Whitsun
terms.text: The feast of Pentecost. Chester moved its play there from Corpus Christi and stretched it to three days between 1521 and 1531.

terms.name: Wholehearted participation
terms.text: Taking part because you are self-motivated, interested and enthusiastic, and not because you were forced or are waiting it out.

terms.name: Wicked problem
terms.text: A problem with many possible solutions and many personal readings of them. Each one is unique, hard to define formally, without a natural stopping point, and every test of a solution affects the people who use it. The paper places game design among them.

terms.name: Wicket
terms.text: A small hoop pushed into the ground in croquet. Players score by knocking their ball through it.

terms.name: Widow
terms.text: An extra hand dealt face down on the table that a player may take in place of their own hand.

terms.name: Widow
terms.text: An extra hand dealt face down that one player may take in exchange for his own or buy at auction.

terms.name: Widow
terms.text: Cards left over after the deal that are set aside and go to the winner of the first trick.

terms.name: Widow (skat)
terms.text: A few cards dealt face down in the centre. The player who wins the bidding may exchange them for cards from his hand, or leave them alone.

terms.name: Wild
terms.text: A die or card that counts as any number the player chooses, as aces in Indian Dice.

terms.name: Wild card
terms.text: A card that can stand in for any other card.

terms.name: Wild card
terms.text: A card that can stand for any other card in the hands of the players holding it. Wild cards make five of a kind possible.

terms.name: Wild eight
terms.text: In Crazy Eights, an eight that can be played on any card, after which the player names the suit to be matched next.

terms.name: Win condition
terms.text: The rule that says when a game is won and the algorithm ends. Wark says SimEarth has none that satisfies.

terms.name: Win state
terms.text: A condition in which the game counts as won; Catlow's chess widens the number of these.

terms.name: Windfall
terms.text: A random lucky event for a player, such as having your number rolled ten times in a row in Catan.

terms.name: Winner and loser effect
terms.text: The tendency of an animal that has just won to win again and of one that has just lost to lose again.

terms.name: Wireframe
terms.text: A plain drawing of simple shapes and placeholder text showing what appears onscreen at a moment, used for sites and apps and, here, for games.

terms.name: Wisdom of the crowd
terms.text: The finding that the middle estimate of many people can be closer to the true value than the estimates of single experts, as long as the people judge independently.

terms.name: Wish panel
terms.text: A display in The Sims that shows what each character wants and how to supply it. Groundcrew copies the idea for real people near each other.

terms.name: Wolf and sheep
terms.text: A game on a chessboard where four white pieces, the sheep, have to trap one black piece, the wolf. Caillois uses it as a game whose outcome mathematics has already settled.

terms.name: Woodpile
terms.text: The stacked, face-down dominoes from which Chinese games draw tiles.

terms.name: Work and play
terms.text: Oriard defines work as action for an outside goal and play as action for its own sake. Work is about the result, play about the process.

terms.name: Work/play dualism
terms.text: The habit of splitting life into two separate halves, work for adults and play for children or for days off, with each half defined by the other.

terms.name: Worker placement
terms.text: A mechanism where players put tokens on action spaces; some games let several players share a space and some do not.

terms.name: Worker placement
terms.text: Players pick single actions from a pool of available ones, usually by putting a token that stands for a worker on the action they want.

terms.name: Working memory
terms.text: The short-term space where a person holds and handles information while thinking. It has a small capacity, so too much at once lowers performance (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

terms.name: Working title
terms.text: The name a team uses for a game before the final title is chosen.

terms.name: World picture
terms.text: Heidegger's term, used by Lee, for seeing the world as a set of things that can be divided up and controlled. Lee finds it in the RISK board.

terms.name: World target
terms.text: Rey Chow's term for a view that scans a whole landscape for points to strike instead of borders to cross.

terms.name: Would You Open the Door
terms.text: A Surrealist parlor game of quick questions: if a named person knocked at your door, would you let them in? The answers start a talk about politics, taste and ethics.

terms.name: Wraparound board
terms.text: A board whose edges are joined so that movement past an edge continues on the opposite side.

terms.name: Yarborough
terms.text: A hand with no card higher than a nine.

terms.name: Yes, and
terms.text: The brainstorming habit of building on someone's idea instead of objecting to it.

terms.name: Yomi
terms.text: A term from Japanese for reading the opponent's intentions through move and countermove, used by designer David Sirlin.

terms.name: Yomi
terms.text: A Japanese idea of knowing your opponent's mind. In play it means guessing what the other player will do, and guessing that they are guessing you, in layers.

terms.name: You-never-win game
terms.text: Shuen-shing Lee's name for a game built so that the player cannot win, as in a tragedy, in order to make people think. September 12th is an example.

terms.name: Younger hand
terms.text: In a two-player game, the player who does not make the opening lead.

terms.name: Yu
terms.text: A Taoist word for following the Way, translated as wandering or flowing. The author reads the cook Ting's story as flow found in a humble job.

terms.name: Z-order
terms.text: The depth position of a fighter in a side-scrolling brawler; enemies cannot hit you while you stand in a different depth.

terms.name: Zero-level heuristic
terms.text: A beginner's rule of thumb that gives a new player some idea of what to try, such as win a trick with the lowest card that will do it.

terms.name: Zero-player game
terms.text: Something that is watched like a game but where nobody influences the result, such as Conway's Life or a race between two raindrops on a window.

terms.name: Zero-sum
terms.text: Describes a game where what one player gains the other loses.

terms.name: Zero-sum
terms.text: A scoring system in which the players' scores always add up to zero, so one player's gain is exactly the others' loss.

terms.name: Zero-sum game
terms.text: A game in which one player's loss equals the other's gain.

terms.name: Zero-sum game
terms.text: A contest where one side's gain is the other side's loss. The author says the research finds many White people treating racial equality as this kind of contest, even when a policy helps all.

terms.name: Zipf's law
terms.text: The pattern that the frequency of an item is roughly proportional to one over its rank. The most common English word is used about twice as often as the second and three times as often as the third.

terms.name: Zugzwang
terms.text: A position where every available move leaves the player lower placed than doing nothing would. The book uses it more widely for positions where most moves cost the player something and helpful ones are rare.

ideas.name: Three findings
ideas.text: The paper reports that collections with different templates can still extend each other, that keywords are a reliable way to find patterns, and that a related patterns field can hold both conflicting and complementing patterns.

ideas.name: Patterns are often called rules or tools
ideas.text: Because Kreimeier brought patterns to game designers in 2002, when only design rules and tools existed, patterns are often reworded as tools or rules. The paper says this confuses what a game design pattern is.

ideas.name: A missing field adds to the fragmentation
ideas.text: Kreimeier's template left out the related patterns field that his own examples had. The paper says this omission is one reason collections do not refer to each other or avoid overlap, and that inconsistent templates are another.

ideas.name: Too many patterns overwhelm new designers
ideas.text: Barney's criticism, cited by the paper, is that novice designers who learn patterns are given too many tools, and find them hard to find, organise and apply.

ideas.name: Keywords are the most suitable way to find patterns
ideas.text: Of the approaches in the six works, the paper favours keywords. They are the one approach used by both collections that have many patterns and take contributions from outside.

ideas.name: Search software and mnemonic names fall short
ideas.text: Kreimeier names search software without saying what it would search on, and Björk and Holopainen's mnemonic names do not hold up with hundreds of patterns. Schell's deck of cards works only for a collection that does not grow.

ideas.name: Lenses avoid contradiction by asking questions
ideas.text: Schell gives questions instead of solutions, so his lenses do not contradict each other and the final decision stays with the designer. The cost is that a lens no longer pairs a problem with a solution.

ideas.name: Conflicts are one kind of relation
ideas.text: Collections that are networks need fields for relations between patterns, and the paper treats a contradiction as one kind of relation. Barney lists four kinds: parent, child, additive and subtractive.

ideas.name: Optional fields make joining easier
ideas.text: Barney's template, the widest of the six, lets a contributor leave out fields such as example games or an image. The paper takes this as a reason for optional fields in a consolidated template, with a few fields required.

ideas.name: A contributor field is required
ideas.text: The collections that accept outside contributions record who wrote or sourced each pattern, as a contributor, references or authors field. The paper makes a reference field required in its template for that reason.

ideas.name: Predictable Consequence and Surprise pull against each other
ideas.text: In the paper's worked example, Predictable Consequence, where the game world reacts the same way under the same conditions, is complemented by Intention and Rules. Surprise contradicts it, and Indirect Control can break it.

ideas.name: The selection of works is intuitive
ideas.text: The six works compared were chosen by intuition, which the paper names as an obvious limit of its method.

ideas.name: Validation and platform stay open
ideas.text: The paper leaves open how patterns in a consolidated collection would be validated and what platform would hold it.

ideas.name: A joined collection is for students
ideas.text: The author says a consolidated collection would need to be more compact than the collections added together to be offered to students. The open question is whether novices find a game design theory easier to learn as a pattern language.

ideas.name: Many games are the same board with changes
ideas.text: Bell finds that Nyout, Patolli and Pachisi are one idea altered. Take the circle away and you have Patolli, take the cross away and you have the Kiowa game Zohn Ahl, fold the circle into the cross and you have Pachisi. A designer can treat a board as a part that is kept while rules and pieces are changed.

ideas.name: A board tells you less than a rule book
ideas.text: Boards were reused for other games. Chess boards were used for draughts, and the fox and geese board for solitaire. Bell warns that because one people used a board for a game, we cannot know the next people did the same. A designer can see that board shape and rules are separate choices.

ideas.name: Games that lose their rules still show their shape
ideas.text: Patolli's rules were lost when priests destroyed Aztec records, but its board, five beans and twelve stones survive. Bell reconstructs it by comparison with related games. When rules are missing, the parts and how they are scored point to likely rules.

ideas.name: One mechanism, many wrappers
ideas.text: Cross-and-circle games turn up in Korea, in Mayan stucco at Chichen Itza and in India. Bell uses this to argue for old links between peoples, or for the same idea arriving twice. A mechanism can be made again in different materials and meanings.

ideas.name: Games change as they cross borders
ideas.text: Pachisi became Ludo in England around 1896, with a cubic die in place of cowries. The game kept the race and lost the royal court. Here a game that travelled kept its core rule and gave up its local objects.

ideas.name: A theme can be added to a race
ideas.text: The Hyena game turns a race along a spiral into a family story: mothers walk to a well, a hyena is released, and the winner becomes the hyena. The track and dice are simple, and the story gives the moves meaning.

ideas.name: Stories on the track
ideas.text: The Royal Game of Goose has numbered spaces with named hazards: an inn, a well, a maze, a prison, death. Landing on one means paying, waiting or going back. The players' only choice is whether to play, so the track decides everything else.

ideas.name: A form that teaches
ideas.text: After Goose, makers produced spiral games to teach children history, geography, botany and astronomy. The same track became a carrier for lessons.

ideas.name: Luck is part of the structure
ideas.text: In Goose a throw of the two dice decides every move, and no choices are left to the players. In Pachisi and Thaayam, a player can split a throw between pieces, or refuse to move, and so gains some control over luck.

ideas.name: Safe spaces change how risk feels
ideas.text: Pachisi castles and Thaayam havens are squares where capture does not happen. The meaning attached to them differs: Thaayam explains them as the sanctity of a guest under a host's roof. A designer can treat a safe square as a rule and as a story.

ideas.name: Partnership changes tactics
ideas.text: In Pachisi, partners win or lose together, so a player sometimes holds back pieces to block enemies or to guard a partner who is behind. A partner who rushes home leaves the other facing two opposing turns for each of his.

ideas.name: Capture can be a tool of the race
ideas.text: In race games a hit piece loses ground and the hitter often gets another turn. Thaayam adds that hitting gives an extra turn, and a twin is protected from single pieces. The same capture rule can work against the pace of a race or add to it.

ideas.name: Exact finishing prolongs the end
ideas.text: Pachisi, Backgammon and Thaayam need an exact throw or a full home table before pieces leave. This keeps a player waiting after his pieces have covered the rest of the track.

ideas.name: The oldest known boards had no recorded rules
ideas.text: Boards from the royal tombs of Ur, about 3000 B.C., are the oldest in existence, yet no account of play survived. Bell offers numbered suggested rules, and marks them as suggestions. A designer can learn to separate what a source shows from what is added to make it playable.

ideas.name: Old games turn into new ones by small changes
ideas.text: Cribbage, invented in the seventeenth century, may have used the old board design from Thebes, a pegged board known over 3,500 years earlier. Bell's point is that a score board is a lasting object.

ideas.name: A new game can take over an old name
ideas.text: The Roman game of twelve lines was replaced by a thirty-six space game from Egypt or Greece, which took the old name. Bell compares this to Sphairistike becoming Lawn Tennis and then simply Tennis. The name stays and the game changes.

ideas.name: A rule can hurt the player who has to follow it
ideas.text: In Zeno's game of Tabula, the Emperor had to use his whole throw if he could, and that forced him to break three pairs and leave eight single pieces. A rule that makes a player use every number can ruin an otherwise sound position.

ideas.name: Dice with no choice are sometimes the whole game
ideas.text: In Chasing the Girls only throws of 6, 1 and doublets count; all other throws score nothing. A designer can make most throws do nothing and let a few carry the game.

ideas.name: A losing player can change role
ideas.text: In Chasing the Girls, a player with one piece left becomes a corner-rattler, moving only between corner points and capturing only on corners. The change of rules for the last piece keeps a trailing player in the game.

ideas.name: Drinking and gambling shaped rules
ideas.text: The seventeenth-century Sixe-Ace variant made a player drink on a throw of 2, and the last players on the board paid for the drinks. Stakes, pools and forfeits are parts of many rule sets.

ideas.name: A name can cover many versions
ideas.text: By the sixteenth century Tables meant any game on a flat surface. Backgammon came back in the seventeenth century as a new variant and was known as gammon in Scotland, tric-trac in France and puff in Germany.

ideas.name: Games rise and fall in favour
ideas.text: Bell notes that chess was the popular game by 1475, backgammon revived in the seventeenth century, was a craze among London writers before 1939, and by 1960 was in eclipse outside the Middle East. A game's rules stay while its audience moves.

ideas.name: Technical words can put people off
ideas.text: Bell blames part of backgammon's decline on its many terms, and so reduces them to a minimum in his account. A game with a long vocabulary asks more of a new player.

ideas.name: One game tradition is many games in sequence
ideas.text: Bell traces Alquerque from temple roof slabs in Kurna, about 1400 B.C., to the Arabic Quirkat of A.D. 976 and the Spanish Alquerque of the thirteenth century. The Spaniards carried it to New Mexico, where the Zuni made a quadruple board into a new game, the Stone Warriors. A game keeps its board and gets new rules at each stop.

ideas.name: Rules are often missing from old sources
ideas.text: The Alfonso manuscript gives Alquerque's moves but Bell says they are not enough to play a game. He adds numbered suggestions: no backward moves, no returning to a point, and a scoring rule for the end. He marks the added rules as his own.

ideas.name: Unfinished boards show what the maker was cutting
ideas.text: One Alquerque board in the roof of the Kurna temple was left half cut after a mistake with a diagonal line. This shows that diagonal lines were part of what makers had to draw.

ideas.name: Compulsory capture keeps the board moving
ideas.text: In Fighting Serpents the opening piece is captured by a short leap at once, and taking is compulsory. This opens the crowded board and makes each early move forced.

ideas.name: Replacing a lost piece with a special one
ideas.text: In Stone Warriors the first piece a player loses is replaced by a Priest of the Bow, which moves in more directions. Loss gives the player a piece with wider moves.

ideas.name: Shaturanga was a battle of four armies
ideas.text: Shaturanga used four armies of infantry, cavalry, elephants and boatmen, one for each player, with allies sitting opposite. It was played on the Ashtapada board, which had earlier been used for a race game. A board for a race was turned into a board for war.

ideas.name: Dice chose which piece could move
ideas.text: In Shaturanga a long die marked 2, 3, 4, 5 told the player which piece to move: ship, horse, elephant, rajah or pawn. If the piece could not move, the turn was lost. A game of war was joined to a throw of chance.

ideas.name: Chance and skill together make a stake game
ideas.text: Shaturanga paid stakes for seizing a throne, capturing a rajah, and building an empire by capturing both enemy rajahs. These payments gave the allies more to play for than one win.

ideas.name: An old account had to be filled in
ideas.text: Bell prints his additions to the Shaturanga rules in italics where the ancient account was missing a rule, such as the stake pool and the turn order. This marks which rules are from the source and which are added.

ideas.name: A ban on gambling reshaped a game
ideas.text: Hindu law punished anyone who played at dice or at Shaturanga for stakes. Players kept the game and dropped the die. Bell suggests that removing luck led to the other changes.

ideas.name: Four players became two
ideas.text: After the die was dropped, the allied forces were merged into one army, and the game for four players became one for two. Bell says this is why chess has two of several pieces. The doubled pieces in modern chess are left from the old allied armies.

ideas.name: Pieces change power when a game changes
ideas.text: When Shaturanga became Shatranj the allied kings became prime ministers whose move was halved, and the ship and elephant swapped moves. The names stayed the same while the powers changed.

ideas.name: A game travels with people who have a reason to move
ideas.text: Bell lists three routes by which Shatranj reached Europe: through Spain with the Moors, through the Byzantine court by marriage and gift, and through the Crusades. Each route was a meeting of courts, soldiers or doctors.

ideas.name: A game can arrive with a story
ideas.text: Firdausi's poem tells how an Indian ambassador brought a board to the Persian court of Chosroes I and challenged the court to solve its mysteries. A wise man solved it in a day and a night. The tale explains how chess came to Persia.

ideas.name: A game carries its time
ideas.text: Bell notes that the European medieval form of chess in Caxton's book of 1474 was little different from the Persian Shatranj of the Crusades. Rules held for four centuries.

ideas.name: Many ways to win make a draw likelier
ideas.text: Shatranj had three ways to win: checkmate, taking all other pieces, and trapping a stalemated king. Even so, drawn games were common, since some pieces had narrow powers and a larger force could not always beat a smaller one placed on favourable squares.

ideas.name: Players change a slow opening
ideas.text: Shatranj's opening was slow, since several pieces moved only a little. Players agreed that the first player could make ten moves at once to set up, and then the second player did the same. This is a house rule that became a custom.

ideas.name: War games can be race boards under another rule
ideas.text: Bell notes that the Ashtapada board was a race board before Shaturanga, that the Tab board of nine by four resembles the ten by three race board of ancient Egypt, and that the chequered chess board served draughts. He treats these as cases of a race board adapted for war.

ideas.name: A new game can be built from two old ones
ideas.text: Draughts was made in the south of France about A.D. 1100 by joining the chess board with the Alquerque moves. Pieces moved as the queen then did, one square on the diagonal, and captured as in Alquerque. The new game took parts from each.

ideas.name: Compulsion of capture is a choice a rule makes
ideas.text: Early draughts had no compulsion, a survival of chess. When France added compulsion about 1535, the old game was called Plaisant and the new one jeu forcé. English draughts descends from the forced game. Whether capture is required changes how a game plays.

ideas.name: Penalties for missing a capture are a design
ideas.text: English draughts lets the opponent return the move, let it stand and demand the capture next turn, or huff the offending piece. Each is a different cost for the same mistake.

ideas.name: Reversing the goal gives a new game
ideas.text: In the Losing Game, played with draughts pieces, each player tries to force the opponent to capture his pieces, and the first to lose all of them wins. The board and moves stay and the aim turns round.

ideas.name: Rules vary for the same pieces
ideas.text: Italian draughts forbids a man to take a king and forces the larger capture. Turkish draughts has men that move forwards and sideways on an unchequered board. Polish draughts allows men to capture backwards. All use the same basic idea of the jump.

ideas.name: A game that took off in a city
ideas.text: Polish or Continental draughts was first played in Paris cafes in 1727, after earlier French versions died out within fifty years. Bell writes that, as now played, it ranks among the major board games. A game grows when a meeting place gives it a steady group of players.

ideas.name: Unequal forces change what each side wants
ideas.text: In the tafl games, a small force with a special piece tries to break out, and a larger force tries to hem it in. In Fox and Geese one fox faces thirteen geese. Each side has a different goal and different powers.

ideas.name: A weighted board needs balance
ideas.text: In Fox and Geese, Bell writes that if the geese are played correctly the fox loses. Later forms raised the geese to seventeen and took away their backward move. A designer can change numbers and moves to adjust a one-sided game.

ideas.name: The edge of the board is a goal
ideas.text: In Tablut and Saxon Hnefatafl, one side wins if the king reaches the board's edge, and the other wins by capturing him. The board shape and the king's goal together set what each side does.

ideas.name: A call-out makes a threat public
ideas.text: In Tablut a player who opens one route to the edge says Raichi, and two routes, Tuichi. The second call means the king cannot be stopped, like checkmate. A spoken rule keeps both players aware of the threat.

ideas.name: A diary gives a game its record
ideas.text: Linnaeus recorded Tablut in his Lapland journal of 20 July 1732. Without that entry the Lapp rules would be unknown. Games survive when someone writes down a rule.

ideas.name: Games hide in other uses of the same object
ideas.text: The Gokstad ship burial held a board with Nine Men's Morris on one side and probably hnefatafl on the other. Triple-purpose boxes in Europe from the fourteenth century carried chess, Nine Men's Morris and backgammon. A single board can carry several games.

ideas.name: A game need not stay with its first meaning
ideas.text: A Nine Men's Morris design on the steps at Mihintale in Ceylon was used as a charm against evil. The same figure was a board in other places.

ideas.name: Fixing the board while the pieces change
ideas.text: A fourteenth-century Italian codex draws Morris pieces as moons, stars, shields, crosses, squares and rounds. Bell reports that all seemed to have the same value and movement, so the shapes may only record the order of play.

ideas.name: A game with a forced win needs a balancer
ideas.text: In Three Men's Morris the first player can force a win by correct play, so Bell suggests dice may have decided the advantage of first entry. In Noughts and Crosses, he notes with A. B. White, the second player cannot win unless the first errs.

ideas.name: Two phases make placing matter
ideas.text: In Seega, Dara and Ludus Latrunculorum, players first put stones on the board, then move and capture them. Bell says skilful placing in the first phase may decide the second. The opening phase builds the position that the second phase tests.

ideas.name: Draws arise from safe walls
ideas.text: In Seega a player can build a barrier behind which only his own pieces move, and those cannot be attacked. Bell names the frequency of draws as a flaw of the game, so the rules add a points win for the larger number of pieces.

ideas.name: Movement and capture can be paired in different ways
ideas.text: High Jump uses the Seega board and moves, but captures by orthogonal jump and does not require capture. The only change from Seega is the capture rule.

ideas.name: An old game can survive at the edge of an empire
ideas.text: Bell suggests that Seega and High Jump survive from Roman Ludus Latrunculorum among Egyptian farmers and Somali herders, each keeping one form of its capture. A game may be lost in a centre and kept at the margin.

ideas.name: A poem as a rules source
ideas.text: The poem Laus Pisonis describes pieces of glass, blocking, trapping between two pieces, and supported lines. Bell reads this as a description of Seega, allowing for metre and rhetoric. When rules are not written, a poet's description can be tested against known games.

ideas.name: A leader piece can unlock a stalled game
ideas.text: Bell suggests that Latrunculorum had a leader that could jump an enemy and break a blocked position, which would prevent games ending with many pieces left. He notes that no source supports or contradicts this.

ideas.name: Unclear rules end in blockade
ideas.text: Bell's suggested Latrunculorum rules end the game if no capture is made in thirty moves. A rule is added to meet a situation the old accounts leave open.

ideas.name: Dice can drive a war game
ideas.text: Tablan and Puluc use throwing sticks or maize ears to decide how far pieces run in a fight along a track. The war game combines a race with capture, and chance decides the pace.

ideas.name: Capture can carry a prisoner
ideas.text: In Puluc a captured piece is put under the capturing piece and carried backwards along the track. If the stack reaches the end the prisoner is slain, and a stack that is hit changes owners. A captured piece stays on the board and travels.

ideas.name: Pieces that are stuck still count
ideas.text: In Tablan a piece that lands on the enemy back row cannot move or be captured, and the winner holds most enemy squares. The pieces become scorers where they stop.

ideas.name: A simpler game can be named as a relative of a larger one
ideas.text: Bell calls Go-Bang a lesser relation of Wei-ch'i, played by children, women and visitors. In his account Go-Bang uses the same board with five-in-a-row as the aim. A simpler goal on a known board makes an easier game.

ideas.name: Changing the goal of a board changes the game
ideas.text: Hasami Shogi (1) wins by five in a row, and Hasami Shogi (2) wins by capturing all the opponent's pieces. Both use the same board and capture.

ideas.name: Mancala is one family with many local versions
ideas.text: Egyptian Mankala'h, Tamil Pallanguli, Ghanaian Wari and Caribbean Awari are different games on boards of pits. Bell uses Mancala as a generic noun for the lot. The shared mechanism is lifting and sowing, and each place changes the counts and the captures.

ideas.name: Sowing joins moving and counting
ideas.text: In Mankala'h, Wari and Chisolo, a move is lifting a pit's seeds and dropping one in each pit beyond. Where the last seed falls decides what is captured or whether the move goes on. The rule makes a move a calculation.

ideas.name: Where the last seed lands decides the move
ideas.text: In Mankala'h an empty pit ends the turn, a pit made two or four by the last seed is captured, and an even pit makes the player lift and sow again. In Wari a last seed that makes two or three in an enemy cup captures it. One landing is tested against several rules.

ideas.name: Capture can run backwards along a row
ideas.text: In Wari, after a capture, the unbroken run of 2s and 3s behind the captured cup is taken as well. A single move can empty a whole row. A rule that chains captures along a line creates large swings.

ideas.name: A rule that prevents a player from winning too fast
ideas.text: Wari does not let a player capture every seed on the opponent's side, as that would leave the opponent nothing to lift. Another rule requires feeding empty cups where possible. Both rules keep the game from ending in one move.

ideas.name: Threats can be counted
ideas.text: In Wari a cup with one or two seeds is threatened when an enemy cup has as many seeds as there are cups between them. Bell turns this into a method for finding threats by counting backwards from the cup. A rule about distance becomes a tool for planning.

ideas.name: A seed can be defended by changing the count
ideas.text: A threatened Wari singleton can be moved on, made safe by adding a seed to the threatening cup so the sowing overshoots, or left as the player prepares a reprisal. In each case the defence works by changing the numbers. No square is blocked.

ideas.name: Hoarding and spreading are rival plans
ideas.text: Bell notes in Wari that a player is safest when many cups bear on different enemy cups, and exposed when several cups bear on one. Slowing the outflow of seeds by lifting lightly loaded cups first is another aim. Position on this board means the spread of counts.

ideas.name: The smaller loss is not always the right move
ideas.text: In one Wari position Bell shows that the move with the smallest immediate loss does not always give the result that counts at the end. Counting what a move costs now and later can give different answers.

ideas.name: Notation lets a game be replayed
ideas.text: Wari moves are recorded by naming the cups, upper case for one player and lower for the other, so a game can be replayed and any position recovered. Bell asks readers to check the method by working a four-move example. A record of moves keeps a game after it is finished.

ideas.name: A game can carry across a long journey
ideas.text: African slaves took their mancala games to Guiana and the Caribbean, where the variants of Awari match the games of Dahomey, Togoland and Nigeria. Bell says a person's form of mancala can show where his ancestors came from. A game can record a migration.

ideas.name: A game can have social rules around it
ideas.text: Awari was played by men, and a woman who played well found men refusing to play her. It was a game for a House of Mourning and was not played after dark because ghosts might join in. Who plays, where and when are customs around the rules.

ideas.name: A board is left rough on purpose
ideas.text: Among the Bush Negroes Awari boards are cut roughly from a log. A board is not brought to a finished state quickly, but smoothed by many hands over many games. The object records the games played on it.

ideas.name: Boards of two shapes avoid a ghost
ideas.text: A village keeps a straight-topped and a curved Awari board, and when a man who preferred one shape dies, the other shape is used for a time. The object choice follows a belief.

ideas.name: More ranks, more laps
ideas.text: Four-rank mancala boards are found in eastern and southern Africa, and in Chisolo a move can run through several laps, sowing on whenever the last stone falls into a loaded hole. Adding rows adds length to a move.

ideas.name: Direction is a rule of its own
ideas.text: In Chisolo each player has to move clockwise on the first move, then choose a direction on the second and keep it. The two players may move in the same direction or opposite ones. Fixing direction after one choice makes the second move a decision about the whole game.

ideas.name: Capture can reach across a board
ideas.text: In Chisolo a lap ending in an empty hole in the front row captures the stones in the two enemy holes on the same file, and the player may also rob one extra hole. A rule that links your pit to the enemy's pits in line gives a move more reach.

ideas.name: Wei-ch'i has simple rules and deep play
ideas.text: Pieces are placed one at a time, never move, and are captured by being surrounded. Bell says oriental scholars have spent years on it and it is not possible to describe the finer points in a few pages. A small rule set can still make a large game.

ideas.name: Territory can be explained with a story
ideas.text: Bell asks the reader to treat each tze as a paratroop unit and the empty points as airfields where supplies can land. A group with an airfield can hold out and a group without one is overwhelmed. A comparison from outside the game can give the rule a picture.

ideas.name: Safety from two separate openings
ideas.text: A Wei-ch'i group with two single-point airfields cannot be taken, since a piece placed on either is captured before it can fill the other. A group needs two exits, or one that can be split in two.

ideas.name: No suicide, and a ban on endless repetition
ideas.text: Wei-ch'i does not allow a piece to be placed where it would be captured at once, unless that move captures. It also bars an immediate recapture in a perpetual attack. Two small rules prevent a loop.

ideas.name: A loss in one place can be made up in another
ideas.text: Bell contrasts Wei-ch'i with chess, where the squares with the kings are supreme. In Wei-ch'i a reverse in one area can be offset by a win in another. The goal is spread across the board.

ideas.name: Handicaps make unequal players equal
ideas.text: The Wei-ch'i winner of three games in a row gives the loser a piece, and if he goes on winning the handicap grows. Bell lists the fixed points where one to nine handicap pieces go.

ideas.name: A game can stand for ability
ideas.text: Skill at Wei-ch'i helped promotion in China and Japan before the twentieth century, as a university degree in a standard subject might do in the West. In Japan players were divided into nine grades and given diplomas.

ideas.name: Etiquette is part of a game
ideas.text: In Wei-ch'i a move once placed cannot be taken back, and a player taps the board with a tze when an opposing piece is one move from capture. Rules of manner sit beside the rules of play.

ideas.name: Fewer pieces at the end mean more skill
ideas.text: Bell says novices have more pieces on the board at the end of a Wei-ch'i game than experts, who may only half cover it. An experienced player sees which positions are decided and leaves them.

ideas.name: A one-player puzzle from a board for two
ideas.text: Solitaire in England used a Fox and Geese board with marbles. The player removes the marble in the middle, then jumps one marble over another into a hole, removing the one jumped, to leave a single marble in the centre. Bell prints a thirty-one move solution.

ideas.name: Dice are very old
ideas.text: Four-sided dice came from Egyptian tombs and Sumerian pyramids, and Etruscan dice about 900 B.C. had opposite faces adding to seven, as in modern dice. Dice also reached prehistoric earthworks in Britain.

ideas.name: Gambling reaches into everything
ideas.text: Tacitus says the Germani staked their freedom on a last cast and kept their word. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries English travellers lost their clothes at Hazard in taverns. In 1020 two kings threw dice for the district of Hising. Dice have been used to settle whatever people value.

ideas.name: A coin can be loaded
ideas.text: Romans played Head or Ship with a copper coin. Bell reports a coin of Nero sawn in two, with an iron weight set between the halves so one side came up more often. Pitmen still use similar crooked coins. A device to keep a throw fair can be turned against fairness.

ideas.name: Two phases can change what a throw is worth
ideas.text: In the bowl game All-tes teg-enuk, five discs alike wins three small tallies in the first phase and four tallies from the opponent in the second. Once the notched tally is taken, the values of the throws alter.

ideas.name: Rules for ending a drawn-out game
