ideas.text: Bell says the second phase of All-tes teg-enuk can become wearisome. His quicker ending puts tallies won in the second phase back into the pool and out of play. A rule can be added after play shows how long a game runs.

ideas.name: Push your luck
ideas.text: In Thirty-six and in Pig a player keeps throwing to build a total, and in Pig a throw of one loses everything scored in that turn. In Thirty-six going over the target puts the player out. On each throw the player decides whether to stop or go on.

ideas.name: Elimination games keep every player in until the end
ideas.text: In Aces in the Pot players lose counters on throws of 1, pass counters on 6, and the last player holding a counter tries three throws without a 6. The result is decided by a chain of passes and losses.

ideas.name: Roles can swap in a betting game
ideas.text: Barbudi has a shooter and a fader. When a half-bet is lost or won they change roles, and a shooter keeps the dice while he wins. The dice and the bets move around the group according to results.

ideas.name: Side bets let everyone play
ideas.text: In Barbudi the other players bet on whether the shooter or the fader will win, and in Hazard players lay odds among themselves. Bell reprints the 1786 table of odds against the caster. People who do not throw still have a stake.

ideas.name: A game's fame can depend on a person
ideas.text: Bell tells of William Crockford, a fishmonger who became a bookmaker, and whose club in St James's Street made Hazard fashionable in the 1820s. He took over a million pounds, but died worth under a sixth of that. The popularity of a gambling game followed a house that organised it.

ideas.name: A game is simplified when it moves to a new group
ideas.text: Hazard came to New Orleans around 1800, where the intricate rules and betting odds were simplified into the Negro's Game and then Craps. Craps spread along the Mississippi among steamboat hands, dockers and cotton field workers, and reached casinos about 1890.

ideas.name: A game without equipment spreads easily
ideas.text: Bell notes that Private or Military Craps needs only two or more players with money, a pair of dice and time. American troops took it all over the world in the Second World War.

ideas.name: Calling out a missed number
ideas.text: In Martinetti a player who could have used a number and passed the dice on loses it to anyone who calls it first. Watching other players' play becomes part of the game.

ideas.name: Dice can be removed as you score
ideas.text: In Drop Dead a thrower scores the sum of the five dice unless a 2 or 5 shows, and then the dice with a 2 or 5 are put aside. The turn ends when all five are dead. Each throw has fewer dice than the last.

ideas.name: A throw can be kept in part
ideas.text: In Indian Dice, a player may put some dice aside after a throw and re-throw the others, up to three throws. The opening player says how many throws all will have. Choice enters a dice game by the right to keep and re-throw.

ideas.name: Dice make groups of games by how many are thrown
ideas.text: Bell sorts dice games by dice used: two-sided dice, then games with one, two, three, five, six, ten and fifteen-plus dice. A game's count of dice changes the odds and the shape of the throw.

ideas.name: The same dice can be pushed or held back
ideas.text: In Thirty-six and in Pig a player decides how long to keep throwing, since a throw of one wipes out the turn. In Drop Dead dice drop out when they show a 2 or 5. The choice is whether to throw again.

ideas.name: A set of throws can stand for a story
ideas.text: Ship, Captain, Mate and Crew requires a 6, then a 5, then a 4, in that order, and the rest of the dice are the crew's score. The order of the needed numbers tells a small story.

ideas.name: Several turns of rolling with parts kept
ideas.text: In Ship, Captain, Mate and Crew and Indian Dice, the player puts aside the dice he wants and rolls the rest, up to three throws. Part of the dice are fixed while others stay open.

ideas.name: Bluffing adds a second game on top of the dice
ideas.text: In Liar Dice the thrower hides the dice and declares a score that may be false. The next player either accepts and has to raise the call, or challenges. The game is about reading the speaker.

ideas.name: Lives give a long game short rounds
ideas.text: Each Liar Dice player starts with three lives. A wrong call loses one, and the first to lose three gets a fourth. A running count lets a loss be a small step.

ideas.name: Auctions can set roles for the round
ideas.text: In Bell and Hammer the cards are sold by auction, and each owner is paid when a particular face turns up. Only buyers take part in the round, and a player out of two rounds is out. The auction decides who can win what.

ideas.name: A game with phases can change when a card is bought
ideas.text: Bell and Hammer's third phase starts as soon as the pool runs short and the inn is open. The rules for payment change at that moment.

ideas.name: The bank's edge is a design fact
ideas.text: Bell says the Crown and Anchor banker's advantage is such that he will always end well in pocket and everyone else well out. He therefore suggests that the bank pass to each player in turn.

ideas.name: Dice marks can follow culture
ideas.text: Chinese dice have a larger, uncoloured one, and the four's pips are painted red, which Bell takes to be a relic of Indian dice from many centuries before. The look of a die carries its history.

ideas.name: A banker rotates when out-thrown
ideas.text: In Strung Flowers and Throwing Heaven and Nine, the banker throws first, the next player throws against him, and the banker changes when someone out-throws him. Everyone takes the role in turn.

ideas.name: Ranking throws as a ladder
ideas.text: Strung Flowers ranks triples, the sequence 4-5-6, pairs with an odd die, and the Dancing Dragon 1-2-3 as the lowest. Throwing Heaven and Nine names its twenty-one throws in a civil and a military series. A ranking gives dice faces an order that has nothing to do with their sums.

ideas.name: The first throw can decide the type of the round
ideas.text: In Throwing Heaven and Nine, the banker's first throw names the suit, civil or military, and a later throw from the other suit does not count. One roll sets the terms for the rest.

ideas.name: A spinner replaces the die
ideas.text: Put and Take uses a six-sided teetotum with instructions on each face: take one, all put, take all, put two, take two, put one. The device gives written results instead of numbers.

ideas.name: Dominoes are dice thrown in advance
ideas.text: Bell says dominoes seem to be a Chinese invention, tablets representing the throw of two dice. The tiles carry the same names as the dice throws and the same civil and military series. A card set can hold the outcomes of a dice game.

ideas.name: Pairing can follow identity or sum
ideas.text: In Chinese dominoes civil tiles pair when identical, military tiles pair by total spots, and 2-4 with 1-2 make the supreme pair. Fishing and Disputing Tens turn on finding matches in a pile.

ideas.name: Counting rules can be strange and fixed
ideas.text: In Fishing tiles with eight or more spots are large fish and score two points a spot, and tiles with fewer than eight are minnows scoring one point only for red spots, rounded up to the next ten. Odd scoring is part of what a game is.

ideas.name: A deal can be prepared by a dice count
ideas.text: In Collecting Tens a croupier shakes four dice, and counts round the players to choose the leader. The leader takes ten tiles and the rest take nine. Chance picks who has the advantage.

ideas.name: A house takes a share
ideas.text: In Collecting Tens, five per cent of the stakes go to the House and the rest to the winner. Playing for money in a house adds a cost to the table.

ideas.name: Ma-jong came from older tile games
ideas.text: Bell says Collecting Tens and Playing Heavens and Nines were the forerunners of Ma-jong, with modified dominoes in three suits and twenty-eight special tiles. A card or tile game grows from earlier ones.

ideas.name: Origin dates are uncertain
ideas.text: Estimates of Ma-jong's age range from the time of Confucius to about one hundred and fifty years. Bell prefers the later date because the game only became popular in China about 1900.

ideas.name: Local rules differ, and the host's book wins
ideas.text: Ma-jong is played differently in northern and southern China, and no two books agree. Bell says the rules in the host's book are accepted as final if a point is in dispute.

ideas.name: The set itself carries the game
ideas.text: A Chinese Ma-jong set has 136 tiles with bamboo backs and bone faces, 128 counters, dice, a tong box and stands. Sets made for foreigners had numerals added to the corner. The objects were changed for new players.

ideas.name: Elaborate set-up prevents cheating
ideas.text: In Ma-jong, dice choose who places the tong, discs set the winds, and each player builds a wall seventeen tiles long and two high, pushed together into a square. A gap at the corner was said to let in the devils of ill-luck, and in practice allowed cheating.

ideas.name: Seating and role are decided by chance and then rotate
ideas.text: In Ma-jong the draw of wind discs gives East, South, West and North their seats and roles. The winds then move round as players win or lose, and East keeps his position while he keeps winning.

ideas.name: A player may break in on someone else's turn
ideas.text: In Ma-jong any player who holds two matching tiles may call Pung on a discard and take it, and a player who passes loses his turn. A call out of turn changes who plays next.

ideas.name: Claims have an order of priority
ideas.text: When two Ma-jong players want one discarded tile, a player completing the hand takes precedence over one needing it for a pung or quong, who takes precedence over one needing it for a chow. Priorities settle disputes.

ideas.name: Declaring a goal binds the player
ideas.text: A Ma-jong player who says he is fishing, needing one tile, cannot change his hand. A player who stands from the first discard gets a bonus. Declaring early adds reward and risk.

ideas.name: Rounds turn into a long game
ideas.text: Each wind in turn is the wind of the round, and a round lasts until each player has been East. A pung of the prevailing wind doubles the player's score. Four rounds make a long game.

ideas.name: Scores can be made to grow quickly
ideas.text: Ma-jong scores are doubled for chosen features, such as a hand of one suit or without chows, and a limit stops the total. Without a limit a single hand could score over a hundred thousand points.

ideas.name: Penalties for wrong calls
ideas.text: A false call of ma-jong with the hand exposed costs the caller double the limit to each player, and a player who discards the tile allowing a special hand pays for all the losers. A rule can punish a mistake that harms others.

ideas.name: A game keeps its name and changes in the next country
ideas.text: Bell notes that when Ma-jong reached America many extra rules were added, so that the Western game differs from the Chinese form he describes.

ideas.name: Dominoes travelled slowly
ideas.text: Dominoes were first reported in Italy in the fourteenth century, perhaps brought by Marco Polo. They reached France and then England, where Strutt in 1801 called them a very childish sport. A hundred and fifty years later they were played over most of the world, even by Eskimos.

ideas.name: The Western set dropped duplicates and added blanks
ideas.text: The Chinese set of thirty-two tiles has no blanks and duplicates its civil tiles. The Western double-six set has twenty-eight tiles with blanks. Bell draws the development in a diagram.

ideas.name: Many games share one set of tiles
ideas.text: Block, Bergen, Forty-two, Bingo and Domino Crib all use a double-six set. Matador, Cyprus and Tiddle-a-Wink use a double-nine set. The same pieces support matching games, trick games and counting games.

ideas.name: Game ends by blocking or running out
ideas.text: The Block Game ends when one player plays his last tile or when no one can play, and scoring counts spots left in hand. A block turns an unlucky hand into a measurable result.

ideas.name: Scoring rewards a pattern
ideas.text: In the Bergen game a double header scores two points, a triple header three, and players near the target score less for them. Making the line of tiles show matching ends is a skill goal inside a matching game.

ideas.name: Dominoes can be played like cards
ideas.text: Forty-two uses bidding, trumps and tricks with a domino set, and Bingo uses trump, tricks and announcements for doubles. A tile set can carry a card game.

ideas.name: Special announcements add excitement
ideas.text: In Bingo a player holding two doubles calls Doubles, with three Triplets, up to seven doubles, Invincible. If he wins the trick he scores. A rare hand carries a name.

ideas.name: A player can end drawing and take a risk
ideas.text: In Bingo a player who turns the trump face down stops drawing and promises to score 70 points. If he succeeds he gains a set, and if he fails the opponent scores double. Ending early is a bet.

ideas.name: A game takes its scoring from another game
ideas.text: Domino Crib borrows cribbage scoring, with fifteens, runs, pairs, a crib and a pegging board, and the board is the cribbage board in the first chapter. Parts of one game are borrowed by another.

ideas.name: Counting to a fixed total turns tiles into numbers
ideas.text: In Domino Crib players add the pips of the tiles they play towards 31, scoring for 15, 31 and pairs. Matching, adding and sequence all appear in one game.

ideas.name: Matching can add up to a number
ideas.text: In the Matador game tiles join when the ends add to ten rather than when they match. Six matador tiles can go anywhere. Changing the relation between neighbours changes what a player looks for.

ideas.name: The number of tiles dealt changes with the players
ideas.text: Cyprus gives a table of tiles by number of players, from four players to ten, and leaves the remaining tiles unused. The deal is chosen so that each player has a fair start.

ideas.name: A double can earn another turn
ideas.text: In Tiddle-a-Wink a player who plays a double gets a second turn. A small bonus rewards a particular tile.

ideas.name: A game is a hobby of making
ideas.text: Bell closes with a chapter on making boards and pieces, because the boards of many games are unobtainable in shops. He lists methods from a red-hot poker line on wood to inlay, veneer, formica, pottery and gilded leather. A designer can make and test a game with plain materials.

ideas.name: Match the method to the original
ideas.text: Bell says that if original boards were simple, crude techniques give satisfying copies, and if elaborate, there are modern materials for them. He warns that a solid underboard can warp weeks after veneer is applied.

ideas.name: Games can be gathered in one box
ideas.text: An antique compendium from western India is painted for Tablan on the top, holds a Pallanguli board inside, has Nine Men's Morris underneath and Cows and Leopards on the lid. Several games share one object.

ideas.name: A writer of rules can fix a standard
ideas.text: Edmond Hoyle began teaching whist in 1741 with manuscript notes, then printed them when pirated copies appeared. The Short Treatise gave the laws of the game, a few rules for beginners and calculations of odds. Over three hundred editions followed, and According to Hoyle came to mean the accepted way of playing.

ideas.name: A group of players can study a game and write down principles
ideas.text: About 1736 gentlemen at the Crown Coffee House in Bedford Row studied whisk, a tavern game, until it became whist, and set out four rules: play from your longest suit, study your partner's hand as much as your own, do not force your partner unnecessarily, and attend to the score. The game changed class by being studied.

ideas.name: A chess master wrote down openings and end games
ideas.text: As-Suli, a champion at the court of Baghdad before A.D. 946, wrote a Book of Chess with ten standard openings, common middle-game problems and a collection of end plays with comments. Bell calls him the first to try to discover the science of the game.

ideas.name: Foreign games were collected from visitors
ideas.text: Thomas Hyde, interpreter in oriental languages to the English court under three kings, met envoys from eastern countries and gathered their games without leaving England. His two books on chess and on backgammon-type games came from these conversations.

ideas.name: Genres are a weak base for a common language
ideas.text: Genres mostly follow what is popular and come from game journalism rather than careful study, and sorting by interaction alone can give 42 genres. The authors look instead for the components that could describe genres.

ideas.name: Mechanics need relations to be useful
ideas.text: The idea that a game is put together from smaller components is useful, but the authors argue that mechanics need a clearer structure, with information on how they relate to each other and how to apply them.

ideas.name: Build the language on interaction, not story
ideas.text: Most earlier game research borrowed from literature, theatre and film, which risks losing sight of interaction. The authors take interaction, between players and between player and game, as the more defining feature of games.

ideas.name: Patterns are not only problem and solution
ideas.text: The authors do not define patterns as problem and solution pairs. They give two reasons: that would treat patterns only as a way to remove unwanted effects, and many patterns describe a characteristic that automatically brings other characteristics with it.

ideas.name: Names are for remembering
ideas.text: Pattern names are meant to be short, specific and idiomatic, to help recall once the description has been read rather than to explain it. Aliases are left out to keep the number of names small, and references to similar ideas in other models do that job.

ideas.name: Test a pattern by taking it out
ideas.text: In analysing a candidate pattern, the authors describe how it is used in example games and then try removing it from those games to explain how the play would change.

ideas.name: Designers use few named mechanics
ideas.text: In interviews with nine professional designers, all used genre, theme and mechanisms easily but named few mechanics. The exceptions for board and card game makers were Bluff, Tension, Action Cards, Storytelling, Trading, Action Points and Cooperation.

ideas.name: Paper Rock Scissors keeps choices open
ideas.text: The pattern promotes tension, either until the choices are revealed or until the result of a long-term strategy shows. It brings randomness unless players can learn about others' activity or keep a record of their behaviour.

ideas.name: Ways to use patterns
ideas.text: The authors list uses without picking one method: idea generation, developing a concept, explaining a design in pre-production, finding competition and patent issues, solving problems, analysing games, sorting games and genres, and exploring new platforms.

ideas.name: Patterns for idea generation
ideas.text: A designer can pick a few patterns at random and try to imagine a game that uses them, or take one pattern and look for a new way to build it.

ideas.name: Patterns for developing a concept
ideas.text: A game concept can be described as a small set of patterns, then fleshed out by choosing subpatterns and studying how the patterns interact, repeating until the detail is enough.

ideas.name: Patterns for analysing games
ideas.text: A pattern collection can be gone through one pattern at a time to see whether, and to what degree, each one is present in an existing game. Games can then be sorted by what they share and differ in.

ideas.name: The same pattern shows up in different games
ideas.text: The authors found the same patterns in very different games, such as Carcassonne and Qix, and Pac-Man and King of the Hill variants of first-person shooters. They take this as a sign that patterns help in understanding interaction.

ideas.name: A pattern collection is a network
ideas.text: The patterns do not form a strict hierarchy but a network with several base nodes. The authors also say that some groups of patterns are normally used together to bring each other about, which sub and superior relations do not cover.

ideas.name: Finding the right pattern is hard
ideas.text: With over 200 candidates, finding the relevant ones for a given situation is a problem, especially for new users. The authors look at ways to sort patterns by use, theme and the structural framework.

ideas.name: Patterns do not take the creativity out
ideas.text: The authors answer the fear that patterns make designers copy each other by saying it comes from mixing up the everyday meaning of pattern with the one used by Alexander. They compare it to an artist who has a greater chance of making something new when familiar with the basic elements of the craft.

ideas.name: Prizes separate players
ideas.text: Boyd held that greed and dishonesty are not part of competitive games themselves. They come in through prizes, which set able players apart from the rest and discourage the less able. In her playground programmes she used games for the play itself, with no reward at the end.

ideas.name: A game is a pretend situation
ideas.text: Boyd wrote in 1934 that play is always an artificial situation, while work is a real one. A game is set up in the imagination and defined by rules the players accept. A child who plays moves out of the real situation into the pretend one and acts as consistently in it as if it were real.

ideas.name: A game is a problem and its solution
ideas.text: For Boyd every game is set up as a problem, and playing the game is the same act as solving it. The pattern of the game gives the starting conditions for the problem. Acting steadily within the frame of the game is the same discipline as any careful problem solving.

ideas.name: A game copies social life in a small space
ideas.text: Boyd called a game a social pattern, a copy of how people are organised, held inside limits of time and space. Players take roles and deal with each other under rules, as people do outside it, and then the game comes to an end.

ideas.name: Rules and strategies come first
ideas.text: In Boyd's view, and in the mathematical theory of games, rules and strategies matter most. Each side picks a plan of behaviour beforehand, and what it meets depends on the plan the other side picked. This differs from everyday talk, where a game means a run of tricks and dishonest moves.

ideas.name: Outside rewards bend the rules
ideas.text: Boyd accepted competition as part of a game. She said outside prizes turn players towards getting round the rules, widen the gap between winner and loser, and push out the enjoyment and spontaneity of play. A game where players avoid the rules by dishonest moves is, to her, a struggle to dominate the others and not a game.

ideas.name: Rules decide what counts in the play world
ideas.text: Simon quotes Huizinga: every game has rules, and they decide what holds inside the world the game makes. The rules bind the players completely and leave no room for doubt. Play happens inside fixed limits of time and place, and the players feel it as different from ordinary life.

ideas.name: Undirected play stays thin
ideas.text: Boyd differed from writers who wanted children's play left alone. She thought play with no adult guidance stays meagre and limited. A leader who joins in, in mind as well as body, can steer play so that it teaches social skills. Her example was Edith, a girl of fourteen who spoke little, and who began to form sentences and join classroom exercises after directed play.

ideas.name: Groups grow by working on a shared problem
ideas.text: For Boyd, people form a group by acting together on something that matters to all of them. Organisation follows from that joint work. A problem that concerns the whole group is solved by the whole group, because deciding it only at the top leaves everyone else with no part in it.

ideas.name: Kinds of group relation run from loose to tight
ideas.text: Boyd listed kinds of group experience. At one end are people doing separate things side by side, who need almost no co-operation. At the other end are activities that need close co-operation, dependence on each other and joining of effort. Each kind came with its own sorts of social relation.

ideas.name: Leadership belongs to the situation
ideas.text: Boyd said leadership is a function and not a trait. Each member leads when they add something needed to the matter in hand, and the adult leader guides the process and stops an aggressive member from ruling the group.

ideas.name: Work is real and play is made up
ideas.text: Boyd said the difference between work and play is not enjoyment, because work can be enjoyed and play can turn into work. The difference is that a work situation is genuine and a play situation is artificial. A child who plays a game accepts its rules and its roles, and also helps to create and hold up the pretend situation.

ideas.name: Players take a game seriously because of the challenge
ideas.text: Boyd asked why a child works hard at something known to be only a game. She gave two causes: the nature of the situation and the child's attitude. The attitude is willingness to accept the problem the game sets, whether it asks for a skill, for beating an opponent or for a shared task. This willingness does away with merit points and badges as a spur.

ideas.name: A game squeezes a long life event into a short one
ideas.text: Boyd compared a game to a well-made drama. It removes what does not matter and puts events close together, so a typical long experience is packed into little time and space. Because of this, a child gets more and different experience from games than from ordinary days.

ideas.name: Folk games grow out of people, not out of adults' plans
ideas.text: Boyd said traditional games were not made by adults to amuse or teach children. They match body development and cultural patterns, and are looser than many real-life situations in how they are organised. She called them social patterns with a stamp of universality.

ideas.name: Taking turns teaches the move from wanting to rule-following
ideas.text: Boyd described growth from self-gratification to self-determinism. In the first, a baby gets what it wants when it wants it. In the second, a child acts by the rules the group made and helps enforce them on others and on self. A game packs this change into one unit, since a player who joins has to follow the rules.

ideas.name: A penalty is accepted when the cause is visible
ideas.text: In Two Deep, a tag game, a frail girl let herself be tagged again and again and had to keep running as the one chasing. After about twenty minutes she began to watch for the runner and got away in time. Boyd said that she took the penalty without complaint because the link from her failure to the result was close, and because the rules were applied to everyone the same way.

ideas.name: Behaviour barred outside is allowed in the game
ideas.text: Boyd noted that play lets a child act in ways that would be offensive in a genuine situation. A game cast list can hold thieves, robbers and kidnappers, yet the robbers only tag, the thieves only steal sticks and the witch carries off Monday while Sunday turns her back. The rules keep the danger small.

ideas.name: A game role is a part and not a character
ideas.text: Boyd separated the role in a game from the role in a play. In baseball the pitcher and catcher are roles, and in a fox and chickens game the fox and hen are roles, but players do not act in character. In Little Sally Waters, Sally stands, turns with eyes shut and points her finger, with none of the weeping the song describes.

ideas.name: Immediate results teach more than advice
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that a game is life in miniature, and that the play group is society in small. When a child takes more than a fair share of turns, the other children protest at once in terms the child follows. She argued that fairness is built through action with quick results and not by being told what is right.

ideas.name: Aggressive players learn to give up extra turns
ideas.text: Boyd saw active children who at first wanted every turn come, under steady leadership, to refuse more than their share and to ask for fairness for a younger or timid child. She held that this came out of playing in the group and could not be handed over as a rule to memorise.

ideas.name: Games without contact steady an unsettled group
ideas.text: A leader worked with youths aged fourteen to sixteen who found it hard to keep to a game. Contact games made them over-excited, so she chose target games between two teams and bowling, where each player takes a turn and adds points to the team score. With no contact and no interplay, they stayed in the game and forgot themselves.

ideas.name: Traditional games are an art form
ideas.text: Boyd put games and folk dances beside painting and music as patterns that express balance, proportion and harmony. She said time has kept the ones that drew a response from each new generation. She added that when music or ballet turned artificial, composers and dancers went back to folk forms.

ideas.name: The game and the leader's part both matter
ideas.text: Boyd held that the spirit of play matters and so does the content. For play to serve social education, the leader needs to join the group and stay one of its members, with the same share in the play as the children, and needs to know the games thoroughly.

ideas.name: Board games grow from daily events
ideas.text: Boyd noted that events such as the capture of slaves, a trip to market or a tribal fight may be the basis of board games like backgammon and chess. The story fades as the game passes between people, but the pattern of the social process stays, like city streets that look clearer from the air once the details are gone.

ideas.name: A close chain of cause and effect makes games teach
ideas.text: Because a game's events come in quick order inside small limits of time and space, Boyd said, cause and effect are plain to the player. The player picks up more than in daily life, much of it without being able to put it into words. A fielder who catches a fly ball behaves as if he had done the physics.

ideas.name: Teach a game as a whole
ideas.text: At the Lincoln school, games and dances were shown as wholes, with details left until the basic pattern was learned and enjoyed. Seventy boys learned basketball to official rules this way, while others failed when it was taught bit by bit.

ideas.name: Group size and age spread were found by trial
ideas.text: Bertha Schlotter found that groups whose mental and chronological ages differed by no more than about two years gave the closest social relations and play, and that twenty children was the largest group she could work with.

ideas.name: Games sort by what they ask of players
ideas.text: Boyd said games may be arranged on a scale by their main factors, such as special body skills, social organisation, co-operative interaction, team play and intellectual content.

ideas.name: A group makes its own rules when given the work
ideas.text: At the Geneva school, girls and a group worker planned a two-week recreation programme with no prizes, no cottage set against another and no special treatment for the well behaved. The groups became clubs, and they began to settle conduct problems among their own members.

ideas.name: One game, play at different depths
ideas.text: Boyd compared a mechanic and an engineer working the same problem at different levels. In dominoes, a child may count only the result of the next move, while an older player works from all exposed pieces and weighs near and far results. The rules stay the same, and players of unlike ability can share one game.

ideas.name: A stable pattern holds varied players
ideas.text: When the basic pattern of a game stays fixed, Boyd noted, players of very different ability are held to a way of behaving that generations of players made. She held that this steadies the nervous system and helps social adjustment.

ideas.name: The game ends and its world dissolves
ideas.text: Boyd described playing as lifting oneself out of a genuine situation into an imagined one, keeping to the rules, playing the assigned role and working with the other players. When the game is over, the whole structure comes apart. She likened this to a cast on a stage, though in a game the players are the ones inside it.

ideas.name: Competition belongs to some games and not others
ideas.text: Boyd accepted competition because many games contain it. In her account a game is a problem, and winning is the last step in solving it and not the chief pleasure. She added that swimming, skiing and skating are not competitive and lose value when made so.

ideas.name: Each replay is a new problem
ideas.text: Even with the same opponents, each play of a game forms a new arrangement, Boyd observed. That makes it a new problem and calls for a new series of moves.

ideas.name: Stakes and publicity pull interest away from the problem
ideas.text: Boyd said prizes, cheering and publicity turn players towards the extras and away from solving the game. She used gambling as the extreme case, since a gambler wants the opponent's money and not the game. Replacing stakes with points and publicity, she asked, may kill interest in the game in the same way.

ideas.name: Games have a design that can be badly made
ideas.text: Boyd called traditional games and dances structural art designs. She watched a teacher join sound traditional dance figures into a new folk game, and the dancers could not pass easily from one figure to the next. Parts that worked alone did not add up to a whole that worked, and she found out the game had been invented by a teacher.

ideas.name: Play with others becomes more than rudimentary
ideas.text: Boyd pointed to children raised among animals, whose play stayed crude and copied the animals, such as running on all fours. She took this to mean that play grows through association in groups.

ideas.name: A well-formed game is not play unless spirit is present
ideas.text: Boyd held that children can be kept busy by a game of sound form and still not be playing. For her, play needs spontaneity and exhilaration shown within the rules and in solving the game's problem. Excitement is not the same as exhilaration, and activity is not the same as spontaneity.

ideas.name: Striving for excellence costs spontaneity
ideas.text: Boyd said learning often means trying to do what one cannot yet do, and putting technique before the activity. Aiming at excellence in play shifts interest to the self and raises competition. She also granted that players may not be joyous while learning a complex game.

ideas.name: Play has its own rules for rough behaviour
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that in play a person may be rough, noisy and unconventional, but that play has its own social controls, code and rules. These are taken on freely, can be enforced, and keep a balance between personal freedom and what the culture demands.

ideas.name: Play patterns keep the customs of a culture
ideas.text: Boyd observed children playing family life, shop-keeping, funerals and school in line with the customs around them. In the same play they show courage, bear pain, respect others' rights and keep to the rules.

ideas.name: The player helps make the role and the activity
ideas.text: Boyd described the player as creating a role while helping to create the activity. This gives the player control over themselves as a player, so what they do or fail to do is their own responsibility.

ideas.name: What a game does for a player depends on several things
ideas.text: Boyd listed what shapes the value of a play activity: the age, earlier play, health and handicaps of the player; the choice of activity and the leadership; the personality of the teacher; and how fully the teacher joins in.

ideas.name: Cheating spoils the game for everyone
ideas.text: Boyd described girls who worked out a group feeling in hide and seek. Cheating started only after they had enjoyed keeping to the rules, and when it did, the game was spoiled so suddenly that the girls protested against the spoiling and not the cheating itself. They then asked for equal, impartial treatment for all.

ideas.name: Players object to turns going to favourites
ideas.text: Boyd gave the case of a child with standing among the others who is chosen again and again for the most wanted roles, when players pick their own successor. Children outside the favoured group objected that it is not fair to always choose only friends. She read this as children forming rules from play.

ideas.name: Rules that block every mistake block learning
ideas.text: Boyd argued that organisations which make rules to prevent errors stop children learning what not to do as well as what to do. A child needs to act, take the result and judge it to build judgement.

ideas.name: A folk dance is played for the dancers
ideas.text: Boyd separated folk dances from ceremonial dances, done to influence fate, and from stage dances, done to influence an audience. Folk dances are done for the pleasure they give to the dancers themselves.

ideas.name: Winning stressed too hard ends the play
ideas.text: Boyd gave the case of school baseball teams that won and were then beaten up by the losers. She said that when winning is stressed too much, the play is killed, and adults then try to bring it back by authority or by preaching about sportsmanship.

ideas.name: Praise for one player spoils the play for others
ideas.text: Boyd held that singling out a child with a high level of skill can raise jealousy in the others where left alone it might have raised emulation. The praised child may start to show off, and everyone is pulled away from the purpose of the activity.

ideas.name: A play that pretends to be enjoyable is not play
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that when the show of enjoyment is played up, the natural life of play dies. She said players who force a game, which she called farced play, are failing to get into the game in their minds. She advised choosing activities that hold interest and stretch the players without overstretching them.

ideas.name: Games with a catch lose interest once the catch is known
ideas.text: Boyd ranked traditional games, whose content keeps drawing players back, above games that make one player the butt of a joke, and above games with a catch that ends interest once found.

ideas.name: Play lasts as long as the challenge holds
ideas.text: Boyd said play depends on interest that comes from seeing the problem and accepting the challenge. Once the thing to be made, the act of skill, the opponent or the group task no longer holds the whole challenge, the attitude of play ends. A player who withdraws in mind while keeping to the letter of the rules has stopped playing.

ideas.name: A game shows a player's own faults at once
ideas.text: In play, Boyd noted, cause and effect sit so close in time and space, and other players answer so quickly, that a player's shortcomings show up straight away. The same closeness gives a reason to overcome them.

ideas.name: Dance, game and drama each hold a player in a role
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that in a dance the player follows the design to the close, in a game the player obeys the rules and plays a role in relation to the other roles, and in a drama the player acts within the frame of the play. When it is over, the player steps out of the role.

ideas.name: Familiar structure frees the player
ideas.text: A player new to a form of play, Boyd observed, is mostly busy working out its structure. Once the structure is established, less attention goes to it and the player is set free to be creative. This happens only when a leader does not press structure and technique too hard.

ideas.name: Aimless excitement is not play
ideas.text: Boyd separated play from purposeless impulse, where incidents have no meaningful sequence. A game, with its definite frame, needs closer adherence to events, more continuity and more self-discipline than free capricious play. She added that within the frame each player can still play a role in their own way.

ideas.name: Telling a player what to do defeats purpose
ideas.text: Boyd said a child's purpose in play can be defeated by interruption, by being told what to do and how, or by help given when persistence would have got the child through. She held that the child wants to be steered and does not want to be handed the answer.

ideas.name: Solving the problem is what matters to the solver
ideas.text: Boyd held that if problem solving were only getting the answer, it would be of little value. The process has value, and effort counts even when the aim is not reached. Having made one's full effort is satisfying even without success.

ideas.name: Prizes redirect effort from the problem
ideas.text: Boyd asked whether awards, emblems and honour rolls turn children's effort to solving the problem or to winning the award. She said those with little chance of success respond badly, and those with ability lose interest in the process itself.

ideas.name: Thinking about the play kills the play
ideas.text: Boyd said that in true play the player does not look inward at personal gains. A child who claps and cries out at a successful move is expressing the end of a successful play and is not stepping back to judge. In her view, making players aware of what play does for them destroys the spirit of play.

ideas.name: Repeating a game builds skill and adaptability
ideas.text: A child delights in playing something over and over, Boyd noted, and the playing is never twice alike though the general pattern is the same. Repetition makes the child more skilful and not more regimented. She held that skill matters most when it grows through use.

ideas.name: Regimentation and spontaneity differ
ideas.text: Boyd defined regimentation as telling players how to play and how to solve the problem. Spontaneity is leaving them to find their own way inside the frame. She warned that yelling and over-excitement under regimentation are taken by adults as a sign of enjoyment and are not.

ideas.name: Self-made play can drift to a side matter
ideas.text: Boyd saw children playing house or a similar game build up a main purpose and then be carried off by a smaller incident that pleased them, carrying on as if it were the main purpose. She called this a creative adventure that is not logical.

ideas.name: Co-operation sits inside competition
ideas.text: Boyd held that in dances, drama and games each participant takes the role needed for the whole activity to go on, so that stronger dancers help weaker ones and actors give fellow actors openings. Players come to see co-operation as necessary even where competition is one of the factors.

ideas.name: Emulation needs a playful signal
ideas.text: Boyd said emulation starts from a stimulus pattern that is itself playful. In her example, a teacher ended a demonstration with French nursery children by saying 'you can't catch me' and running round the court, and the whole group followed laughing. A plain spoken suggestion to run would not have done the same.

ideas.name: Emulating differs from copying
ideas.text: Boyd compared two play leaders. One taught rope-jumping patterns step by step to girls in a line, who copied them. The other sang a song while playing with a ball in time, handed out balls and let the children make up their own plays. The second gave room for original play and the first gave only imitation.

ideas.name: Competition needs nothing at stake
ideas.text: Boyd noted that competition runs through every non-musical game, even among small children, as in hide the thimble. She defined it as seeking to gain what another is trying to gain at the same time, with no ill will, and with nothing material at stake.

ideas.name: A frame of reference leaves room inside it
ideas.text: Boyd saw children dramatising stories or playing house hold to the general pattern while each plays a role in their own way, as long as the requirements of the pattern are met.

ideas.name: Competition and emulation differ
ideas.text: Boyd said both challenge a player by another's shown ability. In a game, competition is move by move, each player or team trying to gain an edge on the other. Emulation is a striving to equal another's skill. Competition used as the only motive is one thing, and competition beside co-operation, empathy and emulation is another.

ideas.name: Competition and winning are two different things
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that competition is the process of one player outwitting another, while winning is centred on the finish. Someone has to win, but a team or person who has enjoyed play without stress on winning is unlikely to be ruled by winning.

ideas.name: Competition added to non-competitive activities
ideas.text: Boyd held that putting contests into skating, swimming, drama or music tends to commercialise them. She also held that a programme with no competition at all removes emulation, strategy and the chance to make judgements and act on them.

ideas.name: Prizes broke up a card group
ideas.text: A small group of men and women met at a public recreation centre to play cards, and word of their enjoyment grew it to over fifty. The contest inside the games had only added to the pleasure until prizes came in. Then people criticised the differences in prize value, winning replaced playing together, and the group broke up, including friendships between neighbours.

ideas.name: Choosing players for roles by contest has costs
ideas.text: Boyd gave the case of two girls who competed for the lead in a school play. The role went to the daughter of a prominent family, and many thought this was unjust. The girl who lost lost faith in honest effort and drifted, and Boyd said she might have done well in another activity had she not met the competitive selection.

ideas.name: Knocking down what a child builds teaches nothing
ideas.text: Boyd said a child who builds a house and has it knocked down does not learn to build sturdier houses. A child can redo a building that fails to satisfy, but destroying it is not the same.

ideas.name: Building blocks teach cause and effect
ideas.text: A child who stacks blocks, finds they fall, and tries again until they stand is dealing with mechanical stress. Boyd said this is intelligent mental behaviour, whether or not it leads to planning a bridge on paper. She added that play materials ought not to set too many problems at once.

ideas.name: Things cannot answer a child's treatment
ideas.text: Toys and objects cannot react to how the child treats them, Boyd noted. Play with things alone reveals a hidden problem but does not solve it, and equipment play stays closer to reflex action unless a dramatic form such as a jump-rope rhyme is joined to it.

ideas.name: Made-up play needs a defined frame to teach discipline
ideas.text: Boyd said imaginative play lacks one thing that organised games and dramatised stories have, which is the discipline of solving problems inside a defined frame. In playing house the frame is only loosely given, and each player acts with general reference to the task.

ideas.name: A leader organised a room into a small town
ideas.text: About fifteen girls began playing house on chalked squares on the floor. The leader gave them paper and scissors for dishes and cut paper babies for the mothers. When the children wanted something to do, she added a school, then a factory with a time schedule struck on the piano, then a grocery and a coal peddler for boys. She insisted that orders be remembered exactly, wrong orders be refused and delivery mistakes be put right, which gave the trade a dignity the children liked.

ideas.name: Each part of a pretend town needs the others
ideas.text: In the same play, dishes from the factory had to be needed by the mothers, the school had to teach the youngest and set work for older ones, and the store had to take orders that the mothers had to place and remember. The leader kept every group tied to the others and to the whole.

ideas.name: A big group of children is like a heap of building material
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that a large group of children has to be organised into a house or be wasted. Where the Polish children's resources were thin, the units could not have kept going without the worker's organising. At around fifty children the worker could go from group to group as a visitor, and above sixty the overflow was given separate games in the corridor.

ideas.name: Play changes experience and does not copy it
ideas.text: Boyd said a child who plays at a train journey is transforming it by selecting and shortening events from a long span of time into a close sequence. Fifteen-month-old Paul built a train from chairs after a trip. Boyd said it is a misconception to call this imitation. A copied game like Patty Cake, she said, is not transformation.

ideas.name: A prompt helps while the child supplies the content
ideas.text: Boyd's example had Paul laying out playing cards in a broken line, and a neighbour running her fingers along them saying 'here comes a train'. Paul then made trains with the cards in several rooms. She held that a prompt, given when imagination is ready, can start play while the child puts in his own content.

ideas.name: Play can run away from its players
ideas.text: Girls of eight and nine playing house made their dolls sick, shared news of worsening illness and drew the shades, until they enjoyed the worry no longer and could not leave the illusion. The play leader announced herself as a doctor, visited each home, and the babies recovered and the shades went up.

ideas.name: A leader plays two parts
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that the worker often plays both player and teacher. The worker keeps the frame of reference intact by objecting when a player acts against it, and does so only when no other player does, since players learn from enforcing the rules on each other as well as obeying them.

ideas.name: Dictated play kills empathy
ideas.text: Boyd held that a coach who tells players exactly what to do, in place of letting them act from their own sense of the situation, defeats their own intelligence. She said this makes a player dependent and not adventurous or experimental.

ideas.name: The same party made two ways builds two groups
ideas.text: Boyd compared two girls' clubs planning a valentine party. In the first, all talk over the programme, ideas clash and adjust, and all make the decorations together. In the second, motions are put, committees are appointed and each does a part. The first draws members together and the second separates them, though the parties look alike.

ideas.name: Groups run from separate activity to shared interest in each other
ideas.text: Boyd described a scale. At one end each member acts mostly alone with little interest in the others, and at the other end members care about one another as persons. Groups held together mainly by a programme break up when the activities stop interesting them. Groups whose interest is in each other last longer and make new programmes.

ideas.name: Conflict inside shared work builds the group
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that when members work on a project for shared satisfaction, differences and conflicts come out and tend to resolve. Free expression of felt difference is the only way to reach consensus. She added that some incompatibilities show up as well, and the group steadies as some members draw closer and others drop out.

ideas.name: Play patterns turn out different from their first use
ideas.text: A group formed for one purpose often grows closeness for another, Boyd observed, as with a clothing workers' union that built a recreation programme, and a sewing class whose members refused any new member.

ideas.name: Rules start still and become active when played
ideas.text: Boyd defined a game as a problem situation set up for a time in the imagination, with playing as the way the problem is solved. In checkers, two players accept the fixed rules, which become active as soon as they are acted on. They move pieces in turn, always in relation to the rules, to each other's changing positions and to the final aim.

ideas.name: A game and a physics problem use the same working method
ideas.text: Boyd said the way a player behaves in a game is identical to thinking inside a frame of reference in physics or philosophy, though the game's behaviour is of a different order. She held that highly organised games are problems whose solution keeps behaviour in a cause-and-effect order.

ideas.name: The game, not the leader, steers behaviour
ideas.text: A play leader showed sixty restless boys and girls aged eight to sixteen how a game controls behaviour. She gathered a few in a circle for a tiptoeing game in which one player stands with eyes shut in the centre and another tries to touch him unheard. The others joined, and the group kept the silence rule for twenty-two minutes in a row.

ideas.name: Players still differ inside a fixed frame
ideas.text: In the same silence game, nothing in the rules stopped one boy crawling to the centre on hands and knees or another taking off his shoes. Boyd said that behaviour in a game is always relative to the frame of reference, and that this leaves room for different ways of solving the problem.

ideas.name: A game's frame is given and a club's frame is made
ideas.text: Boyd contrasted a game, whose pattern is already fixed, with a club, whose frame its members have to create together and keep creating. A club both makes its own social frame and acts in relation to it, which she called self-control in the highest sense.

ideas.name: A ready-made answer removes the challenge
ideas.text: A principal told a club of boys, who had asked whether to give a member who seldom came another chance, that people always get another chance in her school. Boyd said that with the answer supplied, the boys had no reason to go back and work it out together, and no real thinking was needed.

ideas.name: Badges and special privileges work against the group
ideas.text: Boyd argued that a place trying to build integrated groups cannot give privileges or insignia to members rated well behaved, or punish those rated badly behaved. She said both prevent the development of the kind of group where they could grow.

ideas.name: Games make problems that have set limits
ideas.text: Boyd contrasted mathematical problems, which can be stated exactly and solved by formal logic to one correct answer, with social problems, which deal with values in continuous change and call for continuous experimentation. A game sets a problem inside a stated frame, so it can be solved and finished.

ideas.name: Players agree to a contract before the game starts
ideas.text: Boyd said every game has a pattern (Cat and Rat, baseball), fixed rules for that game, and cultural rules that are taken for granted, such as not hurting each other and not giving the game to the opponent. Accepting these is something like a gentleman's agreement. Inside it, players create and solve the game's problem as it changes move by move.

ideas.name: An error in play does not stay on a record
ideas.text: Boyd noted that when a player fails to keep the agreement, the others react at once and everyone, including the one at fault, understands why. The mistake is not written down on a report card, the game goes on like a merry-go-round, and the momentum of the group carries the player along.

ideas.name: Activities run on a scale from watching to joint clubs
ideas.text: Boyd set out six steps of social relation with examples. First is the auditor-spectator, as in theatre or watching sport. Second is individual taking part within a group activity, as in crafts or skating. Third is casual social contact, as in quoits, card and board games and tennis. Fourth is intensive interaction, as in athletic and social group games, country dancing and drama. Fifth is long-term association in an integrated club, and sixth is a federation of clubs.

ideas.name: Card and board games sit low on the scale of co-operation
ideas.text: In Boyd's scale, equipment games such as cards, board games and tennis give only casual social association. Activities in the third and fourth steps need co-operation only while the activity lasts, and young people can stay at the lower steps for years with little concern for others or for building the programme.

ideas.name: Games differ in what they exercise
ideas.text: The type of game situation shapes what a player uses, Boyd noted. Pitching horseshoes is mostly physical, chess is mostly mental, and square dancing is mostly social. In each, the whole person is to some degree active.

ideas.name: Start from what the players already do
ideas.text: At Manteno State Hospital, a leader working with severely withdrawn women reasoned that since they could walk they could move to music, and since they threw chairs about the ward they might throw and catch a volleyball. Many did not respond for months, and one held out nearly two years, but taking part rose from five or six out of fifty to between half and nearly all.

ideas.name: Stable groups help each other
ideas.text: At Manteno, the same patients stayed in the same group with the same workers. In an evening class, one couple could not follow a slightly complex dance figure, and the other couples in turn, without any word from the worker, took them through it.

ideas.name: Simple activities were chosen for a reason
ideas.text: For patients who functioned at a very low level, the Manteno workers kept the problems in the activities easy by choosing activities that are easy to carry out. Boyd said the method still differed from giving exercise or entertainment, since the players were solving problems inside a frame.

ideas.name: Competition in the wrong place keeps out those who need the group
ideas.text: Boyd held that competition on the gym floor between friendly groups is a legitimate part of the game, but that adding competition into other activities, usually by an agency, discourages and drives out the people who most need to take part.

ideas.name: The leader's impartiality sets the tone
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that a leader's partiality towards some members makes others unfriendly or jealous. Where the leader is impartial, the more capable members tend to set patterns that the less capable follow, with neither side aware of it.

ideas.name: A leader brings out a game without changing it
ideas.text: Boyd compared a play leader to an orchestra conductor, who gives a score a different reading without changing the composition. In the same way a play leader brings out values in a game without altering its structure.

ideas.name: A leader learns games by playing them
ideas.text: Boyd said a play leader needs a working knowledge of hundreds of games of many structures, learned by playing and not from a textbook. A leader picks a programme to challenge the players in relation to their developing abilities.

ideas.name: Some games need only one other player
ideas.text: Play that is a group activity stays thin without several players, Boyd noted, but in solitaire, checkers and other card and board games, one or another player is enough.

ideas.name: A slow game loses interest when the high point is far off
ideas.text: Boyd gave I Spy as an example of a game played at slow tempo, where nothing happens to hold attention and the climax is long delayed. The leader may change the game, or keep going and make finishing it something of a challenge, which she called jollying.

ideas.name: Players who do not try moves can find strategy by being beaten
ideas.text: Boyd considered a group of players who neither experiment nor plan their moves. Her answer was for the leader to join as an ordinary player, play strategically without explaining, and win. Players then tend to gain insight one by one, and she said teaching strategy takes away the satisfaction of trying one's own ability.

ideas.name: A simple game can start a player who is not ready
ideas.text: Players need not wait until they can enter a game's imaginative side in full, Boyd noted. They can start with simple games such as throwing at a mark, where success comes easily. Severely withdrawn patients who threw beanbags at random at a hole in a board, over several weeks, began to aim, to smile at a hit and to try again after a miss.

ideas.name: Start the game with little instruction
ideas.text: Boyd advised giving only a rough outline of a game and some demonstration, then starting at once and adding details as they matter. She held that stressing structure over play in the teaching of games kills the play for children and teacher.

ideas.name: Teaching Cat and Rat by gesture
ideas.text: Boyd's way into Cat and Rat with small children had the teacher place the Cat outside a circle and the Rat inside, tell the children to hold hands as a fence and keep the cat out, and then signal at once to let the rat out and shut the gate if the cat got in. She noted that the urge to watch a fleeing object brought even young children in quickly.

ideas.name: A few players can hold the rules for everyone
ideas.text: Only a bare outline of a game's frame of reference, Boyd said, needs to be carried in mind by enough players to maintain the structure. She held that a game keeps running, because at least some of the group take on keeping its structure, pattern and rules.

ideas.name: Complicated card and board games can be taught in stages
ideas.text: Boyd said many games can be taught only stage by stage, including some card and board games as well as active ones. Once players grasp the pattern, the leader gives rules, penalties and scoring when a need arises.

ideas.name: A fast game with changing roles gathers a scattered group
ideas.text: To draw unruly children into play, Boyd advised starting a popular game with no fuss about those who hold back. In her example a leader played catch with one girl, another joined, and a dodgeball game with no sides chosen began with nearly all taking part. The game ran with quick tempo, quick change of roles and no stops, and the two role players in the centre were the focus of interest.

ideas.name: A game has to match what the group can do
ideas.text: Boyd wrote that a group activity needing co-operation depends on a right estimate of what the group has in common. If a leader guesses wrong, a group may play politely, stay withdrawn if the game is beyond them, drift away or break up.

ideas.name: Choosing games by the behaviour they call for
ideas.text: Boyd advised matching the behaviour that is easily evoked at a given age, then choosing traditional games that use it and fit the group's maturity, the place and the occasion. She added that the choice gives players as large a variety of games as is consistent with their value to the group.

ideas.name: Roles can carry a timid player
ideas.text: Boyd held that a leader who plays within a game can assign roles at the right moment and encourage daring or concentration. A timid child caught up in concerted action may act with confidence, and repeated across games this can build a pattern of courage.

ideas.name: Real play depends on imagination being kept up
ideas.text: Boyd said players who cannot set up and keep imagination going are not playing, even if they follow the pattern of the game. If a player drops out in the middle of a swift game, a blunder or a missed chance can follow, as an actor out of character forgets lines.

ideas.name: Prizes grew in value and so did the rivalry
ideas.text: Boyd described a club that added prizes to its meetings to liven them, against its leader's advice. As the prizes rose in value, rivalry rose with them and criticism of the members who bought the prizes began. The social events turned bitter enough to threaten the club.

ideas.name: A game is a fragile kind of system
ideas.text: Burgun says games sit in a narrow strip between puzzles and contests on one side and noise on the other. One rule can break the ambiguity: Tetris lost its tension when later versions added a hold box, five next pieces and a 7-bag that gave pieces in a fixed rotation.

ideas.name: Games sit above puzzles and contests
ideas.text: Burgun maps interactive systems in layers: a puzzle adds a problem, a contest adds competition, and a game adds ambiguous decisions. A jigsaw is a puzzle, a race to finish it is a contest, and chess is a game.

ideas.name: A solved game stops being a game
ideas.text: When players know the right move in every position, no ambiguity is left. Tic-tac-toe is a game for children and a solved puzzle for adults, so whether something is a game depends on who plays it.

ideas.name: Decisions in a game cannot be proved right
ideas.text: Even a winner cannot be sure their choices were the correct ones. So playing is closer to painting than to calculation. Players follow guidelines they can break when a rare chance appears, as when a quick Scout hops over a Heavy in Team Fortress 2.

ideas.name: Theme is not the game
ideas.text: Burgun strips Final Fantasy to numbers and flags to show that a sad death comes from the story, which could sit on a lunchbox as easily. He says the theme is there to support the mechanisms, since the mechanisms are what the game is.

ideas.name: A player can be their own opponent
ideas.text: In Tetris the random generator never wins; the opponent is the player who holds the top score. Score games are multiplayer games played at different times, so one person can play against their old self.

ideas.name: A system with no goal cannot be hard
ideas.text: Minecraft has dangerous monsters, but nobody said survival is the aim, and surviving can never be finished. Without an achievable goal there is no contest, and so no difficulty. Players who add their own goal become the game designer.

ideas.name: Enjoyment is a result, not a part
ideas.text: Burgun says you cannot add enjoyment to a game like an ingredient. It comes from the game working, so he asks designers to talk about interesting decisions and balance, which can be checked, and to describe Puerto Rico by its layered turns and varied strategies.

ideas.name: Games can happen without a designer
ideas.text: A job with goals, rivals and hard choices works as a game, and so does a street fight. These natural games are messy because outsiders can interrupt, which is why designed games are cut off from the outside and kept small.

ideas.name: Games teach how to learn
ideas.text: Burgun says the main value of a game is that it trains the player to make tactics, doubt their own thinking and commit to a plan. The pleasure comes when people feel they have improved at something.

ideas.name: A story is a line, a game is a web
ideas.text: A story has one order of events, but a game offers choices that keep changing as play goes on. A prewritten story is tied to a fixed order, so games that carry one usually use cutscenes, force the player down a corridor, or let play outrank the story.

ideas.name: Ask first whether you need a game
ideas.text: Before designing, Burgun suggests asking if your aim is a story, a character, or a place or object. If so, prose, film or painting may do the job, since a game's rules and rivals do not show a father's love or a magic sword.

ideas.name: Start from one core mechanism
ideas.text: Burgun says a design begins with one simple action and everything else supports it. Parts that do not serve the core can be cut. Cranium shows the problem: its dice-and-move rule has little to do with trivia.

ideas.name: Fewer rules, same depth
ideas.text: Sound design in this book is minimal: only as many rules as it takes to say what matters. Go has about five rules and a possibility space of 2 x 10 to the power 170, while chess has more rules and fewer games.

ideas.name: Rule count and play depth are different things
ideas.text: Chess has more inherent complexity than Go, but Go has far more emergent complexity. What counts is how many moves are meaningful, not how many exist, so a rule set can be short and still deep.

ideas.name: Large amounts of content can hide a thin game
ideas.text: When a game has 100 items or 250 unit types, players chase synergies and stop looking at the core. Magic: The Gathering would wear thin quickly without thousands of cards. Burgun also says the designer cannot see the flaws in such a pile.

ideas.name: Games that need all the space a computer gives
ideas.text: Burgun says people use new technology without restraint at first. Board games, limited by their parts, tend to be more sensible, so he sends digital designers to them for ideas.

ideas.name: Put the design in a web, not a list
ideas.text: Because games are nonlinear, a design document written as a line keeps using terms it has not yet explained. Burgun uses a wiki, or sticky notes on a wall, so that pages can link to each other and the links show.

ideas.name: The designer is wrong often
ideas.text: By the time a game is done, Burgun says no design part is left that the designer had not got wrong at some point. Long planning and prototypes cut the waste, but cutting a spell a programmer spent hours on will still annoy the team.

ideas.name: Input size shapes what the game tests
ideas.text: A chess move is a small input, so the game tests thought. In a real-time strategy game the input is almost unlimited, so speed of hand and managing the interface decide results, and a right plan can lose to faster clicking.

ideas.name: Restrictions are what design is
ideas.text: Burgun says imposing limits on players is not a fault; it is the task. He questions whether looking up and down in Quake added much, since most play happens on one axis, and says input is as open to cutting as features are.

ideas.name: Skill at execution is not a decision
ideas.text: Failing to hit a note in Guitar Hero is no more a decision than tripping over a rug. If one option is clearly ahead, the question was settled before play. Execution tends to pull a game toward a contest, as bowling shows when a rival always strikes.

ideas.name: Harder inputs do not balance a powerful move
ideas.text: Fighting games make a powerful move hard to type in, but players master it in time and the balance breaks. New players are also kept out. Burgun says to balance by cost or delay instead.

ideas.name: Single-player games need randomness
ideas.text: Without it, a game with execution becomes a contest (Guitar Hero) and one without becomes a memory puzzle (Castlevania). Another human mind creates uncertainty in multiplayer games, but alone the player needs random information to keep ambiguity.

ideas.name: Use no more randomness than you need
ideas.text: In a multiplayer game other people supply most of the variety, so extra dice add little. In Catan one player can have their number rolled ten times in a row, and Burgun reports the remark that someone could roll the dice for you and tell you how it went.

ideas.name: Randomness cuts the link between choice and result
ideas.text: When luck drives the outcome, players get mixed signals about whether they played well. A loss may not feel like a real loss. Candy Land has no decisions at all, so Burgun counts it as a luck contest.

ideas.name: Randomness as a way to level skill
ideas.text: Mario Kart 64 gives powerful random items so that weaker players keep up. This lowers the weight of skill and of decisions, which are the features that make a game a game.

ideas.name: Balance is a matter of cost
ideas.text: A move of 50 damage and a move of 10 damage can be balanced if the larger one is slow or costly. A StarCraft Battlecruiser costs more minerals and tech-tree time than a Wraith, and still loses to a crowd of Wraiths in the air.

ideas.name: Balance by starting small and testing
ideas.text: Begin with the least content that carries the play, add only as needed, leave time for testing after the game seems complete, and change only a little at a time. Beta reports are not all trustworthy, since people often mistake their own lack of skill for imbalance.

ideas.name: Do not patch balance with automatic fixes
ideas.text: Burgun lists dynamic difficulty, scaling of enemies to the player and rubberbanding as bandages. They reward weaker play and punish skill, and he says the game then feels lifeless.

ideas.name: Theme helps when a game gets complicated
ideas.text: Go needs no theme, but Zelda's bombs and arrows would be hard to remember as abstract items X and Y. A theme works as a memory aid for verbs. When a player knows the game well it can be removed, as Street Fighter showed when its pictures failed and plain boxes appeared.

ideas.name: Theme can also make a game easier to sell
ideas.text: Burgun admits that abstract games are hard to sell, and a theme makes a game seem welcoming. The task is to add one without hurting the play.

ideas.name: Hex grids treat all neighbours the same
ideas.text: On a square grid a diagonal step goes further than a side step, so designers add costs as a patch. Hexes make every tile equal in distance from its neighbours, which is why war games use them; the cost is that art and four-way controls fit them less easily.

ideas.name: Information type changes solvability
ideas.text: Chess shows everything and can be solved in principle. A game with hidden information has no exact solution but an optimal strategy, such as playing at random in rock-paper-scissors. Adding a mini-map to a scrolling game can silently return it to open information.

ideas.name: Games lean on human limits
ideas.text: Go may be as easy to an alien mind as tic-tac-toe is to an adult. A game has to sit just beyond human mastery, and a game that fits a smarter mind would look like noise to us.

ideas.name: Each pair in an asymmetric game is a new game to balance
ideas.text: Three characters make six matchups including mirrors, ten make 55 and thirty make 465. Burgun says this growth is why fighting games drift out of balance, and he asks designers to keep the number of sides low, under six.

ideas.name: Test an asymmetric game as symmetric first
ideas.text: Burgun asks for a long period of play with one character, since a game that is dull as a mirror match has a thin core. Add differences late, one at a time, and never fix the number of characters in advance.

ideas.name: Too many options become false choices
ideas.text: Street Fighter characters have dozens of moves but only a few real choices such as attack high, attack low, block, throw, jump or shoot. Ten ways to attack high mean that some are simply less useful versions of others.

ideas.name: Do not waste the players' time
ideas.text: Waiting for loading screens, long walks down halls and repeated chores take time and give nothing back. Burgun says a town used only for buying items could be a menu, and board games are kinder to time because parts limit such padding.

ideas.name: Question the parts every game of the type has
ideas.text: Burgun drops equipment, levels and rising stats in his own game Auro, since a hero that grows stronger makes the designer's job harder and the game easier. Characters keep fixed numbers and learn new abilities, such as a counter that reflects damage.

ideas.name: Look outside your own kind of game
ideas.text: Burgun says digital designers copy each other because they know only digital games. He sends them to designer board games, abstracts, sports, children's games, card games and pen-and-paper play, since new ideas come from recombining what you have seen.

ideas.name: Rule changes have side effects
ideas.text: In American football, hard-shell helmets may have made players move faster and more recklessly. Any new rule can have effects the designer did not plan, so sports histories are full of lessons.

ideas.name: Games are machines for behaviour
ideas.text: Because psychology studies behaviour, it informs design. Burgun contrasts games that train the mind with compulsion games like Farmville, which reward every click and leave players empty because the game only uses them.

ideas.name: A pay-off table can help balancing
ideas.text: List the options for two players in a grid and give each outcome a value. His example, "attack or dodge", shows that the dodger who then counterattacks gains most, and values can be tuned to rank the moves.

ideas.name: A hard-to-organise screen points to a design problem
ideas.text: If the pieces of information cannot be arranged clearly, there may be too many or they may not relate closely. Burgun says studying icons and layout shows such design faults, and a clear icon such as a bomb carries a lot of rules.

ideas.name: Teach the rules through the play
ideas.text: Manuals are voluntary and deep but hard to take in; forced tutorials annoy. Burgun's example is the first level of Super Mario Brothers, which teaches by placing things in sequence, and he asks games to teach what they can in this hands-on way.

ideas.name: Games evolve by reinvention
ideas.text: Almost every old game has an earlier game behind it. Pachisi led to Ludo and then Sorry!, and a game found with no predecessor would only mean the predecessor is not yet found.

ideas.name: Pure luck games are contests
ideas.text: Nyout and the Royal Game of Ur are dice races with almost no choices. Burgun counts them as contests, though a wager adds one outside decision about how much to bet.

ideas.name: Gambling thrives without decisions
ideas.text: Roulette and lotteries offer few or no choices and still attract adults, partly through the illusion of control. Burgun adds that poker is a game and that any game can become gambling if money rides on it.

ideas.name: Old games were shaped by many hands
ideas.text: Few ancient games had a single designer. They changed over centuries, so one can watch generations looking for balance, which Burgun calls inspiring for a designer.

ideas.name: Dual goals in hurling add a decision
ideas.text: Hurling has a low goal worth three points and a higher set of uprights worth one but easier to hit. This gives a player a real choice between safe and ambitious scoring.

ideas.name: A playing card deck carries history, not only design
ideas.text: Aces are said to rank high because playing them so was a small act of rebellion by poorer people in the French Revolution. Cultural and economic reasons shaped the deck as well as game design.

ideas.name: War games started as research
ideas.text: A Prussian general used small pieces, a map and dice to study battles, and H. G. Wells's Little Wars (1913) was the first made mainly for enjoyment. Burgun says war is itself a game, since it is a contest of ambiguous decisions, so a war game is both a simulation and a game.

ideas.name: Computers allow new decisions
ideas.text: Spacewar! had two ships, a planet with gravity and a warp that might blow you up. Burgun says it forced players to make choices that no earlier game had asked for, which he calls the promise of digital games.

ideas.name: New features are not new games
