ideas.text: Burgun says Doom, Quake and Call of Duty are variants of the dodging-and-shooting game of 1961. Judged by the decisions a player makes, there may be only a dozen real games with thousands of variations.

ideas.name: More technology does not make a more interesting game
ideas.text: Burgun says Super Smash Brothers could have been made on the earlier NES and that later hardware mostly added colour and sound. He asks designers for ideas, not new machines.

ideas.name: Fantasy simulation is a different aim
ideas.text: Burgun separates a game from a fantasy simulator. A fantasy does not need to be balanced or have ambiguous decisions, so Final Fantasy's repetitive grinding was excused as simulating a world.

ideas.name: Some people feel ashamed of games
ideas.text: Burgun calls this game shame. It explains why games imitate film, chase graphics and talk of immersion, and why a Madden football game copies television football instead of being a game.

ideas.name: A game with no random content turns into a puzzle
ideas.text: The second time through Castlevania or Mega Man, players have memorised parts. Burgun compares it to giving children the same maths test ten times: after a few tries they recall answers and no longer do sums.

ideas.name: More content is not more design
ideas.text: Game boxes brag of 200 spells or 70 guns, and Burgun says this craves bulk when the question is how few mechanisms can carry the idea. Heavy content makes choices false and balance impossible.

ideas.name: Metagames lower the weight of the main game
ideas.text: Extra systems such as unlockables multiply the interactions, make dominant strategies likelier and blur differences between elements. In Team Fortress 2, tying weapons to achievements made players farm achievements instead of playing normally.

ideas.name: Make the screen small enough to need no scrolling
ideas.text: Burgun asks of real-time strategy games why the map has to be so big. A mini-map ends up being the real game, so he suggests tiny units on one screen or tying scrolling to play, since managing a camera has no link to the decisions.

ideas.name: Animations that make players wait have no meaning in turns
ideas.text: In real time, a move's animation is part of its balance. In a turn-based game it only makes the player sit. Burgun's sum is that a one-second animation on every other command wastes twenty minutes in an hour.

ideas.name: Fewer, more meaningful units
ideas.text: Advance Wars has about ten unit types and five or six terrains, and every unit has its own role. Burgun prefers this to Heroes of Might and Magic, with seven resources and stacks of 117 units, whose strength is hard to read.

ideas.name: Leveling up makes a game easier
ideas.text: As characters grow stronger the game gets easier, so designers raise difficulty to match, and every player levels at a different rate. Burgun says balance then becomes close to impossible and the player is left to guess how long to grind.

ideas.name: A discrete map in a continuous costume
ideas.text: The overmap of a Final Fantasy game is really a list of places and a place to grind. Burgun writes it as a menu to show that the walking between them is a chore.

ideas.name: Players differ in skill, and fixes cost something
ideas.text: Items with heavy randomness and rubberbanding hide skill gaps in racers, but they take away the reward for skill. Burgun says handicaps are a plain, honest tool that Go has used for thousands of years.

ideas.name: Make short tracks and routes with trade-offs
ideas.text: A shortcut that is always the quickest is no real choice. Burgun suggests routes where one is longer but gives an item and one is short but harms your vehicle, and small tracks so racers meet more often.

ideas.name: Health bars can be tied to the core mechanism
ideas.text: In Super Smash Brothers a player gains damage instead of losing health, and more damage means being knocked further. Health then feeds the central idea of position.

ideas.name: Protect the jump
ideas.text: A platformer jump works through tension and release. Mid-air steering, a cape or a hover pack shrinks the tension, so Burgun says a designer who boasts of giving the player complete control misreads how limits create the game.

ideas.name: Skill is shown by choosing, not by typing
ideas.text: A move that needs a half circle twice and then three punches tests memory of inputs. Burgun says the pride lies in making wise choices during play.

ideas.name: Third-person views cost information
ideas.text: A big model of the character's back blocks the enemy that may stand behind it. Burgun says to leave large solid things out of the player's view unless hiding information is a mechanism.

ideas.name: Team scores can pull against team play
ideas.text: In Team Fortress 2 players see personal scores, which compete with the team goal. Burgun says soccer players seeing live personal rankings would play for their numbers. Distinct roles with large gaps make teammates need each other.

ideas.name: 3D adds work unrelated to the game
ideas.text: Without depth perception, a 3D platformer player has to judge distance and angles that have nothing to do with platforming. Burgun asks designers to keep gameplay 2D when the screen and controller are 2D.

ideas.name: Monopoly was changed into a luck game
ideas.text: Elizabeth Magie's Landlord's Game made a point about land. When Parker Brothers bought it, the auction on each landing was removed, taking out its core mechanism. What remains has almost no choices and long play with early elimination.

ideas.name: New games ask more of the learner
ideas.text: A new, interesting board game means reading the rules, trying a few turns and reading again. Burgun says rule books are non-linear and often written badly, so the more original a game, the more patience it needs up front.

ideas.name: Area games stall when each side trades one space for one
ideas.text: Chaos in the Old World uses dice and a six gives an explosion. Burgun calls that the easy way out and suggests feints, where you hint at taking tile A and take B, with costs for switching so it does not become rock-paper-scissors.

ideas.name: Long-term plans need predictable futures
ideas.text: Heavy randomness makes planning beyond the next turn impossible. Burgun cites Robo Rally, where pieces move at fixed rates that players alter only a little, and says fewer random outcomes (three tile types, not ten) also helps.

ideas.name: A bid needs many sides to be interesting
ideas.text: If we bid for one victory point that both want equally, the question has no dimension. With extra items, such as a matching half of a set worth five points, each person's wishes differ and bids tell the others something.

ideas.name: Cap bidding to avoid runaway prices
ideas.text: Two players who both badly want an item can push its price to a level that empties the money supply and unbalances the game. Burgun suggests only three or four bid levels, with a rule change when someone goes higher.

ideas.name: Simulation comes second to play
ideas.text: Real conflicts are not balanced, and real vehicles break down. Burgun says to begin with an abstract design and fit a theme on afterwards. Even in war games, area-control games and abstracts offer ways to express movement and combat.

ideas.name: Cooperative games can take mistakes away
ideas.text: When one expert tells everyone what to do, the others lose the chance to explore and err. Burgun says two repairs exist, an all-win-or-all-lose rule or a traitor, though both mean the game is no longer purely cooperative.

ideas.name: Hidden information needs a reason
ideas.text: Pandemic bans showing your hand, but players need to know it, so they keep asking. Burgun says that is a silly rule, and a possible traitor gives a real in-game reason to keep cards secret.

ideas.name: Roles that change during play
ideas.text: In role-selection games the roles are fixed. Burgun suggests letting a role's strength change over the game, so that making a role stronger helps everyone and opens new decisions.

ideas.name: Be wary of convenient numbers
ideas.text: A card game that happens to need exactly 52 cards in four suits may be copying the standard deck. Burgun says to try a half deck, two decks, no face cards, or 17 new cards, in the way you would doubt a unit with exactly 1,000 horsepower.

ideas.name: Abstract games are hard to make and tend toward solution
ideas.text: It is harder to make something simple and interesting. Arimaa was made because computers had partly solved chess. Burgun says random elements and layers of complexity push a solution further away but do not remove it.

ideas.name: A theme is for clarity
ideas.text: Burgun says an abstract game can be as beautiful as a themed one. Add a theme when the game is so complex that actions and pieces need names, not for looks, and not so heavily that it seems silly.

ideas.name: Simple games can leave little room for style
ideas.text: A very small rule set gives fewer odd, lateral moves that confuse rivals or show a player's manner. More complexity gives more space for moves that are not obviously the top choice but also not mistakes.

ideas.name: Party games need rules that stay out of the way
ideas.text: Burgun says a party game can still be a real game if its mechanisms are so light that they do not interrupt the talk. He credits Apples to Apples and Saboteur for using the talk itself.

ideas.name: Collectible cards break balance
ideas.text: Players arrive with different cards, rares are stronger, packs are random and the card pool never stops growing. Burgun says no amount of careful rules cancels these factors.

ideas.name: Deck-building has a built-in balancing act
ideas.text: Victory cards score points but do nothing else, so buying them dilutes your deck. This creates a steady choice between building power and cashing in, though Burgun says luck and add-on content weigh heavily.

ideas.name: A traitor stops one player from taking over
ideas.text: If anyone might be a traitor, a skilled player cannot safely lead everyone. Burgun notes the traitor element tends to swamp other mechanisms and wants a design where the traitor role keeps shifting.

ideas.name: Any activity becomes a game with goals and rules
ideas.text: You can turn Minecraft, Legos or a flight simulator into a game by adding your own goals. Burgun says this adding is the act of game design, so anyone who invents a house rule has designed.

ideas.name: Six qualities of play
ideas.text: Caillois says play is free, separate, uncertain, unproductive, ruled and make-believe. Chess has rules but no make-believe; a child's game of pirates has make-believe but no rules.

ideas.name: A game is ruled or make-believe
ideas.text: Caillois says rules and pretending do the same job: both cut the game off from real life. Playing at pirates needs no rule book, and playing chess needs no pretending.

ideas.name: Play is free to leave
ideas.text: A game a person is forced to play stops being play and becomes a chore. A player can always say "I am not playing any more" at any time.

ideas.name: Play makes nothing
ideas.text: Gambling moves money between players but produces no goods, and at the end the players can begin again from the same point. Caillois calls play a waste of time, energy and skill.

ideas.name: Professionals do not play
ideas.text: Boxers, jockeys and actors who work for a prize or salary are workers. When they play, Caillois says, it is at some other game.

ideas.name: Games happen inside a frontier
ideas.text: A game has its own space and time: a hopscotch grid, a board, a stadium, and a starting and ending signal. Sending the ball out of bounds can bring a penalty.

ideas.name: Rules have no outside reason
ideas.text: Caillois says the rules of a game are absolute inside the game and meaningless outside it. Nothing explains why a bishop moves diagonally except that the rules say so.

ideas.name: Uncertainty lasts to the end
ideas.text: If the result is known in advance, play stops. Card players lay down their hands once the outcome is settled, and a player who wins every time without effort stops enjoying the game.

ideas.name: The player needs room to answer
ideas.text: A game asks for a fresh response after each move, free within the rules. Caillois calls this margin of the player's action a main source of pleasure.

ideas.name: Classifying by equipment mixes categories
ideas.text: Dividing games into card games, sports or parlour games compares unlike things: tool, skill, place. Marbles can be a skill game or, when guessing odd or even, a game of chance.

ideas.name: Four kinds of play
ideas.text: Caillois sorts games by what dominates: competition, chance, simulation or vertigo. Football, roulette, playing pirate and spinning around fall into the four.

ideas.name: Equal chances are made on purpose
ideas.text: In agon, designers build equal starting conditions so a win shows real superiority. Players draw lots for sides and swap positions, and a handicap fixes differences between players.

ideas.name: Exact equality cannot be reached
ideas.text: Moving first in chess, bidding last in bridge, or having the sun at your back all give small advantages. Games answer this by drawing lots and by taking turns at the favoured position.

ideas.name: Agon asks for training
ideas.text: Competitive play needs attention, practice and the wish to win, and the rules apply equally to all. Caillois says this makes the winner's superiority beyond dispute.

ideas.name: Animals have agon, not alea
ideas.text: Young bulls, horses and willow wrens fight within a marked space and do not injure each other. Caillois says only humans wait passively on a verdict they cannot influence.

ideas.name: Alea removes differences between players
ideas.text: In games of chance, skill and training count for nothing, so a beginner and an expert wait on equal terms. A lucky throw can win more than years of work.

ideas.name: Agon and alea are opposite attitudes
ideas.text: In agon the player relies only on himself; in alea he relies on everything except himself. Games such as bridge, dominoes and backgammon join the two by dealing chance hands that skill then plays.

ideas.name: Betting turns agon into alea
ideas.text: Because a fair contest has an uncertain result, outsiders can bet on horse races, football or cock fights. Stakes may change as the match goes on.

ideas.name: Games build cleaner worlds
ideas.text: In real life luck and merit are tangled together. Games, whether agon or alea, replace this with a situation where it is clear what comes from skill and what from chance.

ideas.name: Mimicry is not deception
ideas.text: A child playing train does not try to persuade anyone he is a locomotive. Only spies and fugitives disguise themselves to deceive, and they are not playing.

ideas.name: Spectators play mimicry
ideas.text: Fans who lean with a bowled ball or copy a runner's strain take part in the match by imitation. Caillois says identification with a champion works like a reader's with a novel's hero.

ideas.name: Mimicry has one rule
ideas.text: The only rule of make-believe is that the actor avoids giving the audience a reason to break the spell. The audience in turn agrees not to question the mask or the set.

ideas.name: Dizziness as a purpose
ideas.text: Some games aim only to unsettle the senses: spinning, swinging, sliding, fast descents. Caillois says children and adults freely choose this brief panic and the players often rush to repeat it.

ideas.name: Vertigo needed machines
ideas.text: Caillois says dizziness for adults needed powerful machines, so fairground rides arrived with the Industrial Revolution. People leave the rides pale and dizzy and walk straight to the ticket booth for another turn.

ideas.name: Rides keep the marks of play
ideas.text: A ride is still play because the rider chooses it, it has fixed limits, and it ends when the machine stops. Caillois says watching the riders from a balcony adds to the spectacle without changing this.

ideas.name: Animals play at falling and spinning
ideas.text: Dogs spin to catch their tails, chamois slide down glaciers in turn, gibbons fling themselves from bent branches, and birds drop and open their wings late. Caillois reads these as the animal form of ilinx.

ideas.name: Play begins as noise
ideas.text: Caillois says the first play is shaking, tearing, scribbling and uproar, which he calls paidia. A cat tangled in wool and an infant laughing at a rattle are early examples.

ideas.name: Children test themselves
ideas.text: Children soon bet each other who can stare at the sun, hop, or hold a painful posture longest. Caillois says these are the first small forms of agon, made before any rules are taught.

ideas.name: Rules arrive with equipment
ideas.text: The first named games, such as hide and seek, kite-flying and doll play, appear when conventions and tools appear. At that point the four kinds of play separate.

ideas.name: Ludus is fighting an obstacle
ideas.text: In ludus the player tests skill against a problem made for the purpose, such as a yo-yo, kite or ring puzzle. No rival is needed, though a rival easily gets added.

ideas.name: Ludus joins other kinds
ideas.text: Ludus mixes with agon in chess, with alea in patience and slot machines, and with mimicry in model building. Caillois says it does not mix with ilinx, because its job is to keep a calm mind.

ideas.name: Solitary puzzles turn into contests
ideas.text: A crossword or solitaire game is easily turned into a competition by newspaper prizes or a higher score. Caillois says ludus left alone tends to fade or become a private obsession.

ideas.name: Fashion crazes need rivalry
ideas.text: Yo-yos, diabolos, rebuses and charades rise and vanish together with the crowd playing them. Caillois explains this by the hidden competition inside ludus.

ideas.name: A hobby answers work
ideas.text: A factory worker repeating one movement may build a complete scale model of the machine at home. Caillois reads this as a worker getting back at dull work in a creative way.

ideas.name: Different cultures send paidia different ways
ideas.text: Caillois says Western cultures turned free energy into ludus, with invention and difficulty, while classical China turned it into wan, calm and idle thinking. The choice shows in the games a culture prefers.

ideas.name: Chinese words split play into kinds
ideas.text: The Chinese characters hsi, choua, teou and ton cover acting, skill, conflict, and chance and daring. Caillois says they match his four categories, which suggests the split is not only a Western habit.

ideas.name: Even solo games want an audience
ideas.text: Kite-flyers and top-spinners gather where others can see, and Eskimo cup-and-ball turns into a spoken duel with a crowd. Caillois says play lacks something when it is only a solitary exercise.

ideas.name: Each kind of play needs company
ideas.text: Agon needs rivals, gamblers prefer a crowd at the track to a phone bet, masks are worn for others, and swinging is livelier in a group. A game also holds only a small number of players before it needs an organisation.

ideas.name: Each kind of play has a public institution
ideas.text: Agon becomes sport, alea becomes casinos and lotteries, mimicry becomes theatre and puppet shows, and ilinx becomes the travelling show and the yearly festival.

ideas.name: Each attitude has a matching corruption
ideas.text: When the frame around a game is dropped, the attitude spills into daily life: agon into ruthless ambition, alea into superstition, mimicry into alienation, ilinx into drink and drugs. Pleasure turns into obsession.

ideas.name: Cheats stay inside the game
ideas.text: A cheat pretends to respect the rules and depends on others keeping them, so thrown out he leaves the game intact. Caillois contrasts this with the player who no longer accepts any referee.

ideas.name: Agon is spoiled where no referee is accepted
ideas.text: Players are taught to accept a referee's ruling even if it is wrong, and to take defeat calmly. Caillois says competition turns brutal where no such decision is recognised.

ideas.name: Superstition is chance outside its frame
ideas.text: A gambler who treats dice as a heartless machine plays alea well. One who reads omens, lucky numbers or horoscopes tries to bend chance, which Caillois calls its corruption.

ideas.name: Applause ends the pretence
ideas.text: The fall of a curtain, the end of a masked ball at dawn and the return of a costume to the shop mark where make-believe stops. Caillois says such sharp limits keep players from losing themselves in a role.

ideas.name: Seriousness is allowed, spill-over is not
ideas.text: A player may play very hard or risk a fortune, as long as the game stops at an agreed time and the player returns to ordinary duties. Caillois says the harm comes when the rules of the game keep applying outside it.

ideas.name: Drink replaces the ride
ideas.text: A ride's dizziness stops when the machine stops. Alcohol and drugs bring a similar loss of balance but change the body permanently, which Caillois says is the reverse of play.

ideas.name: Ilinx can turn into addiction
ideas.text: A fairground ride ends when the machine stops, while alcohol and drugs bring the same loss of balance but change the body permanently. Caillois gives the example of ants that feed on a beetle's intoxicating secretion and let it eat their own young.

ideas.name: Ludus and paidia are ways of playing
ideas.text: Caillois says ludus and paidia are not kinds of game but two manners of play. They pass into daily life as opposite tastes, such as noise over a symphony or scribbling over drawing in perspective.

ideas.name: Rules protect from the drives
ideas.text: Competition, chance, simulation and vertigo are powerful urges, and Caillois says they do harm when left free. Games let each urge be satisfied in a limited way, so that players learn to live beside them.

ideas.name: War used to resemble a game
ideas.text: Older war kept to frontiers, strongholds and set objectives, much like a tournament. Caillois says once those limits are dropped, war turns to mass destruction.

ideas.name: Two theories of games and culture
ideas.text: One view says games are leftovers of old rituals; the other, Huizinga's, says culture grows from play. Caillois answers that the spirit of play shapes culture, while particular games are what remains of earlier institutions.

ideas.name: Masks and toys began in ritual
ideas.text: The mask, the kite, the top and hopscotch all served sacred purposes before they became playthings. In Korea a kite carried the community's sins away, and in China it measured distance and carried a rope across a river.

ideas.name: Games from rites
ideas.text: An Egyptian tomb shows the dead playing a board game for their fate in the afterlife, and the Greek games were offerings to a god. Caillois uses these to show that game structures can serve religion before play.

ideas.name: Children play at what adults do seriously
ideas.text: Children play soldiers while armies still exist, play Mass while the church stands, and play with dolls of sacred figures. Caillois says the children's game and the adult activity run side by side.

ideas.name: A new weapon quickly becomes a toy
ideas.text: Children play with water pistols, toy tanks and toy bombers as soon as such things exist. Caillois says Monopoly does not come after capitalism but copies how it works.

ideas.name: A game differs from the activity it copies
ideas.text: A tournament is a game and a war is not; roulette is a game and playing the stock market is not. Caillois says the difference is that in a game nobody may influence the result, and nothing outside the lists is affected.

ideas.name: Games and daily life are opposed
ideas.text: Caillois says play stays closed off and has no lasting effect on institutions, while daily life is full of consequences. A player can say "I am not playing any more"; an adult cannot say that about work.

ideas.name: Games and laws share structure
ideas.text: Rules of law, rhetoric, perspective or liturgy resemble rules of play, yet one does not come from the other. They keep to different domains that cannot be swapped.

ideas.name: Inherited rank became a contest
ideas.text: Where a role was once set by birth, it is now won by merit, competition or examination. Caillois says this carries the principles of agon and alea out of the game and into society.

ideas.name: A list of shared urges
ideas.text: Play and social life share the same impulses: proving superiority, beating a record, hoping for luck, secrecy and disguise, fear, repetition and variation, solving puzzles, respecting and dodging rules, longing for ecstasy. Caillois says a culture honours some and pushes others into play.

ideas.name: Some games push against the culture
ideas.text: Greek stadium games supported the ideal of the city. National lotteries in modern states go against the ideal of earned reward, yet give a chance-based substitute for what work alone cannot promise.

ideas.name: Play absorbs adults fully
ideas.text: Caillois says an adult at play can spend as much energy, skill and attention as at a job. He links the cultural weight of games to this freedom and intensity, which play offers without lasting harm.

ideas.name: A sociology derived from games
ideas.text: Caillois proposes that the kinds of play a culture prefers could explain its path. A culture that favours rank and chance differs from one that favours masks and trance.

ideas.name: Six pairings of the four kinds
ideas.text: The four attitudes can pair in six ways: agon-alea, agon-mimicry, agon-ilinx, alea-mimicry, alea-ilinx, mimicry-ilinx. Caillois sorts the six into forbidden, contingent and fundamental.

ideas.name: A horse race holds three attitudes without mixing them
ideas.text: The jockeys compete, the crowd watches a show and the public bets. Caillois says these meet but do not blend, and betting does not change how the race is run.

ideas.name: Vertigo cancels competition
ideas.text: Dizziness or blind fury removes controlled effort, respect for rules and willingness to accept a referee. Caillois calls agon and ilinx a forbidden pairing.

ideas.name: Disguise cannot cheat chance
ideas.text: Nobody can trick a die or a wheel, and a person asking for luck does not want to appear as someone else. Caillois says alea plus mimicry would turn into magic, which tries to force fate.

ideas.name: Gamblers get dizzy
ideas.text: Winners and losers at a casino lose track of time and money and gamble beyond their means. Caillois says alea and ilinx can sit together because dizziness does not break the rule that the player has to accept the result.

ideas.name: Competition is a show
ideas.text: A match has scenes, applause and a crowd, so a champion and a film star become interchangeable. Mimicry adds to agon provided the athletes do not fool the crowd.

ideas.name: Agon and alea mirror each other
ideas.text: Both need exact fairness and careful measurement, but in agon the player relies on himself and in alea on everything except himself. Card games, dominoes and golf sit between, where the player does as much as he can in a situation he did not make.

ideas.name: Chance can stand for the world
ideas.text: In games that mix skill and chance, chance plays the part of nature, the weather or the gods resisting the player. Caillois calls such a game an ordered, limited image of life.

ideas.name: Mask and trance together
ideas.text: Playing another person can be both liberating and intoxicating, and the mask can pull a player into trance. Caillois says mimicry joined to ilinx leaves play behind and moves into the sacred.

ideas.name: In each pairing one side makes things, the other does not
ideas.text: Agon builds sport and mimicry builds theatre, while alea and ilinx rarely produce anything lasting. Caillois says agon trains faculties, while waiting on chance is passive.

ideas.name: The danger in negative games
ideas.text: In alea the risk is not being able to limit the stakes, and in ilinx it is not being able to stop the disorder. Caillois says people do not grow resistant to either; they are tempted until they give in.

ideas.name: Fairness grows in places that honour merit and chance
ideas.text: Caillois says societies built on merit joined with chance keep trying to raise the part played by justice and lower the part played by luck, and he calls this effort progress.

ideas.name: Games change slowly yet travel widely
ideas.text: Hopscotch, chess and dice show up across ages and continents, while dolls and kites were unknown in Europe until the eighteenth century. Caillois says games last because they matter little.

ideas.name: Games change with the culture
ideas.text: Hopscotch was a labyrinth for the soul, then a plan of a basilica. Chess came from India with four kings, and in medieval Europe one king became a queen, the strongest piece, under the cult of courtly love.

ideas.name: A game trains the habits it reflects
ideas.text: Games popular in a society show its tastes and, by being played, strengthen those tastes. Caillois suggests a society can be read from its games.

ideas.name: A game fits the culture that plays it
ideas.text: Caillois says golf rests on the player's honesty about his own score and truco rests on codified trickery. Each game trains the habit of mind its culture already prizes.

ideas.name: The same game can train different things
ideas.text: The Chinese count chess and checkers among the arts of a scholar, to train a taste for combinations and a calm mind. Caillois warns that such readings of games are unsure and need qualifying.

ideas.name: A game can let off what the culture bans
ideas.text: The Punch and Judy puppet beats his wife, kills the devil and hangs the hangman. Caillois says the audience does not approve; it enjoys a cheap release from rules that bind it in real life.

ideas.name: Four principles spread unevenly
ideas.text: Caillois asks whether agon, alea, mimicry and ilinx are used in different amounts in different societies, as baseball is played more in one country and chess in another. He says the play world is only an island, but the principles affect the whole society.

ideas.name: Two kinds of society
ideas.text: Caillois says some societies run on masks and possession (mimicry and ilinx) and others on offices, careers and rank (agon and alea). In the second kind, birth is a kind of chance and ability is judged by competition.

ideas.name: A festival turns the order upside down
ideas.text: In festivals masks make everyday order vanish, stored wealth is destroyed and rules are inverted. Caillois says this shared dizziness binds loosely joined groups together.

ideas.name: Mask-making is a secret
ideas.text: Masks are made in secret, and women and children are kept from learning they are made by the men. Caillois says the spirits seem real because the makers believe in them as well.

ideas.name: Trance follows a script
ideas.text: Voodoo and Bori possession look wild, yet each god has set costume, props and behaviour, so the person possessed acts as the audience expects. Caillois says the loss of control is drawn from a known pattern.

ideas.name: The audience helps the entranced
ideas.text: Shaman and possessed person are watched by helpers who throw a blanket, strike sparks as stars, and catch them if they fall. Caillois says this cooperation keeps the performance safe and correct.

ideas.name: Make-believe and belief mix
ideas.text: A shaman may hide the pebble he then draws from a patient, and the audience may know it and still accept it. Caillois sets aside which part is acting and stresses that mimicry and trance nearly always occur together.

ideas.name: Children's pretending and possession look alike
ideas.text: An observer likens a person possessed to a child who imagines he is an animal and strengthens it with a piece of clothing. Caillois says the difference is that possession leads to vertigo and does a job for society.

ideas.name: A mask becomes a tool of rule
ideas.text: Secret societies use masks to frighten non-members, punish crimes and keep order. Caillois says initiation teaches the novice the mask is a man in disguise, and then asks him to frighten others.

ideas.name: Civilization pushes mask and dizziness aside
ideas.text: Where a culture grows into order, mimicry and ilinx lose their central place and shrink into games, fiction and fairs. They give the same satisfactions but without madness.

ideas.name: A secret mask is a fragile system
ideas.text: The mask works only while the secret stays unknown, and knowing it spoils the terror. Caillois says this forces strict prohibitions, and when they relax the mask becomes costume and theatre.

ideas.name: The veiled prophet's mirrors
ideas.text: Hakim al-Mokanna wore a veil and said any who saw his face would die. According to one chronicle he showed his soldiers a blaze of sunlight reflected from a hundred women's mirrors, and when he was defeated the mask was called a trick.

ideas.name: Number brings order
ideas.text: Greek thinkers moved from numbers with shape and virtue to abstract numbers for calculation. Caillois says this world of measure has no place for ecstasy and disguise, and leaves room for games of rules and lots.

ideas.name: Stadium games teach loyalty
ideas.text: Greek games, Aztec pelota, Chinese archery and medieval tournaments judged how well a person shot or helped a fallen rival, not only who won. Caillois says limited rivalry teaches respect for the referee.

ideas.name: Exams are agon in the state
ideas.text: Officials chosen by competitive tests are placed on a ladder of ranks. Caillois says this carries the structure of a game into government, though birth often still decides the top posts.

ideas.name: Lots as equality
ideas.text: Greek democrats held that choosing magistrates by lot gave everyone the same chance, and that voting favoured the well-born. Caillois shows alea used as a fair procedure in a city.

ideas.name: Agon and alea answer one problem
ideas.text: Democracies and games both want everyone to start equal. One way is to draw lots so no ability counts; the other is to make everyone use their abilities to the full.

ideas.name: Birth works like a lottery
ideas.text: The Greeks saw talents and privileges as drawn at birth, and some Central American groups believe each person is born with a fixed luck. Caillois sets this against merit, which is won by competing.

ideas.name: Equal rules, unequal start
ideas.text: Wealth, schooling and family decide who starts well, so a rule of fair competition can be formally equal and still be unequal in effect. Caillois compares this to a race in which the runners do not begin on the same line.

ideas.name: Chance enters even a fair test
ideas.text: An examiner who happens to ask the one question a candidate studied helps that candidate, and the others lose. Caillois says an element of chance sits inside agon.

ideas.name: Card games blend both
ideas.text: A winning hand comes from the cards dealt plus the player's knowledge. Caillois uses this to show agon and alea as opposed yet allied.

ideas.name: Chance makes unequal people equal
ideas.text: People who doubt they can win by effort turn to lotteries, where the less able, the unskilled and the able stand on the same footing. Caillois reads this as a comfort for those with little hope in fair contests.

ideas.name: A lottery needs a huge top prize
ideas.text: Tickets are cheap and divisible and the top prize is very large, so the few winners are dazzling. Caillois gives the example of a French sweepstake whose first prize equalled about 250 years of a worker's wages.

ideas.name: Winners are made public
ideas.text: Official publicity follows the lottery winners and reports their plans, which invites readers to try again. Caillois says the large prizes are set to inspire hope of sudden wealth.

ideas.name: Continuous play grows turnover
ideas.text: A casino keeps its wheels turning without pause, and the small steady margin per bet brings a constant profit. A rare solemn draw brings fewer bets than continuous play.

ideas.name: Gambling towns
ideas.text: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo draw visitors who stay a few days of luxury and return to normal life. Caillois calls the stay a pair of brackets in their ordinary lives.

ideas.name: A quiz is a bet
ideas.text: A television quiz looks like a test of knowledge, but each round doubles the risk and shrinks the chance of winning. Caillois calls it a series of wagers dressed as a contest.

ideas.name: One can only be first
ideas.text: Everybody wants to win, but by definition only one person is first, so most people share in the win by following a star. Caillois calls this identification the form mimicry takes in a society of merit and chance.

ideas.name: Stars give hope that skill alone can win
ideas.text: A singer or boxer who rises on voice or muscle alone shows people without money that a way up exists. Caillois adds that such gifts fade with age, so success has to come fast.

ideas.name: Fans copy the idol
ideas.text: Admirers copy a star's haircut, clothes and diet, and in extreme cases mourn to the point of suicide. Caillois says this is mimicry spread thin through the press and cinema.

ideas.name: Kings are stars that cannot leave
ideas.text: A hereditary ruler wins by birth alone, with no effort. Public stories stress that the monarch cannot buy a newspaper or choose whom to love, which makes the position look less enviable.

ideas.name: Two kinds of society, two kinds of order
ideas.text: One kind relies on mask, trance and sacred luck. The other relies on regulated rivalry and fair chance, and writes law. Caillois says the second type begins with law, as in the Roman saying that where there is society there is law.

ideas.name: Mass frenzy returns
ideas.text: Crowd outbreaks such as dancing epidemics, the Nuremberg rallies or the Ghost Dance show mimicry and ilinx breaking out in a world that has pushed them aside. Caillois treats them as proof they were never removed.

ideas.name: Civilization trades trance for technique
ideas.text: Caillois says a culture moves from magical and total control of the world to slower technical control once it agrees to give up frenzy. He calls the trade a wager that few cultures won.

ideas.name: The two suppressed kinds need an outlet
ideas.text: Mimicry and ilinx cannot be removed, so societies give them limited places, such as carnivals and fairs. Caillois says the safest way to contain them is to keep them apart, since their strength lies in the pairing.

ideas.name: The mask has lost its power
ideas.text: In a society without ecstasy the mask no longer changes the wearer. A burglar's mask only hides identity and a gas mask only filters air.

ideas.name: A masked ball runs on conventions
ideas.text: Two dancers at a ball are bound by an unspoken promise of secrecy, and the flirtation follows set conventions with no consequences afterwards. Caillois calls the whole intrigue a game.

ideas.name: Carnival has rules for the onlooker
ideas.text: A passer-by has to play along and pretend to be afraid, or not afraid. If he gets angry he is disqualified, because he has refused the game.

ideas.name: Authorities ban masks first
ideas.text: When carnival frenzy in Rio de Janeiro threatened public services, authorities banned masks alone. Caillois says they knew masks were the core of the release.

ideas.name: Mask and uniform are opposites
ideas.text: A mask hides the face and stands for sudden, frightening power. A uniform shows the face and stands for steady, impartial rule. Caillois sees these as the sign of two kinds of society.

ideas.name: A fairground marks its frontier
ideas.text: Gates, flags and lights mark the edge of the fair, and its dates mark the time. Caillois says that space and season set it apart from routine, as a playing field does.

ideas.name: A fairground holds all four kinds of play
ideas.text: Shooting booths are agon, wheels and fortune-tellers are alea, clowns and dancers are mimicry, and the rides are ilinx. Visitors cannot wear disguises, so only the performers have mimicry.

ideas.name: Fear that turns into laughter
ideas.text: Rides, mirror mazes and haunted houses cause fright and nausea, which becomes relief and laughter as the person steps off. Caillois says the length and strength of the shock are fixed in advance.

ideas.name: Fair traditions stay the same
ideas.text: Everything at a fair follows set habits, down to the nougat, jelly apples and gingerbread pigs. Caillois says play of this kind is agreed disorder: falling and being caught.

ideas.name: Bumper cars undo road rules
ideas.text: Drivers in bumper cars chase, block and collide with each other until bored, all of which road rules ban. Caillois says many drivers wear a solemn face while doing it.

ideas.name: At a fair, dizziness replaces the mask
ideas.text: A fairground gives the same chance for adventure and flirtation as a masked ball, but with vertigo in place of disguise. Caillois adds that this takes the activity outside play.

ideas.name: The circus is a closed society
ideas.text: Circus families pass secrets from father to son, settle disputes inside, and train from infancy. Caillois says this is a way of life and not play, though two of its acts, the tightrope and clowning, belong to ilinx and mimicry.

ideas.name: A safety net changes the game
ideas.text: Circus performers refuse a net, since the risk of death is part of the unspoken agreement with the audience. When the state forces nets on them, Caillois says it falsifies the wager.

ideas.name: The tightrope depends on not thinking
ideas.text: The walker has to calculate distance and effort, yet at the decisive moment thinking paralyses him. Caillois says vertigo is controlled only by obeying it.

ideas.name: Four professions match the four kinds
ideas.text: Caillois pairs sport with agon, the gambler with alea, the theatre with mimicry and the tightrope with ilinx.

ideas.name: The clown copies badly on purpose
ideas.text: The Auguste tries to imitate the others and fails, ending soaked and beaten. Caillois sees an old figure in myth: the dunce who mocks the work of the gods.

ideas.name: A god of parody
ideas.text: The Navajo festival includes a god, Tonenili, who dances out of step and mocks the others, and the Zuni Koyemshis are clowns with fixed traits, such as a coward, a thirsty one and a sad one. Caillois says these masked parodies are known to be relatives in costume.

ideas.name: Satire guards against being carried away
ideas.text: Jesters, caricature and the clown give a comic counterpart to dignity. Caillois says this laughter prevents mimicry from sliding into trance, and could be how a society steps out of the mask-and-trance cycle.

ideas.name: Chance replaces work
ideas.text: Caillois says lottery players swap patient effort for the picture of sudden wealth, so for people who work hard and earn little, play mocks work.

ideas.name: Chance fills the gap in a society changing
ideas.text: A people who suddenly lose masks and possession, without having built competition, may take up chance, since waiting for a draw is easy and fits old magic. Caillois says gambling can then replace work.

ideas.name: Gabon dice
ideas.text: Dice in Cameroun and Gabon have two faces, one carved with a picture such as a woman tilling or a man attacked by a python. Caillois says the pictures act as a visual encyclopedia and as charms, and the game became so ruinous that it was banned.

ideas.name: The Cuban charade lottery
ideas.text: A banker draws one of thirty-six picture symbols, wraps it, sells tickets, and gives a riddle that may point or mislead. Winners get thirty times their bet, and symbols come with companions and valets, which players have to bet together.

ideas.name: Symbols replace numbers
ideas.text: A boy in Cuba adds 2, 9, 1, 4, 8, 3, 5 by saying "butterfly plus elephant plus cat" and gets "deer". Caillois says a lottery's picture code can spread into all of someone's thinking.

ideas.name: The banker can cheat
ideas.text: Because the banker sees all bets before the reveal, he can swap the drawn symbol for one nobody backed. Caillois notes that fraud is easy in such a game.

ideas.name: Gambling takes a share of a country's income
ideas.text: Havana bet over $100,000 a day in 1957, and Puerto Rico's planning board put betting at about half the island's budget. Caillois cites the report's warning that betting weakens savings and trust in work.

ideas.name: Jogo do Bicho began with a zoo
ideas.text: A baron in the 1880s hung a picture of an animal each week at a zoo gate and invited guesses. The game became a street lottery on the last digits of a draw, with each animal tied to four numbers.

ideas.name: Inverted bets teach arithmetic
ideas.text: In Jogo do Bicho a bettor can play a number and every reordering of its digits, so winnings are hard to work out. Caillois says people who can barely read do the sums quickly and accurately.

ideas.name: Dreams choose the bet
ideas.text: Players consult dream manuals: a flying cow means the eagle, a falling cat means the butterfly. A servant able to read omens may come to run the household.

ideas.name: An illegal game needs honest dealers
ideas.text: Bets in Jogo do Bicho pass on slips through three people, and winners collect an envelope by code name. Caillois says that where no complaint is possible, honesty is a necessity because the system would collapse without trust.

ideas.name: Chance competes with work
ideas.text: Caillois says gambling in Brazil keeps money circulating in a closed loop, instead of buying tools, clothes or food. Only the organisers' profits return to general use.

ideas.name: The state treats chance as a rival
ideas.text: Sport earns subsidy from the state, while gambling earns the state taxes. Caillois sets a symmetry: stadium against casino, Tour de France against national lottery.

ideas.name: Agon is useful, alea resists it
ideas.text: Caillois says society tries to reduce chance step by step, since chance is unearned favour and a mockery of work. Of the four kinds of play, only regulated competition carries over into daily life as a working principle.

ideas.name: Chance has few official jobs
ideas.text: Greek magistrates and modern juries are rare cases where lots decide something serious. Caillois says earning a whole living by gambling is seen as suspect almost everywhere.

ideas.name: A socialist state still holds a lottery
ideas.text: The Soviet savings bank let depositors give up interest and join a half-yearly draw, with twenty-five winners per thousand. Caillois says even a system built on merit makes room for chance.

ideas.name: The lottery consoles the loser
ideas.text: In fair competition the loser cannot blame unequal conditions and can only blame himself. Caillois says the lottery gives him a last hope of unearned fortune.

ideas.name: Scholars split the study of games
ideas.text: Child psychologists study leapfrog, sociologists study kites and mathematicians study dominoes, and few look at the same game. Caillois suggests the word "play" may hide quite different behaviours.

ideas.name: Play and culture in Schiller
ideas.text: Schiller wrote that man is fully human only when he plays, and guessed that a nation's taste could be read from its pastimes, from London race tracks to Madrid bullfights. Caillois takes this as an early sign of a sociology of games.

ideas.name: Games as a test, not a training
ideas.text: One writer says young animals play to practise for adult life. Chateau argues that play tests a child's ability to overcome obstacles, and Caillois adds that play is an end in itself.

ideas.name: Play is a test
ideas.text: Chateau says the child does not train for a task but gains a wider capacity to face difficulty. The further a game is from real life, the more it develops aptitude and the less it teaches facts.

ideas.name: Children bet early
ideas.text: Marbles are both a game and a currency, and children stake them on odd-or-even guesses. Caillois says a child notices chance early and has to fit it to his strict sense of fairness.

ideas.name: Rules and cure
ideas.text: Children who could not play or study, and who only pushed and jostled others, improved when an educator taught them to respect rules or to make their own. Caillois says the wish to keep an agreed rule is central.

ideas.name: Games with rules and games of illusion are kinds apart
ideas.text: Playing laundress or soldier is always improvised, while tag or chess depends on exact rules to name a winner. Caillois objects to grouping them just because both need team cooperation.

ideas.name: Team spirit is added on top
ideas.text: Cooperation within a team is an extra layer over an imitation game or a competitive one, and does not form a kind of its own. Caillois says it complicates structures that are otherwise independent.

ideas.name: Fear is the attraction in vertigo
ideas.text: In swinging or tobogganing, the player is not winning out over fear but enjoying a controlled panic and loss of balance. Caillois disagrees with those who read it as courage.

ideas.name: Researchers skip chance and dizziness
ideas.text: Educators and sociologists leave games of vertigo to doctors and games of chance to mathematicians. Caillois says this hides the cultural weight of both.

ideas.name: Probability began with a dice question
ideas.text: A French nobleman believed double six was likely in 24 throws of two dice, found it was not, and asked Pascal. The letters between Pascal and Fermat started the study of probability.

ideas.name: Puzzles led to topology
ideas.text: The bridges of Koenigsberg, ring puzzles and sliding puzzles pushed mathematicians toward new ideas. Caillois adds that combining probability with topology gave the theory of strategic games.

ideas.name: Mathematics assumes full information
ideas.text: Game theory assumes each player knows all the data and acts rationally. Caillois says real play includes error, whim, luck and even the wish to lose.

ideas.name: A pistol duel cannot be fully calculated
ideas.text: Distance, aim and nerves can be put in a formula, but a wasp sting, a tree root or faulty eyesight changes the answer. Caillois says analysis fits only the bare bones.

ideas.name: The sale that gets cheaper each day
ideas.text: A store cuts prices by 20, 30 then 50 per cent over three days while stock runs out. Caillois says the right day to buy depends on the buyer's character, so no formula settles it.

ideas.name: Solved means finished
ideas.text: When a game is mathematically solved, the player loses interest with the uncertainty. Card players stop when the deal is certain and chess players resign once the end is inevitable.

ideas.name: A solved game stops being a game
ideas.text: In "wolf", four white pieces have to win, so a player who knows this has nothing to play for. Caillois imagines a computer that plays chess with every line worked out, where the first move decides the winner, and says it would no longer be chess.

ideas.name: Veterans end a lost game early
ideas.text: A skilled Bolotoudou player stops when he sees he is beaten, before his defeat is plain to others. He also teaches the winning move to a weaker player, because the pleasure is testing one's powers.

ideas.name: Mathematics of a game is a game of its own
ideas.text: Analysis of games grows in its own direction with ever harder situations. Caillois says it ends either in certainty, which spoils the game, or in odds that only help judge risk.

ideas.name: Slot machines hold four kinds of play
ideas.text: Machines mix skill and chance, pretend manoeuvres of an atomic bomber, and a shaking donkey ride for children. Caillois reports 300,000 machines sold in the United States in 1956.

ideas.name: Pinball as contest with industry
ideas.text: A writer says the pinball player feels he beats the combined skill of industry for one coin, with scores written in many zeros. The player can also try to cheat the machine, and the tilt warning sets the limit on that.

ideas.name: Children's mini-lotteries at the sweet shop
ideas.text: Shops near schools sell a draw ticket for a fixed price, and the prize sweet is mixed in as late as possible. Caillois cites this to show that children meet chance early, even where teachers do not allow it.

ideas.name: Play changes with new needs
ideas.text: A writer on American football shows that a mistake in adapting a game to a new place or need can become a new rule or even a new game. Caillois cites this to show how games change.

ideas.name: Four traits, each on a scale
ideas.text: The tool rests on four traits of a board game: rules, randomness, representational backdrop (theme) and interaction. Each runs along a continuum, scored low, medium or high, with finer marks such as medium-low or 0 to 10 allowed.

ideas.name: Seven scores in use
ideas.text: To classify a game, the tool has the user score it on seven differentiators: rule complexity, player reliance, decisive randomness, productive randomness, theme synergy, competitive interaction and collaborative interaction.

ideas.name: Choice is what makes luck feel like agency
ideas.text: The paper follows Knizia in saying that games of luck differ mainly in how much control the player has over the result. Choosing which bet to place is one thing that gives the player agency even when luck decides the outcome.

ideas.name: Luck and skill are not opposites
ideas.text: Following Garfield, the paper treats randomness as separate from skill, so a game can need a lot of skill and also depend a lot on luck. Skill comes from several things, such as rule complexity, player reliance, or the need to draw or sing.

ideas.name: Decisive randomness is usually softened
ideas.text: In modern board games decisive randomness rarely appears without some softening. When it is not softened it tends to be a global effect that hits all players equally, such as which resources Catan produces each turn.

ideas.name: A theme can be tested by taking it away
ideas.text: A game has high theme synergy if the experience is altered a lot when the theme is removed, so that fighting becomes a matter of who rolls higher. Miniatures, maps and rules written to evoke the theme often point to high synergy.

ideas.name: Eurogames play down theme
ideas.text: Games with low theme synergy are more common among Eurogames, which tend to use symbolic wooden pieces such as pawns and meeples so as to bring forward the mechanical side.

ideas.name: Competition and collaboration are not opposites
ideas.text: The paper calls the split between competitive and collaborative games a false dichotomy, as luck and skill are. In Diplomacy a collaborating ally can turn into a rival, and in Tichu partners cooperate to beat the other team.

ideas.name: Interaction in a two-player conflict
ideas.text: A two-player war simulation such as the Commands and Colors series is high on competitive interaction and has none on collaborative, because the two players are always competing and each move is planned to help one side or hurt the other.

ideas.name: Trading adds cooperation
ideas.text: A classic Euro-style game has medium competitive interaction, with few chances for direct attack. The paper says that adding a trading mechanic immediately raises the level of cooperative interaction, since fair trades almost always benefit both sides.

ideas.name: Multiplayer solitaire divides opinion
ideas.text: Two reviewers cited by the paper call Agricola multiplayer solitaire, and one calls that a design failure. The paper notes Agricola has held a top-ten place on BoardGameGeek for over half a decade, and that five of the top ten have strong multiplayer solitaire elements.

ideas.name: Eurogame and Ameritrash profiles differ
ideas.text: Agricola scores mostly medium, with no high extremes, while Descent: Journeys in the Dark is high on more than half its traits, with very high interaction on both scales and more theme synergy. The paper reads Ameritrash games as skewed to the extremes, especially in theme and interaction.

ideas.name: Similar games can be told apart
ideas.text: The tool can also separate two games of the same type. The Castles of Burgundy has the same moderated profile as Agricola but less theme synergy and more randomness, which the paper traces to its dice and less representative pieces.

ideas.name: Mass-market games pair a simple move with a loose overlay
ideas.text: Monopoly and Clue combine a simple roll-and-move mechanic with a loosely player-reliant one, trading in Monopoly and deduction in Clue. The paper says Exploding Kittens has a very similar profile to Monopoly.

ideas.name: A profile can show intended and actual experience
ideas.text: The author suggests designers can use the profile to sketch the experience they want for a prototype and, afterwards, to compare it with how players plot their own experience, so differences show up.

ideas.name: Scores are the author's judgement
ideas.text: The profiles in the paper come from the author's own analysis and are described as subjective, a first step towards a typology specific to board games.

ideas.name: Old words mislead modern readers
ideas.text: The book argues that historians have read medieval words like "drama" and "theatre" in their modern sense and so turned many activities into theatre that were not. For example, the Dunmow Corpus Christi "play" turns out, from its receipts, to be a series of shooting, running and leaping contests.

ideas.name: Play is a part of game
ideas.text: The author follows a scholar's point that the word "play" is historically a subset of the word "game", not the other way round. Ludus and "play" both covered games and sports, so a record of "a play of Saint Andrew" can describe a parish sports day.

ideas.name: A "play" can be a musical event
ideas.text: Payments for "plays" at Durham, Shrewsbury and London may have been for musicians, not actors. If so, a "play book" could be a book of music and a "book bearer" someone who held it for the minstrels.

ideas.name: A script need not be acted to be drama
ideas.text: The author says a text can be a drama in form without being performed, and an enactment can exist without a script. Royal entries with pageants and speeches count as enacted scripts under his usage.

ideas.name: Medieval drama grew from the lay side
ideas.text: Clerics tried to suppress the ludi of ordinary people, and in some places that pressure led towards a vernacular drama run by civic bodies and guilds, whose members wanted entertainment that also showed care for their souls.

ideas.name: Ban on behaviour, not on a form
ideas.text: The author argues the church's long campaign against the theatrum was aimed at lewd gesture and rowdy games, not at scripted biblical or moral plays. Medieval readers knew the theatrum by its gestures and not by its genre.

ideas.name: One word, many activities
ideas.text: Records call a performer a histrio, minstrel, joculator, mimus or player without a fixed sense. In Selby Abbey's accounts, more than 60 percent of the noble companies whose size is given had three or fewer players, too few for the interludes scholars assumed they performed.

ideas.name: Cast size as evidence
ideas.text: No surviving interlude that David Bevington lists calls for fewer than four players. So a troupe of three is more likely to have given music and pageant than a dialogue play.

ideas.name: No ladder from one form to the next
ideas.text: Older histories ran liturgical drama, then biblical cycles, then moralities, then commercial theatre, each replacing the last. The author says this copied Darwinian thinking and that the forms overlapped and went on side by side.

ideas.name: Games used to raise money
ideas.text: Stage plays in churchyards were often king games or other rowdy entertainments run to raise money for the parish. In 1529 London gave one parish a licence for a stage play from summer to Michaelmas and promised none to any other parish in that time.

ideas.name: Moderation is judged by where attention goes
ideas.text: John of Salisbury allows music, sport and entertainment in moderation but cannot name the line. His test is whether the activity draws attention to itself for its own sake; if it does, it is excessive.

ideas.name: Watching suffering
ideas.text: Augustine was troubled that stage tragedy works by drawing intense feeling from the watcher while asking nothing of him. The watcher does nothing to relieve the pain he sees and takes pleasure in it.

ideas.name: Opposition can change a game, not end it
ideas.text: Clerical attempts to stop unholy festivities were often resisted and things went on as before. In some towns the laity swapped the festivities for biblical and moral dramas, which both sides could accept.

ideas.name: The same text is read differently over time
ideas.text: Plays were revised, and even unrevised texts meant different things once the Reformation began. The author warns against treating a play as fixed at the moment it was written.

ideas.name: Contest and chance as the root of games
ideas.text: Isidore of Seville orders his account of play from war to gymnastics, the circus, the theatre, the amphitheatre and games of chance. The author reads this as treating contest and fortune as the two themes running through all of it.

ideas.name: A ban kept a group out by rule
ideas.text: Early church canons barred actors from baptism unless they gave up the stage, let converts attend the games except on Sundays and festivals, and told clergy to leave a wedding feast before the entertainers came in. So watchers were tolerated and performers were shut out.

ideas.name: Where a word points is not fixed
ideas.text: Over time "theatrum" came to mean any place a show could be seen, even a marketplace. Bede's comment on Acts, quoting Isidore on the semicircular building, still treated a marketplace and a theatre as equivalent.

ideas.name: Costume against ordinary dress
ideas.text: The author notes that people in church re-enactments usually wore liturgical garments, not costumes. When Gerhoh complained of masks and men dressed as women, the sources suggest he meant disguise for festive licence, not a scripted part.

ideas.name: The same scene allowed or banned by its effect
ideas.text: A standard legal comment on Innocent III's decree said Nativity and Herod scenes were allowed because they lead people to devotion, while scenes that lead to lewdness on the feasts of Saint Stephen, Saint John and the Holy Innocents were forbidden. The test was what the scene did to its participants, not its subject.

ideas.name: Pretending to be what you represent
ideas.text: Gerhoh of Reichersberg charged that clergy who played Antichrist became what they played. He gave as proof an actor who played a dead man and was found dead, and an Antichrist who was buried and found dead seven days later.

ideas.name: Reform shifts shared meals
ideas.text: Gerhoh complained that his cathedral canons no longer ate or slept together except on rare feasts, when they staged Herod or similar shows. So the canons came together only for entertainment.

ideas.name: A rule of silence and its workaround
ideas.text: Gerald of Wales described monks who kept their rule of silence at table but used fingers, hands, arms and whistles to ask for special foods. He felt he was seated at a stage play.

ideas.name: Sound against sense
ideas.text: Aelred of Rievaulx objected that singers shook and rolled their eyes to ornate music while the crowd stood and gawked. He said the crowd had come to look, not to pray, and that sound was being enjoyed without attention to the words.

ideas.name: Watching against taking part
ideas.text: Aelred and Augustine both separate going to a place to take part in a rite from going to gaze. A hall of onlookers that jeers and snickers counts as a theatre to them, whatever the building is.

ideas.name: The world turned upside down as play
ideas.text: Bernard of Clairvaux compares monks to acrobats who stand on their hands, then separates the monks' game from the theatre's. His reason is that monks play at being mocked and humbled for the sake of those who watch, with David's dance before the ark as the model.

ideas.name: Restraint against imitation in ritual
ideas.text: Honorius of Autun compares the priest at mass to a stage tragedian but uses verbs of signifying, not copying: the silence of the prayer shows Christ as a lamb led without a voice. The author reads this as restrained and symbolic, with no acting.

ideas.name: Colleges swapped rowdy revels for set plays
ideas.text: Cambridge colleges staged Terence at Christmas partly to contain the unruly behaviour of young men, giving the season an educational purpose. Even so, accounts show glass replaced after performances, and in 1578-79 Trinity College hung nets before its windows.

ideas.name: A control can need controlling
ideas.text: Lords of Misrule began as a way to steer energy away from choirboys' antics in the choir. They grew unruly in turn, which led to the 1548 university ban on any Christmas lord of games.

ideas.name: A stage built for the show grows dearer
ideas.text: Oxford paid 18d. in 1538-39 for three days' work on a stage called a proscenium. By 1559-60 the cost had risen from 11s. 6d. to nearly 50s. with more labourers, and the structure was now called a theatrum.

ideas.name: Rules attach to who plays and where
ideas.text: Church rules gave clergy and laity different rules about play. Clerics were told not to watch mimes or play dice, and the rules for the laity began with place: wrestling and dance-songs were banned in the churchyard while matins, mass and vespers were sung.

ideas.name: A rule for one group is extended to another
ideas.text: Bishop Quinel in 1287 applied the language of Innocent's decree on clerics' ludi to lay wrestling and dancing in churchyards. Both were treated as marketplace amusements pushed into a sacred place.

ideas.name: The place decides what the game is
ideas.text: Bishop Lacy in 1451 wrote that laughter, mocking and rough sports belong in places made for viewing, such as the marketplace or theatrum, and not in sacred ground. The same activity was judged by where it took place.

ideas.name: A structure can be the problem
ideas.text: Bishop Grandisson complained in 1339 about a canopy built on posts in sacred ground because it blocked the procession around the church. The author reads this as an objection to the structure and the lay festivity under it, not to a stage play.

ideas.name: Replace by imitating, not duplicating
ideas.text: The author says the clergy did not want laity to become clerics. They wanted lay practice that copied clerical practice in part, such as a feast-day procession in place of a very large feast.

ideas.name: A single word held up a whole theory
ideas.text: A scholar's claim that "miracula" meant saint play rested at last on one record from Dunstable and on one treatise. The author's own count finds seventeen references to ludic miracula up to the early fifteenth century, none before 1400 that clearly names a religious drama.

ideas.name: Roles carry unequal comfort
ideas.text: In a sermon story, players in a summer game took parts as Christ, Peter, Andrew, tormentors and devils. The player who had been Christ said that next time he would be a tormentor or devil, because those parts ate and drank while the others suffered.

ideas.name: Audience rewards shape the play
ideas.text: In the summer game the audience gave food and drink to the tormentors, and whoever tormented Christ most was counted as the most skilful player. The author says this unscripted invention is part of why bishops disliked such games.

ideas.name: A script limits licence
ideas.text: The author contrasts boy bishop ceremonies, which stayed in check while the boys kept to the script, with unscripted summer games, which wandered into mockery of the Crucifixion. He compares feasts of fools that stray past their script in the same way.

ideas.name: An inappropriate person in a role
ideas.text: Some houses called boy bishop ceremonies miracula because a choirboy took the part of a bishop, like the false prophets in Jeremiah who copied true prophets. The practice was allowed, but a Lichfield statute told the subchanter to keep it fitting and honourable.

ideas.name: A word's older sense can survive
ideas.text: Miraculum in older Latin meant a wonder that caused horror or was monstrous, and was linked with lies and distorted masks. The author argues medieval clerics who used "miracula" for rowdy clerical revels were using that older sense, not the later meaning of a divine miracle.

ideas.name: Pretence plus startling effects
ideas.text: Commentators on Jeremiah described the false prophets as people who pretend to be one thing while being another, win a crowd with horror and loud gesture, and mock the truth. The author reads this as the root of the later view of theatre as show and hypocrisy.

ideas.name: Judge an activity by purpose and effect, not by class
ideas.text: In the Franciscan Dives and Pauper, Pauper allows shows, plays and dances done for devotion and honest mirth, without ribaldry, and without keeping people from church services. He does not condemn them because they belong to a class of things, and cites David dancing before the ark.

ideas.name: Two similar dances, different standing
ideas.text: The author contrasts the women of Boston, who danced holding candles as members of a guild, with the cursed dancers of Colbek and the Bury women who walked with a white bull to gain fertility. Each is a dance, and only some were thought fit for holy days.

ideas.name: Contests used the word "play"
ideas.text: A Norfolk witness c. 1410 to 1420 described "diverse plays" played on one ground: shooting, wrestling, running for a spear, and football for cakes, and later grouped them under steracles. Sports with prizes were then plays and shows.

ideas.name: Sign against the thing
ideas.text: The Tretise argues that a feigned miracle is only a sign. By making false tokens, people cheat themselves and show contempt for the real thing, as the tormentors who mocked Christ did. The author reads the objection as one to mockery, not to devout representation.

ideas.name: Play dissolves awe
ideas.text: The tract's theme is that a servant who jokes with his master loses his fear of offending him. In the same way, treating Christ's serious works as play removes the fear of God people are meant to have.

ideas.name: Imitation by the watchers
ideas.text: The Tretise says lay people join in such plays because they see the clergy taking part in jesting. A model set by one group is copied by another.

ideas.name: Watching can be forbidden as well as playing
ideas.text: The tract cites the canons forbidding priests to be a miracle player or to hear or see such playing. The Psalter's plea to turn the eyes from vanity is used to say a priest cannot give himself to the sight of interludes.

ideas.name: Play meaning fight
ideas.text: The Tretise cites Bible verses where people "play" (ludere), and critics have noted that in two of them the word means fighting. The soldiers of Abner and Joab rose to play before the court and were killed; Sarah saw Ishmael playing with Isaac and sent him away.

ideas.name: Counting records tests a claim
ideas.text: If the Tretise targets civic cycle plays, then by 1400 only York and Coventry were known to have cycles, and the only Antichrist play, at Chester, is dated about 1467. The author concludes that the "play of Antichrist" would more likely be a clerical masked game.

ideas.name: Three kinds of play
ideas.text: Following Aquinas, a scholar finds medieval writers sorting play into wicked or devilish play, recreational play that is judged case by case, and spiritual play such as David's dance. Aquinas ordered the question around Aristotle's mean, excess and defect.

ideas.name: Fixed words against loose words
ideas.text: One scholar holds that medieval words for play and players were too indeterminate to say what was meant. The author replies that some terms, such as ludi theatrales as glossed on Cum decorem, had a settled sense even if the activities under them varied.

ideas.name: Context changes how a text reads
ideas.text: Jonas Barish found the Tretise's Bible examples absurd, such as using Elisha's mockers to attack stage plays. The author says the examples make sense once the tract is read as against jeering and parody, not against drama.

ideas.name: Group practice, not individual taste
ideas.text: The author describes what groups allowed and what was common, and sets aside what was idiosyncratic. Group practice was shaped by status, time, place, wealth and the wish to show off.

ideas.name: Processions bind a group
ideas.text: Towns and parishes used processions to show devotion, unity or both, and to mark the group as a body. Groups fined members who shirked their part, and processions never fully replaced the parish ale and its games.

ideas.name: Wealth and size did not decide who staged plays
ideas.text: In 1377 only seven English towns had more than three thousand people, and most towns never produced drama even when they seemed large enough. Exeter, a rich cathedral city of about 2,340, shows little sign of drama. The author names money as the first hurdle and the wish to do it as a second.

ideas.name: Towns trade shows to raise money
ideas.text: New Romney paid the men of neighbouring towns to show their games or interludes and had its own play cried in return. Small places in thinly peopled areas used this cooperation to raise funds.

ideas.name: The sum of group sizes
ideas.text: Of thirty-five Selby Abbey entries that gave the number of players, fifteen were single performers, and about three-fourths of the groups were four or fewer. These fall below the "four men and a boy" Bevington gives for an acting troupe, so the author reads most as musicians.

ideas.name: A licence to play
ideas.text: In 1517 the Warden of the Cinque Ports told New Romney it could not play the Passion without the king's licence. In 1528-29 a commission against stage plays came, and the play stopped for years.

ideas.name: Building the playing ground
ideas.text: For the 1499-1500 Passion play, New Romney had the playing field mown, built a hell and a heaven, and paid for the tormentors' garments and heads. By 1560 the set had at least eight separate stages.

ideas.name: Rehearsal and the cost of the cast
ideas.text: For the 1560 play the town met in church to set who would lend money, labour or a stage. Beer was brought to the church for the players at a rehearsal on 31 March.

ideas.name: Run the same show again
ideas.text: The 1560 New Romney Passion was played on Whit Monday and on two Sundays, and a fourth performance seems to have followed. Takings fell from over £12 at the first to about £4 at the third, yet the author counts it a commercial success.

ideas.name: Spectacle makers and tiltyard assaults
ideas.text: Richard Gibson built court pageants for assaults on a fortress in 1512 and a timber Castle of Loyalty, with drawbridges, ditches and bulwarks, for the tiltyard in 1524-25. The author notes he was a maker of spectacle and not known for dramas.

ideas.name: Allegorical names for roles
ideas.text: The tormentors in the 1555 New Romney Passion play were given names that state a quality: Mischance, False-at-Need, Untrust, Faint-heart, Unhappe and Evil Grace.

ideas.name: The name does not give the content
ideas.text: A Shrewsbury "play" of Saint Katherine in 1525-26 included a lord of misrule, a jester's head and materials for explosions and smoke, with nothing about the saint. The author reads it as a revel.

ideas.name: An old mistake becomes authority
ideas.text: The author traces the idea that miracula meant saint plays to a 1798 paper that misread a text. Once its author had standing, later scholars debated which records fit that meaning instead of asking whether it was right.

ideas.name: Shared illusion against deceit
ideas.text: The author contrasts a devotional play, where the audience knows the illusion is an illusion and enjoys the spectacle, with a clerical Antichrist game meant to entertain with illusions as a trick.

ideas.name: Touch and movement in dance
ideas.text: Hugh of St. Cher, commenting on the line about never joining those who play, glosses "play" as dances. He quotes Jerome that temptation is hard to avoid when fingers touch or feet move.

ideas.name: Role reversal and ransom
ideas.text: On Hock Monday women tied up men and released them for payment, and on Hock Tuesday men did the same to women. Takings on the Monday were usually much larger than on the Tuesday.

ideas.name: Public reversal is the objection
ideas.text: A bishop in 1450 complained of Hock days in which women bound men and men women, "in full view of passers-by". The author thinks the worry was that this was done openly, as a threat to the order of ranks.

ideas.name: Theory against what the records show
ideas.text: Some scholars read carnival-like games as moments when rulers loosen control only to restore it. The author notes that these games were started by the local people and carried on against reforming bishops, so the theory does not match the case.

ideas.name: Substitute, do not only forbid
ideas.text: Bishop Grandisson promoted processions as a lay observance with the decorum of religion without copying liturgy. Lay people in turn took up clerical customs, such as the Easter sepulchre with its watching and lights.

ideas.name: A temporary equality
ideas.text: The author says parish ales set aside rank for a time and invited outsiders in. Contests and shared food and drink would dissolve or redirect tension, though he doubts the Wife of Bath gave up wanting to be first.

ideas.name: Reformers objected to the place
ideas.text: The author suspects reformers disliked parish games less for what they were than for happening in cemeteries and sacred ground. Drinking and dancing there could pollute the area and challenge clerical rank.

ideas.name: Costume in guild processions
ideas.text: The twelve members of the Guild of the Apostles at Louth dressed as apostles. At Beverley a youth dressed as Queen Helen walked with an old man with a cross and another with a spade, to represent the finding of the Cross.

ideas.name: "Play of Saint X" may name an owner, not a story
ideas.text: A record of a "ludus de sancto Thoma didimo" at Lincoln was an Easter liturgical piece. The 1505 "ludum sancti trinitatis" cannot be a play about a Saint Trinity, so it names a guild or church that gave the game.

ideas.name: A ludus is first of all a fund-raiser
ideas.text: The author concludes that a ludus or game was most likely a parish or civic entertainment to raise money. It might contain a scripted play, or only sports, contests, amusements and pageants.

ideas.name: Objects to be seen, not acted
ideas.text: Some ludi were shown, not acted. The Assumption at Lincoln appears to have been a clockwork device, and Canterbury's Becket pageant, carried by four knights, held an effigy and a mechanical angel.

ideas.name: Saint George in street and tableau
ideas.text: Saint George was mostly seen in tableaux, in processions, in the street fighting a dragon, or in folk plays with clowns and Turks. Only Lydd offers a possible enacted life over several years.

ideas.name: London compared with Rome
