ideas.text: William Fitz Stephen wrote that London had "holier" representations of saints' miracles and martyrdoms in place of Rome's theatrical shows, and he also lists ice skating and wrestling. The author reads this as comparing London's liturgy with the obscenity of the ancient theatrum.

ideas.name: A book is not always a script
ideas.text: A Hereford list of pageants for a Corpus Christi procession had no acted drama. An Ipswich man admitted to freedom in 1492 agreed to help with the pageant and correct the Corpus Christi book. The book may hold the order of a procession and speeches for tableaux.

ideas.name: Absence in many records
ideas.text: The author finds no saint plays in the 1389 guild returns, nor in Edwardian inventories, nor in the richly recorded areas of East Anglia, Essex and Kent. In their place he finds processions, church ales and boy bishops.

ideas.name: A mix that satisfied both sides
ideas.text: The church used suppression and replacement, and local people resisted. The result was a blend of folk festivity such as parish ales, Robin Hood games and hockings with approved acts such as processions and Easter sepulchres. When boy bishops were banned they were quickly restored under Mary.

ideas.name: Fill the same season
ideas.text: Reformers saw that to end disorderly ludi they had to give people a licit activity in the same season. The author reads the promotion of Corpus Christi, with its procession, as meant to give the laity both a share in religion and a form of festival.

ideas.name: A costly failure
ideas.text: In 1562 Chelmsford staged four plays, spent more than £21, lost £11, and never tried drama again.

ideas.name: Even rich towns kept to processions
ideas.text: Bristol, second among provincial towns in 1377, left little record beyond processions and pageants for royal visits. Its guild pageants were small enough for one bearer, and by 1530 the Wiredrawers and Pinmakers needed two.

ideas.name: A priest tied to the village
ideas.text: The author suggests parish priests supported ales because they helped call the banns, belonged to the village and its families, and farmed glebe land, so they were both parson and ploughman.

ideas.name: Government decides who stages plays
ideas.text: The author finds cycles in cities that had a firm trade-guild government and no rival power, such as York and Coventry. Where a cathedral shared power or religious guilds ruled, as at Lincoln, he finds processions and small plays.

ideas.name: Conditions make a play possible, not certain
ideas.text: The author says a firm civic government does not guarantee drama. Money and political conditions have to exist first, and then a body decides whether it wants to display itself or feels an obligation to teach.

ideas.name: Marching order shows rank
ideas.text: Coventry's Corpus Christi procession began with the victuallers, who by statute could not hold civic office. It went on through the leather and metal trades and then the wool trades, ending with the Dyers, Drapers and Mercers. The order followed how much and how long each trade held office, not how rich it was.

ideas.name: Share the cost by joining
ideas.text: In 1494-95 Coventry told every guild not paying for the plays to join one that did. Mostly the lesser guilds paid money to the old guilds, which kept making the pageants. In the 1530s a rise of the Cappers and decay of the Cardmakers forced a reshuffle.

ideas.name: A prisoner let out for the play
ideas.text: John Careles, jailed in Coventry in 1556 for his faith, asked to be released on his own recognizance for one day to act in the Weavers' play with his fellows. He returned to jail afterwards.

ideas.name: Route as a claim to space
ideas.text: Chester moved its plays inside the walls in the 1500s. The plays gathered at the barrs, played first in the Cornmarket in front of the abbey gates, then at the Pentice where the mayor sat, then in the main streets. The author reads the route as announcing lay control, while the abbey supplied beer.

ideas.name: Stated reasons and economic reasons together
ideas.text: Chester's banns say the plays were made to strengthen the faith and to exhort the people to devotion, and they also admit money motives. The author does not treat the first as a mask for the second and sees a city taking up responsibility for its citizens' souls.

ideas.name: Summing records can inflate a total
ideas.text: Historians reckoned a Newcastle cycle of twenty-five plays by adding references scattered over 150 years. The author says this ignores changes over time and what is missing.

ideas.name: A small play takes one action
ideas.text: The Newcastle Noah's Dirge ends at the entry to the ark. It has a small cast, no children, no loading of animals, no flood and no dove, and Noah's wife is made to get him drunk. The author takes it as a sign of modest aims.

ideas.name: Cost per member as a measure of scale
ideas.text: Beverley had about a third of York's taxpayers in 1377 (2,663 against 7,248), and its guildsmen paid 4 to 8 pence a play. At Chester in 1561 most Smiths paid 2s. 4d. and the Shoemakers spent 21s. 4d. on their Jerusalem Carriage. The author reads Beverley's pageants as small.

ideas.name: The viewing stand came first
ideas.text: In Beverley's guild ordinances the clauses on the castle and the lights come before any clause on the Corpus Christi pageant, and castles were built every year while plays were not. The author concludes the castles and lights ranked higher than the pageants.

ideas.name: A fine for faulty playing implies a performance
ideas.text: Beverley guild fines included some for not playing as required, so a pageant had speeches or action of some sort. The titles, such as "The Pinnacle" for one of three temptations, point to a single emblematic scene.

ideas.name: Sins assigned to groups of guilds
ideas.text: For the Pater Noster play the governors gave Pride to the Shoemakers, Saddlers, Fullers, Tilers, Ropers and Capmakers together, and gave an eighth pageant, Vicious, to the gentlemen. They were to play at seven places, the same as for the Corpus Christi play.

ideas.name: Taking turns by year
ideas.text: Lincoln's city ludus, called the Corpus Christi or Pater Noster play, usually ran one year, and the cathedral's Assumption and Coronation display ran in the alternate years.

ideas.name: Two sponsors, one calendar
ideas.text: York's Corpus Christi guild put on the Creed Play and the Pater Noster guild its play, each at about ten-year intervals. The citizens saw the city's cycle every year and these two at set intervals.

ideas.name: A partial list taken for a whole
ideas.text: When Chambers and Craig found a list of Bible stories, they concluded a full cycle had existed and its remaining parts were lost. The author says this came from assuming that drama had evolved from church to street, and that recent work finds cycles rare.

ideas.name: Permission to pass through a jurisdiction
ideas.text: The author suggests city governments came to manage religious processions because the processions moved through the city's territory. A mayor welcoming a visitor grants him and his group entry, in the same way.

ideas.name: Processions and plays kept apart
ideas.text: If a play went with a procession, it was staged at the end or in the afternoon of the feast day. Where the plays themselves moved through the city, the procession ran one day and the plays another.

ideas.name: Old Testament scenes for single plays
ideas.text: The author offers three reasons why places with one play often chose Old Testament subjects: they had limited scope in the sources, they suited moral reading, and some people were wary of showing the Passion.

ideas.name: Pictures in the street
ideas.text: The author argues that guilds and city governments had no churches to put paintings and statues in, so they placed their "pictures" in the streets as living scenes for people who could not read. A preacher in the Hundred Merry Tales says to see the creed enacted, go to Coventry.

ideas.name: Display and speech, not story
ideas.text: The author says London's civic and court shows were processions, pageants and formal orations. They had elaborate display but little narrative acted with dialogue, even though London parishes had boy bishops, Hocktide, May games and Palm Sunday prophets.

ideas.name: A staged effect in a parish
ideas.text: In 1536-37 Saint Mary Magdalen Milk had people play God and Longinus, and filled bladders with liquor that ran out of the Cross.

ideas.name: Figures read aloud by a presenter
ideas.text: In Lydgate's mumming of about 1427, a presenter introduces and "reads" Fortune on her island, then four ladies, Prudence, Righteousness, Fortitude and Temperance. They end with a song and Fortune's banishment. The figures do not speak for themselves.

ideas.name: A judgement put off for a year
ideas.text: In Lydgate's Hertford mumming of 1430, six husbands complain of their wives, the wives answer, and the king delays his decision a year and leaves the wives in charge. The author reads this as showing the limit of a prince's power: his court has no process to reverse the matter.

ideas.name: Debasing the characters distances the audience
ideas.text: Lydgate made the Hertford characters rustic, so extravagant gesture and farce became possible. The author says this lets an audience of high rank imagine the situation is not theirs, although the closing line says it is.

ideas.name: Ingredients of a court disguising
ideas.text: The author lists the usual parts of an elaborate disguising: one or more pageant cars with allegorical or romance settings, an interpreter of the scene, a debate, music and finally dancing. At Greenwich in 1514 fifteen men took sides in a tourney before the pageant car was drawn before the king.

ideas.name: Dispute settled by combat, then a judge
ideas.text: In the 1527 Dialogue of Love and Riches, two groups of choristers argued for Cupid and for Plutus. When the case stayed open, three knights on each side fought across a barrier, and an old gentleman declared that princes need both love and riches.

ideas.name: A shift of verse marks a fall
ideas.text: In Medwall's Nature, Man speaks in rhyme royal at first and moves to a tail-rhyme form when he agrees to banish Innocence. The author notes that a form linked with northern writing marks the turn into a fallen world.

ideas.name: Opening as procession and stations
ideas.text: Medwall's Nature begins with processions of Nature and World, who station themselves to point to their opposition. The first part is a formal debate that, in a court disguising, would lead to a ritual battle and a reconciliation.

ideas.name: Remaking the conditions teaches
ideas.text: Modern productions of the plays on moveable carts or stationary pageants have shown what simple stage structures can do. They have also shown the range of verse forms that work as stage speech.

ideas.name: A script is not the performance
ideas.text: What survives on paper tells little about what was said on the day. At York the guilds were told to register their texts, but some never did and others played different words, and the clerk listening at the first stop could not rewrite them into one story.

ideas.name: Separate owners leave gaps and repeats
ideas.text: When each guild owns its own play and does not consult the others, the whole run repeats scenes and contradicts itself. York's Passion sequence shows this, and the book reads it as the guilds acting on their own.

ideas.name: A collection is not a set that was played
ideas.text: The Towneley manuscript holds five plays copied from York and others from nearby places, so it may never have been performed whole. The compiler may have gathered plays to look like the famous series at York and Coventry.

ideas.name: Owning a text is not playing it
ideas.text: A monk named Hyngham owned the Macro plays, but the book notes that collections of play scripts were also a reading genre in monasteries. John Lydgate wrote disguisings and mummings for the court and never a play text.

ideas.name: A long piece can be cut into parts played in turn
ideas.text: The N-Town Passion has two sequences meant for alternate years. The Digby Killing of the Children says last year's show was the Shepherds and Magi, this year's is the Purification and Slaughter, and next year's will be Christ and the Doctors.

ideas.name: The size of a place sets the size of its play
ideas.text: Only large cities with an organised set of guilds could pay for and man a long series of wagons. Smaller East Anglian towns gave single plays, often Old Testament ones, or cut a big project into smaller units.

ideas.name: Costs can be shared and paid back from takings
ideas.text: For the New Romney Passion, richer townspeople lent money for the scaffolds and others gave days of labour. Neighbouring towns also paid in, and the sponsors were repaid from the profit of four days of playing.

ideas.name: A play can travel as a text
ideas.text: The Castle of Perseverance needed at least twenty-two actors and a large stage, and its banns leave a blank for the town's name. The book suggests the text moved from town to town while local people played it, and printed plays offered for acting were small enough for one actor to take several parts.

ideas.name: Collecting money can be part of the play
ideas.text: Mankind is halted before the devil Titivillus enters so that the actors can collect from the audience. The quête is a mark of mummings and folk plays, and the book reads Mankind as closer to a house entertainment than to an inn show.

ideas.name: Clues in a script can be played with
ideas.text: Mankind mentions a hostler and the names of people, so scholars placed it in an inn in Norfolk. The book answers that a host might have written his guests' names into the script for a laugh, so the clues may describe an imagined inn.

ideas.name: A play can sit inside a feast and a season
ideas.text: Mankind has vices called Nought and Nowadays, a mock beheading and a rude Christmas carol, then ends with Mercy steering the audience back to Lent. The book reads it as an entertainment that moves from the year-end revel to the sobriety of the coming fast.

ideas.name: Print turns a play into a text
ideas.text: Printers worked in London while most plays were played elsewhere, and guilds that owned texts gained nothing by selling them. The book adds that a printed play needs no actors, and that the plays with the longest performance lives, such as the York Creed play, were never printed.

ideas.name: A title page can steer how a text is read
ideas.text: Everyman was printed as a Treatise to be read, not a text to be acted. The 1561 printers of Godly Queen Hester called it newly made, drawn from scripture and a lesson in duty, which the book says the text itself does not bear out.

ideas.name: The same text can mean different things in different years
ideas.text: The Chester Antichrist stayed nearly unchanged for seventy-five years. In 1500 it told of a figure to come, in Henry's last years the name Antichrist was aimed at pope and king alike, and under Elizabeth lines were added to the banns so an Expositor would name Catholics as the Antichrists.

ideas.name: A performance can say more than its script
ideas.text: The Chester Smiths played the Purification in 1572 with a gilded face for the child, a Simeon in church clothing, an altar under a Gothic arch and a repaired crown for the Virgin. Cutting lines from the text would not have removed those meanings.

ideas.name: A reader of the script cannot see the gestures
ideas.text: A censor could pass a text that quotes only the gospel words, but the book notes that performers might still act it so as to recall a Catholic rite. Only a censor in the audience would know if the performance strayed from the page.

ideas.name: One play can join several modes on purpose
ideas.text: The Digby Mary Magdalene moves between Bible history, allegory and romance and mixes them. The playwright shows Mary's life in sin as allegory with World, Flesh and Devil so that her fall reads as everyone's, then returns to history for her conversion.

ideas.name: Leaving a scene out can aim attention
ideas.text: The Magdalene playwright leaves out Mary at the Crucifixion and the Deposition, although the stage could hold them. The book says the Passion is left as a backdrop the audience imagines, which keeps the play on Mary.

ideas.name: A large play is a list of structures
ideas.text: The Castle of Perseverance needs a central castle and scaffolds for God and each enemy. The Magdalene adds a tavern, a garden, a rock, a boat, a devil's wagon with hell beneath and a cloud that lifts angels.

ideas.name: An abstract character is still a body on stage
ideas.text: Caro, the flesh, says in his first speech that he sits in a tower, wears flowers and decorates it with taffeta. The speech tells the stage builders what to make, so the quality appears as a large, costumed person with painted cloths.

ideas.name: A name for a quality can be real to the audience
ideas.text: Medieval thinkers held that a quality such as humanity is real and shows itself through particular people, in the way chairness shows in different chairs. On that view a character named Anger or Charity is not a thin idea but the real thing seen through its marks.

ideas.name: Shared stock figures make plays readable
ideas.text: Caesar, Herod and Pilate speak alike, and the boy servants in the Magdalene talk like the shepherds' servants in the cycles. Playwrights and audiences both knew how tyrants and apprentices behave, so a new play could use them at once.

ideas.name: Folk games can be built into a serious play
ideas.text: The Wakefield Master puts a rebellious servant, a plough-play opening, a parody of the Gloria and a shared feast into plays about Christ. The book reads these as chosen uses of festival play, not as a decline from the sacred.

ideas.name: Food shared with the audience changes the scene
ideas.text: The shepherds in the Wakefield plays first hide their food from their apprentice, then produce more than they could eat. At Chester the Bakers threw loaves out to the crowd, as favours are thrown at Mardi Gras.

ideas.name: Merging two lists damages both
ideas.text: In York's Christ and the Doctors the Two Precepts and the last eight commandments are joined into one list, and the Decalogue no longer holds its shape. Chester gives the seventh commandment twice, and Coventry swaps the ninth for a rule against oaths.

ideas.name: Acting out a story raises questions the story leaves unsaid
ideas.text: In the garden scene Christ asks that the cup pass, which invites the question why he does not know the plan. York has an angel explain, Chester stresses one will, N-Town shows a chalice and host, and Towneley repeats the plan of providence.

ideas.name: What a maker includes and omits shows whose interests it serves
ideas.text: The biblical plays leave out most of the church's required lists, such as the seven virtues and the seven sacraments, because they are stories, not teaching sheets. The book argues that what the lay writers brought in and left out defines lay religious life.

ideas.name: A representation can create a staging problem
ideas.text: The Chester Late Banns says God cannot be fitted to a man's face and that gilding the face disfigures the actor, so God is to come as a voice from a cloudy covering. Another note asks how the Chester Fall can make God vanish so Lucifer can take the throne.

ideas.name: Words can be kept while the act is changed
ideas.text: At Chester the Last Supper reports the gospel words of the bread and wine, and the Banns tell the Bakers to speak the same words Christ spoke, so the scene counts as a memorial and not a counterfeit. The book adds that gestures and props could still carry Catholic meaning.

ideas.name: A new play answers old ones played beside it
ideas.text: Bale's Enterlude of John the Baptist was written when the York, N-Town and Towneley Baptism plays could be played the same year. The book reads it as a reply to them, with Bale standing in front as presenter and explainer.

ideas.name: A play may stay inside the line between who may teach and who may urge
ideas.text: Only a bishop or someone he licenses may preach, while any layperson may urge a neighbour to penance. The book argues that lay producers kept their plays to moral urging and avoided technical doctrine, such as the Trinity.

ideas.name: A ban can fix a season
ideas.text: Proclamations from 1549 and 1559 forbid English interludes between May or August and All Saints, the months of church ales, Robin Hood days and summer games. The book reads this as marking an approved play season and shutting down the commoners' one.

ideas.name: One ban is given several reasons
ideas.text: London's rules against plays are justified by services on holy days, apprentices wasting their masters' goods, sedition and plague. The book suggests the fear of crowds spreading sickness covered a fear of speech spreading too.

ideas.name: Audience members who step into the play break it
ideas.text: Thomas More notes that everyone knows the sultan in a stage play is a cobbler, but a spectator who says so aloud may have his head broken by a tormentor. People of low rank at the foot of the scaffold look on, and those who step up and fail to play their parts disorder the play.

ideas.name: Old and new play run side by side
ideas.text: The last Chester cycle was played in 1575, a year before James Burbage built the Theatre in London, and Coventry kept annual plays until 1579. The book argues that the divide between medieval and Renaissance drama is imposed later.

ideas.name: Rising cost wears down a custom
ideas.text: In Beverley, Coventry, Lincoln and Norwich the ruling guilds made other guilds pay for plays and processions without taking part. The book says this tax antagonised people and shows the plays had become a burden before the church or crown acted.

ideas.name: A play can be taken as a picture of a real person
ideas.text: Cardinal Wolsey had John Roo arrested after a Gray's Inn play about a lord governor ruled by dissipation, which he took to be himself. Roo answered that it had been written twenty years earlier.

ideas.name: A staged debate can end without a winner
ideas.text: Wolsey's Love and Riches pageant of 1527 has speakers argue whether love or riches is the greater, knights defend each side at the bar, and an old man ends it by saying both are needed.

ideas.name: A stage villain can be shown as an actor
ideas.text: In Bale's Enterlude the Pharisee and Sadducee pretend to seek truth, and John says they play wicked parts. The true figure, like John, feigns nothing, since he acts in the present and leads the audience into the new age.

ideas.name: The same sign can be read two ways as a scene proceeds
ideas.text: In Wisdom, Anima enters in white cloth of gold under a black mantle, which first suggests a fallen soul. As the dialogue goes on, the mantle is read as original sin, and the audience learns she is pure and has not yet sinned.

ideas.name: A play need not say where or when it is
ideas.text: The opening of Wisdom is set in heaven before the soul is born, though the audience is not told so. They learn it only in the temptation scene, which the book says has caused scholars to argue over who staged the play.

ideas.name: A space where a play is given is negotiated
ideas.text: The book says lay producers of biblical plays took positions normally held by clergy, and that the clergy for a long time let the lay authority stand. Both sides gave and took over the ground where the plays were given.

ideas.name: The record shows what happened every year, not what was special
ideas.text: There is almost no record of performances of the Castle, Mankind or Wisdom, but ales, processions, boy bishops, hockings, king games and Robin Hood games are recorded yearly all over England. The book concludes that moral plays were occasional and rare.

ideas.name: Plays and printing run on different clocks
ideas.text: Most early printed plays appeared ten or twenty years after they were written and first played. Bale's plays of 1538 were printed in 1547 and 1548, after his exile, because they had to wait for a safe moment.

ideas.name: A text can be changed while the rules stay
ideas.text: Chester's Abraham play, probably written in the 1560s or 1570s, adds a bread and wine scene with Melchisedech and a ruling on circumcision, so the old story carries the new church's two sacraments.

ideas.name: One writer going through a whole set gives it one purpose
ideas.text: Most cycles use many verse forms and have no overall plan, but at Chester a late playwright added a single metre throughout, so the cycle shows a sharper aim, such as stress on the old law in the Old Testament plays.

ideas.name: A choice between two versions can be put to an official
ideas.text: In 1575 the Chester guild brought two versions of a play to the mayor for him to choose between. The same city's register let officials check what a guild proposed to play.

ideas.name: Flow comes from matching challenge to skill
ideas.text: Enjoyment appears at the edge between boredom and anxiety, when what the activity asks is just balanced with what the person can do. A beginner hitting a tennis ball over the net can be in flow, and so can an expert in a hard match.

ideas.name: Two players of unequal skill cannot share one game
ideas.text: When two tennis players are mismatched, the weaker one feels anxious and the stronger one feels bored. The same holds for music that is too simple or too complex for the listener.

ideas.name: A game that adjusts itself keeps the balance
ideas.text: The author's hunting dog Hussar ran escape and pursuit circles around him. When the man was tired the dog ran tighter circles, and when he was fit the dog widened them, so the difficulty stayed level for both.

ideas.name: Staying at one level ends the enjoyment
ideas.text: Alex, learning tennis, is in flow at the start. As his skill grows he gets bored, and when he meets a more skilled opponent he gets anxious. Raising his challenge or his skill returns him to flow at a higher level, which is why flow activities lead to growth.

ideas.name: The challenge that counts is the one the player sees
ideas.text: A person may be in a flow activity and feel nothing if they do not perceive the challenges, as a football professional might think only of his contract. Someone else may find flow in raising children.

ideas.name: Enjoyment has eight parts
ideas.text: People in every culture described enjoyment alike: a task one can finish, concentration, clear goals, immediate feedback, effortless involvement, a sense of control, loss of self-consciousness and an altered sense of time.

ideas.name: Games are built to produce flow
ideas.text: Games, sports and art forms were made over the centuries to give enjoyable experience. They supply rules, goals, feedback and a chance of control, and they set players apart from ordinary life with uniforms and special places.

ideas.name: Goals and feedback need to be clear but can be made up
ideas.text: A tennis player always knows what to do and how she is doing. In open-ended work such as painting, the person has to build a private sense of what works. Teenagers inventing a contest on the spot also settle rules and a scoring sense by trial and error.

ideas.name: Any feedback works if it links to a goal
ideas.text: The kind of feedback matters little. A surgeon watches for blood in the cut and a psychiatrist reads a patient's face, and each cares about the signal because it tells them how close they are to their aim.

ideas.name: A trivial goal gives no enjoyment
ideas.text: Staying alive on a sofa is a goal that is met every second, yet it brings no pleasure. The same sort of feedback delights a climber because the aim is hard and could fail.

ideas.name: Competition helps only while the activity stays the point
ideas.text: An opponent forces a player to stretch skills, and Burke called the antagonist a helper. When beating the other person or impressing an audience takes over, enjoyment fades.

ideas.name: Players enjoy the chance of control, not control itself
ideas.text: Chess and dance have rules that make flawless play possible in principle, while a mistake costs little compared to real life. The enjoyable feeling is of exercising control where the result is in doubt.

ideas.name: Risky pastimes are built to shrink the risk
ideas.text: Climbers, divers and racers say they enjoy their ability to control danger, not danger itself. Some climbers call the Matterhorn safer than crossing a Manhattan street because the dangers can be prepared for.

ideas.name: Games of chance feed a feeling of skill
ideas.text: Poker players credit their ability for wins and chance for losses, and roulette players build systems for the wheel. The author links this to divination, an old effort to foresee the future inside a limited set of rules.

ideas.name: Rules limit choices so that action can be effortless
ideas.text: A culture or a game sets arbitrary goals and rules, which rule out many options. That narrowing lets people act with few doubts. Games fill the gaps in the cultural script, mainly in free time.

ideas.name: Too many options weaken commitment
ideas.text: When many equally attractive choices are open, purpose is uncertain and effort drops. The author says that if a game's rules become too flexible, concentration flags and flow is harder to reach.

ideas.name: Rules mean nothing without consequences
ideas.text: If breaking a rule risks nothing, the rule loses meaning and the activity cannot be enjoyed. The book makes the point about family life, where children need both love and known consequences.

ideas.name: Absorption removes the self, then strengthens it
ideas.text: In flow a climber or violinist is very alert but not thinking about who they are. Afterwards the self they reflect on has gained new skills, so it is larger than before.

ideas.name: A team can merge in flow
ideas.text: Surgeons describe an operating team as one organism, like a ballet. A motorcycle gang member in Kyoto described the run as the moment when everyone feels one.

ideas.name: Flow can become a trap
ideas.text: Chess drove Nabokov's character Luchin to see his whole life as moves, and the chess masters Morphy and Fischer turned away from daily life. The author says an enjoyable activity becomes addictive when a person cannot pay attention to anything else.

ideas.name: Flow carries no moral value by itself
ideas.text: Soldiers, burglars, bullfight crowds and bomb designers have all described flow. The book says the experience builds the self but needs to be judged separately by wider social standards.

ideas.name: Pleasure and enjoyment differ
ideas.text: Eating when hungry gives pleasure with no effort, while a gourmet who tracks flavours enjoys the meal. Only enjoyment makes the person more skilled.

ideas.name: Dull tasks can be turned into games
ideas.text: The physicist Maier-Leibnitz tapped his fingers through a set pattern of 888 steps in a dull lecture, and used it to time his own thoughts. A factory worker, Rico, tried to beat his own record for a 43-second task and reached 28 seconds.

ideas.name: A walk becomes a flow activity by five steps
ideas.text: Set an overall goal and subgoals, find ways to measure progress, keep making finer distinctions, build the needed skills, and raise the stakes when it gets dull. City walkers set goals such as timing the lights or keeping to shade.

ideas.name: The same act can be play or chore
ideas.text: Physical exercise done only because it is fashionable stops being enjoyable. Enjoyment depends on how an activity is done, not what is done.

ideas.name: Costly pastimes were not the happiest
ideas.text: In the pager study, people who used expensive equipment or much energy, such as power boating or television, were less happy than people who talked, gardened or knitted. Their pastimes used less material and more attention.

ideas.name: Listening has levels that open as skill grows
ideas.text: Music can be heard first as sensation, then as feeling and picture, then as structure and comparison between versions. Each level gives a listener new goals and new feedback.

ideas.name: Outside pressure spoils performance
ideas.text: Parents who push a child to win prizes at the violin turn music into stress. The pianist Hollander felt ecstasy alone and fear in front of critical adults, and his hands froze at a recital.

ideas.name: Attention is limited
ideas.text: The author estimates a person can handle about 126 bits of information a second, and understanding one speaker takes about 40. Because of that, what enters awareness decides what a life is like.

ideas.name: The mind drifts towards worry without structure
ideas.text: Alone with nothing to do, attention turns to whatever is most troubling. That is why people reach for television or drugs, which supply order cheaply but do not build skill.

ideas.name: Making a puzzle takes more skill than solving one
ideas.text: A person who only solves crosswords depends on a stranger's challenge. A child of eight who started writing his own crosswords had no need for outside patterns and enjoyed it more.

ideas.name: Wordplay trains control of language
ideas.text: Puns and double meanings let children switch between senses of a phrase, such as having Grandma for dinner. The author says the surprise at first gives way to skill.

ideas.name: Science works like a puzzle game
ideas.text: Kuhn writes that the rules of a research paradigm limit acceptable answers and steps, so scientists focus on small problems. Dirac called the making of quantum mechanics a very interesting game.

ideas.name: Riddles carried knowledge in game form
ideas.text: In old Welsh poems, the names of trees stood for letters, so a song about a battle of trees spelled a hidden message. Competition between expert riddlers was often the main intellectual event of a village.

ideas.name: Prisoners invented games to stay sane
ideas.text: Speer imagined a walking trip to Jerusalem, a pilot played eighteen holes in his head every day, and Hungarian prisoners ran a contest to translate a poem, with soap on a shoe as their writing surface. Each of them set goals, watched for feedback and made the task harder over time.

ideas.name: People enjoy work more often than leisure
ideas.text: In the pager study, 54 percent of work responses showed high challenge and high skill, against 18 percent in leisure. Yet people said they wanted to be doing something else more often at work.

ideas.name: Free time lacks the structure that jobs supply
ideas.text: Jobs come with goals, feedback, rules and challenges. Unstructured time needs a person to supply them, so many people fall into passive entertainment that asks for no skill.

ideas.name: Surgery has the features of a flow activity
ideas.text: Surgeons name clear goals, constant feedback, many challenges, a team to coordinate and ritual preparation that shuts out the outside world. Even so, some surgeons who only repeat one simple operation report tedium.

ideas.name: Feedback timing differs between hunting and farming
ideas.text: A hunter chooses quarry and method several times a day, while a farmer decides crops only a few times a year and waits for the weather. The book says hunters forced to farm sometimes died out, and many farmers did learn to enjoy the slow feedback.

ideas.name: A job can be redesigned or a person trained
ideas.text: Making jobs resemble games helps, and training people to spot chances for action helps. The author says neither works well alone, as the welder Joe turned a dull plant into a place to learn while others did not.

ideas.name: Watching replaces doing
ideas.text: Many people watch athletes in stadiums and listen to recorded musicians instead of playing. Such passive leisure uses attention without building skill.

ideas.name: Skills grow only when challenges are renewed
ideas.text: A couple whose early challenges are used up risk boredom. New challenges come from learning the other person more deeply. It is the same loop the Alex diagram shows for any repeated play.

ideas.name: Redefining the rules can change a situation
ideas.text: When three young men robbed twelve-year-old Mark in a park, he followed them and asked for his watch back, treating them as people who could vote on it. They voted two to one to return it.

ideas.name: Teenagers without challenges make their own
ideas.text: Gangs, joyriding and vandalism give young people real chances to use skills that school and suburb do not offer. The book puts much of it down to a lack of worthwhile challenge, and does not blame character.

ideas.name: Adversity becomes a game with new goals
ideas.text: Paraplegic and blind people in the Milan study mastered a new set of challenges, and some called the accident positive because it gave clear goals. One became a regional archery champion from a wheelchair.

ideas.name: Three steps turn threat into a flow activity
ideas.text: The book names unselfconscious self-assurance, attention on the world and the finding of new solutions. A pilot succeeds by fitting herself to the plane's rules and to the air, without trying to force the plane.

ideas.name: Fixing on one plan blinds a player
ideas.text: A soldier who fell with a parachute clawed at his chest where a rip cord usually sits, though a left-handed cord was a few inches away. The author says tight focus on a defence can hide the answer near at hand.

ideas.name: Respond to what appears instead of a fixed plan
ideas.text: The author compares finding goals to a painter who begins with a feeling and changes the picture as colours appear. A painter who holds to a fixed picture produces a trite one.

ideas.name: Goals, challenges and skills imply one another
ideas.text: Choosing to learn tennis implies the challenges of serve and backhand, which imply the skills to build. The sequence can start at any of the three, and feedback keeps the player in the system.

ideas.name: Any goal can give meaning if it has rules
ideas.text: The book says what matters is that a goal supplies clear objectives and rules for action and lets a person concentrate. A beer-bottle collection could do this as well as a cure for cancer.

ideas.name: Effort and goal justify each other
ideas.text: A goal first justifies the effort, and later the effort justifies the goal. A mountaineer who quits at the first hardship shows the goal was not worth much.

ideas.name: Choosing the goal oneself raises commitment
ideas.text: A person who knows they chose their goal is both more dedicated and more willing to change it when it stops making sense. The book calls this being consistent and flexible at once.

ideas.name: A game is well played only when everyone plays well
ideas.text: DeKoven takes readers to watch a professional match that ends 12 to 0. The winning team stops caring, so the game fails even though it had moments of skill. Skilled play has to be shared across both sides for the game as a whole to count as well played.

ideas.name: A hidden handicap changes what a win means
ideas.text: Two friends play Ping-Pong, and one player uses the wrong hand without saying so. The other player wins and feels cheated, because the win said nothing about the match. Telling the other player first would have kept the shared game.

ideas.name: The score does not measure how well people played
ideas.text: DeKoven's test is how well the players played together, not who won. Two people volley in Ping-Pong for an hour with no points and say it was the well-played game they sought.

ideas.name: Players need to renew their agreement to play well together
ideas.text: A shared intention made at the start does not hold itself. Needs shift and players get absorbed in a rule and forget why they are playing, so the aim has to be restated whenever it slips.

ideas.name: A player has to feel safe before being willing
ideas.text: In the mountain-climbing example, a player accepts the risk of falling but not a partner cutting the rope. Willingness rests on knowing that nothing will be risked beyond what was agreed.

ideas.name: Shared conventions let strangers play
ideas.text: Rules such as taking turns and finishing the game work across many games. They give people who have never met a reason to trust each other without first getting to know each other.

ideas.name: The authority over a game can sit with the people playing
ideas.text: Official rules grow when games spread to national leagues, and the players hand control to officials. In a play community the group decides whether a game suits it.

ideas.name: Rules can fall away as trust grows
ideas.text: As a play community builds trust, players look for games with fewer and fewer rules. Eventually they run through the woods playing follow the leader with no named game.

ideas.name: A hint helps only by the amount the other player wants
ideas.text: A clue that says too little does not touch the problem, and one that says too much gives the answer away. In Mastermind, the person who set the code has to judge what the solver needs.

ideas.name: Rules for help work when agreed before play
ideas.text: If players have settled how and when a hint may be asked, the asking does not read as a sign of failure. DeKoven suggests a rule like tapping twice on a peg to ask for a hint.

ideas.name: Fairness develops as players grow
ideas.text: Young children call a game fair if they get the prize. Older players mean equal rules and an equal chance to win, and later a handicap can restore the chance when skill differs.

ideas.name: Some rule-breaking keeps a game going
ideas.text: In musical chairs, DeKoven removed no chairs so no child was out. A child then carried his chair along, the group laughed and all took chairs on the march. The rule broke but the game was still musical chairs in spirit.

ideas.name: Boundaries and bases serve different needs
ideas.text: A boundary lets a player leave the game. A base lets a player stay in but rest, though the player cannot play while safe. In stoop tag, the player who is it has no base, so the chase would stall if all players squatted.

ideas.name: A game needs a way to rest as well as a way to end
ideas.text: Interludes such as halftime, huddles and a bow before a match let players pause the game without ending it. Baseball is full of small pauses between each pitch.

ideas.name: Handing power to officials shifts attention from the community to the game
ideas.text: Players who give umpires the final word can concentrate on playing. Over time the rules turn into regulations kept by others, so the players lose control. DeKoven suggests players take turns as referee.

ideas.name: Watchers change how people play
ideas.text: Spectators remind players that excellence is expected. Players then begin to perform for them, and a coach is needed to bring attention back to the game.

ideas.name: A player who has to prove something stops playing
ideas.text: A player who takes the game personally cannot afford to lose and hogs the ball. DeKoven's coach takes the player out to notice the tightness and the anger.

ideas.name: Players can change a game when it stops working
ideas.text: When a game stops holding one player's gaming mind or overwhelms the playing mind, the cause is an imbalance. DeKoven says changing the game restores equilibrium, so the community keeps the right to do so.

ideas.name: Change one rule at a time
ideas.text: Playing with tic-tac-toe, DeKoven tries the grid size, the length of the winning row, tied-game rules, extra marks and moving pieces. He advises changing one rule, then watching what else has to change to restore balance.

ideas.name: Many rules can change without changing the game
ideas.text: Using letters or colours instead of X and O, or drawing a line through three in a row, leaves strategies as they were. A change that matters is one that needs a new strategy, such as allowing two turns in a row.

ideas.name: A proven game has reasons for each rule
ideas.text: In tic-tac-toe the winning row has to be three. DeKoven tried two in a row and the first player always won. Changing a rule in a balanced game means other rules usually need changing.

ideas.name: Too many changes leave nothing to play
ideas.text: Groups can get so taken with changing rules that they change something every five minutes. They end up without a game to play, and some members feel lost and leave.

ideas.name: Change the game before changing the people
ideas.text: A game is made up for the players, so adjusting the game is less costly than trying to adjust people.

ideas.name: A handicap equalises familiarity
ideas.text: A skilled checkers player starts with four pieces fewer, so the game is new to both. Letting a child win on purpose does not do this, because the child sees through it.

ideas.name: What the score rewards decides the game
ideas.text: Tennis can give points for returns that the other player misses, for bravery, or for keeping a rally going. Each choice makes a different game, and DeKoven suggests giving it a new name.

ideas.name: A game needs a way out as well as a way in
ideas.text: DeKoven worries about a game that cannot be left, since a player who is tired or hurt would be stuck. He lists quitting, giving up, losing and winning as ways out and says each needs to carry no blame.

ideas.name: Freedom to quit lets others enjoy a game
ideas.text: The host who kept asking whether his drinking game suited everyone spoilt it. If players know anyone can leave at any time, they can assume everyone present chose to be there.

ideas.name: Quitting seldom works as a message
ideas.text: A player who throws down the paddle to protest hopes to raise a question. The others hear a sore loser instead, so DeKoven treats quitting as a personal choice.

ideas.name: People may need to watch before they join
ideas.text: A girl stayed in the safe area for weeks, then joined hide-and-seek and played hard. DeKoven concluded she had been checking that she did not have to play, which made her ready to play.

ideas.name: Some games happen to a person rather than with them
ideas.text: In a tug-of-war that starts over a skipping rope, the person never agreed to a game. DeKoven says a game played on someone is not play for them.

ideas.name: Winning is a clear end but does not complete a game
ideas.text: Winning gives an unmistakable stopping point. It also splits players into winners and losers, and the winner has no reason left to play.

ideas.name: The way a game ends changes what players feel
ideas.text: Elimination games draw focus to the last players but leave many waiting out. Cooperative games end with everyone together, and a silly game such as Thar's a bar ends in a pile that nobody wins.

ideas.name: Players who carry a grudge from one game into the next stop playing
ideas.text: DeKoven calls this tournamentality. A player uses each new opponent to pay back an old loss, so quitting and changing the game are no longer open.

ideas.name: A well-played game cannot be repeated exactly
ideas.text: After a game goes well, the players have changed and the same game cannot give the same experience. Efforts to prolong it with more rituals and breaks shrank the game, until players were honouring a memory.

ideas.name: Players can try games that might not work
ideas.text: If everyone shares the trial, a failed game blames nobody. The inventor does not carry the fault, and the group has still shown its willingness.

ideas.name: Themes in games a group enjoys point to other games
ideas.text: A group that enjoys tag and capture the flag likes chasing. A group that likes pool may try marbles or darts, which share aim and contact. DeKoven treats what players enjoy as firmer evidence than what they dislike.

ideas.name: Silliness depends on trust and clarity
ideas.text: Players can be silly together only if everyone can tell it is a joke and feel safe. A person who is actually hurt may be taken as pretending, so silly play needs a way to step out of it.

ideas.name: A place for play is part of a play community
ideas.text: Toy stores, chess clubs and arcades each offer few kinds of game or discourage playing. DeKoven's games preserve combines quiet, active and dancing spaces, with games cared for by everyone.

ideas.name: Rules can say how a game could be played
ideas.text: In New Games, referees describe the rules last used and invite players to adjust them. In hug tag, the group tried no repeat hugs so that the player who is it has a chance.

ideas.name: Playing for keeps works while players can afford to lose
ideas.text: Poker played for pennies, with beer, keeps the play. If a player loses too much, the hurt is real and the game stops.

ideas.name: A stacked game needs players to know it first
ideas.text: Players accept roulette or a slot machine where the house has the higher odds because they know it. Cheating secretly makes them feel the game was changed after they had bet.

ideas.name: Chance and skill are both parts of a card game
ideas.text: In poker, a player works with probability, avoiding an inside straight, and with confidence in a bid. The player can fold, which DeKoven treats as a way of quitting with honour.

ideas.name: Danger can be part of play only by choice
ideas.text: Games with real risk, such as a mountain climb, are play only when every participant knows the risk and chose it. A modern war has people on the receiving end who did not choose it.

ideas.name: Stakes give a game its focus and stop working once they replace the game
ideas.text: Players can play for money, meaning, learning or dignity. When the thought of what happens on winning pushes out the playing, the game is no longer play.

ideas.name: Playing to win and having to win are different
ideas.text: Both follow the same rules. A player playing to win keeps a second voice that says it is only a game, while a player who has to win has one driving voice and no way to leave.

ideas.name: Everyone who competes has to be competing for the challenge to work
ideas.text: A golfer who only wanders the course makes the other player's effort seem foolish. DeKoven says the players need to agree that they are all playing to win.

ideas.name: A visible goal helps a game look legitimate to outsiders
ideas.text: DeKoven's class took games out onto the college quad and chose games with clear aims so that watchers could see an achievement.

ideas.name: Agreements about how to end can themselves be changed
ideas.text: Teams agree to end at a given time or when a winner is named, and still add overtime. DeKoven concludes that the need to finish well outweighs the original agreement.

ideas.name: Players can be surprised by their own play
ideas.text: In DeKoven's account, one part of a person works hard at the game while another part watches and is delighted. A game gives the first part a task that holds its attention.

ideas.name: Games are made to be changed
ideas.text: Zimmerman reads the book as a manual for treating games as things to bend, break and rebuild. Examples include the many tic-tac-toe variants and the many ways to play marbles in the appendix.

ideas.name: A game's worth does not rest on an outside goal
ideas.text: Zimmerman contrasts the book with the claim that games are there to fix education or health. He compares it to a meal valued for taste and company as well as nutrition.

ideas.name: A game is whatever people call a game
ideas.text: The authors reject a tight definition of the word game, since the things called games share only overlapping family likenesses, as Wittgenstein said. They ask how gamelike or how political a thing is, not whether it is one. Of Risk they ask how political it is.

ideas.name: Characteristics are the questions a friend asks
ideas.text: A game is most usefully described by features like length, player count and luck, because those tell a possible player more than the rules do. Calling something a card game tells you about length and luck at once, and a game of thin cardboard pieces that is nothing like a card game would feel like a trick.

ideas.name: Some qualities belong to the players, not the rules
ideas.text: Length, favourite player count and speed depend on who plays. Mancala is played very fast in Africa and slower by Europeans, and chess is slow in the West but quick in the East. A game can change without a rule changing.

ideas.name: Evolved games solve problems that designed games keep meeting
ideas.text: Classic games have been weeded out over long play, so they often show solutions to problems that new designed games run into. Politics has been largely evolved out of classic games, which are mostly two-sided or low in interaction.

ideas.name: Short atoms let a session end well
ideas.text: Players like to end a session by finishing a satisfying unit of play. Poker hands and basketball possessions are short, so people stop when they like. A chess game has no unit shorter than the whole game, so it is hard to squeeze into a spare half hour.

ideas.name: Points make atoms satisfying
ideas.text: Games that record points at the end of each short unit let each unit feel like a small complete game. Chess and go decide only at the end, so they have no such unit, even though go has points.

ideas.name: Long games turn into campaigns
ideas.text: Designers often add content to please serious fans and the games grow, with the atoms getting longer too. Short play then becomes harder to find, and a gap opens for newer shorter games.

ideas.name: A short game costs the player nothing
ideas.text: A short game can be played again for a longer experience, but a long game cannot easily be made short. Poker and basketball do not suffer from short atoms.

ideas.name: The number of sides matters more than the number of players
ideas.text: Football has many players but two sides, so it acts like a two-player game. Politics and kingmaking only arise with three or more sides.

ideas.name: Single-player games run out of content
ideas.text: With no human opponent the surprise has to come from a random setup, hidden information or a simulated opponent. A crossword is spent once it is solved, while a card solitaire deal makes a fresh puzzle each time.

ideas.name: Single-player games let the designer pick the win rate
ideas.text: Because there is only one side, a designer can aim for players winning about 70 percent of the time, which two-player games cannot do. Difficulty levels let players choose their own rate.

ideas.name: Changing the player count changes the game
ideas.text: Scrabble for two and for four play differently, because blocking an opponent and setting up the board pay off differently. Turning a two-player game into one for three or more has many unintended effects.

ideas.name: A game needs rules of thumb to be a game
ideas.text: If a game has no heuristics the players can find, it is random for them and they might as well roll dice. Guess the Digit of pi is the extreme example.

ideas.name: Telling who is ahead and knowing what to do are separate
ideas.text: Money in the Bag has a known winning strategy but nobody can see who is ahead until the end. Money on the Table lets you see the score but gives no clue which button pays more often. Winning play usually needs both kinds of rule of thumb.

ideas.name: Rules of thumb that are too powerful end a game
ideas.text: Nim and tic-tac-toe have heuristics that tell you everything, so once known the game is solved and dull. Rules of thumb that suit a game are clear, rich and satisfying, and need not be powerful.

ideas.name: Beginners need an easy first rule of thumb
ideas.text: In Uno a beginner can even out suits. In go and many European boardgames with many equal options a beginner cannot tell what to do and may give up. Low-powered cards in a trading card game give new players choices they can make.

ideas.name: The same game has different rules of thumb at different skill levels
ideas.text: Chess is friendly to beginners and advanced beginners but intermediate players mostly avoid obvious blunders and wait for a mistake. In go the intermediate player finds many moves that help a bit.

ideas.name: Rules of thumb change as the player base learns
ideas.text: Tic-tac-toe has decent heuristics for small children and few useful ones for adults. Dots and Boxes was played by schoolchildren at random until mathematicians found productive early-game play.

ideas.name: Races and brawls are two ways to make a multiplayer game
ideas.text: A race glues together copies of a one-player game, so players barely affect one another. A brawl adds players to a two-player game, so they hurt one another and eliminate one another. Many multiplayer features follow from which one the game is.

ideas.name: Being out of the game is not the most costly outcome
ideas.text: Playing on with no chance of winning is often more costly to the player than being strictly out, since an eliminated player can rest. How long until the next game starts decides how much it hurts. In poker the next hand starts quickly, in Monopoly it may take an hour.

ideas.name: Three ways to handle elimination
ideas.text: A game can knock players out for ever, leave them in with no chance, or give everyone a chance until the end. The first upsets the player knocked out, the second leaves them to disrupt others, and the third may make only the last part of the game matter.

ideas.name: Tracking points removes the elimination problem
ideas.text: When each subgame or hand scores points, even a losing player cares about how much they lose by. Money in poker does the same after the game is over.

ideas.name: A losing player can still play for something
ideas.text: Players with no chance of winning often play for points or for second place if the game has a simple measure like score or distance. Groups expect this, and dislike it when a player instead steers the result.

ideas.name: Concession is a social rule
ideas.text: Chess has a culture of resigning that solved the problem of hopeless games, and breaking it in a tournament can cause a scandal. Online, players who do not concede may hide a building in a strategy game to drag the game on.

ideas.name: Let the winner remove a hidden loser
ideas.text: Where losing players might drag a game out, a rule that reveals the hidden buildings of a player with no army or economy turns a logically eliminated player into a strictly eliminated one.

ideas.name: Winners can be the ones eliminated
ideas.text: In Old Maid and in footraces the first to finish drops out and the potential losers carry on. The reward of winning softens the annoyance of sitting out.

ideas.name: A race can be made interactive by adding a rule
ideas.text: Mario Kart's shells and the blockades and sending pieces home in Parcheesi add interaction to a race. Without such additions a race has little politics.

ideas.name: Interaction with no choice of target is not politics
ideas.text: In poker you can only take chips from players who choose to play against you, so it is not a chip-taking game. In Risk you can only attack those next to you. Limits on who can be hit limit politics.

ideas.name: Skill stops mattering when everyone can target the leader
ideas.text: In the chip-taking game with chess matches, Kasparov is no likelier to win because others pick him first. The real skill becomes persuading others to attack someone else.

ideas.name: Political play follows the same pattern in every game
ideas.text: Lying low, begging, threatening revenge, offering favours outside the game and waiting to mop up appear whatever the mechanics are. With enough targeted interaction, many games become the same game.

ideas.name: Politics wipes out ways to read the position
ideas.text: If any player can be picked on by group choice, ordinary measures of who is ahead stop telling you much, and so do ordinary strategic rules of thumb. Only social guesses about who will do what to whom stay useful.

ideas.name: A move that is clearly forced causes fewer arguments
ideas.text: If three players have two chips each and one removes a chip from another, there are complaints. If one player has eight chips and is about to win, taking his chip is accepted.

ideas.name: Politics can let lower-skilled players join higher-skilled ones
ideas.text: In free-for-all Magic or Starcraft a low-skilled player can survive because the high-skilled players attract attention. This widens the pool of people who can play together, which matters most for families.

ideas.name: Simple games suit political play
ideas.text: Diplomacy needs no detailed combat tables, because negotiation and betrayal would wash out any such detail. Complex mechanics tend to be lost under politics.

ideas.name: Picking on the leader can be a mistake
ideas.text: In the balloon game with hit chances of 60, 50 and 40 percent, B has a 19 percent chance of winning by aiming at the most accurate thrower and 23 percent by aiming at the least accurate. Instinct says to go for the leader, but that can hurt the attacker.

ideas.name: Hold back and nobody fights
ideas.text: If everyone waits for the others to wear each other down, the game stalls. Rewards for attacking, such as taking resources or cards in Risk, or hero experience in Warcraft III, give players a reason to fight.

ideas.name: Kingmaking survives even when incentives exist
ideas.text: Giving players reasons to attack one player over another cuts politics, but a player who is out of contention no longer cares about those reasons. It needs its own controls, such as keeping losers from having much influence.

ideas.name: Kingmaking is resented because it overwrites everything
ideas.text: A single choice by a player out of the running decides the winner, and the skill and luck of the contenders count for nothing. Fantasy sports leagues have a commissioner to approve trades for this reason.

ideas.name: Players need to feel they contribute to a team
ideas.text: A team game works when each member can see their effect. Designers either balance the roles or give each role something unique, like healing or teleportation in World of Warcraft.

ideas.name: Roles can sit on top of rules
ideas.text: Basketball positions have no special rules, and World of Warcraft tank, healer and damage dealer sit on top of its written classes. Roles that players make up can matter as much as those the rules give.

ideas.name: More dependence on teammates means more anger at them
ideas.text: A swim relay lets you do your utmost whatever your team does. In football or Defense of the Ancients a teammate who drops the ball or dies often costs you the game, so players turn hostile to beginners.

ideas.name: Bridge cuts off table talk on purpose
ideas.text: Partners may not say what they hold, but have to signal through bids and plays. Once the dummy is down, the information flow stops, since otherwise the more skilled player would just tell the partner what to do.

ideas.name: Rules are not the game
ideas.text: The rules of basketball have changed many times and it is still basketball, as Little Red Riding Hood stays the same story with different words. Rules are often changed to keep play the way it was, as when a card is banned in Magic.

ideas.name: Rules can be a barrier to play
ideas.text: Every first-order rule has to be learned before play starts, so too many of them keep people out. Few people learn from a rulebook longer than a page. Most learn from someone who already knows the game.

ideas.name: Fewer rules for the same play
ideas.text: The same play with fewer rules is preferred to more rules, and adding a rule to fix each small problem builds up a messy game. First-order rules cost most, and rules that players have to judge themselves cost more than ones a referee or computer judges.

ideas.name: A computer can hold the rules for you
ideas.text: Players of a computer game can begin with little knowledge because the machine decides what is allowed. Clear rules for the player's own parts still matter, though, while rules for non-player parts may stay vague.

ideas.name: A penalty can turn a ban into a price
ideas.text: If a rule says that doing x causes y, players may do x on purpose and pay y. A time limit meant to speed up a game can make players use all the allowed time.

ideas.name: Teach first-order rules first
ideas.text: A teacher gives a new player only the rules everyone needs, and some rules of thumb. A beginner in chess may know piece values before knowing en passant.

ideas.name: Innovate only where it pays
ideas.text: Players enjoy a comfortable game and always like convenience. A new idea that is no more useful than the old one is harder to learn and probably rougher. Successful games usually have only one or two new things.

ideas.name: The polished later game often wins
ideas.text: Warcraft followed Dune II, the Pokemon trading card game followed Magic, and World of Warcraft followed Everquest. The first game with a new idea rarely gets its details right.

ideas.name: Standards teach the game for free
ideas.text: A player who sees a first-person view with a gun in the picture reaches for the WASD keys. Someone who knows one poker game can pick up another fast, and rules of thumb carry over as well.

ideas.name: A standard may stay for pacing, not for fit
ideas.text: Mining resources to build units in strategy games came from one setting but stayed because it paces the game and gives players an economy against army trade-off to think about. Following a standard also shortens the designer's balancing work.

ideas.name: Break a standard for a reason
ideas.text: Bicycle racing has time trials because drafting makes a mass start measure team help and not individual strength. Taking away health bars in a shooter to feel more real upset players who expected them.

ideas.name: Dedicated decks come from business as well as play
ideas.text: Games like Uno often could be played with a standard deck. Printing a special deck became easy, and a company can own a special deck but cannot sell rules alone.

ideas.name: One game can hold several games that share standards
ideas.text: Hex wargame scenarios, draft and sealed formats in Magic and different battlegrounds in World of Warcraft can be seen as separate games on shared standards. They reuse what the player has already mastered.

ideas.name: Players of open-ended games write their own goals
ideas.text: In an MMO a player may chase levels, gold, friends, looks or helping beginners. Friends playing Hacky Sack may keep the bag up or try stunts. Satisfaction depends on goals the player chose.

ideas.name: Outcomes come in kinds
ideas.text: A game can end with one winner, one loser, a winning alliance, a ranking, or a score of points or time. The kinds can combine, as when a footrace ranks players by their times.

ideas.name: Advice can be stopped by hidden information or time
ideas.text: An expert cannot run a beginner's turn if the beginner holds hidden cards, if there is no time to give orders, or if the game is played in character. The book lists these with skilled control and limits on talking as ways to keep each player in the game.

ideas.name: Cooperative games came with the computer
ideas.text: An opponent gives uncertainty and replay, so people used one when they could find one. The computer supplies an opponent and a network supplies teammates, so players can team up against the machine and win more than half the time.

ideas.name: A cooperative game lacks someone to object to bossing
ideas.text: In bridge the opponents object if a partner tells the other what to do. In Pandemic nobody objects but the player being bossed, who can only say they would rather play.

ideas.name: Winning is partly agreed by the players
ideas.text: The rules may give a points track, but one group plays only for the winner and another plays for place or points. In Starcraft the game gives a score, yet nearly everyone plays only to eliminate the other side.

ideas.name: The kind of outcome shapes play
ideas.text: With a unique winner, players take wild chances near the end and picking on the leader appears. With a unique loser, players tend to pick on whoever is behind. Where first and second place score the same, people still compete for first.

ideas.name: A game where everyone can lose is awkward
ideas.text: In Nuclear War a player has to decide whether second place is preferable to everyone losing. If enough of the group prefers the second, games end with everyone losing.

ideas.name: Long games get called off early
ideas.text: Groups often agree to stop a long multiplayer boardgame when some players are out, and treat the remaining players as winners ranked informally by score.

ideas.name: Real value for points reduces kingmaking
ideas.text: A poker player in fifth place has little reason to give away his chips so that the second-place player comes first. Money makes the value of lower places clear, so players out of the running have something concrete to play for.

ideas.name: Draws fit low-luck games
ideas.text: In a game of little luck, a draw can fairly show that the sides were evenly matched. In a game with a lot of luck, letting luck decide the winner feels natural.

ideas.name: Easy draws spoil the ending
ideas.text: If a player in trouble can force a draw easily, as in tic-tac-toe or chess, games rarely reach a satisfying finish. In children's games, a draw can be welcome because it invites another game.

ideas.name: Who controls the ending matters
ideas.text: When players can influence when the end condition is met, winners rush to end the game and losers try to delay it. Watch for losers who delay forever and for tedious sums that leaders make about when to end it.

ideas.name: Games grow scores even when the rules have none
ideas.text: Chess pieces have point values that players use to tell who is ahead, because a single number says who is winning and by how much.

ideas.name: A game with no ending can be given one
ideas.text: Tetris and arcade games are played until you lose, so some add a goal such as beating a boss. After winning, the game restarts but harder, as in Donkey Kong or Diablo.

ideas.name: Complex games have many point tracks
ideas.text: An MMO has gold, experience, reputation, craft skill and even gear tiers, and the player picks which to pursue.

ideas.name: Points that are spendable invite playing for points
ideas.text: Given the choice, most people take being up 200 dollars at poker over being up 100 when everyone else is lower. Marathon runners care about beating four hours more than finishing 163rd instead of 167th.

ideas.name: One spendable point track tends to snowball
ideas.text: If points can be spent to gain more points, whoever leads spends their way further ahead. Splitting the track into money for power and victory points for winning breaks this loop.

ideas.name: Splitting power from victory has side effects
ideas.text: The player behind in victory points may hold power to close the gap. Players face a choice between a quick win and building up. The loser can say they were close, and can claim most wood as a consolation.

ideas.name: Change the victory condition to fix a play problem
ideas.text: If armies hang back, winning by holding a central area for some turns forces a fight. A Monopoly-like game that ends only when all but one are bankrupt can be changed to reaching a sum of money. The fixes cost extra complexity.

ideas.name: Several ways to win act like several games
ideas.text: Magic and Age of Empires each offer different routes to victory, adding depth and replay. Players have to learn each, and designers find it harder to keep two routes both viable than two pieces.

ideas.name: Rare alternate wins exist for completeness
ideas.text: In reversi a player can win early by turning every piece their colour, and in go a triple ko can end in a draw. These come up so rarely that they are in the rules for logical completeness.

ideas.name: Different goals can even out unequal sides
ideas.text: A wargame can start with one side far ahead and let the other win by surviving for a number of turns. In HORSE, the more skilled player starts with letters against them and needs five shots while the other needs three.

ideas.name: Almost every game starts unevenly
ideas.text: Moving first in chess, seat order at a poker table or a duel between different character classes are all asymmetries. Such effects often wash out at lower skill levels, and moving first in Monopoly hardly seems to matter.

ideas.name: Few games are fully symmetric
ideas.text: Only games where everyone moves at once with the same options, like rock-paper-scissors, have none. Marathons are nearly symmetric because the race is long enough that the start barely matters.

ideas.name: Designers use asymmetry on purpose
ideas.text: Asymmetric starts bring variety and replay, as in Cosmic Encounter, Magic, Starcraft and RPG classes. Single-player RPGs are built on complete asymmetry between player and monsters.

ideas.name: Rotate the advantage
ideas.text: Football teams take turns kicking off, deals rotate in card games, chess matches alternate black and white, and go gives komi for moving second. Short games, or a campaign of many games, also wash an advantage out.

ideas.name: Equipment is a kind of asymmetry
ideas.text: Sports allow own equipment within limits, and some objections to Magic come from deck-building as equipment. Stock-car racing and sealed-deck Magic were created to limit the advantage of equipment.

ideas.name: Going after a low-skilled player helps
ideas.text: In three-player Scrabble, playing right after a low-skilled player is a big advantage, because that player gives you scoring chances. In hearts and poker, seat relative to low-skilled players is a hidden asymmetry too.

ideas.name: Asymmetry marks the difference between one and one and a half players
ideas.text: Thinking of the computer as a player, a highly asymmetric game feels like a pure one-player game and a symmetric one feels like a one and a half player game.

ideas.name: Looks and play can pull apart
ideas.text: Ornate pieces and busy cards please the eye but make the state of the game harder to read, while play wants a simple interface. A fancy-themed chess set is a gift, not the set to play with.

ideas.name: Art direction counts more than technology
ideas.text: World of Warcraft is thought of as having impressive graphics although its technology was not cutting edge. Web games show artistic excellence without it.

ideas.name: Older games harmonise look and play
ideas.text: Playing cards are not too busy and not minimalist. Newer games, art-led games and gift editions more often hide the play, as when a game went from drawings to photographs.

ideas.name: Sound changes how a game is judged
ideas.text: A web game with sound on is enjoyed more and its flaws are easier to overlook. Designers can misjudge an unpolished game by turning sound on or off.

ideas.name: Touch is part of a physical game's pleasure
ideas.text: The weight of chess pieces, shuffling cards and poker chips give satisfaction. Computer RPGs hide dice and use floating numbers because rolling dice on a screen would be an annoyance.

ideas.name: Smell and taste are rarely designed
ideas.text: The scent of new packaging adds to the appeal of opening an expansion or booster pack, but smell is mostly a side effect of other choices in games.

ideas.name: Games hide games
ideas.text: A political game may be really the chip-taking game, and a strategy game has a rock-paper-scissors triangle among its units. Naming the hidden game helps understand a design, whether or not it helps it.

ideas.name: Three ways to build in subgames
ideas.text: A game can contain subgames, as Titan does, be a collection of them, like Mario Party, or be a staged game, like bridge. Each part has its own length, interactivity and appeal.

ideas.name: Subgames shade into metagames
ideas.text: Bidding and play in bridge feel like one game. Magic deckbuilding, Warhammer painting and army choice, and D&D character creation feel more like activities around a game.

ideas.name: A small rock-paper-scissors may sit in a big game
ideas.text: Early units lose to midgame units that lose to late units, so arriving a little late with more pays and planning a huge late army is risky. These triangles are one thing going on, and can be washed out by others.

ideas.name: A broken triangle can break the whole game
ideas.text: If rush is too powerful against turtling, or ranged units beat both air and melee, the problem spills out into the whole game, so the balance of each subgame matters.

ideas.name: Splitting forces makes a subgame
ideas.text: If armies have to be divided over several areas, the game has a resource commitment game inside it. It vanishes if players gain more by putting everything into one area.

ideas.name: Physical skill is a subgame too
ideas.text: Sprinting, throwing and catching are subgames of football. Computer games often include reaction-time subgames and boardgames and card games rarely do.

ideas.name: Having an essential game is not a fault
ideas.text: The problem is when the essential game makes all other mechanics unimportant, as in an overly political game decided only by politics. It takes casual players time to find a game's essence, which may be why few classic games are chip-taking.

ideas.name: Snowball needs power equal to score
ideas.text: Where your score is also your power, as money in Monopoly, a lead feeds on itself. In sports, points are not spendable so they do not snowball. In go, territory is often traded for influence.

ideas.name: Snowball is a problem when it keeps losers playing
ideas.text: Nobody objects that a game ends with a winner. The trouble is a player with no chance forced to carry on. A snowball rule that ends the game quickly may not feel like a snowball at all.

ideas.name: Split score from power to limit snowball
ideas.text: Victory points that cannot be spent, as in sports and European boardgames, break the loop. The cost is a more complicated game. Races do it naturally, and drafting even harms the leader.

ideas.name: Sometimes add snowball on purpose
ideas.text: If a game drags or leaves players waiting, rewards for knocking a player out, as in Risk, make a near-hopeless player's elimination end it. Having 0 percent chance and leaving is preferred to staying in with 1 percent.

ideas.name: Randomness is a catch-up feature
ideas.text: Even an even-handed shake-up, like everyone rolling dice and moving forward or everyone going back to start, helps the one behind more than the leader. Players behind look for high-variance lines and players ahead look for simple ones.

ideas.name: Catch-up rules are usually added on purpose
ideas.text: Mario Kart's shells fire forward, so only those behind can use them, and the Spiny Shell homes in on first place. Some racing games speed up cars that are behind. Warcraft III taxes large armies.

ideas.name: A lead in a game with catch-up is not a big lead
ideas.text: A twenty-square lead in Chutes and Ladders may be worth no more than five squares without the chutes. The real measure of being ahead is the chance of winning, not the distance.

ideas.name: Track win chances as a list that adds to one
ideas.text: Each player's chance of winning is written down at each moment. The spread of the list shows whether the game is snowballing, as it widens, or catching up, as it narrows.
