ideas.name: Hurting the leader and helping the follower are the same
ideas.text: When chances go from 70 and 30 percent to 60 and 40, both things happen. In the model, one player's gain is always another's loss.

ideas.name: Catch-up may be only apparent
ideas.text: If players understand a catch-up rule, a big lead in score is really a small lead in chance of winning, and nobody was ever far behind. Catch-up is real against a simple score-based rule of thumb even when it is not real against win chance.

ideas.name: Two kinds of real catch-up
ideas.text: One kind caps how far apart the chances can get until near the end. The other ends the game for the leader or levels it up when chances spread too far. In a duel the first shooter is ahead only until he misses.

ideas.name: Catch-up keeps a simple and a deeper rule of thumb
ideas.text: A beginner follows the score, and an advanced player learns how the catch-up feature distorts it. This adds a step to climb in the heuristics tree.

ideas.name: A coin-flip catch-up makes leads change often
ideas.text: A missile that may hit or miss makes the lead look random and exciting. Taken too far, sophisticated players see the lead as meaningless and lose interest.

ideas.name: The hardest place is a game you cannot win
ideas.text: The harshest problem of a small chance to win is not losing but playing on with too low a chance. Catch-up that ends or evens out games helps the player behind.

ideas.name: Snowball has useful effects and catch-up has costly ones
ideas.text: Snowball controls length and helps elimination. Catch-up can make early choices irrelevant, spoil the score as a guide, give kingmaking power to the last-place player and lengthen the game.

ideas.name: Over-catch-up empties the middle of the game
ideas.text: If being second pays as well, players avoid getting ahead and everything but the final moves stops mattering. A game where being first is punished becomes less enjoyable once players realise.

ideas.name: Long games need ways to catch up
ideas.text: In a ten-hour game, a player clearly losing for several hours is in too long a state of near-certain loss. Grinding in an RPG lets the player catch up at will, though heavy catch-up can make early choices matter little.

ideas.name: Quiet difficulty adjustment backfires
ideas.text: Players who play well want to be rewarded and will eventually find out, through the internet, that the game was equalising outcomes. It feels like being cheated on.

ideas.name: Players drift apart in skill too
ideas.text: A dozen people who learn chess together will spread in skill over months, so some are permanently losing the have-the-most-skill game. More skilled players teaching less skilled ones works as a catch-up feature.

ideas.name: Who a catch-up rule hits shapes the game
ideas.text: Hurting the leader leads to play for second, hurting a chosen player leads to a political game, and hurting a near player leads to clumps. Each target gives a different style of play.

ideas.name: Audience decides how much catch-up
ideas.text: In a children's race a catch-up feature is likely to be taken at face value. A limit that keeps the loser at 1 percent of the leader's chance may not hold many players, while one at 40 percent may scare off competitive ones.

ideas.name: Press your luck means choosing more or less randomness
ideas.text: Players behind choose riskier plays and those ahead choose safer ones. Hail Mary passes in football, three-point shots in basketball and Can't Stop show it.

ideas.name: A game is a series of interesting choices
ideas.text: Sid Meier's definition counts choices as the core. What matters to players is the number of meaningful choices, which depends on skill. Games with no choices are mostly gambling.

ideas.name: Too few or too many choices spoil a game
ideas.text: Nim and tic-tac-toe between experts have one right move, so there is hardly a game. Beginners at go or in a complex RPG character build feel they are choosing at random.

ideas.name: Most games rise and fall in choices
ideas.text: Monopoly starts with few decisions, has most in the midgame with trades and building, then settles again. Oh Hell builds this in with a changing hand size. Crosswords and solitaire follow the same arc.

ideas.name: Different players feel the arc differently
ideas.text: A beginner at chess has to think hard in the opening, since openings are not learned. A beginner in go is overwhelmed and cannot tell when the game ends. Experts prune the early game with set openings.

ideas.name: Starting with everything gives a falling arc
ideas.text: Risk, Warhammer and Myth begin with a full army and get simpler. Reinforcement rules bring them closer to the classic arc.

ideas.name: Sports and short-atom games have a flat arc
ideas.text: Basketball is about as complex in the first quarter as the third. A tournament is much the same in hour one and hour five. A flat arc is one cost of small atoms.

ideas.name: A raid has an arc even when a character does not
ideas.text: An MMO raid starts with few decisions, builds to a boss fight and ends quickly. This session-sized arc gives the story-like satisfaction, while the raid leader has a rising arc.

ideas.name: Locking options early builds the arc
ideas.text: Strategy games and trading card games make many options unavailable at first and enable them slowly, so the late game is very bushy and may end suddenly with the tree still wide.

ideas.name: Imbalance is a smaller tree than intended
ideas.text: A balance problem means the game offers many choices on paper but only a few are viable. Players then repeat the same ones, and the heuristics shrink to play only the more powerful options.

ideas.name: What counts as balanced depends on the genre
ideas.text: In a strategy game each unit is expected to be useful, so one unit that wins everything is broken. In an MMO most items are expected to be less useful than the top item, so a lot of low-value items is normal but a single dominant helmet is not.

ideas.name: Balance exists at beginner level too
ideas.text: A rush in a strategy game that needs intermediate skill to defend against is a beginner imbalance. Small differences matter more at expert level, so designers worry most there.

ideas.name: More options can mean fewer real options
ideas.text: Adding a less powerful class to six classes leaves an expert with six choices. Adding a more powerful class leaves only one. Banning a card or restricting colours in Magic can increase the number of viable decks.

ideas.name: A new dominant option leaves a design quandary
ideas.text: If one choice is far more effective, the rest of the game has to be tuned either for those who chose well, which crushes the others, or for those who chose badly, which bores the others.

ideas.name: Three degrees of imbalance
ideas.text: An option can be too low-powered, which is sometimes fine. It can be too powerful and drive out its own type, such as the top helmet. Or it can be so powerful it drives out nearly every other choice and decides the game.

ideas.name: A cost lets powerful things exist
ideas.text: If a player may bring as many queens as wanted, something has to offset the queen. A price lets Starcraft have both battlecruisers and marines.

ideas.name: Separate cost from effect to tune balance
ideas.text: The designer picks the effect she wants and then adjusts the cost until things balance. This is easier than adjusting every effect. The price is extra complication, and big games still need bans and fixes.

ideas.name: Triangles protect against collapse
ideas.text: Built-in rock-paper-scissors loops, such as colour A beating B beating C beating A, guarantee a minimum amount of choice. Even if rock only beat paper 10 percent of the time all three would stay in use.

ideas.name: Uncertainty is close to necessary for a game
ideas.text: If a player who never errs at tic-tac-toe or Nim is just running a procedure, the game has gone. Most games sit where there are meaningful decisions and no way to play without error every time.

ideas.name: Luck is not the opposite of skill
ideas.text: Chess and poker both have a lot of skill though poker has much more luck. Tic-tac-toe and slot machines both have little skill though one has no luck and the other nothing but. The two vary independently.

ideas.name: A game with luck is one where a beginner can beat an expert
ideas.text: Two evenly matched Candyland players and two evenly matched chess players both have 50/50 chances. The difference is that a beginner at chess has essentially no chance against Kasparov.

ideas.name: Beginners' games feel more random
ideas.text: Remove a pawn from a game between two beginners and the chances move to 55/45. Do it between experts and it goes to 70/30. Expert games are more sensitive to small advantages.

ideas.name: Luck arrives from four places
ideas.text: Overt random elements, random setup such as who goes first or who sits where, simultaneous choices, and human nature, as when players pick among apparently equal options.

ideas.name: A deterministic game can play as random
ideas.text: Guess the Digit of pi is fixed but a coin flip in practice. Clock solitaire has an outcome set by the deal but unknown to the player, so it counts as random.

ideas.name: People see streaks that are not there
ideas.text: Hot or cold hands in games are often patterns found in random sequences.

ideas.name: Serious games drive luck out
ideas.text: Games with little luck can only be won with a lot of effort, which drives out those unwilling. Designers who are serious players also tend to remove luck.

ideas.name: Reasons players dislike luck
ideas.text: Skilled players want their skill rewarded and want to feel in charge of their fate. A chess player quit backgammon after learning one can make the right move and lose because of it. Luck adds complexity and makes learning harder, because it is hard to tell a losing move from ill luck.

ideas.name: Low luck does not make skilled players win more
ideas.text: Players seek opponents near their own level so win rates drift toward 50/50. In low-luck online games the lower-skilled players leave. Matchmaking pushes everyone toward even odds, though it still makes more even games.

ideas.name: Luck widens who you can play against
ideas.text: A chess player needs a nearly equal partner. Backgammon or cribbage can be played with a spouse or a friend who is much more or less skilled.

ideas.name: Luck lets players blame the dice
ideas.text: Players take credit for wins and blame fate for losses. Casual players with luck also try out styles of play more freely.

ideas.name: Luck makes odd positions that break stagnation
ideas.text: Fischer Random Chess uses randomness against memorised openings. NetHack and Diablo get replay from random dungeons and items.

ideas.name: Luck reduces the load of calculating
ideas.text: Games with more randomness often ask less of players in reading out long sequences of moves.

ideas.name: Dice rolls pull attention
ideas.text: The table at a D&D game watches an important roll to hit, and in late Monopoly everyone watches a roll that may land on a developed property.

ideas.name: Players choose what luck they accept
ideas.text: Expert players dislike luck because it makes them lose and casual players like it. A new game in an old genre, or a sequel, has trouble adding luck. Fluid new genres accept it more easily.

ideas.name: Games evolve toward less luck
ideas.text: Bridge has a dummy that whist lacked, and chess once had dice. Expert pressure can push a game toward fewer people wanting to play it, like a peacock's tail.

ideas.name: Simultaneous-choice randomness is often not seen as luck
ideas.text: Players who dislike dice and cards usually accept uncertainty that comes from their own and their opponents' choices.

ideas.name: Put the randomness at the front
ideas.text: Players tend to like being dealt a hand and working out how to play it, more than planning an attack and then rolling to see if it works. A game that feels decided early, as by an RTS race choice, is too much unless it is very short.

ideas.name: Team Fortress 2 added critical hits for broad appeal
ideas.text: Wild random critical hits were added, testers found the game more enjoyable without knowing why, and hardcore players complained when they understood. Two years on the team counted it a success.

ideas.name: Die-rolling chess keeps all the skill and lowers the reward
ideas.text: Roll a die after chess: 1-2 first player wins, 3-4 second wins, 5-6 chess winner wins. All chess books still apply, but a 60 percent chess winner wins only 53 percent.

ideas.name: The skill chain measures what skill earns
ideas.text: Chess with its little luck has a chain of about 30 steps on the Elo scale, and die-rolling chess about 10. Luck shortens the chain. A tiny game like tic-tac-toe has a short chain from lack of depth.

ideas.name: Skill belongs to the players
ideas.text: How much skill a game has depends on its community of players. On a planet of geniuses chess would be as flat as tic-tac-toe, and on a planet of fools tic-tac-toe would have a long chain of levels. Guess the Digit has a chain of one.

ideas.name: Knowledge can stretch or squash the skill chain
ideas.text: A new strategy game spreads players as they learn it, so random pairings become lopsided. A game that gets solved, like Nim, or one with a powerful easy-to-learn set of rules of thumb, can collapse the chain.

ideas.name: Luck is hard to measure
ideas.text: One way is to see how often a low-ranked player beats a high-ranked one, but extremes are hard to measure and depend on the player base. Another is to take three players each beating the next 60 percent of the time and see how often the first beats the third.

ideas.name: Skill needs a time unit to compare
ideas.text: Longer sessions make a more skilled player almost certain to win, so a skill chain can be stretched by playing longer. Games are compared per unit of time, such as a series of five of one game against a series of three of another.

ideas.name: Skill grows quickest in a new community
ideas.text: Gaining skill depends on luck, on whether the game can be understood, and on useful tools like experienced players, teachers and strategy books. A new game with a young community gives fast improvement.

ideas.name: Luck wears down the return on skill slowly, politics cuts it off
ideas.text: Added luck lowers the return to skill gradually, so there is always some reason to learn. Enough politics makes skill at the game worth nothing, as in chip-taking chess.

ideas.name: Returns to study always shrink
ideas.text: Players learn the most productive rules of thumb first and then more obscure ones, so the thousandth hour of study gains less than the first even in a game without luck.

ideas.name: Skill versus luck is the wrong question for poker
ideas.text: Poker has a large amount of both, and one does not reduce the other. Luck lowers what skill earns in a single hand and not the skill itself.

ideas.name: Hidden information comes in three kinds
ideas.text: There is private information such as a card in my hand, puzzlelike information the player has to work out, and randomness that nobody knows yet, like a die roll.

ideas.name: Private information needs randomness behind it
ideas.text: If hidden facts came out obvious and fixed, both players would know them, so private information is usually produced by a random process like a shuffle or a secret simultaneous choice.

ideas.name: Puzzle information is used up
ideas.text: Nobody wants to do the same crossword or play Myst again once they know the secret. Roguelikes and Mastermind remake their secrets each time, so they can be replayed.

ideas.name: Hidden information shares benefits with randomness
ideas.text: It can be a more acceptable kind of luck, control calculation, give surprise and discovery, and give gameplay in bluffing and deduction. Scouting in strategy games and reading opponents' hands in cards are attempts to uncover it.

ideas.name: Hidden information has costs too
ideas.text: It can add memorising and branching sums, such as playing differently if a king is on the left or right. It is awkward for spectators, and chess and go keep a pure appeal by having none.

ideas.name: Random damage hides breakpoints
ideas.text: If a unit always dealt the same damage, a small upgrade might change a kill from three hits to two, and players would have to remember all such breakpoints. A little randomness washes them out.

ideas.name: Cost is anything between you and the game
ideas.text: Money, time to learn, space, risk of injury and a fast connection are all costs. Some are required, some effectively required, some helpful and some optional.

ideas.name: Preparation varies more than play
ideas.text: NBA games last about as long as a pickup game, but the preparation differs enormously. Some games force preparation, such as a well-equipped character for a raid or a deck for Magic.

ideas.name: Games cost players differently by business model
ideas.text: A game can be unprofitable like tag, sold as equipment, sold as a box, rented, pay to play, or object-based. The model decides what the game looks like to a buyer.

ideas.name: Players can swap one cost for another
ideas.text: Pads trade money for injury risk, rented skis for the cost of buying, and caddies for carrying. Letting time-rich and money-short players trade with money-rich and time-short ones widens the audience, as in buying cards in Magic or gold in World of Warcraft.

ideas.name: Web games win by costing nothing extra
ideas.text: Web games and Minesweeper need no special hardware, which is part of why they are played so widely.

ideas.name: Physical skill is a cost
ideas.text: Games need no physical skill, only eye-hand coordination, or broad physical skill. The more different skills a game needs, the smaller its pool of players.

ideas.name: Faster turns make a game twitchier
ideas.text: A timed chess game is nearly non-twitch, but Starcraft is like Civilization with millisecond turns. It trades less downtime for more skill needed. Few players will accept a game that asks for a hundred productive clicks a minute.

ideas.name: Out-of-reach attributes act like money costs
ideas.text: Height in basketball or very high APM in Starcraft cannot be trained by everyone. People who think they lack it stay away, as they do from yacht racing.

ideas.name: Roles and the metagame need different skills
ideas.text: A quarterback and a lineman, a rogue and a priest, a raid leader and a raider all need different skills. Training discipline and building social networks are metagame skills.

ideas.name: Incompatible skills shrink the audience
ideas.text: Some strategy fans stay with turn-based games because they think real-time is out of reach. Chessboxing joins two skills on purpose, and most games do it by accident.

ideas.name: Getting up to the level of the pack is a cost
ideas.text: It is easy to start chess among casual players and hard when everyone you know is rated 1800 or more. High-luck games lower the barrier since a modest effort lets you win a few games.

ideas.name: A shrinking pool makes entry harder
ideas.text: Low-skilled players leave a low-luck game, so the next beginners face a harder level. Those who were mid-pack become bottom and leave, until a few expert players remain. Fighting games are an example.

ideas.name: Costs can spiral past what players expected
ideas.text: Raiding takes more time for building a character than for the raid. Magic's cost of building a deck rose far beyond the original vision, and the makers spent heavily to cap it. People who learn the true cost may choose not to start.

ideas.name: Match players by what they will invest
ideas.text: Friends, local groups, sports leagues and beginner tournaments all do this. Online, ratings, friend lists and guilds help, though smurfing gets round them. Training and tutorials help new players get up to speed.

ideas.name: Enjoyment needs a more specific word
ideas.text: The authors treat the casual word for enjoyment as too broad and ask which reward a game offers. Rewards include winning, playing well, challenge, aesthetics, excitement, escape and social time.

ideas.name: Rewards continue outside the game
ideas.text: Playgroups remember who won and tell stories, arcade games keep high scores, and Xbox and City of Heroes award badges. Improving at the game is a pleasure in itself.

ideas.name: Games exercise body and mind
ideas.text: Physical games are accepted as exercise, and mental games also give mental fitness. Many non-educational games like Civilization teach knowledge.

ideas.name: Social rewards come before and after play
ideas.text: During the game everyone is busy, but a high school football team or D&D group can form lifelong bonds, and status comes from the group.

ideas.name: Money turns up a game's stakes
ideas.text: Poker needs money to be satisfying, backgammon is improved by it because of the doubling cube, and slots would be uninteresting without it. Bridge players treat points as if they were money.

ideas.name: Gamblers buy a thrill more than a profit
ideas.text: Most gamblers do not expect to come out ahead. They pay for fantasy about money, a kind of status, and the thrill of risk, as with the price of a scary film.

ideas.name: In-game loot sits between reward and mechanic
ideas.text: Loot, virtual currency and experience give power, which distinguishes them from other achievements like beating a monster alone.

ideas.name: Downtime is the most when many players take turns
ideas.text: In a many-player turn-based game with little interaction, a player waits through everyone else's turns. In Titan two players stop to play a miniature wargame while the rest wait.

ideas.name: Share and length of downtime both matter
ideas.text: Poker has plenty of sitting out but never for long, while hockey players play most of the time but sit out for stretches.

ideas.name: Downtime is useful for thinking if the position stays put
ideas.text: Chess nearly needs the opponent's turn for thinking. Random draws at the end of a turn instead of the start help players plan ahead. With many players, the position changes too much to plan ahead.

ideas.name: Make other people's turns interesting
ideas.text: In Monopoly the most useful event for you, someone landing on your property and paying, happens on others' turns, so everyone watches.

ideas.name: No downtime is exhausting
ideas.text: Indoor soccer, where the ball never goes out, tires players more than regular soccer, which tires more than football or baseball. Pauses give players a rest.

ideas.name: Fast AIs hide downtime but online players feel it
ideas.text: In a turn-based game against computer opponents the computer plays at once. Made multiplayer, every long turn is waited through. Real-time strategy removed downtime but added clicking speed and no rest.

ideas.name: Poker lets you pay to avoid downtime
ideas.text: Players stay in hands they ought to leave just to avoid sitting out, and online players run several tables at once.

ideas.name: Busywork has no decision in it
ideas.text: If the player makes no choice, or an arbitrary one, and cannot do it well or badly, it is busywork. Rounding the bases after a home run is busywork that players enjoy, since it marks a big moment.

ideas.name: What is busywork depends on experience
ideas.text: Walking between shops in a first RPG is exciting and in later ones numbing. A beginner finds the Dots and Boxes opening arbitrary, and an expert finds the late game fixed, so both are busywork.

ideas.name: Play can go from baffling, to interesting, to mechanical
ideas.text: Chess, go and Nim all have beginner moves that feel arbitrary and expert moves that are known sequences. Workable beginner rules of thumb fix the first stage, and expert rules of thumb that are not fully deterministic fix the last.

ideas.name: Old games lose busywork
ideas.text: Backgammon went from pieces off the board to starting in play and then to an interesting start, with the doubling cube shortening won games. Chess got faster pawns, castling and the queen. MMOs added questing over grinding and mounts.

ideas.name: Cutting busywork can bring it back
ideas.text: Graphical RPG inventories added the busywork of fitting items in boxes, fixed by auto-arrange and one slot per item. Easier management then led to bigger inventories.

ideas.name: Players skip efforts that return too little
ideas.text: Card counting, memorising chess openings, diving for the ball and conditioning are refused by casual players. A game works or not for an audience by the ratio of reward to effort it asks of them.

ideas.name: A group sets how much effort is expected
ideas.text: A new player in a group that counts cards may feel pushed to do the same, and suffers downtime and fewer wins if not. A serious newcomer in a casual group is told to take it easy.

ideas.name: Calculation pays less and less
ideas.text: In hearts, tracking the queen of spades pays a lot, while tracking every card by player and time pays little more. A game where each extra effort pays less gives experts something to do while beginners keep up.

ideas.name: Chess depth has diminishing returns
ideas.text: Looking one or two moves ahead pays hugely, and looking six instead of four pays little for far more effort. Players naturally learn the highest-paying skills first.

ideas.name: Luck flattens the reward for effort
ideas.text: In hearts, poker or Monopoly an expert's edge over a beginner is small. In chess or go the gap is large, so beginners and experts cannot play together.

ideas.name: Increasing returns to calculation punish beginners
ideas.text: Reading out a sequence to the end is worth a lot and reading four-fifths of it is worth little, as in go life-and-death problems. This makes an arms race that drives people out.

ideas.name: End-of-game arithmetic spoils point games
ideas.text: In go and European boardgames the late game becomes working out exactly what each play does to the score, which may not suit the audience that enjoys the rest.

ideas.name: Rules of thumb reduce the need to calculate
ideas.text: The hearts rule of playing the highest non-winning card saves a lot of counting. Sound heuristics turn lots of calculation paying big into paying a diminishing amount.

ideas.name: Steep reward curves please but do not suit casual groups
ideas.text: Everyone likes seeing effort pay off, but steep curves widen the gap between players. Single-player games can have them since the computer opponents are matched to the player.

ideas.name: Some efforts pay off later or first make things slip
ideas.text: A golfer changing a swing or a fighting-game player learning combos performs lower for a while before improving. Tennis and snowboarding give almost nothing until the basics are learned, which is why people learn twenty boardgames a year and not twenty sports.

ideas.name: Make the enjoyable way the winning way
ideas.text: If a dull grind is the quickest way to advance, some players will quit in disgust, and giving more reward for grinding only makes the grind more attractive. The way that wins most ought to be the enjoyable way.

ideas.name: Several ways to deal with a thankless task
ideas.text: Remove it, raise the reward if it is not unpleasant, cut the effort, or make it hard enough that few bother. Hiding each player's gold stops everyone counting everyone's money.

ideas.name: Letting everyone see the discard pile cuts memory work
ideas.text: It costs time, as players keep looking at it. A designer has to weigh the speed lost against the memory saved.

ideas.name: Randomness and hidden information weaken calculation
ideas.text: Dice in miniatures games and random damage in strategy games stop players from memorising exact outcomes. Bridge's dummy goes the other way and raises the reward of calculating.

ideas.name: Metagame gives rewards the game does not
ideas.text: Status, socialising, self-expression, mastery, money and trophies often come from outside the play. A tournament structure can make rock-paper-scissors entertaining for adults.

ideas.name: The metagame is a place to put design effort
ideas.text: Knowing which metagame structures pay off, such as ratings, leagues, forums and strategy guides, is important. A diagram of life goals and the features supporting each shows where a game has most support.

ideas.name: A microclimate can be mistaken for the game
ideas.text: A player may say chess is wonderful or dull when the group around the game is what is wonderful or dull.

ideas.name: Too many formats split the players
ideas.text: Twelve players at a store where half want sealed and half want constructed make no tournament of eight. Pick three or four of the possible settings and not all twelve switches. People prefer their second choice happening to their first choice being offered but not played.

ideas.name: Downtime gives chat time
ideas.text: An MMO has long waits for a raid to form and the chance to socialise. Small features like a custom chat channel affect how well players can socialise.

ideas.name: Collecting can become its own activity
ideas.text: Magic cards, golf clubs or bike gear are useful in the game, but collecting them can be a metagame activity. Kids who collect Pokemon cards and do not play are players of the metagame, not the game.

ideas.name: Styles and personalities give status
ideas.text: Poker players and sports stars build recognisable styles. A game needs enough ways to play for this, and basketball does where sprinting does not. Titles and visible armour in an MMO are built in for expression.

ideas.name: Cash prizes win respect from outsiders
ideas.text: Winning a large sum persuades relatives who did not follow the game. Ratings and titles are understood mostly inside the community.

ideas.name: Changing the game base can disturb the metagame
ideas.text: Making some cards rarer to support collecting for money could turn a game of skill into one of how much you paid at the start.

ideas.name: Games are cheaper to understand with a familiar conceit
ideas.text: In Magic a dragon outranks an ogre and a Sword of X helps attack. A made-up setting is easier to own but harder to learn. A purely abstract game needs very simple rules, though a simple rule set like go can still give a deep game.

ideas.name: Conceit explains the action
ideas.text: Clue would be less compelling as a purely abstract boardgame. Conceits have been added to games since about 1900, and as early as the sixteenth-century Royal Game of Goose.

ideas.name: Sports build a world around themselves
ideas.text: Baseball's rules are public but the history, heroes and customs around the professional game are ownable. The book reads this as IP of the metagame.

ideas.name: Realism and play pull against each other
ideas.text: A game that models its conceit closely needs many rules because that is how it works in real life. Uno has none, and Squad Leader has a huge number. Partial simulations have to decide how far to go, and players disagree.

ideas.name: Conceits run from none to a full simulation
ideas.text: The authors list ten steps from tic-tac-toe at the abstract end, through chess, Monopoly and Starcraft, to Squad Leader. Full simulations are complex and have small audiences.

ideas.name: Realism can bring a built-in loss
ideas.text: Some wargames let the historical winner nearly always destroy the other side, and the losing player wins by lasting longer. People who dislike realism go elsewhere without complaint.

ideas.name: A licence gives a quick start but a short life
ideas.text: A licensed game has a built-in audience, but it dies with the property and does not reach people who dislike the property. A licensed 1965 card game based on Crazy Eights is forgotten, while the unlicensed Uno of 1971 became a classic.

ideas.name: Licences suit crowded markets
ideas.text: A first-of-its-kind game can use a generic conceit that grows into its own property. A crowded market may need a licence to stand out, but licensed games are almost never long-run hits.

ideas.name: People buy the licence for the licence
ideas.text: If the conceit is a main reason to buy, it is nearly always licensed, as with Battlestar Galactica. Few buy Warcraft games for the Warcraft property. Games are not a reliable way to get people to love a new property, since books and films tell stories more effectively.

ideas.name: Designing the property with the game
ideas.text: Pokemon and Yu-Gi-Oh were designed with the game in mind, and the game players play mirrors the game the characters play. Playing, watching and following the back-story then support each other, as in sports.

ideas.name: Who gets to be the hero
ideas.text: A game with a well-known property that has one or two heroes has to choose between the player being him, which locks it to one player, and cameos, which make the player feel small.

ideas.name: Stories are new in games
ideas.text: Traditional boardgames and card games have none. Early computer games had none, and now almost all do, apart from rhythm, sports and puzzle games. Reading a book between chess turns would not work.

ideas.name: Story and game pull apart
ideas.text: A game worth replaying branches and plays differently each time, while a satisfying story feels inevitable. A heavy story can make a game less replayable, as with Final Fantasy VII against Diablo. Adventure games, being puzzles, lose little.

ideas.name: Even a simple story helps
ideas.text: Games like Doom and Diablo get value from a minimal story in setting expectations, explaining mechanics and motivating goals. Players disagree on how much story matters.

ideas.name: Retelling a game is a kind of watching
ideas.text: Games with highlights, such as football, are easier to recount than continuous ones such as a marathon, and a box score shows how well a game condenses. Tournament poker with big single hands recounts more easily than home poker.

ideas.name: Sports are easy to watch
ideas.text: A five-minute explanation is enough for soccer and chess needs more. People already understand physics, so a dunk or a diving catch is seen as astonishing by everyone, while a brilliant strategy-game move gets blank looks.

ideas.name: Simple state helps watchers
ideas.text: Sports are mostly the score. Poker between hands needs only chip counts, chess shows all its state, and a strategy game hides a large amount. Football's strip with the down and yards, and the coloured line on screen, fixed what the game lacked.

ideas.name: Hidden information hurts watching
ideas.text: Draw poker is duller to watch than stud, and a bridge kibitzer has to move between players. The hole cam made revealing secrets appealing. Computer games where each player has a private screen have hardly any public information.

ideas.name: Watching spreads a game
ideas.text: If it is easy to watch, understand and imagine yourself playing, the game spreads. An audience inspires players to practise and some watchers later play.

ideas.name: Change rules for the watchers
ideas.text: The shot clock in basketball, tiebreakers in tennis and soccer and instant replay in football were partly to improve watching. Tokugawa-era go games before the shogun were played in advance, then replayed, to keep spectators from sitting too long.

ideas.name: Customisation has three levels
ideas.text: Personal style, house rules and choices built into the game. With wide customisation the game feels like a family of games, one for each choice.

ideas.name: Players who customise become balancers
ideas.text: A group adding a Free Parking prize is acting as a game balancer. A player picking a character is choosing for their own benefit, which makes balancing hard.

ideas.name: Some games invite changes
ideas.text: Calvinball, Eleusis, Icehouse, Fluxx and dealer's choice poker are meant to be modified. Chess can be extended by making new pieces, while go is hard to change without making a new game.

ideas.name: Heavy customisation brings attachment and cost
ideas.text: Players grow attached to my character or my deck, but balance gets harder and they expect a stream of new content. Building skills differ from playing skills, and expert templates can put off those who want to build their own.

ideas.name: Balance towards the choices players want
ideas.text: Where players want a flavourful build, keep it within striking distance of the most powerful build.

ideas.name: Guilds make house rules
ideas.text: An MMO that cannot be modded still grows rules, such as a guild's DKP system.

ideas.name: A handicap works when there is a spare quantity
ideas.text: Go has stones, golf has points, and horse racing has weight. Chess cannot lose a piece without becoming a different game, but speed chess can give different times. A handicap also needs ratings so players can see what would make an even game.

ideas.name: Cheating depends on the game
ideas.text: It is hardest in turn-based games with no hidden information, like chess. Random elements, hidden information and real-time play make it easier to hide. Battleship is easy to cheat at and nearly impossible to catch.

ideas.name: Some rule breaking is not called cheating
ideas.text: Offside in football or a desperate handball in soccer are against the rules, but they are easy to catch, have a referee and a fair penalty, are not meant to injure and can happen by accident. Steroids are hard to detect, injure and are not accidental, so they are cheating.

ideas.name: Moderate rule breaking adds drama
ideas.text: Much of sport's excitement comes from violations and penalties, with heroes and villains. This needs referees to catch the violators at least a fair amount of the time.

ideas.name: Suspicion of cheating also harms
ideas.text: Skilled Starcraft players get accused of map hacking. The perception of cheating can drive honest players away, who feel they are falling behind or have to work harder than cheaters.

ideas.name: The code is the referee in a computer game
ideas.text: Cheating usually needs changing the code. The client knows the full state, so there is no way to be sure a player is not using it. Cheats built into a shipped game are more like another difficulty setting.

ideas.name: Sharp play depends on the group
ideas.text: Casual groups find rushing in a strategy game, powerful decks or ringers a breach of manners. Taking back a move is cheating in a serious group and refusing one is sharp in a very casual group.

ideas.name: Sharp play is a gap between rules and spirit
ideas.text: Players see a move as in the rules but against the spirit of the game, much as a law can be obeyed and still give an unjust result. It shows that the rules are not the game.

ideas.name: One person's exploit is another's clever play
ideas.text: Players always look for clever ways to get ahead, so branding them cheaters for a route the designers did not intend is a burden. A patch that removes the behaviour is different from punishing the player.

ideas.name: Announce the style before play
ideas.text: A casual strategy game may announce 20 minutes of no rush. If the assumption is not stated and others do not share it, there is resentment.

ideas.name: Griefing needs out-of-game answers
ideas.text: There are too many ways to annoy people to prevent inside the rules. Offline, others refuse to play with the griefer. Guilds, reputation scores and lasting identities can do it online.

ideas.name: Treat misbehaviour as a balance problem
ideas.text: The question is whether it makes the game less enjoyable for most players. If the system allows too much misbehaviour the fault is with the design. Change the incentives and enforce the rules, since asking players to play as intended rarely works.

ideas.name: Large groups need written conduct rules
ideas.text: Small regular groups can enforce behaviour socially. Anonymous communities need formal rules, such as deck registration in Magic, touch-move in chess and tournament penalties.

ideas.name: A game can last a lifetime or an hour
ideas.text: Tic-tac-toe and chess are similar in structure, yet one gives an hour and the other more than a lifetime. A long lifetime is a goal a game may have, not a defect where it is absent.

ideas.name: Business model decides how long play needs to last
ideas.text: Subscription and object-sale games need long lifetimes. A boxed game can succeed if players feel they got value and stop. Diablo II sold for ten years on repeat play value.

ideas.name: People quit because they are bored or finished
ideas.text: Players blame other events, but in multiplayer games the usual answer is that friends stopped playing. A game can only be finished if it has an ending, which sports and chess do not.

ideas.name: Two ways to hold interest
ideas.text: Offer content to be consumed, which runs out, or offer variability that comes from other players. Soccer and chess stay interesting because opponents keep changing the pressure.

ideas.name: Multiply content, not just add it
ideas.text: Random layouts, such as solitaire deals and NetHack dungeons, character classes, difficulty levels and customisation each make existing content go further.

ideas.name: An ending invites stopping
ideas.text: RPG and puzzle endings and level caps are natural stopping points. Replay assumes there was an end, since nobody replays soccer. Post-completion goals such as player-versus-player play keep people going.

ideas.name: Goals keep play going
ideas.text: Goals can be linear, like harder opponents, or independent, like winning with only marines. A large goal like finishing the story keeps interest and also gives a place to stop.

ideas.name: Global leaderboards feel out of reach
ideas.text: Topping Pac-Man at the local arcade is possible and making the top ten among everyone online is not. Smaller pools such as a guild, server or friends restore the sense it is possible.

ideas.name: Break fine scores into chunks
ideas.text: Dance Dance Revolution adds a letter grade to its points, runners aim for under four hours, and chess has master and grandmaster. Chunks make goals compelling and give stopping points.

ideas.name: In multiplayer games the opponents supply the goal
ideas.text: Winning against them renews itself and gets harder as you improve. A single-player game has to add goals like harder difficulty, achievements and collecting every creature.

ideas.name: Von Neumann theory studies simultaneous single moves
ideas.text: Its subject is games like rock-paper-scissors where two players move at once, encoded in a payoff matrix, looking for equilibrium points. Most of its games are made up to show the core of a bigger problem.

ideas.name: Rock-paper-scissors is the model of balanced choices
ideas.text: In Warcraft III melee beats ranged, ranged beats air and air beats melee. A designer wants every viable strategy neither to dominate nor be dominated by the others.

ideas.name: Delete dominated choices to see what is left
ideas.text: Removing options that pay less whatever the opponent does, one after another, solves many simple games. If only one choice is left for each player, the game has fully collapsed.

ideas.name: The result that looks right may cost both
ideas.text: In the prisoner's dilemma each player betrays and both end with less than if both kept quiet. Change the payoffs, for example by penalising betrayal later, and the result changes.

ideas.name: Two stable outcomes need coordination
ideas.text: In Battle of the Sexes both choosing the same outing is stable, but each prefers a different one and independent players cannot settle which.

ideas.name: Populations behave like Hawks and Doves
ideas.text: A lone hawk does well among doves and a lone dove does well among hawks. In Magic, decks with a chance of beating other decks act this way, though a clever player can predict the field and bring a deck to exploit it.

ideas.name: An unbeatable plan can be random
ideas.text: In rock-paper-scissors, rolling a die to pick each option cannot be beaten even if announced. The price is never doing more than even, even against a player who always plays rock.

ideas.name: Every game has a stable mix
ideas.text: Allowing mixed strategies, every game has an equilibrium. It may not be unique, may not be the highest-paying outcome and may be hard to find.

ideas.name: Positions can be treated as games
ideas.text: In combinatorial theory every position is a game of its own. A position where the first player always loses is called 0, and two unlinked positions are added together by letting players move in either.

ideas.name: Mirroring shows a game minus itself is zero
ideas.text: If a second player copies every move made in a mirror-image game, they never run out of moves first. This is also a workable strategy in games such as two-pile Nim.

ideas.name: Hot positions are worth grabbing
ideas.text: In Domineering a spot that gives whoever takes it another move is hot, and a player wants it before the opponent does.

ideas.name: Von Neumann theory helps design more than analysis
ideas.text: It rarely analyses real games but gives a way of thinking about subgames inside them. Conway's theory can analyse real games like go but only in its narrow domain.

ideas.name: Chess piece values are not in the rules
ideas.text: Players give a pawn one point, a knight three and a castle five, and add up captured pieces to see who is ahead. It is an informal score that came from play.

ideas.name: A hidden-information game for two can be a guessing game
ideas.text: Battleship has each player hide ships on a grid and guess the other's. Clue hides three cards and players ask questions. Mastermind hides a colour code and tells only how many pegs are right.

ideas.name: Blackjack rewards skill against the house
ideas.text: It is unusual among house games because with flawless play the player is favoured, and the house relies on how hard it is to play without a flaw.

ideas.name: Nim is random for a beginner
ideas.text: A new player cannot tell one move from another until close to the end, so they play at random, and once the strategy is known every move but one is equal.

ideas.name: Cosmic Encounter shares wins on purpose
ideas.text: Each turn a random opponent is attacked, which stops lasting alliances, and more than one player can win together. Dune has a complex set of victory conditions that let groups share a win.

ideas.name: Settlers of Catan uses typical European design
ideas.text: A light theme, random elements, victory points that differ from the resources used for actions, a random board and several routes to victory.

ideas.name: Rules that change each deal
ideas.text: In Barbu the scoring changes every deal in a set order, so every round asks for a different way to play.

ideas.name: One stage of a game can differ from another
ideas.text: Skitgubbe has a stage where cards are collected and one where they are got rid of, which work completely differently. Pinochle has bidding, melding and trick taking.

ideas.name: A game can be a thought experiment
ideas.text: The authors made up toy games, such as the chip-taking game, die-rolling chess and the balloon game, to isolate one feature at a time. They are not meant to be played for entertainment.

ideas.name: Scoring by point accumulation rewards frequent play
ideas.text: A rating built by adding points per win mostly shows how often someone plays. Systems that also take points for a loss measure skill more accurately but can discourage players.

ideas.name: Elo gives the odds from two ratings
ideas.text: The winner takes from the loser the same number of points, more for beating a higher-rated player, and any two ratings give the odds of each winning.

ideas.name: Tournament formats suit different games
ideas.text: Round robin works for few players. Swiss pairs similar records. A mix, such as Swiss then single elimination among the top eight, is common. A season is a tournament spread over months.

ideas.name: Werewolf lives on hidden roles and talk
ideas.text: Teams are random and secret, the werewolves kill one townsperson each night, and all vote on a suspect by day. It has two sides, so it has no politics in the book's sense even though it has a lot of discussion.

ideas.name: Game shows use few contestants and a final vote
ideas.text: Survivor lets previously eliminated players vote on the last two, which makes it an extreme case of kingmaking.

ideas.name: A first game can be a race with a theme added
ideas.text: Senet, perhaps the oldest known boardgame from at least 3500 BC, is presumed a race. The Royal Game of Goose, one of the first commercial boardgames, put a theme on a race.

ideas.name: Objective numbers made from subjective grades
ideas.text: Hungarian sports papers printed ranked lists of footballers from season scores. Each score was a young journalist's opinion of one match, and the list averaged those opinions. The averaging is exact, but every number averaged is a judgement, so the list looks more objective than the scores it is made from.

ideas.name: One judge who owns the count
ideas.text: In a Hungarian folktale trapped animals agree that the ugliest will be eaten, and the wolf appoints himself judge. He rates himself and the fox high and the hen low, and the hen is eaten, then the cock. The vote was fair in form, but one voter controlled the result.

ideas.name: Owning the ball makes you the centre
ideas.text: In a class of 40 boys, 37 named Péter as their closest friend because his father could get a real football and nobody else had one. The popularity list followed access to the one thing the game needed, which is how a star-like network forms.

ideas.name: Silver can feel lower than bronze
ideas.text: Studies of Olympic medallists find silver medallists tend to be unhappy and bronze medallists pleased. Silver compares up to gold, bronze compares down to fourth place, so the same ranking position feels different by the comparison used.

ideas.name: Weights are chosen by people
ideas.text: To turn several criteria into one list, each criterion gets a weight, and the book says weights are set by judgement. Changing a weight changes the order of the same items.

ideas.name: Compressing many kinds of pain into one number
ideas.text: The pain scale asks for one number from 0 to 10, with faces, for pain that has physical, emotional, social and other parts. The number is useful to the therapist but drops information, and the patient has trouble finding what zero means.

ideas.name: Rating categories defined by percentages
ideas.text: A graduate-school form asks raters to place a student in the top 5 percent, next 15 percent and so on. The writer notes he uses the top label freely when it means 5 percent and rarely when it means 2 percent, so the size of the band changes the marks given.

ideas.name: Seeking comparisons to suit a purpose
ideas.text: The book quotes the rule that comparing with people who are behind you makes you feel happier, and comparing with people who are ahead of you pushes you harder. Which comparison a player looks at changes what the score does to them.

ideas.name: A rating system predicts, and is corrected by results
ideas.text: Elo gives each chess player a number and an expected score for each game. After the game the number moves by how far the result was from the prediction, so an upset moves it more than an expected win. The system has been carried over to Scrabble, Go, rugby and online games.

ideas.name: A rating can say how sure it is
ideas.text: A player who has not played for a long time has a rating that may no longer hold. Glicko adds a ratings deviation beside the number, so a returning player's old rating is marked as uncertain instead of being taken as exact.

ideas.name: Memory holds a list by structure
ideas.text: Kim learns to recall a tray of objects by practising with many kinds of objects over ten days, and the Boy Scouts use the same game. The book adds that people hold long unstructured lists badly, and that a count in the title of a list, as in a listicle, tells the reader what they will get.

ideas.name: Spacing beats massing
ideas.text: Ebbinghaus found that repeating something several times over a stretch of time works more efficiently than repeating it all at once. Medical students who studied on days 1, 6, 16 and 29 learned more efficiently than those on days 1, 10, 20 and 29.

ideas.name: Cutting a list so that the rest is dropped
ideas.text: Ivy Lee told executives to write six tasks for tomorrow, order them, and do only the first until it is done. Buffett told his pilot to circle the top five of 25 goals and treat the other 20 as things to avoid until the five are done. In both, the ranking has an effect only because the list is cut short.

ideas.name: Ranking one trait is spoiled by the whole impression
ideas.text: A rater who likes a student overall scores the separate traits higher. The writer now rates each trait on its own, and relies on several raters so that their biases partly cancel.

ideas.name: A crowd is accurate only while its members stay independent
ideas.text: At a livestock fair about 800 people guessed the weight of an ox and their median was very close. In a Zurich experiment, people who shared their guesses ended up with a narrower spread of answers centred further from the truth than people who did not.

ideas.name: Diversity and group size
ideas.text: Scott Page's models find that a varied group of problem-solvers reaches more accurate decisions than a group of uniformly high-scoring ones. Studies of experts find groups of five to 15 score more accurately than very large committees.

ideas.name: Rank settles who gets what without fighting each time
ideas.text: In a pecking order each chicken knows who is above and below and gives way, so the group does not fight over every piece of food. Parakeets learn their ranks over about a week, then avoid fights with higher birds and do not waste effort on much lower ones.

ideas.name: Winning raises the chance of winning
ideas.text: Baboon researchers use Elo ratings on thousands of recorded encounters and find that winners become more likely to win next time and losers more likely to lose. A single result then feeds the next one.

ideas.name: Two roads to the top
ideas.text: Dominance gets rank by force and rank is held by fear. Prestige gets rank by skill and rank is held by consent. In The Lion King, Scar rules with a hyena army and Mufasa with the respect he has earned.

ideas.name: Stress feeds the rank loop
ideas.text: High-ranked animals show short bursts of stress hormones that help them win the next contest. Low-ranked animals who are bullied stay stressed for long periods, which lowers their rank further.

ideas.name: Skill used as display
ideas.text: Studies of hunting peoples such as the Hadza find that skilled hunters do not clearly feed their families more. The data fit hunting being used as a sign of status more than as food supply.

ideas.name: Reputation lets help flow one way
ideas.text: In a model by Nowak and Sigmund, a donor who helps a stranger is seen by others, and gains a reputation that makes others more likely to help the donor later. Cooperation can then grow although no single helper is repaid by the person helped.

ideas.name: Removing a rank advantage and finding it small
ideas.text: West Point once grouped cadets by height to stop height affecting early rank. Later data showed height had only a slight effect on promotion, and the grouping was dropped.

ideas.name: Where a rank shows in an act
ideas.text: In Japanese bowing, the angle of the bow shows relative status, from 15 degrees to 45 degrees. In Rome the colour of the toga showed rank. A rank can be carried by a visible sign that anyone can read.

ideas.name: A list is objective when its criterion can be checked
ideas.text: The ranking of the tallest buildings, from Burj Khalifa at 2,717 feet down, is accepted by everyone because heights can be measured. A list of the most influential people of all time is not random, since its names are unsurprising, but it rests on opinion and a new name could be argued in or out.

ideas.name: Different measures of the centre name different leaders
ideas.text: In a network of ten people, Sean and Bill have the most direct links, Sean is closest to everyone, and Ellie, with few links, is first for betweenness because she links two groups. Each measure gives its own top of the list.

ideas.name: Fixed preferences and transitive choices
ideas.text: Rational choice theory says that if you prefer pie to cheesecake and cheesecake to mousse, you also prefer pie to mousse, and you do so on Tuesday as on Monday. The book uses a dessert menu to show the assumption and says people who break it are not called irrational.

ideas.name: People turn down a free gain to punish an uneven split
ideas.text: In the Ultimatum Game a responder who only counts money would accept any positive offer. In studies across cultures responders tend to reject offers below about 30 percent of the sum, so that neither player gets anything.

ideas.name: Enough can be a rule with a number
ideas.text: In the secretary problem you look at the first 37 percent of the candidates and reject them all, then pick the next one who beats everyone seen so far. This gives the highest chance of the top candidate but can still miss them.

ideas.name: The same offer framed as a gain or a loss
ideas.text: Two patients are offered the same treatment, one told there is a 10 percent chance of dying and the other a 90 percent chance of surviving. The second is much more likely to accept, though the numbers are identical.

ideas.name: More options can cost the player
ideas.text: Barry Schwartz separates maximizers, who search for the top option, from satisficers, who stop at a set level. Maximizers face more doubt that they chose well when the options grow. The book lists ways to cut this: limit the options, stop at a set level, and do not worry about what you miss.

ideas.name: Voting can loop though every voter is consistent
ideas.text: With three voters ordering A, B, C as ABC, BCA and CAB, each pair is decided 2 to 1 and the results form a loop. A group of consistent players can have no consistent group order.

ideas.name: The shape of the voting rounds can fix the winner
ideas.text: If a winner is picked by a series of pairwise rounds, the person arranging the rounds can set the leading candidates against each other early and bring in the favoured candidate at the end.

ideas.name: Median grades instead of ranks
ideas.text: In majority judgment each of five voters gives a grade out of 10. For grades 3, 6, 7, 7, 9 the candidate's mark is the middle one, 7, which is the highest grade at least half the voters gave or exceeded. Ties and gaming are handled by further rules.

ideas.name: A circular order with no top choice
ideas.text: In rock, paper, scissors against a random player nothing gives an edge. Human players tend to repeat after winning and to move on to the next hand after losing, and rarely use the same move three times, which a careful observer can use.

ideas.name: Games like rock, paper, scissors in other places
ideas.text: A Japanese version has a tiger, the village chief and the chief's mother. An Indonesian version has an earwig, a man and an elephant. The five-weapon version adds Spock and lizard. All keep the loop.

ideas.name: A loop used on purpose
ideas.text: The US system of checks and balances is described as a loop among executive, legislative and judicial branches so that none outranks the others. A political scientist quoted in the book says it is a useful teaching picture but only partly true.

ideas.name: A link counts more from a page that itself counts
ideas.text: PageRank scores a page by relevance to the query and by the importance of pages that link to it. A link from an important page is worth more than one from an unimportant page.

ideas.name: Votes weighted by order of arrival
ideas.text: Reddit's hot ranking uses a logarithm so the first 10 up-votes weigh as much as the next 100 and those as much as the next 1,000. Early votes shape position most.

ideas.name: Adding an option changes the choice between two others
ideas.text: A buyer leans to the cheap used car until a very expensive new car is shown, after which the cheaper new car looks like a bargain. The new third option reorders the other two.

ideas.name: Spoiler candidates
ideas.text: In the 2000 US presidential election Bush won Florida by 537 votes, and supporters of Gore said a third candidate, Ralph Nader, took enough votes from Gore to change the result. A third option changed the outcome between the two main ones.

ideas.name: The less skilled player rates themselves highest
ideas.text: Students with low marks overestimate their class standing and the strongest students underestimate it. Young drivers overrate their skill and reaction time. A self-rating is least reliable where the person knows least.

ideas.name: Not knowing the rules can open a new move
ideas.text: Ingvar Kamprad took the legs off a table to fit it in his car, and flat-packed furniture followed. Amazon, Uber and Airbnb entered book, taxi and hotel trade by ignoring what those trades took for granted.

ideas.name: Rules without a referee
ideas.text: The book quotes Joseph Brodsky that life is a game with many rules and no referee. It adds that when rules are unwritten it is easier to break them and take an edge.

ideas.name: Measures become targets and then fail
ideas.text: Soviet factories were judged on tonnage, and made chandeliers so heavy they pulled down ceilings. In schools teaching to the test replaces teaching the subject. Surgeons who avoid risky patients keep their figures up.

ideas.name: Players react to being measured
ideas.text: A falling apple is not changed by being watched, but people change what they do when they are scored. Murray Gell-Mann's line quoted here is that physics would be hard if particles could think.

ideas.name: Small leads grow when prizes follow rank
ideas.text: When funds go to the competitors who ranked higher, the ranked-higher gain more equipment and the others cannot challenge them. If most competitors drop out, a few rivals remain.

ideas.name: A reward can pay for the problem
ideas.text: In Hanoi, a bounty paid on rat tails led people to cut tails off and release the rats to breed. In Bogotá, banning cars by plate number led some to buy a second, older car.

ideas.name: Treat a measure like a barometer
ideas.text: A barometer tells you rain is likely, and you take an umbrella. Putting the barometer under water to raise its reading would not change the weather. The point is that a number records something else and acting on the number alone does not alter that thing.

ideas.name: A fixed share at the bottom
ideas.text: General Electric fired the bottom 10 percent each year. Enron graded 1 to 5 and required 15 percent to get the lowest grade whatever the absolute results. The quota makes each person's place depend on the others.

ideas.name: Weights inside a score
ideas.text: FICO's credit score weights payment history 35 percent, amounts owed 30 percent, length of history 15 percent, credit mix 10 percent and new credit 10 percent. Equal weights of 20 percent each would give other scores for the same person.

ideas.name: Players learn a scoring game
ideas.text: A San Francisco group runs lending circles where low-income families learn what is reported to credit bureaus. In one case a participant's score rose 168 points.

ideas.name: A score from patterns, not from stated rules
ideas.text: A traditional scoring rule is written by its designer, such as adding points for each on-time payment. A machine-learned score finds its own patterns in past data, and it can be hard to explain a decision from it.

ideas.name: Round numbers and ranks
ideas.text: A product ranked tenth feels closer to eighth than to eleventh. A price of $19.99 reads as clearly under $20. Seventy-two percent of MBA programmes cite their tier instead of their exact rank.

ideas.name: Rankings began as stars given by experts
ideas.text: In 1906 James McKeen Cattell asked scientists to mark their colleagues with stars, then ranked institutions by the share of starred scientists among their staff. Because the experts were from older private institutions, the method favoured those over newer public ones.

ideas.name: One score for places that differ in kind
ideas.text: Gladwell's example sets Penn State, a large public university known for football, against Yeshiva, a small private one, as items one list has to compare. The book calls this harder than apples and oranges.

ideas.name: Seven indicators with fixed shares
ideas.text: One version of the US News score gave reputation 22.5 percent, graduation and retention 20, faculty resources 20, student selectivity 15, finances 10, graduation rate performance 7.5 and alumni giving 5. The shares were set by the makers, so a different split would order the same colleges differently.

ideas.name: Let the user set the weights
ideas.text: Emanuelle Tognoli suggests rankings where each person moves sliders for the factors. The European U-Multirank lets students choose their own dimensions, and critics doubt that its data are comparable across countries.

ideas.name: Ranking a school that does not exist
ideas.text: Lawyers asked to rank ten law schools put Penn State fifth, though it had no law school. They were rating the name, so a general impression filled in for facts they did not have.

ideas.name: A small rank gap grows
ideas.text: A slightly higher rank this year brings more and stronger applicants next year, which changes the selectivity score, which raises the rank. Noise that is not statistically meaningful can then make a real difference.

ideas.name: What is not counted drops out
ideas.text: Once a few indicators are the basis of a ranking, qualities that are not turned into numbers get less attention. The book notes ranking algorithms ignore things like free speech on campus.

ideas.name: Using a ranking as a first filter
ideas.text: A student applying to PhD programmes took the top 40 or so from the lists, then narrowed by location and by professors whose work interested them. The list cut hundreds to a few dozen and personal taste did the rest.

ideas.name: A cut that most cannot reach
ideas.text: About 18,000 institutions are in a world database, and the top-100 cut takes 0.5 percent of them. Smaller and newer ones with fewer resources can hardly move up.

ideas.name: A cow and a horse
ideas.text: A child can rank a sparrow, a cat, a cow and an elephant by size, but is stuck on the horse, which is taller and narrower than the cow. When items differ in several ways, which feature is used decides the order.

ideas.name: A score that leaves out what it does not measure
ideas.text: Qatar led the 2015 welfare list because its income per head is high and the inequality measure counts income only. The book notes that the country has labour camps and about 700,000 women among 2.5 million people.

ideas.name: Rank gaps below the noise
ideas.text: In the 2017 happiness report, the top five countries scored from 7.47 to 7.54, with no statistically significant difference among them, yet the list put one first.

ideas.name: The next dollar counts less
ideas.text: Stevenson and Wolfers found that happiness rises with income in a logarithmic curve, so each extra dollar adds less than the last. This is the shape the book gives for why richer countries do not look much happier.

ideas.name: Scores turned into ratings and then into words
ideas.text: Freedom House adds three section scores with maximums of 12, 16 and 12, sets bands such as 36 to 40 meaning rating 1, then names the result free, partly free or not free. The maximums are chosen by the makers, and the words are what readers remember.

ideas.name: Naming a group instead of a place
ideas.text: The book proposes that a list say 'these 17 countries are realistic candidates for the top ten' instead of giving exact places, since the scores carry uncertainty.

ideas.name: Reputation builds slowly and breaks fast
ideas.text: Warren Buffett is quoted that it takes twenty years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it. The book adds that reputation spreads outward from close friends through friends of friends, while social media can produce overnight popularity.

ideas.name: Reputation lets cooperation start
ideas.text: In the Nowak and Sigmund model, helping is worth it when the chance of others learning your reputation is larger than the cost of the help divided by its benefit. A helper then gains from being seen even if the person helped never repays.

ideas.name: Three layers of reputation
ideas.text: The book separates who you are, who you say you are, and who other people say you are. The cat who sees a lion in the mirror stands for the second.

ideas.name: Two phases of choosing a top list
ideas.text: The Harris Poll first asks thousands of adults to name companies, which picks the 100 most visible, and then asks a larger group to rate those 100. Naming and rating are separate steps with separate samples.

ideas.name: Eight things a paper needs
ideas.text: Shockley listed the steps to publish: choose a suitable problem, be able to work on it, recognise a worthwhile result, pick a stopping point, present it, learn from critics, finish and submit, and answer referees. The list shows that output depends on many separate abilities.

ideas.name: A few items take nearly all the citations
ideas.text: In 353,268 Physical Review papers, 11 had over 1,000 citations while 245,459 had fewer than 10 and 84,144 had one. A count of what is cited is lopsided in the way word counts and city sizes are.

ideas.name: A window of two years
ideas.text: The impact factor counts citations in one year to articles from the previous two. The book says two years was a compromise between rewarding fast-changing fields and measuring lasting influence.

ideas.name: An editor who raises a journal's own score
ideas.text: An editor-in-chief's list of duties asks board members to cite at least five of the journal's papers a year and to urge others to cite it. Citation counts then reflect that request as much as the papers.

ideas.name: Weights on kinds of attention
ideas.text: Altmetrics gives a news story 8, a blog 5, a patent 3, a tweet 1 and a Facebook or Reddit post 0.25. The book's point is that a person chose these numbers and a different choice orders papers differently.

ideas.name: Early lead can decide the match
ideas.text: The book imagines a football match at 2 to 1 where the chance of scoring again is proportional to goals already scored, which could end 45 to 3. Researchers' citation records behave in a similar way, with early success raising later success.

ideas.name: Success from three mechanisms
ideas.text: Barabási's model says papers with more early citations get more later ones, novelty fades with age, and a quality he calls fitness lets late arrivals still succeed. Future success is predicted by past success multiplied by fitness.

ideas.name: A jury that keeps the status quo
ideas.text: The Paris Salon jury, led by the Academy, admitted religious and historical subjects and refused landscapes and still lifes. Courbet complained that showing at the Salon was the only way to make a name. In 1863 the Salon des Refusés opened, and in 1874 the Impressionists held their own exhibition.

ideas.name: A new gatekeeper replaces the old one
ideas.text: Paul Durand-Ruel bought Impressionist paintings in bulk, held one-person shows and took the work to London and New York, where in 1886 he showed 289 paintings. The jury's monopoly gave way to a market of dealers and critics.

ideas.name: Prices follow a power law
ideas.text: Prices of artworks traded at auction fall on a heavy-tailed curve, not a bell curve. A few artists' works fetch very much more than their followers' works. Pollock's No. 5 sold for $140 million.

ideas.name: Performance is bounded and success is not
ideas.text: Barabási's second law is quoted: performance has a ceiling, success does not. Two artists of similar skill can end very far apart in price and fame.

ideas.name: Stages an artist climbs
ideas.text: The book lists university art spaces, small city galleries, major gallery shows, retrospectives and top museum shows. Moving from one stage to the next is hard, and an artist's rise depends on being linked to people already at the next stage.

ideas.name: A few dealers hold most of the places
ideas.text: One-third of solo shows in US museums go to artists of just five galleries. Two auction houses hold 80 percent of the international fine art auction business.

ideas.name: Points from the company you keep
ideas.text: ArtFacts scores an artist by how many countries and collections hold their work and by the shows they join. A solo show at a museum with thousands of collected artists gives all their points to you, and old exhibitions are discounted and cut off after five years.

ideas.name: A prize that a long list of famous people did not win
ideas.text: Tolstoy, Proust, Kafka, Woolf and Joyce did not win the Nobel literature prize. Bookmakers who set odds on it have no data on how the committee decides, so they need a model of the committee.

ideas.name: The gap opens before the final round
ideas.text: Women hold under 6 percent of Nobel Prizes. The book argues most of this comes from earlier stages, such as the share of PhDs, who is cited and who is nominated, so the committee only sees what the earlier stages passed on.

ideas.name: Players find ways round a ranking
ideas.text: Black-hat optimizers game search engines to reach the top quickly and risk being dropped from the results permanently. The book says a community makes rules and some players then try to get round them.

ideas.name: Order of results can shift undecided voters
ideas.text: An experiment found that biasing search rankings could move the voting preferences of undecided voters by 20 percent or more. Adding alerts about possible bias to the search design reduced the effect.

ideas.name: Three ways to recommend
ideas.text: A system can suggest what friends like, what you liked before, or what fits needs you stated. Real-time systems skip the history and read the clicks of a first-time visitor.

ideas.name: Fewer options make it easier to buy
ideas.text: The book says it pays a seller not to offer too many choices in one category, since a long list overwhelms buyers. Trust in a recommender depends on it being useful and open about how it works.

ideas.name: A short time to catch attention
ideas.text: Netflix says it has about 90 seconds to recommend something before a viewer leaves. It therefore keeps several ranking lists, such as Trending Now and Continue Watching, each ordering the whole catalogue for a different purpose.

ideas.name: Neighbours by taste, not by place
ideas.text: Netflix groups people with others who enjoy the same kind of content, not with people on the same street or in the same country. The book says the result is more accurately called clustered than personal.

ideas.name: An episode that ends before the answer
ideas.text: A series episode ends on an exciting scene and the next picture is withheld. The book links this to stress hormones and then to dopamine on pressing play, a loop that keeps people watching for hours.

ideas.name: A joke that put a shelter in the top 100
ideas.text: In 2013 a group of people gave a Glasgow homeless hostel five stars on TripAdvisor until it reached the top 100 places to stay. The site removed the listing because it did not meet its rules.

ideas.name: A restaurant that did not exist
ideas.text: An Italian food paper made a profile for an imaginary restaurant, La Scaletta, and had friends write top-rated reviews. It reached first place among the restaurants of its town, which showed that the ranking could be made up.

ideas.name: A match needs a yes from both sides
ideas.text: Tinder shows a picture and the user says yes or no. Only when two people each say yes can they start a conversation.

ideas.name: The steps of making a ranked list
ideas.text: The book's flowchart runs: pick the set of items, choose a criterion and a formula, score each item, compare each pair as greater, smaller or equal, and make an ordered list from the results. Each step is a choice by someone.

ideas.name: Make your own ranking
ideas.text: The author advises students and parents to weigh the factors that matter to them. A student he overheard preferred a dorm with a fast internet connection even though the building had bugs.

ideas.name: A crowd that got ahead of the facts
ideas.text: In the South Sea Bubble, shares of a company with little real trade became fashionable and overvalued until holders sold and the market fell. Isaac Newton sold at a profit, bought again at the top and lost £20,000.

ideas.name: Rules about touching pieces
ideas.text: Chess and checkers both say what happens when a player touches a piece, and chess has a spoken phrase, j'adoube, to say the touch means nothing. The rule makes a physical act count as a move, so the players need a way to say otherwise. In chess, a player who touches an enemy piece has to capture it if they legally can.

ideas.name: Penalty left to the opponent
ideas.text: In checkers a player who misses a compulsory capture is only punished if the opponent chooses to huff. The opponent can also let it pass or make the player take back the move. The rule gives the choice to the person harmed, who can weigh the penalty against what the position offers.

ideas.name: Why the capture rule exists
ideas.text: The book says compulsory capture matters because a player may give up two or three men in a row to set up a big capture. Without the rule, the other player could take the first man, then refuse the second and so dodge the trap. A rule can protect a plan that only works if the opponent is forced to act.

ideas.name: Having the move is not having the turn
ideas.text: In checkers, whose turn it is differs from who holds the useful position. The book gives a way to count men and squares to tell who has the move. Players who give up pieces one for one swap that advantage back and forth until someone makes an error.

ideas.name: First player has no clear edge
ideas.text: The book says there is no advantage in playing first in checkers, because the second player ends up with the move. Rules for colour and first turn are often settled by a coin and swapped in later games.

ideas.name: Pieces that change when they cross the board
ideas.text: Checkers men become kings at the far row and gain backward movement. Chess pawns become queens or other pieces. In both games, a plain piece that reaches the far side gains new moves.

ideas.name: Pieces differ in how they move
ideas.text: Each chess piece has its own way of moving and the book rates their relative value, noting that the worth of bishop and knight depends on the position. When every piece type moves in its own way, the board holds many different threats.

ideas.name: Drawn games need defined causes
ideas.text: The book lists several ways a chess game can be a draw, from stalemate to fifty moves without a mate. Without an agreed end for stuck positions, a game can run for ever, so rules name when play stops.

ideas.name: Fifty-move counting
