ideas.text: In chess and checkers, a player with a small advantage can be required to win within a fixed number of moves, or the game is a draw. A move limit means the ending cannot go on indefinitely.

ideas.name: Dice odds for placing a piece
ideas.text: The book works out the chance of a lone backgammon piece being hit. Of 36 dice throws, 11 contain an Ace, so the odds are 25 to 11 against being hit by that number. A piece close to an enemy is hit less often than one at a distance of six, and far pieces are hit mostly by doubles. The odds change how a player places pieces.

ideas.name: Risk against spreading
ideas.text: Backgammon advice says to make points and avoid blots, yet the book admits that spreading men to make points later can be worth the risk. Sometimes it is even useful to be hit, to start from the opponent's home. The player takes on risk to keep more options open.

ideas.name: Dice with choice
ideas.text: In backgammon the player may split a throw between two pieces or use it on one. The book also says the whole throw has to be played if any way allows it. Letting the player choose how to spend the dice keeps luck from deciding every move.

ideas.name: The same board, a different game
ideas.text: Russian Backgammon uses the same board and pieces, but pieces enter by dice and both sides move in one direction. Doubles give extra moves and another throw. A change in start and direction changes who is ahead, since the rear player can hit blots.

ideas.name: Scoring grades
ideas.text: Backgammon counts a single win, a gammon for twice that and backgammon for more. The size of a win depends on how far the loser had got.

ideas.name: Variations as a family
ideas.text: The introduction notes that chapters give many variants and that a player who likes one game will probably like related ones. All-Fours, for instance, comes with All-Fives, Auction Pitch, California Jack and Pedro Sancho. Changing one rule, such as how many points are needed or which cards score, gives a new game.

ideas.name: Different cards score in different ways
ideas.text: In All-Fours the points are High, Low, Jack and Game, and one card can count for all four. In Pedro Sancho the Five and Nine of trumps are worth five and nine. The same pack can give one point per category or a heavy value to certain cards.

ideas.name: Order of precedence in scoring
ideas.text: All-Fours and Pedro Sancho list points in a fixed order so that, if two players would go out at the same moment, the one whose point comes earlier wins. A tie-break written into the scoring removes disputes about who finished first.

ideas.name: Counting down to zero
ideas.text: Auction Pitch and Pedro Sancho start each player with a score and subtract points as they are made, so the first to reach nothing wins. A failed bid adds points back. Scoring downwards makes a loss feel like a step away from the goal.

ideas.name: Auctioning a privilege
ideas.text: In Auction Pitch the right to name trump is sold to the highest bidder, who then has to make as many points as they bid. Players weigh the value of control against the risk of being set back.

ideas.name: A bid is a promise
ideas.text: In Boston and French Boston a player says in advance how many tricks they will take, and the rest play against them. The bid sets a target and a price for missing it.

ideas.name: Bids in order
ideas.text: Boston lists fifteen bids from lowest to highest, with misere hands placed between certain trick counts. A rank order for bids lets players outbid each other simply by saying something higher.

ideas.name: Payment tables
ideas.text: Boston gives a table of chips for each bid and result, so a player does not argue over how much to pay. The table makes a reward scale with risk: a bigger bid pays more, and falling short costs more for each trick missed.

ideas.name: Reversing the goal
ideas.text: A misere hand is played with no trump and the aim is to take no tricks, so the usual strategy turns round. The opponents then try to force the bidder to win a trick. One deck can be used for opposite aims.

ideas.name: A growing pool
ideas.text: When all Boston players pass, each adds a chip to the pool, which goes to the next successful bidder. A pool that grows when nobody acts pushes players towards bidding.

ideas.name: Ending a hand early
ideas.text: In Boston the opponents of a small bidder may all say "I pay" before the second trick and end the hand. Letting players agree to stop shortens a hand whose result is already clear.

ideas.name: Playing alone or in a temporary team
ideas.text: In Calabrasella one player declares and the other two join forces against them. A player can also strengthen their hand by demanding a Three and exchanging with the stock. Teams change every hand and nobody is stuck with a partner.

ideas.name: Rank in play and value in score differ
ideas.text: In Calabrasella the Ace scores 3 points yet is not the highest card in play. The Four is. Separating strength in a trick from worth in points makes players think about which cards to keep and which to risk.

ideas.name: The last trick is special
ideas.text: Calabrasella gives three points and the discard pile to the winner of the final trick. Players are advised to hold high cards back to win it. A reward at the end changes how a hand is paced.

ideas.name: Several ways to capture
ideas.text: Casino has four ways to take cards: pairing, combining, building and calling. Each lets the player use a different feature of the cards on the table and in hand. A single goal can be reached by several moves.

ideas.name: Committing to a build
ideas.text: A Casino player who builds says what total they are aiming at, and an opponent can capture or raise the build. The player cannot raise their own. Publicly declaring a plan gives the opponent a chance to interfere.

ideas.name: Cancelling scores
ideas.text: In Casino a sweep scores a point but a sweep by the other player cancels it, so only the difference counts. A rule that nets out the scores keeps one lucky run from being the whole result.

ideas.name: Eliminating players by round
ideas.text: Commerce removes the two lowest hands after each round until two players are left. Players who are out can talk to the players who are in and try to trap them into answering. The book changes how many leave each round depending on the number of people.

ideas.name: Elimination with a way back
ideas.text: In Commerce an out player who tricks an in player into replying swaps places with them. A player who is knocked out can return by tricking a player still in.

ideas.name: Trading for a price
ideas.text: Trade and Barter Commerce lets players pay a chip to draw a new card or swap with a neighbour for nothing. The paid chips go to the dealer and not into the pool. Having one exchange that costs a chip and one that is free affects how often players change their hand.

ideas.name: Memory as the skill
ideas.text: Concentration is played by turning over two cards at a time and remembering where each one lay. The winner is the person with the most matched pairs, whatever the card values. Remembering what others turned over is the main skill.

ideas.name: A wild card
ideas.text: In Crazy Eights, an Eight can be played on anything and lets the player choose the next suit, the one they hold most of. A single wild card gives a way out when no card matches.

ideas.name: Matching pip or suit
ideas.text: Crazy Eights lets a player match either the number or the suit of the top card. Two matching rules make it unlikely that a player is stuck.

ideas.name: A scoring board
ideas.text: Cribbage keeps score with two pegs per player on a board with holes. The back peg jumps in front of the front one, so the board also shows the last score gained. The score is kept in public.

ideas.name: One hand scored twice
ideas.text: Cribbage scores in the play of the cards, when players add card values toward 31, and again when the hands are shown. Two phases make cards matter in two different ways.

ideas.name: Combinations score in many ways
ideas.text: Cribbage rewards pairs, fifteens, runs, flushes and a Jack matching the start card. One combination of cards can score for several of these at the same time.

ideas.name: A shared hand
ideas.text: The cribbage crib is built from discards by both players and counted for the dealer. A shared pile gives the non-dealer a reason to give away cards carefully.

ideas.name: Small scoring rules around the dealer
ideas.text: Cribbage lets the non-dealer mark three holes at the start, and a player who wins before the opponent has 31 points wins a double. Small rules offset the dealer's turn and give extra weight to a big lead.

ideas.name: Rules for what a mistake costs
ideas.text: Cribbage lists a penalty for almost every slip, often two holes for the opponent, a new deal, or losing the score. Overscoring lets the opponent take points, but underscoring costs nothing and nobody has to help another player count. The cost of a slip depends on who gained from it.

ideas.name: The score decides the style
ideas.text: Cribbage advice says to play off when ahead and play on when behind. The book gives averages of points per hand to tell whether a player is on pace. Knowing the average rate lets players decide how much to risk from where they stand in the score.

ideas.name: A deck with its low cards removed
ideas.text: Calabrasella uses 40 cards, Coon Can 40 and Ecarte 32, each by dropping some ranks from the standard 52. Cutting ranks changes the number of cards each player holds and how often each combination appears.

ideas.name: Six cards or five
ideas.text: Six-card Cribbage plays every card out and gives a point for the last card, while the five-card version stops at 31. The book says six-card scores more points in play, while five-card games are often decided by one point. Hand size changes how long a game is and how much it swings.

ideas.name: Teams in a four-player version
ideas.text: Four-handed Cribbage plays in pairs seated opposite, goes round the board twice for 122 points, and lets only two players handle the board. Moving a two-player game to four needs rules about who sits where and who scores.

ideas.name: A pool split by trick
ideas.text: Division Loo divides the pool into thirds and pays one-third per trick won. A player who declares to play and wins nothing adds chips to the next pool. Payment per trick makes even a small win count.

ideas.name: Declaring before looking
ideas.text: In Division Loo, players decide whether to play only when it is their turn, and are not allowed to peek earlier. Once declared, they have to stay with it. Keeping the cards hidden until a player commits stops them reacting to the others.

ideas.name: A spare hand on the table
ideas.text: The Division Loo dummy hand is dealt to the centre and may be taken by a player in place of their own. Offering a swap to the first player to declare gives an early decision some reward.

ideas.name: Forced leads
ideas.text: In Division Loo, a leader with several trumps has to lead the highest, and the winner of the first trick has to lead trump. Compelled plays take choices away from the leader and shape what the others can expect.

ideas.name: Winning by majority only
ideas.text: Ecarte scores one point for three of five tricks and two for all five, and four tricks is worth no more than three. Past three tricks, extra tricks earn nothing until all five are won.

ideas.name: Offer and refusal
ideas.text: In Ecarte the non-dealer proposes a swap of cards and the dealer may refuse, after which a player who fails to take three tricks gives the other two points. Asking and refusing both carry a risk.

ideas.name: Speed gives away information
ideas.text: The Ecarte advice says to propose quickly, because hesitating shows the hand is uncertain, and to learn the odds by heart. How long a player takes becomes a signal to the other.

ideas.name: Announce a bonus or lose it
ideas.text: In Ecarte a player with the King of trumps scores a point, but only if they say so before playing a card. A scoring chance that depends on a spoken call rewards attention.

ideas.name: Forced to win the trick
ideas.text: In Ecarte the second player has to follow suit and also has to win the trick if able, trumping if needed. A required reply keeps a two-player trick from being a free choice.

ideas.name: Trump chosen from a shown card
ideas.text: In Euchre one card is turned up and each player in turn may accept its suit as trump or pass. Only if everyone passes is a new suit named. The suit is proposed by chance and then confirmed or refused by the players.

ideas.name: Naming trump has a price
ideas.text: A Euchre side that takes the trump has to win three of five tricks or the other side scores two points. Choosing the rule of the hand makes the chooser responsible for the result.

ideas.name: Timing the solo declaration
ideas.text: In Euchre a player can only go alone before the first lead and only when their side made the trump. A special move is allowed only at certain moments, so it is a decision made on partial information.

ideas.name: Partners signal by their plays
ideas.text: Euchre advice says to play a particular card to tell a partner that the Ace remains in your hand. Yet the rules fine a side one point for telling a partner what is held through words or gestures. Players are allowed to signal only with the cards.

ideas.name: Odds-based opening rules
ideas.text: The Ecarte chapter lists ten kinds of hand that are played without asking for new cards and says the value of the trumps does not matter, only their number. It turns a calculation into a lookup table that players learn by heart.

ideas.name: A score marked with two cards
ideas.text: Euchre keeps game score with a Three and a Four, each laid over the other, and the face showing and how much it is covered gives the number. A small physical device replaces a pencil.

ideas.name: Carrying surplus points forward
ideas.text: In the Euchre lap game, points beyond the five needed for a win count towards the next game. A big win then has a lasting effect, so surplus is kept instead of wasted.

ideas.name: Extreme options for the rare hand
ideas.text: Euchre adds jambone, played with the cards open, which scores eight if all five tricks are won, and jamboree, which scores 16 with no play. Rare high-risk or high-reward moves can sit on top of an ordinary game.

ideas.name: The deal is worth a point
ideas.text: In two-handed Euchre the book says to pass the deal only to avoid being euchred, since having the deal counts as a point. Players can put a value on the right to deal.

ideas.name: One game, many head counts
ideas.text: The Euchre chapter gives versions for two, three and six players, plus Napoleon, where everyone plays alone. Three-handed Euchre has one person play against two. Changing the number of players changes how teams form while keeping the same trick-taking.

ideas.name: Adding a card changes the pace
ideas.text: Railroad Euchre adds a Joker that beats the right bower and lets a lone player call for a partner's highest card. The book says this makes the game faster and lone hands more common. One new card can shift which choices players favour.

ideas.name: Playing against the table
ideas.text: In Set-Back Euchre and Napoleon, every player plays for themselves, so the one who takes the trump faces all the others joined together. Opposition forms from the bid and not from fixed teams.

ideas.name: Bid and stop
ideas.text: In Napoleon, a bidder who has won the tricks bid may throw down their cards. If they lead one more, they have to play for all five. Whether to stop is a decision the rules leave to the player.

ideas.name: Paying only for the bid
ideas.text: French Euchre and Six-Handed Euchre award only the number of tricks bid, however many are won. A rule that caps the reward at the stated aim makes overreaching pointless.

ideas.name: Asking for a card
ideas.text: In Go Fish a player asks one opponent for a rank they already hold, and if the opponent has it they have to hand all of them over. The turn continues while requests succeed. The game uses spoken questions and memory to reveal what others hold.

ideas.name: A simple game for children
ideas.text: Go Fish needs no scoring table and no bidding. The chapter on Go Fish is short, and the aim is to complete sets. The introduction calls it one of the simple children's games.

ideas.name: Racing to empty a personal pile
ideas.text: Grabouche gives each team a pile of twenty cards and a shared set of centre piles. A team wins by playing the top card of its pile whenever a centre pile reaches the right number. Players have to judge whether helping a centre pile helps themselves or the other side.

ideas.name: Blocking by what you leave visible
ideas.text: In Grabouche, the cards on a player's table piles are seen by partners but cannot be used by opponents. Players place cards on their table piles to keep the centre from reaching the opponents' card. Public information is used to help a partner.

ideas.name: Banning table talk
ideas.text: Grabouche penalises a player who shows approval or disapproval of a partner's play by letting the opponents place cards in the centre pile. Teams are not allowed to coordinate openly, so skill lies in reading the plays.

ideas.name: Avoiding points instead of seeking them
ideas.text: In Hearts the aim is to avoid tricks with Hearts, and no suit is trump. Players try to get rid of high Hearts and keep low ones. Reversing the aim of trick-taking changes which cards are valuable.

ideas.name: Shortening a suit
ideas.text: Hearts advice says to empty a short suit so that later leads in that suit let you discard dangerous high cards. Holding no cards of a suit becomes useful.

ideas.name: Inferring from a play
ideas.text: Hearts advice says that if the last player plays a very low card the first time a suit is led, they may have few cards of that suit. Players read what others hold from what they choose to play.

ideas.name: Payment depends on who took none
ideas.text: In Hearts, one chip is paid for each Heart taken, and if one player takes none they collect the pool. A player who takes all thirteen pays into the pool instead. Taking everything is punished, so there are risks at both ends.

ideas.name: Jackpot that grows
ideas.text: Heart Jackpot adds a chip each deal and the odd chip from shared splits. It goes to a player who takes no trick at all, and the pot gets larger until someone does. A separate pot makes a rare result more worth reaching.

ideas.name: Lying as the game
ideas.text: I Doubt It asks players to put cards down in a fixed rank order while saying the rank aloud, and the card may be wrong. Anyone may call out "I doubt it". The accuser takes the pile if the player told the truth and the player takes it if not. Bluffing and suspicion become the main skill.

ideas.name: A game about avoiding a loss
ideas.text: Old Maid has no winner to find, only a loser, who holds the one card with no partner. The Queen of Hearts is taken out so that the Queen of Diamonds has no pair. Removing one card leaves another without a pair, and the whole game turns on it.

ideas.name: Scoring from groups, not tricks
ideas.text: Pinochle gives points both for cards in tricks and for melds, such as a marriage or four Aces. Players score by showing combinations in their hand, and a meld cannot be reused for a meld of the same kind. A second route to points makes players weigh what to hold against what to play.

ideas.name: Points held in reserve
ideas.text: In three-handed Pinochle no meld points are added to a score until the player has taken a trick. A rule that points count only after an action keeps a player from banking a score without playing.

ideas.name: Waiting to declare so as not to leak information
ideas.text: In four-handed Pinochle, no melds are allowed until the eldest hand has led, because declaring early would show what the others hold. The timing of a public announcement changes what it gives away.

ideas.name: The same hand, different strengths
ideas.text: Poker ranks hands from one pair to straight flush and breaks ties by the highest card or by splitting the pool. The book says straights are not always played, and that fours beat a straight flush when they are left out. Whether a combination exists changes the order of the rest.

ideas.name: Betting rounds make a game of information
ideas.text: In Poker the betting decides who wins as much as the cards do, because a player who raises can force everyone else out without showing a hand. A raise tells the others something whether true or not.

ideas.name: A forced stake
ideas.text: Poker has an ante or blind from the eldest hand, which guarantees a pool before anyone looks at their cards. A compulsory first stake gives players something to win and gives the first seat a cost.

ideas.name: Limits keep a bet bounded
ideas.text: Poker is played to a limit agreed in advance, and every raise has to stay under it. A cap on bet size limits how much one hand can swing.

ideas.name: Opening needs a minimum hand
ideas.text: In Jackpot Poker a player can only open the betting with Jacks or higher, and a player who breaks the pot without them pays a penalty of twice their bet. A requirement to start separates high-ranking hands from low-ranking ones before any bluffing.

ideas.name: The requirement rises
ideas.text: Progressive Jackpot raises the opening hand to Queens, Kings and then Aces each time nobody opens. Each failed deal makes the next start harder, while the pot grows.

ideas.name: Looking at what others throw away
ideas.text: In Straight Poker with a widow, a player who takes the widow puts their old hand face up, and the next player may pick one card from it. Discards are public and become a source of supply for the next player.

ideas.name: Hidden and shown cards
ideas.text: A Poker variant deals one card face down and the rest face up. The book gives an example where the player with the higher-ranking visible cards loses when the hidden cards are turned over. A mix of seen and hidden cards makes players guess at the part they cannot see.

ideas.name: A wild card with limits
ideas.text: Mistigris, the Joker, can be named as any card not already held, so a pair becomes three of a kind and so on. The rule says what the Joker can stand for in each hand, which keeps a wild card from being open-ended.

ideas.name: Losing the score on a failure
ideas.text: In Rounce a player who plays a hand and takes no trick gets five points added, while each trick taken subtracts one. A failed attempt is costed at five times a success.

ideas.name: Sets and runs
ideas.text: Rummy asks players to group cards into runs (same suit in order) or lays (same rank). The two groupings give each card more than one way to be useful.

ideas.name: Taking the whole discard pile
ideas.text: In Rummy 500 a player can pick up from the discard pile, but has to take every card above the one they want and use the one they wanted at once. Reaching for a useful card has a cost that grows with how deep it lies.

ideas.name: Unmelded cards count against you
ideas.text: In Rummy 500, cards still in hand when another player goes out are subtracted from your score. Holding back sets in the hand is a risk, since they do not count.

ideas.name: Going out hidden
ideas.text: In Gin Rummy, players keep their sets in the hand and only reveal them by saying "Gin" when all cards but one are matched. Keeping the plan secret until the end makes it harder to read.

ideas.name: Closing the stock
ideas.text: In Sixty-Six the leader may turn down the trump card to stop drawing, and loses points if they then fail to reach 66. A player may end the drawing phase early, which turns a game of drawing into a game of counting.

ideas.name: Unrestricted second play
ideas.text: In Sixty-Six the second player to a trick does not have to follow suit until the stock is exhausted. A rule that applies only in a later phase changes how the game feels from early to late.

ideas.name: A bid sets the price
ideas.text: Skat gives every bid a base value by suit and type, then multiplies it by Matadores and by whether Schneider or Schwartz was reached or announced. The size of the payment is known before play begins, so the player can weigh the risk.

ideas.name: Announcing a larger goal
ideas.text: A Skat player may declare they will win Schneider or Schwartz, which raises the reward, but if they miss it their losses grow too. Naming a bigger target raises both sides of the bet.

ideas.name: Giving up midway
ideas.text: A Skat lone player who sees after the first trick that the game is lost can throw down their cards and pay the value of the game. Ending early caps the loss.

ideas.name: Hands shown to the opponents
ideas.text: Open Skat bids expose the lone player's cards, and the book says this gives opponents more chance of defeating them. A visible hand is a handicap that earns a higher score.

ideas.name: Bids that reverse the aim
ideas.text: Skat includes Null, where the lone player has to take no trick, ranked among the other bids. A bid with the opposite goal fits into the same ladder of values.

ideas.name: Two against one
ideas.text: Skat is always played by one lone player against two who join forces, and extra players share the fortune of the two. A fixed three-seat structure with a rotating third player lets more people join.

ideas.name: Nobody wants the trick
ideas.text: Slobberhannes has players try to avoid tricks, and the first to ten points loses. It adds extra points for taking the Queen of Clubs, the first and last tricks. Naming particular cards or tricks as costly makes players avoid them.

ideas.name: Hidden partnerships
ideas.text: In Solo with a called Ace, the holder of the named Ace is the bidder's partner, and nobody else knows who until it is played. Two players have to find out who is on whose side.

ideas.name: Forced play when all pass
ideas.text: If every Solo player passes, the holder of Spadilla has to call an Ace and play. Forcing a play means the hand is always played.

ideas.name: Premium suit
ideas.text: Solo gives one suit, couleur, double value, and Clubs or the previous winning suit usually fills the role. A bonus suit raises the stakes without changing the cards.

ideas.name: Trump cards with special protection
ideas.text: In Solo, high Matadores may be held back without penalty when a lower trump is led. The rule lets players keep their highest card for a later moment.

ideas.name: Declaring more mid-game
ideas.text: A Solo player who wins the first five tricks may lead a sixth card to signal they now go for all eight. Doing so forfeits the payment for five tricks, and the reward doubles if they succeed. A player can raise a bet midway.

ideas.name: Games for one person
ideas.text: Solitaire games are made for a single player who builds sequences on foundations. The game ends when families are complete or when no play is possible. The player's only opponents are themselves and the order of the cards.

ideas.name: A foundation that spells a year
ideas.text: In Anno Domini, the four foundation cards are chosen so that finishing them shows the current year, with the Ten standing for zero. A target can be given a personal meaning.

ideas.name: Doubling as the rule
ideas.text: In Double or Quits, each card on the foundation has to have double the value of the one before. Changing the rule for what fits on a pile changes which cards are useful.

ideas.name: Limited redeals
ideas.text: Solitaire games allow the stock to be dealt again, but one game permits a redeal only if a play was possible in the previous pass. Allowing replays while progress is made prevents endless repetition.

ideas.name: Counting to a target
ideas.text: In Forwards and Backwards, face cards count as 11, 12 and 13 and a card can only be played if it adds up to 14 with the card under it. A fixed sum as the rule for what fits gives every card a partner.

ideas.name: Same cards, different foundations
ideas.text: The solitaire chapter builds on Kings, Aces, Tens, Twos or four corners, in descending, ascending, odd-then-even or both directions. A change to where and how a pile begins gives a new puzzle from the same deck.

ideas.name: Reserves and free cards
ideas.text: Some solitaires deal a reserve packet of thirteen cards or four free cards that can be used when needed. A reserve of spare cards makes the puzzle easier to keep going.

ideas.name: Trading a card before it is revealed
ideas.text: In Speculation, a player who turns up a high trump may sell it to the highest bidder, and unseen cards may be bought too. The game is a market in cards whose value is uncertain.

ideas.name: Cards hidden until their turn
ideas.text: In Speculation each player has three cards face down and turns one at a time to find a higher trump than the turn-up. A player who has shown the highest trump stops turning. Suspense comes from slowly showing cards.

ideas.name: A holder defends their lead
ideas.text: In Speculation, the holder of the highest trump does not turn another card until it is beaten. Success stops a player from taking more risk.

ideas.name: Card order that changes by colour
ideas.text: In Spoil Five, red suits rank high to low and black suits low to high below the Jack, and the Five of trumps, Jack and Ace of Hearts are the three top trumps. The book gives the rhyme "highest in red, lowest in black". The same suit follows a different order depending on its colour, and a short saying helps players remember it.

ideas.name: Cards exempt from following
ideas.text: In Spoil Five the top trumps can hold back instead of following when a lower trump is led. The rank of a card sets whether it is forced to play.

ideas.name: A pool that grows on a stalemate
ideas.text: When nobody wins three tricks in Spoil Five, the pool stays and each player pays in again, up to a half or a third of the first stake. A draw is turned into a larger prize.

ideas.name: Solitaire shaped like a picture
ideas.text: Several solitaires lay out a picture, such as a wheel of 24 packets or a sickle with a handle of Kings. The cards that cannot be played are set aside as ornament, and a won game completes the shape. The goal is a finished picture.

ideas.name: Marriage in solitaire
ideas.text: Solitaire uses the word marriage for placing a card on one of the next rank and the opposite colour. A name from a card meld game is borrowed for a building rule.

ideas.name: Choosing how many cards to draw
ideas.text: In Twenty-One, a player asks for cards until they stop or go over 21. The dealer plays last and has to beat or match them. Each player decides their own level of risk against a known limit.

ideas.name: Dealer acts last
ideas.text: In Twenty-One the dealer shows their hand after all players have stood or drawn, and pays players who did not go over if the dealer busts. Playing last gives a seat the most information.

ideas.name: Ace as one or eleven
ideas.text: The Ace in Twenty-One counts as one or eleven at the holder's choice. A card with two values keeps a hand open.

ideas.name: Two cards that win at once
ideas.text: A natural twenty-one pays double and ends play if the dealer has it, as nobody can then beat the hand. A special result can end a round early and override the usual order of play.

ideas.name: Splitting a pair
ideas.text: A pair in Twenty-One can be played as two separate hands with a stake on each. Letting a player turn one bet into two creates new decisions from the same deal.

ideas.name: Aim lower, same rules
ideas.text: Quinze plays like Twenty-One but aims at 15, for two players. Changing the target number gives a different game from the same mechanism.

ideas.name: War needs no decisions
ideas.text: In War, the players turn up cards and the higher one takes both, and the winner is whoever holds the whole deck. There is no choice, so the outcome is set by the shuffle. The introduction puts it among the games for the youngest players.

ideas.name: Teams by cutting
ideas.text: Whist forms two teams by cutting the cards, with partners sitting opposite. The two highest cutters play the two lowest. Chance decides the partnerships; players do not choose them.

ideas.name: The last card shows trump
ideas.text: In Whist the whole pack is dealt out and the last card, which belongs to the dealer, is shown as trump. Trump is decided by the deal and told to everyone.

ideas.name: Seven choices at the start
ideas.text: In Solo Whist, the eldest hand may pass, propose, call a Solo, bid Misere, Abondance, Open Misere or Abondance Declared. Each is a different target for the same hand, so one deal supports several games.

ideas.name: Signalling with the lead
ideas.text: Whist advice says to lead your fourth highest card, so your partner can subtract its pips from eleven to know how many higher cards are out against you. Players agree on a convention so that a card carries a message.

ideas.name: Rubber play with waiting players
ideas.text: Whist rules say how six players take turns, how substitutes are chosen and how someone sits out after consecutive rubbers. A game for four can be shared by a larger group with rules for who is in.

ideas.name: Dice with a total target
ideas.text: Several dice games add up three throws, or throw a die until the total reaches 21 or goes over. A simple total as the goal makes a game from nothing but dice.

ideas.name: Dice that copy card hands
ideas.text: Poker Dice ranks one pair, two pairs, three of a kind, full house, four of a kind and five of a kind. A set of dice can use the ranking from a card game.

ideas.name: Throwing to pass a chip
ideas.text: In the dice game with chips, a six sends a chip to the next player and a one puts it in the pot. The player left holding the final chip gets three tries to pass it. A single die decides who ends up holding the loss.

ideas.name: Crossing off numbers
ideas.text: In the one-die game with a pad, a player keeps rolling while they cross off new numbers, and when a number repeats the neighbour crosses it off instead. A repeat result hands the play to someone else.

ideas.name: Different scoring of the same throw
ideas.text: Multiplication and Addition dice games throw three dice in the same way but multiply or add the last die. A change in how the score is counted gives a different game.

ideas.name: Matching ends
ideas.text: Dominoes are played by putting a tile so one half matches an open end of the row. A player who cannot match either passes or draws. The row of tiles is the playing area.

ideas.name: Block or draw
ideas.text: Block Dominoes passes when a player cannot match, and Draw Dominoes makes the player draw from the pool until a tile fits. A single rule about what happens when you are stuck changes how long the game is and how much luck matters.

ideas.name: Scoring in multiples
ideas.text: In Muggins, a tile that makes the two ends add to a multiple of five scores that number. Points come from the board position as well as from the hand.

ideas.name: Cutting back a bonus near the end
ideas.text: In a domino game, double-headers and triple-headers score extra, but a player who is close to winning counts them for less. A bonus is capped by how near the player is to finishing.

ideas.name: Tiles used as cards
ideas.text: Domino Poker takes 20 tiles and gives hands ranks such as pairs, flush and full house. Domino Euchre makes the double of the trump suit the right bower. Domino Loo follows Division Loo. Trick-taking and betting games can be moved onto a different set of pieces.

ideas.name: Making seven
ideas.text: In Matador, a tile is matched by playing one whose spots add to seven, and four tiles can be played anywhere. A new matching rule makes a different game with the same tiles, and the blank needs special tiles to be playable.

ideas.name: Tiles that play twice
ideas.text: In the domino game Tiddle-a-Wink, a player who plays a double plays again. A special tile gives its owner an extra move.

ideas.name: Passing out and starring
ideas.text: In Domino Pool, a player whose pips reach 100 leaves the game, and the first out may pay again to return at the score of the next player. A way back gives a knocked-out player a second chance for a price.

ideas.name: Building the table
ideas.text: Mahjong players build a wall of tiles together and throw dice twice to choose where to break it. Setting up the game is part of the play, and the dice decide who draws first from which place.

ideas.name: Seat names that rotate
ideas.text: Mahjong seats are the four Winds, and the East player is the banker, with each player taking a turn as East. The seat gives a role that moves round the table.

ideas.name: Scoring a hand you did not win
ideas.text: In Mahjong, the player who goes out is paid by all, but the other players pay each other the difference between their hands. A player who loses can still be paid more than the winner earned.

ideas.name: Groups worth different amounts
ideas.text: Mahjong scores sets by type: three of a kind of honors are worth more than plain numbers, and hidden sets count double those shown. Sequences score nothing but help to go out. A piece of the hand can be useful for finishing but worthless for points.

ideas.name: Doubling by theme
ideas.text: A Mahjong hand's points double for each doubling combination, such as three Dragons or all one suit, and a hand with six doubles is worth sixty-four times its base score. Stacked multipliers make some hands rare and very large.

ideas.name: A chance to go out versus a chance to score
ideas.text: Mahjong advice says an open-ended run can be completed by eight tiles while a pair can be completed by only two. Holding runs gives more ways to finish even though runs score nothing. What helps a player finish and what scores points are different things.

ideas.name: Reading discards
ideas.text: In Mahjong, players watch discards to guess which suits opponents are collecting, since each player tends to discard their shortest suit. The same public information gives clues about hidden hands.

ideas.name: Dead tiles
ideas.text: A discarded Mahjong tile becomes dead unless claimed straight away. Discarding something no one wants removes it from play.

ideas.name: Priority among claims
ideas.text: When two Mahjong players want the same discard, the one who can pung wins over one who can chow, and a player who needs the tile to go out wins over both. A ranking of claims settles disputes without arguments.

ideas.name: Banker pays and receives double
ideas.text: In Mahjong, East Wind collects double from all if they go out and pays double if another player goes out. A role at the table carries a bigger stake.

ideas.name: A cap on payments
ideas.text: The Mahjong chapter mentions a limit, usually 300 points, on any one hand. A cap stops one hand from deciding a whole table.

ideas.name: Extra tiles add chance
ideas.text: Flowers and seasons are added once the game has been learned, and add an element of chance. A basic game can be taught first and extra components added later.

ideas.name: Named shots
ideas.text: In pool games, the player names the ball they intend to pocket, though not the pocket. A ball pocketed without being called does not count. Declaring intent makes luck count for less.

ideas.name: Penalty by forfeiting a ball
ideas.text: In Eight-Ball style pool, a scratch costs a ball from the player's score, and a player with no balls has the next one replaced on the table. Fouls take away points already earned.

ideas.name: Free choice of the first stroke
ideas.text: In pool the winner of the lead can play first or pass to the opponent. Billiards lets the winner choose balls and who plays first. Whoever holds the choice has to guess which position suits them.

ideas.name: A foul costs points, not the turn alone
ideas.text: Billiards and pool list many fouls, such as touching a ball, a stroke made out of turn or a double touch, and most cost a point or the turn. A long list of fouls gives players a way to check how each stroke was made.

ideas.name: Spotting a ball back
ideas.text: Balls that jump off the table in billiards and pool are put back on a marked spot, or the nearest free place below it. Marking fixed places on the table gives a clear answer when a piece leaves play.

ideas.name: Choice for the opponent after a foul
ideas.text: In billiards, after some fouls the opponent may choose whether balls stay where they are, are replaced, or the stroke is played over. The player who was wronged picks the repair.

ideas.name: Limits on safe play
ideas.text: In billiards, an opponent may reject a third miss in a row and force the player to hit an object ball. A rule can stop players from stalling by staying safe.

ideas.name: Drawing lines to restrict repetition
ideas.text: Balk line billiards draws eight restricted spaces on the table, and a player may only make two shots in a row inside one space. A mark on the board stops one pattern from being repeated.

ideas.name: Shared board, different numbers
ideas.text: A darts board holds 20 numbers plus a bull, and different games pick different parts of it: Cricket uses 15 to 20 and the bull, Killer gives each player a number, Around the Clock goes 1 to 20 in order. One board supports many games.

ideas.name: Closing a number to score on it
ideas.text: In Cricket darts, three hits close a number for a team, and further hits score only while the other side has not closed it. Scoring depends on what the opponent still has open.

ideas.name: Starting with the other hand
ideas.text: In Killer, each player throws the first dart with their other hand, and the wedge it lands in becomes their number. Random assignment gives each person a personal target.

ideas.name: Earning the right to attack
ideas.text: In Killer a player has to hit their own number five times before they can reduce others' hits. A player has to build before they can attack.

ideas.name: Exact finish
ideas.text: In 301 darts, a player has to start by hitting a double and finish by hitting a double that brings the score exactly to zero. A rule that requires an exact finish stretches the end of the game.

ideas.name: Order as the challenge
ideas.text: Around the Clock asks players to hit wedges 1 to 20 in order, and only the right dart in the right order counts. Following a sequence makes a plain board into a test.

ideas.name: Scoring only on a multiple
ideas.text: In Five's, darts count only if the total of three throws is divisible by five. Hitting a number that fits a pattern is more important than hitting high.

ideas.name: Teams that need a count
ideas.text: The ball games chapter gives a range of players for each game, such as "between ten and sixty", with the equipment listed. Writing down player numbers and equipment together lets a group choose a game quickly.

ideas.name: Variation by hand and throw
ideas.text: In the drill game of throwing and catching, the teams change which hand throws and which hand catches. Small changes in how a motion is done give variety to a simple task.

ideas.name: Leaving the circle when you miss
ideas.text: Several circle games remove a player who misses a catch or toss. The last player in wins. Elimination games make the few who remain face the hardest rounds.

ideas.name: More objects than players makes it faster
ideas.text: The beanbag circle game works fastest when there is one fewer beanbag than players. Changing the ratio of objects to people sets the speed.

ideas.name: Time pressure as a rule
ideas.text: In the call-the-name beanbag game, a player has to name a catcher and throw before the person who is It counts to ten. A short count stops players from planning.

ideas.name: Hit or be hit
ideas.text: In several ball games a thrown ball that hits a player passes the role of thrower to them, or the hit player scores a stone against them. Being hit moves a player into a new role.

ideas.name: Guessing who did it
ideas.text: In Guess Ball, one player with their back turned is hit by the ball and has to guess from the other players' postures who threw it. The game rests on reading people's behaviour.

ideas.name: Captured players join the other side
ideas.text: In the ring game of hitting runners, a player who is hit joins the throwers and helps hit the rest. The last runner is the winner. Elimination can add to the other team.

ideas.name: Scoring by closeness
ideas.text: In the jack game, a team scores a point for each ball nearer the target than the opponent's nearest ball. Distance gives a way to rank and score.

ideas.name: Physical limits as rules
ideas.text: Games ask players to stand on one foot, hit the ball only with the free hand or pass it between the legs. A bodily constraint turns a plain ball game into a new one.

ideas.name: Relay as a structure
ideas.text: The passing relay has each row pass a ball down the line, and the last player runs it to the front. The first row to finish wins, and the rest of the row steps back to give space. A repeating task shared across a line makes a race.

ideas.name: Guards and bowlers
ideas.text: In the ninepins game, half of each side defends pins and half throws balls, and guards also feed balls to the bowlers. Splitting a team into attackers and defenders gives each player a role.

ideas.name: Helping a teammate or harming an opponent
ideas.text: In croquet, a player who has hit a ball can use the croquet stroke to send it anywhere they want, which can help a teammate or hurt an opponent. The same move is used for both aims, and croquet advice says a player who races for arches alone may gain less than one who breaks up opponents.

ideas.name: A role after finishing
ideas.text: A croquet player who has done the full course can retire by striking the stake, or become a rover. A rover can travel anywhere to help their side and hurt the other. Finishing early can turn a player into a helper.

ideas.name: Two versions of one stroke
ideas.text: Croquet has tight and loose croquet. In the tight one the player puts a foot on their ball and sends the other away; in the loose one the two balls are struck together. A small change in a rule about contact changes what the stroke does.

ideas.name: Hiding and finding
ideas.text: Hide-and-Seek has It count to twenty, search, and chase the first person found, who has to reach home base. Home base is the safe place to reach.

ideas.name: Guiding with warm and cold
ideas.text: In the thimble hunt, the hider may call "warmer" or "colder" as searchers move, or play music louder as they come close, but may not mislead them. Hints that say how close but not where guide the search step by step.

ideas.name: Hidden in plain sight
ideas.text: In the variation of the thimble game, the object is placed where it can be seen without moving anything, and a player who spots it acts as if still looking, then sits down. Hiding the fact that you have found the answer is part of the game.

ideas.name: A board with an order
ideas.text: Hopscotch has players throw a stone into box 1, hop in, kick it out, and go on to the next number, losing their turn if they miss or step on a line. The court sets the order, and touching a line ends the turn.

ideas.name: Scoring by nearness to a stake
ideas.text: Horseshoes scores one point for the closest shoe, two if both are closer, three for a ringer and six for two ringers. If both players have a double ringer they cancel. Cancelling stops equal efforts from scoring.

ideas.name: Rules about talking
ideas.text: Horseshoes rules ban speaking or moving in a way that bothers the opponent during a throw. A rule about conduct belongs with the rules about the board.

ideas.name: Baseball made simple
ideas.text: Kickball is described as baseball with a rolled ball that is kicked, three outs and nine innings, easier for beginners. A known game can be made easier by changing the equipment.

ideas.name: Chase games and their variants
ideas.text: The Tag chapter lists ways of changing a chase: no tagging while you stoop, safe when touching iron, a tagged player holding their hand on the spot, cooperating by crossing between the chaser and the chased. A single rule applied to a basic chase gives a new game.

ideas.name: Safe places
ideas.text: In Tag variants, a player is safe if touching iron, wood or stone, or while stooping a limited number of times. A safe spot limits the chaser, and a cap on its use stops a player from staying safe for ever.

ideas.name: Tag that spreads
ideas.text: In one Tag version, the first player tagged becomes It's partner and joins hands to chase the rest. The chasing side grows as players are caught.

ideas.name: Changing the course mid-chase
ideas.text: In the aisle chase, players stand in lines holding hands and the leader calls "Right face" so all turn and the aisles change direction. A rule that changes the paths lets the chase surprise the runners.

ideas.name: Shared control of a court
ideas.text: Volleyball allows several players on a side to hit the ball, but no one more than twice in a row, and only the serving side scores. Limits on touches force a team to pass among themselves.

ideas.name: Skill built in stages
ideas.text: In Jacks, the player picks up one jack at a time, then two, then three, up to all twelve, before winning. Each round raises the demand on the same action.

ideas.name: Winning marbles
ideas.text: Marbles games are played for the marbles themselves: in the ring game, the shooter keeps any marbles knocked out. The pieces are the stakes, so the game has no separate score.

ideas.name: Paying to try
ideas.text: In the marble and die game, a player who knocks the die off wins a marble from the keeper and a miss costs one. The keeper wins or pays on every try.

ideas.name: Games played for the pieces
ideas.text: The marble games each use a different way to win marbles: shooting from a ring, tossing at a hole, rolling at a wall, shooting at a die, or passing under bridges. The same pieces are the means and the stakes, and the games are told apart by how they are won.

ideas.name: Paying for a miss
ideas.text: In several marble games, a player who misses adds a marble to the row, pays the keeper or leaves the shooter in the ring. A miss makes the next attempt harder or more costly.

ideas.name: A bridge keeper
ideas.text: In the bridge marble game, a keeper pays marbles for each arch a player shoots through and collects one for a miss, and the keeper changes every round. A banker role in a game goes round the table.

ideas.name: The tool that is allowed
ideas.text: In Pickup Sticks one stick is different and may be used to lift others. One permitted helper stick makes the task easier without removing the challenge.

ideas.name: Losing the turn by touching
ideas.text: In both Jacks and Pickup Sticks, a player's turn ends when they move a piece they were not picking up. The rule rewards a steady hand.

ideas.name: Take away the sight
ideas.text: Blind Man's Buff and its variations blindfold one player, who has to catch or guess a person by touch, voice or a cane. Removing one sense turns a simple chase into a puzzle.

ideas.name: Changing places on a call
ideas.text: In the numbered Blind Man's Buff, the blindfolded player calls two numbers and those players swap seats while he tries to catch one. A named swap gives a moment of risk to the people called.

ideas.name: Disguised voice
ideas.text: In Blind Man's Buff with a cane, the person holding the other end may disguise their voice while answering three questions. The guesser identifies a person from a few answers.

ideas.name: Making others fail
ideas.text: In Cushion Dance, players dance in a ring trying to make their neighbours knock over the cushions without doing so themselves. The penalty for letting go of hands or knocking one is leaving the game. Players try to make others slip while staying safe themselves.

ideas.name: Rotating roles in a ring
ideas.text: Duck Duck Goose has the tapper pick a goose, who chases them round the circle. Whoever reaches the empty spot first sits there, so a role passes with a race.

ideas.name: Sound as the clue
ideas.text: In Marco Polo, the player who is It keeps their eyes shut and finds others by the sound of their answers. Hearing is the only way to find the others.

ideas.name: Asking permission
ideas.text: In Mother May I, players ask "Mother, may I?" before every step, and the Mother can say yes or no. The Mother has to remember where everyone is, and loses the position if she forgets.

ideas.name: Seats run out
ideas.text: Musical Chairs has one chair fewer than players, and one chair is removed each round. The player who finds no seat when the music stops is out. A shrinking supply makes each round tighter.

ideas.name: Memory test with objects
ideas.text: In Observation, players look at 20 objects for half a minute and then write what they remember. The most correct names win. The game measures attention over a fixed time.

ideas.name: Blind aim
ideas.text: In the Pinata and Pin the Tail on the Donkey, a blindfolded and spun player aims at a target. Spinning removes the sense of direction, so the result comes from luck and from remembering the room.

ideas.name: Breaking a wall
ideas.text: In Red Rover, a named player runs at a wall of linked hands, and if they fail to break through they join the wall. Players move from one team to the other through a test.

ideas.name: Hunt with a list
ideas.text: In a scavenger hunt, each team gets a list of things to find, either named or as clues. The first team back with the items or their locations wins. Clues make the list a puzzle first and a search second.

ideas.name: Obey only the right command
ideas.text: In Simon Says, players follow a movement only if the leader says "Simon says", and those who follow an order without it are out. The game tests attention to the form of an instruction.

ideas.name: Points from the numbers
ideas.text: High Low Jack pool gives points for the highest ball, the lowest ball and the nine ball, as the card game does, plus the most balls. Pool scoring can borrow categories from a card game.

ideas.name: Scores kept as buttons
ideas.text: Continuous Pool keeps points on a string of buttons over the table, with penalties taken from the score instead of the table. The scoring tool is built into the room.

ideas.name: Claiming a group by the first pocket
ideas.text: In Eight Ball, whichever group of balls is pocketed first decides who plays solids and who plays stripes. A choice made by an early event stands for the rest of the game.

ideas.name: The last target is special
ideas.text: In Eight Ball the Eight ball can only be pocketed after all your own balls, and pocketing it in the wrong pocket or with the cue ball loses. A key target that can be reached only at the end gives a game a clear last step.

ideas.name: Balls worth their number
ideas.text: Fifteen-Ball Pool credits each pocketed ball with its number, so the winner is the player with the highest total and not the most balls. Giving unequal values to pieces changes what counts as a worthwhile shot.

ideas.name: Playing in numerical order
ideas.text: Chicago Pool sets the balls along the cushions and has players pocket them in order from one. Nine Ball uses nine balls in a diamond and wins with the nine, even by hitting the lowest ball first. A sequence turns an open table into a series of steps.

ideas.name: Winning by a shortcut
ideas.text: In Nine Ball a player can win by pocketing the nine using the lowest ball on the table, without pocketing the others. A rule that allows a combination skips the long route.

ideas.name: Charades without words
ideas.text: A Charades player cannot speak, sign letters or use props. The referee holds the topics, settles disputes and watches the time. Banning words forces the player to find another way to carry a meaning.

ideas.name: Agreed signs
ideas.text: In team Charades, teams can agree on gestures before the game for a book, a movie, a song or an action, but cannot discuss them once play begins. A shared code made in advance replaces talking.

ideas.name: Answers by acting together
ideas.text: In "What did you see", the leader asks a team and the team answers with a physical action all of them copy. The book asks for variety and originality in the answers. A joint answer is shown by the whole group.

ideas.name: Paper-and-pencil games
ideas.text: Dots, Hangman and Tick-tack-toe need only paper and pens. In Dots, a player who completes a square adds their initial and takes another turn. A game can be played with no equipment bought.

ideas.name: Two strategies in Dots
ideas.text: The book gives two plans for Dots: block the opponent from making squares, or set up the board so that one line completes many squares. A simple board gives players a choice between defence and setting traps.

ideas.name: Naming from memory in turn
ideas.text: In Geography, players take turns naming a place and each has to keep a mental list of what has been said. A repeat or a blank puts a player out. The only equipment is memory.

ideas.name: Wrong guesses build a picture
ideas.text: In Hangman, each wrong letter adds a part to the drawing of the figure, and the figure's completion ends the game. A visible count of mistakes works as a clock.

ideas.name: A game that often ends level
ideas.text: The book says Tick-tack-toe often ends in a draw because neither player can get three in a row. When both players see the same moves, the result is predictable.

ideas.name: Games carry beliefs in their parts
ideas.text: Flanagan builds the book on the claim that a game's rules of progress, winning and losing paradigms, codes of conduct and ways of interacting hold beliefs, as marble and chisel shape a sculpture. A designer who changes these parts changes what the game says.

ideas.name: A game is a machine for social relations
ideas.text: A hopscotch map with numbers, a very large map, or two maps side by side each set up a different relation between players: points, a height advantage, a race. Onlookers who distract the hopper add unwritten play that the group accepts.

ideas.name: Real options make a game
ideas.text: Costikyan holds that a story is linear and a game is not, because a game depends on decisions with real alternatives. A player may choose one way in one game and another way in the next, and the more linear a game gets, the less it is a game.

ideas.name: Games loosely defined
ideas.text: Flanagan sets aside the strict definitions of Crawford, Costikyan and Salen and Zimmerman, which need conflict and a quantifiable outcome. She treats games as situations with guidelines and procedures, which lets her include artists' play with no winner.

ideas.name: Play moves with technology and economy
ideas.text: Doll play was organised during the American industrial revolution, when household roles needed restating, and money-centred board games such as Monopoly came with changes in banking and property. A change in how people live shows up in what they play.

ideas.name: Players test the edge of the rules
ideas.text: In hockey, chess or house play, players look for what is allowed and push at it. Cheating, open play and social comment are all ways of using the gap between the rules and what players expect.

ideas.name: Doll play copied the home
ideas.text: An 1888 account describes a girl getting her dolls up, giving them breakfast and lessons, dinner and bed, matching her own day. Armstrong reads this as record keeping about the culture disguised as play.

ideas.name: A broken illusion stops play
ideas.text: Mechanical dolls of the late nineteenth century, such as Edison's talking doll, were unpopular with girls and often failed to work. Without the sense of being alive, the doll was only a heavy object, and nobody engaged with it.

ideas.name: What a group plays shows its values
ideas.text: Sutton-Smith argues that a group's preferred pastimes are one way its values appear. Swinging in Rococo painting, sanctioned by doctors for the ruling class, shows leisure shaped by rank and propriety.

ideas.name: Childhood and leisure are recent inventions
ideas.text: The idea of childhood as a separate stage is about four hundred years old in Europe and North America, and leisure time came from the industrial split between work and social life. Both shaped what counts as play and who gets it.

ideas.name: The Sims builds consumption into its core loop
ideas.text: Characters turn happy through purchased goods, and expensive chairs please them more than plain ones, so the player needs an income to keep buying. Flanagan reads this as a mirror of real consumer messages, while noting players can also use it with irony.

ideas.name: The Sims lets players move room functions
ideas.text: A player who puts a large chair and television in the kitchen finds the characters just as happy as in the bedroom. That freedom lets players rework what a home is for, even though buying things stays the main route to wellbeing.

ideas.name: Too much control removes the point of play
ideas.text: Flanagan notes that the pull of house games comes from moving through them and pushing limits, more than from arriving. A player who can control everything has nothing left to find out.

ideas.name: A mancala board already has the parts of a game
ideas.text: Flanagan lists five in a board that is thousands of years old: territories (the hollows), actions (moving stones), rules (direction, number of seeds), tokens and feedback (the count collected). The same list fits modern boards.

ideas.name: The same family spans chance and strategy
ideas.text: Mancala without counting seeds is a game of pure chance, and with counting it becomes a game of strategy with complete information. A change in what players track alters the kind of game.

ideas.name: Chance has been used to feel possible
ideas.text: Csikszentmihalyi and Bennett argue that people who consult chance, as in divination, feel their plans can cope with what may come, so their state is nearer play than worry. Senet, played on a journey to the afterlife, mixes chance with a race against fate.

ideas.name: Special squares change the direction of play
ideas.text: In the Egyptian Hounds and Jackals, two holes send a piece backward and two give an extra turn, while the two tracks stay independent. Snakes and Ladders still uses the same idea of squares that move a piece.

ideas.name: A board game can carry a message
ideas.text: The twelfth-century Alea Evangelii turned a Tafl game into a religious allegory, one of the first uses of a board game as an ideological tool. Later sugoroku and American morality games did the same for Buddhist teaching, nationalism and moral conduct.

ideas.name: Abstraction helps a game travel
ideas.text: Chess, Go and backgammon have abstract boards and stable rules, which let them move across regions, religions and cultures. Games that add detail and theme become tied to a place and a time.

ideas.name: One structure carries many themes
ideas.text: Sugoroku keeps one roll-and-move form like Snakes and Ladders and changes the theme: Buddhist doctrine, a journey through Edo, poems, actors, soldiers, the National Diet. The printed sheet made each version cheap and portable.

ideas.name: Matching games run on talk
ideas.text: In E-awase, nobles paired painted shells and debated the matches, so chance and judgement calls gave them a reason to talk. The game was a device for conversation more than for winning.

ideas.name: Rules can build a moral world
ideas.text: In Mansion of Happiness, landing on Piety moves a player toward the mansion and landing on Cruelty sends the player back. More than half the spaces carry a virtue or a vice, so the board states what the makers valued.

ideas.name: Game makers change games to suit their time
ideas.text: When Parker Brothers reissued Mansion of Happiness in 1894 they removed the vices of Immodesty and Passion, swapped women for men in the house of correction, and added poverty to the vices. The rules changed with the publisher's view of the audience.

ideas.name: Point values show what a game rewards
ideas.text: In The Checkered Game of Life a Happy Old Age earned fifty of the hundred points needed, Wealth ten, and Matrimony and Truth none. The scoring table is a ranking of values.

ideas.name: A familiar form can be reskinned to argue the opposite
ideas.text: The game of Stanley's journey across Africa reused the travel game and put a white officer leading porters, so that play supported colonial belief. Flanagan warns that "it's only a game" is often a shelter for bias.

ideas.name: A game can start as a protest
ideas.text: Magie designed The Landlord's Game to show the harm of land monopoly under Henry George's single tax, and she let players adapt it to their region. Parker Brothers refused it as too complicated, too educational and too political before taking Darrow's near copy.

ideas.name: Anti-Monopoly turns the board's starting state around
ideas.text: Ralph Anspach's game begins with the board already held by monopolies, and players compete to restore a free market. A square that sent players to jail now sends them to a price war.

ideas.name: Games mirror the culture that made them
ideas.text: Hofer calls American games from the 1840s to the 1920s a window on a nation changing through immigration, cities and industry. Early mass-produced titles centred on the home and on moral teaching before turning to money, war and word play.

ideas.name: An unreachable goal changes the game
ideas.text: In Giacometti's Circuit, a ball rolls round a groove, and the only hollow that could be a goal lies outside the groove. Nothing the player does can reach it, so the board shows a closed system with endless motion and no ending.

ideas.name: A board can place a theme in its layout
ideas.text: Giacometti's No More Play sets thin figures among holes on two sides, with a bombed-out middle that opens to graves. A familiar form (two sides facing across a board) is used to hold war and death.

ideas.name: Meaningful play depends on visible links
ideas.text: Salen and Zimmerman say play is meaningful when the link between an action and its outcome is both discernible and integrated into the whole game. Flanagan adds that the social setting matters too: board game sales rose in the Depression of the 1930s.

ideas.name: A machine's theme can be swapped without touching its mechanism
ideas.text: In the 1940s Genco and Seeburg sold changeover units that re-themed pinball and shooting games for war, such as Chicken Sam turned into a shooting range for an enemy figure. The mechanism stayed the same while the meaning changed.

ideas.name: Games as processes, not outcomes
ideas.text: Fluxus artists treated games as processes that could carry ideas, using humour, touch and chance. Cards and boxes took the place of a finished object.

ideas.name: A rule set may leave play and result to the players
ideas.text: Brecht's Swim Puzzle Box tells players to arrange beads so a word never occurs, but the box holds only a seashell. Water Yam's seventy event cards leave each task's success to the group and chance.

ideas.name: A reconfigurable board lets players act on the subject
ideas.text: Fahlström fixed his pieces with magnets so players could move them and take sides in a political scene. His boards used Monopoly-like rules inscribed on the work, including text read as part of play.

ideas.name: Changing the space of a sport changes the game
ideas.text: Orozco's Ping Pond Table multiplies the table by four, so four people play and the net becomes an open space between them. His pocketless Oval Billiard Table has no goal, and viewers hit the swinging ball to see what happens.

ideas.name: A handicap keeps unequal players in one game
ideas.text: In Go, a weaker player may be given more stones or a smaller board, and the rules stay the same. The game adjusts to the people instead of dropping the contest.

ideas.name: Changing a turn order changes who thinks of whom
ideas.text: In Lilian Ball's GO ECO, an odd number of players means no one holds a fixed side, since each player occupies another side next turn. The change was meant to push players to see viewpoints other than their own.

ideas.name: Chess changed as its society did
ideas.text: Yalom traces the queen: absent before the tenth century, then the weakest piece moving one square, then the most powerful as women held more power in Europe. Islamic sets avoided realistic human figures and used abstract pieces.

ideas.name: Pieces are defined by what they can do
ideas.text: To teach chess one shows the board, then maps abilities onto figures. If a piece is missing, an eraser can stand in for a bishop, because a piece gets its powers from the rules, whatever it looks like.

ideas.name: Different games can model the same battle in different ways
ideas.text: The Greek game Polis traps a piece between two of the opponent's, echoing a phalanx. In chess the knight's move makes such a line less important.

ideas.name: Changing the senses used changes the game
ideas.text: Takako Saito made chess sets of vials of liquid with smells, boxes identified by weight or sound, and tubes of spices. Players have to learn the pieces by touch, smell or hearing before the rules can be used.

ideas.name: Removing the colour difference removes the contest
ideas.text: Ono's All White Chess Set is painted all white, with a plate saying to play as long as you can remember where your pieces are. Flanagan reads white as the colour of surrender, so the usual opposition between two sides has no marker.

ideas.name: A third side changes a two-sided game
ideas.text: Catlow's Rethinking Wargames gives chess three players: white royalty, black royalty and the pawns. When five turns pass without a capture, grass grows on the board, and the pawns win by delaying violence long enough for talk.

ideas.name: A duality can oversimplify
ideas.text: Huizinga warns that dividing life into two camps, us and them, makes competition easy to start and leaves out shades of difference. Flanagan sees Catlow's added role and wider outcomes as a way to answer this limit of two-sided games.

ideas.name: Widening the win states changes agency
ideas.text: Catlow's chess gives the pawns new power and adds outcomes beyond one side winning. Giacometti's boards go the other way and question whether acting in a game can lead anywhere at all.

ideas.name: Language play makes a play space from words
ideas.text: Crystal says language games cut across region, class, age and culture. Flanagan treats secret languages, riddles, limericks and puns as forms in which words are the material of play.

ideas.name: One sign can carry two meanings
ideas.text: Two carp in a Chinese wedding gift stand for a married pair, and the same sound yu also means abundance. A Dutch painting of a slipper hints at a love affair because slippertje can mean a slip. The viewer needs to know the second meaning to see the joke.

ideas.name: Hidden wordplay brings the audience into the work
ideas.text: Jarry made the name Ubu a palindrome and hid word puzzles in the play, which invited the audience to piece together a criticism aimed at themselves.

ideas.name: Puns were once used to read signs
ideas.text: Early writing had few signs for many meanings, so a sign could be read in several ways. Diviners looked for puns in the sound and look of words, so interpreting became a ritual act.

ideas.name: Puns stop one fixed reading
ideas.text: Duchamp's Anemic Cinema pairs spinning disks with punning sentences, so the images and text offer many meanings and no lesson. The viewer is left room to interpret.

ideas.name: A procedure can stand in for the author
ideas.text: Tzara's recipe is a rule set: choose an article, cut out each word, shake the bag, copy the words in the order drawn. The poem comes from the procedure, which shifts authorship from the writer to the process.

ideas.name: Automatic writing has rules too
ideas.text: The Surrealist instruction is to write fast without thinking, and if the flow stops, to leave a gap and start the next sentence with a letter chosen at random in advance. Chance operations set the limits within which the writer is free.

ideas.name: Chance replaces premeditation
ideas.text: Surrealist games and procedures aim to free words and images from rational order by using chance and indeterminacy. Brotchie and Gooding link this to a political aim to transform objects, behaviour and ideas.

ideas.name: Information limits change a word game
ideas.text: In the exquisite corpse, players either see only the last person's contribution or follow a fixed pattern of parts of speech. The pattern keeps the sentence grammatical while no one controls the whole.

ideas.name: Games can be made from instructions
ideas.text: Ono's Sun Piece asks the reader to watch the sun until it becomes square, and Touch Poem for a Group of People says to touch each other. These instruction cards act as little programs that turn a viewer into a participant.

ideas.name: Cage framed everyday acts as play
ideas.text: Cage's teaching in New York placed a magic circle around ordinary actions, which turned them into games and moved them into fantasy. Fluxus then used such cards to make situations that are artworks.

ideas.name: Letters can be made touchable
ideas.text: Knowles's Finger Book of Ancient Languages gives each English letter an object sewn into cloth, such as a pin for p and a feather for f. A reader touches each zone to spell words, so reading becomes a bodily search.

ideas.name: Players can add to the text
ideas.text: In Holzer's Please Change Beliefs, internet users upload new truisms to a list that is shown at timed intervals and open to change. The audience supplies the content, and the participation is part of what the piece is.

ideas.name: The player's body can interact with the text
ideas.text: In Text Rain, a camera tracks participants and letters of a poem fall on their silhouettes, so players catch letters on an arm and gather phrases. Players find the poem is about bodies and language.

ideas.name: Fluxus made a multiplayer play space
ideas.text: Fluxus moved play from galleries to everyday venues and treated the joke as a method, aiming at collective identity over the individual artist. Maciunas wrote that Fluxus tends toward anonymity.

ideas.name: All games are performative
ideas.text: Flanagan notes that any game needs some action from players, such as thinking, guessing, running or tossing. Theatre does the same when actors pretend, as children do with a dollhouse.

ideas.name: Chance can be a method
ideas.text: Arp tore up drawings and fixed the pieces where they fell, and he called the result ordered by the law of chance. He saw chance as a systematic way to remove the artist's will, and not as accident.

ideas.name: Folding a paper hides earlier moves
ideas.text: In the drawing form of exquisite corpse, each player draws on a folded section so the next player cannot see what came before. Small link lines can run across the fold, or one word can be handed on, so the final picture looks joined up.

ideas.name: A game of questions can reveal the group
ideas.text: Would You Open the Door asks for an instant decision about a person and sets off talk about politics and ethics. Flanagan notes it was close to an existing French parlor game, with the cast of names changed to suit the group.

ideas.name: Retelling changes the picture
ideas.text: In chain drawing, each person has five seconds to look and then draws from memory. The point is to compare how the first, middle and last drawings differ after passing through many hands.

ideas.name: Games used as a way of working
ideas.text: The Surrealists made games in order to make art, so a game was part of their research and not only the product. Exquisite corpse pooled thought across the group and produced work that went beyond one author.

ideas.name: Winning can mean finding something
ideas.text: In these games, winning might be to experience or make something new, puzzling or surprising, or to touch a process that shows how the mind works. At other times a performance is pure amusement.

ideas.name: Dressing up can blur a pair of opposites
ideas.text: Cahun's self-portraits move between pairs such as schoolgirl and weightlifter or geisha and Buddha through costume. Seeing the roles changed so easily shows them as made, as in a charades-like guessing game.

ideas.name: Artists can turn a process into the whole game
ideas.text: Gutai artists staged events and made objects that were games in their entirety, instead of using games behind the scenes to make a fixed work. Kanayama's painting machine let him make art while he napped and set up a game space run by rules.

ideas.name: A plan can design the work
ideas.text: LeWitt's plans were preset rule sets for a wall drawing, and he wrote that the plan would design the work, in some cases with millions of variations and in others a limited number. Both kinds are finite.

ideas.name: Guests given instructions become participants
ideas.text: In Kaprow's 18 Happenings in Six Parts, guests received instructions like game rules on how to move through rooms, sometimes bending into uncomfortable positions. They were called participants and not spectators.

ideas.name: Absurd rules add physical play
ideas.text: Fluxus festivals included soccer on stilts, balloon javelin and table tennis with large holes in the paddles. The Handicap Run had players run while drinking vodka, eating oatmeal, grinding coffee and shouting.

ideas.name: A work can pass the authority to the audience
ideas.text: In 4'33'' the pianist plays nothing, and listeners create their own piece from the sounds in the room. Cage's chance operations changed who composes and who listens.

ideas.name: Repeating one action makes it a game
ideas.text: Knowles's Identical Lunch had different people eat the same tuna sandwich on wheat toast with a glass of buttermilk at the same place and time on many days. Each lunch was documented, and the series itself was the piece.

ideas.name: A written rule leaves a space for unwritten rules
ideas.text: "Follow a line" is explicit, but players have to decide whose line, where to and why. Flanagan argues that Fluxus work lives in these implicit rules, which players settle as they move from an everyday action into the magic circle.

ideas.name: An open score shows how people behave
ideas.text: In Ono's Cut Piece the audience cuts off pieces of her clothing, one at a time. Some audiences mobbed her and others held back, and she said she did not want to control the ripples.

ideas.name: One planned error keeps people looking
ideas.text: Cadere's wooden bars follow a colour code from mathematical permutations, with one error placed in each. From a distance they seem striped, and the viewer who tries to decode the pattern starts a conversation with the work.

ideas.name: Putting a board game on people changes it
ideas.text: In human shogi, the board game becomes a performance and a social event with players, facilitators and spectators. Flanagan says the move reskins, replays and rewrites the game all at once.

ideas.name: A player can play with a game instead of playing it
ideas.text: Schleiner's OUT projected America's Army onto buildings in New York and had players talk with the regular online players about war. She used an existing game as the setting of a live performance.

ideas.name: Rules can set up a long personal game
