ideas.text: Ostojic's Looking for a Husband with an EU Passport ran from 2000 to 2005, with rules set, conditions met and challenges overcome, from an advertisement to a wedding, a visa and a divorce party. Flanagan reads it as role-play about borders and intimacy.

ideas.name: Play hard, play fair, nobody hurt
ideas.text: These three principles guided every New Games event, and the games were meant to change how people of different ages, ethnicities, genders and incomes met. Brand's softwar added that a conflict could be regional, refereed and cushioned.

ideas.name: Changing what players do can matter more than the theme
ideas.text: In the New Games match Slaughter, forty players compete for four balls and moving baskets, and instead of pushing players off the mat, they pull each other from one area to another. Designers did not make games about Vietnam or racism, and put the change into the action.

ideas.name: A game changes when people leave it
ideas.text: Brand's Theory of Game Change says a game is not altered by winning, judging or watching it, but by leaving it and starting a new game elsewhere. If the new one works, it may alter or replace the old one.

ideas.name: The mechanic is the message
ideas.text: Flanagan holds that knowledge in games comes through doing, so what a player does with the game's verbs matters to the meaning. She writes that a game's mechanic is its message.

ideas.name: Play makes nothing
ideas.text: Caillois says play creates no wealth or goods, so that property is exchanged but nothing is produced and nothing is harvested. Flanagan finds conceptual art close to this, because it favours the system and process over a product.

ideas.name: Critical games often lack a clear winner
ideas.text: Salen and Zimmerman and Crawford would say a game needs at least a winner or loser, and many artists' games are abstract or open. Flanagan points out that automatic writing, Fluxus action and a finished exquisite corpse can each be read as a quantifiable outcome.

ideas.name: Play belongs to a place
ideas.text: Flanagan holds that play is universal but each experience of it is tied to a place and culture. The same act may count as play in one square and not be seen as play in another. Steve Symons's Aura is moved to many squares unchanged, which she reads as treating the site as secondary.

ideas.name: Play needs agreement
ideas.text: Play can only start when the people involved decide it can, and this includes bystanders. A game played in a public square asks passers-by, who never agreed, to be part of it.

ideas.name: A street game hides who is playing
ideas.text: In Cruel 2 B Kind, teams of two "kill" others with acts of kindness such as a compliment. Players cannot tell who is a player and who is a bystander, so strangers may be hit by accident.

ideas.name: Captured players join the capturer
ideas.text: A Cruel 2 B Kind player who is picked off joins the team of the person who did it. Teams grow until two crowds meet in one final showdown.

ideas.name: Passers-by become game pieces
ideas.text: Flanagan notes that Cruel 2 B Kind uses outsiders as non-player characters, and players act kindly for points rather than out of kindness. In Vem Grater, players left clues and graffiti around a university, and the cleaning staff had to undo them.

ideas.name: Taking play outdoors does not by itself give power
ideas.text: Flanagan argues that moving a game onto the pavement is not empowering on its own. If the aim is to help people reclaim a city, that aim has to be built into the mechanic and the setting.

ideas.name: A hopscotch grid can be a map-making tool
ideas.text: In mapscotch, cards ask players to chalk hopscotch patterns on the pavement on themes such as labour or human rights. A very simple old rule set is used to draw out how a city treats different people.

ideas.name: A walking game can be a short rule set
ideas.text: Chain Reaction has players change direction whenever they see a lead object, such as a Starbucks cup, and stop at a release object, such as an independent bookshop. They map each walk, and the maps differ from one neighbourhood to the next.

ideas.name: Three rules can make a game
ideas.text: Suyin Looui's Transition Algorithm has three steps: visit a neighbourhood that is changing, photograph it, and bring home a souvenir that was not bought. The game sends players to places of change and records what they see.

ideas.name: Players can set their own rules
ideas.text: In the Cell Phone-Free Temporary Autonomous Zone, people in a set place and time follow rules that they ideally decide for themselves. Badges mark who is part of the zone.

ideas.name: Less technology can leave more room for the place
ideas.text: Flanagan observes that the locative projects most aware of space often use little or no technology. She suggests the lived experience of a place comes first and the technology second.

ideas.name: A giant game piece draws a whole city in
ideas.text: In the Big Urban Game, three teams moved huge inflatable pieces through neighbourhoods towards one bridge. The public voted online or by phone on the route, and neighbours who rarely met ended up playing together.

ideas.name: A game asks who has time to play
ideas.text: Flanagan asks of drift games and street games: who is free to wander, and who walks because work or the day requires it? A game that assumes free time and free movement is built for some players and not others.

ideas.name: Swapping the picture does not change the system
ideas.text: Butler's argument, as Flanagan uses it, is that reskinning a stereotype is not enough. Larger change comes from altering the categories and relations that a system rests on.

ideas.name: Games carry beliefs whether or not designers intend it
ideas.text: The Sims rewards earning and buying, and Grand Theft Auto rewards success through crime. Neither was made to teach, but players take in the world view anyway.

ideas.name: A game with no win state has no built-in conflict
ideas.text: September 12th lets the player only fire or not fire missiles at a town. With no goal there is no obstacle, no opponent and no learning curve, and any conflict is inside the player.

ideas.name: One action can carry the whole argument
ideas.text: September 12th has one move: fire. Each shot brings rubble and mourners, and the survivors turn into terrorists, so the rules themselves say that violence breeds violence.

ideas.name: An impossible task can be the point
ideas.text: In Madrid the player keeps candles lit for those killed in the bombings, but cannot move fast enough to save them all. The failure is built to make the player think about remembering.

ideas.name: A mechanic can pull against its theme
ideas.text: In Hush the player has to stay calm and type a lullaby on time to keep a baby quiet during a raid. The wish to be calm clashes with the fear of being found, and the baby's cry grows harsher as the player fails.

ideas.name: Random cards can start a design
ideas.text: The Hush team drew the mechanic "Singing" and the theme "Human Rights" in a Values at Play exercise. The odd pairing led to the core idea.

ideas.name: A story and its controls can disagree on purpose
ideas.text: In The Intruder the player earns each line of the story by winning a mini-game, yet the story is about harm to a woman. The gap between easy play and a dark tale is meant to make the player feel part of the harm.

ideas.name: A failure state can move the story on
ideas.text: One mini-game of The Intruder moves the story on when the character falls into a trap. In most games that would mean failure and a restart.

ideas.name: Most games give the player the command post
ideas.text: Chesher is quoted saying the cursor signals that the machine is waiting for the player's order. Flanagan notes that players are nearly always cast as powerful agents, and The Intruder puts them in an uncomfortable spot instead.

ideas.name: A game can play itself
ideas.text: Eddo Stern's Fort Paladin has robotic fingers play America's Army again and again, with the same grenade, the same enemies and the same respawn. Watching it shows how little a player's choice changes in a closed system.

ideas.name: Game events can reach the player's body
ideas.text: Tekken Torture Tournament passes injuries to the on-screen fighters on to the real players. In Dark Game, two rivals lose their sight.

ideas.name: Players can undo a game from inside it
ideas.text: In Domestic Tension, viewers could shoot paintballs at a man by webcam. Some formed a human shield that took turns aiming the gun away from him, so the play was turned against the rules.

ideas.name: A win state can be kept up as an illusion
ideas.text: In Darfur Is Dying the player has a clear goal, to survive one week, so it feels like an action game with a smooth learning curve. Reaching it does not end the real crisis.

ideas.name: Success can raise the price of play
ideas.text: A camp that does well in Darfur Is Dying attracts raiders, so the player has to rebuild again and again. The more the player achieves, the more danger the game sends back.

ideas.name: The character chosen changes what is possible
ideas.text: A Darfur Is Dying player picks a character by age and gender. A girl who fetches water carries more than a small boy and less than an adult, and she also faces extra danger.

ideas.name: A game can point to action outside itself
ideas.text: Darfur Is Dying has a Take Action Now button that lets the player write to the US president, petition Congress or send the game on, which links the game to the world outside it.

ideas.name: Hidden effects can make every win look the same
ideas.text: Oil God has the player raise oil prices by starting wars and disasters, with no way to tell which acts raise the price most. Persuasive Games' game rewards every move, so Flanagan calls it a you-always-win game.

ideas.name: Games can start talk instead of giving answers
ideas.text: Frasca writes that these games aim to trigger discussion, not to find solutions. The model need not be accurate if it prompts people to think about other ways of handling an issue.

ideas.name: A serious game can fail in two ways
ideas.text: Flanagan says such a game has to keep what makes a game enjoyable and still send its message. It can lose either one, ending dull and didactic, or entertaining and hollow.

ideas.name: Facts between levels can change how a game reads
ideas.text: Vagamundo is an arcade game in which a migrant avoids flying bottles and fights a giant cockroach. Between its levels it shows facts about border crossing and deaths, so the comic play sits next to serious data.

ideas.name: A game can be a safe place for hard subjects
ideas.text: Flanagan says a simulated world lets players step back and think about problems, and may be the safest outlet for exploring terrible ones. She also says play only happens when players feel comfortable.

ideas.name: A tragedy form needs the player to lose
ideas.text: Lee links games for change to tragedy, where the player is not meant to win because that keeps the form. Brecht and Boal ask audiences to stay aware that they are watching or playing a model.

ideas.name: Work and play can be given the same screen
ideas.text: Metapet has players train office workers in a made-up biotech firm to be more efficient. The game copies the constant checking and upkeep of networked jobs, and asks what that costs.

ideas.name: Games about care drew many women players
ideas.text: Flanagan reports that games of everyday tasks, such as social talk and tending characters, attracted many women players. Women are still few among the people who make games.

ideas.name: Rules are constraints that start invention
ideas.text: Flanagan says even playing house has implied rules for actions and space. Rules of operation give both designer and player constraints that provoke new ideas.

ideas.name: Designers follow repeatable steps
ideas.text: Flanagan lists the usual cycle: set a goal, build a minimum set of rules and pieces, make a paper or acted prototype, play test, revise, repeat. The cycle can be run on one small goal or on the whole game.

ideas.name: Add a values check to every loop
ideas.text: The critical play method asks the designer to set a values goal next to the design goal and test both on each round. A game is checked for being playable and for whether its values come through in play.

ideas.name: Plan for several play styles and for subversion
ideas.text: Flanagan suggests a noncompetitive way to play beside a competitive one. She also asks designers to leave room for players to bend the system.

ideas.name: Test with people who do not usually play
ideas.text: Designers are asked to leave the studio and test with a wide range of players, including nongamers. They look for dead ends, dull stretches and uneven difficulty.

ideas.name: The finished game can say something other than intended
ideas.text: Flanagan notes a gap between what a maker intends and what gets made. Varied testers can show whether the concept still comes through once the game is done.

ideas.name: A design process can share authority
ideas.text: Flanagan asks for less hierarchy in making games, with the usual designers, ideas and players not always the same. Playtesting with the community an artist wants to reach is part of this.

ideas.name: Made things have politics
ideas.text: Following Langdon Winner, Flanagan says artifacts carry politics, and games hold the norms and biases of their makers and their time, often unnoticed. The method a maker uses shapes what a game means.

ideas.name: Past examples give designers a list of tactics
ideas.text: Flanagan turns the book's cases into moves a designer can try: write instructions, use rude language, make puppets of people, make words touchable, shift the point of view. She says this gives a name to techniques that might go unnoticed.

ideas.name: Games distil daily life
ideas.text: Flanagan says games take the everyday actions of players and boil them down, and they carry the motives and values of their designers. The game then makes a place unfamiliar enough for play to begin.

ideas.name: Play is never innocent
ideas.text: Citing Sutton-Smith, Flanagan reminds readers that play has been used to pass on culture and to change it, and has also served other purposes. A locative game cannot be taken as freeing just because it is play.

ideas.name: A game and a playing of it are different things
ideas.text: Wake separates the game as a set of rules and parts from each performance of it, which happens once, at a particular time and place. Jenga's fifty-four blocks are real objects, but the game only exists when people stack and pull them.

ideas.name: Open rules invite players to fill the gaps
ideas.text: Wake argues that games leave deliberate gaps, spots of indeterminacy, so that every playing differs. Designers steer players towards behaviour they can anticipate, but only partly, so players also argue over rules, hack and mod.

ideas.name: Pieces that stand for players pull the body into the game
ideas.text: In Rhino Hero, players put a wooden hero on a shaky tower of folded cards. Reviewers write about their trembling thumbs and old-age tremor, which shows that the player's own body becomes part of the game's challenge.

ideas.name: A board arranges people as well as pieces
ideas.text: The Monopoly board prints its text facing four sides and sets play running clockwise round the table. A War of Whispers uses a round board with no opposite sides, so players sit as members of one council.

ideas.name: Table size decides how close players sit
ideas.text: A Monopoly board is about twenty inches across, so hands pass dice, cards and money across it and fingers sometimes touch. Wake sees this closeness as part of what a board does.

ideas.name: An object becomes a toy when someone plays with it
ideas.text: Sicart argues that a stick is just an object until a person picks it up. Its weight and bark then shape what the player does, and the player's use changes what the stick is.

ideas.name: A piece matters less as a token than as a toy
ideas.text: The miniaturists in the survey differ. Some treat a figure as a toy whose paint and look matter. Others treat it as a game token that could be a coin. The rules of irrelevance say the look of a game piece does not matter to the rules.

ideas.name: One object can serve several uses at once
ideas.text: Miniatures are objects, craft material, toys or tokens, display art and prompts for imagination. A respondent can paint a figure for display, field it in a tournament and invent its backstory.

ideas.name: Making and customising pieces is part of play for many
ideas.text: Painters describe hours of steady concentration, and some change figures by joining parts from different sets. For these people the crafting is as much the hobby as the game that follows.

ideas.name: What happens to a prop happens in the story
ideas.text: A respondent leaves a snapped elf sword unrepaired because it counts as battle damage. The physical figure and the imagined fiction change together.

ideas.name: A game with no choices can still carry a meaning
ideas.text: Nielsen shows that three games about women's lives used purely chance-based movement. In Pank-a-Squith the player always reaches Parliament, and only the length of the journey varies.

ideas.name: The same roll-and-move device can carry different messages
ideas.text: Pank-a-Squith promises a certain win, while Womanopoly gives the player cast as the woman a harder start: two sixes against one to begin. The mechanic is common, and the rule set around it makes the point.

ideas.name: A skipped turn can start a conversation
ideas.text: Space 44 of Womanopoly tells both players to miss a turn and talk about what the space says about daughters and sons. The usual penalty is used to make players stop and discuss.

ideas.name: A game can work without being played
ideas.text: The Ladder of Academic Success was printed with a board but no rules. Its readers understood it as a joke about women's careers from the board alone.

ideas.name: How a board looks shapes the world players think they are in
ideas.text: Lee names three things in a board: its artwork, the way it shows data, and the rule-governed space for moves. Together they give players a view of the game world as well as a place to move.

ideas.name: Where the score sits changes how a game feels
ideas.text: Lee notes that a victory point track around the board makes everyone's position visible and gives a race-like feel. Hidden point tokens or a count at the end give a different feel.

ideas.name: Moves happen on the table and in the game world at once
ideas.text: A player moves a cube on a board, and that move changes the imagined state of the world. Lee says rules link the two kinds of move.

ideas.name: A rule decides what a physical move means
ideas.text: Pushing a pawn across a chessboard is limited only by physics, but a legal move in chess needs the players' agreed rules. Without them it is only a piece being pushed.

ideas.name: Changing from borders to influence changes how players look at a map
ideas.text: In RISK a player holds whole territories and attention goes to borders. In Area Control games several players share a region, so attention goes to many targets at once.

ideas.name: A theme does not decide what a game teaches
ideas.text: Lee finds that even cooperative games set against war, such as Spirit Island, keep a territorial view of land. The way the board and rules treat space carries the message.

ideas.name: A map of routes makes players look at flow
ideas.text: Pandemic and Freedom print lines between cities. Players watch roads, spread and rescue rather than borders and conquest.

ideas.name: Theme and rules can pull against each other
ideas.text: In Photosynthesis, players grow trees but compete for territory and score by removing the tallest trees. Germaine says the game could be re-themed with soldiers on a battlefield and play the same.

ideas.name: The words in a rulebook shape how players treat pieces
ideas.text: Photosynthesis lets players buy seeds with light points. Germaine says that wording makes the trees feel like units of resource and not like living things.

ideas.name: Scoring rules can reward variety
ideas.text: In Ecosystem, a card scores for where it sits and the whole layout scores for few gaps in animal types. Players are pushed towards mixed habitats.

ideas.name: A limit on the board can show a limit in the world
ideas.text: The hexagonal board in Photosynthesis restricts how far trees spread. Germaine says this can make players think about habitats running out of room.

ideas.name: Replaying lets players test other approaches
ideas.text: Germaine says that because each replay allows a different strategy within the written rules, eurogames push players to reflect on the system and not only on one session.

ideas.name: Who can play depends on time, space and money
ideas.text: Pobuda notes that campaign games need a very large table left untouched for days, plus free time and spending power. These needs shut out people who lack them.

ideas.name: Learning the rules can keep newcomers out
ideas.text: Game shops trained staff to demonstrate rules because understanding them is a barrier to entry. A respondent who was ridiculed after a hurried explanation of Catan still avoided events years later.

ideas.name: Players keep wanting physical parts even when a digital copy exists
ideas.text: During lockdown, players moved to Board Game Arena and Tabletop Simulator, yet physical sales also rose. The online version of Ticket to Ride raised sales of the boxed game.

ideas.name: Cost can lead groups to share games
ideas.text: MacCallum-Stewart notes that a large boxed game can cost fifty to ninety pounds, so friends often pool money. One person buys it and brings it to play with others.

ideas.name: Extra components sell more copies
ideas.text: In the Scythe campaign, the Collector's edition at $99 outsold every other level together, while the base game at $59 sold under half as many.

ideas.name: Extras count when they change play
ideas.text: Booth found backers favoured higher tiers with extra play pieces, but fewer chose items such as signed copies, wine glasses or visits with the creators.

ideas.name: More physical parts leave less to imagine
ideas.text: If a red cube stands for a disease, players picture it themselves. A plastic virus model does that picturing for them, so Booth says the imaginative load drops.

ideas.name: Many parts create bookkeeping, and apps appear to handle it
ideas.text: Gloomhaven has scenario books, thirty boards, monster cards and dials to track. Fans built at least fifteen apps to take over the calculations.

ideas.name: The platform a game is funded on shapes the game
ideas.text: Werning's reading of Kickstarter is that it favours modular designs where new characters and places can be added. Booth adds that campaigns show near-finished games and many miniatures.

ideas.name: A rule keeps its meaning only inside its theme
ideas.text: Altice says that copying Sagrada's dice-drafting rule into another setting would lose the stained-glass idea the dice stand for. Mechanics carry meaning along with function.

ideas.name: The same action can be built in different ways
ideas.text: Jumping in the Super Mario video game depends on controls, physics and collision. Jumping in the Mario game book depends on picking a numbered page. Altice says the two have the same name but are built differently.

ideas.name: A re-skin imports the rules of the base game
ideas.text: Monopoly with a Mario theme still has players buying and trading property. Altice says this treats the Mushroom Kingdom as a real estate market.

ideas.name: A small board can be made from pieces that recombine
ideas.text: Bandai's Mario game cut the world into thirty-six map panels drawn from a shuffled deck, so each game builds a different world. Milton Bradley's strips could only be laid in one order.

ideas.name: Paper comes before code
ideas.text: Trammell notes that scientists, musicians and game designers often start with a paper mock-up before writing it in software. The analogue version is the base that the digital version is built on.

ideas.name: A score threshold is a made-up line
ideas.text: Wark reads Katamari Damacy as a game where the ball wins once it passes an exact size. Trammell quotes her to show how a game can make a chosen number seem like a natural truth.

ideas.name: Game spaces can feel closed to some players
ideas.text: Pobuda describes a games shop basement where a newcomer was ignored by the group at her table and the Dungeon Master never met her eye. Her survey found 36 per cent of respondents had avoided public events.

ideas.name: Physical pieces can exclude players
ideas.text: Booth notes that players with disabilities may find it harder to move pieces, roll dice or play tiles. Wake's reviewers also point to shaky hands in dexterity games.

ideas.name: Play leaves traces on the objects
ideas.text: A role-playing mat holds six years of erased marker pen, so crooked lines that were once tavern walls still show as stains. The object carries a record of the sessions played on it.

ideas.name: A tabletop session depends on many objects at once
ideas.text: A Dungeons and Dragons session has a screen, character sheets, dice, a vinyl mat and miniatures. Warren says these objects and the players circulate imagination and feeling among them.

ideas.name: A manual can describe a character by what it does
ideas.text: The Super Mario manual describes Bowser as one who spits fire and who can be killed several ways, with points only if you use fireballs. Altice says the characters are written in the language of play.

ideas.name: Games can be told, shown or interacted with
ideas.text: Following Hutcheon, Altice sorts media by how they engage: novels tell, films show and games invite interaction. The interactive mode adds the body, which is why story is not always what carries across from game to game.

ideas.name: Play comes before culture
ideas.text: Huizinga argues that play is older than culture, because animals play without being taught. Young dogs invite each other to play with gestures, keep to a rule not to bite hard, and pretend to be angry. So the main marks of play are already there before humans.

ideas.name: Play does not need a purpose to explain it
ideas.text: Theories say play releases spare energy, trains the young or relaxes the tired, and each one treats play as serving something else. Huizinga says none of them explains why a gambler loses himself or why a crowd goes wild at a football match. He wants play described in itself, as its players take it.

ideas.name: The five marks of play
ideas.text: Huizinga sums play up as free, outside ordinary life, tied to no material gain, kept within its own time and space, and run by fixed rules. Playing also draws people together into groups. A child playing trains, who says not to kiss the engine or the carriages will not think it is real, shows several of these at once.

ideas.name: Play is voluntary
ideas.text: Play on order is no longer play, only a copy of it. A grown person can leave play alone or stop at any time. It is done in free time, and it is never a task.

ideas.name: A game is a world with its own limits
ideas.text: Play starts and then ends, and it happens inside a space marked off beforehand. Huizinga lists the card table, the tennis court, the stage and the court of justice as the same kind of place. Each is a temporary world inside the ordinary world, where special rules apply.

ideas.name: Play makes order
ideas.text: Inside the play-ground a complete order holds, and the smallest step away from it spoils the game. Huizinga notes that the words for playing come from beauty: tension, balance, contrast, variation, resolution.

ideas.name: Tension tests the player
ideas.text: The uncertainty of play tests courage, endurance and skill. It also tests fairness, because a player eager to win still has to keep the rules. A solitary puzzle and a football match both depend on it.

ideas.name: Rules hold the whole world up
ideas.text: Huizinga quotes Valéry: nobody can doubt the rules of a game. If they are broken, the play-world collapses and ordinary life returns, as when an umpire's whistle ends a match.

ideas.name: The spoil-sport matters more than the cheat
ideas.text: A cheat still pretends to play, so the game goes on. A spoil-sport leaves or breaks the rules and shows how fragile the shared world is. Boys' games send the spoil-sport away. Huizinga adds that spoil-sports sometimes found new groups with rules of their own.

ideas.name: A game can outlast its playing
ideas.text: Players who shared a game feel set apart together, and this can hold after play ends. Not every game of marbles makes a club, but clubs grow out of this feeling.

ideas.name: Play is serious and not serious together
ideas.text: Children, footballers and chess players play in deep earnest, and nobody laughs. Yet they know they are playing. The line between play and seriousness moves, and each can turn into the other.

ideas.name: Laughter and comedy are not the same as play
ideas.text: Huizinga separates play from laughter, the comic and folly. Grown dogs chasing each other do not make us laugh, and chess is played without a smile. Play sits outside the pairs wise and foolish, true and false, right and wrong.

ideas.name: Contest and showing are the two roots of play
ideas.text: Higher forms of play are either a contest for something or a representation of something, and the two can join. A game can act out a contest, or become a contest over who acts something out most convincingly.

ideas.name: Children pretend by making an image
ideas.text: A child playing a prince, a witch or a tiger makes an image of something more beautiful or dangerous than themselves, and almost believes it. The child does not fully lose sight of ordinary reality.

ideas.name: Ritual has the form of play
ideas.text: Huizinga argues that a sacred rite and a game cannot be told apart in form. The temple, the magic circle, the chessboard and the tennis court are all marked-off ground where rules apply. He builds on Plato, who described a right way of living as a set of games, sacrifices, songs and dances.

ideas.name: The knowing and the pretending sit side by side
ideas.text: Huizinga draws on accounts of initiation feasts. The men carve the masks and make the ghost noises themselves, while the women know who is under each mask but shriek anyway, because the done thing is not to spoil the game. Belief and make-believe are not separated.

ideas.name: Being an animal and playing an animal
ideas.text: A dancer in a kangaroo dance is the kangaroo for himself, and is playing the kangaroo for outside observers. Huizinga says the word play suits this state because it holds belief and make-believe together.

ideas.name: Riddles are a shared contest of knowing
ideas.text: In Vedic feasts, priests asked each other riddles about the origin of the world, and solving them was as necessary as the sacrifice. The answer is found by knowing the rules and the secret names, not by reasoning it out.

ideas.name: The riddle can cost a head
ideas.text: In old stories, a player who cannot answer loses their life. Yājñavalkya wins a thousand cows in Vedic riddle-play, and an opponent loses his head. Huizinga says the story is play-like because the contest is the point, not whether anybody really died.

ideas.name: A catch-question traps by its own rules
ideas.text: A riddle with a second correct answer the asker did not expect leaves the asker caught in the trap. Alexander's question to ten wise men, who answered least accurately, was turned back by a judge who said each answered as wrongly as the other, so nobody could be put to death.

ideas.name: Equal footing is part of a question game
ideas.text: In the Questions of King Menander, the sage says the wise talk without anger when cornered, unlike kings. Frederick II took a rude reply calmly for the same reason. Huizinga reads this as the game needing both sides to speak as equals.

ideas.name: Philosophy began as a challenge
ideas.text: The Greek word problema meant something thrown before you. Early philosophers spoke in the first person, attacked rivals, and used aporias that led from an opponent's own premises to two opposite conclusions. Huizinga reads this as the riddle's shape.

ideas.name: Opposites in conflict as the pattern of the world
ideas.text: Early thinkers saw life as a struggle of opposites, as in yin and yang. Heraclitus called strife the father of all things, and Hesiod named a helpful Eris and a harmful one. Huizinga links this to a society that was itself built on contest.

ideas.name: Play and seriousness once formed one medium
ideas.text: Huizinga says the riddle began as a sacred game and later split into mystic philosophy and recreation. He argues it is wrong to say seriousness fell into play or play rose into seriousness. The two modes were separated later by civilization.

ideas.name: Personification is a play of the mind
ideas.text: People give life to ideas and objects without stating a belief in them. St Francis honoured Poverty as his bride, and a person scolds a collar-stud. Huizinga says belief and unbelief mix in this, which makes it play.

ideas.name: The Romans made gods for moments of tension
ideas.text: In the rite of indigitamenta, the Romans set up shrines to Fear, Paleness and the Voice that warned of the Gauls. Huizinga calls this a way of giving a dangerous feeling a fixed form so a crowd could be calmed.

ideas.name: Exaggeration is a play habit
ideas.text: Children and myths both enlarge things beyond belief, such as a carrot as big as God or Thor sleeping in the thumb of a giant's glove. Huizinga says this is not to be taken wholly seriously and belongs to the play attitude.

ideas.name: Drama stays closest to play
ideas.text: Of the three kinds of poetry, drama keeps its link to play because it is an action. Latin and the Germanic languages call a drama a play, and performing it playing. Greek tragedy and comedy both began as sacred or festive acts and were staged as contests at the feast of Dionysus.

ideas.name: A contest with an audience
ideas.text: Greek dramatists competed for the feast of Dionysus, and the crowd followed the tension like a football crowd. A chorus rehearsed for a year. Huizinga says this agonistic frame is what keeps drama within play.

ideas.name: Sophists treated argument as sport
ideas.text: Sophists travelled, charged fees for set pieces such as the fifty-drachma lecture, and challenged anyone to ask them questions. Crowds applauded them like athletes. Gorgias called his Encomium on Helen a game.

ideas.name: Reasoning games depend on accepting the rules
ideas.text: Catch-questions work only if the opponent accepts the logic of the game without objecting, as Diogenes did not. Huizinga wonders whether all logic rests on tacit agreement about terms, as chess rests on its pieces.

ideas.name: School once meant leisure
ideas.text: The Greek word behind school meant free time. Huizinga says Greek knowledge grew out of leisure, not training for useful jobs. As civilization took the young man's time, the word came to mean systematic work.

ideas.name: Universities ran on contest
ideas.text: Medieval scholars argued in public disputations, grouped themselves into nationes, and Abelard spoke of besieging a rival from the Hill of St Genevieve. Huizinga reads this competition as a play-form. He cites Erasmus, who said a learned debate need not treat a new idea like a rule broken in cards.

ideas.name: Contest is useful and has limits
ideas.text: Huizinga says the play-character keeps verbal contest tolerable and legitimate. It turns false only when cleverness serves an aim that is wrong in itself, as with Callicles. For most sophists the aim was the personal satisfaction of being right and winning glory.

ideas.name: Courts and kings play too
ideas.text: Huizinga says courtly culture adopts play-forms easily, because a small circle ruled by awe of majesty already has its rules and fictions. At Charlemagne's court, scholars took classical names, such as Alcuin as Horace. Pippin and Alcuin played a riddle game of question and answer.

ideas.name: Games are patterns to be learned
ideas.text: Koster says the brain is mainly a consumer of patterns, and a game is a pattern packed in a clear form. A child learns tic-tac-toe by playing it until every match is a draw, and loses interest once the pattern is grasped.

ideas.name: Fun is learning
ideas.text: Koster argues the pleasure of a game comes from mastering a problem or taking in a pattern, not from winning or looking. The brain releases a reward when we learn, so a player grinning at a solved puzzle is showing fun.

ideas.name: Boredom signals the end of teaching
ideas.text: When a game offers no new pattern, the player says they are bored. Koster lists six ways this happens, such as mastering everything in the first five minutes or facing a pattern that looks like noise.

ideas.name: Order and chaos are balanced
ideas.text: Koster says a game moves between too little new information and too much. An adult drops tic-tac-toe because it is too plain, and drops a game with a flood of unexplained rules because it looks like noise.

ideas.name: Noise is a pattern not yet understood
ideas.text: Static has patterns, Koster says, and what seems random is often a failure of our understanding. A first listen to jazz sounds odd until the listener picks up the beat and the flattened fifth.

ideas.name: Formal games are limited
ideas.text: Koster says the more tightly rules define a game, the sooner it can be fully worked out. Tic-tac-toe has only 125,168 possible games, so a player can see every outcome, while games with human psychology in them last longer.

ideas.name: Games are meant to be outgrown
ideas.text: Koster says any game that teaches is destined to become routine, because learning something means it is over. His own example is a typing game where sharks eat words, which gave up trying new tricks after level twelve or fourteen.

ideas.name: Games model reality, mostly through maths
ideas.text: Koster says rules are mathematical, so even abstract games reflect something about the world. Many teach odds, territory and power, which he ties to human survival.

ideas.name: Space is the first lesson of games
ideas.text: Most games, Koster says, teach the player to read a space, whether a grid or a graph of links. Tic-tac-toe teaches the lines of power across a grid.

ideas.name: A game cannot be learned in one turn
ideas.text: Even a dice game, Koster says, is played over many turns so the player can explore the possibility space. Players learn about odds by rolling again and again.

ideas.name: New games come from a new dimension
ideas.text: Koster argues shooters stopped changing once they gained power-ups, scrolling and bosses. Tetris, he says, led to variants with hexagons and 3-D, and he suggests a puzzle built on time as a new direction.

ideas.name: Add to a game by adding a dimension, not more of the same
ideas.text: Koster says designers often add more weapons instead of a new kind of challenge. A modern platformer keeps the old get to the other side goal and adds secrets and time limits.

ideas.name: Speed training suits reflex games
ideas.text: Koster says developing speed before precision is not useful, so action games push the player faster as they improve. Strategy games rarely have time attack because their tasks do not rest on reflex.

ideas.name: Thoroughness is a subtler skill
ideas.text: Koster says asking the player to find secrets teaches patience and checking every angle. He sees this as more widely useful than rote reflex.

ideas.name: Fiction wraps the pattern and is set aside by players
ideas.text: Koster compares a game's story to a maths word problem. In checkers the crowned piece could be called a wolf and the game would not change.

ideas.name: A game's core is separate from its theme
ideas.text: Koster says Deathrace is mechanically a game of catching objects on a flat field. He holds that its violent dressing is not what the game teaches, though he does not excuse the dressing.

ideas.name: Games and stories teach in different ways
ideas.text: Koster says games teach by experience and handle objects and actions well, while stories teach by empathy and inner life. The moment Floyd sacrifices himself in Planetfall happens outside player control, so it is not part of the challenge.

ideas.name: The word fun covers several different pleasures
ideas.text: Koster names mastery, aesthetic appreciation, physical thrill and social standing. He keeps the word fun for the first, which is mentally mastering a problem.

ideas.name: Fun is contextual
ideas.text: Koster says fun comes when an activity is practice, not for real. A team that says it went out to have fun is treating the game as practice, and a team that says it went to win is not.

ideas.name: Flow and fun are different
ideas.text: Flow, Koster says, comes from using a skill already mastered, while fun comes from learning. Meditation can bring flow without fun.

ideas.name: Different people take to different games
ideas.text: Koster says people vary in how they learn and in what they find easy to see. A person with high spatial or verbal ability leans toward sports or word games.

ideas.name: No game suits everyone
ideas.text: Koster says a formal system fits some kinds of mind more than others, so a difficulty ramp is likely to suit some players and not others. He compares it to books, which are bought mostly by people of certain groups.

ideas.name: Cheating shows the player has understood
ideas.text: Koster says someone who cheats is choosing a wider battlefield than the game and is using cunning. Duellists who shoot before the other has finished pacing are more likely to have children, so cheating pays in a plain evolutionary sense.

ideas.name: Exploits circumvent the challenge
ideas.text: Koster says an exploit uses a loophole inside the rules, so expert players find it first. Others resent it because the game meant to teach a technique and the loophole skips it.

ideas.name: Players make a game predictable
ideas.text: People want to win, Koster says, so they reduce risk by learning patterns. Running an easy level two hundred times to bank lives is like storing food for winter.

ideas.name: A game's destiny is routine
ideas.text: Koster says fun is a process and routine is where it ends, since learning removes the need to learn again. Designers who want games to stay fun work against how the brain operates.

ideas.name: Games need a set of working parts
ideas.text: Koster lists preparation, a sense of space, a core mechanic, a range of challenges, a range of abilities and skill in using them. Without preparation a game is left to chance, and without a range of challenges it is used up fast.

ideas.name: Learning needs feedback and a cost for failure
ideas.text: Koster says results vary with skill, easy encounters do not pay experts, and failure costs something. In chess the variable feedback is the opponent's reply.

ideas.name: The Mastery Problem favours the skilled
ideas.text: Koster says competition removes the players who most need practice, because they are knocked out in their first match. Head-to-head games supply endless new challenges, yet beginners who face experts tend to quit.

ideas.name: A checklist can reveal what a game lacks
ideas.text: Koster gives questions such as whether the player prepares, whether more than one ability helps, and whether failure forces a retry. A no to any one marks a system worth rethinking.

ideas.name: Every system serves the game's lesson
ideas.text: A designer's sole responsibility, Koster says, is to know what the game is about and make it teach that. No system belongs in the game if it does not contribute to that point.

ideas.name: Fewer systems can be enough
ideas.text: Koster says classic games fit a few systems together neatly, as checkers has just two ludemes. Modern console games pile on many, which Koster ties to the need to keep adding challenges.

ideas.name: Designers try to keep games from running dry
ideas.text: Koster lists emergence, story, head-to-head play and player-made content as tactics. He notes each has a catch, such as emergence tending to open loopholes.

ideas.name: People repeat what has worked
ideas.text: Koster says players pick the same kind of character or solution each time. A friend of his has played the big silent type in dozens of role-playing games.

ideas.name: Mastered games can become a trap
ideas.text: Replaying a game you have fully mastered only to feel powerful betrays the game's purpose, Koster says. Playing for style points at least sets a new challenge.

ideas.name: Complex genres shut out newcomers
ideas.text: Koster says a new game genre gains rules until a priesthood of expert players forms and the barrier to entry rises. He wants games that appeal to the broad public.

ideas.name: Knowing too many games can limit a designer
ideas.text: Koster says designers sample many games and grok them fast, so they fall back on known solutions. He suggests the most inventive take ideas from outside games.

ideas.name: Activities can be mapped on a grid
ideas.text: Koster crosses solo, collaborative and competitive with experiential, constructive and deconstructive, for any medium. He fills it in for music to show that playing, making and analysing all sit on one chart.

ideas.name: Games are not always fun in the strict sense
ideas.text: Practising piano or writing can be hard work and still fulfilling, Koster says. Interacting with a game can likewise be thought-provoking or painful and still hold a pattern to learn.

ideas.name: Entertainment and art differ by degree
ideas.text: Koster says media provide information, entertainment comforting information and art challenging information. Mere entertainment becomes art when its communication is novel or very skilled.

ideas.name: Abstract systems can carry meaning
ideas.text: All media are formal systems, Koster says, so a game made of rules can still say something. Minesweeper works like an Impressionist picture because the thing you seek is never shown and repetition with variation teaches it.

ideas.name: Games convey general points more readily than specific ones
ideas.text: Koster says it is easy to make a game showing that small groups can beat large ones, but hard to show a particular rescue like the one in a film about Private Ryan. A designer needs to learn what the medium carries.

ideas.name: Content design and experience design are different jobs
ideas.text: Koster compares game design to dance and film, where a director shapes the whole experience above the writer or choreographer. He says game teams are not yet set up this way.

ideas.name: The dressing shapes how the rules feel
ideas.text: Chess might not have lasted, Koster says, if its pieces were different kinds of snot. A mismatch between a game's core and its theme can harm the experience.

ideas.name: Test a game with the dressing removed
ideas.text: Koster proposes playing with no graphics, music or story. If the bare rules are fun, the dressing can focus and magnify them, but no dressing changes the core.

ideas.name: Rules can carry a message
ideas.text: Koster describes a game where power comes from followers but healing comes from friends, and friends leave as you gain power. The goal of keeping the tribe alive makes sitting at the top a choice the player has to weigh.

ideas.name: Games shape players like a trellis
ideas.text: Koster says a game steers its players as a trellis steers a plant, and the plant also grows to escape it. He says games now produce only fun and boredom, and wants rules built with intent to teach chosen things.

ideas.name: Three paths with no fixed order
ideas.text: The author wrote the title without or and without and, so the three paths need not be taken together, in a set order, or one before another. He says empowerment need not come before prosperity or joy, and joy could lead to empowerment.

ideas.name: A game whose rules were not written for you
ideas.text: The author asks what a person has to do to survive and prosper in a game that was not made for them. Example: the Williams sisters faced hostility in tennis, and many Black parents steered children to basketball, which was thought more welcoming.

ideas.name: Some people choose a field by how it treats them
ideas.text: The author says some Black people skip careers such as interior design or wine because those fields seem unwelcoming, whatever their talent. The choice of game follows what players expect to happen to them.

ideas.name: Playing a game to leave it
ideas.text: Tope Awotona and Adah Ojile spent years inside large companies learning how they worked, building contacts and skill. They then started their own firms, using the first game to prepare for the second.

ideas.name: Playing, changing and leaving in one plan
ideas.text: Charles Blow's plan to move Black voters to chosen Southern states uses all three paths at once. People relocate (leave), use the existing voting rules (play) and aim for a majority that can alter the rules (change).

ideas.name: Skill is necessary but may not be enough
ideas.text: The author says competence is necessary for Black professionals but does not guarantee reward, while for White men it is enough but not necessary. Example: an overqualified Black candidate may be labelled a diversity hire, and an underqualified White one seldom draws comment.

ideas.name: The same mistake can score differently
ideas.text: In the author's study, White male leaders were forgiven errors as human, while Black leaders, most of all Black women, were marked down as unsuited to the role. The same move by different players is read differently.

ideas.name: Knowing and showing are different skills
ideas.text: Mastery is learning a thing and performance is showing it. A student can earn an A+ in Spanish and not speak with native speakers, and a fluent speaker can get a B. Managers also split between those who want it right and those who want it done.

ideas.name: Fix the win before you play
ideas.text: Carla Harris reached an unusual client meeting and her manager counted it as no win. She says she needed to agree in advance that the meeting was a win and the sale a separate one, since she could not control the sale.

ideas.name: A win can be hollow
ideas.text: Anthony Foxx's pollsters told him a transit line through a Black neighbourhood would lose votes. He kept it, saying a win that meant giving up what he thought right for the city would be hollow, and the project later helped his standing.

ideas.name: Showing a high score can bring a penalty
ideas.text: Black students who scored highest on a test section were the most reluctant to make their scores public. In a football study, Black players were penalised for celebrating after a touchdown and White players were not.

ideas.name: Same number of contacts, different reach
ideas.text: Two people who each know three others can have very different reach. The one whose three contacts come from separate circles is linked to eleven people, and the one in a closed group is linked to three.

ideas.name: Two riders, one message, two outcomes
ideas.text: Paul Revere and William Dawes rode similar distances in 1775 and met about the same number of people. Revere told the local brokers, such as the tavern owner and the doctor, so his news spread, while Dawes told people inside closed groups, so his news stayed put.

ideas.name: Networking can feel unclean and cost people
ideas.text: In a law firm study, lawyers who saw deliberate networking as dirty did less of it and billed fewer hours. Women, introverts and people with less power were more likely to see it that way.

ideas.name: Unequal partners can both gain
ideas.text: An investor funded the author's house flip in exchange for a share of the profit. The author notes that the investor was not giving a gift, since he earned more than a bank would pay, and nobody was exploited.

ideas.name: Mentoring and sponsoring are different jobs
ideas.text: Mentors give advice and support, and sponsors use their rank to push your case. The studies cited say women and people of colour get more of the first than the second.

ideas.name: Ask people who know you to speak for you
ideas.text: The author suggests asking those who know you well to pass your name through their own networks. It avoids the problem of having to praise yourself or to stay quiet.

ideas.name: A sponsor need not look like you
ideas.text: In one company, almost 60 percent of the people Black executives named as key to their rise were White. Just under 40 percent were senior Black colleagues, who were a very small share of the staff.

ideas.name: Use the rules without depending on them
ideas.text: The author says using the master's tools is open to you so long as they are not your only support. At Morehouse College, David Thomas says, students learn this and know when to put the tools down, as Dr King did by choosing nonviolence over the courts and violence.

ideas.name: Inside pressure and outside pressure work together
ideas.text: Deval Patrick says outsiders demanding more and faster helped him inside government. When the Clinton White House weighed dropping affirmative action, his blunt outside view helped lead to a policy of mending it and not ending it.

ideas.name: Small wins can prepare large ones
ideas.text: A run of small changes can slip past an organisation's resistance where one big change would set it off. The author adds that a small change matters to the person it reaches, as with the man who throws starfish back to the sea one at a time.

ideas.name: Three kinds of impact
ideas.text: The author separates change in institutions, in individuals and in inspiration. Obama's term helped inspire many but, to some, changed institutions little. In Rwanda, women in parliament rose from 33 to 64 percent after a quota let people see it done.

ideas.name: Holding a seat can cost the holder
ideas.text: William Darity says he has never felt like an insider in economics and notes that many prominent Black economists had heart attacks young. The author says breaks from the dance floor may be needed, such as one woman's rule of not doing White on weekends.

ideas.name: A few promoted people can steady the system
ideas.text: Writers cited say that promoting a few members of a group can make the system look fair and weaken the group's push. Research found White leaders promoting a small number of Black people in times of unrest.

ideas.name: Changing the game is about the attempt
ideas.text: The author counts the push as the point and the result as secondary. Over time it brings no win, sometimes a small win and occasionally a big one.

ideas.name: Speaking up costs socially and helps personally
ideas.text: Black people who confronted racism were disliked more by White observers but reported lower blood pressure and a higher sense of autonomy. The author says staying silent carries its own costs.

ideas.name: The complaint is judged by who makes it
ideas.text: Black people who confronted bias were labelled complainers even in studies where discrimination was certain to have taken place. The author reads the reaction as being about who is speaking, not about the facts.

ideas.name: Wanting to be liked or wanting to be respected
ideas.text: In one study of interracial conversations, the White partner mostly aimed to be liked and the Black partner mostly aimed to be respected. The author says people who feel they belong care less about being liked and speak up more.

ideas.name: An apology has three parts
ideas.text: The author lists recognition (I understand the problem), remorse (I regret it) and repair (I will make it right and stop it recurring). The airline reply to his letter contained all three, including a change to staff training.

ideas.name: Treat freedom as a journey
ideas.text: Angela Davis says that if freedom is a destination, then once you arrive nothing is left to do. She prefers to treat it as a continuing journey and to call hope a discipline that has to be practised and made again.

ideas.name: The struggle makes joy and knowledge
ideas.text: Davis says Black people have always made joy inside the struggle and not after it, and she points to the blues. She adds that a movement produces knowledge of its own, since the idea of intersectionality grew out of one.

ideas.name: Removing struggle can remove the strength it builds
ideas.text: In a story told in a fourth-grade class, children cut open a chrysalis to help a butterfly out, and it could not fly because it never worked its wings. The author links this to overprotected children and to the benefits of unsupervised play.

ideas.name: Groups under threat tend to band together
ideas.text: Studies of disasters, hijackings and crowds find that people in danger usually form a shared identity and coordinate, in place of each looking out for themselves.

ideas.name: A boycott works only when many take part
ideas.text: One rider refusing a bus in Montgomery is insignificant, but a whole community of riders can topple the system. The author adds that individual duties need to stay visible, or people ease off.

ideas.name: Turning what people have into what they need
ideas.text: Ganz says the central task of a movement is to show people they hold resources and then turn these into collective power. In Montgomery the resource was the ability to walk.

ideas.name: Nonviolent movements won more often
ideas.text: A study of over a century of campaigns found nonviolent movements reached their goals about 53 percent of the time and violent ones about 26 percent. The authors link this to the larger numbers of people a nonviolent movement can draw in.

ideas.name: Respect is something you do
ideas.text: A fellow organiser told Ganz that respect is what you do and not what you have, and gave four steps: listen and hear, ask and learn, show respect, and be yourself.

ideas.name: A leaderless group still has a hidden structure
ideas.text: Jo Freeman argues that dropping formal leadership only hides an informal structure no one can hold to account. The author describes leadership as roles shared by a group that takes on responsibility.

ideas.name: A goal's clarity matters more than how likely it is
ideas.text: The author says a plan needs a specific target, not a likely one. Reaching the moon seemed impossible but was concrete enough to plan for. Exploring the whole universe is too vague to plan for.

ideas.name: Pay and profit can rise together
ideas.text: Zeynep Ton argues that treating staff as a cost to cut can raise running costs and lower profits. A study in India found workers made fewer errors on days when they had just been paid.

ideas.name: Rephrase a goal to fit the rule in force
ideas.text: Yoshino and Glasgow say programmes aimed at a legally protected group are now risky, so they advise aiming at interests and experiences. After three law firms changed fellowship eligibility to anyone with a commitment to diversity, the lawsuits were dropped.

ideas.name: Widen the pool and then train
ideas.text: OneTen found most of its members' middle-skill jobs asked for a degree that the work itself did not require. Its lessons for employers were to widen the net, to coach and not only scout, and to pay people enough.

ideas.name: Reach people where they already are
ideas.text: Vot-ER lets hospital staff wear a badge with a question and a QR code so patients can register to vote during a visit. The idea began when a mother and children could prove their residence for housing by registering to vote.

ideas.name: Push at two levels at once
ideas.text: Vot-ER worked with clinicians on the ground and also lobbied the medical association, which in 2022 formally named voting a social determinant of health. The author says combining the two is likelier to fix a change in place.

ideas.name: Meet urgent needs before asking for participation
ideas.text: Link Health connects patients to unused public benefits first, then talks about voting months later. Its founder says that once pressing needs are met, people can think beyond survival.

ideas.name: Why people stay, speak or leave
ideas.text: Hirschman says people delay leaving if they believe speaking up will work, and stay if they feel loyal. When people cannot leave, they use their voice more.

ideas.name: Leaving is not the same as losing
ideas.text: The author says people may hesitate to leave out of pride or a wish not to look like quitters. He argues that leaving can show agency, or can be a plan to rest and direct energy elsewhere.

ideas.name: Your own venture lets you set your own rules
ideas.text: The author says an entrepreneur can choose how to run the business. A landlord can be a slumlord or can keep housing safe and affordable, and the choice expresses values.

ideas.name: Go round a funding rule
ideas.text: Adah Ojile found that $700,000 of early money paid for about three engineers in the United States but for forty-five in Nigeria. He built his firm around that gap and not around competing with Silicon Valley on spending.

ideas.name: Look for demand nobody is serving
ideas.text: At sixteen the author bought sale candy at a discount shop and resold it at school, where none was sold, and made $50 to $75 a week until stock was confiscated. Wally Amos began by baking cookies for meetings with music and film executives.

ideas.name: Success measured by the work, not the title
ideas.text: A university president told the author he missed the contact with students he had as a dean and took the promotion because it was what you do. The author concludes that the actual work done is what gives a job meaning.

ideas.name: A setback can redirect a path
ideas.text: Vanessa Williams lost her title after photos were published and then moved into singing and acting, which she says she had wanted all along. The author's own dismissal led him to a job with more freedom.

ideas.name: Two separations with different purposes
ideas.text: The author says an incubator protects a group from a harmful setting, while segregation protects a hierarchy. So a Black neighbourhood and an all-White club may look alike but serve opposite motives.

ideas.name: A secure base lets people go further
ideas.text: HBCU students were about 40 percent more likely to study abroad than Black students at mainly White colleges. The author links this to research showing children with a secure base roam and explore more.

ideas.name: A small support group helps people stay
ideas.text: The Posse Foundation sends groups of ten students to one college. Among its alumni, 70 percent said the posse helped them stay on track when about a third had thought of dropping out.

ideas.name: Groups began as practical fixes
ideas.text: Black employees at Xerox formed groups to share sales practice and to ask that job openings be posted openly. By 1980 the company had 22 Black vice presidents.

ideas.name: A group open to all can still draw objections
ideas.text: Most employee resource groups admit anyone who supports their aim. Even so, some White staff felt left out, and a CEO quoted by Friedman called the groups divisive.

ideas.name: Pressure raises the pull to leave
ideas.text: The author says the need to retreat to enclaves grows as hostility from the dominant group grows. Examples are the founding of historically Black colleges after exclusion and the northward migration of families during Jim Crow.

ideas.name: Asking people whether they want in or apart
ideas.text: In 1865 General Sherman asked Black ministers whether freed people wanted to join society or live separately. Nineteen of the twenty voted to live apart, and one, aged 26, voted to join.

ideas.name: Move people to where their votes count
ideas.text: Richard Pollak urged hippies in the early 1970s to move to Vermont and register, and the state turned from red to blue. Charles Blow proposes the same for Black voters in chosen Southern states.

ideas.name: A plan needs a way to move people
ideas.text: Tracy Dumas suggests five ways to get people to relocate: planting new congregations from big churches, targeting remote workers, moving Black-owned firms, funding young movers and helping them register. Without registering, the author notes, the whole strategy is useless.

ideas.name: A group name can hide variety
ideas.text: Black people differ in politics, region, class and origin, and Davis cautions that the concepts we use may not fit the facts. At Harvard, 67 percent of Black students are of West Indian or African descent.

ideas.name: Relative winning makes equality look like a loss
ideas.text: Studies found members of a dominant group more threatened by equality between groups than within their own group. Some opposed policies that would help them if the policies also narrowed the gap.

ideas.name: A life that goes well has five goals
ideas.text: The author names physical health, mental health, loving relationships, financial security and purpose as the building blocks of the win. He says each person answers for themselves what winning means.

ideas.name: More money stops adding happiness
ideas.text: Kahneman found happiness rose with income up to about $75,000 in 2010, around $110,000 in 2025, and stayed flat above that. The author uses this to argue that chasing more power or wealth feeds the ego and not wellbeing.

ideas.name: Choose your own goals and rules
ideas.text: The author ends by saying the real win is the power to make your own goals and even your own rules, whether you play, change or leave the game.

ideas.name: Facts do not change a need-driven habit
ideas.text: The author compares a smoker who has seen every warning and every cost and still smokes. He says education about racism fails for the same reason, because the behaviour is held in place by need and defence, not by missing facts.

ideas.name: Justice asks why, charity asks what
ideas.text: Marshall Ganz says charity asks what is wrong and offers help, while justice asks why it happens and tries to change it. He says the second question brings pushback.

ideas.name: Support comes when people see cruelty
ideas.text: The author says major movements with White participants arose in the context of visible cruelty, such as the murder of George Floyd, and not from plain disparity. Without cruelty, he says, unequal outcomes become mundane.

ideas.name: A condition set by a buyer
ideas.text: The author's mother asked a car dealership whether it had Black salespeople and said she would not buy from one that had none. He calls it a small act of changing the game by using purchasing power.

ideas.name: A game is a machine that makes play
ideas.text: A game does little until people use it, like a pocket knife or a car engine. Hopscotch is only lines on the ground and a stone until rules and players arrive. The designer builds the machine and the play comes out of using it.

ideas.name: Six elements make up every game
ideas.text: Actions, goals, rules, objects, playspace and players are present in any game. Soccer shows all six: kicking and running, scoring, the ban on hands, the ball and nets, the field, and the teams. Games differ in how they combine them.

ideas.name: Rules both allow and limit
ideas.text: Rules say what players cannot do as much as what they can. In soccer the ban on hands is what makes the bicycle kick or well-timed tackle possible at all. The limits give players something to work around.

ideas.name: A goal is what turns a toy into a game
ideas.text: A soccer ball alone is a toy that can be thrown or drawn on. Inside a game with a goal, the ball takes on special meaning. Without a goal, players tend to invent one.

ideas.name: A goal can drive play or only start it
ideas.text: In soccer, scoring sits behind every action. In Exquisite Corpse, a folded paper drawn on in turn, there is no score, and the goal of making a drawing together only sets the play going.

ideas.name: Changing one action changes the whole experience
ideas.text: Dear Esther keeps the first-person walking and looking of a shooting game but removes shooting. That one removal turns it into a game of exploring a story world.

ideas.name: The designer shapes play only at a distance
ideas.text: The designer fixes the elements, but players choose when, why and how to play. Surprising results appear when players act inside the system, which is why testing and revising are needed.

ideas.name: Games can have narrow or wide spaces of possibility
ideas.text: Queers in Love at the End of the World gives ten seconds and a few choices, so its space is narrow and focused. Minecraft lets players build ships, rollercoasters and cities, so its space is wide. The more focused the experience, the smaller the space.

ideas.name: The space of possibility can grow during a game's life
ideas.text: Until 1980 nobody tried jumping under the basketball backboard from one side of the basket to the other. When Dr. J did it, a new set of moves was added to the game.

ideas.name: Constraint makes a goal worth pursuing
ideas.text: In soccer, banning hands makes putting the ball in the net a puzzle, where carrying it would be easy. Flywrench combines flapping with colour-matching, and Octodad uses a floppy octopus body, so each game gets its feel from what it blocks.

ideas.name: Direct and indirect actions trade control for discovery
ideas.text: Hitting a pinball is direct, but what the ball then does to ramps and bumpers is indirect. More direct actions give finer control. More indirect actions give less control and more finding out how the world behaves, as in Proteus.

ideas.name: Goals range from firm to loose
ideas.text: Soccer has a countable goal. Slam City Oracles has a score so silly it works as a joke. Dog Eat Dog counts tokens, but only to decide how the story ends. Sunset stacks three goals: a task, a day's list and the game.

ideas.name: Flow is one experience among several
ideas.text: Flow arises when challenge fits skill, and designers use it to set difficulty. The authors say games can also aim at other things, such as a hard story or the absorption of ninja, depending on what the designer wants to explore.

ideas.name: Challenge comes in three kinds
ideas.text: A game can test skill, test whether the player reaches the goal, or test the player's ideas through its content. In the game about a woman's balanced life, the posing task is hard and so is the content, since early life choices make later poses harder.

ideas.name: Chance and strategy pull against each other
ideas.text: More chance leaves less room for strategy. Darts has skill and no chance. Roulette has almost no skill and nearly all chance. Poker mixes them, since players see only 7 of the 52 cards by the end.

ideas.name: Uncertainty can exist without chance
ideas.text: Basketball has no dice, yet players cannot know how the ball will leave the rim or where teammates will be. Players cope by reading the changing game state quickly.

ideas.name: Play is a loop of decisions and feedback
ideas.text: The player acts, the game shows what happened, and the player decides again. In Nidhogg, moving, stabbing, a screen change towards the goal, and the serpent at the end are all feedback. Even Howling Dogs, a text game with no score, works this way.

ideas.name: The timing structure sets the kind of thinking
ideas.text: Chess gives each player time to read the board and think. Speed Chess has sixteen players moving at once, so nobody can follow the whole state and play turns instinctive.

ideas.name: Abstraction has three uses
ideas.text: It can remove representation altogether, as in Go. It can simplify an everyday activity, as Pong does to tennis. It can model a real system as a game, as Pandemic does with the spread of disease through cubes on cities.

ideas.name: Even abstract games carry a theme
ideas.text: Chess is called abstract, yet its pieces suggest a war over territory. The king is slow, the queen quick, the pawns many, and the shapes of their moves match those roles. Theme gives players a handle on how the world works.

ideas.name: Theme can be tight or light
ideas.text: Way ties its theme of wordless communication to every goal and action. Kentucky Route Zero uses theme mainly as mood. Chess carries a light theme over a full set of rules.

ideas.name: Story can sit in the rules, the world or the players
ideas.text: Braid tells story through level texts, a menu and time rewinding. Gone Home tells it by moving through a house. Dog Eat Dog lets players make the story. In Conversations We Have in My Head, story is the whole activity.

ideas.name: The same game can be reshaped for a new setting
ideas.text: Jenga Giant uses big blocks for bars and gardens, where the fall is a spectacle. Tiny Games asks where the player is before offering a game. The Jenga variants show that context can change a game's form.

ideas.name: Kinds of play open more options than genres
ideas.text: Genre points a designer at what similar games already do. Asking what kind of play to give players, such as fast choices, slow strategy, story or cooperation, opens more options. The kinds mix like ingredients in a dish.

ideas.name: Yomi gives competitive games depth
ideas.text: In Nidhogg a player guesses her opponent will parry, he guesses she thinks that and jumps, and she guesses again. The layers appear when both players chase an explicit goal and each has to read the other.

ideas.name: Competition has several shapes
ideas.text: Nidhogg is player against player. Canabalt compares scores, even in tournaments where a crowd watches players take turns. Desert Golfing is player against the game. Each puts pressure on a different part of play.

ideas.name: Symmetry and asymmetry apply to both competing and cooperating
ideas.text: In Johann Sebastian Joust every player has the same moves. In Spy Party one player hides as a party guest and the other is a sniper with one bullet. In cooperation, Portal 2 gives both players the same actions while Pandemic gives different roles.

ideas.name: Symmetrical cooperation leaves roles to the players
ideas.text: In Portal 2 both robots shoot portals, run and jump the same way. Because the game assigns no role, players decide between themselves who does what.

ideas.name: Symbiotic cooperation makes working alone close to impossible
ideas.text: In Way the player who moves cannot see the full puzzle, and the player who watches can. They have to invent body-language signals to pass the information across.

ideas.name: Skill games shape who will keep playing
ideas.text: Super Meat Boy takes hundreds of failed tries to master timing. Games asking for exact skill need more practice, which narrows who commits to them but raises the weight of a win.

ideas.name: Experience-based play can sit inside a competitive frame
ideas.text: Ninja has a goal of hitting a neighbour's hand, yet most groups play for the pose and the shared silliness. The designer has to leave room in the space of possibility for this.

ideas.name: Chance mixed with strategy needs managing
ideas.text: Threes adds a random tile after each move but shows the next tile's colour. In Android: Netrunner players shuffle decks they built, so they put three copies of a key card in a 45-card deck to improve the odds of drawing it.

ideas.name: Too much chance removes decisions
ideas.text: Candy Land is a spinner and a move, with no choice at all. Young children enjoy it for its pictures and make-believe, but the lack of decisions is what many older players find thin. The authors compare chance to a spice that can be too much or too little.

ideas.name: Whimsy can come from the body, the controls or the concept
ideas.text: In Hit Me players strain to press buttons on each other's hats. In QWOP the keys map to thighs and calves so the runner collapses. In Tenya Wanya Teens a panel of unlabelled buttons sends the character to the wrong task.

ideas.name: A light rule set can still support role-playing
ideas.text: Lesberation uses a hand of object cards and verb cards, with no character sheets, and players agree each move as a group. Rules only give structure to a story that players could otherwise act out without a game.

ideas.name: Stories can be made by players or authored by makers
ideas.text: In Lesberation players produce the story, which is emergence. In The Path the makers wrote the six sisters and the woods, and the player only unfolds them, which is progression. Howling Dogs does the same with branching text.

ideas.name: Absorption leads to unselfconscious performance
ideas.text: Johann Sebastian Joust players are so busy keeping their controller steady that they forget how they look, so the audience sees a dance the players do not notice. Coffee: A Misunderstanding does the opposite and keeps players aware of awkwardness.

ideas.name: Simulation uses abstraction to argue
ideas.text: The Landlord's Game was made to show how rents enrich owners and impoverish tenants. The McDonald's Videogame links a farm, a plant, a restaurant and a board room to make a point about the chain.

ideas.name: Simulations can be seen from above or from within
ideas.text: The McDonald's Videogame shows the whole system in simple form. Papers, Please puts the player at a passport desk, stamping and refusing, and shows a whole government through one repeated job.

ideas.name: Players meet a game in five layers
ideas.text: Sensory, information, interaction, frame and purpose follow one another and loop back. What a player sees leads to what they understand, what they think they can do, what they bring from outside, and why they play.

ideas.name: Simple controls and flat views are easier to enter
ideas.text: 3D games with WASD and mouse, or a console pad of fifteen buttons, are hard for many people to learn, the authors say. Even a text game like Alabaster assumes knowledge of how interactive fiction works. A two-dimensional game with left, right and hug asks for less.

ideas.name: Seeing is different from understanding
ideas.text: At the start of Journey, the player sees a figure, a hill and sand. Moving the sticks shows the figure is theirs, and sand shifting under it confirms the material. Data becomes information and then knowledge.

ideas.name: A landmark can guide without telling
ideas.text: A large mountain visible from everywhere in Journey gives players a goal and a sense of direction. Theme parks use the same device, called a weenie.

ideas.name: Full information still leaves hidden thoughts
ideas.text: In chess, every piece is in view, yet the players still guess each other's plans. That guessing is yomi. Because the amount to think about is large, chess suits turns with no clock.

ideas.name: Hidden cards create guessing about roles
ideas.text: In Android: Netrunner the Corporation hides Agendas and the Runner tries to steal them, and each knows only part of what the other holds. Players have to imagine how someone on the other side thinks.

ideas.name: Real-time pace overloads even full information
ideas.text: In basketball everyone can see everything, yet the speed of play makes it impossible to process all possible moves. That keeps the outcome open.

ideas.name: A mental model is built by playing
