ideas.text: Anna Anthropy's reading of the first screen of Super Mario Bros. shows a figure on the left, open ground to the right, and nothing else to do but move right. Soon a question-mark brick and an enemy teach jumping.

ideas.name: Affordances can be seen, hidden or false
ideas.text: In Braid the key invites picking up, the large keyhole invites unlocking, and the goomba's face warns of danger. Rewinding time has no visible sign and is learned from a one-time prompt.

ideas.name: The screen and the controller are separate
ideas.text: Players look at a screen and press buttons elsewhere, and even touch screens seldom match gestures to what appears. That gap between seeing and doing is something designers have to bridge.

ideas.name: Rich feedback still needs repetition to read
ideas.text: Drop7 gives seven kinds of feedback for one match: sound, lit row, rotating disc, particles, shrinking, score and falling discs. New players see a disc vanish without knowing why until repeated plays teach them the number rule.

ideas.name: Consistent response lets players learn the rules
ideas.text: In Drop7 a disc always falls to the top of its column and breaks when the numbers add up. If it sometimes broke on touch or fell while held, players could not work out their part in the game.

ideas.name: Practice moves effort from mechanics to experience
ideas.text: New basketball players think about dribbling and foot position. With repetition these become automatic and attention goes to the game itself. Drop7 helps by using falling and breaking, which people already know.

ideas.name: Players feel own-fault failure differently from the game's fault
ideas.text: Juul found that failures blamed on the player feel more acceptable, since skill can improve. Failures blamed on the game, such as a level that seems unbeatable, tend to make players quit.

ideas.name: What players bring from outside frames the game
ideas.text: Someone seeing an anvil on a cliff edge expects it to fall, from life or cartoons. The Kinect pose game about women's life stages uses expectations about women's roles, and Train changes them by revealing the setting of its history only at the end.

ideas.name: Players come to a game for different reasons
ideas.text: Bartle named achievers, explorers, socializers and killers. In The Path an achiever collects all 36 objects and 144 flowers, while an explorer in Proteus wants to see the whole island. Types can shift in a single player.

ideas.name: Authored games may not need player types
ideas.text: In a game like Howling Dogs the maker plans the experience and the player takes it as given, like reading a novel. The authors suggest Kentucky Route Zero suits being taken as the makers planned, not forced into a play style.

ideas.name: Designers cannot see a design until it is played
ideas.text: A game cannot be played until it is made, and its qualities show only in play. Iteration answers this by moving round concept, prototype, playtest and evaluation.

ideas.name: Iteration is adaptive where much industry work is predictive
ideas.text: A predictive process assumes the maker is right the first time. An adaptive one leaves room for errors and new ideas. Games are experiences more than tools like typewriters or ATMs, so the authors choose adaptive.

ideas.name: The cycle has older roots
ideas.text: Shewhart's Plan-Do-Study-Act used data to raise the consistency of Bell Labs products. Dreyfuss's Think-Sketch-Show-Evaluate looked at the user of a telephone or vacuum cleaner. Software design added requirements, prototype, review, revise.

ideas.name: An idea begins as a question
ideas.text: The first output is not a plan but a question such as how might we make a game where unicorns joust with dinosaurs. Brainstorming then produces what if questions, and the most promising is built.

ideas.name: Prototype fast to find what the idea can do
ideas.text: The sooner a game leaves the world of ideas and becomes paper cut-outs, quick code or the designer's own body, the authors say, the sooner it shows its play. Prototyping can also uncover things concepting would never have raised.

ideas.name: A playtest is the answer to the prototype's question
ideas.text: The prototype asks what if, and the playtest answers it, along with questions about whether players grasp the goal, feel the hoped-for emotion, understand the interface and get clear feedback.

ideas.name: Evaluation returns to the questions of the start
ideas.text: After seeing players struggle to make a unicorn pick up a lance, the designers ask why and how might we make it easier. This is why the cycle is circular and the evaluate and conceptualize steps blur.

ideas.name: Reading playtest feedback is like diagnosis
ideas.text: A comment like this game is too intense is hard to act on. The authors compare it to a doctor who builds evidence from what a patient says and from watching them.

ideas.name: Failing early and often is part of the method
ideas.text: Reiner Knizia is quoted as saying all his designs were flawless until they were playtested. The authors advise getting through early loops quickly so problems appear while they are cheap to fix.

ideas.name: Design values are asked as questions
ideas.text: Their questions cover experience, theme, point of view, challenge, decision-making, skill and chance, context and emotions. Answering them gives a team a shared picture of what they are making.

ideas.name: Design values let a team check new ideas
ideas.text: When an idea arrives that excites people but may not suit the game, the team asks whether it fits their design values. This settles disputes and shows whether the idea belongs in this game or a later one.

ideas.name: A design value can be a feeling the player is meant to have
ideas.text: Jenova Chen wanted Journey to make the player feel lonely, small and full of awe. That aim guided choices about the world and the sand dunes, and was checked in each round of prototyping.

ideas.name: The platform a game is made for shapes its design values
ideas.text: Journey was made for a living-room console, and Sony asked for a single-player game. So the other player appears and disappears in the world and the game does not rely on anyone being online.

ideas.name: A real place can give a design value
ideas.text: The team visited sand dunes and noticed how pleasant it was to climb and how hard it is to slide down. This led to sand-surfing in Journey, which feels like reality but is not possible in reality.

ideas.name: Testing can show that actions work against the aim
ideas.text: Early Journey prototypes had boulder-pushing and pulling over obstacles to encourage cooperation, but playtesters pushed and fought. The team changed to equal access to resources, and replaced chat with one signature tone.

ideas.name: Design values can grow out of a notebook of notes
ideas.text: Justin Smith wrote down short ideas like indie Angry Birds and later found ones that connect. For Desert Golfing, that gave values of minimal play, a certain world look, a satisfying single stroke, a sense of endlessness and sharing found by players.

ideas.name: Leaving sharing to players can be a design value
ideas.text: Desert Golfing has no leaderboard. Its colours change slowly and a stroke total is shown, so players discuss them in person and online without a built-in competition.

ideas.name: Design values can come from dissatisfaction with other media
ideas.text: Naomi Clark disliked how a genre of animation set monsters in power over young women. Her card game Consentacle gives both characters equal power and bases its play on consent.

ideas.name: A design value can be borrowed from the way another game feels
ideas.text: Naomi noticed that hidden information in Android: Netrunner made the two sides' dealings feel intimate. In Hanabi, players see everyone's cards but their own and have to help each other, which led to a value of collaborative decision-making.

ideas.name: A constraint can be chosen to shape cooperation
ideas.text: In the advanced version of Consentacle players may not talk about which cards to play. They guess each other's actions instead, which Naomi called collaborative yomi.

ideas.name: A game about cooperation can drop the winner
ideas.text: Consentacle gives no win or loss. It rates how well the pair did on a scale like a magazine quiz, and shows how the points were spread between them.

ideas.name: Design values give research a direction
ideas.text: With a clear set of values, looking at other games and media has a purpose and does not drift. Naomi's search for ideas was led by her values.

ideas.name: Design values answer questions in the middle of work
ideas.text: They are guideposts that keep a team aiming at one play experience. When something unplanned comes up, the team can ask whether it serves the values.

ideas.name: Documents keep a team on the same page
ideas.text: Without records, team members hold different understandings of the game, repeat work or leave tasks undone. The authors use three kinds: a design document, schematics and a tracking spreadsheet.

ideas.name: A design document can be short
ideas.text: Many people picture 500 pages, but an indie game may need 10 to 20. With a new team more detail is likely at first, and the right level shows up as the team learns how it works together.

ideas.name: Design documents resemble scripts and specifications
ideas.text: A film script tells a crew what to shoot. A software requirements document lists parts and use cases because users act differently. Story-heavy games lean towards scripts and systems-heavy games towards specifications.

ideas.name: A design document is kept alive across iterations
ideas.text: Each trip round the cycle changes the game, so the document gets new sections and loses others. Keeping it current takes time but matters most for complex games and bigger teams.

ideas.name: Early documents list the game's basic elements
ideas.text: The authors suggest asking how many players, what their goals are, what the main actions are, which objects and what playspace there are, and what rules govern all of these.

ideas.name: Schematics serve as wireframes, storyboards and blueprints
ideas.text: A wireframe shows what is onscreen. A storyboard plans how a scene is seen, and an animatic adds motion. A blueprint gives exact sizes, such as how each section of the Pong paddle sends the ball at a different angle.

ideas.name: A single wireframe cannot show play
ideas.text: The Pong wireframe shows paddles, net, ball, court and scores but not their interaction. As a rule of thumb the designer draws key changes, such as when a point is won, how the next begins and how the game ends.

ideas.name: A simple game may only need notes on drawings
ideas.text: Pong is simple enough that annotated schematics could replace the design document. The team would still write design values and carry out art direction separately.

ideas.name: A tracking spreadsheet is a shared agenda
ideas.text: The authors' team uses six sheets: overview, for discussion, task list, ongoing responsibilities, asset list and completed tasks. Kept online, it can be seen by a collaborator in another city and doubles as a meeting agenda.

ideas.name: Tasks are sorted by size
ideas.text: Long-range tasks are guideposts, mid-range are milestones, short-range take days and immediate tasks are quick fixes. Each larger kind is made up of the smaller, and timeframes are given to the larger two.

ideas.name: Keeping finished tasks saves repeat work
ideas.text: The completed-tasks sheet records the work done and questions asked in each phase, so the team does not go back over ground it has already covered.

ideas.name: Small teams mix roles
ideas.text: Roles of design, programming, art, sound, testing and management often overlap in one person. Local No. 12 shares game design and project management, and then gives each member a lead area such as narrative, visuals or playtests.

ideas.name: Teams balance autonomy against alignment
ideas.text: More freedom in a role makes people feel committed, while more alignment keeps the team in step. Spotify's approach is to give each project a clear goal everyone agrees on and then leave the way to reach it to team members.

ideas.name: Shared design values allow freedom
ideas.text: When everyone knows what the team values about the play experience, members can explore their own solutions towards it. Frequent check-ins show how one person's decisions affect others.

ideas.name: Agreement and consent differ
ideas.text: A person can be okay with a decision without agreeing with it. The authors say noticing the difference avoids hidden tension, and that consensus is worth the time it takes.

ideas.name: A team agreement is useful when things go badly or well
ideas.text: It records goal, member status, ownership, expected participation, roles, decisions and term. It settles questions such as who owns a game that ends up in a museum or one that is never finished.

ideas.name: Decisions come in classes
ideas.text: The authors split them into creative, process and business decisions, and say a team can decide for each what agreement means: majority, two-thirds or consensus.

ideas.name: Team tools can be the simplest ones
ideas.text: For file sharing, task tracking and communication, the authors suggest the simplest, most familiar and least costly tools. They have tried specialist task software several times and gone back to a shared spreadsheet.

ideas.name: Meetings need a few basics
ideas.text: The authors list goals, an agenda, talking rights, a way of deciding, action items and notes. Full-team meetings stay above the level of immediate tasks, and smaller meetings go into details.

ideas.name: Rotating the note-taker spreads the load
ideas.text: Notes follow the agenda and sit in a shared place. They feed the task list and the design document so a team can look back at earlier meetings.

ideas.name: Quiet members need routes to be heard
ideas.text: Posing questions to the group, prompting soft-spoken people and allowing written feedback before or after meetings all help. Prototyping and playtesting can also settle a design argument that talk cannot.

ideas.name: Three kinds of team conflict need three responses
ideas.text: Procedural conflict is about how the team works and can be fixed by trying changes. Affective conflict comes from differing values and calls for listening. Substantive conflict about the game is handled by returning to the design values.

ideas.name: Playtests can settle substantive arguments
ideas.text: Instead of relying on team opinion, playtesting shows strengths and weaknesses of the game, provided the team is willing to learn from what testers do and say.

ideas.name: Failure is handled by asking what was learned
ideas.text: Spotify's Henrik Kniberg is quoted as asking not whose fault it was but what was learned and how it will be fixed. Looking back at the prototype and its test often answers that.

ideas.name: Six kinds of failure differ in usefulness
ideas.text: Jamer Hunt's list is abject, structural, glorious, common, version and predicted. Predicted failures are the ones iteration invites, since they give the team a safe place to experiment with limited risk.

ideas.name: Ideas can come from anywhere
ideas.text: Chris Bell made Way after getting lost in a Tokyo fish market and finding his way by gesturing with an older woman. The game kept only the kernel, nonverbal communication, and dropped the market.

ideas.name: Brainstorming has set rules
ideas.text: Osborn's rules include quantity over quality, deferring judgment, no buts, going wild, drawing and combining. Replacing but with and, as in and what if the tubes lead to rooms of coins, keeps ideas moving.

ideas.name: Brainstorming also builds agreement
ideas.text: Beyond producing ideas, it gets team members building on each other and valuing every idea whatever their role, and helps a team agree on what matters.

ideas.name: Mashing up two ideas can beat either original
ideas.text: In idea speed-dating, unicorns jousting with dinosaurs meets soccer in the dark with a light-up ball. The pair writes a merge, such as creatures fighting for the ball to find their way home.

ideas.name: A how might we question stays neither too narrow nor too wide
ideas.text: How might we create a competitive game is too broad. A game about unicorns and dinosaurs chasing a glowing ball in the dark is too specific for early work. How might we create a game about creatures finding their way home sits between.

ideas.name: One idea per sticky note allows sorting
ideas.text: Square notes and thick markers limit each note to one short idea, so notes can be grouped into clusters and read from across the room. The authors photograph the groups and copy them into a shared document.

ideas.name: Random word cards can push toward odd combinations
ideas.text: For a game about healthy eating, shuffled cards might give gigantic, jumping and broccoli. The authors add a few unexpected verbs and adjectives to keep results unexpected.

ideas.name: Motivation gives a design its angle
ideas.text: Like a journalist's angle, a motivation tells the designer what to ask. Six are listed: what the player does, constraints, a story, personal experiences, abstracting the real world, and the player.

ideas.name: A game can start from an activity that is already enjoyable
ideas.text: Douglas Wilson began Johann Sebastian Joust from moving in slow motion on a playground, then added a game system. Slow music makes the controllers more sensitive, so players have to move slowly.

ideas.name: Games can be built on what the player may not do
ideas.text: In vvvvvv the player cannot jump and flips gravity to cross even a small step. In soccer the limit is on the hands. Play comes from working around the obvious route.

ideas.name: Technology limits have shaped game design
ideas.text: The Atari 2600 used rectangular pixels, so Breakout made rectangular bricks a feature. Canabalt came from the challenge of Super Mario with one button, a game jam brief.

ideas.name: A story can be found by exploring
ideas.text: Gone Home does not resolve scenes through character actions. The player walks an empty house, reading letters and listening to tapes, and assembles the family's story from objects.

ideas.name: A story-led design asks about the player's role
ideas.text: The authors suggest asking whether the player watches or acts, how many paths exist, which nouns and verbs carry the story, and what the player is left thinking about afterwards.

ideas.name: A personal experience can be abstracted
ideas.text: dys4ia is a journal about anna anthropy's hormone therapy. Way is based on Chris Bell's trip through a fish market but does not set the game there. A designer chooses how autobiographical to be.

ideas.name: Modelling a system means choosing a point of view
ideas.text: In The McDonald's Videogame the player moves from pasture to feedlot to restaurant to board room, each level with different actions. The model shows how hard it is to stay profitable without cutting corners.

ideas.name: Ask what an abstraction leaves out
ideas.text: A real system is simplified into rules, and the authors say the removed details matter as much as the kept ones. They also ask whether the player is part of the system or above it.

ideas.name: Personas keep a particular player in view
ideas.text: A team picks one main persona and two others to also keep in mind. Questions about where, when and with what else the player plays, and what else they like, help widen the design.

ideas.name: Design values act as scaffolding
ideas.text: They hold the game's shape and stop a team spending time on parts that dilute the vision. A rule of thumb for a changing value is to ask whether it strengthens the player's experience and what the game says.

ideas.name: Drifting is different from moving forward
ideas.text: New ideas arise while making a game, and some are kept for a later game. The authors say that telling the two apart takes practice.

ideas.name: A prototype tests whether an exciting idea is in fact exciting
ideas.text: Making ideas tangible shows unexpected results, which is the aim of iteration. Industrial designers do the same with a peeler's grip and balance, but game designers test play.

ideas.name: Games may make things harder on purpose
ideas.text: A peeler is refined to make peeling easier. A game stresses challenge or mood over ease, so a prototype tests whether the experience matches what was intended. Not every game aims to be enjoyable, but it needs interesting choices.

ideas.name: Prototype from a question
ideas.text: Questions like whether the main activity is enjoyable, whether players grasp the theme or whether the palette works decide what to build next.

ideas.name: Rough prototypes protect the designer from attachment
ideas.text: Polish delays answers, the authors argue, and also makes ideas feel finished, which makes them harder to judge objectively.

ideas.name: Change little between prototypes
ideas.text: Altering one rule or variable can set off many emergent effects, so a team playtests before making too many significant changes.

ideas.name: A paper prototype can settle basic layout questions
ideas.text: While cutting paper paddles and balls for Ping!, the authors had to decide where the score sits, how it is counted and where the ball enters, either auto-served from the centre or from a paddle.

ideas.name: A basic kit is enough for paper prototypes
ideas.text: The authors list paper, markers, scissors, glue, tape, rulers, dice and tokens. Paper prototypes answer what is onscreen, what the playspace is, which objects and actions exist, and how the play is meant to feel.

ideas.name: Physical prototypes capture how a game feels
ideas.text: Killer Queen began as an outdoor field game for two teams of ten, with a Queen, Workers, foam swords, rubber balls and a bomb. Playing it at festivals let the makers watch teams build strategies before turning it into an arcade videogame.

ideas.name: A digital prototype can be built from an ordinary tool
ideas.text: The authors tested Losswords through Skype chat, with one person playing the game logic by sending book passages and scoring replies on word count, length and rarity. It took an hour of planning instead of days of code.

ideas.name: Most games go through a dozen or more playable prototypes
ideas.text: The early ones model the actions players repeat, because if those are not enjoyable the game will not be either. Design values are checked and sometimes revised as discoveries arrive.

ideas.name: Art and sound can come first
ideas.text: Tale of Tales began The Path from the Red Riding Hood theme seen through horror, plus music. Designing the character Ruby first showed what all six sisters would be.

ideas.name: Art and sound need early trials
ideas.text: The Path started with reference music, and the composers later wrote its score. The authors say sound shapes mood, so trying different tracks in a playable prototype can change testers' responses.

ideas.name: An interface prototype can be pictures in presentation software
ideas.text: For Losswords the authors drew each screen in image software and linked them in presentation software to show how players move. Those screens also served as the base for the art.

ideas.name: Technology tests show what can and cannot be done
ideas.text: Peter Lu tried the Kinect for the pose game and found its limits, then adjusted smoothing and speed to reduce lag between body and screen character. New technology can be hyped beyond its ability.

ideas.name: A core prototype can be circles and squares
ideas.text: Jane Friedhoff made two circles bounce off squares with physics and no goals for Slam City Oracles. Because bouncing and smashing was the whole experience, that was enough to judge it.

ideas.name: A complete prototype is rough but whole
ideas.text: Kevin Cancienne finished Dog Park for an exhibition where players met it with no instruction. He did not polish the code, but he made the entire game playable to see players' reactions.

ideas.name: Prototype notes record why, what and how
ideas.text: The authors record the reason for each prototype, what was done, and how, so it can be rebuilt. Unaddressed ideas go on a to-do list and design changes go into the design document.

ideas.name: The playtest answers the prototype
ideas.text: Playtests can last minutes or months, and the team or outsiders can supply the answers. Early on they show whether the game runs and the parts balance. Later they show whether players understand the game.

ideas.name: Playtests reveal what designers did not intend
ideas.text: The authors list exploitable cracks, unclear parts, spots that are too easy or too hard, and emotions different from those hoped for.

ideas.name: Internal testing can alter the design
ideas.text: While trying Ping! the authors tuned paddle and ball speeds, then found that a paddle that shrinks on each hit and grows on each score felt like part of the game world.

ideas.name: Change one thing at a time
ideas.text: In rapid testing, changing several variables at once hides which change did what. One change per test shows its effect on the game as a whole.

ideas.name: Developers' advice is shaped by the game they would make
ideas.text: They give sharp feedback but often propose solutions. The authors suggest sharing the design values and weighing suggestions against them.

ideas.name: Friends are kind, so watch what they do
ideas.text: Friends tend to say positive things. The authors say to notice where they seem to enjoy themselves, where they struggle and what their faces show.

ideas.name: A family can test how a game treats people it assumes less about
ideas.text: Local No. 12 tried The Metagame with a friend's family, ages 13 to 70, to see how the youngest and oldest reacted to pop culture references they did not know.

ideas.name: A target audience can be gathered early
ideas.text: Chris Hecker built a community round Spy Party with convention booths and a website. Players who wanted the game gave feedback soon after the first playable version, and showed whether he was heading the right way.

ideas.name: Five to seven new players is a working range
ideas.text: Fewer gives too little variation and more costs too much time. A person is a new player only once, so finding fresh testers is a continuing task.

ideas.name: An exploit can show what the game is for
ideas.text: A Dog Park player won by barking nonstop. Kevin Cancienne saw other players chase and wrestle the barker, as dogs do, and so kept barking but reduced its points.

ideas.name: Different prototypes suit different testers
ideas.text: Paper, physical and code prototypes suit the team and other developers. Art and playable ones add friends. Core prototypes add the target audience, and complete ones suit everyone. Experienced players can join from the start.

ideas.name: Playtests ask a lot of testers
ideas.text: Eric Zimmerman and Nathalie Pozzi compare early playtests to a dinner party where some food is unappetising or uncooked. The team has to be ready before asking people to try something it knows is broken.

ideas.name: Place matters to a playtest
ideas.text: A loud cafe or bar may seem lively, but it spoils a test of a game that needs focus and undivided attention.

ideas.name: Designers lose the feel of their own game
ideas.text: After repeated play the Ping! team could no longer tell how hard it was to move paddles or how long a volley lasted, so they asked others. Outsiders keep difficulty reasonable and interactions clear.

ideas.name: Much of a playtest is nonverbal
ideas.text: A laugh, a comment mid-play, white knuckles on a hard part and bored glances at a phone are all clues. Video helps capture them.

ideas.name: The designer has to watch without stepping in
ideas.text: It is painful to see testers fail to understand something that seems obvious, yet that is what the team came to find. The four tasks are introduce, observe, listen and discuss.

ideas.name: Listening differs from observing
ideas.text: Observing is watching what testers do. Listening is hearing them say aloud what they are doing, why they choose and what confuses them.

ideas.name: Ask testers open questions
ideas.text: The authors give how did playing the game make you feel and tell me how you figured out the goal as examples. Their aim is to hear the tester's reactions, not to hand over the designer's.

ideas.name: Record who, when, where and what happened
ideas.text: The authors record tester names and contact details, the date and place, the prototype tested and the note-taker, then notes on gameplay, visuals and audio, bugs, comments, observations and ideas.

ideas.name: Video is used with notes pointing to the moments
ideas.text: Recordings help the team review a session, but notes with times or levels marked let them find the relevant bits instead of re-watching hours of footage.

ideas.name: Input and feedback are different
ideas.text: Mattie Brice and Lana Polansky argue that designing around players can water down a game's message. Input changes the game to suit testers. Feedback is information the designer weighs without having to act on it.

ideas.name: Playtesting can calibrate expression
ideas.text: Jonathan Blow does not want ideas from testers but does test, to check that his games give the experience he intends. Many arts do the same through workshops, table reads and critiques.

ideas.name: Evaluation works like diagnosis
ideas.text: Playtest notes are symptoms and the design values are what the game is meant to show. Treatments range from small fixes to large changes.

ideas.name: Evaluation follows what, where, why and takeaway
ideas.text: First list small observed moments without interpretation, then note where in the game each happened, then guess why, then agree on a specific takeaway.

ideas.name: A suggested change may hide a different problem
ideas.text: If a tester says to make the score bigger, the cause may be that they miss score changes in fast play. A bigger number may not fix it, and a summary screen between matches could.

ideas.name: Evaluate against a checklist drawn from the design tools
ideas.text: The authors suggest asking about actions, goals, challenge, information, feedback, decision-making, perceptions, context, takeaways and emotions, after rereading the design values.

ideas.name: Responses may be unintended strengths or intended ones
ideas.text: Players may call a game too hard or too short when that was planned. Bending convention marks experimental design but can also signal an oversight, and design values help tell which.

ideas.name: A player doing it wrong shows something
ideas.text: A high school student said testers played the game wrong. The authors reply that the design may need work, or the testers' way may be more intuitive than the planned one. Either finding helps.

ideas.name: Revision has six steps
ideas.text: The team reviews, incubates, brainstorms, decides, documents and schedules. The time for incubating grows with the size of the problem.

ideas.name: Brainstorming fixes can overload the design
ideas.text: New ideas are welcome, but the team picks what the next prototype needs and writes down the rest for a future project.

ideas.name: Make a decision that can be built
ideas.text: Deciding is quicker than long debate, the authors say, and reaching the next buildable prototype is worth more than the ideal answer.

ideas.name: Each loop of the cycle poses and answers one question
ideas.text: The team theorizes a question in conceptualizing, shapes it in prototyping, answers it in playtesting and interprets it in evaluating. A loop may repeat a question or move to a new part of the game.

ideas.name: Failure is raw material for iteration
ideas.text: The authors open the chapter with a line from Beckett about trying and failing again, and say creativity is more about failure than success.

ideas.name: One game can pass through many forms while its goal stays fixed
ideas.text: The Metagame was a game show, a conference card game, a boxed party game and a magazine insert over five years. Its aim of giving people a playful structure for talking about pop culture never changed.

ideas.name: A conference can act as a large playtest
ideas.text: The conference version of The Metagame was played by more than 3,000 people. It showed the makers what worked about the card information, images and conversations before the boxed edition.

ideas.name: A new play setting calls for a new design loop
ideas.text: Moving The Metagame from conference halls and bars to living rooms and classrooms led to new play modes for smaller groups and tight loops on the rules booklet.

ideas.name: Playtests can shape the content of a game
ideas.text: For the broader version, testers of different ages and cultures named television shows, fashions and artworks, and much of the card content came from those suggestions.

ideas.name: A quick design can rest on long experience
ideas.text: Johann Sebastian Joust took shape in a 48-hour game jam, but it followed a year of work with motion controllers and then over two years of building a stand-alone version. The authors count four years in all.

ideas.name: A discovery can come from a happy accident
ideas.text: While testing controller sensitivity, Douglas Wilson and Nils walked towards each other and shoved to make the other lose. That showed that the game they wanted was a duel, not a race.

ideas.name: A game that others run alone needs its own teaching
ideas.text: Making Joust ready to run without its designer meant building menus and a setup guide that explained how to play. That took two years, ten times longer than the first design.

ideas.name: Some mood-based games need art before they can be tested
ideas.text: The Path could not be playtested for emotional effect until its environments, art and sound were well developed. So early cycles built a world to walk through, with little gameplay.

ideas.name: A live-editing tool blurs prototype and playtest
ideas.text: In Quest 3D, changing a character's behaviour or the sky's colour took effect at once, so Tale of Tales played in the world and changed it at the same time, like playing with dolls.

ideas.name: A design value can mean removing finished work
ideas.text: After hearing the finished soundtrack, the makers of The Path cut many small puzzle tasks and made the game about exploring. The authors call this being willing to kill your babies, though they would not advise a first game to follow that path.

ideas.name: A constraint can carry a theme
ideas.text: anna anthropy took a timer from another Twine game and a call for 10-second games, and set a queer couple's last 10 seconds before the world ends. The time limit stood for the pressure she felt in a long-distance relationship.

ideas.name: Playtests can be for function only
ideas.text: anna anthropy tested Queers in Love at the End of the World just for technical faults such as a broken timer or dead links. She did not seek ideas or input on content.

ideas.name: Not every game needs a full iterative process
ideas.text: Queers in Love fits the authors' method only partly, they say, and time and resources for iteration cannot be assumed. Sometimes all a maker has is a short time.

ideas.name: Iteration and production have opposite attitudes to failure
ideas.text: During iteration the team avoids getting things exactly right and fails faster. During production the work has to be right, such as server code sturdy enough for internet traffic.

ideas.name: A design is done when its parts are decided and tested
ideas.text: The authors list a complete game prototype, tests with the target audience, new players and experienced players, met design values, art direction, a sound code base, most final text and a current design document.

ideas.name: New and experienced testers show different things
ideas.text: New players show how learnable the game is. Experienced players show that it holds up over repeated play without losing interest or becoming too easy to master.

ideas.name: Placeholder assets can remain when design is complete
ideas.text: A game with many dinosaurs may have a few finished ones and only placeholders for the rest. Making the remaining models is production.

ideas.name: Production needs who, what and by when
ideas.text: The team lists people, tasks and deadlines, marks tasks that depend on others, and doubles its time estimates because people tend to underestimate.

ideas.name: Regular meetings in production keep a team honest
ideas.text: Weekly or more frequent meetings show how much was done. If nothing is reported, the team knows to set aside more time.

ideas.name: Games meet needs that daily life leaves open
ideas.text: Many people spend long hours in games, and the book reads this as a sign that games supply rewards, teaching and company that daily life does not. Players in World of Warcraft raids and Rock Band practice are examples.

ideas.name: A game can be a deliberate response to hardship
ideas.text: Herodotus tells of the Lydians, who played games on one day and ate on the next to survive a famine for eighteen years. The book reads this as play that gave people structure and a sense of power when they had little of either.

ideas.name: A game has four defining parts
ideas.text: Every game has a goal, rules, a feedback system and voluntary participation. Story, graphics, scores, levels and competition are added to strengthen these four, and are not needed to make a game.

ideas.name: A game is a chosen unnecessary obstacle
ideas.text: Bernard Suits defined playing a game as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles. In golf a player could drop the ball in the hole by hand, but agrees to stand far away and use a club.

ideas.name: Rules turn an ordinary task into a game
ideas.text: Scrabble is spelling words, which is typing. It becomes a game because players hold only seven tiles, cannot pick letters, have to build on words already played, and have a fixed number of each letter.

ideas.name: A game need not be winnable
ideas.text: Tetris cannot be won, because the pieces only fall faster until the player fails. Players still play because of the strength of its visual, number and difficulty feedback.

ideas.name: Three kinds of feedback in one game
ideas.text: Tetris shows rows vanishing on screen, a score that climbs, and a difficulty the player can feel rising. The book names these visual, quantitative and qualitative feedback.

ideas.name: Digital games tighten the feedback loop
ideas.text: In a computer game the response to an action is immediate and countable, and the game can raise difficulty only when the player is doing well. This keeps players near the edge of their skill.

ideas.name: Players may prefer playing to winning
ideas.text: In games with strong feedback, being absorbed can please more than winning, and winning ends the game. The book uses this to argue that gamers are not mainly people who want to win.

ideas.name: Players can learn the rules from the feedback
ideas.text: In Portal the player starts in a room with no instructions and works out the goal and physics by watching how the game responds. The four parts stay the same, but feedback comes first and the rules come last.

ideas.name: Players take a game seriously
ideas.text: Because the goal and feedback are worth caring about, players wrestle with limits for a long time. The book says a game matters to the person playing it, even though it is chosen.

ideas.name: Chosen hard work differs from imposed hard work
ideas.text: Work done for someone else often fails to fit our strengths, gives no view of what it adds to, and has no visible pay-off. A game offers work that suits the person and is chosen.

ideas.name: The opposite of play is depression
ideas.text: Brian Sutton-Smith is quoted saying this. The book describes play as an optimistic sense of one's ability together with a rush of activity, the reverse of depression.

ideas.name: Relaxing pastimes can leave people lower
ideas.text: Experience sampling studies find that watching television or window-shopping leaves people less motivated afterward, while playing sports, board games and video games leaves them more interested and in a higher mood.

ideas.name: A game is built from many kinds of work
ideas.text: A single player may meet high-stakes work, busywork, mental, physical, discovery, team and creative work. Different kinds suit different people at different times.

ideas.name: Fiero grows with difficulty
ideas.text: The harder the obstacle that was beaten, the bigger the rush of triumph. It involves reward circuits tied to addiction, and people everywhere show it with the same gesture.

ideas.name: Games make flow quick and reliable
ideas.text: Csikszentmihalyi found flow in chess, climbing and dancing, where it took years of skill. Video games gave a goal, rising challenge, voluntary play and fast feedback, so flow could start within seconds.

ideas.name: Reality can be given a game's structure
ideas.text: Csikszentmihalyi argued in 1975 that schools and workplaces leave people bored and anxious, and that work with chosen goals, matched obstacles and constant feedback would give more flow.

ideas.name: Sudnow and Breakout
ideas.text: David Sudnow played Breakout for three months. The paddle shrank and the ball sped up as bricks fell, so difficulty tracked his skill, and each brick gave a beep and a flicker. He stopped playing after one flawless game.

ideas.name: Too much flow and fiero can wear a player out
ideas.text: Flow uses up mental and physical resources and cannot be kept up all the time. Fiero is linked to the feeling of addiction. Designers add fatigue systems and resting bonuses to limit hours, but players find ways around limits.

ideas.name: Hours of play can cause regret
ideas.text: Clive Thompson found he had played thirty-six hours in one week and felt pride and emptiness together. The book says players tend to start doubting once play passes about twenty hours a week.

ideas.name: Outside rewards do not last
ideas.text: The book cites a University of Rochester study of 150 graduates. Those who reached money, fame and looks were not happier, while those who worked on strengths and relationships were happier for two years.

ideas.name: Four rewards that come from within
ideas.text: The book groups intrinsic rewards into satisfying work, the hope or experience of success, social connection, and meaning. Games supply all four without paying money or raising status.

ideas.name: Self-made rewards are renewable
ideas.text: Sonja Lyubomirsky is quoted saying a reward a person made themselves can be made again. Activities that reward themselves build resilience, while bought pleasures need to grow to keep working.

ideas.name: Work needs a goal and actionable steps
ideas.text: A clear goal with no known way to progress is a problem, and a goal with next steps is work. The book says designed work carries a guarantee of progress, and that this guarantee is what draws players.

ideas.name: A World of Warcraft quest spells out its parts
ideas.text: A quest scroll gives a goal, the reason it matters, where to go, step-by-step instructions and the proof to bring back. Players seldom doubt they can finish a quest, only when they will fit it in.

ideas.name: More work is the main reward
ideas.text: In World of Warcraft, finishing a quest brings further quests, and the book calls this a bigger reward than points or gold. Each new task is slightly harder than the last, enough to interest and not enough to cause anxiety.

ideas.name: Players ask for long levelling
ideas.text: Players take about five hundred hours to reach the top level. When Age of Conan was said to need two hundred fifty hours, fans called that too little effort. The process of improving is the draw.

ideas.name: Visible results make work satisfying
ideas.text: The heads-up display flashes +1 strength and +1 stamina, the avatar wears finer armour, and quest histories can be shown. Each way of seeing progress lets players watch their abilities grow.

ideas.name: Phasing shows a player's effect on the world
ideas.text: After a player helps a faction win an area, that player sees a camp there where others still see enemies. The book says seeing an effect on the world is among the things people want most from work.

ideas.name: Office work often hides its results
ideas.text: Matthew Crawford and Alain de Botton are cited to say that when the chain from effort to result is long and many people share it, people struggle to feel what they did. Games give a small group direct and fast results.

ideas.name: Casual games give short bursts of satisfying work
ideas.text: Games such as Peggle and Bejeweled take minutes to learn and play. The book reports that most senior executives surveyed play them while working, to feel less stressed.

ideas.name: Players fail most of the time and keep playing
ideas.text: Nicole Lazzaro found that gamers fail about four times in five. Researchers at the M.I.N.D. Lab measured heart rate, skin sweat and smile muscles in Super Monkey Ball 2 players and found excitement and joy peaked after a failure.

ideas.name: A failure can show the player's own effect
ideas.text: In Super Monkey Ball 2 a missed shot sends the monkey spinning into space. The player laughs and sees that their action did this, so they believe the next attempt can go differently.

ideas.name: Random or passive failure removes the wish to try again
ideas.text: Clive Thompson is quoted saying failing only pleases if the game is fair and you had every chance. If a loss seems random, the player loses a sense of agency and with it the hope.

ideas.name: Every puzzle and level is meant to be solvable
ideas.text: A video game is built so that a player with enough time can pass every level. This built-in assurance is why players meet very hard content with hope.

ideas.name: Mastery ends the interest
ideas.text: Raph Koster argues that a game holds attention only until it is mastered, because learning is what the player enjoys. A game that is always won becomes dull, so players move on.

ideas.name: Fun failure stretches out learning
ideas.text: If failure is pleasant, the player stays longer in the stage where success is near but not certain. That extends the game before the obstacle stops being an obstacle.

ideas.name: Hope of success keeps players engaged more than success
ideas.text: Winning leaves the player with nothing to do, while a failure that can be retried still gives a mission. The book says the hope of success can be more exciting than success.

ideas.name: Players thrive on goals they can reach
ideas.text: Randolph Nesse suggests low mood is the body's way of stopping effort on goals that cannot be met. Games give a steady supply of goals the player knows are reachable.

ideas.name: Rock Band ties difficulty to real musical action
ideas.text: Higher levels ask for more complex chords and drum patterns, closer to real playing. Each band member picks a level, so a beginner and an expert can play one song together.

ideas.name: Rock Band turns failure into partial success
ideas.text: When a player is booed off stage, the game shows the percentage of the song completed, even if only a third. Failure becomes a measure of progress, and the crowd booing and band scowling are meant to be funny.

ideas.name: Teammates can revive a failing player
ideas.text: In Rock Band a player who fails can be saved by a bandmate's skilful play, up to twice. A save needs real effort from another player, so one member's failure pushes the others.

ideas.name: Instant feedback shows where the player went wrong
ideas.text: Rock Band marks each note hit or missed and the singer sees pitch on a staff. Players can find the exact place they stumble and change it in real time.

ideas.name: Playing together carries the hope of success
ideas.text: The book says people want others to see their strengths. Rock Band offers home play, bar nights and tournaments, and a 2008 study found most non-musician players were inspired to pick up a real instrument.

ideas.name: An asynchronous game gives a reason to stay in touch
ideas.text: In Lexulous, a Scrabble variant on Facebook, players take turns whenever they like. Each started game commits two people to a dozen or more small exchanges, and many players use it to talk to their mother.

ideas.name: Waiting for a turn builds anticipation
ideas.text: Because a player does not know when the other will return, there is a build-up before each move. The book quotes a player who says you have to be addicted and patient.

ideas.name: FarmVille adds a social layer to solo work
ideas.text: Players tend their own farm, with tasks that take twelve hours to four days, and visit friends' farms as neighbours. Pop-ups ask them to help neighbours, and a free daily gift invites a return gift.

ideas.name: Gifts and favours in a game create a habit of reciprocity
ideas.text: The gifts in FarmVille are not real, yet each one helps the receiver's goals in the game. Seeing that someone helped your farm makes you want to help back, and this repeats daily.

ideas.name: Playing together builds prosocial emotions as a side effect
ideas.text: The author describes falling in love while solving the adventure game Grim Fandango with her husband. Time spent working on puzzles together gave chances to admire, sympathise and share a goal.

ideas.name: Teasing in a game builds trust
ideas.text: Dacher Keltner calls a tease a social vaccine: a small hurt that shows the teaser could hurt but does not. Letting yourself be teased shows trust and gives the other person a moment of higher status.

ideas.name: Silly actions in party games lower status on purpose
ideas.text: WarioWare: Smooth Moves asks players to flap their arms or mime a hula hoop within five seconds. Looking silly in front of others signals trust in them.

ideas.name: Teaching a friend a game gives pride
ideas.text: A study of over one thousand gamers placed naches eighth among feelings they wanted from play, and 53.4 percent said training friends and family raised their enjoyment. Paul Ekman links it to group survival.

ideas.name: Players need company even when they do not interact
ideas.text: A study of over 150,000 World of Warcraft players found they spent about 70 percent of their time on solo missions. They said seeing others doing their own tasks in the same world made them feel not alone.

ideas.name: Light contact may make social play easier for shy players
ideas.text: Nicole Lazzaro suggests that mental tasks plus easy contact in an online world could teach introverts to find company rewarding. The book says no study has tested this yet.

ideas.name: Players choose between friends and strangers
ideas.text: Game designer Daniel Cookman says the choice depends on whether the player is lonely. A study found players under eighteen spend 61 percent of their game time with people they know.

ideas.name: Single-player games can be played as a group
ideas.text: One person plays and others watch, advise and encourage. In Braid, a hard puzzle game, players revisit puzzles they have solved to guide friends through them.

ideas.name: Games can rebuild community habits
ideas.text: Robert Putnam wrote that people bowl alone. The book argues gamers are building new habits of staying in touch, through asynchronous turns, teasing, mentoring and shared worlds.

ideas.name: A kill count has no value but can have meaning
ideas.text: In April 2009, Halo 3 players reached ten billion kills against a fictional enemy. The book separates value, meaning importance and consequence, from meaning, the sense that your action matters to a larger group.

ideas.name: Meaning needs only a chance to contribute
ideas.text: The book says players need a way to join others who care about the same large goal and a chance to see its scale. The goal can be arbitrary.

ideas.name: Story gives a frame for actions
ideas.text: Game developer Trent Polack says story sets the stage for meaning and frames what the player does. In a shooter, the story changes the pleasure from destroying things to acting where it matters.

ideas.name: A shared story and effort for all make a cause
ideas.text: Two conditions turn a game into a cause: a story that many players share, and actions that each benefit all other players. Halo adds forums, wikis and video sharing to build this.

ideas.name: A service record joins one player to a larger history
ideas.text: Halo keeps a public record of every match a player has played, with heat maps and charts. Millions of these records together make a history of the 'Great War'.

ideas.name: A fictional museum can make fiction felt
ideas.text: The Halo Museum of Humanity was made by a marketing group as an online museum from the twenty-seventh century, with documentary-style videos. Players reported chills, though the war it honours never happened.

ideas.name: A built environment shows what people can do together
ideas.text: The book compares Halo's thirty-four settings, made by over 250 people in three years with 54,000 pieces of audio, to a cathedral. Players feel awe at the work behind the space.

ideas.name: Epic spaces are very old
ideas.text: Gobekli Tepe in Turkey, more than eleven thousand years old, has stone circles with pillars three metres high and winding passages. Some archaeologists think building it came before farming and pushed people to cooperate.

ideas.name: Sound is part of an epic space
ideas.text: Halo's score mixes Gregorian chant, strings, percussion and Qawwali singing, chosen to give a feeling of weight and age. Players describe goose bumps when they hear it.

ideas.name: Players build knowledge as a shared project
ideas.text: Halo players wrote over 21 million forum posts, and its largest wiki has nearly six thousand articles by 1.5 million users. Halowiki has over a thousand sections of tips and strategy written by players.

ideas.name: A game can use the real world as its context
ideas.text: In NCAA Football 10, players pick a real college team and every online point adds to its score. Weekly online matches mirror the real schedule, and a team can win online after losing in reality.

ideas.name: Choosing a chore makes it voluntary
ideas.text: In Chore Wars nobody is assigned a task. Every player picks from a pool of adventures, so each is a volunteer, and players also think about strategy, such as fast easy chores against slow big ones.

ideas.name: Extra restrictions make an ordinary task a game
ideas.text: Chore Wars players add limits to a chore, such as a time limit for double points, a stealth rule, or doing it while singing or walking backward.

ideas.name: A player can set the reward to suit the task
ideas.text: In Chore Wars the household writes the adventures and sets their points, so a disliked chore such as cleaning the bathroom can be worth one hundred points.

ideas.name: An avatar keeps a record that housework does not
ideas.text: A clean kitchen gets dirty again, but points earned stay. The book says watching an avatar level up makes the work feel like personal growth.

ideas.name: A game can be dropped after it has done its work
ideas.text: The book expects Chore Wars to become dull as players improve. Even then, the shared memory of doing chores together may change how the household views chores.

ideas.name: A real-life game needs to be optional
ideas.text: The book says an alternate reality game has to stay a true alternate. Making Chore Wars compulsory would remove much of its effect.

ideas.name: A game can be a way to see what you want
ideas.text: The book says games show people what they want: satisfying work, hope of success, social contact and meaning. It cites Maslow, who wrote that knowing what we want is rare and hard.

ideas.name: Helping inside a game may lead to helping outside it
ideas.text: Three studies of over three thousand young players found that more time in games where players help each other went with more helping of friends, family and strangers.

ideas.name: Born-digital students expect feedback and challenge
ideas.text: Marc Prensky is quoted saying students demand to be engaged or they get enraged. The book says school gives obstacles that are required, standard, and recorded permanently if failed.

ideas.name: A school can be a game from start to finish
ideas.text: Educational games help a little, but Quest to Learn builds each course and assessment from game mechanics. Students level up by taking more quests, with no permanent mark for failing one.

ideas.name: Levelling replaces one chance at a grade
ideas.text: A student who fails a quest tries another to gain points. The book says this swaps negative stress for positive stress and puts attention on learning, not performing.

ideas.name: Students are matched by strengths
ideas.text: The expertise exchange lets Rai list mapmaking, a skill she had not counted, and a team needing a digital mapper can find her. This gives respect based on contributions made.

ideas.name: Teaching a character can replace a quiz
ideas.text: A student teaches the software character Betty how to divide mixed numbers. The student shows what they know by explaining it and does not feel tested. The book links this to naches.

ideas.name: A game can be built to treat a health problem
ideas.text: The author made 'SuperBetter' after a concussion. It turns three recovery strategies into a superhero game with allies, power-ups and lists of triggers. The strategies are optimism, support and reading symptoms like a gauge.

ideas.name: Asking for help can be given a role
ideas.text: In 'SuperBetter' each ally has a part in a story, such as a mentor who calls daily or a friend who keeps scores. This gives helpers a clear job and makes asking easier.

ideas.name: Achievements feel larger when someone else grants them
ideas.text: In 'SuperBetter' a friend or relative awards achievements for real acts, such as ignoring email for a day. The book says an achievement given by another person means more.

ideas.name: A goal list keeps hope when one outcome is uncertain
ideas.text: 'SuperBetter' has a list of superhero to-dos from easy to ambitious. The book says it lowers the fear of failing at full recovery, because there are other goals to pursue.

ideas.name: Rules can be shared without software
ideas.text: The author posted the rules of 'SuperBetter' on a blog and added a hashtag so players could find each other. She notes a game can be a set of rules one person passes to another, like chess or hide-and-seek.

ideas.name: New Games asked everyone to play
ideas.text: The New Games movement held that nobody has to sit out for lack of skill, and that competition is about playing harder and longer, not about winning. Earth ball needs several people to move a six-foot ball.

ideas.name: Players act as the judges of a new game
ideas.text: Bernie DeKoven wrote that players of a new game are its officials. If a game does not work they try to fix it, and each takes responsibility for finding what they can enjoy together.

ideas.name: Three questions for judging a real-life game
ideas.text: The book lists when and where a game is needed, who is invited, and what core activities its mechanics are to multiply.

ideas.name: Points for real strengths
ideas.text: Plusoneme lets anyone send a plus-one with a reason, such as plus-one backbone for sticking up for an idea, in thirty-seven strengths. The sender need not be a member and the receiver's plus-ones stack.

ideas.name: A feedback system can exist without being a game
ideas.text: The author says Plusoneme has no goals or limits, so it is a gesture toward a game. It asks what constant positive feedback would do to motivation.

ideas.name: A voluntary game inside a forced activity changes its mood
ideas.text: In airport security lines a person cannot opt out, but can opt in to Jetset. The book says this moves attention from outside pressure to the stress of a game the person chose.

ideas.name: Jetset makes the place part of the game
ideas.text: Players score souvenirs only at real airports, found by GPS, and levels match the airport they are in. The game's security agent role has banned items and a line that grows.

ideas.name: Rewards from inside do not run out
ideas.text: Ian Bogost says airlines make miles harder to earn once many people earn them, while pride and social connection can be given to everyone without limit.

ideas.name: Day in the Cloud links two planes and the ground
ideas.text: Passengers on two flights in opposite directions solve puzzles tied to altitude, and the planes with the higher score win. The puzzles are too many for one person, so planemates and friends on the ground help.

ideas.name: A game that is optional leaves others alone
ideas.text: About half the fliers on the Day in the Cloud tests played and half did not. The book says people who sleep or read well can ignore it.

ideas.name: Rewards from outside can weaken an activity people already enjoy
ideas.text: Economists found that paying for something people enjoy lowers their motivation. The book says game points carry little outside value, but could still distract from the first reason for the activity.

ideas.name: Measuring effort helps people improve it
ideas.text: Lord Kelvin is quoted saying what cannot be measured cannot be improved. Real-time data and numeric targets let players see progress and try harder.

ideas.name: Nike+ turns running into a levelled game
ideas.text: A sensor in a shoe sends speed and distance to a music player. Each mile earns a point, six levels follow martial-arts belt colours, and trophies mark fastest times.

ideas.name: Live pace makes it easier to run fast
ideas.text: Seeing the pace in real time lets a runner notice slowing down, and the numbers falling as they speed up give reward at once. The author ran over two minutes faster on her first run.

ideas.name: Players write their own challenges
ideas.text: In Nike+ anyone can create a competitive or collaborative challenge, from a two-person rivalry to a team race. One public challenge asks runners to cover 24,902 miles, around the earth, by 2027.

ideas.name: An avatar that looks like you changes behaviour
ideas.text: At Stanford, people who saw a look-alike avatar gain or lose weight as they exercised did about eight times more repetitions. A random avatar had no such effect.

ideas.name: Players care for creatures that depend on them
ideas.text: Judith Donath argues that characters who seem to need us trigger a wish to nurture. The Nike+ Mini pouts after a slack week, and the author runs more to make it happy.

ideas.name: Tracking data lets any activity be turned into a game
ideas.text: Foursquare, running with Nike+ and a wished-for writing counter all rely on sensors or self-reports. Once progress is recorded, goals, challenges and achievements can be added to any activity.

ideas.name: A game can reward trying new things
ideas.text: Foursquare gives trophies for checking in at ten, twenty-five, fifty and a hundred different places in a city. Staying at one favourite place earns a title, but new places earn trophies.

ideas.name: The mayor rule makes a rival from a stranger
ideas.text: Whoever checks in most at a place is its mayor, and a rival can take the title. Some cafes give the mayor free drinks, which also brings the players back to the cafe.

ideas.name: Stats can make people record what they do
ideas.text: Because players want accurate scores, they remember to check in, and that makes it easier for friends to find them. The book says the game points attention to real rewards.

ideas.name: Players who are strangers look for each other
ideas.text: In the Comfort of Strangers, players on phones with Bluetooth hear a whisper when another player passes. Players on one team gain a life and players on the other lose one, and nobody knows who is on which team at first.

ideas.name: Not knowing who plays makes finding a player a comfort
ideas.text: The designers made players feel lost on purpose. Meeting another player is reassuring even if they are on the opposite team, since they understand that you are in the same game.

ideas.name: Games can be set in a place and a time window
ideas.text: Because few people play yet, players organise games online for one neighbourhood and hour. Festivals such as Igfest, Come Out and Play, and Urban Play gather enough people.

ideas.name: A community comes from shared interest plus a way to interact
ideas.text: The book says two steps turn strangers into a community: build a shared interest, then give them a chance and means to interact about it. A multiplayer game does both.

ideas.name: A short community still counts
ideas.text: Communitas can last for days, hours or minutes, and the book says even a short burst can bring an isolated person back into social life or change how they see a place.

ideas.name: A museum game turned members into contributors
ideas.text: In Ghosts of a Chance, fictional curators asked players to make artworks for two ghosts' stories. More than six thousand people took part online and two hundred fifty attended the exhibit.

ideas.name: A game lowers the risk of making art
ideas.text: Because it was a game and not an art contest, people who would not offer artwork felt free to try. Others took part by discussing and analysing the works.

ideas.name: Treating game objects as real brings players inside an institution
ideas.text: The player-made artworks were entered in the museum's collection database and handled with white gloves like other objects. The book says this removed the wall between curators and visitors.

ideas.name: A shared score makes two strangers allies
ideas.text: In Bounce a young caller and an older person find life experiences they share, such as swimming in the Pacific, within ten minutes. Both aim at the same score, which creates a connection.

ideas.name: A role name can make a participant comfortable
ideas.text: The older players were called senior experience agents. The book says this set a playful tone and gave them confidence to take part.

ideas.name: The game's result can be a made thing
ideas.text: At the end of Bounce the shared answers were turned into a short poem that players could print or email. The book says players left feeling they had made something together.

ideas.name: A game for strangers may be given only to trusted people
ideas.text: The Bounce team shared the phone number with trusted friends and festival visitors, to avoid griefers. A live matchmaker paired callers with seniors.

ideas.name: Happiness advice sounds hokey and is resisted
ideas.text: Sonja Lyubomirsky found that people resist tested happiness activities as corny. The book says such activities need a package that does not feel like cheerful advice.

ideas.name: Happiness is social, so private self-help falls short
ideas.text: Eric Weiner is quoted saying self-help turns people inward when they need to look to other people. The book says happiness activities need to be done with friends, strangers and coworkers.

ideas.name: Knowing what helps is not the same as doing it
ideas.text: Tal Ben-Shahar is quoted saying people drop theories once they see how hard practice is. The book says reading about happiness leads most readers to do nothing.

ideas.name: Three crowd games turn advice into public play
ideas.text: Cruel 2 B Kind, Tombstone Hold 'Em and Top Secret Dance-Off turn acts of kindness, thinking of death and group dancing into games for large groups.

ideas.name: A hack is light and free
ideas.text: In the book a hack is cheap to adopt and needs no special equipment or skill, and hackers freely share it. The ten-two rule is the example: work ten minutes, rest two.

ideas.name: Happiness hacking turns research into mechanics
ideas.text: The book defines it as translating positive-psychology findings into game mechanics. Mechanics let designers raise the difficulty and add novelty so an activity stays challenging, and put it in a social setting.

ideas.name: A place can be scored for friendliness
ideas.text: The jen ratio is found by watching a space for an hour and tallying kind and unkind contacts. Keltner reports that the ratio in the United States is trending toward zero.

ideas.name: One person alone cannot change a public place
ideas.text: The book says raising a space's friendliness would need a crowd, and no custom exists for strangers to be kind together. A game supplies a reason and a method.

ideas.name: Cruel 2 B Kind borrows from Assassins
ideas.text: In Assassins, players get named targets and hunt them with water guns. In Cruel 2 B Kind there are no named targets, the game is short and local, and a hit with a gesture recruits the other player.

ideas.name: Rock-paper-scissors settles simultaneous attacks
ideas.text: Each secret weapon beats one and loses to another, such as a hearty welcome over a thank-you. If both players use the same weapon, both run and wait thirty seconds.

ideas.name: Hidden players make everyone a possible target
ideas.text: No names or photos are given, so any stranger might be a player. The only way to find out is to use a gesture on them, which turns ignoring people into noticing them.

ideas.name: Making the game short and small raises its effect
ideas.text: The designers cut the length to an hour or two and the area to a few blocks so that the game would change the local mood. Teams grow as hit players join their hitters.

ideas.name: Bystanders are included on purpose
ideas.text: Each friendly contact with a non-player raises the jen ratio even if it scores nothing. The designer estimates players attack about five non-players for every player.

ideas.name: Playtesting sorted the weapons
ideas.text: Gestures that did not draw positive reactions were dropped from the list. The designer filmed games and counted visible smiles and curiosity against blank or negative looks.

ideas.name: Courage and uncertainty make kindness exciting
ideas.text: Paying a compliment takes nerve, and time is short because another player may target you. Players cheer after a hit, and the cheer grows with the misfires on the way.

ideas.name: A game can be released as a free hack
ideas.text: Cruel 2 B Kind has no software or fee. It has a six-minute video and a one-page cheat sheet, and organisers do not need permission. It has been played in more than fifty cities.

ideas.name: A game can be taken up by an unlikely group
ideas.text: Organisers at a gothic festival in Utrecht ran it to get goths and non-goths to play together. The book reads this as proof that a plain activity meant to benefit people can become mischievous play.

ideas.name: Cemetery poker links play to remembering death
ideas.text: Tombstone Hold 'Em asks players to read tombstones as playing cards. The designer says players report thinking about death and lost loved ones more positively afterward.

ideas.name: Happiness can be approached sideways
ideas.text: John Stuart Mill held that people cannot chase happiness directly and gain it as a by-product of other goals. Happiness hacks follow this: Tombstone Hold 'Em is a card game on its face, and the reminder of death comes as a side effect.

ideas.name: A game can use the features of a place as its pieces
ideas.text: In Tombstone Hold 'Em the shape of a headstone gives the suit and the last digit of the death year gives the value. Because every cemetery has headstones, the game can be played in any cemetery and cannot be moved to a room elsewhere.

ideas.name: Touch and partnership bring players close
ideas.text: Tombstone Hold 'Em is played in pairs, and a pair has to touch both stones and each other at the same moment to claim a hand. The designer chose this because cooperation and touch build trust between strangers.

ideas.name: A game gives permission to break habits
ideas.text: Players in a cemetery are doing something that custom does not expect there. McGonigal says a crowd carries the social weight to change what counts as normal, and that the more people play, the safer it feels.

ideas.name: An added obstacle moves attention off the self
ideas.text: Top Secret Dance-Off asks players to dance without moving their feet, or upside down, or with a tree. Because the player is busy with the odd rule, there is less room for worry about looking foolish.

ideas.name: Restricting the usual moves widens who can do well
ideas.text: When the usual dance steps are ruled out, grace counts for less and silliness, invention and enthusiasm count for more. People who do not think of themselves as dancers can still do well.

ideas.name: Feedback can be made to come only in positive form
ideas.text: Viewers of a dance video can add a point of beauty, humour, sneakiness or exuberance, or leave nothing. The rule keeps comments friendly and lets players post videos they would otherwise keep private.

ideas.name: A disguise lowers the player's guard
ideas.text: Every Top Secret Dance-Off player wears the same partial mask in every quest. The mask and the superhero theme free players from the picture they hold of themselves as non-dancers.

ideas.name: A hack can be built cheaply and spread by word of mouth
ideas.text: Tombstone Hold 'Em needs playing cards, chips and a cemetery, and its rules were posted online for anyone to adopt. Top Secret Dance-Off was launched in days on a low-cost social network service.

ideas.name: Players need to see that their action had an effect
ideas.text: The developer of the Guardian game said the main point was to give people an "I rock" feeling, through clear purpose, visible impact and steady progress. The results page showed totals found by the crowd, such as repayments ordered from members of parliament.

ideas.name: Most crowd projects fail for lack of a crowd
ideas.text: More than half of online collaborations never reach the number of participants needed to start. McGonigal estimates 200 million public requests for participation, which works out to about 8.5 people for each.

ideas.name: Wikipedia can be read as a game
ideas.text: Its editors describe pages as places, vandal fights as battles, long articles as dungeons, and edit counts as experience points. They also note that players of online worlds stay at high involvement for about six to eighteen months, and so do heavy editors.

ideas.name: Money can lower the wish to take part
ideas.text: Studies show that paying people for something they would do from interest makes them less likely to do it unpaid later. Money is also limited, so it caps how much participation a project can support.

ideas.name: Match what is asked to what the crowd can do
ideas.text: Folding@home asks PlayStation 3 owners only to leave a console running, which every owner can do. The project reached supercomputing milestones within six months and drew one in twenty-five users of the network.

ideas.name: Difficulty can adjust to the player
ideas.text: In Free Rice, a wrong answer makes the next question easier and a right one makes it harder, so players stay at the edge of their ability. Each right answer also adds virtual rice to a bowl that is later converted into real rice.

ideas.name: A reward system can be shaped so that only honest play pays
ideas.text: McGonigal says players will do whatever earns the most reward, so the rules need to make honest taking part the only way to earn it. The Bungie job listing describes the same aim: rewards that cannot be exploited by players against each other.

ideas.name: An epic win changes what a player thinks is possible
ideas.text: Gamers describe wins such as finishing an office battle they thought impossible, or coaching an underdog team to a title. After each, the player sets a new idea of the highest outcome and tries again.

ideas.name: A real-world task can be written like a quest
ideas.text: The Extraordinaries gives each mission a story, a step-by-step list and a few minutes of work. In one, a player photographs a defibrillator and tags its location so that emergency services can direct people to it.

ideas.name: Showing the outcome of a small act extends its reward
ideas.text: After a player maps a defibrillator, the organiser links news of any later use to that location. The player can then learn that the object they found helped save a life.

ideas.name: A request for help can be matched to a person nearby
ideas.text: Groundcrew lets people post a wish and alerts others close by. The first wish was a latte for a tired dancer, delivered in five minutes by someone who saw it on the system.

ideas.name: Sensitive tasks can be locked behind earned trust
ideas.text: In Groundcrew, work with older people, such as shopping or companionship, is open only to agents with enough reputation points who also pass a background check. The points work as a record of reliability.

ideas.name: Attention paid to others can be a task in itself
ideas.text: In Lost Joules, players with smart meters try to save energy and others place virtual bets on whether they will. Players without meters still have a role, which is to value other people's efforts.

ideas.name: Every multiplayer game begins with an agreement
ideas.text: Players accept the same rules, turn up at the same time, concentrate together and try hard so that the game works. The word compete comes from a Latin verb meaning to strive together, and players of online games thank each other with the message GG after a match.

ideas.name: Children protect a game from being played wrongly
ideas.text: In Tomasello's experiment, children of two and three learned a new game, and when a puppet played it by invented rules they objected and tried to correct it. He takes this as early evidence of shared intentionality.

ideas.name: Many players prefer to play together than against each other
ideas.text: Surveys cited in the book find three of four players prefer co-op mode to competitive play. Co-op play avoids the anger, aggression and humiliation that can come with losing.

ideas.name: Players can extend a game by building levels
ideas.text: Little Big Planet shipped with 45 levels, and players published 1.3 million within a year. Halo 3's Forge lets players arrange weapons and vehicles to make new maps and share them.

ideas.name: Players can build a shared world without playing at the same time
ideas.text: In Spore, each player acts alone but the creatures and cities they meet were made by other players and fetched from a database. More than 144 million objects had been shared.

ideas.name: A story told in fragments needs players to assemble it
ideas.text: The Lost Ring spread its story over podcasts, blogs, videos, messages from characters and real objects hidden in 27 countries. Players translated and joined the pieces on a wiki of 943 articles.

ideas.name: Spreading content over languages and places forces players to rely on each other
ideas.text: Clues in The Lost Ring appeared on regional sites in several languages and in physical places around the world. No single player or country could collect them all.

ideas.name: Designers cannot predict how far players will take a game
ideas.text: The creative team of The Lost Ring played its blindfolded labyrinth race slowly and badly in testing. Players then trained every weekend in many cities, cut average times from 3 minutes 30 seconds to 59 seconds, and held their own world championships.

ideas.name: Roles built on personal strengths give every newcomer a task
