ideas.text: The Lost Ring offered six strengths from positive psychology, each with a role in the sport: engineers, runners, coaches, captains, referees and storytellers. A twelve-question test placed each player.

ideas.name: God games exercise three habits of thought
ideas.text: Games such as Civilization and Spore ask the player to take a long view, to think about a world as linked parts, and to try small experiments before committing. McGonigal links these to the habits needed to manage the planet.

ideas.name: A game's ending can point the player back at the world
ideas.text: In Spore a player who reaches the centre of the galaxy gets a staff of life and a message to look for the third rock from the sun. The game ends with a call to care for real life.

ideas.name: Imagining the worst first can lead to solutions
ideas.text: In World Without Oil, players began with stories of theft, riots and shortages, and about halfway through moved to neighbourhood cooperation and lower use of oil. The game ended in cautious optimism.

ideas.name: Compressed time lets a scenario run long
ideas.text: One real day in World Without Oil stood for one week in the story, so the 32-day game covered 32 weeks. Players were also asked to live parts of their real days as if the shortage were true.

ideas.name: Meters tied to player actions close the loop between story and scenario
ideas.text: The World Without Oil dashboard showed regional measures of quality of life and stability that rose with hopeful, cooperative forecasts and fell with accounts of hardship. Players could see the effect of what they wrote.

ideas.name: A game played by many can work as a study of a problem
ideas.text: Einstein is quoted as calling games the most elevated form of investigation. McGonigal reads this through chess: its positions multiply to 72,084 after two moves each, and its players have recorded and shared their play for centuries.

ideas.name: A score can show personal progress without ranking
ideas.text: The Superstruct survivability score ran from 0 to 100 for each player. Summed together, the points moved the in-game survival horizon for humanity from 2042 to 2086.

ideas.name: A creative task can have set traits
ideas.text: A Superstruct superstructure had to join groups that did not already work together, tackle a problem too large for one group, use the different skills of each part, and be new. Players wrote theirs as wiki pages with fields such as name, motto, mission and who we need.

ideas.name: A player can be asked to start from real strengths
ideas.text: Superstruct began by asking players to describe themselves in 2019, using real skills and real communities. The instruction was real play, not role play.

ideas.name: Real action with evidence from the player can anchor a game
ideas.text: Each EVOKE mission asked for a task in the player's own community, such as helping someone start a home garden. Players posted a blog, video or photo, and other players checked it and awarded points for traits such as sparks and local insight.

ideas.name: A game can run over a very long time
ideas.text: The Long Game was proposed as one move a year, played on a single day worldwide, in rounds of fifty moves. No player would see the start and end, but the game would link people now with those later.

ideas.name: Games can combine comfort, coordination and thrift
ideas.text: The conclusion lists what games did for the Lydians and still do: they raise daily quality of life, organise large groups around shared rules, and let people enjoy themselves while consuming less. It adds a fourth role today, which is to carry serious content about real problems.

ideas.name: Ten thousand hours of play can build a skill
ideas.text: Citing Gladwell's practice figure, McGonigal says young people in the United States play about ten thousand hours of video games by age twenty-one. She argues the skill this builds in online players is working together at large scale.

ideas.name: A rule set grows by changing one rule at a time
ideas.text: Bridge came out of Whist by small steps. First the dealer could name the trump and a partner's hand was laid open, then all four players could bid, then only the scoring changed. Each step kept almost everything else.

ideas.name: Changing only the scoring changes how people play
ideas.text: Auction Bridge and Contract Bridge have the same cards, bidding and play. In Contract Bridge only the tricks that were bid count towards a game, while in Auction Bridge every trick counts. The book says that single difference alters strategy a lot.

ideas.name: Fix waiting time with the structure of a round
ideas.text: In a cut-in Bridge game, a player who is cut out waits a long while for the rubber to end. Four-Deal Bridge makes a round of exactly four deals, one dealt by each player, so nobody waits more than fifteen or twenty minutes.

ideas.name: Lay down in advance what happens when a rule is broken
ideas.text: Contract Bridge has a long list of laws, each naming what follows a wrong call or a card played out of turn. The book says their purpose is to prevent arguments, and that experts and tournaments observe them without question.

ideas.name: Hidden information can be turned into public information by a mistake
ideas.text: A card shown by accident becomes a penalty card and stays face up. The partner of the player who showed it has to ignore what he learned from seeing it. The rules name an accident as a source of information and say how to handle it.

ideas.name: The same game can be reshaped for a different number of players
ideas.text: Bridge needs four, and the book shows versions for three (Cutthroat, Trio, Towie) and for two (Draw Bridge, Honeymoon Bridge). Each keeps the auction and play but changes who owns or sees the dummy hand.

ideas.name: Games can be adapted for a party of many tables
ideas.text: Progressive Bridge sets up one table per four guests, with fixed four-deal rounds. Winners move to a lower-numbered table and swap partners, so over the evening everyone plays with and against many others and a total is kept per person.

ideas.name: A shared number lets players judge a hand without talking
ideas.text: The point count gives every high card a value, and tables say what totals normally reach a game or a slam. Two partners can then read each other's strength from the size of a bid alone.

ideas.name: Calls can carry meanings agreed beforehand
ideas.text: A bid of four no-trump after a trump suit is agreed asks the partner how many aces he holds, and the answer is given by which suit he bids. The calls work as a code. Their meanings come from what the partners agreed, and the words alone do not carry them.

ideas.name: Reversing the aim reverses how a hand is played
ideas.text: In Hearts the aim is to avoid certain cards. A player who has already taken a hearts card no longer minds taking more, and so the players who are painted work together against the others. What a player wants can change partway through a hand.

ideas.name: Add a reversal so a losing player has a way back
ideas.text: Taking every penalty card in Black Lady, called shooting the moon, either cancels the hand or gives the player a gain. In Omnibus Hearts a plus-ten card is added, so a player stuck with penalties can try to offset them. Players then have something to aim for besides avoiding cards.

ideas.name: A pass before seeing what arrives keeps choices honest
ideas.text: In Black Lady each player chooses three cards to pass left before looking at the three that come from the right. The player has to judge risk from his own hand alone.

ideas.name: A rule can remove an argument even if it removes a tactic
ideas.text: The Black Lady rule says a player holding that card has to get rid of it at the first chance. The book says its purpose is to stop quarrels about favouritism, though favouritism in self-interest is part of the strategy.

ideas.name: Scoring by exact match changes the tension of every hand
ideas.text: In Oh Hell! a player scores only by winning exactly the number of tricks bid, so winning extra tricks counts as a bust. The last bidder can see how the others bid and may bid to make the total uneven, and other players cooperate or spoil according to their own bids.

ideas.name: A growing hand size gives a game a shape
ideas.text: In Oh Hell! the first deal gives one card each, the second two, and so on up to a full pack. A zero bid is easy early and hard later, so the book suggests scoring it differently as hands grow.

ideas.name: Hidden partnerships create suspense during play
ideas.text: In Solo the player names an ace he does not hold and its holder becomes his partner without saying so. Partnerships become clear only when the called ace is played, so the other players guess during the hand.

ideas.name: A bid can hide the true plan
ideas.text: In Solo each bidder says only enough to outbid the last, which hides how high in value his hand is. The winning bidder may then name any higher game than the one he bid.

ideas.name: Shared and private spaces can sit side by side
ideas.text: In the two-player race game Screw Your Neighbor, both players add to centre stacks, but each parks cards only on his own side stacks. The book also says it is never legal to count a pay-off pile, so a number stays hidden by a rule.

ideas.name: Betting adds bluffing to a game of ranked hands
ideas.text: In Poker a hand wins either at a showdown or because no one is willing to meet a bet. Because the second way exists, a player can win with cards that rank lower than the others hold by getting them to give up.

ideas.name: Introduce a game by playing it, with rules one at a time
ideas.text: The book advises starting the cards at once and telling a child what to do at each point, giving rules as each need arises. When a dispute touches a rule, the adult says that the rule is so, so the child sees that rules are not made up to suit the moment.

ideas.name: Name the mood a game is meant for
ideas.text: The book sorts games by number of players and by mood: hilarious games that survive rowdy talk, social ones that tolerate chat, and serious ones that need close attention. It marks games that are quick to teach.

ideas.name: Betting adds a second layer to a game of ranked hands
ideas.text: In Poker each turn to bet offers three actions: drop, call or raise. Betting goes round until the stakes are level, so a player pays to stay in. The rank of hands says who is ahead, while betting decides how much that is worth.

ideas.name: A cost to stay in makes chance and nerve both matter
ideas.text: Poker's expected-value advice is about odds: a four-flush completes in about one try in five, so the pot has to hold at least four times the stake. The book gives such comparisons for several hands, which shows a player weighing a risk against a payoff in each turn.

ideas.name: Limits shape how far betting can run
ideas.text: The book describes a fixed limit, a pot limit and table stakes. Under pot limit, bets in a seven-player game can climb from 7 to 238 chips within a few turns, so the book recommends a maximum anyway. The choice of limit changes how big the bets get.

ideas.name: Hiding and showing information make different games
ideas.text: Draw Poker keeps all five cards hidden. Five-Card Stud shows all but one card, and betting begins with the highest-ranking visible hand. Seven-Card Stud shows four of seven. The book notes a stud player decides after seeing nearly all of every other hand.

ideas.name: One skeleton can produce many variants
ideas.text: The book lists dozens of Poker games in the section on Dealer's Choice. Cincinnati puts five shared cards in the middle, Omaha cuts a player's own cards to two, and Hold'em reveals three shared cards at once. A change to how many cards are shared or when they appear gives a different game.

ideas.name: Letting the dealer choose the game keeps a session varied
ideas.text: In Dealer's Choice each dealer names the game and any wild cards, provided it can be explained quickly. The next dealer is not bound by the last one's choice. Each player in turn gets to decide the game.

ideas.name: A split pot rewards two different aims
ideas.text: In High-Low Poker the highest and lowest hands share the pot. In Seven-Card High-Low Stud a player may declare high, low or both, and one who declares both has to at least tie each way. The book says simultaneous declarations, using concealed tokens, remove the advantage of position that spoken declarations give.

ideas.name: The player who acts later learns more
ideas.text: The book prefers declaring with hidden tokens revealed together because speaking in turn gives an edge to those who speak last. Speaking in turn lets later players learn from earlier ones, and revealing the tokens together takes that away.

ideas.name: Starting stakes and forced bets keep a pot alive
ideas.text: Blind and Straddle makes the first players post bets before looking at cards, and each next player may double. Jackpots demands a pair of jacks before a player may open, and if no one opens, everyone antes again. Either way, there is always something in the pot.

ideas.name: Wild cards change what counts as a top hand
ideas.text: When wild cards are used, five of a kind becomes the top hand and ties between equal hands become possible. In Deuces Wild two pairs are close to worthless. The book gives separate advice for that game, so a wild card changes the whole ranking.

ideas.name: A written rule for an accident keeps play moving
ideas.text: Poker has a list of what to do when a card is exposed in dealing, a bet is made out of turn or a player has too few cards. A player with too few cards may play on but cannot make a straight or flush; one with too many has a dead hand. Each fault has a named result.

ideas.name: Table manners belong to the group
ideas.text: The book says each group sets its own ethics, and that words such as 'go ahead, call me, I'm always bluffing' are accepted misrepresentation. It notes partnerships are contrary to the spirit of Poker, so husband and wife are to treat each other as opponents.

ideas.name: Two directions out of one early game
ideas.text: Coon-Can brought together two ideas: scoring by melding and scoring by going out. American players developed one idea into Rummy, Gin Rummy and Knock Rummy, and the other into Five Hundred Rum, Canasta and Samba. A game can split by which of its scoring ideas gets more weight.

ideas.name: A fixed order of a turn makes a simple game
ideas.text: In Basic Rummy each turn is draw, then meld if wished, then discard. The player may lay off cards on any melded set, including an opponent's. Play is that three-step turn, repeated.

ideas.name: A changing target for each deal gives a game a shape
ideas.text: Contract Rummy has seven deals with a different required first meld each time, from two groups up to three sequences with a complete band. Hand sizes rise from ten to twelve cards. The target steps up as the game goes on.

ideas.name: Penalty for cards left, not winnings alone
ideas.text: In Basic Rummy the winner collects from each player according to the value of the cards still in that player's hand, even cards that were in matched sets but not melded. Holding cards back has a price.

ideas.name: Where you score changes what you do
ideas.text: Rummy split into games about going out first (Gin Rummy, Knock Rummy) and games about scoring for melds (Canasta, Five Hundred Rum). The same card sets and draw-meld-discard turn lead to different play depending on which action pays.

ideas.name: Knock Rummy removed the need to show sets
ideas.text: In Knock Rummy sets stay hidden in the hand, whether or not they have been laid down, and a player ends the hand by knocking. A knock shows every hand at once, and the undercut means knocking carries a risk.

ideas.name: Ending a hand early is a risky choice with a built-in counter
ideas.text: In Gin Rummy a player may knock once his unmatched cards total ten or less. The opponent can lay off on the knocker's sets, and if he ties or beats the knocker's count he takes a bonus for undercut. Ending the hand is therefore a gamble on your opponent's hand.

ideas.name: Layered bonuses reward small and large wins
ideas.text: Gin Rummy pays the difference in counts, a 25 bonus for gin or undercut, 100 for the game, and 25 for each hand won, with doubling for a shutout. A player who wins many small hands is paid for it at the end.

ideas.name: Keeping track of discards turns a game of chance into one of deduction
ideas.text: Gin Rummy advice says to follow what the opponent picks up and throws away, to see which of your own combinations can still be completed. A combination that needs one of three cards is weaker than one that can use any of four.

ideas.name: Scoring can run as several games at once
ideas.text: Hollywood Gin enters a player's first win in one game, his second in two games, and later wins in three games. Three scoresheets run at the same time and end separately.

ideas.name: A two-player game becomes a team game by pairing duels
ideas.text: Four-hand Gin Rummy deals two packs so that two members of one partnership each play a duel against a different opponent, and the net of both results scores. This works for any even number up to about twelve.
ideas.page: under 'Gin Rummy for Four or More'

ideas.name: Raising the threshold for a first move slows leaders
ideas.text: Canasta sets a minimum value for a side's first meld, and the minimum rises with the side's accumulated score. A side far ahead has to meet a higher bar to start scoring.

ideas.name: Freezing a pile limits what players can take
ideas.text: In Canasta, a pile with a wild card or red three on top, or one taken before the side has melded, can only be taken with a natural pair. The book advises throwing a wild card on purpose to freeze it against opponents who have melded.

ideas.name: Big targets give small hands a reason to wait
ideas.text: Canasta advice is to avoid early melds because a hand with fewer than its original eleven cards is crippled. A side may not go out until it has built one canasta. Players hold cards back to build toward a larger prize.

ideas.name: Hoarding is an error as much as squandering
ideas.text: The book says more mistakes in Canasta come from hoarding wild cards than from spending them. A side tries to keep even with opponents in canastas, and completing the first one of the deal puts pressure on the others.

ideas.name: Variants come from stacking small changes on a popular game
ideas.text: The book lists nine changes that were added to Canasta, from a third pack of cards to melding sequences, and says they produced Samba, Bolivia, Chilean and Italian Canasta, named after places. Each variant is a short list of rule edits to the original.

ideas.name: Penalties for unfinished plans make people finish them
ideas.text: In Brazilian Canasta an uncompleted meld towards a wild-card or sequence canasta costs 1,000 points when anyone goes out. A player who starts such a meld pays for leaving it unfinished.

ideas.name: Forcing a player to take a card can disrupt his plan
ideas.text: In Panguingue a player has to draw and meld a discard that fits his melds if any other player demands it, which can break up a pair he needed to go out. So one player can upset another's plan on a turn that is not his own.

ideas.name: Dropping out before play is a decision with a price
ideas.text: In Panguingue every player may drop from the deal before play, and in clubs pays a forfeit that goes to the winner. The book says Pan gives less chance than other Rummy games to improve the starting hand, so the choice comes first.

ideas.name: A hand that can only shrink changes the strategy
ideas.text: In Panguingue the original ten cards never change except by subtraction, since a drawn card is either melded at once or shown to everyone. Players plan their melds knowing what they hold.

ideas.name: A game that is a race to an exact count
ideas.text: In Coon-Can and Panguingue a player wins by melding exactly eleven cards from a hand of ten, so the last card has to come from the draw. A player can run out of cards in hand and still be unable to win.

ideas.name: A matching rule makes a simple game
ideas.text: In Eights, a card may be played if it matches the last card in either suit or number. A player who cannot play draws until he can. An eight is wild and the player names the next suit. The game needs nothing more than the two ways to match and the wild eight.

ideas.name: Optional special cards can be added in layers
ideas.text: The book lists additions to Eights: a queen of spades that makes the next player draw five, twos that stack draws of 2, 4, 6 and 8, a jack that skips a turn. Each addition is a card with its own effect, added to the basic game.

ideas.name: A shared layout gives everyone the same open moves
ideas.text: In Fan Tan the four sevens are laid in a row, and the eights and sixes of the same suit become playable next to them, building up to kings and down to aces. Anything a player lays down opens a move for the next.

ideas.name: Passing has a cost
ideas.text: In Fan Tan a player who cannot play pays a chip into the pool. A player who passes while holding a legal card pays more and has to also pay the holders of cards that were blocked. The rule discourages hiding cards.

ideas.name: A turn that does not rotate
ideas.text: In Michigan the next turn goes to whoever holds the next higher card of the suit, not to the player on the left. A sequence ends at a stop, when the next card is missing, and the player who made the last play starts again. The order of turns follows the cards.

ideas.name: Unclaimed prizes carry over
ideas.text: In Michigan chips on the boodle cards stay there if no one plays the matching card, and grow with each new ante until someone wins them.

ideas.name: An auction for an extra hand tests how players value cards
ideas.text: In Michigan the dealer may swap his hand for the widow or sell it to the highest bidder. The strategy advice says there is little reason to pay more than about five chips unless the hand is unusually low in rank.

ideas.name: Paying for the number of cards left ends a round fairly
ideas.text: In Snip, Snap, Snorem and Michigan the winner collects one chip from each player for every card still held. Everyone has a reason to shed cards quickly even after a loss.

ideas.name: Tricks can be a way to shed cards
ideas.text: In Enfle tricks have no value. A player who cannot follow suit has to pick up all cards played to the trick, and the first to get rid of every card wins. The usual trick-taking rules are used to make a game about emptying your hand.

ideas.name: Letting a player refuse or beg gives each hand a small negotiation
ideas.text: In Seven-Up the player to the dealer's left says whether he stands or begs. If he begs, the dealer can accept, giving the beggar a point, or refuse, and the trump is changed by dealing more cards. A single choice decides who carries the risk.

ideas.name: Being too ambitious is punished
ideas.text: In Auction Pitch a bidder who makes fewer points than he bid loses the amount of his bid from his score and can drop below zero. Bidding last, the dealer has an advantage and can take risks.

ideas.name: A larger bid can be a way back
ideas.text: In Smudge, a player whose score is not negative who bids four and makes it wins the game at once. A player below zero who does it gains only the four points. The rule lets a leader finish but gives no shortcut to someone behind.

ideas.name: A game with five cards each finishes quickly
ideas.text: The Triumph family gives each player five cards and aims at winning three of the five tricks. Napoleon, Euchre and Forty-Five all use that shape, with the bidder naming trump by leading or by acceptance.

ideas.name: A bid of the same value as winning everything pays asymmetrically
ideas.text: In Napoleon, a bid to win all five tricks pays ten if it succeeds but only five if it fails. Wellington and Blucher raise the loss to ten and twenty, so they outrank it. The payout structure sets the order of bids.

ideas.name: Unusual card ranks make a game recognisable
ideas.text: In Auction Forty-Five the five of trumps is highest, then the jack and the ace of hearts. In the black suits the low cards rank above high ones, summed up as 'highest in red, lowest in black'. In Euchre the jack of trumps and the other jack of the same colour rank at the top.

ideas.name: The dealer can have the last word in an auction
ideas.text: In Auction Forty-Five the dealer may say 'I hold' and match the last bid, which keeps the right to name trump if nobody bids higher. The dealer's seat carries a privilege.

ideas.name: Rules of caution matter more when the score is close
ideas.text: The Euchre advice notes that at 4-2 the side with 4 points will often accept the turn-up whatever its cards, so the other side cannot be maker and win by playing alone. The right move depends on the score.

ideas.name: Players keep their own score with cards
ideas.text: In Euchre each side tracks points by showing a three and a four in a pattern that changes with the score. The tool for counting is part of the pack.

ideas.name: Speed-up variants appear when players want quicker games
ideas.text: Railroad Euchre, played by commuters, adds a joker, lets a lone player call for a partner's highest-value card, carries excess points forward as laps, and doubles a game if the loser scored nothing.

ideas.name: Dealing the whole pack changes a game from guessing to planning
ideas.text: Five Hundred was made in 1904 for Euchre players who wanted more skill, by dealing the whole pack out. The book says it became as popular as Auction Bridge for twenty years. More known cards means more to reason about.

ideas.name: A table of bid values sets the order of auctions
ideas.text: In Five Hundred a bid beats an earlier one if its scoring value is higher, and a table of values orders every suit and no-trump bid. Nullo is placed above eight spades and below eight clubs. The scoring table doubles as the ranking of bids.

ideas.name: One bid only, so the bidder has to judge once
ideas.text: In Five Hundred each player has one chance to bid. The strategy advice says to make the highest safe bid, stretching to reach six or seven tricks but being careful above that. A single turn forces a decision.

ideas.name: Temporary alliances against the leader
ideas.text: In three-player Five Hundred, Skat and Schafkopf, the two players who lost the bidding combine against the bidder for one hand, and each gathers his own score. Players change from rivals to allies each deal.

ideas.name: The extra hand lets the winner of the auction improve
ideas.text: The contractor in Five Hundred takes the widow and discards three cards. The advice is to expect one or two tricks of help from it, and never to bid in hope of finding one specific card. A widow adds uncertainty to the bid.

ideas.name: One game rescaled for each number of players
ideas.text: The book gives Five Hundred for two, three, four and five by changing the pack (25, 33, 43 or 53 cards), the use of a dead hand and how partners are named. In five-hand play the contractor with a big bid may name two partners.

ideas.name: The same trick game can be played with points in cards
ideas.text: In Sixty-Six and Skat players win cards that carry points (ace 11, ten 10, king 4, queen 3, jack 2) and not just tricks. A player who takes at least 61 of 120 wins. Counting what is in the tricks gives a different goal from counting tricks.

ideas.name: Closing a game early can be a choice
ideas.text: In Sixty-Six a player may turn down the trump card on his turn, stopping all drawing and forcing everyone to follow suit. The last trick no longer scores. A player closes when he believes he is ahead.

ideas.name: A false claim has a price
ideas.text: In Sixty-Six a player may declare at any time that he has reached 66. If right he wins, but if he has fewer his opponent scores two game points.

ideas.name: Small prizes within a hand
ideas.text: The marriage in Sixty-Six scores 40 in trumps and 20 elsewhere, and the nine of trumps may be swapped for the face-up trump card. These small events happen alongside the main aim of taking tricks.

ideas.name: Bid a number, not a game
ideas.text: In Skat a bid is only a number of points, which has to match the value of some game the player will name after winning. The value depends on multipliers not all known until play ends, so the bidder may find he has overbid.

ideas.name: Several games can sit inside one deal
ideas.text: Skat offers eight possible games from a single deal, including suit games, grand with only jacks as trumps, a reject game to take few points, and two null games. The bidding decides which one is played.

ideas.name: Hidden cards can be traded for risk
ideas.text: In Skat the Player who takes up the widow and discards two cards loses twice the bid if he fails, while one who plays without it risks only the bid. Taking more information costs more if the plan fails.

ideas.name: Showing your hand can be part of the bid
ideas.text: In Skat a Player can declare that he will play open, laying his hand face up, and raise the base value of the game to 59. The player gives up his secret in return for the higher value.

ideas.name: A permanent trump suit made of unusual cards
ideas.text: In Schafkopf the trumps are fourteen cards: the four queens, the four jacks and the diamonds. They are always trumps, so every suit has fewer ordinary cards.

ideas.name: A nobody-wanted hand has its own game
ideas.text: In Schafkopf, if all three decline the widow, the hand becomes Least, where the aim is to take as few points as possible. Skat has Reject for the same purpose. So a deal nobody bids on is still played.

ideas.name: Increasing difficulty of bids as a ladder
ideas.text: Six-bid Solo ranks its bids from solo up to call solo, in which the bidder promises to win all 120 points and asks for a named card from another player. Frog, its cousin, has just three bids and is described as an easy introduction.

ideas.name: Compulsory rules push a player to take risks
ideas.text: In Klaberjass a player who sees a trump has to follow suit and, when a trump is led, has to win it if he can. Being forced to win changes what hands are worth.

ideas.name: Some scoring is for special holdings, announced in a script
ideas.text: In Klaberjass the players announce a sequence before leading, using set phrases, and only one player may score for sequence. The highest sequence wins by a set of tie-break rules.

ideas.name: Hidden information in a bid can be restricted by agreed phrases
ideas.text: In Klaberjass a player asking 'How high?' or otherwise getting unwarranted information about the opponent's sequence loses the deal. The player who announces a sequence gives only as much as needed to decide who scores it.

ideas.name: A proposal to cancel the deal is a bluff tool
ideas.text: The schmeiss in Klaberjass offers to abandon the deal. If the other accepts, a new deal; if refused, the proposer has to play the shown suit. The book calls it a psychological weapon that can bluff a dealer out of a stronger hand if used sparingly.

ideas.name: A card face value is not its value in the bid
ideas.text: Klaberjass advises counting about 40 points of trumps, side aces and tens to take, but says a lone jass plus an ace and a ten beats four trumps without it. The three extra cards served after the bidding are worth about 20 points on average, so they count in the bid.

ideas.name: Two kinds of scoring run together
ideas.text: Pinochle scores for melds shown in the hand and for cards won in tricks. Melds can be scored before play and reused in different classes, for example one queen in a marriage, sixty queens and a pinochle. Two separate ways to earn points feed one total.

ideas.name: Melding after a win ties scoring to trick play
ideas.text: In Two-Hand Pinochle, a player may meld only after winning a trick, and each new meld needs at least one new card from the hand. So winning tricks is what gives a player the right to score melds.

ideas.name: A game can have two phases with different rules
ideas.text: In Two-Hand Pinochle the early play has a draw from the stock and no need to follow suit. After the stock runs out, players have to follow suit, trump if void, and win a trump lead if they can. The shift makes the second half a different game.

ideas.name: Remembering what has gone is a skill the game rewards
ideas.text: The Pinochle advice says the most skilled players know all twelve cards held by the opponent at the end, and if one cannot, to count trumps and aces. A game of open information in the endgame rewards memory.

ideas.name: Declaring you have won can end the game early
ideas.text: In Pinochle a player may claim to have reached 1,000, after which the tricks are examined. If right, he wins even though the opponent holds a higher score; if wrong, he loses.

ideas.name: Revealing a hand to end the play when the contract is already covered
ideas.text: In Auction Pinochle if the bidder's melds already equal or exceed his bid, the contract counts as made and no cards are played. The auction can be settled by what is shown, without play.

ideas.name: Three levels of failure
ideas.text: Auction Pinochle separates conceding before leading, which costs single bete, from playing and failing, which costs double bete. Giving up early is cheaper than being beaten.

ideas.name: Payments tied to a common pool soften big swings
ideas.text: In Auction Pinochle the kitty absorbs the loss of a player who was forced to open and conceded without looking, and takes part like a player on high bids. The pool is formed from equal contributions and divided at the end.

ideas.name: Bidding on hope loses
ideas.text: The advice for Auction Pinochle says the costliest error is bidding on hope instead of on the cards held. A player may expect the widow to add about 20 points, but does not expect it to fill a meld unless five different cards would do so.

ideas.name: Scaling a game up with more copies of the cards
ideas.text: Double-Pack Pinochle uses 80 cards, four of each rank, deals twenty to each of four players, and raises minimum bid to 500. Quadruple melds are counted as two doubles. It is the same game on a larger scale.

ideas.name: A game dropped out of fashion when another idea took over
ideas.text: Partnership Pinochle was given up after the vogue for bidding games, and survives as Partnership Auction Pinochle. Two-Hand Pinochle lost out to Gin Rummy and Canasta. The book records how games rise and fall with what players like.

ideas.name: Draw and play on a small board makes score visible
ideas.text: Cribbage points come so fast that the game needs a board with two pegs per player. The rear peg jumps ahead of the front one, so the two pegs also show how far a player moved last. The board keeps the score and also shows the last move.

ideas.name: Cards used as numbers instead of ranks
ideas.text: In Cribbage face cards count ten and aces one, and suits matter little. Players add card values to a running total with a limit of thirty-one, and score for hitting fifteen, pairs and runs. Adding up values takes the place of ranking cards.

ideas.name: Giving cards to a shared hand forces a trade-off
ideas.text: Each Cribbage player puts two cards into the dealer's crib. The dealer wants to give valuable cards, the other player wants to give cards that will not score. The book says dangerous cards to give are fives, sevens, eights and cards next to each other.

ideas.name: Two phases score differently
ideas.text: Cribbage scores once during play, when cards are laid in turn, and again when each hand is shown. Combinations in play depend on the order and on the opponent, while those in the show depend only on the cards.

ideas.name: A rule that lets the opponent steal a missed score trains attention
ideas.text: Muggins allows the other player to claim a score you overlooked, and the book says to waive it when a beginner plays an experienced player. The rule can be turned off for teaching.

ideas.name: Winning big when the loser is far behind
ideas.text: A Cribbage game lost before the loser reaches the halfway mark is a lurch and counts double. Rubicon Bezique likewise gives the winner both totals if the loser has under 1,000. The size of the win is made to depend on how far behind the loser was.

ideas.name: Pick a form of a game suited to the number of people
ideas.text: Cribbage is for two and the book adapts it for three (five cards each, a triangular board) and four (partnerships). Casino adds three- and four-hand versions, and notes that in the partnership game there is little scope for cooperation.

ideas.name: Capturing by number and by building
ideas.text: In Casino a card from the hand takes table cards that match it or add up to its value. A player can also build, laying a card on another to make a total he can capture later. Declaring the build stops the opponent taking it without the right card.

ideas.name: A game where face cards only pair
ideas.text: In Casino jacks, queens and kings have no number value, so they can only be taken by matching rank. The book says that follows from the cards being used mostly to represent numbers.

ideas.name: Casino rewards memory
ideas.text: The book calls it a training school for observation, memory and inference. Face cards go by pairs, so if you hold one in the last hand its mate is on the table or in the opponent's hand.

ideas.name: A scoring claim that ends the game early
ideas.text: Casino allows counting out: a player may stop play at any time and claim the winning score, which is checked. A right claim wins and a wrong claim loses the game.

ideas.name: Solitaire is a layout and a rule about moving cards
ideas.text: The book describes a solitaire as laying out a tableau, turning cards from the stock, and building piles in order onto foundations. A vacancy in the tableau, called a space, is described as having a lot of value for moving cards.

ideas.name: Hidden cards in a layout give a solitaire its difficulty
ideas.text: In Klondike twenty-eight cards are dealt into seven piles with only the top card face up. A move pays off when it lets a covered card be turned up. Cards face down give the player a reason to prefer moves that reach them.

ideas.name: A fixed number of passes through the stock limits play
ideas.text: Klondike allows one pass through the stock. Canfield, in the gambling house, let a player turn cards one at a time with one pass or three at a time with three passes. The book reports the average player got only five or six cards out.

ideas.name: A bet that pays per card sets the odds
ideas.text: In Canfield's gambling dive a pack cost $50 and the house paid $5 for each card put on the foundations, and $500 for all 52. The book says the odds were right for the house, which made a fortune.

ideas.name: A solitaire can become a race
ideas.text: Pounce is Canfield for several players, each with their own pack and tableau, sharing foundations in the centre. The first to empty a reserve pile wins. The book says players set rules of procedure to avoid chaos.

ideas.name: A solitaire may be scored like golf
ideas.text: In Golf the player's score is the number of cards left in the tableau, and Double Golf compares scores or plays nine holes. If a tableau is cleared, cards left in hand count as minus strokes.

ideas.name: Some solitaires are decided by one early plan
ideas.text: In Forty Thieves the talon strings out before the first space appears, so the player has to plan from the start how to make it. Kings are a nuisance because they can only go to spaces.

ideas.name: Luck can be reduced by letting suits and sequences be rearranged
ideas.text: The book calls Spider the solitaire with most room for skill in overcoming the luck of the deal. Piles are built down in any suit, but only same-suit runs move as a unit, so the player decides when to follow suit and when to open spaces.

ideas.name: Do the move that leaves a choice open for later
ideas.text: The Spider example advises placing a card that can go on either of two others, so it can move again if a natural play appears, and moving higher cards before lower ones. A flexible move is worth more than a fixed one.

ideas.name: A solitaire can be lost by the layout before play
ideas.text: The book says Scorpion is bound to be won unless a card is buried under the next lower card of its own suit, or a criss-cross exists. A player who spots one can abandon the deal. The outcome can follow from the layout.

ideas.name: A last-chance move gives a stuck game one more turn
ideas.text: Scorpion deals the last three cards (the merci) after other moves stop, and La Belle Lucie allows one card to be pulled out after the third deal. The book says that pull is almost always needed to win.

ideas.name: Pairs that add to a number replace matching suits
ideas.text: In Pyramid two available cards are removed together if their values add to 13, with kings removed alone. The matching rule is arithmetic and not suit or colour.

ideas.name: A game with no choices at all
ideas.text: In the Clock each card turned over sends the player to the pile with that number, and the game is won if everything is turned up before the fourth king. The book describes the moves, and none of them are decisions.

ideas.name: A tableau can be a fixed loop of moves
ideas.text: Gaps removes the aces and fills each gap with the next higher card of the suit to the left. The catch is that no card may be moved into the gap after a king, so the game stops when all gaps are blocked, with two redeals allowed.

ideas.name: Solitaire layouts differ by what is open
ideas.text: In Beleaguered Castle and Fortress the whole pack is laid out face up in two wings, only the end card of each row is available, and aces go to a central column. All the cards are visible, so the difficulty lies in the order of moves.

ideas.name: Foundations that do not start from the same card
ideas.text: In Calculation the four foundations start with an ace, two, three and four, and each is built up in steps of 1, 2, 3 or 4. The player sorts turned cards to four waste piles, and the hint is to keep one pile for kings.

ideas.name: Borrowing a scoring system turns a card game into a puzzle
ideas.text: Cribbage Solitaire uses Cribbage's scoring to make the highest total over a run through the pack. The book says an average is about 85, so a player wins by reaching 121.

ideas.name: Rank the targets by how hard they are to reach
ideas.text: Poker Solitaire asks for the highest score over rows and columns of a 5 by 5 square, and ranks hands by difficulty in this game and not by Poker rank. Flushes are easy, straights are hard.

ideas.name: A strict order of moves can make a two-player game
ideas.text: In Russian Bank, two players use separate packs and take turns on the same centre piles. Rules of precedence say which move has to be made first, such as playing to the centre before anything else, and breaking the order ends the turn.

ideas.name: A game can let one player hand cards to another
ideas.text: In Russian Bank a player may load the opponent by building on the opponent's stock and waste pile, which gets rid of his own cards but adds to the other's.

ideas.name: A game of skill with no general rules
ideas.text: The book says Russian Bank needs close attention and the more skilled player nearly always wins, yet it gives no general rules because the most effective plays need analysis case by case.

ideas.name: Fixed house rules remove the dealer's choices
ideas.text: In a Blackjack gambling house the dealer has to take a card on 16 or less and stand on 17 or more. In social games the dealer uses judgement. The same game has a rigid version and a flexible one.

ideas.name: One player against everyone else, each bet settled alone
ideas.text: In Blackjack the dealer plays against each other player separately and settles each bet on its own. A player bets only against the dealer, with a table minimum and maximum.

ideas.name: Optional moves give a player more control
ideas.text: Blackjack lets a player split a pair into two hands or double the bet and take one card. Each choice raises the stake in return for fewer chances to change course.

ideas.name: Advice is a table of conditions
ideas.text: The Blackjack advice is a list: stand on 17 or more, stand on 13 to 16 if the dealer shows 6 or lower, hit on 12 or under, double on 11. The player decides by comparing his total with the dealer's visible card.

ideas.name: The position of a player in the order affects the right choice
ideas.text: The Blackjack advice says a player after several others have stood stands on low counts such as 12 or 13, because the dealer, seeing many counts to beat, has every reason to hit and may go over.

ideas.name: Staying in the game after losing all chips
ideas.text: In Thirty-One and Chase the Ace, a player with no chips continues on his honour until he loses again, then is out. A last life can be added without extra chips.

ideas.name: Passing on an unwanted card to a neighbour
ideas.text: In Chase the Ace each player may swap his card with the player on his left, who has to accept, to avoid holding the highest card, which pays a chip. The dealer cannot swap and instead may cut the pack for a new card.

ideas.name: Buying and selling a turn-up card
ideas.text: In Speculation the dealer may sell the turned-up trump card to the highest bidder, and the price goes to the dealer. Later, any new high trump can be sold by its owner, and buyers may bargain for unturned cards. Trading is part of the game.

ideas.name: Betting the pot caps risk
ideas.text: In Red Dog the largest bet is the number of chips in the pot, so the pot can always pay. The book calls it a betting game for fast action and light thought, seldom played for high stakes.

ideas.name: A betting game can be reduced to counting
ideas.text: The Red Dog advice is to count the cards you cannot see and compare winners and losers. With 47 unknown cards, 23 of them out of reach, the odds are 24 to 23. As cards are shown, the counts change.

ideas.name: Banker rotates by winning or losing
ideas.text: In Chemin-de-fer the bank passes to the player on the right whenever the banker loses, while a winning banker stays on. Anyone may pass the bank, and the banker cannot take out winnings until he does.

ideas.name: Fixed drawing rules remove decisions
ideas.text: In Chemin-de-fer the opponent has to stand on 6 or 7 and has to draw on 4 or less, and has an option only on 5. The banker follows a table. Little remains for the players to decide.

ideas.name: A betting layout lets players place stakes on cards without taking part in play
ideas.text: In Stuss players put chips on cards of a spade suit laid on the table, and a coin on top of the chips turns the bet into one that the card will lose. The dealer's turns settle all bets.

ideas.name: The house takes a fixed share built into the odds
ideas.text: In Roulette the green zero section means the house pays 35 to 1 on a single number but there are 37 or 38 outcomes. The house share is 2.7 per cent on the European wheel and 5.26 per cent on the American one, and no betting system changes that over many spins.

ideas.name: Chess has pieces with distinct powers
ideas.text: Each of six kinds of piece has its own way of moving, from the king's single step to the knight's jump that nothing can block. The pawn moves straight but captures diagonally, so it can be blocked without being able to fight back.

ideas.name: A special rule can preserve an old balance
ideas.text: The en passant capture exists so that a pawn advancing two squares still meets an attack from pawns on both adjacent files. If it is not used at once, the right is lost.

ideas.name: A rule that gives a trailing player something to play for
ideas.text: Queening lets a pawn become any piece on reaching the far side. The book says this keeps the fight going in positions that would otherwise be drawn, because the struggle becomes about getting a pawn through.

ideas.name: Written notation makes games studied afterwards
ideas.text: The book describes the English descriptive notation and the algebraic one, which names every square by a letter and a number. The algebraic form is shorter and removes ambiguity.

ideas.name: Hiding the opponent's pieces changes chess into a game of inference
ideas.text: Kriegspiel uses three boards and a referee who says only 'no' to an illegal try, announces captures and the direction of checks, and never says what was taken. Each player infers where the other pieces are from these answers.

ideas.name: War is a game of hidden information and chess is not
ideas.text: The Kriegspiel text points out that the chess comparison to war fails because in chess the position of both forces is fully known, whereas in war it is not. Kriegspiel adds what chess lacks: not knowing where the other side's pieces are.

ideas.name: A different start changes a well-studied game
ideas.text: Battle Chess lets players place pieces behind a screen, within the first three ranks. Reversing the knights and bishops was tried in a tournament and suggested by a world champion as a way out of stagnant opening play.

ideas.name: Captured pieces can come back
ideas.text: In Bughouse each captured piece is put back on the board wherever the captor wishes, subject to a few restrictions. The aim shifts to stripping the opponent's king of defenders.

ideas.name: Reversing the object of a game
ideas.text: Giveaway Chess makes a player lose all his pieces on purpose to win, and a player has to capture whenever able. The book notes that the plausible opening move P-Q3 loses. The same board and pieces serve an opposite goal.

ideas.name: Small positions can teach end-play
ideas.text: The Little Game of Chess and Peasants' Revolt start from a few pieces on the board. The book says that analysis shows White wins the first, though beginners make many mistakes in either side.

ideas.name: Forcing a capture makes combinations possible
ideas.text: In Checkers a player who can capture has to, and the book says the average player falls into a two-for-one shot within a dozen moves. Because captures are compulsory, a player can force an opponent into a position that costs him two pieces.

ideas.name: Draws among experts led to rule changes
ideas.text: Checkers tournaments once let players pick openings, and too many games were drawn. The fix was to draw the first two moves by chance (47 playable openings), later the first three (about 150), with each player playing both sides of the opening.

ideas.name: Changing the starting position keeps a solved game open
ideas.text: Other ways to avoid draws in Checkers are Eleven-Man Checkers, where two matching pieces are removed by chance, and Contract Checkers, where pieces are replaced when two chosen king-row squares empty. The book reports fewer draws in test matches with each.

ideas.name: Stacking pieces changes what a capture means
ideas.text: In Stack-Up Checkers a jumped piece goes under the jumper and a stack moves in both directions. Nothing leaves the board, and a stack belongs to the colour on top.

ideas.name: Reversed aims make the same pieces play differently
ideas.text: The Losing Game in Checkers asks players to get rid of all their pieces and has no draws. The player whose turn it is to move usually wins an ending, the opposite of the regular rule for counting the move.

ideas.name: A game with no capture can still be a contest
ideas.text: In Pyramid Checkers pieces jump but nothing is removed, and the aim is to move one's own pieces into the squares the opponent started on. If a player's pieces get arranged so that some cannot reach the goal, he loses at once.

ideas.name: Fox and Geese is an asymmetric puzzle
ideas.text: Four geese that only move forward try to corner one fox that moves both ways. The book says it is an easy win for the geese, so it is more a puzzle than a game. The two sides have different pieces and different goals.

ideas.name: The same family of games changes by country with small rules
ideas.text: Spanish, Italian, Polish and Turkish draughts differ in compulsory maximum capture, whether a single piece can capture a king, the size of the board and the direction pieces may move. Each rule set is a short list of differences from the English game.

ideas.name: Dice decide how far, the player decides which stone
ideas.text: In Backgammon each die gives a number of points to move, which can be used together on one stone or one each on two stones. Doublets are played four times. A player has to use both numbers if possible and the higher one if only one can be used.

ideas.name: A single piece is a risk and two are a wall
ideas.text: In Backgammon a point with two or more stones of one colour is closed to the opponent, and a lone stone, a blot, can be hit and sent to the bar. Two stones together are safe.

ideas.name: A hit costs time, not the piece
ideas.text: A hit stone in Backgammon returns to the bar and has to re-enter before any other move, so the cost is turns. The book says each hit costs the owner at least 1 to 4 turns and that no-hit games are rare.

ideas.name: Doubling the stake brought a game back into fashion
ideas.text: The book says Backgammon spurted in popularity around 1925 after the doubling rule was introduced, which added scope for skill and quickened play. A player offers to double, and the other either takes it or drops and loses the current stake.

ideas.name: A doubling cube hands the right to raise to the player who accepted
ideas.text: The doubling cube sits centred at the start. When one player accepts a double, the cube moves to his side so only he may redouble. The cube shows who may double next as well as the current stake.

ideas.name: Losing by a wider margin costs more
ideas.text: A Backgammon loser who has borne off no stone loses double (gammon), and one who still has a stone in the winner's home table or on the bar loses triple (backgammon). The margin of defeat matters, as in lurched games elsewhere.

ideas.name: Two styles of play: race or ambush
ideas.text: The forward game tries to lose as few turns as possible, while the back game gives the opponent a long lead and holds points in his home table, hoping to hit a blot later. The book says an expert playing a beginner will usually go deliberately for a back game.

ideas.name: A wall that moves
ideas.text: The walking prime is six adjacent closed points that the owner shifts forward by laying a blot ahead and covering it from the back. Doublets of 4-4 and 5-5 can break it by moving stones too far.

ideas.name: Adding spectators as a team
ideas.text: Chouette lets extra players join a two-player game: one plays alone in the box and the rest advise a captain who plays. When anyone proposes a double, each team member decides whether to drop and pay.

ideas.name: Starting from an unusual position makes a familiar game new
ideas.text: Dutch Backgammon starts with all the stones off the board and Acey-Deucey adds a special roll of 1-2, which lets the player name any doublet and roll again. Russian Backgammon has both players move the same way round the same board.

ideas.name: A lopsided setup
ideas.text: Snake starts White with only six stones on the board and nine on the bar. White's aim is to enter, hit and build a prime. The book says it is an extreme form of the back game problem.

ideas.name: Three in a row as a power
ideas.text: In Morris making a mill lets the player remove an opposing piece. A mill opened and closed again counts as a new mill, so two mills allow one to stay closed while the other shuttles. The shuttling double mill is the most deadly form.

ideas.name: Winning early can lose
ideas.text: The Morris advice shows that forcing a mill straight away may lose, since the opponent's pieces then lock yours in and you run out of moves. The book notes that with correct play both sides probably draw.

ideas.name: Surrounding scores in Go
ideas.text: Go has one kind of piece placed on a grid's crossings, and the aim is territory. A group lives while it touches an empty point, and dies when enclosed. A final score is the empty points a player surrounds minus the stones he lost.

ideas.name: Two eyes make a group safe
ideas.text: A group that has two separate enclosed empty points cannot be captured, because the opponent can only fill one at a time. So empty points are what keep a group safe.

ideas.name: A game can end when both players agree nothing more is worth trying
ideas.text: Go ends by agreement when both players think all ownership is settled. A player disputing a claim has to invade the space and make a living group there. Play ends when no one is willing to try.

ideas.name: The first player may have a forced win unless a rule bars it
ideas.text: The book states that on the 19 by 19 board the first player in Go Moku can force a win, and the rules ban making two open threes at once. Tic-Tac-Toe is a draw with correct play. Limits on board size or piece count can have the same effect as a ban.

ideas.name: Pieces that match by number
ideas.text: Dominoes are tiles with two numbered halves. A tile may be played if one end matches an open end of the layout. The set of twenty-eight is every pair of numbers from blank to six, and each number appears at eight ends.

ideas.name: A single rule on what to do when stuck splits the family
ideas.text: In the block game a player who cannot play passes, while in the draw game he draws from the boneyard. Everything else can stay the same.

ideas.name: Variety of numbers in the hand keeps options open
ideas.text: The advice for the block game is to keep as many different numbers in hand as possible, choosing which tile to play according to which numbers remain in hand.

ideas.name: A change of matching rule makes a new game
ideas.text: In Matador, adjacent ends have to total seven, so a 6 calls for a 1. Four tiles, called matadors, can be played anywhere. That one change, matching by a sum instead of by the same number, is the whole difference.

ideas.name: Scoring from the layout, not from the hand
ideas.text: In Sniff, after each play the numbers on the open ends are added, and a total that is a multiple of five scores for the player who made it. The first doublet opens on four sides, and its unsprouted sides do not count.

ideas.name: Drawing tiles by choice
ideas.text: In Sniff a player may draw from the boneyard even when able to play, to hunt for a scoring tile. The book says a player with three or four more bones than his opponent can sometimes score on successive turns to earn more than the cost.

ideas.name: Bets among players against bets against the house
ideas.text: In home Craps players bet among themselves by fading the shooter's stake, while in gambling houses all bets are against the house. The same dice game works with either arrangement.

ideas.name: One first roll can decide, or start a longer test
ideas.text: In Craps a first roll of 7 or 11 wins and 2, 3 or 12 loses. Any other number becomes the shooter's point, and he rolls repeatedly until the point or a 7 shows.

ideas.name: A near-even bet still favours the house
ideas.text: The Craps pass bet is 251 to 245 in actual odds but pays 1 to 1, so the house has an edge of about 1.4 per cent. Chuck-A-Luck's single number bet gives the house about 7.9 per cent.

ideas.name: A bet can pay less than its odds
ideas.text: In Chuck-A-Luck, a bet on any triple pays 30 to 1 though the true odds are 35 to 1. High, low, odd and even bets lose when a triple shows, which gives the house only 2.78 per cent.

ideas.name: Bluffing is the core of a dice game
ideas.text: In Liars' Dice a caller says what he rolled, and it need not be true. His opponent may claim a higher hand, lift the screen to challenge, or roll again. A lifted screen ends the round, and the one who lied loses.

ideas.name: Rerolling with a commitment
ideas.text: In Liars' Dice a player who rolls again has to claim a higher hand than the last claim and cannot go back to challenging. Once he chooses to roll again, he can no longer challenge.

ideas.name: Dice with fewer rolls and held dice make a game of choice
ideas.text: Poker Dice and Yacht give a player three rolls per turn, with dice set aside after each roll. Then Yacht lets a turn be filed under any unused category, even for zero.

ideas.name: Each category is used once
ideas.text: In Yacht a player picks one of twelve boxes after each turn and cannot use it again, so a roll that missed has to be spent somewhere. The book says low boxes like Aces can cover a roll that missed.

ideas.name: A bonus rewards doing well on a group of categories
ideas.text: In Yahtzee a player with a total of 63 or more in the number boxes (aces to sixes) earns 35 extra. The sum creates a target across six turns.

ideas.name: Memory as the main skill
ideas.text: In Concentration all cards are face down and a player turns up two at a time, keeping any pair. When they do not match they are turned back, and the skill is remembering what was shown. The book says children of seven can beat adults.

ideas.name: Asking for a card gives away information
ideas.text: In Authors a player has to hold a card of a rank to ask for it, and may not ask for a card he has. So asking for the ace of spades tells the table he holds an ace. The rule makes every request a clue.

ideas.name: Penalties for breaking a rule are paid to everyone
ideas.text: In Authors, asking wrongly or not showing a book costs the offender a chip to each other player. The cost is spread across all.

ideas.name: Children make their own rules and the book accepts it
ideas.text: The book says that if children set a rule of their own, such as the turn continuing when a drawn card matches the last named rank, adults are told not to quote the rule book.

ideas.name: A simple version first, then the full one
ideas.text: Go Boom starts without face cards for the youngest, with the ace low, and adds the face cards when children know the game. Each deal is a separate game at first, and a running score comes later.

ideas.name: Rank and suit combined to give two ways to follow
ideas.text: In Go Boom a player has to follow the suit or the rank of the lead. A player who cannot draws from the stock. This doubles the chance of a legal play and shortens the game.

ideas.name: A party game that ends by watching
ideas.text: In Pig, players pass cards round the table at once, and the first to hold four of a kind puts a finger to his nose. Everyone else has to copy, and the last to notice is the Pig. The signal to end is seen, and nobody says anything.

ideas.name: Lying is allowed, so doubting becomes the skill
ideas.text: In I Doubt It each player says he is putting down a stated rank, though the cards can be anything. The book advises arranging the hand in the order of ranks to be called, cheating early, being honest in the last five or six turns and doubting when the ranks you need were called early.

ideas.name: The last play is always shown
ideas.text: In I Doubt It the winner puts his last batch of cards face up, because everybody is bound to doubt him. The final move is checked in public.

ideas.name: A game where nobody chooses
ideas.text: Old Maid and Beggar-Your-Neighbor and War are decided by the shuffle. The book says plainly that Beggar-Your-Neighbor depends entirely on luck, and that in War it takes so long to win all 52 cards that players agree to count wars won.

ideas.name: A payment that grows with the card shown
ideas.text: In Beggar-Your-Neighbor an ace demands four cards, a king three, a queen two and a jack one. If a face card comes up during the payment, the duty reverses. The turn of a single card passes a debt back and forth.

ideas.name: A reflex game needs rules about hands
ideas.text: In Slapjack the rules say cards are turned away from the owner, turning and slapping use the same hand, the lowest hand nearest the jack wins when many slap, and a wrong slap costs a card. The book adds that these are to be enforced to avoid mayhem.

ideas.name: A player who has lost everything can still return
ideas.text: In Slapjack a player with no cards stays in until the next jack. If he slaps it first he continues, otherwise he is out.

ideas.name: A parlour game uses almost nothing
ideas.text: The book says most parlour games need pencils and paper, sometimes not even that. Some are real games, some are only stunts, and some are intellectual contests that interest keen competitors.

ideas.name: A hidden word can be reached by rhyme and mime
ideas.text: Dumb Crambo has one player give a rhyming clue, and the others mime words that rhyme, which are not spoken. Players guess the mime and so reach the secret word.

ideas.name: A hide and seek with no winner
ideas.text: In Hot Buttered Beans the players help the seeker by calling cold, warm, hot or burning. The book says there are no winners or losers and each player takes a turn at seeking.

ideas.name: Hidden in plain sight
ideas.text: In Hunt the Thimble the object sits in view in a cluttered room. A seeker who sees it sits down silently and does not stare, so the others cannot tell. The last seeker is the target of gentle jibes.

ideas.name: Free-for-all play needs calling and challenge rules
ideas.text: Anagrams has no turns for spotting words, so the book lists rules for who calls first, what a longer word does against a shorter one, what counts as a foul, and how a challenge is settled by a dictionary chosen in advance.

ideas.name: A shared stock of letters can be taken from other players
ideas.text: In Anagrams a player may use a tile in the middle and a word before another player to make a new word. Owners can add to their own words to make them harder to steal.

ideas.name: A game with no equipment but the world
ideas.text: In Alphabet the players find each letter from A to Z on signs and number plates, and may play alone, in competition or co-operatively. The book lists safety rules for drivers and a rule about graveyards that sends players back to A.

ideas.name: A bluff in a word game
ideas.text: In Ghosts, players add letters in turn and each hopes not to complete a word. A player may challenge the one before him to name a word starting with the letters so far. The book says it is often necessary to bluff by calling a letter with no word in mind.

ideas.name: Losses spell out a word
ideas.text: A player who loses a round in Ghosts takes the next letter of GHOSTS, and with all six he is out. The loss counter is also a word, and the last one left wins.

ideas.name: A category chain
ideas.text: In Geography each player names a place that begins with the last letter of the previous place. The same format works for any category, and the book says to define it carefully at the start to avoid arguments.

ideas.name: A solved game becomes a children's game
ideas.text: The book says players soon find that correct play by both sides in Tic-Tac-Toe leads to a draw, so the game is mostly played by young children who have not yet found how to force a draw.

ideas.name: Every player fills the same grid with the same calls
ideas.text: In Word Squares and Poker Squares each person writes one called letter or card into a 5 by 5 square, never to be moved, and scores rows and columns after twenty-five calls. The calls are the same for everyone, so the difference is where each person puts them.

ideas.name: Scoring by what others did not write
ideas.text: In Guggenheim each space scores 1 point for every other player who did not write the same word. The more common an answer, the less it earns.

ideas.name: Hidden ships, shared guesses
ideas.text: In Battleship each side hides ships on a grid and fires a salvo at squares. The opponent reports how many hits on which ship without saying which shots hit. A sunk ship reduces the owner's next salvo by the number of shots it represented.

ideas.name: Yes or no questions halve the possibilities
ideas.text: The book says that if every question in Twenty Questions removes half the subjects, twenty questions can tell apart 1,048,576 things. That works only if each question is chosen to split what remains in half.

ideas.name: Naming a guess every turn keeps pressure on
ideas.text: In Twenty Questions the questioner has to make a specific guess after each question. The clue of animal, vegetable or mineral can give odd results, such as a wooden table counted as a vegetable.

ideas.name: A refinement where the answerer has to produce names
ideas.text: In Botticelli the questioner asks something that has a name as answer, and It has to supply a name beginning with the announced letter. If It cannot, the questioner may ask a direct yes or no question.

ideas.name: Secret agreements are fair only if they are shared
ideas.text: The glossary defines a convention as an understanding between partners about what their bids or plays mean, and says it is not unethical if the opponents are also informed. So what matters is whether the opponents know the code.

ideas.name: Terms for sharp practice mark where manners stop and rules start
ideas.text: The glossary names coffee-housing as sharp practice that is unethical but not cheating, and a psychic bid as a bid not justified by the cards held. The game has words for moves that sit between permitted and forbidden.

ideas.name: Game goals are justified by looking backwards
ideas.text: In daily life a goal is worth chasing because of what it is or what follows from it. In a game the goal is worth chasing because of the kind of activity chasing it produces. A marathon runner does not take a taxi to the finish line, since arriving is not the point.

ideas.name: Goal and purpose in a game can differ
ideas.text: The goal of party Charades is to win, but the purpose is to have a pleasant evening. A player so competitive that everyone is miserable has met the goal and missed the purpose.

ideas.name: A designer shapes agency, not only a world
ideas.text: A game sets a goal, picks the abilities the player may use and builds obstacles that fit both. Super Mario gives a run and a jump that are only just enough for the chasms in front of the player, and the chess knight's odd leap fits the problems of the board.

ideas.name: Games record agency the way other arts record other things
ideas.text: Painting records sights, music records sounds and stories record events. Games write down a way of acting, so it can be kept and handed to another person. The role-playing game Sign hands players the experience of inventing a sign language in silence.

ideas.name: Tokens only matter inside the game
ideas.text: Before a board game starts, nobody cares about the green tokens. During play they cause sweating palms. Afterwards they go into a plastic bag. The caring is created by the rules and ends with them.

ideas.name: Players may hold back their own skill to keep a game tense
ideas.text: The author declines free lessons in racquetball because one player pulling far ahead would end the pleasure of the matches. Between games he guards the struggle; during a game he plays all out to win.

ideas.name: Players cannot stay aware of the reason for playing while playing
ideas.text: A child who slips money to a losing father in Monopoly, so the game never ends, has kept the purpose in view and spoiled the game. Absorption needs the win to look like a real end for the length of play.

ideas.name: Dropping a game is not like losing a value
ideas.text: When a Charades game is making guests bicker, players do not weigh winning against other things. Winning simply stops mattering, and the game's ends fade from sight.

ideas.name: Some games work by stopping skill from growing
ideas.text: In a drinking game where each player names a candy bar nobody has named yet, the failures are the memorable part. A person who memorised lists of candy bars would be missing the point. Such games are played rarely so nobody gets skilled at them.

ideas.name: Choosing a game is itself evidence for striving play
ideas.text: People talk about which game to play in terms of interest, beauty and fascination, not excellence or prizes. A group where each member is likely to lose at some game still plays it, because the struggle is the attraction.

ideas.name: Players of unequal skill keep playing games they will probably lose
ideas.text: In the author's board game circle one member is most skilled at calculation, one at bluffing, one at careful planning. Each still plays games suited to the others, and a local chess club welcomes a grandmaster and does not flee from one.

ideas.name: A game can narrow what a player has to think about
ideas.text: Daily life asks for many values to be weighed at once. A game cuts these to a few clear ones, such as score and position. This makes it easy to enter the game and easy to judge whether a move was elegant.

ideas.name: A scoring system makes values look simpler than they are
ideas.text: In the video game Knights of the Old Republic, a moral choice is followed at once by a Light or Dark score. The critic Sicart says this makes morality seem simple. The author replies that simplicity is the point of a game, and the risk lies in carrying the expectation of clarity back into life.

ideas.name: Player and character stand differently in games and in theatre
ideas.text: An actor playing a bank robber stuck in a vault may choose to have him act foolishly because the story needs it. A game player trapped in the same situation wants to escape. The player's real wish to escape is what produces the thrill of a game.

ideas.name: An outer self keeps watch over an inner game self
ideas.text: The outer self chooses the game, can stop it when it stops being worth playing, and changes the rules with house rules. The author's Sign group agreed never to reveal what they had tried to communicate, which only makes sense if winning is a temporary interest.

ideas.name: A player can feel loss and delight together
ideas.text: A person can be agonised at losing and also see that the game was beautiful. The author explains this as two layers: the inner game self suffers while the outer self enjoys the struggle. His Go teacher Joe replayed a position so a fine game could go on.

ideas.name: Fixed and clear aims are why games are easy to enter
ideas.text: The clear, narrow goals of a game make a new way of acting visible, which helps a player step into it.

ideas.name: Restrictions can add options
ideas.text: A house in an open field limits movement but creates the options of inside and outside. In the same way, making a basket in basketball is a new action that exists only because of the rules.

ideas.name: Games hand over ways of acting from the inside
ideas.text: Spyfall gives one player a spy card and the others a shared location. Team players have to hint that they know the place without telling the spy. Playing it trains a person to listen for vagueness and bluffing, which they might then use in a committee meeting.

ideas.name: Free play and structured games give different things
ideas.text: The critic Sicart argues that a designer ought only to offer a stage and let players do as they like. The author argues that rules and goals are what let a game pass on a specific way of acting, so a store of such games builds a wider range of agency than free play can.

ideas.name: Strict rules in the short term can widen what a person can do later
ideas.text: Zen monks greet everyone with a loud hello without thinking; climbers practise easy routes without bending their elbows so that hip rotation becomes natural; yoga gives exact postures. The author argues game rules work the same way, by walking a player into a way of acting they would not reach alone.

ideas.name: Games hand over modes of acting that suit particular tasks
ideas.text: Pandemic gives one shared goal with different abilities per player, Monopoly a self-centred drive to ruin others, Risk a self-interest with temporary alliances, Imperial an agency of shaping others' incentives. The author says playing 1830 helped him understand how corporations reason.

ideas.name: Narrow ways of acting are useful if a person can switch
ideas.text: A narrowed mode looks only at a small set of reasons, but a person who can cycle through many modes sees more reasons in total than one broad mode could hold. The author compares this to carrying a Swiss Army knife of agencies.

ideas.name: A game can crowd out other experience
ideas.text: If a person plays one game so often that they skip other kinds of life experience, the range of their agency shrinks. The author says slot machine designs with a ludic loop work this way, and that the same techniques have moved into mobile games such as Candy Crush.

ideas.name: Go teaches comparison of many fights at once
ideas.text: A Go teacher told the author that chess is one fight and Go is ten at once, so the player keeps comparing the value of each and gives up one to play elsewhere. He says this habit of stepping back carried over to his daily choices.

ideas.name: Games are not the only route to new modes of acting but they are quick and exact
ideas.text: Careers and hobbies can also teach a mode of agency. A game compresses one mode into a short, narrow and clearly stated form. That makes it easier to enter than a whole life project, though less rich.

ideas.name: Representation is one value of games, not the whole of it
ideas.text: Critics praise games such as Train, where players ship yellow pieces by rail until they learn they are carrying prisoners to camps, or September 12th, for what they say about the world. The author accepts this and adds that a game can also be valued for the quality of the player's own striving.

ideas.name: A new art form can be hidden by borrowing the standards of an older one
ideas.text: Early art photographers blurred their pictures to look like paintings and only found photography's own strengths after dropping that aim. The author warns that praising games only as fiction or film may do the same.

ideas.name: Players can feel three different kinds of fit
ideas.text: A spectator can see that a move solves a problem. A player also feels that their own decision was right, and, near the limit of their skill, that all their abilities were only just enough. In the author's rock climbing, warm-up climbs give the first two and a desperate climb gives the third.

ideas.name: The tense, awkward movement near a limit looks clumsy but feels harmonious
ideas.text: A climber on easy routes moves elegantly; the same climber at the edge of ability clutches and lunges. The player feels the closest fit in the second case while an onlooker sees the first as more graceful.

ideas.name: A game can be about clumsiness on purpose
ideas.text: In QWOP, four keys control a runner's thighs and calves, so running is hard; in Octodad the player moves an octopus with a limb on each trigger; in Minotaur in a China Shop the controls are erratic. The designers build an experience of not being able to do what you mean to.

ideas.name: Difficulty can be wanted for the fit, not the prize
ideas.text: The author argues players pick hard games for the feeling that their whole ability meets the task. This explains why a first-try flash feels satisfying with no earlier failures to make a story of.

ideas.name: Strategy players stop noticing the look of a game
