ideas.text: Dor found that new players soak in graphics and music while experienced players drop them and watch only what matters for winning. This is why chess pieces and Starcraft tiles repeat simple shapes.

ideas.name: Judging a game needs playing it
ideas.text: A review based on a game's code or box art, or after twenty hours spent only in the character creator of Oblivion, is rejected by players. The author reads this as showing that players treat a game as a work met through play.

ideas.name: Variants and speedruns are different games
ideas.text: Speedrunning Super Mario is a legitimate way to play; it is another game played with the same program. Chess variants likewise are different games on the same pieces.

ideas.name: Rules fix what the experience is
ideas.text: In Bridge, the ban on speaking makes the game one of deduction; in Poker, the ban on looking at others' cards makes it one of reading behaviour; in free climbing, the ban on pulling on gear forces a different solution for each rock face.

ideas.name: A climbing gym's colour-coded holds are a rule that sets the experience
ideas.text: A beginner who uses every hold on the wall is playing freely but never meets the movement the route setter shaped.

ideas.name: Some games only make sense after many playings
ideas.text: In 1830, a par value has to be set in the first round, but its meaning shows only when the player knows how stock and track interact. In Dream Quest, cards that look powerful early may lock the deck in. The author concludes reviewers who play a handful of times have not met such games.

ideas.name: A game's community can be part of the game
ideas.text: Netrunner releases new cards monthly and drops older sets after two years, so the pool of play keeps shifting. Designers watch the meta and make new cards to break dominant strategies. The author says this makes the community part of what has to be encountered.

ideas.name: Party games and stupid games are different categories
ideas.text: Cards Against Humanity is a party game where skill is unimportant, but success is the pleasure, so it is not a stupid game. Finger jousting is a stupid game where failure is the pleasure, yet it grows more entertaining as players gain skill, so it is not a party game.

ideas.name: A designer cannot fix where the player looks but can tilt it
ideas.text: The general prescription only says to play and then attend to one's own activity, but the activity itself draws attention to where agency was most active. Climbers think about movement, not the taste in their mouth.

ideas.name: In a game, each player appreciates something different
ideas.text: At a dance performance everyone looks at the same event. In a game each player attends to their own run through it, so no two players have quite the same object of appreciation.

ideas.name: A first playing of a puzzle is its truest one
ideas.text: After a puzzle is solved, repeat plays are shadows of the first. The author uses this to show games do not all call for repeated exploration the way interactive computer art does.

ideas.name: Narrowing solutions tightens the experience
ideas.text: A climbing route with tiny holds forces slow, precise, calm movement from almost everyone. The same is true of single-answer puzzles in adventure games.

ideas.name: A designer can plan for different kinds of players
ideas.text: Magic's designers aim at one player wanting a feeling, one wanting self-expression and one wanting to prove skill, and try to make the game work when they meet.

ideas.name: The same effect can be reached by shaping the roles
ideas.text: In Android: Netrunner, the corporation cannot attack and plays hidden cards; the hacker attacks and plays open cards. These differences produce a game of bluff on one side and deduction on the other.

ideas.name: A designer can steer people without forcing them
ideas.text: In Alexander's A Pattern Language, a shared lounge placed between offices and the kitchen draws casual meetings, and a longer alternative path lets people avoid it when they want. The author uses this to compare a game designer with an urban planner.

ideas.name: A game designer can set the goal itself
ideas.text: City planners and governments can set rules and incentives but can hardly set what people want. A game designer names the player's goal and abilities and expects the player to take them up.

ideas.name: A tiny choice space can produce intense feeling
ideas.text: In The King Is Dead each player has eight cards and plays each once, all in the open. The author reports that players describe a slow cage fight and some feel close to sick, then ask to play again.

ideas.name: Swapping goals quickly can itself be the game
ideas.text: BUTTON and WarioWare fire mini-games for a few seconds each. The player grabs one goal and drops it for another, and the laughter comes from the wrenching of agency.

ideas.name: Credit for a fine solution is shared between designer and player
ideas.text: In Portal a player can invent a way across a trench that the designers never planned. The player acted, but the designers built a physics and a wormhole gun that make such solutions possible. The author says responsibility is spread between both.

ideas.name: Comedy can come from showing how fluid a player's goals are
ideas.text: In WarioWare and B.U.T.T.O.N. the player is told to want one thing for a few seconds and then another. The author compares this to books that joke about being books.

ideas.name: Game designers are kin of planners and governments
ideas.text: City planners, traffic engineers and lawmakers also set rules for free agents and wait to see what comes out. A game designer differs by being able to set the agent's goal and abilities too.

ideas.name: A game can be made of social roles alone
ideas.text: In Werewolf a referee taps a few players as werewolves who know each other, while villagers know nothing. Each day all talk and vote to remove someone; each night the werewolves remove a villager. The whole game is built of who knows what.

ideas.name: A game can teach what trust consists of
ideas.text: In Hanabi each player holds their cards facing outward so everyone sees them except the holder, and gives one limited hint per turn. Players have to read what was not said. The author says this shows trust is about anticipating what another needs.

ideas.name: Time pressure changes a cooperative game
ideas.text: Space Alert has players program their next actions at once in a short timed phase, so they shout and coordinate in a rush. Hanabi gives unlimited time and tests memory and inference instead.

ideas.name: Opposing players can be helping each other
ideas.text: The author and his spouse try to wreck each other's plans in a board game and then talk over whether the game was interesting. Their competing agencies are temporary; their lasting agencies cooperate to make a struggle.

ideas.name: Agreeing to play does not make every attack acceptable
ideas.text: The author imagines picking a cocky novice to crush in public, or proposing the lying game Diplomacy to a spouse who hates lying. Both players agreed to play, yet the game fails them because the match is wrong.

ideas.name: A game can only turn a contest into something valuable when skill, taste and design line up
ideas.text: Players need roughly equal skill, a game that suits their tastes, and a design that channels attacks into interesting problems. An insult contest or a whipping contest is a design that cannot do this for most people.

ideas.name: The same people and same intentions can have different results under different rules
ideas.text: The author's playground bullies were harmless-feeling in basketball, where their efforts went into guarding and blocking, and hurtful in dodgeball, where the ball hit faces. The only thing that changed was the game design.

ideas.name: Asymmetric roles create a society
ideas.text: In Root, the Marquise de Cats builds and suppresses, the Eyrie programs a rigid plan that collapses if one step fails, and the Woodland Alliance starts with nothing and spreads sympathy. The uneven roles give uneasy alliances and mutual stomping.

ideas.name: A game can be described as an art installation
ideas.text: The author invents an art review of an installation where four people sit at a table, exchange numbered placards, and may not discuss what they are doing. It turns out to describe contract bridge.

ideas.name: Games show a social arrangement from several seats
ideas.text: A player of Root can be the comfortable power or the resourceless insurgent in the same struggle. The author says this lets games offer perspectives on a society, not only on an individual.

ideas.name: Fiction and fact are mixed in a video game
ideas.text: When a player shoots another in an online shooter, the killing is invented but the win, the speed and the outwitting are real. Research that finds fictional violence screened off does not cover the real parts of play.

ideas.name: Game goals are unusually easy to read
ideas.text: The author lists three traits: it is obvious whether a goal was met, different goals are measured on one scale, and results can be ranked. Daily life gives none of these for goals like wisdom or a child's happiness.

ideas.name: A game does not need a score
ideas.text: A Scoreless Super Mario would still be a game with goals and obstacles, but players could not rank runs. The author says most players want a score and choose one.

ideas.name: Formal competition pushes subtle games toward countable goals
ideas.text: Skateboarders in the afternoon compete over style and difficulty without naming a winner. When contests were formalised, emphasis moved to jump height and number of spins.

ideas.name: Multiple scoring routes still use one currency
ideas.text: In Taj Mahal, points come from sets of goods, chains of palaces or bonus tiles, all converted to victory points. The author says this makes different goals comparable in the way daily values are not.

ideas.name: A work incentive scheme at Disney turned into a whip
ideas.text: Laundry workers had their names on a board in green, yellow or red by speed. Output rose and injuries and skipped breaks followed. Workers called it the electronic whip and said they could not ignore the pull of the game even while resenting it.

ideas.name: A step counter can replace the thing it was bought for
ideas.text: A person wears a FitBit for health and ends up chasing step totals, and drops yoga and weights because the device does not count them. The author calls this value capture.

ideas.name: Numbers travel well because they lose context
ideas.text: A written report on a student holds much detail but is hard to average. A grade is easy to move and sum into a grade average, yet it hides how it was reached and looks more objective than it is.

ideas.name: Games can be used for self-help where the target is simple
ideas.text: Duolingo uses points and clear targets for learning a language, a goal that loses little when turned into a game. The author notes that the risk grows when the target is subtle, such as health or wisdom.

ideas.name: A heuristic needs checking against what it stands for
ideas.text: Thirty minutes of exercise before breakfast is a rule of thumb for health. The author says a person steps back from time to time to ask whether the rule still serves that aim.

ideas.name: Aesthetic judgement does not follow from rules
ideas.text: The author cites writers who hold that no description of a work lets anyone predict whether they will value it, and that every proposed principle, such as symmetry being beautiful, has been broken by a work people admire. This sets aesthetic reflection against the clear scoring of a game.

ideas.name: Winning is only a road to the value in striving play
ideas.text: An achievement player counts more wins as more value. A striving player asks afterwards whether the struggle was worth it, and answers in terms that the game does not supply.

ideas.name: Playing and then reflecting trains both flexibility and control
ideas.text: A yoga teacher told the author that flexibility needs strength to guide it. He argues that dipping into a narrow game goal and then judging it from outside trains both abilities.

ideas.name: Patterns and mechanics overlap in meaning
ideas.text: Pairs such as area control and conquer, bidding and bidding, or aim and shoot and aiming and shooting appear in both collections. The paper concludes that separating the two by level of abstraction does not work.

ideas.name: Both patterns and mechanics can serve design and analysis
ideas.text: An earlier view held patterns to be for design and mechanics for analysis. The authors point out that published work uses patterns mainly to analyse games, while mechanics have been used for design insight, so both serve both purposes.

ideas.name: Relations between patterns are tendencies
ideas.text: The paper says the relations between patterns are to be read as general consequences or possible combinations, not hard links. They may occur in the mechanics that carry out the patterns, but players are not guaranteed to see them.

ideas.name: Mechanics lose meaning outside their game
ideas.text: Mechanics found in two different games are only alike in the way family members are, because a small change in a design can change the play. The paper advises treating mechanics named outside a specific game with care.

ideas.name: Patterns, mechanics and a layer between
ideas.text: The authors give patterns the place of social interaction and mechanics the place of the physical space where interaction happens, with contextualization as the layer where the two meet.

ideas.name: Players and designers care about different layers
ideas.text: Players are mostly concerned with mechanics and use patterns without noticing. Designers study other games on purpose to find the patterns in them, and use that study as a frame of reference so their design does not drift without their choosing.

ideas.name: Developers and researchers care about different layers
ideas.text: Developers work directly with mechanics to turn them into code, and the paper says they always add their own readings of what the designer meant. Design researchers sit mostly between general patterns and the relations among them.

ideas.name: A shared language is not enough
ideas.text: A shared design language does not remove differences in how designers, developers and players picture a game. The authors say it works as a base for conversation that builds shared understanding.

ideas.name: First impressions decide whether players stay
ideas.text: Because players read a new game through patterns they already know, the paper says the first impression carries weight: a player without a favourable first impression is likely to move on to another game.

ideas.name: Same mechanic, different verdict by context
ideas.text: Quickscoping in the Call of Duty games is used to show that a mechanic can be nearly identical in two games and still be judged differently, depending on the context it sits in and the tactics it is compared with.

ideas.name: Contextualization is a process of communication
ideas.text: The authors do not think contextualization can be broken down into a template. They see it as a process of communication, described through shared cues such as language, gestures and illustrations.

ideas.name: A game sits between work and play
ideas.text: Oriard sees work and play as the two ends of a line, with games between them. A game is play with effort and rules in it, or work done in a playful way. His example is the Virginian in Wister's novel, who runs a cattle business as a game and so stays a boy at heart while working.

ideas.name: The word game once meant gambling
ideas.text: In colonial America game mostly meant gambling, which was the least accepted pastime. Over the nineteenth century it came to mean a playful contest by agreed rules. Oriard also notes that game could mean a scheme or a trick, as in playing games with someone.

ideas.name: Two attitudes to the same rulebook
ideas.text: Sportsmanship follows the rules and a code of manners. Gamesmanship follows only the rules and treats loopholes as clever play. The coach Stagg said British players keep the spirit of the rules and Americans the letter, and that he would still rather lose than win by a trick.

ideas.name: Loopholes make rulebooks longer
ideas.text: American football has far more rules than soccer or rugby. Oriard says this is because rule makers kept adding rules to stop players evading the old ones. Each new clever tactic produced a new rule.

ideas.name: Referees and long rules show distrust
ideas.text: The economist Veblen read the need for umpires and thick rulebooks as proof that players try to cheat each other. Stagg read the same rules as the setting for fair play. Oriard accepts both readings as true of American sport.

ideas.name: A violent game brings in a governing body
ideas.text: College football in the 1890s caused so many injuries that newspapers asked for it to be banned. In 1905 President Roosevelt called the colleges together and the National Collegiate Athletic Association was formed to regulate the rules.

ideas.name: Calling a conflict a game can make force look fair
ideas.text: Roosevelt described frontier fights between settlers and Indians as one-to-one contests with equal chances, such as a race to reload a gun. Oriard says this turned conquest into a fair match and hid the size of the forces behind it.

ideas.name: A rule is fair only if everyone accepts who made it
ideas.text: The Virginian hangs his friend Steve and says Steve knew the rules and played the game. Oriard asks who made the rules, who gains from them and who acts as umpire. When a rule is imposed on someone who has not accepted it, it works as force.

ideas.name: Which game you name shows what you value
ideas.text: Calling something a gentleman's sport suggests fixed values and a stable order. Calling it poker suggests a fluid world where an underdog can win. Oriard shows that the choice of game for a metaphor carries a view of how society works.

ideas.name: Some games are won by leaving the game
ideas.text: In the novel the courtship of Molly and the Virginian is a contest in which winning is possible only when both stop playing it. Oriard calls it an anti-game.

ideas.name: Poker as skill with a dealt hand
ideas.text: The Virginian says a person with the right nature wins poker with whatever hand is dealt, even a lame horse or an empty gun. Games of cards give a picture of life where luck sets the hand and skill decides how it is played.

ideas.name: Players may be shut out of a game
ideas.text: In Wharton's novel Lily Bart cannot play the game of business and speculation. She is expected to play another game, finding a husband, with money at stake in both. Oriard uses this to show that who may play which game can be fixed by rank or sex.

ideas.name: Games have losers who started behind
ideas.text: Writers who disliked the game metaphor pointed out that some players have little chance from the start because of sex, race or class. A game with an equal start and a fair field is a claim that has to be checked.

ideas.name: Word contests are games too
ideas.text: In The Virginian cowboys compete in wit and in tall tales, a liars' contest, where the winner gains respect and nobody is hurt. The prize is the loyalty of the other men.

ideas.name: Competition needs a limit on severity
ideas.text: Roosevelt wrote that some competition is needed, but if it becomes too severe the whole group suffers. He named fair play as the means of controlling it.

ideas.name: Games grow out of work and danger
ideas.text: Frontier people made contests from what they needed to survive: shooting, racing, wrestling, and community jobs like barn raising. Oriard says these games gave status and turned risky skills into ritual.

ideas.name: Rules by custom against rules by statute
ideas.text: In Cooper's turkey shoot a flint misfires and the men argue whether the shooter gets another shot. They agree he is entitled to one, but the sheriff rules it a miss. Oriard says fair play works through custom and agreement, law through written statutes and their interpretation.

ideas.name: Three limits a hunter sets for himself
ideas.text: Natty Bumppo's code has three parts: do not waste, kill cleanly, take no undue advantage. The sheriff, by contrast, measures success by the number of birds and fish he brings down. Oriard contrasts measuring by quantity with measuring by quality.

ideas.name: Judging the means or the ends
ideas.text: Natty shoots a deer out of season and a panther that threatens a girl with the same care, and sees no difference. The law punishes the first and rewards the second. In Oriard's summary, the law judges ends and the hunter's code judges means.

ideas.name: A fair system needs shared agreement on what fair is
ideas.text: The real fair play settlements worked because their members agreed on what was fair. Oriard says the town in The Pioneers had no such agreement across its classes, so a fair play system could not have held there.

ideas.name: Sportsmanship needs an outside authority, gamesmanship does not
ideas.text: Oriard says sportsmanship looks to timeless values known through tradition. Gamesmanship looks to no authority outside the game, so its rules justify themselves and onlookers are needed to confirm who won.

ideas.name: A contest of equals against a contest of mismatched players
ideas.text: Frontier games assumed equal players, and winners were said to earn their win rather than inherit it. In nineteenth-century love games a man and woman were called partners, but the woman risked more and had more to lose.

ideas.name: A game with a hidden contest
ideas.text: Love games said the two players were partners and that marriage was a win for both. Oriard says the word game gave away that the situation was a contest with losers.

ideas.name: Refusing an advantage as part of the game
ideas.text: In The Deerslayer Natty will not fire at an enemy who has no loaded gun. He puts down his rifle and offers a fair fight, though the enemy tries to trick him. Oriard shows the hero defined by the advantages he will not use.

ideas.name: A contest framed to look equal
ideas.text: Cooper's Indian war scenes show single fights between one white man and one Indian, shaped like sporting contests. Oriard notes that the end of the same novel is a massacre by soldiers and that numbers and force decide it.

ideas.name: Play was allowed in its place
ideas.text: Puritans did not ban all play. They objected to play on the Sabbath, play that led to gambling, and play that was immoderate or untimely. Oriard says the question was the time and kind of play, not play itself.

ideas.name: Seasonal work gives seasonal play
ideas.text: Southern planters worked hard at planting and harvest and then rested, so visitors saw them as lazy. New England worked at a steady pace. Oriard shows that the rhythm of work shapes when and how much people play.

ideas.name: Cheating can move a game from luck to skill
ideas.text: In the humorists' tales a player who cheats is playing a game where the deal counts for less and the players' wit counts for more. The most typical tales end with the trickster being tricked, as when a gambler gets a deck with all four jacks removed.

ideas.name: Outcheating the cheater
ideas.text: A common story had a clever player take advantage of others and then be beaten by someone cleverer. In Longstreet's horse swap the clever trader ends with a horse that is blind and deaf. Oriard shows readers enjoying the game of wits more than any single winner.

ideas.name: When everything is a contest
ideas.text: In Southwestern humour horse races, weddings, dances, camp meetings and steamboat trips all become contests. Oriard says this showed a society where rank had to be won by wit and chance rather than inherited.

ideas.name: A fair fight can be a joke and a boast
ideas.text: A hunter in one tale fights a panther with bare hands, offers odds on himself and announces his own fight, then says he won with no gouging. Oriard reads the no gouging as a joke that still marks a real rule.

ideas.name: Winning a dare can cost the winner
ideas.text: Sut Lovingood wins a dozen marbles by jumping into a house wall as far as he can, and his head is damaged. Oriard uses the story to ask what a win amounts to when the contest has no larger point.

ideas.name: Ritual fights give status to both sides
ideas.text: In the tall tales fights follow rules and both winner and loser gain standing, so the game settles disputes in place of law. When the game turns spiteful, as in Sut Lovingood's bets on other people's misery, it stops working.

ideas.name: Holiday ends the rivalry of the season
ideas.text: After the hunt the trappers meet and drink, sing, tell lies and wrestle. Their feuds are dropped and fights end in reconciliation. Oriard notes that Irving shows hunting rivalry as sharpening wit and the holiday as healing it.

ideas.name: A pause for festival does not cost work
ideas.text: Kirkland complains that her neighbours have no day set aside for gaiety at the end of the harvest. She argues that people would work as much after an interval of gaiety.

ideas.name: Play and sport differ in a contest
ideas.text: Women writers of the West separated play, such as dances, picnics and gardens, from sport, which meant hunting, violence and winning. Oriard notes that men's writing was also unsure about this and that the line was not absolute.

ideas.name: The same word can mean a fair contest or a scheme
ideas.text: In dime novels game could mean a shooting match under fair play or the plot of a villain. Murder, hunting buffalo and robbery were all called games. Oriard reads this as a sign that readers felt both attitudes toward the same activity.

ideas.name: Game words spread from the card table to everyday speech
ideas.text: Dime novels were full of poker idioms such as playing your cards and playing trumps, and heroes named Poker Jack or Ace High. Oriard thinks cheap fiction carried these words from gambling saloons up to respectable speakers, until Roosevelt used them.

ideas.name: Fairness may be owed only to an equal
ideas.text: Pat Garrett wrote that he owed a fair fight only to a man of high reputation and equal social standing. A man like the Kid could be shot with every advantage. Oriard shows that fair play depended on who the opponent was.

ideas.name: Losing gracefully as a rule of the game
ideas.text: A boys' magazine hero tells his team to play honestly and to admit defeat like a gentleman. They lose to opponents who tamper with cartridges and saddles, and keep their manners. Oriard reads this as a moral win.

ideas.name: Law itself can be played as a game
ideas.text: Baldwin described lawyers' contests as struggles for standing with bets placed all round. In these stories a game replaces justice as the way disputes are settled.

ideas.name: How you play the hand you are dealt
ideas.text: An epitaph in Lewis's Wolfville stories says life is not about which cards you hold but about how you play a low-ranked hand. The characters talk of life in poker terms. Oriard shows the idea that skill and honesty matter more than the deal.

ideas.name: You cannot bluff the game itself
ideas.text: A Wolfville gambler says life is stud poker where Destiny holds a hidden ace. You cannot hold six cards, deal twice or bluff Destiny. You can only play the five cards that belong to you, and play honestly.

ideas.name: A gambler who follows a code
ideas.text: In Bret Harte's stories the professional gambler is a gamesman by trade and a sportsman by instinct. He accepts fate, pays what he owes and plays fair. Oriard says readers could take him as hero or as a fatalist who gave up.

ideas.name: Mixed audiences read the same game two ways
ideas.text: Oriard shows genteel magazines presenting the frontier gambler as a noble sportsman and cheap novels presenting him as a trickster. The same figure and the same game carried different values for different readers.

ideas.name: Cheating is disgrace, losing is not
ideas.text: In Southern race week, schools, shops and courts closed, and winning by cheating would have shamed a gentleman more than losing. Bets were paid without argument. Oriard says the contest was a public display of honour rather than a fierce rivalry.

ideas.name: Give the pursued side a start
ideas.text: Southern hunters offered the fox a head start, called law, and avoided night hunting. Oriard says the code tried to offset the inequality of human advantage over animals by placing limits on the more powerful side.

ideas.name: Rules and ritual make a violent act tolerable
ideas.text: Southern society officially disliked dueling but accepted it because it had rules, seconds, formal steps and often ended without blood. Oriard says its sport-like form let public ritual take the place of private revenge.

ideas.name: A contest played to save face
ideas.text: In Swallow Barn two neighbours each refuse to win a lawsuit over land neither wants, because honour requires it. A lawyer arranges a settlement in which one takes the land and both keep their honour. Oriard describes the suit as turning into a fox chase.

ideas.name: The one who sets the terms can win
ideas.text: Mike Brown challenges the devil to a duel and expects fair play, but lets the devil choose the ground. The devil picks a swamp where Mike sticks fast, and calls himself no gentleman. The story shows a loophole in the terms of a match.

ideas.name: Style is part of the contest
ideas.text: Ned Hazard fights a bully with a cheerful face as if in mere sport, refuses to strike a man who is down and offers a fair field. Oriard says the manner of winning shows class as much as the result.

ideas.name: Playing to win against playing for play
ideas.text: Oriard's reading of Southern sport is that the planters defined themselves as a leisure class, so they had to be seen to play, yet also to work. They needed to look both industrious and leisurely.

ideas.name: A contest has to be hard enough to count
ideas.text: Whitehead's hunter complains that a hunt is like shooting deer in a park when it becomes too easy. Oriard shows the Southern code treating the quarry's skill and chance as part of what made the hunt worth doing.

ideas.name: Absorption in the chase
ideas.text: Elliott asks his readers whether, in the middle of a fox chase, they can still say their name, or whether they have a wife or child. A person who can answer such questions is only half a sportsman. Oriard quotes this as a picture of play that takes over the whole attention.

ideas.name: Equality in play can stop at the edge of the game
ideas.text: Tucker says friends who raced and wrestled as boys learned not to claim privilege in a fight with those treated as equals in play. Oriard notes that the sense of equal terms in games was then used to argue that an unequal system was fair.

ideas.name: Letting the quarry win
ideas.text: When a wounded deer escapes into the water, Cornelia begs the men not to shoot because he has won his life, and they lower their guns. Oriard presents this as women writers' answer to the hunt, in which the chased animal counts as a winner.

ideas.name: Play without stakes
ideas.text: A Southern woman's novel notes that at the family parlour games nothing was staked. Women writers kept the spirit of play and rejected gambling, racing and dueling. Oriard says this separated play from the competitive contest.

ideas.name: Gambling and showy hosting can ruin a household
ideas.text: In Dupuy's novel a planter loses his estate first through lavish hospitality and then through speculation. Oriard says hosts competed to out-entertain each other in a way as ruinous as heavy betting.

ideas.name: The prize shows what a community values
ideas.text: Marcus Warland comes home with a blue ribbon for an essay, where readers expected a fox's tail. He gives it to his foster mother. Oriard uses the scene to show that a trophy names what the winner cares about and who he plays for.

ideas.name: Players may stake different things
ideas.text: Simms's hero stakes the fate of his region and country in a war game, while the turncoat plays for his own gain. Oriard says the first plays the open game and the second the sly one, and links the two to class.

ideas.name: A fair fight can favour the other side
ideas.text: In Simms's novels a patriot offers a captured British sergeant a fair fight with broadswords, a weapon that gives the sergeant the advantage. Fair play is shown by what you hand the opponent.

ideas.name: Playful manner before a fight
ideas.text: Before a duel with a traitor Jack Bannister drops his stern tone and acts like a boy in a playground. Oriard says Simms's heroes fight in a sporting manner, and in his novels this redeems battle from murder. The hero still says war is a duty and not a sport.

ideas.name: Fair play sorts people into groups
ideas.text: In Simms's romances the heroes gamble at cards and dice for pleasure, and the villains gamble viciously and cheat. Oriard says the author sorted the same sporting practices into those he admired and those he rejected.

ideas.name: A prize that is given away
ideas.text: In postwar Southern fiction young men race one another for a fox's tail that each will give to a lady. The contest is among rivals and the trophy goes to a third person. Oriard reads the scene as a gentle form of manly rivalry.

ideas.name: Prize money changes why people play
ideas.text: A hero in one novel races for the name of his family's horses and objects to purses and side bets, which would turn a race into a money matter. Oriard shows two ways of seeing a race: sport for its own sake, or a contest for stakes.

ideas.name: Keeping score is not enough to make a game
ideas.text: In Huckleberry Finn the feuding families acknowledge rules and keep score of who has shot whom. Oriard says this shows violence dressed as sport, where rules and scores are present but the harm is not play.

ideas.name: Laughter in the face of defeat
ideas.text: Confederate writers show Jeb Stuart's soldiers dancing before a battle and singing as they ride to it, and say their mirth is evidence of game. Oriard calls this doomed playfulness, in which the way of facing a loss is itself praised.

ideas.name: One player treats it as war, the other as sport
ideas.text: In The Bostonians Olive describes her contest with Basil as a fight to the death, while he enjoys it as sport and answers in a joking tone. Oriard says Basil sees a game because he thinks women have no real power.

ideas.name: Contests are not always equal
ideas.text: Olive warns Verena against a contest that is not equal. Oriard uses this to say that contests between men and women then could not simply be fair, however the language of sport described them.

ideas.name: When the opponent is also the prize
ideas.text: In the love game described by Oriard, the person a man plays against is the one he wants to win, and she is supposed to win by losing. Both sides use the language of a contest but want different outcomes.

ideas.name: Treating a person as a card
ideas.text: Pardon in The Bostonians thinks of Verena as a high card to be played in a tour of paid lectures, as her father did. Oriard picks out how game words turn a person into a piece in someone else's hand.

ideas.name: A game with unevenly matched players is no longer sport
ideas.text: Godey's Lady's Book printed pictures of the sports of love, and also warned against men who sport with women's affections. Oriard says the sports of love become unsporting when the players are unevenly matched.

ideas.name: The early rounds are light and the stakes rise
ideas.text: In The Coquette, Eliza's flirtations seem an innocent pastime at first. When the stakes grow serious she loses everything. Oriard says the person who agreed to play is caught by her own wishes as much as by the other player.

ideas.name: The role fixes the available moves
ideas.text: In courtship a woman of the period was expected to be alluring yet restrained, so she could only act by hints and evasion. Oriard says these became the moves of the game and made inequality part of its ritual.

ideas.name: Not playing may be safer than playing
ideas.text: Virtuous women in cautionary novels did not play the game of love at all, because losing meant shame or death. Oriard shows the choice to sit out as itself a rule set by society.

ideas.name: Game words that warn
ideas.text: In Sedgwick's novel the words of the lottery and the whist table are used for a suitor who wagers on marrying and says the game is his. Oriard says the author used game language to mark danger for those who view marriage as a gambler does.

ideas.name: An early board game on courtship
ideas.text: A board game of 1858, The Game of Coquette and Her Suitors, has players as a parson, doctor, sailor, farmer, artist, merchant, soldier or mechanic. The first to reach the centre of the board wins the Coquette. Oriard notes most board games of the time were meant to teach, so this one is unusual.

ideas.name: Croquet shows how to move other people
ideas.text: In Stowe's croquet scene one suitor says the game teaches you to use friends and send enemies away, because a player may knock another's ball into a new place. The other characters say that many people are croqueted along by partners and parents. Oriard shows a rule used as a picture of power.

ideas.name: The winner gives the prize away
ideas.text: Eva wins the croquet match and offers the prize to Sophie, the runner-up. Oriard reads this as giving up the competition once it is won.

ideas.name: The same stake weighs differently on different players
ideas.text: Lily Bart plays bridge for money she cannot afford to lose, while the rich players treat the money as markers of winning and losing. In the same way a debt to Gus Trenor is a game to him and survival to her. Oriard says stakes are not the same for all who sit down.

ideas.name: Declining to play costs standing
ideas.text: In the Trenor circle, anyone who plays at all has to play high or be thought priggish or stingy. Lily starts unwillingly, then likes winning and runs up debts. The group sets how high the stakes go and who may stay out; the rules of the game do not.

ideas.name: The people with money choose the game
ideas.text: Wharton writes that the rich contribute least to society's amusement and yet decide what form it takes. Oriard uses the line to show that the rules of a social game belong to those who can pay for it.

ideas.name: The rules of the game invoked as a debt
ideas.text: Gus Trenor tells Lily it is not playing fair to take his help and give nothing, and says she is dodging the rules of the game. Oriard shows a claim of fair play used to demand a favour that no rule had stated.

ideas.name: A contest whose visible purpose differs from its real one
ideas.text: Wharton remembers archery club meetings where women wore veils that hindered their aim, because the complexion mattered more than winning. Oriard reads the sport as a display for the marriage market rather than a test of skill.

ideas.name: Winning and losing can both do harm
ideas.text: Lily Bart is ruined as a loser in the marriage game, and Undine Spragg wins it and loses her character. Oriard compares the two to show that the cost of playing can fall on the winner too.

ideas.name: A player cannot be content with a draw
ideas.text: Edna Pontellier will not play the flirtation game that ends in a draw between equals. She has too much at stake, and her desires are not met by a tie. Oriard shows the result of a game depends on what each side wants from it.

ideas.name: Wishing for risk where no risk is allowed
ideas.text: Edna bets on horses at the racetrack and swims far out, because her home life gives her no place for risk. Oriard reads the gambling and swimming as her wish for agon, a test of strength against the world.

ideas.name: Roles and masks that come off after play
ideas.text: Alcott describes a village of young people who frankly grieve or rejoice when they lose or win and wear masks only in play, taking them off soon after. Oriard says playing at love with low stakes removes the sting of rejection.

ideas.name: A rule that makes players say what they do not feel
ideas.text: In a story Dolly tells her brother, as the rules dictate, that she does not like the gymnast, though she does. Oriard says the game requires a denial, and the confusion ends only when she stops playing and states her wish.

ideas.name: A person as the stake of a game
ideas.text: In James's novels a woman's fate is decided by a contest among others, with moves and countermoves over her. She is a stake or plaything and not a contestant. Oriard says these games are about power, though they present themselves as something gentler.

ideas.name: Fate, will and chance as four kinds of game
ideas.text: Oriard sorts the metaphors by how much choice a player has. In the game of life everything is will. In the sport of the gods everything is fate. In the desperate game fate and will clash. In the sport of chance the will is subject to random events.

ideas.name: Dice were once read as an answer from God
ideas.text: In the Bible land was divided and an apostle was chosen by lot, because casting lots left the decision to God. For this reason strict Protestants forbade gambling: using dice for a pastime was playing with God's judgements. Oriard shows the same mechanism read as chance by some people and as divine will by others.

ideas.name: Fortune's game of lifting and dropping
ideas.text: In Boethius the goddess Fortune says she spins her wheel and enjoys lifting the low and lowering the high. She tells the philosopher he may climb only on the condition that he will not complain when her sport requires his fall.

ideas.name: An opponent who tests but stops short of breaking
ideas.text: Luther explained Jacob's wrestling with God as a game in which God plays with his saints, tempting them toward despair to strengthen their faith but never beyond their endurance. Oriard presents it as an opponent who sets the difficulty.

ideas.name: Bargaining with the more powerful side
ideas.text: Increase Mather prayed with a promise of what he would do if God did what he asked, and pushed the arrangement toward a contest. Oriard notes this wrestling for a blessing was common in Puritan writing.

ideas.name: Holding the card that would end the game
ideas.text: In The Golden Bowl Maggie holds one card, a spoken accusation, that would end the game her father is enjoying. She decides never to play it and steps out to the terrace so the others can keep their illusion. Oriard calls the renunciation her cleverest move.

ideas.name: The same game with a spiritual or a money prize
ideas.text: Washington Gladden wrote that life is a contest whose prize is becoming what we are meant to be. Zebediah Flint wrote that the game of life is getting on and prospering. Oriard says the two descriptions meet in the middle. Both keep the contest and name the prize differently.

ideas.name: Taking part counts as winning
ideas.text: Oriard argues that in the success writing the game placed winning in the playing itself. Wealth was never declared more important than the act of acquiring it. The value lay in the process and not in the result.

ideas.name: The word game changed from frivolity to serious effort
ideas.text: In 1707 the minister Benjamin Colman said God and sacred things were never to be called our game, since game suggested frivolity. By 1914 Gladden used game to mean competition and striving in its most serious form. Oriard shows that the same word can mean opposite things at different times.

ideas.name: A free player earns the prize
ideas.text: Gladden took it for granted that players of life's game freely choose to compete and earn what they win. Oriard notes that this is the reverse of the earlier belief that the result depends on the sovereign God, not on the player.

ideas.name: Stages with a reward at the end make a board game
ideas.text: Perkins drew the steps by which a soul moves toward salvation or damnation, in 1592. Oriard points to the likeness with a race board game such as Goose, published five years later, which also depends on chance as Perkins's Christian depended on God's will. Later moral board games joined the two patterns.

ideas.name: A board game that teaches through advance and retreat
ideas.text: Nineteenth-century board games like The Game of Human Life and The Mansion of Happiness taught children Christian living by rewarding virtue and punishing vice. Alcott's Little Women draws on a Pilgrim's Progress board game from her childhood. Oriard says children's play mirrored what adults believed about a moral life.

ideas.name: A personal score card
ideas.text: Franklin took one virtue each week for thirteen weeks, four rounds a year, and marked every fault in a book. He also planned each hour of the day. Oriard compares this to a board game: a course, a score card and a progress toward a reward.

ideas.name: Teaching through the game children already play
ideas.text: Cotton Mather wrote that he watched what games his children played and reminded them of pious lessons suited to the play. Oriard sets this beside Franklin's own use of games for success rather than salvation.

ideas.name: Losers perform a task
ideas.text: Franklin and a friend agreed that whoever won each chess game could set a task, such as part of the Italian grammar to learn by heart, and the loser did it before the next meeting. As they played about equally, they taught each other the language. The stake is work and not money.

ideas.name: What chess teaches
ideas.text: In his essay on the morals of chess Franklin says it builds foresight, circumspection, caution and perseverance, and that life is a kind of chess with points to gain and opponents to face. He adds that a more skilled player can help the less skilled avoid mistakes to keep the match equal.

ideas.name: The opponent is your own tendency to err
ideas.text: Oriard notes that Franklin plays down rivalry. In chess and in life the real opponent is the player's own habit of making mistakes, an idea later success writers inherited.

ideas.name: A race in which everyone who finishes the course is crowned
ideas.text: Gladden wrote in 1868 that Greek races gave one prize for many runners, but in the races of life all who run are crowned, because people are matched against difficulties and not against each other. Oriard calls it a game without an opponent.

ideas.name: Everyone can win because the win is inward
ideas.text: Beecher said people are unequally equipped for the race of life, but since victory is inward, all can win by taking part in the struggle. Abbott said the pursuit of life is itself the prize. Oriard shows the win condition moved inside the player.

ideas.name: A career laid out as spaces on a board
ideas.text: Carnegie's lecture marks each turning point in turn: choice of a career, start in life, openings to success, second step upward, and so on, with the wrong path of speculation marked too. Oriard compares it to a game board with rewards at the end.

ideas.name: Each player sets the win condition
ideas.text: Later success writers said success meant whatever the individual wanted it to mean, and moved the contest from the social world into the mind. Oriard says this made winning possible for all who felt outside power, since the goal was whatever the player chose.

ideas.name: Two games called business
ideas.text: Oriard finds two games in business novels: speculation, treated as gambling and condemned, and productive enterprise, treated as an honourable sport. The same word described both a vice and a calling, depending on how the play was done.

ideas.name: A race can be run by foul means
ideas.text: William Matthews asks whether life is a scrub race in which you have to blind the man on your right and trip the one on your left to come out ahead. He answers that the true race is another one. The question separates a race with fair play from a race without limits.

ideas.name: Struggle changes from battle to sport
ideas.text: Oriard says liberal preachers moved from the language of war to the language of athletic contest between 1850 and 1914. Total war had made battle terrible, and sport carried an ethic of fair play. Calling a struggle a sport changed how the struggle was felt.

ideas.name: A game assigned for a week
ideas.text: In Little Women, Mrs. March gives her daughters a week-long game based on Pilgrim's Progress, in which each girl is a pilgrim carrying her own burden and developing a habit. Oriard notes that moral board games of the time followed the same idea.

ideas.name: Games lie between play and striving
ideas.text: Oriard says all games fall on a line between pure play and pure striving. Marden's success game slid toward play: he wrote that the player loses sight of the hope of victory in the zest of the game and seeks the pleasure of the chase.

ideas.name: A game against your own faults
ideas.text: Oriard says the game of life moved the contest inward. Players competed against their own faults and not against other people. This differs from the Western and Southern sporting myths, where a rival had to be beaten.

ideas.name: Chance is denied to keep the game fair
ideas.text: Thayer and Marden said there is no such thing as luck in a world of law and order. Oriard explains that luck would have meant disorder and no equal opportunity. Whether a game includes chance says what a culture claims about fairness.

ideas.name: More tickets, higher odds
ideas.text: Hardwicke compared success to a lottery in which the person with the most tickets has the highest chance of the prize. He argued that wider knowledge and skill act as extra tickets.

ideas.name: The player who does not play fair is the villain
ideas.text: Frank Merriwell's stories rest on a simple contest between Frank and an opponent who does not play fair, such as a crooked umpire or an unscrupulous speculator. Oriard says the playing field becomes a picture for the whole world.

ideas.name: Exploiting an opponent who plays fair
ideas.text: In The American the Bellegardes agree to the rules and the stake, which is a marriage, and then withdraw permission when it no longer serves them. Newman stays a sportsman, and at the end a friend points out that they had counted on his fairness all along.

ideas.name: Handing your hand to a friend
ideas.text: Christopher Newman tells a friend that when he left business he made over his hand to someone else and could take up the cards again if he liked. Oriard uses the picture of a player who can leave a game and return to it.

ideas.name: Playing only if you can sweep the board
ideas.text: Holland's villain says he will sweep the board, fairly or foully, or not play. He plays for two stakes at once, present profit and future power, and ends the story whimpering that he is played out. Oriard shows a player whose need to win everything ends the game for him.

ideas.name: Swept along by the game's logic
ideas.text: Silas Lapham is warned that speculation is like betting on the turn of a card. Once in, he is carried along by the game and tries to buy out his competitors to hold the whole game in his hand. His escape comes by refusing his partner's games altogether.

ideas.name: A contest where the players hit each other
ideas.text: Phelps describes a strike as an unskilled, futile boxing match in which the strikers bash each other more than their real opponents. Oriard notes this anticipates a scene in Ralph Ellison's Invisible Man.

ideas.name: Power changes what the same game does
ideas.text: Two characters in Howells's A Hazard of New Fortunes speak the same language of winning and little games. Fulkerson has no wealth, so his play hurts nobody. Dryfoos has wealth, and his play ruins others and in the end himself. The same rules weigh differently on whoever holds more power.

ideas.name: A player willing to take any rules
ideas.text: Fulkerson will adapt to whatever set of rules he finds, because for him business is a game with no larger context. A player like this wins by following rules, and never asks whether the rules harm anyone. The book calls him a pure type of the sporting businessman.

ideas.name: Raising the stake can raise the pull of the game
ideas.text: In Webster's novel the narrator says the players care about the play and not the stake. The bigger the stake, with everything lost by the loser, the more eager the players become. The titans fight over a corner on wheat, and the danger adds to their zest.

ideas.name: Naming the opponent as a force hides the people hurt
ideas.text: When a novel makes the rival Chance or Force instead of a person, readers stop seeing the farmers and buyers who suffer when the contest ends. The book says these novels ignore the real results of market play. In The Pit a corner on wheat raises bread prices, yet the story is told as a duel with fate.

ideas.name: Meaning can come from who plays, not from the move
ideas.text: In The Octopus the other ranchers play a small game of bribery, and Magnus Derrick plays the same game as a mighty gamble. The book says the greater the man, the greater the risk and the greater the game. The bribery is the same, and it counts for more when Derrick does it.

ideas.name: Declaring fair play can create the game
ideas.text: Ahab insists that there is a sort of fair play between himself and the whale. Whether the universe agrees does not matter, the book says: by declaring it, he makes the contest exist.

ideas.name: A long struggle told as moves and replies
ideas.text: The book follows Ahab and the sea turn by turn. He crushes his quadrant, a typhoon wrecks the masts, he builds his own compass, the log line parts, and he says he can mend all.

ideas.name: Giving up safeguards to meet an opponent on its terms
ideas.text: When a storm hits, Ahab refuses lightning rods and asks for fair play even though his side has less power. The book says the side with less power can match its opponent only by playing on the opponent's terms.

ideas.name: Accepting the deal is different from giving in to the dealer
ideas.text: Stubb treats the deal as a joke and submits. Ahab accepts the cards but plays them actively, and the book calls the difference 'crucial'.

ideas.name: A loss that is chosen can read as a victory
ideas.text: A sporting frame, unlike a war frame, lets defeat carry meaning. Ahab dies still grappling the whale, which he calls unconquering. The book says spiritual warfare implies destruction, while a game implies a chance of victory beyond defeat.

ideas.name: Inside and outside views of one game differ
ideas.text: To Ahab the chase has stakes and rules and is heroic. To Ishmael, watching from outside, it is madness laid over a different reality. The book says a game makes sense only on its own terms and seems meaningless from beyond them.

ideas.name: Stubb: if all is predestined, life is mere play
ideas.text: Stubb reasons that if every act is predestined, then life is mere play: pretending that striving matters when it changes nothing.

ideas.name: Hidden knowledge can settle a contest before it starts
ideas.text: Hank Morgan fights Merlin with thirteen centuries of knowledge, so the match was never open, though Hank talks in the words of poker and baseball. The book calls this gamesmanship by the one with power. A game described with the words of fair play can still be decided in advance.

ideas.name: A bluff works because few will call it
ideas.text: Hank bluffs the knights by playing his hand for a hundred times its worth. He says that forty-nine times in fifty nobody dares to call.

ideas.name: A chain in which the first move decides the rest
ideas.text: Twain's Satan compares human life to a row of bricks stood on end: one push topples each in turn, and nothing changes the order after the first event.

ideas.name: Chance can block you or open a door
ideas.text: The book says that at mid-century chance was seen as an obstacle to self-made success, as in the business panics of 1837 and 1857. By 1900 the naturalists treated it as the opening that makes a bid possible.

ideas.name: Talk of luck does not track how much luck there is
ideas.text: The book says luck was denied most loudly when markets were unstable and luck mattered most. It was admitted openly once a few controlled the markets and luck mattered less.

ideas.name: Chance and contest working together
ideas.text: The book finds the naturalists most interesting when chance makes a contest possible: it gives Magnus Derrick, Jadwin and Cowperwood the chance to compete for wealth, and then also assures their defeat. A story of pure chance, such as the lottery in McTeague, reads differently from one of pure contest, such as London's boxing tales.

ideas.name: A chance event can still have causes
ideas.text: In Crane's story the New York Kid loses a dice game, and that starts a chain of events that ends by preventing a murder. The book says the story warns against thinking that chance wipes out responsibility. A random draw feeds into later events that people still answer for.

ideas.name: A player is also a piece
ideas.text: In Crane's version of the game, characters both play and are played upon by chance. At some point in the sequence of events, the book says, responsibility is assigned to them.

ideas.name: A game can slide into another kind of game
ideas.text: In The Blue Hotel a friendly card game turns into a quarrel. One player's board-whacking changes a game of luck into a contest of pride, and an accusation of cheating pushes it into a fight. What the players do changes which game is being played.

ideas.name: Everyone around a game shares what comes of it
ideas.text: The Easterner says every sin is the result of a collaboration. Johnnie cheated, the Easterner kept silent, the cowboy provoked and Scully allowed it. The book says the ending holds the bystanders responsible along with the two men who fought.

ideas.name: Open lives crave rules
ideas.text: Don DeLillo says people whose lives are unshaped may secretly want rules and boundaries. He adds that inside games we look for ideal moments or structures, though that search can turn out to be a cruel delusion.

ideas.name: A court can aim at a fair contest instead of the truth
ideas.text: Legal scholars cited in the book say the adversarial system sets prosecution against defence to reach justice. They define justice as a fair contest under rules that give both sides an equal chance to win. The aim is the fairness of the contest, not finding out what happened.

ideas.name: Same pastime, different job
ideas.text: In Margaret Walker's Jubilee the master hunts foxes for pleasure, and slaves hunt possum and raccoon to eat. His sport depends on their work in the kitchen and fields, so the cook's Christmas is as much labour as any other day. The same holiday is a game for one household and a job for another.

ideas.name: A code stays a rule when only one side keeps it
ideas.text: In 1920s Westerns the hero proves himself by playing fairly against opponents who do not. Earlier, both hero and villain obeyed the code. The book says the stories then claim an orderly universe because fair play wins anyway.

ideas.name: The player's code and the written law can pull apart
ideas.text: Western fiction often sets law against the game: law against justice, law against what is right. In some books the two are on the same side, as when a hero who fights with fists and shakes hands afterward prevents a lynching.

ideas.name: A catchphrase empties when it is copied
ideas.text: By the 1930s Western writers used games, playing one's hand and trump cards as gestures because convention called for them. The book says the idioms then did less work than in the first books that used them.

ideas.name: Play with nothing at stake outside the doing
ideas.text: In Lonesome Dove the heroes drive stolen cattle from Texas to Montana for no reason other than doing it. The book says such adventure approaches play in the purest sense, an occasion to show qualities nobody now needs.

ideas.name: A football season can stand in for older rituals
ideas.text: The book argues that in the South football took the place of duelling, hunting and private gambling as a public show of physical risk controlled by a code. A new game can take over the job an older ritual once did.

ideas.name: A star's identity can outlast the game
ideas.text: Southern novels give a series of football heroes whose retirement leaves them without a reason to live. Jim Randolph in Thomas Wolfe's The Web and the Rock is the first.

ideas.name: A stake can be the game's own currency
ideas.text: In Matthews's Hardball the only prize is power itself, not power to pass a particular law. In Vaughan's career game the prize is satisfaction and pay.

ideas.name: Watching a game versus joining it
ideas.text: The book contrasts politics, a game played by a shrewd few and watched by many, with business, a game anyone can join from the mail clerk up. The same word game gives the crowd two different roles.

ideas.name: A game set so everyone wins
ideas.text: Vaughan tells employees that prizes can be won by all and that competition is not a big factor in a career. A game with this setup has no losers and no opposing side.

ideas.name: A no-lose game
ideas.text: William Nickels's Win the Happiness Game gives players a goal that cannot be lost: self-knowledge, self-satisfaction and contentment with life as it is. Each player decides what happiness means. The book calls it an easy game that anyone can win.

ideas.name: A game printed inside a book
ideas.text: Nickels's dust jacket unfolds into a game board. Readers also tally progress on score cards at the end of each chapter.

ideas.name: A game can argue a point
ideas.text: The 1968 board game 50 Easy Steps to the White House parodies Monopoly and other success games, and satirises American politics. Its route runs from the ghetto to the White House, and one square tells the player to choose George Wallace as running mate and defend it on television.

ideas.name: Winning against defeat names no competitor
ideas.text: Norman Vincent Peale urged readers to win victories over defeat. The book notes that this names no rival and no outside obstacle, so it says nothing while reassuring.

ideas.name: Fixed rules can make a hostile world feel safe
ideas.text: Donald Meyer reads Peale's game of life this way: because the game has fixed ground rules, the world is not truly hostile, and to be an identity is just to give yourself to the rules.

ideas.name: Cash McCall asks what a game is without rules or a win
ideas.text: Cash McCall asks how you can play without knowing the rules, or if no rules exist, and what the point is if you cannot win.

ideas.name: Following a rule you do not agree with
ideas.text: Cash McCall says he did not make the rules and only plays. He thinks little of the kick for the extra point after a touchdown, but it is in the rule book, so that is how the game is played.

ideas.name: Winning can mean you keep playing
ideas.text: In Gaddis's J R the boy says that if you play to win, then even when you win you have to keep playing.

ideas.name: Play money and real money can look the same
ideas.text: In J R a boy builds a company empire out of paper, which is the play money of his game, the real money of finance, and nothing when the empire collapses.

ideas.name: A poker table with a fixed number of chips
ideas.text: Ringer pictures the earth as a poker table with a set number of chips, each player trying to pile up as many as possible during the time he is in.

ideas.name: The score can matter more than the prize
ideas.text: Adam Smith's Money Game says investors play for the game itself. The trophies could be swapped for plastic beads or whales' teeth, he writes, as long as there is a way to keep score.

ideas.name: Equal chance to throw is not equal result
ideas.text: Peter Berger wrote that anyone can throw some dice and counted the system fair for that reason. Gilder wrote that the lottery of life depends on most players not winning.

ideas.name: One round tells little about chance
ideas.text: Gilder says chance moving towards order is not assured in any one lifetime, and that it can only be shown to work in the long run.

ideas.name: Several side games run inside one game
ideas.text: Hedrick Smith lists the games politicians play at once: turf games, access games, career games, money games and blame games. Each has its own logic, and the book says these can pull a player away from the aim the main game states.

ideas.name: A game you cannot leave
ideas.text: Marilyn French argues that once one partner made power the basis of a relationship, the other had two options: leave entirely or play. Whatever she did then became part of a contest. In her account the game is the only one available.

ideas.name: Outstanding play and still no place
ideas.text: In Beckham's novel a Black ballplayer climbs an outfield wall to catch a fly ball at his tryout and still does not make the team. The book uses the scene to say that winning is not open to him whatever his skill.

ideas.name: A win that changes nothing outside the game
ideas.text: The book says a trickster who outwits a powerful opponent wins personally but leaves the arrangement of power as it was. In Chesnutt's conjure tales a man gains comfort while the order around him stays in place. A win can count inside the game and not at all beyond it.

ideas.name: Games players choose and games forced on them
ideas.text: Several Black writers separate the creative, community-building word games played among friends from the destructive games forced on them by whites. One word, game, covers both.

ideas.name: A prize held out and never paid
ideas.text: Ellison's narrator is kept running, chasing prizes that the white world holds out and will not hand over. At each stage, doing what is asked brings no reward.

ideas.name: A staged fight for those who hold the power
ideas.text: In Invisible Man blindfolded boys pummel each other for the amusement of the town's white leaders. Later fights among Black characters leave the distribution of power unchanged.

ideas.name: Breaking an opponent's timing
ideas.text: In Ellison's prologue a clumsy boxer knocks out a fast, scientific one, having stepped inside his opponent's sense of time.

ideas.name: The word play can mean two things
ideas.text: Frederic Henry asks Catherine to play chess, and she asks to play with him. For him love is like chess or bridge, and for her it is a religion. The book says play means very different things to the two lovers.

ideas.name: A contest in three acts
ideas.text: Hemingway describes a bullfight in three phases: the lances, the banderillas, and the final faena that ends in death. The chance draw of the bull comes first, a short middle act follows, and everything leads to the last.

ideas.name: In games, avoiding defeat stands in for avoiding death
ideas.text: Hemingway wrote that in games we are fascinated by victory, and we replace the avoidance of death with the avoidance of defeat. He added that it takes more courage when death is a closer partner to the game.

ideas.name: A handshake ends a contest only if both accept it
ideas.text: Cohn treats his fight with Romero as a gentleman's contest that closes with a handshake and no hard feelings. Romero refuses the handshake and keeps fighting from the floor.

ideas.name: How a player takes a loss shows what the game is to them
ideas.text: Jake says Cohn was not angry at being beaten at tennis. The book reads that calm as a sign of purposelessness, since he plays for no stake that matters to him.

ideas.name: Solving a position instead of beating someone
ideas.text: Philip Marlowe keeps a chess board in his flat for working out problems alone. The book says he plays chess as he approaches life, to solve the puzzle and make the game intelligible, not to clear the world of evil.

ideas.name: Playing above the rules
ideas.text: William Kennedy describes Billy Phelan as a gamester who accepted the rules and played by them but also played above them.

ideas.name: A fair start for a deadly contest
ideas.text: Houston proposes to settle a quarrel with Mink Snopes by laying a pistol on a fence post, each man backing off one post on his side, counting three and running for it. Mink shoots him from hiding instead. The book uses the scene to set an old habit of equal terms against a new habit of winning by any means.

ideas.name: Same trade, played for pleasure or for profit
ideas.text: Pat Stamper swaps horses as a gambler plays cards, for the pleasure of beating a worthy opponent as much as for gain. Flem Snopes trades only for power and profit. The book says play makes barter a social relationship, while acquisitiveness makes it exploitation.

ideas.name: A series of different contests decides one prize
ideas.text: In Faulkner's A Courtship two men compete for a woman in dancing, racing, drinking, eating and a 130-mile foot race.

ideas.name: One player can pull a whole town into their game
ideas.text: Tom Sawyer draws the entire adult population of St. Petersburg into his imaginative play. The book calls this the harmless version of a superior being who sports with lesser ones.

ideas.name: Some choices are kept out of chance
ideas.text: Dede offers to flip a coin to settle whether to marry, and Elam refuses, saying love is too big to take a chance on.

ideas.name: Perpetual play loses its pull
ideas.text: In Hawthorne's version of Pandora, children in a paradise with no tasks and nothing but games become discontented, because they cannot play hide-and-seek for ever. The narrator says that when life is all sport, toil is the real play.

ideas.name: Play is defined by where the aim lies
ideas.text: Horace Bushnell defined work as activity for an end and play as activity as an end.

ideas.name: Three ways to relate work and play
ideas.text: The book sorts writers into three groups: those who want a balance, each in its proper time; those who want work abolished for pure play; and those who treat the two as one whole.

ideas.name: What play frees you from changes
ideas.text: The book lists work, tyranny, mechanisation, inhibition, violence and self-destruction as things play has meant freedom from. Which one counts depends on the period.

ideas.name: Work done as sport
ideas.text: Thoreau wrote that earning a living can be a pastime if one lives simply and wisely. He told readers to make getting a living their sport and not their trade.

ideas.name: Play beside danger
ideas.text: Hawthorne's Miriam plays in the sunlight at the mouth of a cavern. In Moby-Dick the whales mate and suckle in the middle of the slaughter.

ideas.name: Children's play teaches the laws of the world
ideas.text: Emerson wrote that a child among baubles is learning the action of light, motion, gravity and muscular force. In a later essay he called children's plays educative nonsense.

ideas.name: Why a community bans a pastime
ideas.text: Puritan bans on sport protected three things: economic security, the safety of lives and property, and the Sabbath. Sledding and football inside town limits risked injury and damage, and gambling led to financial ruin.

ideas.name: Rules on paper and play in practice differ
ideas.text: The book says Puritan laws against popular recreations were mostly ineffective. Church members and nonmembers both played with little inhibition.

ideas.name: Organising play adds aims beyond the play
ideas.text: When teams, leagues, rankings, championships, statistics and records come in, players are working toward things outside the activity. The book says the prophets of college sport after the Civil War cared about character building and not play.

ideas.name: Play is promoted for its uses
ideas.text: Churches built gymnasiums to pull young people away from temptation, and employers backed working-class play so that work would go faster and crime would fall. Play was recognised, but only for what it did for something else.

ideas.name: A week with no work wears the players out
ideas.text: In Little Women the girls try a week of only play. After one day they are weary of it, and their mother says to keep regular hours for work and play.

ideas.name: A game can carry a lesson
ideas.text: The March sisters play a game of Pilgrim's Progress, which the book describes as moral striving in the form of play. The rules of the game are a story with a message.

ideas.name: Play defined as what you are not obliged to do
ideas.text: In the whitewashing scene Twain says work is whatever a body is obliged to do and play is whatever it is not obliged to do. By that line, Tom and Joe on Jackson's Island are no longer playing, since they stay on long after they are tired of it.

ideas.name: One player can bring others into his game
ideas.text: Tom Sawyer gets the adults of the town to go along with him in treating the world as a place for play. The children's game becomes a shared set of pretences.

ideas.name: A pretend game needs everyone to share it
ideas.text: Tom wants to tie Jim to a tree as a joke and plays pirates and robbers. Huck loses patience when he says the swords are lath and the elephants are a Sunday School outing. The people outside the pretence pay for it.

ideas.name: Play holds inside a boundary
ideas.text: On the raft Huck is free and has no one to answer to. On the shore the same play has no power over the feud, the con men or the killing. The raft works like a space marked off from the world.

ideas.name: The word game covers cruel contests as well as pastimes
ideas.text: In Huckleberry Finn the feud, the con men's schemes and the torturing of dogs in Bricksville are all called games. The book calls them versions of false play that refuse to see the world as it is.

ideas.name: Play does not sort right from wrong
ideas.text: Huck's lazy days with Jim and his lazy days with Pap are described in nearly the same words. The book says play has no moral conscience, and that the two sets of days differ only in what threatens them.

ideas.name: Hiding a fact that changes the game
ideas.text: Twain keeps back the news that Jim is already free while Tom stages an escape. The book says he cheated the reader, because the pretence of the final chapters rests on a fact the reader was not given.

ideas.name: Work and play can be mixed for a moment only
ideas.text: Hapgood writes of a spell in Italy when work was play and play was work. The mixture gives way when passion breaks both.

ideas.name: Cheating with nothing at stake
ideas.text: Lardner describes golf matches where rich members cheat whether or not anything is at stake. The cheating has become a habit of the game and is separate from any wish for the prize.

ideas.name: Fixing a contest ends belief in all contests
ideas.text: The gambler Wolfsheim fixes the World Series. The narrator treats this as toying with the faith of a whole nation in the result.

ideas.name: Social games run on scripts
ideas.text: Amory's courtships are games of lines and poses, with set phrases and rules nobody breaks. Rosalind ends one with a score and a rain call.

ideas.name: A game without a referee
ideas.text: Amory calls life a football game with every one offside and the referee got rid of, with everyone claiming the referee would have ruled for them. The picture shows what a referee does: he settles which claim counts.

ideas.name: Play can be set against the game
ideas.text: Salinger and Holmes use play for freedom and game for posing and pettiness. Holden says a game is a game only if you are on the side where the hot-shots are.

ideas.name: Playing without caring for the score
ideas.text: Seymour plays Ping-Pong hard and with joy, with no interest in the score. At soccer he runs down the field and waits so the goalie can get set, and his team finds this unendearing.

ideas.name: Aim less
ideas.text: Seymour tells Buddy to try not aiming so much at marbles, so that shooter and shot become one. The advice is to stop trying to win by control.

ideas.name: A feel that cannot be called up
ideas.text: Rabbit's touch on the court comes and goes, and one unforced golf swing sends the ball straight. The next swing, in A Month of Sundays, is just as unthinking and slices into the rough.

ideas.name: A pastime turns into work as it becomes routine
ideas.text: Rabbit plays golf weekly at a country club and says it feels more like work. His practice swing is smooth, but anxiety comes in when he faces the ball.

ideas.name: Control against touch
ideas.text: In sixties basketball novels, free-lancing players who live by touch meet coaches obsessed with patterns and control. The book reads this as the game's work and play pulling apart.

ideas.name: The same game can stand for different things over time
ideas.text: Twain saw baseball as a symbol of the rush and push of his century. From the 1930s writers made it a garden in a land of machines, the summer game.

ideas.name: Football novels set love of the game against management
ideas.text: The football novel of the sixties puts a hero who loves the game for its own sake against management that regiments his life on and off the field.

ideas.name: A calendar of games
ideas.text: In Couples the ten pairs live by a wheel of parties and games, with basketball and touch football at weekends and a Sunday evening with no game. Summer is the season of many games and autumn the season of duty.

ideas.name: Hard times raise the number of games
ideas.text: In the 1930s Monopoly, dance marathons, roller derbies, six-day bicycle races and softball all spread, and laws against gambling eased. The book reads some of these as efforts to keep up hope.

ideas.name: A festival of play ends
ideas.text: The Marble Faun stops at the Carnival, but Couples follows the couples back into the world after the carnival. When the parties stop, the same people turn to earnest matters.

ideas.name: A game with a ruler
ideas.text: Kesey invents a game called Power, in which the winner has thirty minutes when everything he says is law. Wolfe takes it as an allegory of the Pranksters' own hierarchy.

ideas.name: A group that rejects games makes its own
ideas.text: The Pranksters call the straight world a set of games, yet they divide into those on the bus and those off it, and an old personality game returns.

ideas.name: Play ordered by an organiser
ideas.text: The book says Kesey ends up like a recreation director of the 1910s, insisting on play for the benefit of young souls. Play that is ordered by an organiser is the thing the book calls antiplay.

ideas.name: A game closed to outsiders
ideas.text: At the Pranksters' graduation party the music is wired only to their own headphones. Outsiders look on puzzled or angry while the circle around Kesey closes.

ideas.name: Rules and community, set against spontaneity
ideas.text: Sennett wants play as children do it, with rules, seriousness and shared pleasure, in place of play as spontaneity. Lasch gets his model of such a game from contests of speech and body in Aristotle.

ideas.name: A prank can break up a serious meeting
ideas.text: Kesey brings the Day-Glo bus to a Berkeley rally and tells the students they are playing the Pentagon's game. Wolfe says it deadened the rally.

ideas.name: Play used as a method of protest
