ideas.text: The Yippies exorcised the Pentagon, scattered money before the Stock Exchange, and put a pig up for president. The book says the politics of play freed culture more than it changed politics.

ideas.name: A style gets copied by sellers
ideas.text: Hippie entrepreneurs sold the signs of rebellion and mass advertisers took up the style. The book says the playfulness of the young was soon part of middle-class life.

ideas.name: Singing together, against playing alone
ideas.text: The scenes of blues in Hughes, McKay and Hurston show play shared by a crowd, unlike the lone self of earlier writers. The dance floor and the jook are crowded.

ideas.name: Play that carries grief
ideas.text: Ellison's blues keeps painful details alive and lifts them into something part tragic and part comic. The book calls this playful tragedy, and sets it against white writers who saw play without pain.

ideas.name: Sports words describe the rest of life
ideas.text: The book argues American writers used game and play to criticise, justify or celebrate ordinary life. Sport is a metaphor for life in the country.

ideas.name: Where tradition is thin, rules take its place
ideas.text: In the book's account, American society relied on laws and gamelike rules of behaviour. The book adds that a faith in competition and a level field made life look like a game.

ideas.name: Players turn to self-fulfilment
ideas.text: By the 1970s and 1980s free agency, endorsements and end-zone dances showed players treating sport as a place for themselves and not for the team. Courts sided with players over owners.

ideas.name: Courts may protect the game itself
ideas.text: The author suspects that earlier rulings which freed baseball owners from antitrust law came from a belief that the game is a public possession, ranking above any one player.

ideas.name: Leisure can keep people occupied
ideas.text: The Grand Inquisitor in Dostoyevsky would have people work and, in their free hours, live like children with songs and dances. The book reads this as a picture of a consumer culture.

ideas.name: Complexity is not a count of mechanics
ideas.text: The paper reports that how complex and engaging a game is does not follow simply from the set of mechanics it uses. What counts more is how the mechanics interact and how each one is carried out in that particular game.

ideas.name: Few mechanics, deep game
ideas.text: Chess is tagged with four mechanics and Go with two, yet both open up a huge range of strategies. A six-year-old can learn the moves and an adult can spend years on the tactics, so a short mechanic list says little about how hard a game is to play well.

ideas.name: Same mechanic, different weight
ideas.text: Worker placement is simple in Agricola, where each action space holds only one family member in a round. It is harder in Stone Age, where spaces need different numbers of workers and a die decides the reward, and harder again in Paladins of the West Kingdom, where workers come in several types.

ideas.name: Same number of mechanics, different complexity
ideas.text: A game that pairs hand management with card play conflict resolution can be more complex than one that pairs acting with card drafting, although both use cards and both carry two mechanics.

ideas.name: Complexity and rating move together only a little
ideas.text: Across the top 10,000 games, a higher complexity rating goes with a higher average rating, with a correlation of 0.48. The paper adds that BoardGameGeek mostly hears from keen players, so this cannot be read as true of all players.

ideas.name: Number of mechanics is moderately tied to complexity and rating
ideas.text: The number of mechanics a game has correlates at about 0.34 with its complexity and 0.33 with its rating. Some highly rated games, such as Gloomhaven with 19 mechanics, carry a lot of them.

ideas.name: The type of mechanic does not change the rating
ideas.text: When the paper averages the ratings of the games that use each mechanic, it sees no clear difference between mechanics. It concludes that which mechanics a game has does not decide how well it is rated.

ideas.name: Mechanics that go with higher complexity
ideas.text: Of the 182 mechanics, 25 have an average complexity above 3 out of 5 across the games that use them. Order counters, loans and ownership have the highest averages.

ideas.name: Hand management is rising and dice rolling is falling
ideas.text: The share of games using hand management grew from 4.4% in 1980 to 25.7% by 2020. More than 55% of the 1980 games used dice rolling, and the share has fallen since, even though dice rolling is still the most common mechanic overall.

ideas.name: Popular mechanics bias co-occurrence counts
ideas.text: The pairs that turn up most often together are made of the mechanics that turn up most often anyway: dice rolling, hand management and variable player powers. The paper therefore turns to mutual information, which removes that effect.

ideas.name: Worker placement is the most connected mechanic
ideas.text: Worker placement appears in 48 of the 66 pairs with mutual information above 0.65. It is most often paired with auction and turn-order mechanics, which the paper reads as games where players choose single actions also tend to bid for items or resources that improve their position.

ideas.name: Worker placement leans on other mechanics
ideas.text: The paper reads worker placement's many links as reliance on other mechanics: turn order, auction, pattern movement, pieces as map and physical removal help settle the order of turns, how the action spaces are built and what the outcomes are.

ideas.name: Auctions and turn order depend on each other
ideas.text: The paper explains the high link between auction types and turn-order mechanics by the fact that the order of bidding is usually set by a turn-order structure. Five Tribes, Keyflower and Railways of the World are named as examples.

ideas.name: Pattern movement and static capture go together
ideas.text: Their mutual information is 0.77. Chess and Onitama are given as games that use both.

ideas.name: Alliances and negotiation go together
ideas.text: The pair has a mutual information of 0.68 and appears in games such as Rising Sun and Cosmic Encounter.

ideas.name: Most strongly linked mechanics concern actions
ideas.text: Most pairs with mutual information above 0.65 are about what players can do and how it is resolved, rather than about how the game is laid out.

ideas.name: Mutual dependency between mechanics does not predict appeal
ideas.text: The average mutual information of the mechanic pairs in a game shows no clear link to its rating, complexity or BGG rank. The paper finds no relationship between using mechanics that depend on each other and how appealing a game is.

ideas.name: Some mechanics are for all kinds of game
ideas.text: Dice rolling, hand management and variable player powers sit in the cluster of mechanics used in every domain. The paper explains this by the many ways each can be set up, and by the fact that each fits both simple and complex designs.

ideas.name: Abstract games leave out some mechanics
ideas.text: Mechanics used in every domain except abstract games, such as worker placement and network and route building, tend to rely on hidden information, a theme or randomisers like dice, which games such as Chess and Go do without.

ideas.name: Mechanics that suit one domain only
ideas.text: Pattern movement appears only in abstract games, ownership only in strategy games, and singing and hot potato only in party games.

ideas.name: Mechanics are coarse labels
ideas.text: A single mechanic name covers many different ways of setting it up, so the label alone does not settle how a game feels. The paper also notes that its data comes from avid players, not casual ones.

ideas.name: People change rules because they like a game
ideas.text: The more widely a game is played, the more house rules it collects, and players often change a game most when they like it most. The author notes that game inventors make many arbitrary choices, such as how many cards to deal or how much money to start with, and cannot test every combination. Backgammon grew out of Tabula and modern chess out of Shatranj this way.

ideas.name: Fix a luck problem by evening out the start
ideas.text: In Monopoly the last player to move finds the properties already bought. Starting players on different squares, or auctioning the turn order, cuts that disadvantage without touching the rest of the game.

ideas.name: Replacing a dice roll with an auction
ideas.text: In Auction Monopoly every unowned property is bid for. Players bid too much too early the first time and run out of cash, so the game turns into a test of judging what a property is worth, and a player needing one property to finish a set sees the bidding rise.

ideas.name: A rule that adds money to the board can empty the bank
ideas.text: Putting penalty payments on Free Parking sounds harmless. The author reports the cash flow rises just enough to keep the second-ranked player going while the leader barely feels rent, and the bank may run out before anyone wins.

ideas.name: A challenge rule adds contact between players
ideas.text: Trivial Pursuit has almost no interaction. Letting a player say 'challenge' to a wrong answer, with a wedge lost for a failed challenge and gained for a correct one, gives each player a reason to watch the others.

ideas.name: The same cards can run under other win conditions
ideas.text: Trivial Pursuit questions work without the board. Playing to a total, to one answer per category, by discarding a pile of cards, or by winning squares of a tic-tac-toe grid each changes what a player wants.

ideas.name: Doubling the points for each extra unit lets a trailing player catch up
ideas.text: In Big Boggle, if each added letter doubles a word's score, one long word found by one player can outweigh many short ones. A player far behind can come back when the board holds a common ending.

ideas.name: Making a guess reveal something about yourself
ideas.text: In Double Jotto each guess also tells the opponent how many letters it shares with your own secret word. Players now look for guesses that learn a lot and give away little.

ideas.name: Allowing one lie changes what a reply means
ideas.text: In One-Lie Jotto and One-Lie MasterMind each answerer may give one false reply. No answer can be fully trusted, so the guesser has to keep a record of what would fit if any single reply were false.

ideas.name: Letting the code change cuts the luck of a lucky guess
ideas.text: In Interactive MasterMind the codemaker may change the code between guesses as long as every earlier answer stays true. A lucky first guess no longer wins, because the maker can switch to a code that gives the least revealing reply.

ideas.name: Asking for two guesses at once removes information
ideas.text: Double Guesses makes the codebreaker place two rows before any answer arrives. He cannot use the first answer to choose the second guess, so the player needs a sense of probability instead.

ideas.name: Moving a piece of equipment can act as a handicap
ideas.text: In Nerf Ping Pong the net can be angled or set nearer the more skilled player. Two players can try placements until each wins about half the time.

ideas.name: An advantage can be made fair by rotating it
ideas.text: In three-handed hearts the player to the dealer's left keeps an extra card and gets a large edge. The game stays fair because everyone takes that seat in turn, so the players agree on a number of deals divisible by three.

ideas.name: Zero-sum scoring invites short alliances
ideas.text: In Zero-Sum Hearts the scores always add up to zero. A player close to an extreme low score can be stopped only by others working together for a moment.

ideas.name: Agreeing a source of words decides what the game rewards
ideas.text: Tournament Scrabble depends on memorising one dictionary. For casual play, groups use an atlas, the Bible or a phone book, and a challenged word has to be found within a set time.

ideas.name: Giving back the wild tile raises luck and allows comebacks
ideas.text: If any player may take a blank from the board by putting the matching letter in its place, a blank can be used again and again. Bingos come within a few turns, luck rises, and a player behind can recover.

ideas.name: A category bonus needs members that can be checked
ideas.text: A bonus for words in a chosen category causes arguments when members are unclear, such as whether BONE is a colour. State names, chemical elements or months avoid disputes, as does naming a reference book in advance.

ideas.name: Changing the shape of the board can break scoring squares
ideas.text: On a toric Scrabble board all the triple word squares sit next to each other, so one word could cross two. The author adds a patch: only one of the adjacent triples counts. A change of geometry often needs a second rule to repair what it upsets.

ideas.name: Changing the aim changes the game's tactics
ideas.text: In Extinction Chess the pieces and moves are the same but the goal is to keep one of every kind. Queen trades become fatal, a single remaining knight has to be guarded like a king, and games end quickly.

ideas.name: A game can fail for reasons the box does not show
ideas.text: Games have been published that always favour one side, never end, or leave a rule unclear. The author's advice is to treat the equipment as material for a new game and test the rules by playing.

ideas.name: Unequal sides cannot be balanced exactly by changing movement
ideas.text: In Tablut the king escapes in games between equal players. Maths shows that with unequal forces and aims no rule change gives exact balance unless a draw is the right result, and Tablut has none. The remedy is to handle the choice of side instead.

ideas.name: Bidding hands the choice of side to the players
ideas.text: In Tablut players bid how many moves the king will need to escape, and the lowest bidder plays the king but loses if he fails. Each side then carries a price the players set themselves.

ideas.name: The pie rule makes the first player care about the second
ideas.text: When one player makes the opening move and the other picks a side, the first player has an incentive to make the position close. In Hex it removes the need to guess which centre hexes to ban.

ideas.name: More choices let players balance finely
ideas.text: Letting one player make two moves and the other one before the choice of side much increases the number of possible starting positions. The more positions to choose from, the closer the balance.

ideas.name: Playing two boards at once cancels a side's advantage
ideas.text: When each player has White on one board and Black on the other, the winner is the first to win either board. Neither player can count on knowing a target score, which is the flaw of playing two games one after another.

ideas.name: Take a balanced game, unbalance it, then race
ideas.text: In Double Unbalanced Chess both White armies have an extra queen, so each player is nearly certain to win with White. The contest becomes who wins faster with White and lasts longer with Black.

ideas.name: New rules for mixed decks come from the game's own logic
ideas.text: When two aces of trumps tie, pinochle's rule that the first one played wins works. In multi-deck poker, five of a kind outranks a straight flush because it is rarer, and suits stay equal since they matter nowhere else. Common sense and the spirit of the game guide these choices.

ideas.name: A bigger set of suits changes how cards are distributed
ideas.text: In six-suited bridge, 13 cards spread over six suits make voids and singletons common and long suits rare. Expert bidders are as unsure as beginners at first.

ideas.name: Combining games turns choosing where to move into the main skill
ideas.text: In Chess-Checkers-Chinese Checkers players move on any one of three boards and win two out of three. The question becomes which board to spend a move on. An odd number of games prevents ties.

ideas.name: Choosing the board after the roll keeps the decision informed
ideas.text: In the three-game dice combination, rolling first and then picking a board gives the player real information to act on. Choosing the board before the roll removes it.

ideas.name: One game, many ways to cooperate in a team
ideas.text: A team can take turns without talking, or it can discuss everything with a captain deciding ties. The first is simple to run and the second gives more strategic discussion.

ideas.name: The win condition decides how a multiplayer game feels
ideas.text: With three croquet balls each, 'first ball home', 'all balls home' and 'lowest total of finishing places' lead to different plans: sacrifice two balls for one, hinder the rear ball, or avoid finishing last.

ideas.name: Three-player pure strategy games push players to gang up
ideas.text: In a three-way chess game, a player who gets ahead is attacked by the other two. A doomed player has to pick which rival wins. Players end up lying low and talking, which turns chess into a small diplomacy game.

ideas.name: Two ways around petty diplomacy
ideas.text: One is to put one player against a team of two. The other is a three-player shogi variant that turns the game into two against one whenever two players attack the third, and then rewards the lone player with a more powerful king.

ideas.name: Deals with yourself break trading games
ideas.text: If one player runs three nations in a trading game, he can give one nation a generous deal and repay it later. The fixes are caps on such trades, equal exchanges, or a limited number of vetoes by the opponent, which then become something to bargain over.

ideas.name: Adjust payoffs from what was actually used
ideas.text: In Mah-jongg, players can raise the value of hands that never came up in a session and lower the ones that scored most. After a number of sessions, all hands pay roughly alike.

ideas.name: A retreat rule costs the attacker
ideas.text: In Risk with Retreats the defender may withdraw to a neighbouring territory, the attacker loses one army, and has to move in. This means an attack needs at least three armies.

ideas.name: A rule can change where armies are placed
ideas.text: In Nuclear Risk, the country on a drawn card is wiped out. Players avoid piling armies into a country whose card they do not hold, since that card could be played against it.

ideas.name: Simultaneous moves need written orders
ideas.text: In the Risk variation with simultaneous movement, both players write their moves, compare them, and settle collisions with a formula in which a two-to-one force loses nothing. Writing keeps everyone honest.

ideas.name: Scoring changes how a hand is played
ideas.text: The same bridge hand is played differently in rubber and duplicate scoring. In duplicate an overtrick can matter more than safety, so a player may risk the contract.

ideas.name: A table can pay back a lopsided deal
ideas.text: In Compensation Bridge the side with fewer high-card points receives the score the other side could typically expect, taken from a computer study of thousands of deals. It reduces luck without removing it.

ideas.name: Variants favour whoever knows them
ideas.text: In dealer's choice poker, the dealer picks the game and probably knows it most thoroughly. The author advises choosing a game that gives the dealer a large edge, and warns that unfamiliar variants cost money.

ideas.name: Paying to pass on a card changes who gets extreme hands
ideas.text: In the poker game Push a player may pay to push an up card to his neighbour. Pots grow, players fold less, and hands of both high and low kinds turn up more often.

ideas.name: Which rule set a game uses is a design choice with side effects
ideas.text: Chinese rules for Go are easier to state, and Japanese rules differ mostly in scoring and suicide moves. The author says they give almost the same result when both players make the same number of moves.

ideas.name: Komi puts a price on moving first
ideas.text: Go adds points to the second player's score. The common value is 5.5 in Japan, a fraction to avoid ties, while a study of professional games put the first-move edge at about 7. No one can say the exact figure.

ideas.name: Board size alone can open a game up
ideas.text: Smaller Go boards help beginners, and a bigger one would give experts new ground if the 19x19 board ever ran out of secrets.

ideas.name: Joined edges can kill a game
ideas.text: The author reports Toric Go did not please the author as much as the standard game and would likely end in one big seki at high levels, since neither side can form two eyes.

ideas.name: Changing the unit of a move changes the whole game
ideas.text: In Omino Go a player places up to four connected stones instead of one. Tactics shift and a game takes much less time. The author also suggests giving each player a different set of shapes to find which shapes win most against which.

ideas.name: Forbidding a tactic leaves a different game
ideas.text: In One-Capture Go the player cannot sacrifice stones to build a wall, since the first capture ends the game. A single eye of two or more points is now enough for safety. Players still stake out territory as in ordinary Go, because the no-passing rule makes the side that runs out of safe moves lose.

ideas.name: A rule can turn a drawn-out game into sudden death
ideas.text: Without passing or recapture, One-Capture Go has the tension of overtime in hockey. At the end a player with fewer safe moves has to fill his own eye and let the opponent capture.

ideas.name: A different grid changes how hard capture is
ideas.text: On a hexagonal grid a stone needs six enemy stones to be captured instead of four. Paper and coloured pencils make it easy to test other grids, and regular shapes let players carry what they learn across the board.

ideas.name: If a board makes survival too hard, add a rule that protects groups
ideas.text: Rosette is Go on a hexagonal grid. Forming two eyes is difficult there, so a ring of six stones around a point makes the group permanently safe.

ideas.name: Handicaps serve the reasons people play
ideas.text: The author argues that people play to enjoy themselves and to learn, and a handicap serves both. Players who refuse one because only an even fight counts have to change how they think about competition.

ideas.name: A handicap that moves with results makes the less skilled player want to win
ideas.text: In Go the handicap changes by one stone when a player wins three games in a row. The less skilled player tries to lower it and the more skilled player tries to keep or raise it, so every game also moves the handicap.

ideas.name: A game with depth suits a handicap
ideas.text: Go can be played at many levels of skill, so stones placed in advance give an uneven pair a game both can win without changing what the game is. A one-rank gap gives the less skilled player the first move without komi.

ideas.name: Handicap is easy in shogi and hard in chess
ideas.text: In chess, a player down a piece can trade pieces to simplify to an endgame. In shogi, captured pieces return to the board by dropping, so trading adds mobility instead of removing it, and a handicap by removing pieces costs the more skilled player less than expected.

ideas.name: A handicap can leave the character of the game unchanged
ideas.text: The author asks for a handicap that has several levels and does not markedly change what the game is. Trivial Pursuit does it with extra questions in a winner's categories, Scrabble with the dictionary, and chess with removed pawns.

ideas.name: Carrying handicap points across sessions
ideas.text: In Trivial Pursuit with handicaps a player gets a point for each win and carries it to later sessions. More points mean more categories needing two questions in a row. Players now also try to raise their handicap, which gives them a second aim.

ideas.name: Knowledge can be the thing to level
ideas.text: In Scrabble with challenges, a trained player beats an average one by hundreds of points because he knows the dictionary. Dictionary odds lets the less skilled player consult it freely and brings the margin down.

ideas.name: A takeback gives the less skilled player one look ahead
ideas.text: In chess or Go, the less skilled player can undo his last move once after seeing the reply, but not twice in a row.

ideas.name: Handicaps can add extra moves, points, money, armies, guesses, time or a lesser goal
ideas.text: Many games can be handicapped this way. The author tells players to experiment until everyone wins about as often as everyone else.

ideas.name: A game of Eleusis is the scientific method
ideas.text: In Eleusis the dealer's secret rule stands for a law of nature, and players test guesses by playing cards. Martin Gardner noted this, and experienced players call their turn as dealer their turn to be God.

ideas.name: Penalties price the cost of testing a guess
ideas.text: In Eleusis a wrong card costs two penalty cards and a wrong string costs twice its length. A player pays more for a bolder test, and the dealer's cards give nothing away about which in a string was wrong.

ideas.name: An exception to the penalty rule invites bold plays
ideas.text: When a Prophet is overthrown the player whose card was wrong takes no penalty cards. Players will therefore try unusual or deliberately wrong plays in the hope of catching the Prophet out.

ideas.name: A secret rule of middle difficulty serves everyone
ideas.text: In Eleusis the dealer scores more, and the players enjoy the round more, with a rule that is neither too simple nor too complex. Rules that let about one-quarter of the cards through are easier to find than those that allow half. New dealers tend to underestimate how hard their rule is.

ideas.name: The setter of a puzzle needs a score too
ideas.text: Eleusis scores the dealer at the highest player score, unless the Prophet's marker comes early, in which case the dealer gets twice the cards before the marker. Players who finish quickly pay the dealer less. A ten-point bonus for players who never dealt makes up for the dealer's usual lead.

ideas.name: Stealing makes a word unsafe until it is long
ideas.text: In Anagrams a word on the table can be taken by anyone who adds tiles and rearranges it. A player adding only an S gives opponents an easy steal, so a player looks for a longer change that is harder to take.

ideas.name: Unequal pieces make the order of play matter
ideas.text: In mancala games every pebble is the same, so the only choice is which pit to pick. In The Glass Bead Game coloured gems are worth 1 to 5 points and stones are worth nothing. The player chooses which bead goes in each pit, and moves can number in the hundreds.

ideas.name: Where a score is kept can still leave it at risk
ideas.text: In The Glass Bead Game, an indirect capture lets a player take a gem from the opponent's storehouse if the opponent has none on his side of the board. Points stored are not safe until the game ends.

ideas.name: A rule absent from the original can be repaired by adding it
ideas.text: The old Halma rules let a player block the opponent's win by leaving a piece in his own starting corner. The author adds that a player wins when the opposite corner is full, whoever owns the pieces.

ideas.name: One quantity can set how far a piece moves
ideas.text: In Fields of Action a piece moves exactly as many squares as there are pieces next to it at the start of the move. Crowded pieces move far and lone pieces are stuck, so a special rule lets isolated pieces move freely if they end beside two others.

ideas.name: Equipment from one game can become the pieces of several others
ideas.text: An ordinary checkers set plays Mini-Halma, Salta and Fields of Action when pieces are numbered with stick-on labels.

ideas.name: Give offence more reward by changing what a capture takes
ideas.text: In Crossings only the piece landed on was captured. Epaminondas lets the head of a phalanx capture the whole opposing phalanx, which gives attackers more force. The scale is also larger, with more pieces and a bigger board.

ideas.name: Close a loophole that makes one reply always draw
ideas.text: In Epaminondas, if the second player copies each move symmetrically about the board's centre, the game always ends in a draw. A rule against moves that create left-right symmetry on the far row removes the copy strategy.

ideas.name: Keep the pieces and change only the opening
ideas.text: Othello and Reversi are the same game except for how the first four pieces are placed. This is why many near-identical Othello clones could be sold.

ideas.name: In some games doing less is the more powerful plan
ideas.text: The author says the right strategy in Reversi and Othello is to avoid capturing more pieces than needed for most of the game. That limits the opponent's choices and often makes him give up key squares such as corners late in the game.

ideas.name: Replace an object that does not work
ideas.text: The incomplete Ming-Mang rules had a capture aim, yet pieces in a corner could never be taken, so a draw was always available. The author gave the game the aim of Go, walling off territory, and made capture a means to that end.

ideas.name: Start new rules on a small board
ideas.text: The author recommends trying the Ming-Mang territory game on an 8x8 board first and moving to a larger board when the small one feels limiting.

ideas.name: A territory only counts if it cannot be taken
ideas.text: In Modern Ming-Mang a wall is secure only when no enemy move can ever capture a piece in it. White's apparently complete wall in one diagram is still under threat because Black can place a piece that threatens to return and capture four.

ideas.name: Forbid repeating a position unless the other player was to move
ideas.text: The rule stops draws by repeating moves without outlawing every back-and-forth. It also leaves a player a way to use the repetition rule against the opponent.

ideas.name: A no-check rule turns a chess variant into a race
ideas.text: In Racing Kings the aim is to reach the last rank with the king and checks are illegal, so the game is about speed. Trading pieces helps the opponent develop more than the small gain helps you.

ideas.name: Dice can decide which piece moves instead of how far
ideas.text: In Modern Chaturanga the roll names the type of piece that may move, and doubles let a piece move twice. A player has to plan around which pieces may be forced to wait.

ideas.name: A game can rest on an ally relationship
ideas.text: In Chaturanga a captured raja leaves its army frozen. The ally's raja can take command by reaching the empty throne, and a one-time swap of captured rajas may restore both armies. Players have to weigh whom the swap helps.

ideas.name: Score by position as well as by capture
ideas.text: Chaturanga gives points for the last raja, for sitting on an enemy throne and for capturing a raja with a raja. Moving a raja two squares from an enemy raja gives the other side the first chance but, if the dice allow a double move, doubles the reward.

ideas.name: A version without dice makes order of moves the puzzle
ideas.text: Played as pure strategy with no scoring, Chaturanga becomes a contest to eliminate both rajas. The need to take into account the order in which the armies move complicates tactics considerably.

ideas.name: Extending a flat game into three dimensions needs new thinking
ideas.text: Commercial 3D chess often fails because it carries two-dimensional moves into space without allowing for the differences in geometry or for how hard it is to picture moves. In some versions a king cannot be mated even three queens down.

ideas.name: A piece can be redesigned so an old goal works again
ideas.text: The hook mover makes two perpendicular moves in a plane, and on an empty board it cuts off planes the way a rook cuts off ranks and files. A king and rook can then force mate in 3D.

ideas.name: Another world with its own laws changes where the battle happens
ideas.text: In Parallel Worlds Chess the middle board has no captures and every piece moves like a queen. Pieces move between levels, players can win on one level, and a common tactic is to promote pawns as sacrifices on the board you are losing.

ideas.name: A limit on the first turn reduces the advantage of moving first
ideas.text: In Parallel Worlds Chess, White makes only two moves on the first turn, though later turns allow three.

ideas.name: The first player's edge drives rules of Five-in-a-Row
ideas.text: In plain Five-in-a-Row Black's second stone has to be away from the centre. Renju adds a swap option, a choice between two stones, and Black-only prohibitions, because a plain first move wins too often.

ideas.name: Board size balances the first player
ideas.text: Renju is played on a 15x15 board because a larger board tends to favour the first player too much while a smaller one results in too many draws.

ideas.name: Balance can be made by restricting the more powerful side's shapes
ideas.text: In Renju Black may not make double threes, double fours or an overline, but White may. The author calls Renju an example of how far serious players tune a game to balance both sides.

ideas.name: A joined board has no centre
ideas.text: On a toric Renju board a line of five may continue over an edge and no point is the middle, so it does not matter where the first move is made.

ideas.name: A game of not enough places
ideas.text: Conspirators gives every piece a goal but provides one shelter fewer than pieces. The loser is the player stuck with the piece outside, like a strategic game of musical chairs.

ideas.name: A chain you build can be used by either side
ideas.text: In Philosopher's Football the ball moves by jumping lines of stones, so a chain you build toward your goal can help the opponent jump the ball back. The authors advise delaying jumps and building the chain first.

ideas.name: Handicap by moving the start
ideas.text: Philosopher's Football can be handicapped simply by moving the ball's starting position nearer the goal the more skilled player defends.

ideas.name: More than one way to win makes the board work in many directions
ideas.text: Hexade and Havannah give three different winning formations, so one stone can threaten to join several. In Havannah a ring is almost impossible to complete but its threat gains time for a fork or bridge.

ideas.name: The larger board can become the favourite
ideas.text: Havannah was sold on a 169-cell board, but experienced players in Holland prefer the 271-cell board with an extra ring of hexagons.

ideas.name: Make the komi a track
ideas.text: In Lotus a marker on a 19-point track begins three points toward the second player. A player who passes moves it toward himself, and the final position scores points. This combines komi, passing and scoring in one device.

ideas.name: Capture by flipping makes suicide a second capture
ideas.text: In Lotus a captured group changes colour instead of leaving the board. If the capturing group has no liberties after flipping, it flips again, so some moves look like captures and act as suicides.

ideas.name: Allowing a move for one piece type changes safety
ideas.text: In Medusa a rosette is safe only while it stays together, since a player can break it by moving a stone. Suicide can be a temporary sacrifice that lets a player surround and flip five enemy stones.

ideas.name: Everyone can play the same letters in a different way
ideas.text: In Crossword Squares each player calls one letter and everyone writes it into their own hidden grid. Each player ends with a different crossword from the same letters, and the skill lies in using the letters opponents call.

ideas.name: Scoring that doubles per extra letter keeps long words equal to overlaps
ideas.text: Crossword Squares gives 10, 20 and 40 points for three, four and five letters. A five-letter run like SCATS then scores the same whether read as one word or as two overlapping four-letter words.

ideas.name: Allowing a challenge turns a spelling game into a bluff game
ideas.text: In Ghost a player who names a letter that does not finish a word can be challenged by someone who thinks no word starts that way. The challenged player has to name a word or lose a letter.

ideas.name: Letting letters go on either end enlarges the options
ideas.text: In Super Ghost a player can add a letter before the sequence, so PERSO can become MPERSO or UPERSO. Counting the possibilities is very hard.

ideas.name: Crash gives information without revealing the word
ideas.text: A player answers each guess with only the number of letters in the right position. Guessers need several words at a time, four in the first salvo, three in the second, and so on, which fits play by post.

ideas.name: A winning rule can be calculated, yet the game stays playable
ideas.text: In Nim, the position can be turned into binary numbers and added with 1+1=0. A player to move at a nim-sum of zero loses against error-free play, and any other position can be moved to zero.

ideas.name: Reversing the object changes little of the strategy
ideas.text: In Misere Nim the loser is who takes the last object, yet the winning strategy is nearly the same as in Nim. The differences are near the end: avoid leaving an even number of single-object piles, and with one pile left take all but one.

ideas.name: Adding a dimension makes a solved game hard again
ideas.text: Nim on a rectangular or triangular array lets players remove a line of objects from any row, column or diagonal. The same simple idea becomes much more challenging.

ideas.name: Cutting a position into two equal halves lets the second player mirror
ideas.text: In a Nim variation where objects separated by a gap cannot be taken together, the first player loses if he leaves two identical sections. The second player imitates each move in the other half.

ideas.name: A Nim-like game can have an elegant winning pattern
ideas.text: Tsianshidsi, played with two piles, lets a player take from one pile or the same number from both. The safe pairs 1-2, 3-5, 4-7, 6-10 and so on always give a way back to another safe pair.

ideas.name: Rules of colouring turn a map into a board
ideas.text: In the simplest map-colouring game neighbouring regions may not both be coloured and the first player with no move loses. Giving each player different colours, or two colours each, makes the game harder.

ideas.name: A game can have a non-square board that favours no corner
ideas.text: Chomp works on any rectangle larger than 6x6 that is not a square, and the player forced to take the corner square loses.

ideas.name: Some simple games are still unsolved
ideas.text: In Sprouts the player who makes the last move wins, but for all but the simplest starts nobody knows which of the first or second player wins with error-free play.

ideas.name: Completing a shape earns another turn
ideas.text: In Dots-and-boxes a player who closes a square puts in his initial and moves again. Play comes to a point where players run out of safe moves, and the game is hard to analyse.

ideas.name: Rules about steps can make an arithmetic race
ideas.text: In Arithmetic Croquet each player names a number, steps of up to 8 are allowed, and a step cannot equal the opponent's last step or its difference from 9. Passing the hoops at 10, 20 and so on by rule makes a new player feel lost at first.

ideas.name: Without one fixed choice that always wins, randomness is the plan
ideas.text: In Finger Baseball both players show fingers at once and the batter scores if they match. A player who always shows the same number is read by the opponent, so the plan with the highest long-run result is a weighted random mix, but players still become predictable.

ideas.name: Games that never move or remove pieces can go on paper
ideas.text: Because pieces in One-Capture Go, Hex and Havannah stay where placed, players can colour regions with two pencils. They can then try any grid they draw.

ideas.name: In some connection games, defence and offence are the same
ideas.text: Octagons mixes half-octagons with squares, and a half-octagon touches seven spaces against four for a square. The inventors of other connection games say that attack is served by a sound defence, and a player who can block never needs to worry about linking.

ideas.name: A threat made twice in one turn cannot be answered
ideas.text: In Octagons a player may fill two squares per turn. If he threatens two connections in different parts of the board, he can fill both key squares at once.

ideas.name: Spread moves out, because close stones do the same job
ideas.text: In Octagons stones too near one another may duplicate each other. A move that turns out to be unnecessary is like handing the opponent an extra turn.

ideas.name: Hidden rules turn a party into a trading game
ideas.text: In Haggle each player gets an envelope with 12 cards and two secret sheets of scoring rules. Players trade cards and information, and the host scores the envelopes afterward.

ideas.name: Cap the top cards and reward the low ones to keep trading lively
ideas.text: The author tells the host to limit high-valued cards, for example by scoring zero for four or more hearts, and to add bonuses for low ranks. A player dealt many cards of one suit then gains no large advantage, and nobody can easily see which suit to collect.

ideas.name: Add a few odd rules at the end to fit the crowd
ideas.text: In Haggle a host can drop or add a whimsical rule at the last minute if more players turn up. Cross-references between rules make play interesting, but the host has to check they do not contradict one another.

ideas.name: Trades of equal numbers keep a hand intact
ideas.text: In Super Babel all trades are one for one or three for three, so every player can still make a ten-card hand. Players may bargain openly, whisper in another room, ally or work alone.

ideas.name: Score by how hard a holding is to get
ideas.text: An alternative Super Babel table gives points by the average number of cards needed to be dealt a hand, such as 15 for four of a kind and 40 for nine cards of one suit. Unequal trades then become possible, and a card can be used in only one combination.

ideas.name: A bid in time makes an acting game into a contest of confidence
ideas.text: In charades with bidding a player says how quickly he can get his team to guess a phrase and bids shorter times against the other team. The lowest bidder acts. His team gains a point if it guesses in time and loses a point if it does not.

ideas.name: Handicaps can be drawn from a deck
ideas.text: Experienced charades players write handicaps such as hands behind the back, mittens, back turned or eyes closed on cards and turn one up before each act. Bidders can see the handicap before they bid.

ideas.name: A tournament format follows from equipment, players and time
ideas.text: The host chooses round robin, single or double elimination, or Swiss pairing by looking at the number of players, how many games can run together and how many rounds there is time for. With 18 players, one croquet set and time for four games, three groups of six and a final works.

ideas.name: A tiny space can still hold a full game
ideas.text: The author's front-lawn pitch-and-putt course and his five-tree kickball course were both made from what he had. Against an imagined opponent, Mr. Par, he tried to beat his own lowest score and set records, which kept a solo game going.

ideas.name: Difficulty can be tuned by distance and target size
ideas.text: In Kickball Golf the author rates holes by distance, tree diameter, obstacles and slope. He changed par values as his skill rose, so that breaking par stayed hard.

ideas.name: The way of playing follows the equipment
ideas.text: Kicking a light ball with bare feet worked more accurately than with shoes. The author used one stroke for long shots and another for putts under 25 feet.

ideas.name: Playing the route as one continuous journey changes the plan
ideas.text: In Kickball Ricochet the ball is not reset to a tee. A player thinks about where a shot leaves the ball for the next hole, as a pool player thinks about the position of the cue ball.

ideas.name: Reduce the roster of base-runners to fit a small field
ideas.text: In the author's backyard baseball there were three bases, no stealing and only one runner per team at a time. A runner on first could be forced out at home, and a run usually came from a hit that kept the runner from being forced out at third.

ideas.name: A scoring system can let a player win more points and still lose
ideas.text: The author notes that in tennis a player can win most of the points without winning a set, and most of the games without winning the match. He proposes a match made only of tiebreakers, won by the first to seven, as a closer match to the points won.

ideas.name: Harsh conditions are fair when shared
ideas.text: Croquet with wickets on slopes and near trees is amusing because everyone plays under the same conditions.

ideas.name: A winner can become a hazard to the others
ideas.text: In Poison croquet a ball that finishes the course becomes poison and eliminates any ball it hits, so the game goes on until only one ball is left.

ideas.name: The doubling cube makes skill matter more in chance games
ideas.text: Because a player decides when to raise the stakes and when to refuse, the cube rewards judging odds. The author says it suits other race games with mixed luck and skill, such as Parcheesi or Sorry!.

ideas.name: Owning the cube has a value
ideas.text: A player with about a 25 percent chance of winning is at break-even when deciding whether to accept a double. Often accepting is still right, because holding the cube lets him redouble if the game turns, and the earlier in the game, the more that is worth.

ideas.name: The state of the match changes the right choice
ideas.text: In a ten-point match a player down eight to one may need to take almost any double, because giving up another point would make the match hard to win. The author adds that a double usually needs more than 50 percent, since it gives the cube to the opponent.

ideas.name: A team against one player makes a social game from a two-player one
ideas.text: In the chouette one player faces a team whose captain moves the pieces. Winners and losers rotate the roles of captain, box player and last in line. The author says the idea suits other games, especially those with a doubling cube.

ideas.name: Old games show which rules were once different
ideas.text: In Tabula all pieces start off the board and enter by dice rolls, and both players move in the same direction with three dice. Fayles adds a sudden-death rule that failing to use all three dice loses the game at once.

ideas.name: A hit can move a piece, trap it, or do nothing
ideas.text: In ordinary backgammon a hit blot goes to the bar. In Plakato it is pinned under the hitter until the hitter moves. In Moultezim and Gioul a lone piece cannot be hit at all.

ideas.name: A reward that is built to be double-edged
ideas.text: In Gioul a double lets a player play every double from his own up to 6-6, but he has to use them in ascending order. If he cannot use one, his opponent takes over the rest, so a big roll may help the opponent.

ideas.name: Condition on entry delays contact
ideas.text: In Dutch Backgammon all pieces start off the board, none moves until all have entered, and no blot may be hit until one piece reaches the inner table. These rules put fighting off until later.

ideas.name: Different stakes can be woven into the score
ideas.text: In Acey Deucey a roll of 1-2 doubles the stakes and lets the player choose a double. The 1,000-point scoring gives 100, 200 or 1,000 for kinds of win plus a point for each piece and pip left to the loser.

ideas.name: Playing the old rules makes clear why modern games chose theirs
ideas.text: Anglo-American Checkers has forward-only men and a free choice among captures. International Checkers has backward capture, long-range kings and a maximum-capture rule, and other regions changed one or two of those parts. Comparing them shows what each rule in the set does to play.

ideas.name: Sources disagree because players use names loosely
ideas.text: The author warns that Pool, Spanish and other checkers are named inconsistently, so the same name can mean two different sets of rules.

ideas.name: A small set of knobs generates a family of games
ideas.text: Regional checkers vary movement of men, which pieces may be captured, direction of capture, whether to take the most, where kings stop, and whether jumped pieces are removed at once.

ideas.name: A capture rule that keeps pieces on the board changes what a capture means
ideas.text: In Lasca a jumped piece goes beneath the jumper and a jumped stack gives up only its top piece. A single capture can free a friendly piece trapped underneath.

ideas.name: A game's key idea can be lifted out and rebuilt
ideas.text: Emergo takes Lasca's stack idea and drops forward movement, promotion and the checkers setup. It has a hexagonal board, pieces entered one at a time, and mandatory maximum captures.

ideas.name: Order of entering is a strategic choice
ideas.text: In Emergo it helps to enter all your checkers first and take the initiative, but a tall shadow piece can give the opponent a big return. Losing several checkers to one piece can pay if you recapture and hold a tall stack.

ideas.name: Play tends toward fewer, taller stacks
ideas.text: Emergo moves toward fewer pieces whose average height is larger.

ideas.name: Add win conditions that pull in opposite directions
ideas.text: In the Parton game with back-row pawns the owner wants to lose his back-row pieces and may not promote them. A player can win by losing them all or forcing the opponent to promote one, and loses by capturing them all.

ideas.name: A scoring win lets a player win without clearing the board
ideas.text: In Dragon a complete victory needs all enemy pieces taken, but a player can still win a demi-victory by having more pieces left. A rule that kings may not end captures on the edge of the board makes it harder for the less powerful side to draw.

ideas.name: A piece that only its own kind can take
ideas.text: In Kinger a kinger can be captured only by an enemy kinger, but may not end a capture on the edge. The two rules pull in opposite directions, one making it safer and the other more exposed.

ideas.name: Move the object of one game into another
ideas.text: Royal Checkers applies the object of chess, capturing a royal piece, to a checkers setting in two forms: a royal pawn that behaves like any man and a royal queen that moves like a king.

ideas.name: More directions of movement complicate tactics without more rules
ideas.text: Hexdame puts International Checkers on a hexagonal grid with six lines. Draws become rarer because three kings can always beat one, where International Checkers needs four.

ideas.name: One principle can be tried across many games
ideas.text: The author says that ideas from chess variants, such as Refusal Chess, can be tried in nearly any abstract two-player game. He finds that making chess variants gives him ideas for other games.

ideas.name: Changing the setup makes memorised openings useless
ideas.text: In Pre-Chess players place their back-row pieces in turn. Opening theory no longer helps, and players have to meet many kinds of positions. Grandmaster games have been published.

ideas.name: Pieces with shorter reach lead to a different game
ideas.text: Shatranj has a general who moves one diagonal step and an elephant that jumps two squares. The author says it has depth and positional play missing from modern chess.

ideas.name: Piece values come from long experience
ideas.text: An early Shatranj writer gave values of rook 5, knight 3 and a third, general 1 and two thirds, and counted a kingside elephant above the queenside one because it works with the general.

ideas.name: Dice can decide which piece moves
ideas.text: In Dice Chess the throw names the piece type to move and a player rolls again if the piece is missing or blocked. Tournament players use it for light relaxation.

ideas.name: Cheap dice may not be fair
ideas.text: The author warns that with inexpensive dice a 6 may come up noticeably more or less often than a 1, which matters when odd and even decide who moves.

ideas.name: Banning checks restricts where a king can go
ideas.text: In Checkless Chess a player may not check unless it is mate. Opponents have to avoid squares that give check, so a king in the centre can cramp their pieces.

ideas.name: Hide the setup to skip the opening
ideas.text: In Screen Chess both players arrange their half of the board behind a screen. The first meeting of armies happens in the middle game, with bishops on opposite colours and one pawn per file the only limits.

ideas.name: Giving away your pieces can be the aim
ideas.text: In Giveaway Chess capture is compulsory, kings are captured like other pieces, and the first player to lose everything wins. Players try to force the opponent to capture.

ideas.name: Two moves per turn replace check
ideas.text: In Double Move Chess check and checkmate are removed, because a player can walk into check and then escape or capture the king with the second move. Games end quickly, which suits playing by post.

ideas.name: Let the other player pick which move you make
ideas.text: In Refusal Chess a player may reject the opponent's move once, so the opponent has to play a different one. In Compromise Chess a player offers two moves and the opponent chooses. The author says the first can be applied to almost any abstract two-player game.

ideas.name: Change what counts as the target
ideas.text: Kinglet tells players to capture all eight enemy pawns, not the king, and the player who has to promote his last pawn loses. The author says this was part of his inspiration for Extinction Chess.

ideas.name: A piece's value depends on the board
ideas.text: A grasshopper is worth almost a knight early, when the board is crowded with pieces to jump over, and less than a pawn after many exchanges.

ideas.name: A forced extra move makes the game faster
ideas.text: In Avalanche Chess the pawn push after each move exposes kings easily and sends passed pawns quickly toward promotion. Details such as promotion by the pawn's owner and a ban on en passant after a push settle odd cases.

ideas.name: A piece with unlimited power is limited by its twin
ideas.text: In Emperor King Chess each king may jump to any square, but not onto a defended enemy emperor. They cancel each other, so a piece cannot simply be picked off, and the end game turns on attacking the emperor's last defender.

ideas.name: Testing a rule from a huge game in a small one
ideas.text: The author added the emperor's power to ordinary chess kings to learn how emperor endgames work without playing 1,000 moves of Tai Shogi.

ideas.name: Piece powers can be lent by a neighbour
ideas.text: In Knight Relay Chess pieces a knight's move from their own knight can move like knights, and knights themselves neither capture nor are captured. Powers are gained and lost as pieces move.

ideas.name: A king with wide powers is given a forced reply
ideas.text: In Rettah the king combines queen and knight, but when checked it has to capture the checking piece even if that exposes it. Players win by capturing the rettah.

ideas.name: Two boards can double the geometry
ideas.text: In Alice Chess a piece moves on one board and is then transferred to the matching square on the other, which has to be empty. This makes the board 8x8x2, and a move is legal only if legal where it is made.

ideas.name: Two targets double attack and defence
ideas.text: In Double King Chess a player wins by capturing either king, so one piece forking both kings can win. Each side has two queens, two kings and many targets to cover.

ideas.name: Teamwork in a speed game turns on a shared clock
ideas.text: In Double Bughouse each team has one player on each board, a captured piece goes to the partner, and either player running out of time or being mated loses it for the team. A player about to be mated can stop moving and hope his partner wins first.

ideas.name: Single-use powers add timing decisions
ideas.text: In Missile Chess every piece starts with a one-shot missile that captures on any square it could move to. Variants give different numbers to different pieces, let the player share a fixed total among them, or add shields.

ideas.name: Save a power or spend it
ideas.text: In Teleportation Chess a player who spent his knight's teleport too early lost the advantage, and the author's note says White ought to have kept it in reserve. With a one-time power, the skill lies in choosing when to use it.

ideas.name: One token system can carry many different powers
ideas.text: In Exotic Chess a checker under a piece stands for a special power. Queens destroy a piece one or two squares away, rooks push pieces along a line, knights rearrange the eight squares around them, and so on.

ideas.name: Merging piece moves makes new pieces
ideas.text: Capablanca's Chess adds an archbishop and a chancellor, and earlier games added a centaur and a champion. Combining knight with bishop or rook is the same idea that built the queen.

ideas.name: A bigger board with more powerful pieces ends fewer games in draws
ideas.text: Capablanca and Lasker preferred a 10x8 board with extra pieces to ordinary chess because games were faster, more exciting and less likely to be drawn.

ideas.name: A promotion limit stops free gains
ideas.text: In Grand Chess a pawn promotes only to a piece the side has lost, and may not enter the last rank if none is lost. It still attacks along that rank.

ideas.name: Balance two kinds of mover
ideas.text: Wildebeest Chess is built so that the number of riders equals the number of leapers. The camel is worth less than a knight because its larger range reaches fewer squares, and so hinders it.

ideas.name: Stalemate is a design choice
ideas.text: The author thinks chess is illogical in drawing a stalemate and prefers Shatranj's rule that the stalemated player loses.

ideas.name: Check which source a rule set came from
ideas.text: Murray's History of Chess printed Chu Shogi rules with major errors, copied by later books. Correct rules were researched in Japan and brought to the West in the 1970s.

ideas.name: Giving a piece an unusual power calls for rules about its capture
ideas.text: The lion in Chu Shogi can move two squares, capture and keep moving, or capture without moving. To keep lions on the board, a lion may take an unprotected lion two squares away, and after a lion is captured by another kind of piece the opponent cannot take a lion back except with a lion.

ideas.name: Piece values rank pieces and change as the game goes on
ideas.text: In Chu Shogi the author ranks pieces from the lion to the pawn instead of giving points, because a big board and slow movement mean a small gain may not be used in time. A lion is worth more than two free kings early but less than a free king in an endgame.

ideas.name: Skilled players look to see which pieces have gone before they trade
ideas.text: In Chu Shogi the player left with more rook-like pieces has a kind of air superiority that helps advance and promote, so swapping one high-ranking piece for two or three low-ranking ones needs care.

ideas.name: Playing by post suits a certain kind of player
ideas.text: The author lists people who have no nearby opponents, who spend time on a train, or who feel rushed over the board. Playing two games at once with one opponent doubles the play for the same postage and lets each take the first move.

ideas.name: Chance in a mailed game can be taken from a shared public number
ideas.text: Players agree that the next roll comes from, for example, the closing Dow Jones average and its change. Both can check the number later, so nobody can reroll, and no third party is needed.

ideas.name: Removing the dice also removes luck as an excuse
ideas.text: In the diceless system each player picks a roll from his list and crosses it off. The odds of a roll are either one or zero for both players to see, and the author notes that using up all rolls with one die number leaves blots exposed until the sheet is replaced.

ideas.name: Open the draw and luck turns into foresight
ideas.text: In Open Scrabble all tiles lie face up in a string and players draw from either end. The game has no luck in theory, but nobody can look far enough ahead to calculate what the opponent can then draw.

ideas.name: A game earns its quality by how people feel after many plays
ideas.text: The author says tic-tac-toe fails the lasting interest test with adults, because after a few games every game is a draw, while chess and Go keep teaching players new things.

ideas.name: Depth can be measured
ideas.text: If two players are one rank apart when the winner takes two games in three, a game's depth is the number of ranks between a beginner and the champion. A larger depth means players keep learning for longer.

ideas.name: Depth is not the only quality a game has
ideas.text: The author lists the possibility of reversals and close finishes, some originality, no unnecessary complexity, not too many draws, no marked tilt to one side, and also aesthetics and playing time. A variation that only varies the game, neither improving nor harming it, still counts as a new game.

ideas.name: A rule change can have effects nobody planned
ideas.text: The author warns that a change that looks right may have an undesirable result that is hard to foresee, so each one needs to be played to find out.

ideas.name: More choices let a player's skill show
ideas.text: Rules that give more options let a player control the outcome and try other plans. Examples are three dice with a choice of two, a few rethrow options, or coins spent to change a roll by one.

ideas.name: Rethrows can be given unevenly to handicap
ideas.text: Giving one player more rethrow options than another offsets the first-move advantage. The author suggests keeping them to four or five each so that deciding when to use one stays hard.

ideas.name: Help the attacker when waiting is the winning plan
ideas.text: In some games sitting back and doing nothing wins until the opponent loosens his position, which leads to long games with little happening. The author prefers making pieces more mobile, rewarding attack, or reducing defence, as chess promotion does, or as a larger soccer goal would cut scoreless draws.

ideas.name: More interference between players makes a game richer
ideas.text: The author says the more a player can affect what the others do, the more interesting a game usually is, as with the challenge rule in Trivial Pursuit.

ideas.name: Try changing the target, adding a second way to win, or changing the amount of equipment
ideas.text: Examples include fewer captures to win Pente, three kings in a diagonal for checkers, six hotels in a row for Monopoly, and different numbers of pieces, cards or money.

ideas.name: The ko rule from Go works for other games
ideas.text: Banning any move that recreates an earlier position stops draws by repetition. It also makes threats elsewhere on the board matter, since a player can make a threat that has to be answered and then make the move the rule had forbidden.

ideas.name: Ideas travel between games
ideas.text: The author suggests reading the chess chapter for ideas even if you do not play chess, since Refusal and Compromise work in any two-player strategy game. He says the aim of variants is enjoyment, and many games were found by trying things out.

ideas.name: One naming of spaces records any grid game
ideas.text: Algebraic notation names each space by letter and number, so the same method records chess, a hexagonal game or Tablut. The chess descriptive system could not do that because each square had two names.

ideas.name: A hexagonal board can be improvised from circles
ideas.text: Poker chips or other thin round objects glued in a pattern have the same neighbour relations as hexagons. Wargame stores sell hex grids, and tape on acrylic gives a checkerboard with clean lines.

ideas.name: Games are played with, not just received
ideas.text: Henry Jenkins's foreword says talk about games has moved from asking what a game does to the player to asking what the player does with it. A group once wanted to build play spaces that turned 'bad' kids into 'good' ones by repeating 'good' values, and the foreword calls that a reductive model of what a game teaches.

ideas.name: Rehearsing a choice in a space with no real cost
ideas.text: The foreword compares a player building a role-playing character with Fagin in the musical Oliver!, who tries out several imagined lives in a song before deciding to think again. A game lets a player try a villain or a hero, fail, restart and try another course within one afternoon.

ideas.name: The player is partly to blame
ideas.text: Will Wright is quoted as saying that games are the only medium that lets us feel guilt. In a film we can blame the author, but in a game we pressed the button that put the character in that situation.

ideas.name: What a game does not allow shapes its ethics
ideas.text: A designer can narrow the options so that a player facing a dangerous scene can only shoot or flee. The ethical system of a game comes from what it permits and from what it leaves out or discourages.

ideas.name: Design and play are both needed
ideas.text: The foreword names two jobs: putting a moral picture into a game, and building a way of playing around it. In its example, a mother and her young son both played The Sims and used the game to talk about changes in their family that were hard to say plainly.

ideas.name: Many games reduce ethics to a 'good' or 'evil' tree
ideas.text: Sicart (chapter by Miguel Sicart) says most commercial games with moral choices use branching decision trees on a scale of 'good' and 'evil'. He argues that ethics is also the reasons behind the systems we live by, so a game's ethics lies in the systems through which a player chooses and experiences its world.

ideas.name: Rules and story can pull in opposite directions
ideas.text: In Call of Duty 4 the opening makes the player look around but never gives a weapon, and the player's character is executed. In Fallout 3's Tempenny Tower a quest offers three outcomes, killing the ghouls, killing the humans or arranging a truce, and the truce fails once the player leaves (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

ideas.name: Most design tries to remove friction; ethics may need it
ideas.text: Usual design advice says a player is always told why an action has its result, so the designer takes friction away. Sicart argues that for ethical play the designer adds friction between what the rules ask and what the setting means (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

ideas.name: A game that tells the player how moral they were takes the thinking away
ideas.text: Knights of the Old Republic and Fable show an interface item that turns choices into a place on a moral scale. Sicart says this removes friction by computing the player's values for them (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

ideas.name: Rewarding a move the story calls harmful
ideas.text: In Shadow of the Colossus, each defeated colossus makes the player's avatar look sicker, yet his stamina meter rises a little, so the rules treat each fight as progress while the pictures show him getting ill (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

ideas.name: A mechanic can change meaning at the end
ideas.text: In Braid the player moves left to right to help a princess away from a monster, then the sequence is rewound and it shows she was running from the player's own character. The player then reads the same action with a different meaning (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

ideas.name: Design objects carry values
ideas.text: Latour and Winner, cited by Sicart, argue that a made thing has values built into it. Sicart says that reading stops short, since it assumes players follow instructions without question, whereas players interpret and take the values as their own (chapter by Miguel Sicart).

ideas.name: A player may separate in-game acts from real values
ideas.text: Teenager Rachel regularly cares for stray cats, yet in Zoo Tycoon sold newborn zoo animals at once for money and said it was fine in a game. Koo and Seider take this as the main problem for games meant to teach social behaviour (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Content messages are only part of what a game says
ideas.text: A first guess is that a game teaches whatever themes sit in its plot and pictures, so rating systems sort games by violence. Koo and Seider note that studies find only correlation, and that a game with a plainly helpful message did not reliably lead to helpful responses (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Games add rules to content
ideas.text: Koo and Seider say video games share story, characters and images with film and books, and add a system of rules that shapes what players do (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Reskinning does not change what a game teaches
ideas.text: Changing Space Invaders so the player shoots litter instead of aliens teaches little about litter, because the action is still aiming and shooting. Koo and Seider argue that prosocial games need new rules, not a new picture on old rules (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Monopoly's rules make its claim
ideas.text: Monopoly models capitalist economics through rules such as investing in owned property to raise income. Koo and Seider say a Monopoly edition set in another city keeps the same activity of buying and developing, though a national parks edition does change the claim, because parks are not usually things to buy and improve (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Rules can carry a profession's values
ideas.text: In S.W.A.T. 4 shooting a suspect who poses no immediate threat costs points or fails the mission, and so does failing to shoot when needed. A player learns what the profession counts as acceptable by playing inside those rules (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: The rules, not the topic, set the role
ideas.text: Zoo Tycoon looks like animal care, but its rules ask the player to invest money in assets that earn income, which is the same loop as a railroad game. That is why a girl who cares for animals at home treats animals as stock in the game (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Different players can read one game differently
ideas.text: Two girls of the same age played Zoo Tycoon: Rachel took the tycoon role, while Katarina treated it as a design medium and ignored the in-game advice to maximise points, using a cheat code to avoid failing. Cheat codes can work as a sanctioned way to set one's own goal (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Playing a rule can prompt a player to criticise it
ideas.text: Rachel objected that in Zoo Tycoon trees lose value and cost nothing to clear-cut, with no ecological price. A teacher could use such a remark to discuss why a designer wrote a rule that way and how to change it (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Lessons may not carry over to real life
ideas.text: Seminary students on their way to give a talk about the 'Good Samaritan' were no more likely to help a person in need than others, and being late predicted who stopped. The authors use this to warn that what a player learns in a game may stay in the game (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Talk around a game is part of the game
ideas.text: Hint guides, forums, friends and teachers shape how players read a game, and Gee calls this wider setting the Game with a capital G. A forum thread on whether to spare a character in Grand Theft Auto IV is one example (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Players can make values the mechanism
ideas.text: The board game Scruples makes disagreement about values its basic mechanism. The authors suggest a multiplayer game where players negotiate and debate a stated situation, such as allowing a risky medical procedure, could work as a just community (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: Real actions can feed into a game
ideas.text: A car dashboard that grows trees on screen when fuel use is low, and a campaign site that awards points for making phone calls, change behaviour directly. The player's real acts count as the moves, so nothing learned in the game has to carry over into life (chapter by Gene Koo and Scott Seider).

ideas.name: A dilemma with no consequence is easy to answer
ideas.text: The questions in Ultima IV, delivered by tarot cards at the start, only set the player's class and starting place. Staines suggests having a similar dilemma come back later in a form that costs the player something, such as shopkeepers who stop talking to a player who gave to a beggar (chapter by Dan Staines).

ideas.name: Variations on one dilemma prompt thought
ideas.text: Moral philosophers change a dilemma slightly each time, as with the trolley dilemma. Staines suggests following a beggar dilemma with one about stealing food for a sick child, so a player who answers each differently has to compare them (chapter by Dan Staines).

ideas.name: A plainly 'good' side and a plainly 'evil' side give nothing to weigh
ideas.text: In Fallout 3's Megaton quest a kindly sheriff asks the player to save the town and a cartoonish villain pays the player to blow it up. Staines argues that a 'good' temptation needs reasons the player could half-believe, and that these two characters show no feeling worth thinking about (chapter by Dan Staines).

ideas.name: A score turns a moral choice into a character statistic
ideas.text: Because Fallout 3 awards karma points, the choice between hero and villain works like choosing hair colour for a character. Staines says real moral situations are rarely labelled that plainly (chapter by Dan Staines).

ideas.name: A multi-sided choice engages more than a two-sided one
ideas.text: In the Oasis quest a mutant tree asks to be killed, and two leaders each want his seeds slowed or spread, giving three options with no compromise. Staines finds it holds the player's interest more than Megaton does, and notes that it offers no way to bring the parties to talk (chapter by Dan Staines).

ideas.name: A game alone does not teach; the lesson around it matters
ideas.text: Staines argues that a game is paired with classroom work in his plan. For example, students who chose to spare or kill a prisoner in Mass Effect could be grouped by choice and debate it, so the abstract argument is tied to something they did (chapter by Dan Staines).

ideas.name: Rules alone do not make an act moral
ideas.text: Capturing a piece in checkers is not immoral, because a moral reading needs some fiction around the action. Švelch quotes a remark that it matters whether you arrange blocks in the 'best' position or save a princess from a monkey (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: Futile choices can still produce guilt
ideas.text: In Silent Hill 2 the player can have the avatar try to save a character who is being attacked but cannot succeed. A reviewer reports guilt at running away and leaving her to die (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: A game can reveal that its player was misled
ideas.text: In BioShock, a radio voice named Atlas asks for help and the player can only do as told. Halfway through, Atlas proves to be the villain and the avatar his puppet (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: Visible point values show who set the rules
ideas.text: In Mass Effect, ending a negotiation peacefully gives 8 Paragon points and killing everyone gives 25 Renegade points. Švelch notes this arbitrariness shows the consequences come from the designers, and that the points can unlock missions, so a player may choose for gameplay reasons (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: Five weaknesses of moral choices in games
ideas.text: Švelch lists choices that are imposed, quantified, polarised, predictable and inconsistent. In Mass Effect choices come almost only in conversation, so the game announces that a moral choice is coming (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: A balanced outcome keeps the choice about morals
ideas.text: In BioShock, saving or harvesting the Little Sisters ends up balanced in gameplay terms, because saving them is later compensated with gifts. A player therefore cannot choose on rewards alone (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: Delaying consequences stops players undoing them
ideas.text: Players save and reload after a major decision to see the result. The Witcher delays some consequences by hours of play so a player cannot calculate or reverse the outcome (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: Playing styles decide how much a player is engaged
ideas.text: Strategizing, meta-gaming and exploration are driven by gameplay and tend to reduce moral engagement, while honest play and role-playing are driven by the fiction. A player may switch between them, for example by killing innocents in Baldur's Gate II to lower a reputation score and hire evil companions (chapter by Jaroslav Švelch).

ideas.name: A game world can have ethics of its own
ideas.text: Simkins says killing an orc in Neverwinter Nights has no moral weight outside the game, but inside it the player may be hailed as a hero for saving a town or called a villain for killing a peaceful orc. The player is no more at fault than the writers of a television drama are for their lead character (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: Games can be a place to practise living with a set of values
ideas.text: Simkins says a player can try one set of values, find the world reacts to them, then start again with another set and compare. Out of the game the consequences of an act stay with the person (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: Principles are easy to build in; practice is harder
ideas.text: Simkins says a designer can state principle through mechanics, such as the alignment on two axes of 'good' against 'evil' and law against chaos in Planescape: Torment or the Karma counter in Fallout 3. Showing the practices of a culture, and letting a player take it up, is harder because much of the work falls to the player (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: Playing from the inside gives a critical view
ideas.text: Simkins says a reader of a novel or a film viewer judges as an outsider, but a player acts as an insider. When the character's choices are reflected back at the player, the player can examine their own ethics in light of the character's situation (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: A decision that saves resources can overshadow the story
ideas.text: In Final Fantasy VI the player may let a character stay on a bridge to hold off enemies or may help him. One participant chose the story that felt in character, then felt cheated on learning he could have kept the character and his resources, since this made the right answer a matter of winning (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: A death carries more weight when others react
