ideas.text: In the same game, the character's daughter appears later in the party and pines for her father, so the player's choice shows up in another character's life. Simkins calls this mirroring (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: A freedom to choose is not a freedom to control the outcome
ideas.text: In Oblivion a gladiator champion asks to be slain, and the game does not let the player refuse. Simkins suggests the game could have let the player refuse and had the arena officials respond, since freedom in a game, as in life, is the freedom to make choices and not to control their results (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: A simple score can clash with a complicated world
ideas.text: Fallout 3 has a Karma counter that rates a character as 'good' or 'evil', yet the setting is a lawless wasteland where most people just survive. Simkins notes a radio host and other broadcasts that comment on the player's deeds from several viewpoints, and suggests each community could give its own opinion of the player's actions (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: The four design principles need to fit each other
ideas.text: Simkins finds that the games players liked most often fall short in one of consequence, mirroring, social context or freedom, and that a design suffers when one part contradicts the others. A detailed reaction system beside a clumsy score is one example (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: In multiplayer play the boundary around the game needs upkeep
ideas.text: Simkins says that in a game with other people, in-game acts affect real players, so how far antisocial play is allowed has to rest on the consent of everyone affected. He says a magic circle around a game does not hold itself up and a boundary has to be maintained (chapter by David Simkins).

ideas.name: Reward for observing and predicting keeps a closed system going
ideas.text: In Plato's cave, prisoners win honours for correctly predicting the shadows, and so they would kill anyone who tried to free them. Travis says a game that rewards choices within a set range works the same way, and teaches nothing beyond the ethics it already assumes (chapter by Roger Travis).

ideas.name: Light or dark choices can lead to the same result
ideas.text: In Knights of the Old Republic the player decides to kill or befriend a character, and the game turns that into points and whether she can join the party. Travis notes neither changes the player's ability to finish, and even the double ending brings victory by either path within one light-and-dark system (chapter by Roger Travis).

ideas.name: A game's boundary can be used to comment
ideas.text: Travis says Oblivion tries to widen choice until the edges of its system disappear. Grand Theft Auto IV shows that its hero Niko has no choice but to commit the violent acts that carry the story, which begins to use the boundary as a comment on the game (chapter by Roger Travis).

ideas.name: Two outcomes can be equal in play while differing in story
ideas.text: Travis argues that Bioshock offers a choice to harvest or save the Little Sisters but pays the player the same either way. He reads this as a point the game makes about choices in games, and a later scene, where the player is made to disarm a device on a command phrase, shows the player was controlled all along (chapter by Roger Travis).

ideas.name: Other players can break open a closed game
ideas.text: Travis says players of World of Warcraft who advise each other on quests often reach a deeper understanding of how its rules and stories work. In the cave comparison, any fellow prisoner might be the one who has left and come back (chapter by Roger Travis).

ideas.name: Real life lacks the map a game gives
ideas.text: Nordlinger compares living without a philosophy to playing World of Warcraft without a quest-guide add-on. In the game a player knows why they chase each task, and in life people often do not know why they go to school or follow a career (chapter by John Nordlinger).

ideas.name: Online games hold players by their own choices
ideas.text: Nordlinger made a short film in which three players in Everquest 2 are told by a voice from the kitchen to go outside. He presents their hold on them as compelling community, competition, story and abstract reward, like the shadows in Plato's cave (chapter by John Nordlinger).

ideas.name: The same moment of pressure can go two ways
ideas.text: Nordlinger sets Arjuna's doubt before battle in the Bhagavad Gita, which ends in understanding, against Leeroy Jenkins, whose group rushes into a fight and fails. He adds that in a game the player can repeat the attempt and try every alternative (chapter by John Nordlinger).

ideas.name: Power is easy to show where reward and punishment are quick
ideas.text: Nordlinger describes a high-level player killing low-level newcomers for no gain. He uses Nietzsche's idea that only punishment holds back base desires, and says this shows more plainly in a game, where consequences are faster and power is clearer than in life (chapter by John Nordlinger).

ideas.name: Playing is testing a guess
ideas.text: Hoffman, using Gee, describes play as trying something, forming a guess about what it means, trying again and accepting or rethinking the guess. She calls this the same procedure as the scientific method and also the root of curiosity and learning (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

ideas.name: A game can be an argument
ideas.text: Hoffman notes Monopoly began in 1903 as The Landlord Game by Elizabeth Magie, to illustrate the consequences of land monopoly. The set of play interactions under a rule set carries that thesis (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

ideas.name: In most games death means failure
ideas.text: Designer Randy Smith, quoted by Hoffman, says that because games are about goals that are scored, and inability to reach them leads to failure, a game's version of death is often a light nuisance. Death works as a difficulty adjuster that penalises without making the player quit (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

ideas.name: The same loss feels different when a character is long-lived
ideas.text: In single-player games a character is soon replaced, but in a persistent online game a player may spend months on a chosen character, so its death feels personal. Some players ask for permadeath for that reason, though Hoffman cites a survey where 2 percent asked for harsher death penalties (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

ideas.name: Showing the aftermath changes what a kill means
ideas.text: In Super Columbine Massacre RPG! the bodies of victims stay on the map, where in most games they vanish. Hoffman says this, and the use of real photographs, makes the player look at their act, and that it upset many players because it broke the usual rule that death means temporary failure (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

ideas.name: Games let a player beat death in a made world
ideas.text: Hoffman uses Ernest Becker's argument that people deal with fear of death through heroism, immortality and aggression against rival beliefs. She reads a game's hero and its repeated defeat of death as that same drive (chapter by Erin Hoffman).

ideas.name: Judge the activity, not the game
ideas.text: Phelps says claims such as 'games are good' or 'games are harmful' fail to say what is measured. He proposes the unit of study be the activity that arises where a game's design, the social practices around it and the player's own purpose meet (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: Slowing a player down can be a design aim
ideas.text: In Passage the player has five minutes and watches a character age. In The Graveyard an old woman walks slowly and takes minutes to sit on a bench, and a player who wants to rush has to wait. Phelps argues both ask the player "why?" in the face of hurried activity (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: Playing the other side can remove stereotypes
ideas.text: Phelps describes playing the two shooters in Super Columbine Massacre RPG! and coming to see them and their victims as people rather than as media images. He quotes Gee that a game lets you experience the other from the inside (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: A game can let a player find the system's flaw
ideas.text: In Vigilance 1.0 the player watches a town through surveillance and corrects citizens, and crime seems to fall while paranoia rises. Phelps cites Bogost's reading that the player sees the harm of constant watching by running the system (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: A world can mourn by leaving something out
ideas.text: In Flower the player steers a petal across fields while the flower, stuck on a city windowsill, dreams. Phelps places it with works that show the absence of nature to counter what Jared Diamond calls landscape amnesia (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: A game can be like a lesson it comments on
ideas.text: In Portal the player solves test chambers set by an authoritarian voice that promises cake. Phelps felt the early chambers were chore-like and the choice to disobey the voice in the last chamber was the first real choice, and he reads the game as a parody of testing and drilling in school (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: A game that expects one reading of its scoring can mislead
ideas.text: Phelps tried to work out the hidden rule for unlocking songs in Rock Band 2 and stopped listening to his friends. His group later found they had unlocked every song already, and the scoring had hidden that (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: Play with others can draw out a person's voice
ideas.text: Phelps cites Mary Watkins that play and dialogue let a child see through others' eyes and dream of what has not yet happened. He also cites Justine Cassell's five tenets for games: hand design authority to users, value subjective knowledge, allow many kinds of users, give users a tool to express their voice, and encourage collaboration (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: Group goals force different play styles to meet
ideas.text: Thomas and Brown, cited by Phelps, note that in World of Warcraft high-level tasks can only be finished by large groups of players with different play styles. Around Portal, fans fill different kinds of roles, such as map makers, speed runners, story theorists and comic sharers, matching Bartle's four player types (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: A simulation needs the player to be in it
ideas.text: Dörner's town simulations had players act as a mayor over ten turns and found that players who asked why questions reached higher scores. Phelps argues they were missing the subjunctive, since a player in absolute control of a town is not implicated by its outcome (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: Rules that persist make a system learnable
ideas.text: Phelps names three properties of rule sets: serialised, so events build on earlier ones; persistent, so rules stay the same and any change can be seen; and interactive, so the world responds to the player. Constantly changing rules would not allow systemic thinking (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: Plague makes the player carry the result of a choice
ideas.text: In Quest Atlantis's Plague a player gathers views on a scientist's plan to make a living organism to test cures, and the townspeople respond to the player's decisions. Phelps lists guiding questions for such design, including how a perspective is legitimised through player choice and how consequences are made meaningful (chapter by David Phelps).

ideas.name: The same game can draw out different reasoning
ideas.text: Gilbert interviewed fourteen young online gamers and sorted them into three models. One player used two characters, a nice one and an evil one who scams her cousin, and cited only a rule against giving out personal information, while another considered the whole game community (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: "It's just a game" shrinks the circle of concern
ideas.text: Three players Gilbert calls individualistic all justified their acts that way. One player altered a game's design to get free items, and when the company acted, it deleted the accounts of everyone who had traded with her (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: Fairness can be applied narrowly
ideas.text: A player gave a prized item to a stranger who won a dice roll rather than to a friend who begged for it, because he would have been angry if treated the other way. Later he took kills by tagging every monster first, since the rules allowed it, which others disliked (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: A rule can be judged by what it does for the community
ideas.text: A fifteen-year-old explained that a limit on trade values in Runescape stopped real-world trading edges, but also meant players could no longer set prices themselves. Gilbert counts this as thinking about why a rule exists, beyond fairness (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: Belonging to a group seems to widen concern
ideas.text: None of the three individualistic players was in an in-game group, while all communal players except two newcomers or less-tested ones were. A group needs members to be considerate and keep roles, and Gilbert suggests it is a stepping stone beyond the self (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: Early help from another player may set an example
ideas.text: Two of three players who got 'strong' help from another online player fit the communal model, and most who were excluded or taken advantage of did not. Gilbert guesses players copy those who helped them, and that the game design could reward helping new players (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: Talk about a game extends its effect
ideas.text: Gilbert says one of the easiest steps is to encourage young people to talk about ethical issues they meet in games, because his interviews gave a space for that reflection that his subjects eagerly filled (chapter by Sam Gilbert).

ideas.name: Games in a home bring a new gathering place
ideas.text: The Wii was placed with the main family television, unlike earlier consoles kept in children's rooms. Bryant and Drell say this puts a game system where families gather, as earlier with television, and where patterns of interaction form (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: The child often picks the game
ideas.text: Family ritual theory assumes a parent sets rituals, but Bryant and Drell note video game choice is more often made by the child, both at purchase and at play. They say the theory has to allow influence to run from child to parent (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: Games can model sportsmanship
ideas.text: In sports games some show taunting and 'poor' sportsmanship and others show encouragement. The authors add that the way family members treat each other during play also becomes a model for interaction outside it (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: A family game has five design questions
ideas.text: Bryant and Drell turn family game design into five questions: who will play, where, what, why and how. Each one has a list of prompts, for example whether the game encourages independence or interdependence, and who the characters are (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: Designing for the least experienced player pushes new ideas
ideas.text: A family game has to work for the weakest game player while keeping the skilled one interested. The authors say this can push developers toward fresh play; children under about eight bring small hands, simple problem solving and a small vocabulary (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: Pairs can be easier to design for than whole families
ideas.text: A game for preschoolers can be made for one child and one carer, with simple play and one-to-one teaching. Teen boys often say they enjoy one-to-one play with a father, and fewer skill levels need covering (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: The device decides who can play
ideas.text: The PlayStation 2 looked old to developers but sat in about 43 percent of homes, often with young parents. The Wii was placed in main living areas and had the highest adult use, so it suited play across ages (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: A simple controller makes room for beginners
ideas.text: Dance pads, balance boards and plastic instruments let people who do not read game controllers join in. The device adds cost for the developer and the buyer, and it also marks the game out in a crowded market (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: Setup effort works against a family habit
ideas.text: A game with long setup is less likely to become a weekly ritual. An online world that needs only a connection can become a weekly meeting between a grandparent and a grandchild in different states (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: A shared goal can carry a value
ideas.text: Instead of individual points, a game can give a collective goal that players donate to. In Coins for Change, children's points were pooled to decide how real money went to charities, which gave players a reason to talk about values (chapter by J. Alison Bryant and Jordana Drell).

ideas.name: Games are agreements about conduct
ideas.text: Khetrapal notes that players are outraged when a partner breaks a stated rule. This shows that play, which looks like pure pleasure, also includes a shared sense of fair behaviour and personal blame (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Challenge at the edge of ability keeps players engaged
ideas.text: Gee's principles, cited by Khetrapal, say a game stays motivating when it works near the limit of the player's skill. Simple problems come first so the player can find a pattern and use it on harder ones (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Showing the other side deepens a moral case
ideas.text: In Covay's study of Dax Cowart, a burned man who asked to stop treatment, learners speak to the patient, nurse, doctor, lawyer and mother. Whatever side a learner picks, the program shows evidence against it (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Writing your own dilemmas raises sensitivity
ideas.text: In ETGAR, students played through dilemmas from school, family, work and more, then wrote their own. Points were made unpredictable on purpose to resemble life, and the study reported gains in moral development (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Four conditions help technology teach
ideas.text: Roschelle and colleagues, cited by Khetrapal, found learning works when students engage actively, work in groups, get frequent feedback and see links to the real world. Khetrapal proposes checking games against these four (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Eyes make a drawing read as a feeling being
ideas.text: Khetrapal cites work showing that giving cartoon characters eyes helps children treat them as living agents with feelings, not machines, which helps children learn about other minds (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Two senses at once can lower load
ideas.text: Presenting animation with spoken narration lets a learner store information in two ways, easing the strain on working memory. Khetrapal cites Mayer's finding that people learned more from both together (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Skill at a game is not proof of understanding
ideas.text: Khetrapal asks for transfer tests: children apply what they learned to a new situation. A child who handles moral problems inside a game may not do so outside it (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: School use of games has practical limits
ideas.text: A UK teachers' report found game content clashed with the curriculum. A survey found teachers needed support materials, lacked time to learn the software, and met school rules that slowed installing it (chapter by Neha Khetrapal).

ideas.name: Feeling able to choose affects moral conduct
ideas.text: Bandura says moral behaviour depends on believing one's choice can matter. In Milgram's study everyone polled said they would have quit, yet only 35 percent of actual participants did (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: Reward and punishment do not explain why an act is wrong
ideas.text: The authors say a player who is only rewarded or punished does not learn why behaviour counts as moral. Reflection, such as that prompted by role play, finds contradictions that build moral reasoning (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: People are easiest to persuade when they know a little
ideas.text: Because well-formed schemata are hard to change, beliefs shift most when a person knows enough to follow an argument but is not yet committed to one view (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: Fables suit how ideas are first stored
ideas.text: In the tortoise and the hare, the characters are nameless and simple, with no side plots. The authors say this keeps the number of elements low, matching the way young minds build early schemata (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: Hearing others narrate turns solo play into social play
ideas.text: Ryokai and Cassell found children told fuller stories and took more points of view after hearing recordings of other children narrating play. The authors conclude that a single-player adventure game can still support social narrative play (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: A lesson has to be part of the plot
ideas.text: Edutainment often placed lessons inside a game that had nothing to do with them. The authors say a moral lesson has to drive the story forward, or it gets in the way of deeper thinking (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: Open worlds leave the moral topic to the players
ideas.text: In Second Life there is no storyline except what residents bring. Gambling and virtual sex caused controversy and were banned or regulated, so whether play turns to moral talk depends on how the world moves from play to reflection (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: A game can support moral thinking but not force it
ideas.text: Games are weak at prescribing beliefs and strong at offering experiences. Players bring their own values, so persuasion depends on how their ideas meet the game's and does not run one way from game to player (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: A shooting game can teach by letting you decline
ideas.text: In September 12, the player can fire a missile or not. Firing destroys what is near and civilians weep and turn into terrorists; the cursor invites a shot, and the lesson lies in whether the player fires (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: Players found grey choices most satisfying
ideas.text: The designers of Fable say they regret the first game's 'good' or 'evil' split. Players had found its morally unclear events most rewarding, so Fable II added greyer choices and personal cost (chapter by Lance Vikaros and Darnel Degand).

ideas.name: Every game is a loop of choice and answer
ideas.text: Swain says all games, solo or multiplayer, turn-based or live, run on a player making a choice and the system responding. By practising the loop, players learn how the system works (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Make the player's action match the real action
ideas.text: In Gran Turismo 4 the player steers, accelerates and brakes as a driver does, with a wheel and pedals if wanted. Practice with no real cost teaches racing skills in detail (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: What a game fails to punish also sends a message
ideas.text: Grand Theft Auto IV does not penalise running over pedestrians, and its makers are accused of saying that such acts are acceptable in real life. Swain uses this as the opposite case to a designed message (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Generic templates teach little about a system
ideas.text: Jenkins and Hinrichs found most educational games failed because they used stock templates such as Pac-Man in place of original rules showing how the topic works. Swain asks for custom mechanics (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Experts give facts, designers turn them into rules
ideas.text: In Peacemaker the team of Israelis, Palestinians and Americans used experts to build about forty real actions per side. The experts shape the system and test it, but the designers write the closed set of rules (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Players can find real strategies without being told
ideas.text: Testers of The Redistricting Game, with no training, started to use packing and cracking at once. Experts in the session were surprised, since the rules led logically to what real redistricters do (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Ranked objectives guide each design choice
ideas.text: Gran Turismo 4 uses real car data to simulate racing; Burnout Paradise uses invented cars and tuning for spectacle. Each game's aim decides how realistic its numbers are (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Start with the cheapest prototype
ideas.text: The Redistricting Game began as a 14 by 20 grid on poster board with coloured sticky notes, built in the second week by four people. Its first play led to a three-hour debate, before any digital work began (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Tension can carry the message
ideas.text: Peacemaker's makers wanted tension because the conflict is delicate and every action has gains and costs. One action per turn, plus gauges that move sharply, communicate that to the player (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Real data adds credibility
ideas.text: Madden uses real passing statistics for real players. The Redistricting Game uses the same map and variables for either party, with only names and jokes changing, and pairs quotes from both sides (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Choosing who the player is carries a value
ideas.text: The SurgeWorld team tried playing a doctor, nurse or commander, then let the player make choices for every group. This shows each role's duties and strains, and in the game triage means labelling some patients unsalvageable (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: Measure learning with before-and-after tests
ideas.text: Swain describes testing players on the topic, having them play, testing again and comparing. He notes that assessing a changing game takes more complex statistics than assessing film or books (chapter by Chris Swain).

ideas.name: A game is safe ground for risk
ideas.text: Rouse argues Grand Theft Auto III works because the harshest result is a restart, so players try acts they would never do in life. Ethics designers can use this for uncomfortable ground (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: Whether a game reaches the self depends on how real and virtual identity relate
ideas.text: If the two are fully separate, a lesson stays inside the game. If they meet, as when a player feels responsible for a character, ethical thinking can carry across (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: Forms that block progress break immersion
ideas.text: In Veritas University, menu-driven forms and visible scoring halted play until the player answered. This encouraged thought but reminded players they were being tested, and the game held players less than the team had hoped (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: Giving two enemies one fate unsettles
ideas.text: In the Knights of Astrus tutorial, a player has to choose the same fate for a bully guard and the guard he bullied: kill them, tie them up or let them go. The authors say this sets the tone that no choice is ideal (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: One ending can hide different routes
ideas.text: Knights of Astrus gates the story so every player reaches one ending and gets the ship repaired. How the parts are obtained depends on the player's choices, which later become material for discussion (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: Learning content and enjoyment need balance
ideas.text: Veritas University ended up heavy on ethics and light on play; Knights of Astrus had polished mechanics and weaker scenarios. The authors say early audience feedback is the way to find the balance (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: Open play and an open question gather more than a test
ideas.text: The first plan for Knights of Astrus was to teach ethical models and compare players' actions with them. Philosophy advisers led the team to leave play open and ask players why they chose, using a journal (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: A game can leave scope for players to write dilemmas
ideas.text: Because Knights of Astrus was built with a map editor and files for dialogue, students in a philosophy course could write their own variants. The authors expect shared play to build a community around the game (chapter by Rudy McDaniel and Stephen M. Fiore).

ideas.name: Letting a player act from today's values shows what the past rewarded
ideas.text: In Mission US the player controls Nat in 1770 but can choose as a modern person would. If the player chases a customs official who kicked him, the game shows the cost; a runaway servant's ad can be refused (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: Adding learning objectives lengthens a game
ideas.text: The Mission US team found each new objective took more play minutes and more budget, and blurred the others. They cut scope and set each day to about twenty minutes so it fit a forty-five minute class (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: A random mix of scenes gives each player a different witness
ideas.text: At the Boston Massacre each player sees four of eight short animations, one from each pair, one favouring Patriots and one Loyalists. That gives sixteen combinations, and a deposition afterwards asks what the player saw (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: Weighting one side can offset a leaning
ideas.text: Expecting students to favour the Patriots, the team made a friendly Loyalist, Constance, and a bullying Patriot, Royce. The authors admit this may have tilted the balance the other way and made some takeaways inaccurate (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: Accuracy is traded against cost and understanding
ideas.text: Historians and developers scored changes for priority and difficulty. The team simplified 1770 speech but avoided modern slang, and showed handwritten items with a click for a modern-font copy, since comprehension came first (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: Students sorted characters by kindness at first
ideas.text: In class, students placed the redcoat Hugh White under Patriot because he was nice to them. Others argued friendliness does not show loyalty, and discussion showed characters can hold competing loyalties (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: Designing is itself ethical reflection
ideas.text: The authors say how a team shows history, people and events reveals its beliefs. Talks between designers, historians, researchers and teachers brought out hidden values, which they urge teams to state openly (chapter by Karen Schrier, James Diamond and David Langendoen).

ideas.name: Ethics comes from play, not from topic
ideas.text: Macklin says Re:Activism is not ethical because its subject is serious. Ethics is created through action in play and how the design responds, so a game has to be played before its meaning shows (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: Serious aims clash with the idea that play changes nothing
ideas.text: Caillois held that play leaves the world as it was. Games for change aim for lasting change, which adds a hard task: they also have to remain enjoyable enough to play (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: A race can crowd out the point of a game
ideas.text: In Re:Activism the first players to rush between sites won; a team that lingered at Stonewall, talked to two strangers and staged a re-enactment ended last. The scoring penalised the team that got the most out of a site (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: A losing result can reveal a design flaw
ideas.text: Macklin's team first thought the game was broken. Then they saw the yellow team's slow play showed what the game could become, and made racing one strategy among others, with fewer sites and more bonus challenges (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: Games take shape through the player
ideas.text: Hocking says a film tells one case and the audience induces a meaning, while a game builds a system in which the player can deduce one. Macklin warns serious games against sliding into delivering fixed facts (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: Street games need ways to show they are games
ideas.text: Matching bandannas marked teams as an organised game. Later runs gave teams a visible video camera in place of hidden phones, and a related game handed passers-by official-looking cards to start play (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: Unwritten social rules can clash with written game rules
ideas.text: In Re:Activism, teams hurried, photographed without asking, or lacked background to explain a petition when a stranger questioned it. Macklin counts these as conflicts between game rules and everyday manners (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: Each live run is another playtest
ideas.text: With event games in public, the context changes every time, and players such as other game designers gave feedback that shaped later versions. Macklin's team plans an open kit so other cities can run their own (chapter by Colleen Macklin).

ideas.name: People expect to act more ethically than they do
ideas.text: In Milgram's study, students predicted at most 3 percent would give the top shock, yet 26 of 40 did. Balzac says people picture themselves acting as they do in an ethics class, calm and informed (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Knowing is not doing under pressure
ideas.text: Sport psychology shows a gap between knowing a skill and using it when tired or distracted. Balzac says ethics needs practice in the same way: notice the problem, recall the rule, check fit and choose (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: An abstract scenario gives the right answer too easily
ideas.text: Balzac says that without personal stakes, almost everyone chooses the ethical option. His pandemic flu games earlier involved calm table talk; adding a chance of catching the flu produced denial and panic (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: A full role reduces anonymity
ideas.text: Players handed a plain role such as a CIA agent broke the rules more often than those given detailed characters. A developed persona frees a player to try things while still keeping them tied to the role's sense of right (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Players may become what they fight
ideas.text: In Operation: Atlantis, the agents of SHIELD began as detectives and by the last days framed suspects, kidnapped and killed. The enemy, SWORD, had been almost harmless and law-abiding (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: A game can move players toward ethical action
ideas.text: In Nexus, a mass murderer on the run made a series of sensible choices that led him to help find a cure for a plague. By the end he could not bring himself to double-cross the others (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Conflicting goals produce dilemmas
ideas.text: When rivals such as the CIA and KGB had no goals beyond stopping a villain, they cooperated within hours. Balzac added detail and gave each group goals that could not all be met so tension returned (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Start with plots and goals, not the dilemma
ideas.text: Balzac says dilemmas come from complex plots and clashing goals. Starting with the dilemma narrows imagination too early; a well-built scenario has as many main characters as players (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: How fast players solve problems is a signal
ideas.text: If a long dispute ends in minutes, the answer was too simple or nothing was at stake. If players hand over resources quickly, the resources are not valued highly enough (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Games of twenty to eighty players suit this method
ideas.text: Smaller games lack enough interaction for dilemmas to appear naturally; beyond eighty or a hundred, players split into sub-plots and the bigger picture is lost (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Humour and open questions open a debrief
ideas.text: A remark that SHIELD subverted democracy to stop villains provokes defence when said sternly and can be heard when said lightly. Balzac asks open questions and repeats players' own words in a tone of real interest (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: Neutral observers show how a dilemma looks from outside
ideas.text: Shadows watched the pandemic flu game and later asked players why they chose. Players said they were caught up in the moment, and one doctor noted that no drill had ever made doctors fall ill (chapter by Stephen R. Balzac).

ideas.name: A designer's possibility space can narrow without notice
ideas.text: Brathwaite says twenty-five years of ratings letters and sales worries made her ask only whether a game was fun, how it would be rated and whether stores would sell it (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: The rules are the game
ideas.text: Brathwaite says the board, pieces, graphics and viewpoint exist only to let players act out the rules. She typed the rules for Train on a Nazi-era typewriter, since any other way felt like cheating (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: Built-in ambiguity makes players complicit
ideas.text: In Train, the derail rule leaves open what happens to passengers who will not re-board. Players have been seen to kill them, save them, hide them in a pocket or send them to Denmark (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: A message can sit in what players do
ideas.text: Sharp says Brathwaite shows and tells nothing in Train. Players pack tokens into boxcars and move them to a station, and the horror arrives from their own acts and the word on the terminus card (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: Players with prior knowledge may resist the aim
ideas.text: Some players who knew or guessed Train's subject derailed cars or made refuges they called Denmarks. The rules allowed it, so the game held more than one reading (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: A game that needs no play can still spread its idea
ideas.text: Sharp notes that people who only read about Train, or watched others play, still discussed its mechanics. He asks whether a game of this kind needs to be played at all to be valued (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: Showing in a gallery has both a gain and a cost
ideas.text: A gallery can lift games out of the idea that they are mass entertainment and invite careful attention. It can also turn them into objects to look at, not touch, and reach only people who already agree (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: Two traps weaken serious games
ideas.text: Sharp names embedding a fixed rhetorical position in the decisions, and modelling the system poorly. He says Train avoids both by modelling a system and not telling the player which choice is right (chapter by Brenda Brathwaite and John Sharp).

ideas.name: Which games reached number one
ideas.text: Paths of Glory, Tigris and Euphrates, Puerto Rico, Agricola, Twilight Struggle, Pandemic Legacy: Season 1 and Gloomhaven are the seven games that held first place on BoardGameGeek between 2001 and 2022. The author could not check the source list against other records, since none were public.

ideas.name: Reading the rules gives more than the database
ideas.text: BoardGameGeek's tags were not complete enough for the analysis, so the author read the rules and played the games. Set collection is not tagged for every game, and the author added it for Puerto Rico and Twilight Struggle after reading the rules. The paper recommends analysing games directly.

ideas.name: Card play is the common core
ideas.text: Card play is the core mechanism in three of the seven games and tile placement records players' decisions on the board. Dice rolling is less common among these games, although it is the most common mechanism on BoardGameGeek as a whole.

ideas.name: Players handle mostly cards
ideas.text: Cards are the components players handle most and they dictate the actions available. They are played from the hand to add or remove tiles and bits on the board, as in Twilight Struggle, Pandemic Legacy and Gloomhaven.

ideas.name: Hexagons suit realistic territory
ideas.text: Hexagonal grids appear in games that model territory more realistically, because the distance between the centres of adjacent hexagons is always the same. Square grids are simpler and appear in many older games.

ideas.name: Agricola shows chained mechanisms
ideas.text: In Agricola the core action is worker placement. A worker on a shared space leads the player on to tile placement, managing bits, playing cards and collecting resources, and set collection comes in during production, conversion and scoring.

ideas.name: Randomness is low or medium and asymmetry recurs
ideas.text: The seven games have low or medium randomness, and player asymmetry comes up again and again. The author reads this as support for player agency and strategic depth.

ideas.name: Conflict is shrinking
ideas.text: The paper says that apart from the two wargames, the games have no direct conflict between players: Puerto Rico and Agricola compete constructively, and Pandemic Legacy and Gloomhaven are cooperative, so all players can lose together. The author reads this as a move away from the classic form of player elimination.

ideas.name: Games are getting shorter, and complexity stays high
ideas.text: The more recent number one games tend to play in one to two hours, while complexity is usually above 3.5 out of 5.

ideas.name: Game type labels are contested
ideas.text: The paper notes doubts about calling Tigris and Euphrates a Eurogame because of its constant conflict, and about Gloomhaven, which BoardGameGeek treats as thematic. Some players also say Twilight Struggle is not a wargame because it lacks military tactics.

ideas.name: Progression runs through connected spaces
ideas.text: The author proposes that showing progress through networks and grids of connected, ranked spaces is a possible compound ludeme in modern board games, handed from game to game and changing the play.

ideas.name: Components and themes fit the ludeme idea less well
ideas.text: Physical components, colour schemes and themes seemed less related to the ludemic approach than board structure did, but they matter for analysing a game as a system.

ideas.name: Ludemes pull a system apart
ideas.text: The paper found it confusing to analyse a game as a system when the ludemic approach tends to isolate single elements, and that the ludemic approach gave less clear results than expected.

ideas.name: BoardGameGeek leans towards long games
ideas.text: BoardGameGeek users tend to prefer long, complex games, some taking over two hours to play and nearly an hour to explain, which the paper treats as a bias in the ratings.

ideas.name: Rules vary by place and household
ideas.text: The author found that rules differ from country to country, region to region and even street to street, so she drew on family memories as well as official rulebooks. Only tournament and gambling games have fixed rules. The rest is settled by the people at the table, as when a family agrees what happens if a Charades player says the word aloud.

ideas.name: Penalties can be softened for beginners
ideas.text: The book leaves out most penalties for breaking rules so that an eight-year-old playing Charades for the first time can have a do-over. A rule that ends a turn or a game is also a choice about who is playing.

ideas.name: Many variations come from changing one rule
ideas.text: Giveaway Checkers keeps every rule of checkers but flips the aim to losing all your pieces. Italian, Spanish and International Checkers each change the board size, how kings move or which jump is forced. A new game can be a single changed rule on an old one.

ideas.name: Pieces that gain powers give a race to aim for
ideas.text: A checkers piece that reaches the far row is crowned and can then move backward. The book says games are often won by the first king, so players race one piece across while guarding their own back row. A reward at the far end of the board shapes how every piece moves.

ideas.name: The same pieces can be given different powers
ideas.text: Chess pieces differ in how they move and capture. The knight is the only one that can jump, the bishop stays on one colour, the king moves one square. The book describes each piece by placement, moves and captures. That list shows what makes one piece different from another.

ideas.name: Starting with fewer pieces teaches the game
ideas.text: The chess variations The Pawns Game, The Queen and Pawn Game and The King and Pawn Game take away most of the pieces. Players learn how pawns and the king work before meeting the whole set. Go on a 9x9 board is offered for the same reason.

ideas.name: Handicaps let unequal players share a board
ideas.text: In five-player Chinese Checkers one player moves into an empty corner, which helps them, so a less experienced player such as a young child takes that place. Matching partners by size in Chicken Fights is the same idea. A rule can be adjusted for who is sitting down.

ideas.name: Scoring methods can differ yet agree
ideas.text: Chinese and Japanese Go count territory in different ways. One counts occupied points and the other counts captured stones, yet the book says they usually give a comparable result. Two rules can lead to the same winner.

ideas.name: Scoring can reward rare answers
ideas.text: In Categories a word scores one point for every other player who did not write it. If everyone wrote bear, nobody scores. This pushes each player to guess what the others will not think of, and so to avoid the obvious answer.

ideas.name: Bluffing needs a way to check
ideas.text: In Hollywood Connections a player can challenge a link between two actors and ask for the film. If the bluffer cannot name one, a point is lost, and if the film is real the challenger loses. A bluff is only worth making where the other side can test it.

ideas.name: Hidden information drives social games
ideas.text: In Mafia and Killer a few players know who they are and the rest do not. The Moderator controls who learns what, and the dead can watch but not talk. All the play is talking, accusing and voting.

ideas.name: A rule can add roles to fit group size
ideas.text: Mafia suggests one-third to one-quarter of players as Mafia, and Killer sets the number of kills by player count. Extra roles such as Witness or Masons are added only when the group is large. Rules can be written as a table of settings that change with the number of people.

ideas.name: Rotating seats stops one team winning for ever
ideas.text: In Bunco the winning team stays at the head table and the losing team moves down, while partners are split and re-paired each round. Over six rounds everyone plays with and against everyone. Movement rules shape who meets whom.

ideas.name: Variations come from groups, not designers
ideas.text: The author says Bunco, which spread by word of mouth, has more rule variations than any other game in the book. Groups add their own prizes, scorecards and wipe-out rules. A game that is passed on freely gets adapted to each group's taste.

ideas.name: Questions that split the field help guessing games
ideas.text: In Twenty Questions the most effective questions cut the remaining possibilities roughly in half. Opening with animal, vegetable or mineral does this. A guessing game with a limited number of turns rewards questions that narrow the field quickly.

ideas.name: Varied guesses give more information
ideas.text: In Jotto the book advises against guessing a word that differs from the last by one letter. A quite different word tests more letters at once. Each turn tells the player something, and how much depends on the guess.

ideas.name: Elimination can leave players with nothing to do
ideas.text: Musical Chairs removes a player and a chair each round. A pamphlet in Britain urged teachers to drop it because it favoured the biggest and heaviest children. The variation Musical Laps removes chairs but keeps everyone in, so no one waits out.

ideas.name: A prerequisite order gives structure to a dice game
ideas.text: In Beetle a player needs a 1 for the body before anything else, and a 2 for the head before feelers or eyes. A roll that cannot be used is wasted. Rules about what comes first turn a plain roll into a build.

ideas.name: Safe zones give a chase game its shape
ideas.text: Fox and Geese gives geese a safe centre once the fox leaves it, and the book says the game is more riotous without one. Capture the Flag has a jail that can be reached by a teammate's touch. Where players can rest and be rescued decides how the chase goes.

ideas.name: Rescue rules keep captured players in the game
ideas.text: In Capture the Flag and Hide and Seek a captured player waits in jail or at home base until a teammate frees them. A rescuer can free only one at a time, and if the rescuer is caught they join the jail. Capture does not have to mean leaving the game.

ideas.name: Chasing games turn on how a player gets caught
ideas.text: In Ringoleavio a captured hider has to be held until the hunter says a set phrase. In Hide and Seek a hider can be caught just by being spotted and named. In Tag, a touch is enough. How capture works sets how fast a game of chase goes.

ideas.name: A game can end by running out of players or by running out of time
ideas.text: Red Rover ends when one team has won all the players, or at a set time, when the bigger team wins. Capture the Flag ends when a flag is captured, or at a time limit, when the team with more prisoners wins. A time limit needs its own way of deciding the winner.

ideas.name: Long games get a shorter rule
ideas.text: Kick the Can can go on if jailbreaks keep freeing captured players, so the book makes the first player caught three times It. Freeze Tag can drag on if frozen players are thawed too often, so the book allows them to stay frozen. A rule can be added when play stops moving toward an end.

ideas.name: Moves that free others change a chase game
ideas.text: In Kick the Can a free hider can kick the can and free every captured player at once. In Ringoleavio one touch of the base and a shout sets all prisoners running. One free action can undo all the work of the seeker.

ideas.name: Capturing can turn a player into a helper
ideas.text: In Sharks and Minnows, Dragon Tag and Blob Tag a tagged player joins the chasers. The group doing the chasing gets bigger as the group being chased gets smaller. Each catch makes the next one easier.

ideas.name: Penalty letters spread out the cost of mistakes
ideas.text: In Spud and Ghost a player who is hit or caught gets one letter of the game's name. Reaching the last letter ends their game. The loss builds up over rounds, and the player who got a letter often becomes the next Caller.

ideas.name: Less experienced players can be moved into easier roles
ideas.text: Johnny Ride a Pony puts the lightest player at the wall as the anchor of the pony. In Chicken Fights partners are matched by size. In Chinese Checkers a younger child takes the open corner. The roles on a team can be given out on purpose.

ideas.name: Attacking the target can cost the attacker
ideas.text: In Skully, hitting an opponent's cap earns the shooter extra boxes, and the cap in No Man's Land is stuck there until another player knocks it out. In marbles, a shooter left in the inner circle becomes a target and its owner can lose all the marbles won. A player who is ahead is easier to attack.

ideas.name: Players can set the distance of a game by setting lines
ideas.text: In Over-the-Line players choose a pole, streetlight or shirt as the lines for single, double, triple and home run, and a ball that passes a line puts an imaginary runner on that base. A game can be played on any street because the players mark the board themselves.

ideas.name: Race games can use public things as pieces
ideas.text: In Are We There Yet? players spot licence plates from states along a route, and only one player can claim each plate. From A to Z uses signs and trucks. The board is whatever passes the car window, and a first-come rule settles who owns a find.

ideas.name: A game can be played for rivalry or for company
ideas.text: The book offers From A to Z and the travelling scavenger hunt as cooperative games, with one list and no winner, for families who want less sibling rivalry. The same equipment gives a different game when the aim changes from beating others to finishing together.

ideas.name: Tie-breaking rules need to be simple
ideas.text: In the Licence Plate Game two words of the same length are separated by which comes first in the alphabet, so clot beats colt. A tie in Anagrams goes to the longer word, and then to a vote. A fixed rule for ties ends arguments quickly.

ideas.name: Only one side can score at a time
ideas.text: In badminton, only the serving side scores. If the server loses a rally, the other side gets the serve but no point. A point therefore has to be won twice, once by gaining the serve and once by winning a rally on it.

ideas.name: A foul can count as a strike but never as the last one
ideas.text: In baseball the first two foul balls count as strikes, but a foul cannot be a third strike unless caught in the air. The rule stops a batter being put out by hitting the ball in an awkward direction, while still adding a cost to each foul.

ideas.name: A cost for a risk can be spread over the game
ideas.text: The book notes that stealing a base brings both gains, such as distracting the pitcher and forcing errors, and the cost of being caught. Experts think the gains can sometimes outweigh the cost. A risky move is worth including when it can pay for itself.

ideas.name: Scoring can wait for later moves
ideas.text: In bowling a spare adds the next roll and a strike adds the next two, so a frame's score cannot be written until later rolls happen. The last frame gives extra rolls, which is why the top score is twelve strikes instead of ten. A reward can be delayed and still be fair.

ideas.name: An exact target changes which move scores
ideas.text: In Twenty-one basketball, a player on 20 points has to miss a foul shot on purpose, so as to score the last point from a rebound. Darts needs the last throw to be a double that brings the score to exactly zero. Exact totals make a bigger score no use.

ideas.name: Losing all you have gathered raises the stakes
ideas.text: In 3-2-1 a player who misses all three shots in a turn loses every point built up. In Skully, a cap stuck in No Man's Land waits to be knocked out. A penalty that wipes out progress makes careful play and risky play both worth thinking about.

ideas.name: Letters give losers a slow, visible countdown
ideas.text: In HORSE each miss on a copied shot gives a letter, and the first player to spell the word loses. Players can see how near the end they are. The same device appears in Ghost and Spud.

ideas.name: The leader of a round sets the task
ideas.text: In HORSE the player who makes a shot decides what the other has to copy. If the first shooter misses, the right to set the shot passes over. The player in the lead picks the difficulty.

ideas.name: Equipment can be arranged to cut down luck
ideas.text: The numbers on a dartboard are in a seemingly random order, placed in 1896 by a carpenter so that small numbers sit beside large ones. A near miss on the 20 hits a 1 or a 5. The layout punishes loose aim and lessens lucky shots.

ideas.name: Rewards for hitting can be combined or limited
ideas.text: In croquet a player who scores a wicket and hits a ball in the same stroke gets only the bonus for the hit. Scoring two wickets in one stroke earns one bonus. Rules about stacking rewards keep one lucky stroke from running away with a turn.

ideas.name: A finished player can stay in as a threat
ideas.text: In Poison croquet a player who completes the course stays on as a poison ball that can remove any other ball by hitting it. Poison balls are removed by being hit or by passing through any wicket. A player who finishes early goes on to hunt the others.

ideas.name: A game scales to the number of people
ideas.text: Bocce splits the eight balls so that one player throws four, two players throw two each, or four players throw one each. Croquet gives each player one, two or three balls depending on the numbers. Basketball half-court games add a referee or teams of two when more people come.

ideas.name: Rules for small groups replace missing roles
ideas.text: Baseball with fewer players lets the second baseman double as right fielder, and the batting team supply its own catcher. Wiffle Ball uses imaginary runners instead of bases. A game can be written so that missing positions are covered.

ideas.name: Players can police their own fouls
ideas.text: In the basketball games in the book, the offensive player calls his own fouls. The book also drops penalties for a croquet ball played out of turn and simply returns it. Informal games lean on trust and quick fixes in place of referees.

ideas.name: Rules change with time
ideas.text: The early Knickerbocker rules from 1845 let a fielder get a runner out by hitting him with the ball, called for an underhand pitch and gave the win to the first side to reach 21 runs. Hitting the runner was later outlawed. Rules of famous games were once different.

ideas.name: Letting players choose whether to take part
ideas.text: The book says dodgeball can be played by all as long as everyone gets to choose whether to play. A game with a danger of being hit works only for people who agreed to risk it.

ideas.name: Whole teams can be eliminated, or players can be brought back
ideas.text: In basic Dodgeball a hit player is out. In Prison Dodgeball a player who is out waits on the side and returns when a teammate catches a ball. In Dr. Dodgeball a fallen player gets up when the doctor tags them. How elimination works decides how long each player waits.

ideas.name: A hit can have a graded cost
ideas.text: Army Dodgeball makes a hit on an arm or leg disable that limb for the rest of the game, while a hit to the head or body puts the player out. The loss grows with each injury instead of being all or nothing.

ideas.name: Home scoring and official scoring can differ
ideas.text: Horseshoes at home gives 3 points for a ringer and 1 for a leaner. Official play ignores leaners and cancels ringers thrown by both players. A simple scoring rule helps beginners and a more complex one tests finer skill.

ideas.name: Cancelling can stop runaway scoring
ideas.text: In official horseshoes, one ringer each cancels, and two each cancels, so only the difference in ringers counts. Points are earned by being ahead of the other player in that round.

ideas.name: Winning by a margin makes the end of a game open
ideas.text: Table tennis has to be won by two points, so a 20-19 score may go on to 22-20. Badminton and volleyball use the same margin. A game may not end at the first moment someone reaches the total.

ideas.name: Taking turns to serve evens out chances
ideas.text: Table tennis players each serve for two points regardless of who wins them, and before 2001 they alternated every five. In doubles the order of serve passes round the four players. A fixed rotation gives everyone equal turns at the privilege.

ideas.name: A rule can reduce the advantage of going first
ideas.text: In tetherball the server can be made to wait until the receiver hits the ball or the ball wraps four times. The book says this evens out the advantage of serving, and can even work against the server.

ideas.name: A move can help the opponent now to help yourself later
ideas.text: In tetherball a player facing an awkward ball can make a sacrifice wrap, hitting it once toward the opponent so as to set up an easy hit the other way. Giving up ground for one move can pay off on the next.

ideas.name: Field size can change the rule
ideas.text: The book says touch football can have fewer downs on smaller fields and more downs on larger ones. With an odd number of players one person can be quarterback for both sides. Rules about attempts can be set to match the space.

ideas.name: Handicapping by weight keeps teams close
ideas.text: International tug-of-war puts team weight into nine categories, from Ultra Featherweight to Catchweight with no limit, and allows one substitute who weighs the same or less. A race of strength is made equal by matching totals.

ideas.name: Players can referee themselves under an honour code
ideas.text: In Ultimate Frisbee players call their own fouls and line violations, and a disputed call can be replayed. The game's philosophy, called the Spirit of the Game, puts fair play first. Some games add observers who judge only when asked.

ideas.name: A player who cannot run has to pass
ideas.text: In Ultimate a player holding the disc may only pivot, has ten seconds to throw, and a step is a turnover. Taking away running forces every move to go through a teammate.

ideas.name: Rotation shares out the positions
ideas.text: In volleyball a team that wins the serve rotates one place clockwise, so every player serves and takes each spot at the net. Rotation removes the chance of a player stuck in one role.

ideas.name: Two ways of scoring change who can come back
ideas.text: Sideout scoring in volleyball lets only the serving team score. Rally point scoring awards the point to whoever wins the rally. The second makes every rally count and tends to shorten a game.

ideas.name: Common house rules can be written once for many games
ideas.text: The book's General Rules fix who deals, how the deck is cut, that dealing goes clockwise, and that aces are high. A play out of turn stands unless another player asks for a retraction. A shared set of defaults leaves each game only its differences to explain.

ideas.name: A chain of payments can decide a game by luck
ideas.text: In Beggar My Neighbour a face card makes the next player pay one to four cards, and a face card in the payment reverses the debt. Nobody makes a decision. The book calls it a game of chance more than skill.

ideas.name: The dealer has a different job from the players
ideas.text: In blackjack players bet only against the dealer, who plays last and wins ties. A natural for a player passes the deal to them. The roles are unequal and rotate.

ideas.name: Bidding turns a card game into a conversation
ideas.text: Bridge bids tell a partner about a hand in a few moves and each bid has to outrank the last, like an auction. A point count by Charles Goren turns the cards in a hand into a number to bid on.

ideas.name: Partners play opposite roles with shared information
ideas.text: In Bridge the declarer's partner lays down a hand face up, and the declarer plays both. Two people are on one team but only one of them makes the choices.

ideas.name: Past success can raise the stakes
ideas.text: In Bridge a side that has won a game is vulnerable, so game bonuses and penalties for failing go up. The score at the table changes how risky the next bid is.

ideas.name: A turn can make a plan, and the opponent can break it
ideas.text: In Casino a player can build a pile and call it, meaning to capture it next turn. The other player can capture it first with a matching card. A stated plan gives the opponent information to use against it.

ideas.name: Points can come from several different features of one hand
ideas.text: A Casino hand scores for the most cards (3 points), the most spades, the ten of diamonds (2), the two of spades, each ace and each sweep. A player has several targets, each worth a different amount.

ideas.name: One hand can have an advantage built in
ideas.text: In cribbage the dealer gets the crib, a second hand that only the dealer counts. The deal alternates so that the advantage moves between players. The book says the game is named for this advantage.

ideas.name: Scoring happens during play and again at the end
ideas.text: Cribbage players peg points while they play cards, for fifteens, pairs and runs made in the shared count, and again in the show, where they count the combinations in their own hands. Both stages share some features but reward different skills.

ideas.name: Order of counting can decide a close game
ideas.text: In cribbage the nondealer counts first, and if that player reaches 61 or 121 the game ends, even if the dealer would have counted more. Position at the table can matter more than total points.

ideas.name: A track with two pegs lets players check their own count
ideas.text: A cribbage board gives every player two pegs, so if they lose track the back peg still shows the previous score. A tool can store past state as well as the present.

ideas.name: A shared total sets a limit that all players watch
ideas.text: In the cribbage play, both players call a running total that cannot go past 31. A player who cannot play calls go, and the other earns a point for it. A single number visible to all gives each card a different value depending on the moment.

ideas.name: Tips often say what to keep back
ideas.text: Cribbage advice is to hold fives for the hand and not lead a five, since four in thirteen cards are worth ten. It says to keep small cards so as to play the last card for a point. Choosing what to hold is as much a decision as choosing what to play.

ideas.name: Players can add variety by changing what they are dealt
ideas.text: Cribbage can be played with five, six or seven cards, with each player giving up one or two to the crib, to different final scores such as 61, 121 or 181. Dealing a different number of cards changes how much choice there is.

ideas.name: Ranking can be rewritten for a game
ideas.text: In Euchre the jack of the trump suit is the highest card, and the jack of the same colour is second, counted as trump. In other suits the jack ranks below the queen. A game can set up its own order of cards.

ideas.name: A bidding round can be short and public
ideas.text: In Euchre each player in turn can accept the turned-up card's suit as trump or pass, with a second round if all pass. The bid is taken in seconds and the whole table knows who chose the trump.

ideas.name: Taking a larger risk can earn a larger reward
ideas.text: A Euchre maker who plays alone scores 4 points for winning all five tricks, against 2 for a team. A lone defender also scores 4 for a march. The partner sits out, so the choice costs the team a hand.

ideas.name: Forcing a choice avoids a deadlock
ideas.text: In the Stick-the-dealer variation of Euchre the dealer has to name a trump suit if everyone else passed, so no hand is thrown in. A forced decision keeps play moving, and it also makes the dealer's position riskier.

ideas.name: The same game can be made for different numbers of players
ideas.text: Bridge has versions for two players (Double Dummy and Honeymoon Bridge) and for three, where one player takes the dummy hand. Casino is played with two, three or four players. Casino for four becomes a partnership game. Games adapt to the people present.

ideas.name: A game can turn the usual aim upside down
ideas.text: In Hearts players try to avoid taking points, and the lowest score wins. Taking every heart and the queen of spades, shooting the moon, turns the penalty into a gain. The same cards punish most players and reward one.

ideas.name: Passing cards before play changes the hand
ideas.text: In Hearts every player passes three cards to the left without seeing what they receive. The book advises passing high spades if holding few, so as to avoid taking the queen. A hand can be reshaped before the first card is led.

ideas.name: A restriction on opening moves holds back a risk
ideas.text: In Hearts nobody may lead a heart until one has been discarded, unless a player has only hearts. Until then hearts cannot be forced on others. A rule about what can start a round decides when the danger arrives.

ideas.name: Removing cards makes the deal equal
ideas.text: Hearts for three, five, six or seven players takes out named cards, such as the two of clubs, so that every player holds the same number. A deck can be adjusted to the players.

ideas.name: Many variants change only the scoring
ideas.text: Spot Hearts counts each heart at its face value instead of one. Pink Lady adds the queen of hearts as another 13 points. Omnibus Hearts gives the ten of diamonds a negative value. Changing the points on a card can change a game's feel.

ideas.name: A bid can be the target as well as the promise
ideas.text: In Oh Hell a player scores only by winning exactly the number of tricks bid, so winning more earns nothing. Success depends on reading the hand and controlling the result as well as on winning.

ideas.name: The number of cards dealt can change from round to round
ideas.text: Oh Hell starts with one card each and adds one each deal, up to the most the deck allows, and the last deal has no trump. Every round has a different size and a new level of difficulty.

ideas.name: A game can have two phases with different rules
ideas.text: In two-handed Pinochle, melds are laid down after winning tricks and the hands are refilled from the stock. After the stock runs out, players have to follow suit, have to trump if they can, and can no longer meld. The rules tighten at the end.

ideas.name: A claim can be risky for the one who makes it
ideas.text: In Pinochle a player may claim to have reached 1,000 points at any time. If right, the player wins. If wrong, the player loses. A claim is a bet on your own count.

ideas.name: Poker has a fixed round of choices
ideas.text: Each round of poker offers check, bet, call, fold or raise, and ends when everyone has checked or answered the bets. Most house rules limit raises to three. A tight list of choices keeps a game with many players manageable.

ideas.name: Hand ranks follow how rare the hands are
ideas.text: The book lists poker hands from royal flush down to one pair, along with the odds of getting each in five cards, from 1 in 649,740 to 1 in 2.36. The less often a hand comes up, the higher it ranks.

ideas.name: Friends can set the stakes low
ideas.text: The book says games between friends have low limits on the ante, on the raise and on the size of the pot, and that coins, matchsticks or Monopoly money can stand in for chips. The way a game is played at the table can be set by the people around it.

ideas.name: Showing some cards lets players read each other
ideas.text: In Seven-Card Stud most cards are face up, so players see part of each hand, and the dealer even names possible flushes and straights. The player with the highest visible cards bets first. Information that is public shapes the betting.

ideas.name: A shared board changes what a hand is worth
ideas.text: In Texas Hold'em each player has two private cards and five shared ones, and may use two, one or none of their own. A player who uses only the shared cards is playing the board and splits the pot.

ideas.name: Seeing everything except your own hand
ideas.text: In Indian Poker players hold a card on their forehead facing out and bet on what they see in everyone else's. A game can reverse who has the information.

ideas.name: The rummy turn is draw one and discard one
ideas.text: A player takes the top of the stock or the discard pile and then discards a card, and melds or lays off at any time. The rule gives each turn the same shape, and a discard tells the next player what is not wanted.

ideas.name: A faster ending makes a different game
ideas.text: Knock rummy and gin end the hand when a player knocks with a low deadwood total, instead of waiting for someone to lay down every card. If the knocker does not have the lowest count, the knocker is penalised. Ending a hand early is a risk.

ideas.name: A threshold can be set by the first card
ideas.text: In Oklahoma Gin the card turned up first fixes how many points are needed to knock for that hand. The goal changes from hand to hand, and an ace means a player has to either knock on 1 or go gin.

ideas.name: Taking from a pile can cost more than one card
ideas.text: In 500 Rum a player can take any card from the spread-out discard pile, but has to take every card above it and has to use the chosen card at once. The more tempting the card, the more it costs.

ideas.name: A score can go down
ideas.text: In 500 Rum a player's hand score is the value of cards melded on the table minus the value of cards still held. A player who holds too many high cards can lose points in a round.

ideas.name: Opening requirements can rise with the score
ideas.text: In Canasta a side has to lay down a first meld worth a minimum of points, 15 if its score is below zero, 50 to 1,499, 90 to 2,999 and 120 above that. A side ahead has to do more to begin, so the rule keeps a lead from running away.

ideas.name: Wild cards need limits
ideas.text: In Canasta wild cards can never form a meld alone, a meld needs at least two natural cards, and no meld may hold more than three wild cards. A wild card can be as flexible as a game allows, but each limit keeps the cards from being used without effort.

ideas.name: A frozen pile raises the cost of taking
ideas.text: In Canasta a discarded wild card or black three freezes the discard pile, so only a player holding two matching natural cards can take it. A discard can be a defence as well as a way of getting rid of a card.

ideas.name: Bonuses can differ for how the result was reached
ideas.text: Canasta pays 500 for a natural canasta and 300 for a mixed one, and 100 extra for going out concealed. The way you earn a result changes its score.

ideas.name: Rule books disagree and the group decides
ideas.text: The Canasta section describes a dispute about whether a player has to ask a partner before going out and whether the partner may refuse. Some books say the partner always has to say no. A rule that is unclear gets settled by agreement at the table.

ideas.name: Partners can share an obligation
ideas.text: In Canasta the first meld made by one partner counts as the opening requirement for the other as well. Teams can share goals and costs.

ideas.name: A hand can be won without counting tricks
ideas.text: Whist has no bidding and no dummy. The only target is the number of tricks beyond the first six, and the first side to reach 7 points wins. A game can be short in rules but still need a lot of attention.

ideas.name: Memory is the main skill in some card games
ideas.text: In Concentration all cards are laid face down and players turn up two at a time, keeping any matches. The book suggests playing alone as practice, since the more you play the more you remember.

ideas.name: Matching rank or suit gives players two ways to play
ideas.text: In Crazy Eights a card can be laid if it matches the top card in rank or suit, and any eight can be laid whatever the top card is. A player who has nothing has to draw until a card fits. With two matching features there is a higher chance of a play.

ideas.name: Special cards can be added as variations
ideas.text: The book lists house rules for Crazy Eights: a queen skips the next player, an ace reverses the direction, a two makes the next player draw two. Each rank is given a job. A game can be extended by attaching actions to cards.

ideas.name: Asking for what you hold is a way to give away information
ideas.text: In Go Fish a player may only ask for a rank already in the hand, so every request tells the table what that player holds. The book advises remembering who asked for what.

ideas.name: A bluff game needs a way to call it
ideas.text: In I Doubt It a player lays cards face down and says what they are, and anyone can say I doubt it. The cards are turned over, and either the liar or the doubter takes the pile. Telling the truth at the end is part of the strategy.

ideas.name: Passing can replace winning
ideas.text: Old Maid has no winner. Players take cards from one another's hands and the player left with the odd queen loses. The only aim is to avoid losing.

ideas.name: A reaction game rewards speed
ideas.text: In Pig the first player with four of a kind puts a finger on the nose, and the last to copy gets a letter. Slapjack is won by slapping the pile when a jack appears. Speed of response decides these games, and knowing the cards does not.

ideas.name: Real time can replace taking turns
ideas.text: In Spit both players play at once, as fast as they can, using one hand and one card at a time. A game does not have to give each player a separate turn.

ideas.name: A solitaire game is a puzzle with fixed odds
ideas.text: Idiot's Delight is won in about 1 game in 10. Accordion is so hard that some players have never won it in decades. Klondike lets the stock be gone through twice, and Pyramid three times. A one-player game sets its difficulty with rules about moves and passes through the deck.

ideas.name: A free space can be limited to certain pieces
ideas.text: In Klondike only a king can go into an empty column. In Scorpion only kings are moved into a free space, and Black Spider repeats this. Restricting who may use a gap decides how useful it is.

ideas.name: A house rule can change winning odds
ideas.text: Yukon deals all the cards onto the layout and lets any face-up card be moved with all those on top of it. The book says it is easier to win than Klondike. Letting players move more at once makes a puzzle easier.

ideas.name: A layout can hide information in rows
ideas.text: Klondike deals seven columns with one more face-down card in each, and only the top card is face up. Moving cards turns up new ones, so the puzzle is partly about finding out what is hidden.

ideas.name: A toy challenge has no rules except patience
ideas.text: The book's last section tells readers to build a house of cards with cheap cards on a surface that does not slip. It says the most important rule is to have patience. Not every game has a winner or a score.

ideas.name: The game becomes the form of daily life
ideas.text: Wark argues that games have stopped being a pastime beside life and become the pattern life follows. Work is a rat race, politics is a horse race and the economy is a casino, and each ends in a win or a loss.

ideas.name: Games as allegories, not copies
ideas.text: Wark holds that games do not stand for the world the way a picture does. They work as allegories, carrying the abstract rules by which choices are made in the world. In The Sims a rise through jobs by points echoes how careers run outside the game.

ideas.name: Trifling to understand the form
