ideas.text: A player can ignore winning and play with style to see how the game is built. Wark says this lets the player learn how the wider game-world falls short of the claims it makes about fair contests and level fields.

ideas.name: Learning a game is learning its algorithm
ideas.text: A player finds the rules by trial and error and gradually works out what each choice does. Wark quotes Galloway that to play is to play the code, and gives The Sims, where every object and person has a value that can be found out.

ideas.name: The game is more consistent than the world
ideas.text: Wark says everyday life seems an uneven version of the game, which runs on rules that always give the same result. A Sim looks crude next to a person, but the game's rules are easier to know than the rules of daily life.

ideas.name: Saving turns time into something reversible
ideas.text: In a game a mistake can be undone by going back to a saved state. Wark says this removes the one loose end of daily life, that time runs one way. In The Sims, a player who forgot to save has no earlier point to go back to.

ideas.name: Failure is measured and taught by the numbers
ideas.text: In The Sims the bar graphs show how needs fall when the player is busy elsewhere. A Sim who is not taken to the toilet in time wets himself, and the player learns through counted failure.

ideas.name: Characters and images carry a score
ideas.text: Players enjoy wrecking Sims because images are cheap, Wark says, but the algorithm still counts everything. Even a house without doors is scored as hunger rises.

ideas.name: A higher level is just more
ideas.text: Wark argues that names for levels, such as Scholar or Theorist, only label a larger number. In The Sims, climbing a career feels like a change of kind but is a change of amount.

ideas.name: The look is a skin, the numbers decide
ideas.text: In The Sims 2 the player chooses gender, colour, hair and clothes, but these do not alter play. Hidden values for charisma or creativity fix which careers a Sim can succeed in.

ideas.name: The trifler and the cheat
ideas.text: Suits describes the trifler as one who keeps the rules and drops the goal, and the cheat as one who keeps the goal and drops the rules. Wark sees players of The Sims who ignore the goal and tell stories or build houses as triflers.

ideas.name: Constraint is what a game offers
ideas.text: Wark says a game gives a consistent set of limits. A Sims player can try endless sofas and tables, yet the sequences built in by the designers are fixed, so the freedom is within those limits.

ideas.name: Work in the games trade is not a game
ideas.text: Wark points to EA Spouse's account of crunch time at a game studio. A Sim moves from job to job in measured steps, but a person in the real trade works twelve hours a day, six days a week, with nowhere else to go.

ideas.name: The meter always runs
ideas.text: A player writes to the makers of The Sims asking for no meter on items bought. Wark reads this as showing that the counting belongs to the whole game-world and cannot easily be removed.

ideas.name: A game is a contest over nothing
ideas.text: In a game nobody fights over minerals or labour contracts, and the rules treat every player the same way. Wark says that is the difference between a game and a world where the stakes are real.

ideas.name: A game reaches the world through its materials
ideas.text: Wark points out that a PlayStation contains coltan dug in the Congo. The game is closed off by its rules, but the machine it runs on depends on mining, wars and the destruction of animal habitats.

ideas.name: Starting over after defeat
ideas.text: Wark frames history as a run of levels, each opened only after the one before is cleared, where a defeated player starts again. Time in a game is counted in equal units, so a level can always be played once more.

ideas.name: Strategy games model resource allocation
ideas.text: In Civilization III everything is a quantity to be moved from one use to another. The player taxes, invests in science or culture, and sees that a small change in one variable can have a big effect elsewhere.

ideas.name: A database replaces a story
ideas.text: Wark says a strategy game turns descriptions into a database and a storyline into a way of moving through it. The Civilopedia is a reference book for the game's world, and the player picks combinations from it.

ideas.name: The player is a manager and a designer
ideas.text: In Civilization III the player works within limits, finds out by trial and error which variables depend on which, and starts over when a plan fails. Wark says this is the work of a game designer too.

ideas.name: The possible is real inside the game
ideas.text: Wark says that if the algorithm can produce an outcome from the database, it exists in the game. In Civilization III any mix of resources the rules allow can be tried, and the actual world is just one of the outcomes.

ideas.name: Every choice of side plays the same game
ideas.text: In Civilization III it does not matter whether the player picks Babylon, China or Zulu-land. Wark says the logic of the game is the same for all, so whoever wins plays by one set of rules.

ideas.name: Analog movement is turned into yes and no
ideas.text: In Katamari Damacy the player twists a stick by degrees, but the game turns this into a decision. A ball is big enough to become a star or it is not, and the stick movement only decides how quickly the player gets there.

ideas.name: Every game ends in a decision
ideas.text: Wark says that all games are digital in the sense that they come down to in or out, goal or no goal. Even a board game is a machine of human motion and objects that ends in a ruling by a referee.

ideas.name: A threshold needs to be marked
ideas.text: The task of Sisyphus is to roll a rock up a hill with no mark for the top, so it never ends. In Katamari Damacy a small icon shows the size the ball has to reach, so effort ends in a decision.

ideas.name: The digital allows saving
ideas.text: Because a game is digital, Wark says, a finished ball can be saved and comes back unchanged. What is saved does not decay, but if the system crashes it may be lost altogether.

ideas.name: Scale can change while the form stays
ideas.text: The Katamari ball starts with household objects and grows until it gathers whole towns and then stars. Wark says the same rule works at each scale, as a tiny electric switch can set off a missile.

ideas.name: Moves come before rules
ideas.text: Wark asks which came first, play or the game. He suggests rules grew out of moves: a transgression is marked only after someone has made the move. Now the game leads and play follows.

ideas.name: Play can go on, a game stops
ideas.text: The task of Sisyphus is a move that never crosses a line. A game, in Wark's reading, stops and starts again and again, because each run produces a score and then ends.

ideas.name: Games began in military research
ideas.text: Wark quotes Herz that nearly every part of an arcade or console traces back to a defence grant. The same technology that served command and control later became a form of entertainment.

ideas.name: The designer is also an artist
ideas.text: Takahashi, who made Katamari Damacy, is a sculptor who says he does not play games. Wark says the artist can work from inside the game, leaving something of the hand in the code.

ideas.name: Contest alone wears a culture out
ideas.text: Wark cites Huizinga that when competition dominates, decline follows in time. He suggests a style of play that moves away from the either-or of winning and losing.

ideas.name: Games once stayed in set-apart places
ideas.text: Caillois placed games of competition and chance in special zones with their own rules, outside daily life. These fields, courts and arenas are the places Foucault called heterotopias.

ideas.name: Two aims for two kinds of play
ideas.text: Wark says aesthetic play aims to be free and calculated games aim to be fair. In each case the aim only holds inside the place built for it.

ideas.name: Rules chosen by the maker
ideas.text: The Oulipo writers set themselves arbitrary rules to see what kinds of play followed. Wark says this suits a time when the margins that held games have disappeared.

ideas.name: All four kinds of play at once
ideas.text: In Vice City chance, competition, dizziness and spectacle all appear together. A player takes chances, competes, drives through a world of drugs and noise and watches destruction, all inside one set of rules.

ideas.name: A game of crime in which cheating is not possible
ideas.text: Vice City is about breaking the law, but its player cannot break the game's rules. Even the cheat codes are part of the rules, so every move that looks wrong is a move into another game.

ideas.name: Fixed reward, fixed rule
ideas.text: Each mission in Vice City pays exactly one thousand dollars. Wark says this shows the game does not care about description, only about the relations between numbers.

ideas.name: Setting and story are decoration
ideas.text: In Vice City the criminal world, the art and the story are surface. The player uses them to find the steps of the algorithm, as a way of guessing the rules.

ideas.name: Game theory and gamer theory
ideas.text: Game theory starts with a calculating agent weighing odds, as a prisoner in a cell does. Wark says gamer theory asks how the player becomes an agent at all, and how a player decides when to act in the middle of a battle.

ideas.name: Targeting is done in two steps
ideas.text: In Rez the player holds the trigger to pick targets and releases it to fire, so aiming is separate from shooting. Wark says this puts the act of targeting ahead of the target.

ideas.name: Abstracting the enemy
ideas.text: The shapes in Rez are colourful and abstract, and the story about why one shoots is minimal. Wark says the game's interest lies in the act of targeting and not in who or what is hit.

ideas.name: Repeating the same time
ideas.text: A level of Rez can be replayed any number of times, and time inside it is measured in the same units each run. Wark says this makes game time repeatable and without the wear that time has outside.

ideas.name: Access follows protocol
ideas.text: In Rez every point may connect to every other, but only some links open at a time. Wark says play is the work of negotiating the rules that decide which points open.

ideas.name: The story is an alibi
ideas.text: The story in a game, Wark says, excuses the player for treating something as a target. In Rez the player saves a network, and in other games plays the villain, but the story is not the point of the play.

ideas.name: Games are not morality tales
ideas.text: Wark says the story of a game cannot be read as a moral. He proposes reading it as an allegory of how signs are held together in the game and not held together outside it.

ideas.name: Boredom is a lack of room for action
ideas.text: Wark describes boredom as being in a space where one cannot act, or where acts add up to nothing, like waiting in an airport. A game such as State of Emergency lets the player change the space, which displaces some of it.

ideas.name: Choosing your own necessities
ideas.text: In a game a player picks which circumstances to push against. Wark says this is a freedom the world does not give, since in a game the demands are chosen and the limits are set from the start.

ideas.name: A game's limit is given in advance
ideas.text: Boredom comes back, Wark says, whenever a player reaches the end of what a game offers. In games the limit is known from the start, which he counts as a feature of the form.

ideas.name: When there is nothing to trifle with
ideas.text: Wark finds State of Emergency has little room to play with style. Every object in it appears only as a way to win, so the game turns back to dullness.

ideas.name: Designers keep adding new games
ideas.text: Wark argues that the game industry answers boredom by producing new rules, new moves and new contests. Boredom with one game is moved onto the next one.

ideas.name: Three ways through a game
ideas.text: Wark notes that Deus Ex can be played by stealth, by violence or by negotiation. Each gets from beginning to end, but the player still works through it level by level.

ideas.name: Four endings as a puzzle
ideas.text: Deus Ex has four endings, each tied to a group seeking power. Wark arranges them on a Greimas square to show that the game's possible ends hang together as a set.

ideas.name: A game with several endings shows its rules
ideas.text: A story has one ending, but Deus Ex has four. Wark says this reveals a little more of the rules by which the game makes meaning.

ideas.name: Playing as an alternation
ideas.text: In Wark's account a player in play moves between being apart from a target and being joined to it. Deus Ex stealth mode reverses this, since the aim is to avoid becoming a target.

ideas.name: The maker of rules as a fourth character
ideas.text: Wark sets player against worker, then asks who is neither. The gamer is the non-player and the hacker is the non-worker, a person who makes both moves and rules.

ideas.name: Game engines make worlds to act in
ideas.text: Wark says a game engine presents a world as made for the player to act upon in a way set by the rules. A book or film is for looking at, while the engine's world gives the player actions.

ideas.name: The party ending
ideas.text: Deus Ex has a fifth ending where all the characters, whatever their side, party together. Differences stay but are no longer in opposition. Wark notes that it still sits inside the game.

ideas.name: A model that counts consequences
ideas.text: SimEarth lets players choose energy sources and uses, and it shows effects they did not plan. More farming raises the population and also the methane from rice fields and cattle, which warms the planet.

ideas.name: A game with no satisfying end
ideas.text: Wark says SimEarth lacks a clear win condition, since the usual result for most runs is that the people leave in spaceships. He reads this as showing the limit of gamespace, which leaves out the by-products of its choices.

ideas.name: Games change by variation and selection
ideas.text: Wark likens game forms to living forms: designers breed new versions from old ones and the market selects which survive. SimEarth left no sequel, while The Sims lived on and Spore offered more than one world.

ideas.name: The player is played by the game
ideas.text: In a God game the player seems to be in control, but Wark says the game plays the player. The gamer is an avatar of an abstract principle and answers to the game.

ideas.name: Games as a way to think about now
ideas.text: For Wark, games are the form in which the present can be felt and thought. To study them is to rethink cultural history after the digital game; it is more than adding a new medium to a list.

ideas.name: Play has a location
ideas.text: Inner life sits inside a person and the outside world sits beyond the skin. Play is in neither; the book gives it a place in the space between a baby and the carer. A child playing with a teddy on a bed is using objects from the world to carry something from inside.

ideas.name: Playing is doing and takes time
ideas.text: To control what is outside, a person has to act, not only think or wish. The book says this is why playing is doing and why it takes time, as when a two-year-old arranges train parts one by one on a table.

ideas.name: Hold a paradox without solving it
ideas.text: The baby made the transitional object and also found it. The book asks adults never to ask which is true. Resolving the paradox by thinking it through loses the value that the paradox carries.

ideas.name: The question is never asked
ideas.text: Between adults and the baby there is an agreement not to ask whether the baby thought the object up or it came from outside. Play keeps working only while that question stays unasked.

ideas.name: A third area of experience
ideas.text: Human life has an inside, an outside, and a third area where the two are allowed to meet and no one demands a ruling. The book names art, religion and imaginative work as living there.

ideas.name: Exact fit that goes on too long turns into magic
ideas.text: At the start a carer needs to answer needs almost exactly. If this continues for too long, the object that behaves exactly as wanted becomes no more real than a hallucination, so a small amount of failure makes things real.

ideas.name: Washing the blanket breaks something
ideas.text: Parents carry the blanket on journeys and let it stay dirty and smelly. Washing it breaks the continuity the baby relies on, and the object's meaning can be lost.

ideas.name: Fantasying and playing look alike but differ
ideas.text: A woman sat doing nothing while in her head she painted, worked and walked in the country, and nothing happened. Playing joins dreaming and living; fantasying stays shut off and freezes.

ideas.name: Excitement of the body spoils play
ideas.text: When physical excitement becomes obvious in a child's play, the playing stops or is spoiled. The excitement of play itself comes from a different source.

ideas.name: Where the excitement of play comes from
ideas.text: Play is exciting because of the shaky meeting of what the player imagines and what is actually there. The book calls this precariousness, the same thing that gives magic its pull.

ideas.name: Games manage the frightening side of play
ideas.text: Playing can become frightening. The book says games and their organisation can be read as an attempt to head off that fear.

ideas.name: An organiser is a sign
ideas.text: If an organiser has to take charge, the book takes it to mean the children cannot play creatively. Responsible adults are to be available, but need not enter the play.

ideas.name: Copied play is not play
ideas.text: A youngest child joined her older siblings' games on the basis of compliance, struggling to act the part she was given. The others felt she was not adding anything, and she watched herself from outside.

ideas.name: Playful adults make playing easier
ideas.text: Children play more easily when the adult with them is free to be playful. In the book, the author puts his ear to a teddy in his pocket and says he heard it speak, and the child takes up the idea.

ideas.name: The moment the player surprises themself
ideas.text: In a play session the moment that counts is when the child surprises himself or herself, not when the adult gives a clever reading. A reading given before the material is ready produces compliance.

ideas.name: Content does not matter, absorption does
ideas.text: To understand playing, look at the child's absorbed, near-withdrawn state and ignore what the toys are. The playing child lives in an area that is hard to leave and hard to enter.

ideas.name: Play is a stretch of stages
ideas.text: The book gives a sequence: baby and object merged; object pushed away and taken back; being alone in the presence of someone; two people's play areas overlapping. Shared play grows out of the earlier stages.

ideas.name: Alone in the presence of someone
ideas.text: A child can play alone when a loved, reliable person is nearby and comes back to mind after being forgotten. That person is felt to reflect back what happens in the play.

ideas.name: Play grows into culture
ideas.text: The book traces a direct line from transitional phenomena to playing, from playing to shared playing, and from shared playing to cultural experience.

ideas.name: Playing needs trust
ideas.text: Playing belongs in the space between a dependent baby and a carer whose care the baby takes for granted. Where trust is missing, a patient or a child cannot play at all.

ideas.name: Play can be used by the player to heal
ideas.text: Edmund, two and a half, put the string at the bottom of a bucket like bedding and laid toys in it like a cot, after climbing on and off his mother's lap. The book reads this as him showing the ebb and flow of his dependence without anyone interpreting.

ideas.name: Play through objects carries dreams
ideas.text: Diana laid toys around her two soft animals' heads, as the dreams they were having. She gathered fragments of the outside world and used them to carry something from inside.

ideas.name: Play works on adults too
ideas.text: The book holds that what is true of children's playing is true of adults, shown in the choice of words, the tone of the voice and the sense of humour.

ideas.name: One game, two meanings
ideas.text: A woman played the card game patience for hours and said she did not exist while doing it. Told as a dream, the same game could be read as a struggle with fate over four royal families. The same activity can be fixed habit or live play.

ideas.name: Throwing and losing, toes that stay
ideas.text: A baby on the author's knee played at biting and throwing wooden spatulas on the floor, then fingered her toes. The book reads it as testing that spatulas can be thrown and lost but toes cannot be pulled off.

ideas.name: Only in playing is a person free to be creative
ideas.text: The book claims that a child or adult is creative, and uses the whole personality, only while playing, and that a person finds the self only through being creative.

ideas.name: Communication happens in playing
ideas.text: Apart from direct communication, which the book ties to illness or extreme immaturity, communication is possible only in playing. Edmund conveyed his need for closeness through string and a bucket of toys while adults talked.

ideas.name: A made thing does not heal the missing self
ideas.text: An artist can be praised everywhere and still not have found the self being looked for. The book says the self is not found in products of body or mind, however fine they are.

ideas.name: Rest is needed before reaching out
ideas.text: A person who can rest after work may still not reach the resting state from which a creative reaching-out can start. The book says trust in a reliable setting is what lets that resting state happen.

ideas.name: Looking for a pattern too early takes the nonsense away
ideas.text: A therapist who hunts for sense in a patient's scattered talk makes the patient leave the nonsense behind out of hopelessness. The book gives a sequence: relaxation in trust, then playing, then the sum of these making a sense of self.

ideas.name: Knowing too much steals the player's creativity
ideas.text: The author kept silent for long stretches and wrote withheld readings in his notes. His reward came when the patient made the reading herself, an hour or two later.

ideas.name: An idea given too early is lost
ideas.text: An interpretation made by the patient could have been stolen from her if he had made it earlier in the session. Ideas that people reach themselves belong to them.

ideas.name: Wasted time and used time
ideas.text: A session of three hours let the patient move from formless wandering to being present with the author. A fifty-minute session could not have done the work.

ideas.name: A question points to a self
ideas.text: The patient noted that one could say there is a self from the question she asked, as from searching. The book reads the question as coming from her creativity, which comes after relaxation.

ideas.name: Playing is the base of experience
ideas.text: Opportunity for formless experience, and for motor and sensory creative impulses, is the stuff of playing. In Winnicott's account the whole of experience is built on it.

ideas.name: Creativity is wider than art
ideas.text: The book keeps creativity for any attitude to outside reality, and lists a picture, a garden, a hairstyle or a meal cooked at home as things that could be creations.

ideas.name: Creation can block sight of creativity
ideas.text: The author says studies of famous artists look for reasons for greatness but miss the impulse. The finished work stands between the observer and the artist's creativity.

ideas.name: Living by someone else's rules feels empty
ideas.text: The book describes people who have tasted creative living and know that most of their time is spent as if caught up in the creativity of someone else, or of a machine.

ideas.name: Creative impulse shows in small acts
ideas.text: The impulse appears when anyone looks in a healthy way at something or does something on purpose, such as prolonging a cry to enjoy a musical sound. It is as present in a child enjoying breathing as in an architect who suddenly knows what to build.

ideas.name: Creativity depends on the setting
ideas.text: The quality of the environment at the start decides whether a person lives creatively. A description of the player alone cannot touch where creativity comes from.

ideas.name: Play is neither inside nor outside
ideas.text: The book asks where play is, if it is neither a matter of inner psychic reality nor of external reality, and gives it a place in the potential space between baby and carer. Tagore's line, children play on the seashore of endless worlds, opens the chapter.

ideas.name: Alone in the presence of someone
ideas.text: The child is first alone only while someone is present. Play develops on the assumption that a reliable person is there, even when the child pays no attention to them.

ideas.name: The time limit of a carer's absence
ideas.text: The book gives the feeling of the mother's existence a lifespan of x minutes. After x plus y minutes the baby's distress is mended on her return; after x plus y plus z the baby is harmed and return no longer repairs it.

ideas.name: Play with no climax
ideas.text: The phenomena of the play area have no climax, unlike instinctual satisfactions. They can be intense without an end point, as with the interplay between the edges of two curtains.

ideas.name: Playing is intense without being a drive
ideas.text: Instinct and frustration are thoroughly studied, but the book says the intensity of playing, which has no climax, has not been described with comparable force.

ideas.name: With no set game, all of it is creative
ideas.text: A baby who has met a carer reducing her adaptation step by step plays with no set game, so everything is made by the baby and is first-time-ever. Everything physical is imagined into something.

ideas.name: Every object is a found object
ideas.text: An observer sees that the baby's play has been done and felt before, and that its toys were adopted. For the baby, each detail is an example of creative living, so each toy is found as if new.

ideas.name: A child who cannot settle cannot play
ideas.text: A deprived child, in Winnicott's account, is restless, unable to play, and has little capacity to take part in cultural life. A loss of reliable people means a loss of the play area.

ideas.name: Filling someone else's play space
ideas.text: A carer or analyst who has set up a space for play can ruin it by pouring in their own readings. What comes from someone else, in that space, is felt by the child as persecuting.

ideas.name: Originality sits on tradition
ideas.text: In any cultural field a person cannot be original except on a basis of tradition. No one repeats except as deliberate quotation, and the book calls plagiarism the sin that cannot be forgiven.

ideas.name: The use of this space varies person to person
ideas.text: Inner reality is relatively constant and the actual world is common property. The third area varies widely, from minimal to maximal, according to the sum of a person's real experiences.

ideas.name: Play and culture take time and space
ideas.text: Playing and cultural experience link past, present and future, take up time and space, and get concentrated deliberate attention, but without too much of the deliberateness of trying.

ideas.name: Fed is not the same as brought up
ideas.text: A baby can be fed without love, but loveless or impersonal management does not produce an autonomous child. The book says trust and reliability make the space where play can fill the gap.

ideas.name: Two needs of those who care for children
ideas.text: The first is to protect the early relationship so that trust can build and the child can play. The second is to put each child in touch with elements of the cultural heritage that fit the child's capacity and phase.

ideas.name: Poverty of play has two sources
ideas.text: Play capacity is cramped by a failure of confidence. It is also cramped when the adults in the child's world fail to introduce cultural elements at suitable stages.

ideas.name: The first rule agreed with a baby
ideas.text: The book calls the agreement never to ask the baby whether it created the object or found it a rule of the game that everyone knows. Without it the object would lose its role.

ideas.name: Using an object requires that it survives being attacked
ideas.text: The book gives a sequence: the subject relates to the object, finds it outside, destroys it, the object survives, and then the subject can use it. A child bites the breast or throws a toy and the toy is still there.

ideas.name: Surviving means not hitting back
ideas.text: In the book, survival of an attacked object means the object does not retaliate or change its quality. There is no anger in the destruction, though there is joy at the object's survival.

ideas.name: Waiting beats telling
ideas.text: The author came to wait for years for understanding to arrive in the patient, and says he enjoys the patient's joy more than he enjoyed feeling clever. The principle is that the patient has the answers.

ideas.name: Using a thing is not exploiting it
ideas.text: By use, Winnicott does not mean exploitation. A person who can use objects uses parents, siblings and home, and then uses the analysis in the same way.

ideas.name: The first mirror is a face
ideas.text: A baby looking at the carer's face sees itself, if she reflects it back. A baby who sees only her mood or her fixed face learns that looking gives perception of her and nothing back, and its own creativity begins to wither.

ideas.name: Being seen comes before seeing
ideas.text: The book gives a chain: when I look I am seen, so I exist; then I can afford to look and see; then I look creatively. A player who is noticed has the nerve to look closely at the game.

ideas.name: Predicting a mood
ideas.text: A baby who cannot rely on a carer's face studies it as people study the weather, to judge when it is safe to be spontaneous. This strains the baby, and the book describes the baby as organising withdrawal.

ideas.name: Giving back what is brought
ideas.text: The book describes the work of a therapist as long-term giving back to the patient what the patient brings, like a face that reflects what is there. It is tiring and does not depend on clever readings.

ideas.name: A drawing game with no rules
ideas.text: The author offers a sixteen-year-old the squiggle game, which he calls the game with no rules. She asks if a drawing can go any way up, and he says there are no rules.

ideas.name: A game that shows how a player acts
ideas.text: In the squiggle game Sarah said she would make a line as difficult as possible, and later called one of her own drawings cramped, not free and spreading. The author took the drawing as the main communication and let her expand on it.

ideas.name: A game may not be spontaneous
ideas.text: After nine drawings Sarah said the squiggle was not spontaneous: she was always trying to make an impression. The game gave her room to say so because it did not matter here.

ideas.name: Every detail fed back into play
ideas.text: By the stage of a unit self, the child constantly matches inner reality with samples of the outside world. The book says this shows up in the use of symbols and in creative playing.

ideas.name: Everyone survives a small quarrel
ideas.text: The author tells a girl that her task is to live through relationships that turn a little sour, in which she is a bit angry and a bit disillusioned, and everyone survives. The idea repeats the survival of the object.

ideas.name: The game of the king of the castle
ideas.text: The book reads the rhyme as a statement of personal being that implies the death of rivals. The challenger is named at once, the king is knocked off, and the challenger becomes king. The Opies call the game very old and quote a Roman version.

ideas.name: Handing over too early ends the game
ideas.text: The author says adults who abdicate on purpose, just as the young come to take their place, leave them stuck as the establishment. In terms of the game, the adult leaves just when the young are about to knock them over.

ideas.name: Confrontation gives rebellion something to push against
ideas.text: The young need an adult who stands up, does not hit back or hold a grudge, and is not simply nice. Without this the adolescent wins too early and the imaginative striving is lost.

ideas.name: A paradox that is left standing
ideas.text: The tailpiece proposes that a stage exists before objectivity, when the baby lives in a conceived world, and that the paradox of the move to perception is for allowing, not for solving.
